cards.desc: Continuation of the descending thoracic aorta from the aortic hiatus at T12 to its bifurcation at L4, lying slightly to the left of the midline on the lumbar vertebral bodies.
cards.att: Begins at the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at the lower border of T12, descends on the bodies of L1 to L4, and ends at L4 by dividing into the two common iliac arteries; the median sacral artery continues from the bifurcation.
cards.sup: Unpaired ventral branches: coeliac trunk (T12), superior mesenteric (L1), inferior mesenteric (L3). Paired lateral visceral: inferior phrenic, middle suprarenal, renal, gonadal. Paired parietal: four lumbar arteries.
cards.act: Arterial supply to the abdominal viscera and posterior abdominal wall, and through the common iliac arteries to the pelvis and lower limbs.
cards.rel: Anteriorly: coeliac plexus, body of pancreas, splenic vein, left renal vein and third part of duodenum. To the right lie the inferior vena cava and cisterna chyli; to the left, the left sympathetic trunk and duodenojejunal flexure.
cards.clin: Abdominal aortic aneurysm is usually infrarenal and presents as an expansile pulsatile mass above the umbilicus, with back pain and shock on rupture. The bifurcation lies at the supracristal plane (L4), the surface landmark used for palpation and for aortic compression.
cards.exam: Q. At which vertebral levels do the three unpaired ventral branches of the abdominal aorta arise? A. Coeliac trunk at T12, superior mesenteric artery at L1, inferior mesenteric artery at L3.

cards.desc: The smallest, lowest slip of pectoralis major, arising from the anterior wall of the rectus sheath below the sternocostal part.
cards.att: Origin: anterior lamina of the rectus sheath, from the aponeurosis of external oblique. Insertion: fibres ascend and twist to reach the highest and deepest point of the lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus.
cards.sup: Medial pectoral nerve (C8, T1).
cards.act: Adducts and medially rotates the arm; with the sternocostal part it extends the flexed arm and depresses the shoulder girdle in climbing.
cards.rel: Lies deepest of the three parts at the insertion because of the twist of fibres; superficial to the upper rectus sheath and the sternocostal part below the fifth costal cartilage.
cards.clin: The twisting of the abdominal fibres creates the bilaminar tendon and the rounded anterior axillary fold; the lowest fibres are the ones classically avulsed in a pectoralis major rupture during bench press. Selective congenital absence of the lower parts occurs in Poland syndrome.
cards.exam: Q. Which fibres of pectoralis major insert highest on the humerus? A. The abdominal fibres, because the tendon twists through 180 degrees.

cards.desc: Most lateral muscle of the first layer of the sole, along the lateral border of the foot.
cards.att: Origin: lateral and medial processes of the tuberosity of the calcaneus, the plantar aponeurosis and the intermuscular septum. Insertion: lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the fifth toe, with a slip to the tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal.
cards.sup: Lateral plantar nerve (S2, S3).
cards.act: Abducts and flexes the fifth toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint; supports the lateral longitudinal arch.
cards.rel: Lies in the first layer with flexor digitorum brevis and abductor hallucis; the lateral plantar vessels and nerve pass forwards between it and flexor digitorum brevis.
cards.clin: The first branch of the lateral plantar nerve, the nerve to abductor digiti minimi, is entrapped between abductor hallucis and quadratus plantae in Baxter neuropathy, a cause of chronic heel pain that mimics plantar fasciitis but without morning stiffness.
cards.exam: Q. What is the nerve supply of abductor digiti minimi of the foot? A. The lateral plantar nerve (S2, S3).

cards.desc: Most medial and superficial of the three hypothenar muscles, forming the ulnar border of the palm.
cards.att: Origin: pisiform, tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris and the pisohamate ligament. Insertion: medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the little finger and the dorsal digital expansion.
cards.sup: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8, T1).
cards.act: Abducts the little finger at the metacarpophalangeal joint; assists flexion of that joint and extension of the interphalangeal joints.
cards.rel: Superficial and medial to flexor digiti minimi brevis, with opponens digiti minimi deep to both; the deep branch of the ulnar nerve passes between it and flexor digiti minimi brevis.
cards.clin: Wasting of the hypothenar eminence with loss of little finger abduction is an early sign of ulnar nerve lesion at the wrist or elbow; it is the standard muscle for ulnar motor nerve conduction studies.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle forms the medial border of the hypothenar eminence and what is its nerve? A. Abductor digiti minimi, supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8, T1).

cards.desc: Most medial muscle of the first layer of the sole, forming the fleshy medial border of the foot.
cards.att: Origin: medial process of the tuberosity of the calcaneus, flexor retinaculum, plantar aponeurosis and intermuscular septum. Insertion: medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe, with the medial head of flexor hallucis brevis.
cards.sup: Medial plantar nerve (S2, S3).
cards.act: Abducts and flexes the great toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint; braces the medial longitudinal arch.
cards.rel: Its upper border forms the roof of the porta pedis, through which the plantar vessels and nerves enter the sole after leaving the tarsal tunnel; it covers the medial plantar neurovascular bundle.
cards.clin: A common tether at the abductor hallucis fascia causes distal tarsal tunnel and Baxter nerve entrapment. The muscle is released or transferred in hallux valgus and clubfoot surgery, and it is the muscle wasting first noticed in medial plantar nerve lesions.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve supplies abductor hallucis? A. The medial plantar nerve (S2, S3).

cards.desc: Most superficial and lateral of the thenar muscles, lying directly under the skin of the thenar eminence.
cards.att: Origin: flexor retinaculum, tubercle of the scaphoid and tubercle of the trapezium. Insertion: lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb, with a slip to the extensor expansion.
cards.sup: Recurrent (muscular) branch of the median nerve (C8, T1).
cards.act: Abducts the thumb at the carpometacarpal and metacarpophalangeal joints, moving it anteriorly at right angles to the palm.
cards.rel: Superficial to opponens pollicis and the superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis; the recurrent branch of the median nerve enters its deep surface.
cards.clin: The muscle tested in carpal tunnel syndrome: the patient abducts the thumb vertically against resistance with the hand flat. Thenar wasting with loss of palmar abduction is the classic median nerve sign, and it is the muscle used for opponensplasty assessment.
cards.exam: Q. Which single muscle best tests the median nerve in the hand? A. Abductor pollicis brevis, tested by palmar abduction of the thumb.

cards.desc: Deep muscle of the posterior forearm whose tendon emerges between the superficial extensors to form the lateral border of the anatomical snuffbox.
cards.att: Origin: posterior surface of the ulna below anconeus, the interosseous membrane and the posterior surface of the radius distal to supinator. Insertion: lateral side of the base of the first metacarpal, often with slips to the trapezium and abductor pollicis brevis.
cards.sup: Posterior interosseous nerve (C7, C8).
cards.act: Abducts and extends the thumb at the carpometacarpal joint; assists abduction of the wrist.
cards.rel: With extensor pollicis brevis it winds round the lateral border of the radius superficial to the radial extensors of the wrist, forming the outcropping muscles; both tendons occupy the first extensor compartment and form the anterior boundary of the anatomical snuffbox.
cards.clin: Stenosing tenosynovitis of its tendon with extensor pollicis brevis in the first extensor compartment is de Quervain's disease, positive on Finkelstein's test. The tendon is a graft source for basal thumb joint reconstruction.
cards.exam: Q. Which tendons occupy the first extensor compartment of the wrist? A. Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis.

cards.desc: Vein of the left posterior mediastinum draining the middle left posterior intercostal spaces and joining the azygos system.
cards.att: Formed by the union of the 4th to 8th left posterior intercostal veins, descends on the left side of the vertebral bodies from about T5 to T8, then crosses to the right at about the level of T7 or T8, behind the aorta, oesophagus and thoracic duct, to join the azygos vein; it frequently communicates below with the hemiazygos vein and above with the left superior intercostal vein.
cards.sup: Tributaries: 4th to 8th left posterior intercostal veins and the left bronchial veins.
cards.act: Returns blood from the left middle intercostal spaces to the azygos vein and thence to the superior vena cava.
cards.rel: Lies on the left of the vertebral bodies with the descending thoracic aorta anterolateral to it and the thoracic duct and azygos vein to its right; it crosses behind the aorta.
cards.clin: Part of the azygos collateral pathway that enlarges in obstruction of the superior or inferior vena cava. Its variability matters in posterior mediastinal and spinal surgery.
cards.exam: Q. Which intercostal veins drain into the accessory hemiazygos vein? A. The 4th to 8th left posterior intercostal veins.

cards.desc: The thick multipennate middle portion of deltoid arising from the acromion, the only truly multipennate part of the muscle.
cards.att: Origin: lateral margin and superior surface of the acromion. Insertion: deltoid tuberosity on the lateral surface of the humerus, in common with the other parts.
cards.sup: Axillary nerve (C5, C6).
cards.act: The chief abductor of the arm from about 15 to 90 degrees, after supraspinatus initiates abduction.
cards.rel: Overlies the subacromial bursa, the supraspinatus tendon and the greater tubercle; the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels run on its deep surface about 5 to 7 cm below the acromion.
cards.clin: Paralysis after surgical neck fracture of the humerus or shoulder dislocation causes loss of abduction and a flattened shoulder contour with loss of sensation over the regimental badge area. The multipennate structure gives power at the cost of range.
cards.exam: Q. Why is the acromial part of deltoid multipennate? A. To generate the power needed to abduct the arm against gravity beyond 15 degrees.

cards.desc: Triangular muscle of the medial compartment of the thigh, lying deep to pectineus and adductor longus.
cards.att: Origin: body and inferior ramus of the pubis, between gracilis and obturator externus. Insertion: upper part of the linea aspera and the lower part of the pectineal line of the femur.
cards.sup: Obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4).
cards.act: Adducts the thigh and assists flexion at the hip.
cards.rel: Lies behind pectineus and adductor longus and in front of adductor magnus. The anterior division of the obturator nerve descends in front of it and the posterior division behind it, so the muscle separates the two divisions.
cards.clin: Its relation to the obturator nerve makes it the key landmark in obturator nerve block and in obturator neurectomy for adductor spasticity in cerebral palsy.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle separates the anterior and posterior divisions of the obturator nerve? A. Adductor brevis.

cards.desc: Most anterior muscle of the adductor group, forming the medial boundary of the femoral triangle.
cards.att: Origin: front of the body of the pubis in the angle between the crest and the symphysis, by a narrow tendon. Insertion: middle third of the linea aspera of the femur.
cards.sup: Obturator nerve, anterior division (L2, L3, L4).
cards.act: Adducts, flexes and medially rotates the thigh at the hip.
cards.rel: Its medial border forms the medial boundary of the femoral triangle, and it helps form the floor of the triangle with iliopsoas and pectineus; lower down it forms part of the posterior wall of the adductor canal with adductor magnus. Adductor brevis and the anterior division of the obturator nerve lie behind it.
cards.clin: Its narrow tendinous origin is the commonest site of adductor strain or groin pull in footballers. Chronic traction can produce ossification in the tendon, the rider bone of horse riders.
cards.exam: Q. What forms the medial boundary of the femoral triangle? A. The medial border of adductor longus.

cards.desc: Large triangular composite muscle forming the posterior wall of the adductor compartment, with an adductor part and a hamstring part.
cards.att: Origin: adductor part from the inferior pubic ramus and ramus of the ischium, hamstring part from the inferolateral part of the ischial tuberosity. Insertion: adductor part into the gluteal tuberosity, linea aspera and medial supracondylar line; hamstring part by a rounded tendon into the adductor tubercle of the medial femoral condyle.
cards.sup: Adductor part by the obturator nerve, posterior division (L2, L3, L4); hamstring part by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L4).
cards.act: Powerful adductor of the thigh; the adductor part also flexes and the hamstring part extends the hip.
cards.rel: Pierced by the four perforating arteries near the linea aspera. The osseoaponeurotic adductor hiatus between its aponeurotic insertion and the adductor tubercle transmits the femoral vessels into the popliteal fossa.
cards.clin: At the adductor hiatus the femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery, a fixed point where the vessel is tethered and vulnerable. The adductor tubercle is the palpable landmark for the medial collateral and medial patellofemoral ligaments and for measuring limb length.
cards.exam: Q. What is the dual nerve supply of adductor magnus? A. Obturator nerve to the adductor part and the tibial division of the sciatic nerve to the hamstring part.

cards.desc: Retroperitoneal endocrine gland capping the upper pole of the kidney within the renal fascia, separated from the kidney by a septum of fat.
cards.att: The right gland is pyramidal and lies higher, behind the inferior vena cava and against the bare area of the liver; the left is semilunar and lies along the medial border of the upper kidney behind the lesser sac and pancreas. Each has a cortex (zona glomerulosa, fasciculata and reticularis) and a medulla of chromaffin cells.
cards.sup: Three arterial sources: superior suprarenal from the inferior phrenic artery, middle suprarenal from the aorta, inferior suprarenal from the renal artery. A single vein drains each gland: the short right vein directly into the inferior vena cava, the longer left vein into the left renal vein. Preganglionic sympathetic fibres from the greater splanchnic nerve synapse directly on medullary cells.
cards.act: Cortex secretes aldosterone, cortisol and androgens; the medulla secretes adrenaline and noradrenaline as a modified sympathetic ganglion.
cards.rel: The right gland lies behind the inferior vena cava and the bare area of the liver and in front of the diaphragm. The left lies behind the lesser sac and the body of the pancreas with the splenic artery, in front of the diaphragm and left crus.
cards.clin: The short right suprarenal vein draining straight into the inferior vena cava makes right adrenalectomy and right adrenal vein sampling technically hazardous. Bilateral haemorrhagic infarction in meningococcal septicaemia is the Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome. Phaeochromocytoma arises from the medulla.
cards.exam: Q. Where does each suprarenal vein drain? A. The right directly into the inferior vena cava, the left into the left renal vein.

cards.desc: Almond shaped mass of grey matter in the dorsomedial part of the temporal pole, just in front of and above the tip of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle.
cards.att: Continuous above with the tail of the caudate nucleus and with the substantia innominata, and below with the cortex of the uncus. Connected by the stria terminalis, which arches in the floor of the lateral ventricle to the septal area, hypothalamus and anterior thalamus, and by the ventral amygdalofugal pathway to the hypothalamus and brain stem; it receives olfactory fibres through the lateral olfactory stria and has reciprocal links with the hippocampus, prefrontal cortex and dorsomedial thalamus.
cards.act: Core limbic nucleus for fear and emotional memory: it attaches emotional value to sensory input and drives the autonomic, endocrine and behavioural responses to threat.
cards.rel: Lies deep to the uncus, above the tip of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle, in front of the head of the hippocampus, lateral to the optic tract and below the lentiform nucleus.
cards.clin: Bilateral destruction, as after herpes simplex encephalitis or bilateral temporal lobectomy, gives the Klüver-Bucy syndrome of placidity, hyperorality, hypersexuality and visual agnosia. It is a common focus in temporal lobe epilepsy, whose auras include fear and an unpleasant smell, and it is removed in amygdalohippocampectomy for intractable seizures.
cards.exam: Q. Name the main efferent pathway of the amygdala and its destination. A. The stria terminalis, running in the floor of the lateral ventricle to the septal area and hypothalamus.

cards.desc: Small triangular muscle on the posterolateral aspect of the elbow, continuous with the medial head of triceps.
cards.att: Origin: posterior surface of the lateral epicondyle of the humerus. Insertion: lateral surface of the olecranon and the upper quarter of the posterior surface of the ulna.
cards.sup: Radial nerve (C7, C8, T1), by the branch to the medial head of triceps.
cards.act: Assists triceps in extending the elbow, stabilises the elbow joint and abducts the ulna during pronation.
cards.rel: Covers the posterior part of the annular ligament and the radioulnar joint; forms the floor of the anconeus triangle between the lateral epicondyle, olecranon and radial head.
cards.clin: The soft spot between the lateral epicondyle, radial head and olecranon overlying anconeus is the standard site for elbow joint aspiration and arthroscopy portal placement. Anconeus is used as a rotational muscle flap in elbow surgery.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve supplies anconeus? A. The radial nerve (C7, C8, T1), via the branch to the medial head of triceps.

cards.desc: Gyrus of the inferior parietal lobule that arches round the upturned posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus.
cards.att: Continuous in front with the supramarginal gyrus, below with the middle and superior temporal gyri, and behind with the occipital cortex; corresponds to Brodmann area 39.
cards.sup: Angular artery, a terminal cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery.
cards.act: Association cortex where visual, auditory and somatosensory information converge; in the dominant hemisphere it is essential for reading, writing and calculation and forms part of the wider Wernicke area.
cards.rel: Lies behind the supramarginal gyrus in the inferior parietal lobule, above the posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus, in front of the occipital lobe and above the temporal lobe.
cards.clin: A lesion of the dominant angular gyrus produces Gerstmann syndrome: agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia and right-left disorientation, often with alexia. Non-dominant lesions contribute to contralateral neglect and dressing apraxia.
cards.exam: Q. What are the four components of Gerstmann syndrome and where is the lesion? A. Agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia and right-left disorientation, from a lesion of the dominant angular gyrus.

cards.desc: Smaller terminal branch of the internal carotid artery, supplying the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes.
cards.att: Arises at the bifurcation of the internal carotid lateral to the optic chiasm, runs medially above the optic nerve (A1), joins its fellow by the anterior communicating artery, then turns up in the longitudinal fissure and arches round the genu of the corpus callosum as the pericallosal artery, ending near the parieto-occipital sulcus.
cards.sup: Medial striate artery (recurrent artery of Heubner), medial frontobasal (orbitofrontal), frontopolar, callosomarginal with its paracentral branch, and pericallosal arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere from the frontal pole to the parieto-occipital sulcus, a strip over the superolateral margin including the leg area of the paracentral lobule, the corpus callosum, and, through Heubner artery, the head of the caudate and anterior limb of the internal capsule.
cards.rel: Lies above the optic nerve and chiasm at its origin, in the longitudinal fissure between the hemispheres, on the corpus callosum; forms the anterior part of the circle of Willis with the anterior communicating artery.
cards.clin: Occlusion causes contralateral weakness and sensory loss maximal in the lower limb, urinary incontinence and abulia, sparing the face and hand. The anterior communicating artery is a common site of berry aneurysm, whose rupture or expansion can compress the optic chiasm.
cards.exam: Q. Which part of the body is chiefly affected in anterior cerebral artery occlusion, and why? A. The contralateral lower limb, because the leg area lies in the paracentral lobule on the medial surface supplied by this artery.

cards.desc: The aqueous-filled space of the eyeball bounded in front by the cornea and behind by the iris and the pupillary part of the lens.
cards.att: Bounded anteriorly by the corneal endothelium, posteriorly by the anterior surface of the iris and the central lens, and peripherally by the iridocorneal angle, where the trabecular meshwork and the scleral venous sinus (canal of Schlemm) lie. It communicates with the posterior chamber through the pupil.
cards.act: Holds aqueous humour, which nourishes the avascular cornea and lens and maintains intra-ocular pressure. Aqueous is secreted by the ciliary processes into the posterior chamber, flows through the pupil, and drains through the trabecular meshwork into the scleral venous sinus and thence to the anterior ciliary veins.
cards.rel: Lies in front of the iris and behind the cornea; the angle recess is bounded by the root of the iris and the anterior surface of the ciliary body.
cards.clin: Obstruction at the iridocorneal angle causes acute angle-closure glaucoma with a painful red eye, a fixed mid-dilated pupil and a hazy cornea, treated by laser iridotomy. Blood in the chamber is a hyphaema and pus is a hypopyon.
cards.exam: Q. What is the route of aqueous humour drainage? A. Ciliary processes to posterior chamber, through the pupil to the anterior chamber, then trabecular meshwork to the scleral venous sinus.

cards.desc: Small artery of the third part of the axillary artery that crosses the front of the surgical neck of the humerus.
cards.att: Arises from the third part of the axillary artery, runs laterally deep to coracobrachialis and the short head of biceps across the front of the surgical neck, and anastomoses with the posterior circumflex humeral artery to complete an arterial ring round the neck.
cards.sup: Gives an ascending (arcuate) branch that runs up the intertubercular sulcus with the tendon of the long head of biceps into the head of the humerus, plus small branches to the shoulder joint and deltoid.
cards.act: Principal blood supply of the head of the humerus, with lesser supply to the shoulder joint and adjacent muscles.
cards.rel: Lies on the surgical neck, deep to coracobrachialis, the short head of biceps and deltoid; the much larger posterior circumflex humeral artery and the axillary nerve pass behind the same neck through the quadrangular space.
cards.clin: Because its ascending branch dominates the supply to the humeral head, displaced anatomical neck and four-part proximal humeral fractures carry a high risk of avascular necrosis of the head.
cards.exam: Q. Which artery chiefly supplies the head of the humerus? A. The ascending (arcuate) branch of the anterior circumflex humeral artery.

cards.desc: Compact, densely myelinated commissural bundle crossing the midline in the upper part of the lamina terminalis, immediately in front of the columns of the fornix.
cards.att: Connects the two temporal lobes, chiefly middle and inferior temporal gyri and the amygdalae, and interconnects the anterior olfactory nuclei and olfactory structures of the two sides.
cards.act: Interhemispheric transfer between temporal and olfactory regions; supplements the corpus callosum.
cards.rel: Lies behind the lamina terminalis and in front of the columns of the fornix; forms the anterior boundary of the interventricular foramen with the fornix. The third ventricle lies behind it.
cards.clin: The anterior commissure is one of the two landmarks of the AC-PC line used to set stereotactic coordinates in functional neurosurgery and imaging atlases. It is preserved when the corpus callosum is agenetic or surgically divided, and may carry residual interhemispheric transfer after callosotomy.
cards.exam: Q. Which commissure lies in the lamina terminalis and connects the temporal lobes? A. The anterior commissure.

cards.latin: valvula semilunaris anterior valvae trunci pulmonalis
syn: anterior semilunar cusp of pulmonary valve
cards.desc: One of the three semilunar cusps of the pulmonary valve, set anteriorly at the junction of the right ventricular outflow tract and the pulmonary trunk; the other two are the right and left cusps.
cards.att: Attached by its convex margin to the wall of the pulmonary trunk, forming a pocket-like sinus; its free margin carries a central thickening, the nodule, flanked by thin lunules. It has no chordae tendineae or papillary muscles.
cards.act: Opens passively during right ventricular ejection and closes in early diastole, the sinus filling to appose the three cusps and prevent regurgitation into the right ventricle.
cards.rel: Faces forwards and slightly to the left, lying immediately behind the left third costal cartilage and the sternum; the aortic valve lies posteroinferior and to its right. Unlike the aortic sinuses, the pulmonary sinuses give off no arteries.
cards.clin: Closure of the pulmonary cusps produces the P2 component of the second heart sound, best heard in the left second intercostal space. Pulmonary stenosis, often congenital and a feature of the tetralogy of Fallot and congenital rubella syndrome, gives an ejection systolic murmur there.
cards.exam: Q. Name the cusps of the pulmonary valve. A. Anterior, right and left semilunar cusps.

cards.desc: Terminal continuation of the nasociliary nerve that leaves the orbit medially and reaches the nasal cavity and the skin of the tip of the nose.
cards.att: Arises from the nasociliary nerve in the medial orbit, leaves through the anterior ethmoidal foramen, runs across the cribriform plate area beneath the dura, descends into the nasal cavity through the nasal slit beside the crista galli, and emerges between the nasal bone and the lateral nasal cartilage as the external nasal nerve.
cards.act: Sensory to the mucosa of the anterosuperior nasal septum and lateral wall, the anterior ethmoidal air cells, and the skin of the dorsum and tip of the nose.
cards.rel: Runs with the anterior ethmoidal artery along the roof of the ethmoid at the frontoethmoidal suture, between the medial rectus and superior oblique in the orbit.
cards.clin: Vesicles on the tip of the nose in herpes zoster ophthalmicus, Hutchinson's sign, follow this nerve's external nasal branch and warn of ocular involvement, because both come from the nasociliary. It is the afferent limb of the sneeze reflex, and its accompanying artery is ligated for bleeding from the anterosuperior part of the nasal septum.
cards.exam: Q. What is the anatomical basis of Hutchinson's sign? A. The external nasal branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve and the ciliary nerves both arise from the nasociliary nerve.

cards.desc: Deep artery of the front of the forearm running on the interosseous membrane.
cards.att: Arises from the common interosseous branch of the ulnar artery just below the radial tuberosity, descends on the front of the interosseous membrane between flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus, and pierces the membrane at the upper border of pronator quadratus to end in the dorsal carpal arch.
cards.sup: Muscular branches to the deep flexors, nutrient arteries to the radius and the ulna, a slender median artery accompanying the median nerve, and terminal branches to the dorsal carpal arch.
cards.act: Chief supply of the deep flexor compartment of the forearm and of the shafts of the radius and ulna.
cards.rel: Accompanied throughout by the anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median nerve, and covered by flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus; pronator quadratus lies in front of its terminal part.
cards.clin: Vascularised bone graft from the distal radius is raised on this vessel. Its companion nerve, when compressed, causes anterior interosseous syndrome: loss of the OK sign from paralysis of flexor pollicis longus and the profundus to the index finger, with no sensory loss.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve accompanies the anterior interosseous artery and what is the sign of its palsy? A. The anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve; inability to make the OK sign.

syn: anterior interventricular part of the great cardiac vein
cards.desc: Cardiac vein ascending in the anterior interventricular groove beside the anterior interventricular (left anterior descending) artery.
cards.att: Begins near the apex of the heart, ascends in the anterior interventricular sulcus, then turns to the left in the coronary sulcus, where it is continued as the great cardiac vein and drains into the left end of the coronary sinus.
cards.act: Returns venous blood from the anterior walls of both ventricles and the anterior part of the interventricular septum, the territory of the left anterior descending artery.
cards.rel: Accompanies the anterior interventricular artery in the sulcus, lying superficial to it beneath the epicardium and adjacent fat.
cards.clin: An important landmark during coronary artery bypass grafting to the left anterior descending artery, and a route for retrograde cardioplegia and for lead placement in cardiac resynchronisation therapy.
cards.exam: Q. Into what does the anterior interventricular vein continue? A. The great cardiac vein, which drains into the coronary sinus.

cards.desc: The larger of the two cusps of the left atrioventricular (mitral) valve, hanging between the mitral orifice and the aortic vestibule.
cards.att: Attached to the anterior third of the mitral annulus and in fibrous continuity with the left and non-coronary cusps of the aortic valve; its free margin and ventricular surface receive chordae tendineae from both the anterolateral and the posteromedial papillary muscles.
cards.act: Closes the mitral orifice in ventricular systole; in diastole it swings back and forms the posterior boundary of the left ventricular outflow tract.
cards.rel: Separates the mitral inflow from the aortic outflow; the aortic valve lies immediately in front of and above it, and the left ventricular outflow tract lies on its ventricular side.
cards.clin: Systolic anterior motion of this leaflet obstructs the outflow tract in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy. Prolapse of the anterior leaflet directs the regurgitant jet posteriorly on echocardiography. Rheumatic disease thickens and fuses the cusps, giving the fish-mouth mitral stenosis.
cards.exam: Q. Which valve is in fibrous continuity with the anterior mitral leaflet? A. The aortic valve, through its left coronary and non-coronary cusps.

cards.desc: The largest of the three cusps of the right atrioventricular (tricuspid) valve, guarding the right atrioventricular orifice; the others are the posterior and septal cusps.
cards.att: Attached to the anterior part of the tricuspid annulus, extending from the infundibulum to the inferolateral wall of the right ventricle; its chordae tendineae arise mainly from the anterior papillary muscle, which is reached by the moderator band.
cards.act: Closes the right atrioventricular orifice during right ventricular systole, preventing regurgitation into the right atrium.
cards.rel: Lies behind the sternum at the level of the fourth and fifth costal cartilages; the right ventricular outflow tract lies anterosuperior, and the membranous septum with the atrioventricular bundle lies close to the septal cusp attachment.
cards.clin: In Ebstein anomaly this leaflet remains attached at the annulus and becomes large and sail-like while the septal and posterior leaflets are displaced apically. Tricuspid regurgitation gives a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border increasing with inspiration (Carvallo sign) and a giant v wave in the jugular venous pulse.
cards.exam: Q. Which papillary muscle supplies the chordae of the anterior tricuspid leaflet? A. The anterior papillary muscle of the right ventricle, reached by the moderator band.

syn: anterior papillary muscle of right ventricle
cards.desc: Largest papillary muscle of the right ventricle, projecting from the anterior wall into the cavity.
cards.att: Arises from the anterior wall of the right ventricle and from the septomarginal trabecula, which reaches its base from the interventricular septum; its chordae tendineae pass to the anterior and posterior cusps of the tricuspid valve.
cards.sup: Right coronary artery.
cards.act: Contracts at the start of systole to keep the tricuspid cusps apposed and prevent their prolapse into the right atrium when ventricular pressure rises.
cards.rel: Lies against the anterior wall of the right ventricle with the trabeculae carneae; the septomarginal trabecula (moderator band) crosses the cavity to its base, carrying the right branch of the atrioventricular bundle.
cards.clin: The septomarginal trabecula reaching this muscle carries the right bundle branch, so the anterior wall of the right ventricle is excited early; the band is a landmark for the right ventricle on echocardiography and prevents overdistension of the chamber.
cards.exam: Q. What does the septomarginal trabecula carry, and where does it end? A. The right branch of the atrioventricular bundle, ending at the base of the anterior papillary muscle of the right ventricle.

cards.desc: Main artery of the anterior (extensor) compartment of the leg, running from the back of the knee to the front of the ankle.
cards.att: Arises as the smaller terminal branch of the popliteal artery at the lower border of popliteus, passes forwards above the upper border of the interosseous membrane into the anterior compartment, then descends on the anterior surface of the membrane and the lower tibia, and becomes the dorsalis pedis artery midway between the malleoli at the level of the ankle joint.
cards.sup: Anterior tibial recurrent, muscular branches, anterior medial malleolar and anterior lateral malleolar arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the extensor compartment muscles, the anterior part of the ankle and the skin over the front of the leg.
cards.rel: Accompanied by the deep fibular nerve, which crosses from lateral to anterior and then lies lateral to the artery in the lower leg; lies between tibialis anterior medially and extensor digitorum longus, then extensor hallucis longus, laterally; venae comitantes on either side.
cards.clin: Vulnerable in fractures of the upper tibia and in anterior compartment syndrome, where rising compartment pressure causes deep pain on passive plantarflexion, weak dorsiflexion, and numbness in the first web space; distal pulses may still be present.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the anterior tibial artery enter the anterior compartment of the leg? A. Through the gap above the upper border of the interosseous membrane.

cards.k: anterolateral head of lateral papillary muscle of ventricle
syn: anterior head of anterolateral papillary muscle
cards.desc: Anterior of the two heads into which the anterolateral papillary muscle of the left ventricle is usually divided.
cards.att: Arises from the anterolateral wall of the left ventricle, at the junction of its anterior and lateral walls in the middle third; its chordae tendineae pass to the anterior halves of both the anterior and the posterior cusps of the mitral valve.
cards.sup: Dual supply from the left anterior descending artery through a diagonal branch and from the circumflex artery, unlike the single supply of the posteromedial muscle.
cards.act: Tightens the chordae at the onset of systole so that the mitral cusps meet and do not prolapse into the left atrium.
cards.rel: Projects from the anterolateral wall into the left ventricular cavity, lateral to the interventricular septum and anterolateral to the posteromedial papillary muscle, the only other papillary muscle of the left ventricle.
cards.clin: Because of its dual coronary supply the anterolateral papillary muscle is far less often ruptured after myocardial infarction than the posteromedial, which has only the posterior descending supply. Rupture causes sudden severe mitral regurgitation and pulmonary oedema.
cards.exam: Q. Which papillary muscle of the left ventricle ruptures more often after infarction and why? A. The posteromedial, because it has a single blood supply, whereas the anterolateral has a dual supply.

cards.desc: Narrow blind-ended muscular tube of gut with abundant lymphoid tissue, arising from the posteromedial wall of the caecum about 2 cm below the ileocaecal junction.
cards.att: Base is fixed where the three taeniae coli converge on the caecum; the tip is mobile and lies retrocaecal (commonest), pelvic, subcaecal, pre-ileal or post-ileal. Suspended by the mesoappendix.
cards.sup: Appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery, running in the free edge of the mesoappendix. Veins drain to the superior mesenteric vein. Lymph to ileocolic nodes. Visceral afferents accompany sympathetics to T10.
cards.act: Gut-associated lymphoid tissue; no essential digestive function.
cards.rel: Base lies deep to McBurney's point, at the junction of the lateral and middle thirds of the line from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. A retrocaecal appendix lies against the iliacus and psoas major.
cards.clin: Appendicitis pain begins periumbilically (visceral, T10) and shifts to the right iliac fossa when the parietal peritoneum is irritated. A retrocaecal appendix gives a positive psoas sign; a pelvic appendix gives a positive obturator sign and tenderness on rectal examination. The appendicular artery is an end artery, so gangrene and perforation follow quickly.
cards.exam: Q. How is the base of the appendix found at operation? A. By tracing the taeniae coli of the caecum to their convergence.

cards.desc: Curved continuation of the ascending aorta in the superior mediastinum, arching upwards, backwards and to the left over the root of the left lung.
cards.att: Begins behind the right half of the manubrium at the level of the sternal angle (T4 to T5 disc) and ends on the left side of the lower border of T4, where it becomes the descending thoracic aorta. Branches in order: brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery, left subclavian artery.
cards.sup: Gives the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries; the ligamentum arteriosum joins its inferior surface to the left pulmonary artery.
cards.act: Conducts the entire cardiac output from the ascending aorta to the head, neck, upper limbs and descending aorta; baroreceptors in its wall, supplied by the vagus, regulate blood pressure.
cards.rel: On its left lie the left phrenic nerve, left vagus and the left superior intercostal vein; the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under it lateral to the ligamentum arteriosum. Medially and below lie the trachea, oesophagus, thoracic duct and left recurrent laryngeal nerve; the left brachiocephalic vein crosses in front.
cards.clin: An aneurysm or a dilated left atrium can stretch the left recurrent laryngeal nerve and cause hoarseness (Ortner cardiovocal syndrome). Postductal coarctation just beyond the left subclavian gives radiofemoral delay, upper limb hypertension and inferior rib notching from enlarged intercostal arteries.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve hooks around the arch of the aorta and where? A. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve, immediately lateral to the ligamentum arteriosum.

cards.desc: Main artery of the thumb, a branch of the radial artery in the deep palm.
cards.att: Arises from the radial artery as it turns medially between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous into the palm, descends along the ulnar side of the first metacarpal deep to the oblique head of adductor pollicis, and divides at the head of the metacarpal into the two proper palmar digital arteries of the thumb.
cards.sup: Two proper palmar digital arteries running along the sides of the thumb to the pulp; the radialis indicis artery to the radial side of the index finger arises from it or from the radial artery alongside.
cards.act: Dominant blood supply of the thumb.
cards.rel: Deep to adductor pollicis and the long flexor tendons, lying on the first metacarpal; the deep branch of the ulnar nerve crosses the deep palm nearby.
cards.clin: As the dominant supply of the thumb it must be identified and preserved in thumb replantation, pollicisation and adductor pollicis release; its dorsal counterpart, the first dorsal metacarpal artery, carries the kite flap used to resurface the thumb.
cards.exam: Q. Which artery gives the princeps pollicis? A. The radial artery, as it enters the palm between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous.

cards.desc: Cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery that ascends in the central sulcus.
cards.att: Arises from the terminal branches of the middle cerebral artery at the lateral sulcus and runs upwards and backwards in, or along, the central sulcus towards the superolateral margin.
cards.sup: Supplies the cortex on both banks of the central sulcus, the lower part of the precentral and postcentral gyri, that is the face, tongue and upper limb areas.
cards.act: Perfuses the primary motor and primary sensory cortex for the face and upper limb.
cards.rel: Runs between the artery of the precentral sulcus in front and the artery of the postcentral sulcus behind, on the lateral surface above the lateral sulcus.
cards.clin: Occlusion gives contralateral weakness and sensory loss of the face and upper limb with the lower limb spared, the classic cortical pattern of middle cerebral artery territory stroke.
cards.exam: Q. Why does a middle cerebral artery stroke spare the leg? A. Because the leg area lies in the paracentral lobule supplied by the anterior cerebral artery, while the face and arm areas lie on the lateral surface supplied by the middle cerebral artery.

cards.desc: Cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery ascending in the precentral sulcus.
cards.att: Arises from the terminal branches of the middle cerebral artery at the lateral sulcus and runs upwards and forwards in the precentral sulcus.
cards.sup: Supplies the posterior parts of the middle and inferior frontal gyri including the premotor cortex, and the anterior part of the precentral gyrus.
cards.act: Perfuses premotor cortex and, in the dominant hemisphere, the motor speech area in the posterior part of the inferior frontal gyrus.
cards.rel: Lies in front of the artery of the central sulcus, above the lateral sulcus, on the frontal operculum.
cards.clin: Occlusion in the dominant hemisphere infarcts Broca area and produces an expressive, non-fluent aphasia with comprehension preserved.
cards.exam: Q. Which artery supplies Broca area? A. The precentral (prerolandic) branch of the middle cerebral artery in the dominant hemisphere.

cards.desc: Paired pyramidal hyaline cartilage sitting on the upper border of the lamina of the cricoid at the back of the larynx.
cards.att: Has an apex bearing the corniculate cartilage, a base articulating with the cricoid at the synovial cricoarytenoid joint, an anteriorly directed vocal process giving attachment to the vocal ligament and conus elasticus, and a laterally directed muscular process receiving posterior cricoarytenoid behind and lateral cricoarytenoid in front. Thyroarytenoid and vocalis attach to its anterolateral surface, the transverse and oblique arytenoids to its posterior surface.
cards.sup: Laryngeal branches of the superior and inferior thyroid arteries; motor supply of all attached muscles is the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
cards.act: Rotation and gliding at the cricoarytenoid joint swing the vocal process laterally or medially, thereby abducting or adducting the vocal fold and altering the length and tension of the vocal ligament.
cards.rel: Piriform fossa lies lateral to it, the laryngeal inlet and aryepiglottic fold anterolateral, the cricoid below and the corniculate cartilage above.
cards.clin: Arytenoid subluxation or dislocation is a recognised complication of difficult intubation and presents with hoarseness and a fixed cord. Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy leaves the cord in the paramedian position because the arytenoid cannot be abducted.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle attaches to the muscular process of the arytenoid to abduct the vocal cord? A. Posterior cricoarytenoid, the only abductor of the vocal cord.

cards.desc: First part of the aorta, about 5 cm long, running upwards, forwards and to the right within the fibrous pericardium.
cards.att: Begins at the aortic orifice of the left ventricle behind the left half of the sternum at the level of the third costal cartilage, and ends at the level of the sternal angle where it becomes the arch. Its origin shows three dilated aortic sinuses (of Valsalva) and ends distally at the sinotubular junction.
cards.sup: Branches: right coronary artery from the right (anterior) aortic sinus and left coronary artery from the left (posterior) aortic sinus; the posterior (non-coronary) sinus gives no branch.
cards.act: Delivers the left ventricular output to the arch, and through the coronary arteries supplies the heart itself during diastole.
cards.rel: Enclosed with the pulmonary trunk in a common sleeve of serous pericardium; the transverse pericardial sinus lies behind it. The right atrium and superior vena cava lie to its right, the pulmonary trunk to its left, and the right pulmonary artery and right main bronchus behind.
cards.clin: Dilatation of the aortic root occurs in Marfan syndrome and cystic medial degeneration. Type A dissection involves the ascending aorta and is a surgical emergency because it can rupture into the pericardium and cause tamponade. Rupture of the ascending aorta bleeds into the pericardial cavity, since this segment is intrapericardial.
cards.exam: Q. Which vessels arise from the ascending aorta? A. Only the right and left coronary arteries, from the corresponding aortic sinuses.

cards.desc: Retroperitoneal segment of large intestine, about 12 to 15 cm long, running from the caecum in the right iliac fossa up to the right colic (hepatic) flexure.
cards.att: Continues from the caecum at the level of the ileocaecal junction, ascends in the right paracolic gutter, and turns left and forwards at the right colic flexure to become the transverse colon. Covered by peritoneum on its front and sides only.
cards.sup: Ileocolic and right colic arteries from the superior mesenteric artery, through the marginal artery of Drummond. Veins to the superior mesenteric vein. Lymph to ileocolic and right colic nodes. Parasympathetic supply from the vagus, sympathetic from T10 to T12.
cards.act: Absorbs water and electrolytes; transports faeces towards the transverse colon.
cards.rel: Posteriorly lies on iliacus, quadratus lumborum, the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves and the lower pole of the right kidney. The right paracolic gutter lies laterally, and the greater omentum and coils of ileum lie anteriorly.
cards.clin: The right paracolic gutter is a route for pus to track from a perforated appendix to the subphrenic space, and from the gallbladder down to the right iliac fossa. Carcinoma here presents late with iron deficiency anaemia rather than obstruction, because the contents are fluid and the lumen is wide.
cards.exam: Q. Why does right-sided colon cancer present with anaemia rather than obstruction? A. The lumen is wide and the contents are liquid, so bleeding occurs long before obstruction.

cards.desc: Long vertical vein on each side of the posterior abdominal wall, deep to psoas major, connecting the lumbar veins to each other and to the azygos system.
cards.att: Begins below from the common iliac or iliolumbar vein, ascends in front of the roots of the lumbar transverse processes behind psoas major, and joins the subcostal vein to become the azygos vein on the right and the hemiazygos vein on the left.
cards.sup: Receives the lumbar veins and communicates with the inferior vena cava and with the internal vertebral venous plexus.
cards.act: Provides a collateral channel carrying blood from the lower limb and pelvis to the superior vena cava, bypassing the inferior vena cava.
cards.rel: Lies deep to psoas major and to the lumbar sympathetic trunk, anterior to the roots of the transverse processes and lateral to the vertebral bodies.
cards.clin: Main collateral pathway in inferior vena caval obstruction, when it enlarges greatly. A femoral or umbilical catheter may be misdirected into the left ascending lumbar vein and mimic an aortic position on a frontal radiograph; the vein is also a source of type II endoleak after endovascular aortic repair.
cards.exam: Q. What does the ascending lumbar vein become after it joins the subcostal vein? A. The azygos vein on the right and the hemiazygos vein on the left.

cards.desc: The lower fibres of trapezius, running upwards and laterally from the lower thoracic spines to the scapular spine.
cards.att: Origin: spinous processes and supraspinous ligaments of the lower thoracic vertebrae, about T5 to T12. Insertion: an aponeurosis gliding over the medial end of the spine of the scapula, inserting on the tubercle of the scapular spine.
cards.sup: Accessory nerve (CN XI) for motor supply, with proprioceptive fibres from the ventral rami of C3 and C4.
cards.act: Depresses the scapula; acting with the descending part it produces upward rotation of the glenoid cavity, essential for elevating the arm above the head.
cards.rel: Deep to skin and superficial fascia; overlies rhomboid major, erector spinae and latissimus dorsi; its lateral border helps form the medial boundary of the triangle of auscultation.
cards.clin: Weakness of the lower fibres allows scapular dyskinesis and impingement. Complete accessory nerve injury during posterior triangle lymph node biopsy causes drooping shoulder and inability to raise the arm above the head.
cards.exam: Q. Which two parts of trapezius combine to rotate the glenoid cavity upwards? A. The descending (upper) and ascending (lower) parts, acting as a force couple with serratus anterior.

cards.desc: Ring-shaped first cervical vertebra with no body and no spine, carrying the skull.
cards.att: Consists of anterior and posterior arches and two lateral masses with transverse processes containing foramina transversaria. The anterior arch bears the anterior tubercle in front and a facet for the dens behind; the posterior arch bears the posterior tubercle and a groove for the vertebral artery and the first cervical nerve. Concave superior facets articulate with the occipital condyles, flattish inferior facets with the axis. The transverse ligament attaches to tubercles on the medial surfaces of the lateral masses.
cards.sup: Vertebral artery grooves the posterior arch; segmental supply from the vertebral and ascending cervical arteries.
cards.act: Transmits the weight of the skull to the axis; the atlanto-occipital joints allow flexion and extension, the nodding movement of yes.
cards.rel: Transverse process is palpable between the mastoid process and the angle of the mandible. The vertebral artery, internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein and the last four cranial nerves lie close to the transverse process.
cards.clin: Axial loading, as in diving into shallow water, splits the ring as a Jefferson burst fracture, usually without cord injury because the fragments spread outwards. Rupture of the transverse ligament allows atlanto-axial subluxation and cord compression.
cards.exam: Q. Why does the atlas have no body? A. Its body has fused with the axis to form the dens, which is retained against the anterior arch by the transverse ligament of the atlas.

cards.desc: Main artery of the axilla, continuing the subclavian artery and supplying the shoulder region and upper limb.
cards.att: Begins as the continuation of the subclavian artery at the outer border of the first rib and ends at the lower border of teres major, where it becomes the brachial artery; pectoralis minor crossing it divides it into three parts.
cards.sup: First part: superior thoracic artery. Second part: thoraco-acromial and lateral thoracic arteries. Third part: subscapular, anterior circumflex humeral and posterior circumflex humeral arteries, giving one, two and three branches from the three parts.
cards.act: Supplies the shoulder girdle, the walls and contents of the axilla, the lateral part of the breast, and through its continuation the whole upper limb.
cards.rel: Enclosed with the brachial plexus in the axillary sheath; the cords of the plexus are named from their relation to its second part. The axillary vein lies medial to it throughout, and the axillary nerve and radial nerve lie behind its third part.
cards.clin: At risk in anterior shoulder dislocation and proximal humeral fracture, and may be compressed against the humeral head. It can be ligated between the thyrocervical trunk and the subscapular artery because the scapular anastomosis restores flow, but ligation distal to the subscapular origin threatens the limb.
cards.exam: Q. What divides the axillary artery into its three parts? A. Pectoralis minor: the first part is proximal to it, the second behind it, the third distal to it.

cards.desc: Large vein of the axilla draining the whole upper limb, lying medial to the axillary artery.
cards.att: Formed at the lower border of teres major by the union of the brachial venae comitantes with the basilic vein, ascends medial and slightly anterior to the axillary artery, and becomes the subclavian vein at the outer border of the first rib.
cards.sup: Receives tributaries corresponding to the branches of the axillary artery, together with the cephalic vein, which pierces the clavipectoral fascia to join it, and the thoraco-epigastric vein.
cards.rel: Lies medial to the axillary artery and partly overlaps it; the medial cord of the brachial plexus, the ulnar nerve and the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm lie between the vein and the artery. The lateral (humeral) and apical groups of axillary lymph nodes lie along it.
cards.clin: Used for infraclavicular central venous access; its walls are held open by surrounding fascia, so a tear can draw in air and cause air embolism. Effort thrombosis (Paget-Schroetter syndrome) affects the axillary and subclavian veins, and dissection along the vein in axillary clearance risks lymphoedema.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the axillary vein begin and end? A. At the lower border of teres major, from the brachial veins and basilic vein, ending at the outer border of the first rib as the subclavian vein.

cards.desc: Second cervical vertebra, identified by the dens projecting upwards from its body.
cards.att: The dens has an anterior facet for the anterior arch of the atlas, a posterior groove for the transverse ligament, and gives attachment to the apical ligament at its tip and the alar ligaments from its sides to the occipital condyles. Large superior articular facets lie on the body and pedicles for the atlas, a strong bifid spine gives attachment to semispinalis cervicis and the inferior oblique, and the foramina transversaria transmit the vertebral arteries.
cards.sup: Segmental branches of the vertebral and ascending pharyngeal arteries.
cards.act: Forms the pivot for the median and lateral atlanto-axial joints, at which the atlas and skull rotate, the movement of shaking the head for no; about half of all cervical rotation occurs here.
cards.rel: The dens lies behind the anterior arch of the atlas and in front of the transverse ligament and the spinal cord. The vertebral artery turns laterally over the axis before ascending to the atlas.
cards.clin: Fracture of the dens, especially type II at its base, unites poorly and threatens the cord. Hyperextension injury fractures the pars interarticularis bilaterally, the hangman fracture or traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2. The dens erodes in rheumatoid arthritis, so intubation risks atlanto-axial subluxation.
cards.exam: Q. What keeps the dens in place and what happens if it fails? A. The transverse ligament of the atlas; rupture or dens fracture allows atlanto-axial dislocation and compression of the spinal cord.

cards.desc: Unpaired vein of the right posterior thoracic wall that links the inferior and superior venae cavae and drains most of the posterior intercostal spaces.
cards.att: Usually formed at about the level of L1 or L2 by the union of the right ascending lumbar vein and the right subcostal vein, sometimes arising from the inferior vena cava; enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus or the right crus, ascends on the right of the vertebral bodies, then arches forwards over the root of the right lung at the level of T4 to open into the superior vena cava.
cards.sup: Tributaries: right posterior intercostal veins of the 4th to 11th spaces, right subcostal vein, hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins, right superior intercostal vein, right bronchial, oesophageal, mediastinal and pericardial veins.
cards.act: Returns blood from the posterior thoracic and upper abdominal walls to the superior vena cava, and provides an alternative route between the caval systems.
cards.rel: Lies to the right of the thoracic duct and the descending thoracic aorta, in front of the vertebral bodies and right posterior intercostal arteries, behind the oesophagus at its arch; the right lung root lies below its arch.
cards.clin: The principal collateral channel in obstruction of the superior or inferior vena cava, when it dilates and is visible on chest radiograph. An azygos lobe of the right lung forms when the vein migrates abnormally through the upper lobe, drawing a fissure with it.
cards.exam: Q. At what level does the azygos vein arch to enter the superior vena cava? A. At the level of T4, arching over the root of the right lung.

cards.desc: Single midline artery on the ventral surface of the pons, formed by the union of the two vertebral arteries, supplying the pons, cerebellum and inner ear.
cards.att: Formed at the lower border of the pons (pontomedullary junction) by the union of the two vertebral arteries, ascends in the basilar sulcus of the pons within the pontine cistern, and divides at the upper border of the pons into the two posterior cerebral arteries.
cards.sup: Branches: anterior inferior cerebellar artery, labyrinthine (internal auditory) artery, pontine branches, superior cerebellar artery, and the terminal posterior cerebral arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the pons, midbrain, cerebellum, internal ear and, through the posterior cerebral arteries, the occipital and inferomedial temporal lobes.
cards.rel: Lies on the clivus behind the dorsum sellae, with the abducent nerve emerging at the pontomedullary junction beside it and the oculomotor nerve passing between the superior cerebellar and posterior cerebral arteries at its termination.
cards.clin: Basilar occlusion causes bilateral pontine infarction and the locked-in syndrome: quadriplegia and anarthria with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movement. Occlusion of the labyrinthine artery causes sudden ipsilateral deafness and vertigo.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve passes between the superior cerebellar and posterior cerebral arteries? A. The oculomotor nerve, hence its compression by a posterior communicating aneurysm or uncal herniation.

cards.desc: Large superficial vein on the medial side of the forearm and arm that becomes a deep vein in the arm.
cards.att: Begins at the ulnar end of the dorsal venous network, ascends on the ulnar side of the front of the forearm, passes in front of the medial epicondyle, and pierces the deep fascia at about the middle of the arm to run with the brachial artery and join the brachial veins at the lower border of teres major as the axillary vein.
cards.sup: Receives the median cubital vein and often the median vein of the forearm at the elbow, together with tributaries from the medial forearm and arm.
cards.rel: Accompanied by the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm below the elbow and by branches of the same nerve in the arm; after piercing the deep fascia it lies medial to the brachial artery.
cards.clin: The vein of choice for peripherally inserted central catheters because of its straight course into the axillary vein, and it is transposed and anastomosed to the brachial artery to create a dialysis fistula when forearm vessels have failed.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the basilic vein pierce the deep fascia? A. At about the middle of the arm, at the hiatus basilicus in the medial intermuscular septum.

cards.desc: Flat middle part of the sternum, formed by fusion of four sternebrae, lying between the manubrium above and the xiphoid process below.
cards.att: Articulates with the manubrium at the manubriosternal joint (sternal angle, a symphysis) and with the xiphoid at the xiphisternal joint. Costal notches take the lower half of the 2nd costal cartilage, the 3rd to 6th cartilages, and the upper part of the 7th. Gives attachment to pectoralis major, to transversus thoracis internally and to the rectus sheath aponeuroses below.
cards.sup: Internal thoracic artery through perforating and sternal branches; contains red marrow throughout life.
cards.act: Protects the mediastinum and forms the anterior anchor of the rib cage, moving forward and upward with the ribs in inspiration.
cards.rel: Behind it lie the anterior mediastinum, the pericardium and the right ventricle with its outflow tract; the internal thoracic vessels descend about 1 cm lateral to its border.
cards.clin: Sternal puncture for marrow aspiration is done in the body at the level of the 2nd or 3rd intercostal space. Median sternotomy splits it for cardiac surgery; the xiphisternal joint lies at the T9 vertebral level.
cards.exam: Q. Which costal cartilages articulate with the body of the sternum? A. The 2nd (lower half) to the 7th (upper part), with the 3rd to 6th articulating with the body alone.

cards.desc: Main artery of the arm, the continuation of the axillary artery on the front of the arm.
cards.att: Begins at the lower border of teres major, descends on the medial side of the arm and then on brachialis in front of the humerus, and ends in the cubital fossa at the level of the neck of the radius by dividing into the radial and ulnar arteries.
cards.sup: Profunda brachii (deep brachial), superior ulnar collateral, inferior ulnar collateral, the nutrient artery to the humerus and muscular branches; terminates as the radial and ulnar arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the flexor and extensor compartments of the arm, the humerus and the elbow, and carries the entire blood supply of the forearm and hand.
cards.rel: The median nerve crosses it from lateral to medial in the middle of the arm. In the cubital fossa it lies between the median nerve medially and the tendon of biceps laterally, covered by the bicipital aponeurosis; the ulnar nerve leaves it in the upper arm to pass behind the medial epicondyle.
cards.clin: The artery used for blood pressure measurement and the brachial pulse, felt medial to the biceps tendon. In supracondylar fracture of the humerus, injury or spasm produces forearm ischaemia and Volkmann ischaemic contracture; pain on passive extension of the fingers with a weak radial pulse is the warning sign.
cards.exam: Q. At what level does the brachial artery divide, and into what? A. At the level of the neck of the radius in the cubital fossa, into the radial and ulnar arteries.

cards.desc: Flat muscle on the lower half of the front of the humerus, lying deep to biceps brachii and crossing only the elbow joint.
cards.att: Origin: lower half of the anterior surface of the humerus and the adjacent medial and lateral intermuscular septa. Insertion: tuberosity and anterior surface of the coronoid process of the ulna.
cards.sup: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6); the lateral part receives a twig from the radial nerve (C7).
cards.act: The main flexor of the elbow, working in all positions of the forearm because it inserts on the ulna and is unaffected by pronation and supination.
cards.rel: Forms the floor of the cubital fossa with supinator; the median nerve and brachial artery lie on it medially, the radial nerve between it and brachioradialis laterally; biceps brachii lies superficial.
cards.clin: Direct trauma to the muscle is a common cause of myositis ossificans at the elbow. Supracondylar fracture fragments may pierce it and injure the underlying brachial artery and median nerve, and it is the muscle interposed in anterior elbow dislocation.
cards.exam: Q. Why is brachialis called the workhorse flexor of the elbow? A. Because it inserts on the ulna and therefore flexes the elbow with equal power in supination, pronation and midprone positions.

cards.desc: Most superficial and lateral muscle of the forearm, forming the prominent lateral border of the cubital fossa.
cards.att: Origin: upper two-thirds of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus and the anterior surface of the lateral intermuscular septum. Insertion: lateral side of the base of the styloid process of the radius.
cards.sup: Radial nerve (C5, C6, C7), in the arm before the nerve divides.
cards.act: Flexes the elbow, most powerfully with the forearm in the midprone position; it is a shunt muscle rather than a true supinator or pronator.
cards.rel: Forms the lateral boundary of the cubital fossa; the radial nerve and radial artery lie deep to it in the forearm, the artery emerging at its medial border where the radial pulse is felt.
cards.clin: An anomaly among flexors: it flexes the elbow yet is supplied by the radial nerve. It is paralysed with the wrist extensors when the radial nerve is injured in the spiral groove, but spared in a posterior interosseous nerve lesion, so preserved brachioradialis localises the lesion below the elbow; the brachioradialis jerk tests C5 and C6.
cards.exam: Q. In which position of the forearm does brachioradialis act most powerfully, and what nerve supplies it? A. The midprone position, supplied by the radial nerve (C5, C6, C7).

cards.desc: Oblique ridge of fibres on the lateral surface of the midbrain running upwards and forwards from the inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate body.
cards.att: Arises from the inferior colliculus, carrying also some fibres of the lateral lemniscus, and terminates in the medial geniculate body.
cards.act: Conveys the auditory pathway from the midbrain to the thalamic auditory relay.
cards.rel: Lies below the brachium of the superior colliculus on the lateral surface of the midbrain, above the trigeminal lemniscus, deep to the medial geniculate body in front.
cards.clin: A unilateral lesion causes little clinical deafness because auditory information is represented bilaterally above the cochlear nuclei; the deficit is limited to subtle contralateral sound localisation difficulty.
cards.exam: Q. What does the brachium of the inferior colliculus connect? A. The inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate body.

cards.desc: Band of fibres passing on the lateral surface of the midbrain from the region of the optic tract and lateral geniculate body backwards to the superior colliculus and pretectal area.
cards.att: Carries retinal fibres from the optic tract and cortical fibres to the superior colliculus and pretectal nuclei.
cards.act: Carries the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex to the pretectal area and visual input for reflex eye and head movements to the superior colliculus.
cards.rel: Lies between the pulvinar above and the brachium of the inferior colliculus below, crossing the lateral surface of the midbrain.
cards.clin: Lesions in this pretectal region interrupt the light reflex pathway while sparing the near response and cause the upgaze palsy of Parinaud's syndrome, classically from a pineal tumour.
cards.exam: Q. Which fibres in the brachium of the superior colliculus are lost in a pretectal lesion? A. The afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex, giving light-near dissociation.

cards.desc: The thickest and strongest tendon in the body, formed by the triceps surae and inserting on the heel.
cards.att: Formed by union of the tendons of the two heads of gastrocnemius and of soleus about the middle of the leg; the fibres spiral about ninety degrees as they descend and insert into the middle part of the posterior surface of the calcaneus.
cards.sup: Blood supply from branches of the posterior tibial and fibular arteries; sensory innervation from the tibial and sural nerves.
cards.act: Transmits the plantarflexion force of the triceps surae to the heel, giving the push off in walking, running and jumping.
cards.rel: The retrocalcaneal bursa lies between the tendon and the upper part of the posterior surface of the calcaneus, and a subcutaneous bursa lies behind it. The sural nerve and small saphenous vein lie along its lateral border; the tibial neurovascular bundle and deep flexor tendons lie deep and medial to it.
cards.clin: Ruptures typically 2 to 6 cm above the insertion, a relatively avascular watershed zone, with a palpable gap and a positive Simmonds or Thompson calf squeeze test. Its integrity is tested clinically by the ankle jerk (S1, S2).
cards.exam: Q. Why does the calcaneal tendon usually rupture 2 to 6 cm above its insertion? A. That segment is a relatively avascular watershed zone between its proximal and distal blood supply.

cards.desc: Largest and strongest tarsal bone, forming the heel and transmitting body weight to the ground behind the talus.
cards.att: Parts: body, calcaneal tuberosity with medial and lateral processes, sustentaculum tali, anterior process, and the fibular (peroneal) trochlea laterally. Articulates above with the talus by anterior, middle and posterior facets and in front with the cuboid. The calcaneal tendon inserts on the middle of the posterior surface; the plantar aponeurosis, abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis and abductor digiti minimi arise from the tuberosity; the groove below sustentaculum tali carries the tendon of flexor hallucis longus.
cards.act: Transmits body weight to the ground, acts as the lever arm for the calf muscles and forms the posterior pillar of the lateral longitudinal arch.
cards.rel: The sinus tarsi and tarsal canal between calcaneus and talus hold the interosseous talocalcaneal ligament. Medially the tarsal tunnel structures cross it; the fibular tendons pass on either side of the fibular trochlea laterally.
cards.clin: A fall from a height causes a compression fracture of the calcaneus, often bilateral and associated with a burst fracture of the lumbar spine, and Böhler's angle is reduced. A calcaneal spur at the origin of the plantar aponeurosis is associated with plantar fasciitis, and the medial process is the usual site of heel pain.
cards.exam: Q. What injuries are typically associated with a calcaneal fracture from a fall on the heels? A. A fracture of the opposite calcaneus and a compression or burst fracture of the thoracolumbar spine.

cards.desc: The largest carpal bone, lying at the centre of the wrist in the distal row, with a rounded head, a constricted neck and a body.
cards.att: Its head articulates proximally with the lunate and with the scaphoid, the trapezoid lies on its radial side and the hamate on its ulnar side, and distally it articulates chiefly with the base of the third metacarpal and partly with the second and fourth. It gives attachment to the deep intercarpal ligaments and to a slip of adductor pollicis from its palmar surface.
cards.rel: Forms part of the floor of the carpal tunnel with the other carpals; the deep branch of the ulnar nerve and the deep palmar arch cross its palmar aspect. It lies at the centre of the arc of wrist movement.
cards.clin: The base of the third metacarpal and the capitate lie in the axis of the wrist, so the capitate is the pivot about which the wrist moves. Its proximal pole receives a retrograde blood supply and can undergo avascular necrosis after a scaphocapitate fracture, in which the capitate head is fractured and rotated.
cards.exam: Q. Which is the largest carpal bone and with which metacarpal does it mainly articulate? A. The capitate, articulating mainly with the base of the third metacarpal.

cards.desc: Small lobe on the posterior surface of the liver, bounded by the inferior vena cava on the right, the fissure for the ligamentum venosum on the left and the porta hepatis below.
cards.att: Bounded above by the diaphragmatic surface, below by the porta hepatis, on the right by the groove for the inferior vena cava and on the left by the fissure for the ligamentum venosum. Connected to the right lobe by the caudate process, which forms the upper boundary of the epiploic foramen.
cards.sup: Receives portal and arterial branches from both the right and left systems; drains directly into the inferior vena cava by several small hepatic veins, independent of the three main hepatic veins.
cards.act: Functionally independent liver segment (segment I) in the Couinaud scheme.
cards.rel: Lies in the anterior wall of the superior recess of the lesser sac. The inferior vena cava is immediately posterior and to the right; the oesophageal groove and lesser omentum lie to the left.
cards.clin: Because it drains straight into the inferior vena cava, the caudate lobe is spared and hypertrophies in Budd-Chiari syndrome, giving the classic enlarged caudate on imaging. Its dual inflow and separate drainage also make it a separate resection unit, removed with the specimen in hilar cholangiocarcinoma.
cards.exam: Q. Which liver segment is the caudate lobe and why does it enlarge in Budd-Chiari syndrome? A. Segment I; it drains directly into the IVC by its own small veins, bypassing the obstructed main hepatic veins.

cards.desc: C-shaped mass of grey matter of the corpus striatum arching over the thalamus and following the concavity of the lateral ventricle, with a head, body and tail.
cards.att: Head bulges into the floor and lateral wall of the anterior horn of the lateral ventricle; the body lies in the floor of the ventricular body; the tail curves into the roof of the inferior horn and ends in the amygdaloid body. Joined to the putamen by grey bridges crossing the anterior limb of the internal capsule.
cards.sup: Head supplied by the medial striate artery of Heubner from the anterior cerebral artery; body and tail by lateral striate (lenticulostriate) branches of the middle cerebral artery and the anterior choroidal artery.
cards.act: With the putamen forms the striatum, the input station of the basal ganglia, concerned with the initiation and control of movement and with cognitive and associative motor learning.
cards.rel: Separated from the lentiform nucleus by the internal capsule; the thalamus lies medial to its body with the stria terminalis and thalamostriate vein in the intervening groove; the lateral ventricle lies on its ventricular surface.
cards.clin: Selective atrophy of the caudate head in Huntington's disease produces the boxcar appearance of dilated frontal horns on CT and MRI. Infarction of the head from occlusion of Heubner's artery may cause abulia and contralateral facio-brachial weakness.
cards.exam: Q. What separates the caudate nucleus from the lentiform nucleus? A. The internal capsule, crossed by grey bridges of striatum.

cards.desc: Blood filled chamber of a cardiac ventricle, between the atrioventricular valve above and the outflow tract leading to the great artery.
cards.att: Each cavity has an inflow part, roughened by trabeculae carneae and papillary muscles, and a smooth outflow part: the conus arteriosus in the right ventricle and the aortic vestibule in the left. The right cavity is crescentic in cross section because the septum bulges into it; the left cavity is circular and its wall is about three times thicker.
cards.sup: Right ventricular cavity receives blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve and empties into the pulmonary trunk; the left receives from the left atrium through the mitral valve and empties into the aorta.
cards.act: Fills in diastole and, on systolic contraction, ejects the stroke volume, the two ventricles delivering equal outputs.
cards.rel: Right cavity lies behind the sternum and forms most of the anterior surface of the heart; the left cavity lies posterolaterally and forms the apex and the left border; the interventricular septum separates the two.
cards.clin: Cavity size and wall thickness on echocardiography separate concentric hypertrophy of pressure overload from dilatation of volume overload. Mural thrombus forms in the cavity over an akinetic infarcted segment and may embolise to the brain or limbs.
cards.exam: Q. Why is the right ventricular cavity crescentic in cross section? A. Because the thicker left ventricle and its septum bulge into it.

cards.desc: First unpaired ventral branch of the abdominal aorta, arising at the level of T12 just below the aortic hiatus and dividing after about 1.5 cm into three branches.
cards.att: Arises from the front of the abdominal aorta at the T12 to L1 level, passes forwards and slightly to the right above the pancreas, and ends by trifurcating behind the omental bursa.
cards.sup: Left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the foregut derivatives: abdominal oesophagus, stomach, duodenum as far as the major duodenal papilla, liver, gallbladder, pancreas and spleen.
cards.rel: Surrounded by the coeliac plexus and its two ganglia, overhung by the median arcuate ligament and the crura, with the omental bursa and lesser omentum in front and the splenic vein and pancreas below.
cards.clin: Median arcuate ligament (Dunbar) syndrome: compression by a low-lying ligament causes postprandial epigastric pain, weight loss and an epigastric bruit. Slow coeliac occlusion is tolerated because the pancreaticoduodenal arcade connects it with the superior mesenteric artery.
cards.exam: Q. Name the three branches of the coeliac artery and the gut region it supplies. A. Left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries; the foregut.

cards.desc: Short wide artery, about 1.5 cm long, arising from the front of the abdominal aorta at T12 and trifurcating into the left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries.
cards.att: Arises immediately below the aortic hiatus at the T12 to L1 level between the crura of the diaphragm, runs forwards over the upper border of the pancreas, and ends by dividing into its three branches.
