cards.sup: Left gastric artery (smallest), splenic artery (largest) and common hepatic artery; it may also give an inferior phrenic or a dorsal pancreatic branch.
cards.act: Carries the arterial supply of all foregut derivatives, with pain from these organs referred to the epigastrium.
cards.rel: Lies behind the omental bursa and the peritoneum of the lesser sac, embedded in the coeliac plexus, with the caudate lobe of the liver above and the body of the pancreas and splenic vein below.
cards.clin: Classical trifurcation is present in about 90 percent of people; hepatosplenic, gastrosplenic and hepatogastric variants and a common coeliacomesenteric trunk are recognised, and these variants must be defined on CT angiography before pancreatic or liver surgery.
cards.exam: Q. Which foregut structures does the coeliac trunk supply and where is their pain referred? A. Stomach, proximal duodenum, liver, gallbladder, pancreas and spleen, with pain referred to the epigastrium.

cards.desc: Narrow ependyma-lined canal running the whole length of the spinal cord within the grey commissure, the persistent lumen of the embryonic neural tube.
cards.att: Continuous above with the cavity of the fourth ventricle at the level of the obex; expands below in the conus medullaris as the terminal ventricle.
cards.act: Contains cerebrospinal fluid; largely obliterated in the adult and of no significant conducting function.
cards.rel: Lies in the grey commissure between the anterior and posterior grey commissures, with the anterior white commissure in front of it and the posterior median septum behind.
cards.clin: Pathological cavitation around the canal, syringomyelia, interrupts the decussating spinothalamic fibres in the anterior white commissure and produces a suspended, cape-like dissociated sensory loss of pain and temperature with preserved touch and proprioception.
cards.exam: Q. Why is sensory loss dissociated in syringomyelia? A. The cavity interrupts decussating pain and temperature fibres in the anterior white commissure while the dorsal columns are spared.

cards.desc: Large superficial vein on the lateral side of the forearm and arm, ending in the deltopectoral groove.
cards.att: Begins at the radial end of the dorsal venous network, winds round the radial border of the forearm on to its front, ascends lateral to biceps in the arm, runs in the deltopectoral groove between deltoid and pectoralis major, and pierces the clavipectoral fascia to end in the axillary vein.
cards.sup: Receives the accessory cephalic vein in the forearm and gives off the median cubital vein at the elbow; drains the radial side of the hand, forearm and arm.
cards.rel: Lies in the superficial fascia throughout; in the deltopectoral groove it accompanies the deltoid branch of the thoraco-acromial artery and lies within the deltopectoral triangle below the clavicle.
cards.clin: Approached in the deltopectoral groove for venous cutdown and for the insertion of cardiac pacemaker leads. At the wrist it is anastomosed to the radial artery to form the radiocephalic (Brescia-Cimino) dialysis fistula.
cards.exam: Q. What structure does the cephalic vein pierce to reach the axillary vein? A. The clavipectoral fascia.

cards.desc: Largest part of the hindbrain, lying in the posterior cranial fossa behind the pons and medulla and below the tentorium cerebelli, consisting of two hemispheres joined by the median vermis.
cards.att: Attached to the brainstem by three paired peduncles: superior to the midbrain, middle to the pons, inferior to the medulla. Divided by the primary fissure into anterior and posterior lobes and by the posterolateral fissure into the flocculonodular lobe.
cards.sup: Superior cerebellar artery from the basilar, anterior inferior cerebellar artery from the basilar, and posterior inferior cerebellar artery from the vertebral artery.
cards.act: Coordination of movement, regulation of muscle tone and posture, maintenance of equilibrium, and motor learning. Vestibulocerebellum controls balance and eye movements, spinocerebellum posture and gait, cerebrocerebellum planning and timing of skilled movement.
cards.rel: Fourth ventricle lies in front of it between it and the pons and medulla; tentorium cerebelli separates it from the occipital lobes above; the cerebellar tonsils lie close to the foramen magnum.
cards.clin: Cerebellar lesions produce signs on the same side as the lesion: intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, dysmetria, nystagmus, scanning speech and hypotonia. Midline vermian lesions give truncal ataxia, and medulloblastoma of the vermis is a common posterior fossa tumour of childhood; raised pressure may force the tonsils through the foramen magnum.
cards.exam: Q. Why are cerebellar signs ipsilateral to the lesion? A. Because cerebellar output pathways cross twice, in the superior cerebellar peduncle decussation and again in the corticospinal decussation.

cards.desc: Narrow ependyma-lined channel about 15 to 18 mm long traversing the midbrain and joining the third to the fourth ventricle.
cards.att: Connects the third ventricle above with the fourth ventricle below; surrounded by the periaqueductal (central) grey matter.
cards.act: Conducts cerebrospinal fluid from the third to the fourth ventricle. It contains no choroid plexus.
cards.rel: Separates the tectum behind from the tegmentum in front; the oculomotor nucleus and trochlear nucleus lie in the periaqueductal grey ventral to it at superior and inferior collicular levels respectively.
cards.clin: Being the narrowest part of the ventricular system, the aqueduct is the commonest site of obstruction; congenital stenosis or a pineal or tectal tumour causes non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus with dilated lateral and third ventricles and a normal fourth ventricle.
cards.exam: Q. Which ventricular dilatation pattern indicates aqueduct stenosis? A. Dilated lateral and third ventricles with a normal-sized fourth ventricle.

cards.desc: The thin, highly vascular, deeply pigmented posterior part of the vascular (middle) coat of the eyeball, lying between the sclera and the retina.
cards.att: Extends from the margin of the optic nerve behind to the ora serrata in front, where it continues as the ciliary body. It is loosely attached to the sclera by the suprachoroid lamina and firmly attached to the retinal pigment epithelium by its basal complex (Bruch's membrane); its layers are the suprachoroid lamina, vascular layer, choriocapillaris and basal complex.
cards.sup: Supplied by the short posterior ciliary arteries; drained by the four or five vorticose (vortex) veins that pierce the sclera behind the equator. Sensory and autonomic fibres come from the short and long ciliary nerves.
cards.act: Nourishes the outer layers of the retina, including the photoreceptors, and its pigment absorbs stray light within the eyeball.
cards.rel: Lies internal to the sclera, separated by the perichoroidal space containing the ciliary nerves and vessels, and external to the retinal pigment epithelium.
cards.clin: Choroidal melanoma is the commonest primary intra-ocular malignancy of adults. Age-related macular degeneration involves Bruch's membrane and the choriocapillaris, and new vessels grow through breaks in Bruch's membrane in the wet form.
cards.exam: Q. Which vessels supply the choroid, and which drain it? A. The short posterior ciliary arteries supply it and the vorticose veins drain it.

cards.desc: Fringed, highly vascular fold of pia mater covered by ependyma, invaginated into the lateral ventricle along the choroid fissure.
cards.att: Extends from the interventricular foramen backwards along the body of the ventricle and forwards into the inferior horn; enlarged at the atrium as the glomus. It is absent from the anterior and posterior horns.
cards.sup: Anterior choroidal artery from the internal carotid, and posterior choroidal branches of the posterior cerebral artery; drained by the internal cerebral vein.
cards.act: Secretes cerebrospinal fluid and forms the blood-cerebrospinal fluid barrier.
cards.rel: Lies along the choroid fissure between the fornix and the upper surface of the thalamus; continuous through the interventricular foramen with the plexus of the third ventricle.
cards.clin: The glomus is a common site of physiological calcification seen on CT and a useful midline landmark; displacement indicates a mass. Choroid plexus papilloma, most often in a child, may cause hydrocephalus by overproduction of cerebrospinal fluid as well as by obstruction.
cards.exam: Q. Which parts of the lateral ventricle have no choroid plexus? A. The anterior (frontal) and posterior (occipital) horns.

cards.desc: Small parasympathetic ganglion, about 2 mm across, lying in the posterior orbit between the optic nerve and lateral rectus, about 1 cm in front of the optic canal.
cards.att: Parasympathetic (motor) root from the nerve to inferior oblique, from the inferior branch of the oculomotor nerve, carrying preganglionic fibres from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus that synapse here. Sensory root from the nasociliary nerve and sympathetic root from the internal carotid plexus both pass through without synapsing. Its branches are the short ciliary nerves.
cards.act: Relay station for parasympathetic supply to sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle, mediating the light reflex and accommodation.
cards.rel: Lies lateral to the optic nerve and medial to lateral rectus, with the ophthalmic artery above and the short ciliary nerves passing forwards from it around the optic nerve.
cards.clin: Damage or a viral ganglionitis produces a tonic (Adie) pupil: a dilated pupil with light-near dissociation, sector palsy of the iris and denervation supersensitivity to dilute pilocarpine.
cards.exam: Q. Which fibres actually synapse in the ciliary ganglion? A. Only the preganglionic parasympathetic fibres from the oculomotor nerve; sensory and sympathetic fibres pass through.

cards.desc: Arched gyrus on the medial surface of the hemisphere lying immediately above the corpus callosum, between the callosal sulcus below and the cingulate sulcus above.
cards.att: Continuous behind, through the isthmus, with the parahippocampal gyrus; connected to the hippocampal formation, anterior thalamic nucleus and adjacent medial cortex through the cingulum, the association bundle in its white matter.
cards.sup: Branches of the anterior cerebral artery, chiefly the callosomarginal artery; the posterior part also receives supply from the posterior cerebral artery.
cards.act: Part of the limbic lobe and of the Papez circuit; involved in emotional response, autonomic control, motivation, pain affect and the initiation of behaviour.
cards.rel: Lies between the corpus callosum below and the medial frontal and paracentral gyri above; the paracentral lobule lies above its middle part.
cards.clin: Bilateral infarction of the anterior cingulate region from anterior cerebral artery occlusion causes akinetic mutism and abulia. The anterior cingulate is the target of cingulotomy for intractable pain and severe obsessive compulsive disorder.
cards.exam: Q. Name the components of the Papez circuit in order. A. Hippocampus, fornix, mammillary body, mammillothalamic tract, anterior thalamic nucleus, cingulate gyrus, cingulum, parahippocampal gyrus, back to the hippocampus.

cards.desc: Larger terminal branch of the subscapular artery, winding round the lateral border of the scapula.
cards.att: Arises from the subscapular artery in the axilla, passes backwards through the triangular space between teres minor, teres major and the long head of triceps, and curves round the lateral border of the scapula into the infraspinous fossa deep to teres minor and infraspinatus.
cards.sup: Muscular branches to subscapularis, teres major and minor and infraspinatus, and branches that anastomose with the suprascapular and dorsal scapular arteries on the dorsum of the scapula.
cards.act: Supplies the scapular muscles and forms a key limb of the scapular anastomosis.
cards.rel: Traverses the triangular space, bounded above by teres minor, below by teres major and laterally by the long head of triceps; it lies deep to the scapular muscles once it reaches the infraspinous fossa.
cards.clin: Pedicle of the scapular and parascapular fasciocutaneous flaps used in head and neck and limb reconstruction. As a major channel of the scapular anastomosis it maintains limb perfusion after ligation of the axillary artery proximal to the subscapular origin.
cards.exam: Q. Through which space does the circumflex scapular artery pass? A. The triangular space, bounded by teres minor, teres major and the long head of triceps.

cards.desc: Subcutaneous S-shaped long bone lying horizontally at the root of the neck, the only bony strut connecting the upper limb to the axial skeleton.
cards.att: Medial two-thirds are convex forwards and rounded, the lateral third is concave forwards and flattened. It articulates medially at the sternoclavicular joint and laterally at the acromioclavicular joint. Landmarks: subclavian groove on the inferior surface, conoid tubercle and trapezoid ridge laterally, and the impression for the costoclavicular ligament medially. Pectoralis major, deltoid, sternocleidomastoid, trapezius, subclavius and sternohyoid attach to it.
cards.act: Acts as a strut holding the shoulder away from the trunk and transmits force from the upper limb to the axial skeleton.
cards.rel: The subclavian vessels and the trunks of the brachial plexus pass behind its middle third, separated from it by subclavius and the clavipectoral fascia. The apex of the lung lies behind its medial end.
cards.clin: It is the first bone to ossify (fifth to sixth intrauterine week) and the last epiphysis in the body to fuse (sternal end, about 25 years), which makes it useful for age estimation. Fracture is commonest at the junction of the middle and lateral thirds: the lateral fragment is pulled down by the weight of the limb and the medial fragment up by sternocleidomastoid.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the clavicle usually fracture and how do the fragments displace? A. At the junction of the middle and lateral thirds; the medial fragment is pulled up by sternocleidomastoid and the lateral fragment drops with the weight of the limb.

cards.desc: The anterior, unipennate portion of deltoid arising from the lateral third of the clavicle.
cards.att: Origin: anterior border and superior surface of the lateral third of the clavicle. Insertion: deltoid tuberosity of the humerus, blending with the other parts.
cards.sup: Axillary nerve (C5, C6).
cards.act: Flexes and medially rotates the arm; assists abduction once the arm is abducted, and stabilises the humeral head anteriorly.
cards.rel: Separated from the clavicular head of pectoralis major by the deltopectoral groove, which contains the cephalic vein and the deltoid branch of the thoracoacromial artery.
cards.clin: The deltopectoral groove along its medial border is the standard approach to the shoulder joint and the site for infraclavicular access to the axillary vessels. Anterior deltoid transfer is used to restore elbow flexion or shoulder function in brachial plexus palsy.
cards.exam: Q. What structure lies in the groove between the clavicular part of deltoid and pectoralis major? A. The cephalic vein, in the deltopectoral groove.

cards.desc: The upper head of pectoralis major, arising from the front of the medial half of the clavicle.
cards.att: Origin: anterior surface of the medial half of the clavicle. Insertion: lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus, its fibres lying most anterior and lowest at the insertion.
cards.sup: Lateral pectoral nerve (C5, C6, C7).
cards.act: Flexes and medially rotates the arm; adducts the flexed arm across the chest.
cards.rel: Separated from the clavicular part of deltoid by the deltopectoral groove containing the cephalic vein; lies anterior to the sternocostal part at the insertion.
cards.clin: Tested by asking the patient to push the hands forward at shoulder level, or by flexing the arm against resistance while the fold is palpated. Poland syndrome typically spares the clavicular head while the sternocostal part is absent.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve supplies the clavicular head of pectoralis major? A. The lateral pectoral nerve (C5, C6, C7).

cards.desc: A small triangular muscle forming the posterior part of the pelvic diaphragm, behind levator ani.
cards.att: Origin from the tip of the ischial spine by its apex; inserted by its base into the lateral margin of the coccyx and the lowest piece of the sacrum. It lies on the pelvic surface of the sacrospinous ligament and is coextensive with it.
cards.sup: Branches from the ventral rami of the fourth and fifth sacral nerves (S4, S5).
cards.act: Supports the pelvic viscera and pulls the coccyx forwards after it has been pushed back during defaecation or childbirth.
cards.rel: Levator ani lies in front, gluteus maximus and the sacrotuberous ligament behind the sacrospinous ligament; the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels cross the ischial spine behind its origin; the greater sciatic foramen lies above and the lesser below.
cards.clin: Sacrospinous ligament fixation for vaginal vault prolapse places sutures through the coccygeus and ligament; the pudendal nerve and vessels and the sciatic nerve lie close to the ischial spine and are at risk. The ischial spine is also the landmark for pudendal nerve block in labour.
cards.exam: Q. What is the nerve supply of coccygeus? A. The ventral rami of the fourth and fifth sacral nerves.

cards.desc: Main arterial trunk of the neck, ascending within the carotid sheath and dividing into the internal and external carotid arteries.
cards.att: The right arises from the brachiocephalic trunk behind the right sternoclavicular joint; the left arises directly from the arch of the aorta in the superior mediastinum. Both ascend in the carotid sheath and divide at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, at the level of C4.
cards.sup: Gives no named branches in the neck; its terminal branches are the internal and external carotid arteries.
cards.act: Conveys blood to the head and neck.
cards.rel: Within the carotid sheath the internal jugular vein lies lateral and the vagus nerve posteriorly between them. Anteriorly the infrahyoid muscles and sternocleidomastoid; posteriorly the transverse processes, sympathetic trunk and the anterior tubercle of C6 (carotid tubercle of Chassaignac).
cards.clin: Compressed against the carotid tubercle of C6 to control bleeding. The carotid sinus, at the bifurcation, is a baroreceptor supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve; pressure on it can cause reflex bradycardia and syncope. The bifurcation is the usual site of atheromatous plaque and of endarterectomy.
cards.exam: Q. At what level does the common carotid artery divide? A. At the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, level with the C4 vertebra.

cards.desc: Branch of the coeliac trunk that runs to the right along the upper border of the pancreas towards the free edge of the lesser omentum.
cards.att: Arises from the coeliac trunk, passes forwards and to the right along the superior border of the head of the pancreas, and ends near the upper border of the first part of the duodenum by giving off the gastroduodenal artery and continuing as the hepatic artery proper.
cards.sup: Gastroduodenal artery and hepatic artery proper; the right gastric artery arises from one or the other.
cards.act: Supplies the liver, gallbladder, stomach, duodenum and part of the pancreas.
cards.rel: Forms the upper border of the epiploic foramen region as it enters the lesser omentum, lying anterior to the portal vein and to the left of the bile duct; the coeliac plexus surrounds its origin and the omental bursa lies behind.
cards.clin: Its gastroduodenal branch lies behind the first part of the duodenum and is eroded by a posterior duodenal ulcer, causing massive haematemesis. A replaced or accessory right hepatic artery from the superior mesenteric artery occurs in about one in five people and must be identified before pancreaticoduodenectomy.
cards.exam: Q. Which branch of the common hepatic artery lies behind the first part of the duodenum? A. The gastroduodenal artery.

cards.desc: Extrahepatic bile duct about 3 cm long, formed at the porta hepatis by union of the right and left hepatic ducts.
cards.att: Formed in the right end of the porta hepatis anterior to the right branch of the portal vein, descends in the free edge of the lesser omentum, and is joined on its right side by the cystic duct to form the bile duct (common bile duct).
cards.sup: Arterial supply from the cystic artery and the right hepatic artery, through a fine axial plexus running at the 3 o'clock and 9 o'clock positions. Lymph to the cystic and hilar nodes.
cards.act: Conveys bile from both hepatic ducts towards the bile duct and duodenum.
cards.rel: Lies to the right of the hepatic artery and anterior to the portal vein in the hepatoduodenal ligament. It forms the medial boundary of the cystohepatic triangle of Calot.
cards.clin: Mirizzi syndrome is obstruction of the common hepatic duct by a stone impacted in the cystic duct or Hartmann's pouch. The duct is at risk of injury during laparoscopic cholecystectomy when it is mistaken for the cystic duct, hence the critical view of safety.
cards.exam: Q. What forms the common hepatic duct and what does it become? A. Union of the right and left hepatic ducts; it becomes the bile duct after receiving the cystic duct.

cards.desc: One of the two terminal branches of the abdominal aorta, running from the aortic bifurcation to the pelvic brim.
cards.att: Arises at the bifurcation of the abdominal aorta at the level of the fourth lumbar vertebra, a little to the left of the midline; passes inferolaterally along the medial border of psoas major for about 5 cm and divides in front of the sacroiliac joint into external and internal iliac arteries. It normally gives only small branches to peritoneum, psoas, ureter and surrounding tissue.
cards.act: Conveys the whole arterial supply of the pelvis, perineum and lower limb.
cards.rel: The ureter crosses the bifurcation anteriorly, and on the left the superior rectal vessels and the apex of the sigmoid mesocolon lie in front; the right common iliac artery crosses in front of the left common iliac vein and the beginning of the inferior vena cava; the sympathetic trunk, obturator nerve and lumbosacral trunk lie behind.
cards.clin: Aorto-iliac occlusive disease gives Leriche syndrome: buttock and thigh claudication, absent femoral pulses and impotence. The ureter crossing the bifurcation is the standard landmark for identifying it at pelvic surgery, and the site where a ureteric calculus commonly lodges.
cards.exam: Q. At what vertebral level does the aorta divide into common iliac arteries? A. The lower border of the fourth lumbar vertebra.

cards.desc: The vein formed in front of the sacroiliac joint by the union of the external and internal iliac veins, ending by forming the inferior vena cava.
cards.att: Formed in front of the sacroiliac joint; the two veins ascend and unite at the level of the fifth lumbar vertebra to the right of the midline to form the inferior vena cava. The left vein is longer and more oblique and receives the median sacral vein; both receive iliolumbar and sometimes lateral sacral veins.
cards.act: Returns all venous blood from the lower limb, pelvis and perineum to the inferior vena cava.
cards.rel: The right common iliac artery crosses in front of the left common iliac vein; the right vein lies behind and then lateral to its own artery; the common iliac veins lie in front of the fifth lumbar vertebra and the sacral promontory.
cards.clin: May-Thurner (Cockett) syndrome: chronic compression of the left common iliac vein between the overlying right common iliac artery and the fifth lumbar vertebra causes left iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis and left leg swelling.
cards.exam: Q. Why is left leg deep vein thrombosis commoner than right? A. The left common iliac vein is compressed by the overlying right common iliac artery, May-Thurner syndrome.

cards.desc: A fibrous ring at the apex of the orbit that surrounds the optic canal and the medial part of the superior orbital fissure and gives origin to the four recti.
cards.att: Attached to the body of the sphenoid around the margins of the optic canal and to the lower margin of the superior orbital fissure, including the infra-optic tubercle and the spina recti lateralis on the greater wing. From it arise superior, inferior, medial and lateral recti.
cards.act: Provides a common fixed posterior origin for the four recti, so their pull is directed from the orbital apex to the globe.
cards.rel: Passing through the ring: optic nerve with the ophthalmic artery, the superior and inferior divisions of the oculomotor nerve, the nasociliary nerve and the abducent nerve. Passing through the superior orbital fissure outside the ring: lacrimal, frontal and trochlear nerves and the superior ophthalmic vein.
cards.clin: The anatomical basis of the retrobulbar block, where anaesthetic is placed within the muscle cone. Lesions at the orbital apex involving the ring produce total ophthalmoplegia with visual loss, while a lesion of the superior orbital fissure alone spares vision. Pain on eye movement in retrobulbar neuritis arises because the optic nerve sheath is tethered to the ring.
cards.exam: Q. Which structures enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure outside the common tendinous ring? A. The lacrimal, frontal and trochlear nerves and the superior ophthalmic vein.

cards.k: communicating branch of nasociliary nerve with ciliary ganglion
syn: sensory root of the ciliary ganglion
cards.desc: Short branch running from the nasociliary nerve backwards and laterally to the posterosuperior angle of the ciliary ganglion, forming its sensory root.
cards.att: Arises from the nasociliary nerve as it crosses above the optic nerve in the posterior orbit, and joins the ciliary ganglion posterosuperiorly. Its fibres traverse the ganglion without synapsing and leave in the short ciliary nerves.
cards.act: Conveys general sensation from the cornea, iris and ciliary body back to the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve.
cards.rel: Lies between the optic nerve medially and lateral rectus laterally, above the ciliary ganglion, alongside the ophthalmic artery.
cards.clin: These fibres form the afferent limb of the corneal reflex; their loss in a trigeminal lesion or after trigeminal ablation gives corneal anaesthesia and neurotrophic keratitis with painless ulceration.
cards.exam: Q. Do the sensory fibres reaching the ciliary ganglion from the nasociliary nerve synapse there? A. No, they pass straight through into the short ciliary nerves.

cards.desc: Slender muscle of the anterior compartment of the arm running from the coracoid process to the middle of the medial surface of the humerus.
cards.att: Origin: tip of the coracoid process of the scapula, by a tendon common with the short head of biceps brachii. Insertion: middle third of the medial surface and border of the humerus.
cards.sup: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6, C7), which pierces the muscle.
cards.act: Flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder; helps stabilise the humeral head.
cards.rel: Pierced by the musculocutaneous nerve; forms the lateral wall of the axilla with the humerus and biceps; the axillary and brachial arteries and the median and ulnar nerves lie medial to it.
cards.clin: Called the perforated muscle because the musculocutaneous nerve passes through it; the nerve can be entrapped there causing weak elbow flexion and numbness on the lateral forearm. It is a landmark for locating the neurovascular bundle in the arm.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve pierces coracobrachialis? A. The musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6, C7).

cards.desc: The transparent, avascular anterior one-sixth of the fibrous coat of the eyeball, more curved than the sclera and the eye's principal refracting surface.
cards.att: Continuous with the sclera at the limbus (corneoscleral junction). It has five layers from before backwards: corneal epithelium, anterior limiting lamina (Bowman's layer), substantia propria or stroma, posterior limiting lamina (Descemet's membrane) and the corneal endothelium.
cards.sup: Avascular; nourished by the aqueous humour, the tear film and the capillaries at the limbus. Sensory supply is by the long and short ciliary nerves, from the nasociliary branch of the ophthalmic nerve, CN V1.
cards.act: Provides about two-thirds of the refractive power of the eye and, with the sclera, protects the intra-ocular contents.
cards.rel: Bounded in front by the tear film and precorneal conjunctival epithelium, behind by the aqueous humour of the anterior chamber; the iris lies behind it across the anterior chamber, and the limbus surrounds it.
cards.clin: Its dense sensory innervation makes corneal abrasion intensely painful and provides the corneal reflex, afferent V1 and efferent facial nerve. Being avascular and immunologically privileged, it is the most successfully transplanted tissue. A Kayser-Fleischer ring at the periphery of Descemet's membrane indicates Wilson's disease.
cards.exam: Q. Name the five layers of the cornea from anterior to posterior. A. Epithelium, Bowman's layer, stroma, Descemet's membrane, endothelium.

cards.desc: The anterior, ridged part of the inner surface of the ciliary body, bearing about seventy radiating ciliary processes.
cards.att: Occupies the anterior two to three millimetres of the ciliary body, immediately behind the root of the iris; behind it lies the smooth orbiculus ciliaris (pars plana), which reaches the ora serrata. The zonular fibres of the lens are attached in the valleys between the ciliary processes.
cards.sup: Supplied by the major arterial circle of the iris, formed by the long posterior and anterior ciliary arteries; innervated by the short ciliary nerves.
cards.act: Its ciliary processes secrete the aqueous humour and anchor the suspensory ligament of the lens.
cards.rel: Lies behind the peripheral iris and in front of the pars plana; the ciliary muscle lies external to it within the ciliary body, and the posterior chamber lies in front of it between iris and lens.
cards.clin: The ciliary processes are the target of cyclodestructive procedures, such as transscleral cyclophotocoagulation, to reduce aqueous production in refractory glaucoma. The smooth pars plana just behind it, 3.5 to 4 mm behind the limbus, is the safe entry point for vitrectomy and intravitreal injection.
cards.exam: Q. Which part of the eye secretes aqueous humour? A. The ciliary processes of the corona ciliaris.

cards.desc: Wide venous channel about 2 to 3 cm long in the posterior part of the coronary sulcus, the main venous drainage of the heart.
cards.att: Lies in the atrioventricular groove between the left atrium and the left ventricle on the diaphragmatic surface, and opens into the right atrium between the opening of the inferior vena cava and the right atrioventricular orifice, guarded by the valve of the coronary sinus (Thebesian valve).
cards.sup: Tributaries: great cardiac vein, middle cardiac vein, small cardiac vein, posterior vein of the left ventricle and the oblique vein of the left atrium (vein of Marshall), which marks its left limit. It is a derivative of the left horn of the sinus venosus.
cards.act: Returns about 60 per cent of the coronary venous blood to the right atrium; the remainder reaches the chambers directly through the anterior cardiac veins and venae cordis minimae.
cards.rel: Left atrium above, left ventricle below, the circumflex artery running with it in the coronary sulcus; the fibrous pericardium and oblique pericardial sinus lie behind.
cards.clin: Cannulated for retrograde cardioplegia in cardiac surgery and for placing the left ventricular pacing lead in cardiac resynchronisation therapy. It is markedly dilated when a persistent left superior vena cava drains into it, a finding on echocardiography.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the coronary sinus open, and what guards its opening? A. Into the right atrium between the inferior vena caval opening and the right atrioventricular orifice, guarded by the Thebesian valve.

cards.desc: The largest commissure of the brain, a thick arched plate of white matter in the floor of the longitudinal fissure connecting the neocortex of the two hemispheres.
cards.att: From front to back: rostrum, genu, trunk (body) and splenium. Fibres of the genu sweep forward as the forceps minor into the frontal lobes, those of the splenium sweep back as the forceps major into the occipital lobes, and fibres passing laterally over the lateral ventricle form the tapetum.
cards.sup: Pericallosal artery from the anterior cerebral artery along most of its length; the splenium is also supplied by the posterior pericallosal branch of the posterior cerebral artery.
cards.act: Interhemispheric transfer of sensory, motor and cognitive information between corresponding cortical areas.
cards.rel: Forms the roof of the lateral ventricles and of the third ventricle region; the cingulate gyrus lies above it across the callosal sulcus, the fornix and septum pellucidum below the trunk, and the anterior cerebral arteries run on its upper surface.
cards.clin: Section of the corpus callosum for intractable epilepsy produces disconnection syndromes including alien hand. Infarction of the splenium with the left occipital cortex produces alexia without agraphia: the patient can write but cannot read what has been written.
cards.exam: Q. Which part of the corpus callosum is damaged in alexia without agraphia? A. The splenium, together with the left occipital cortex.

cards.desc: Paired dorsolateral erectile columns of the penis, each beginning as a crus attached to the ischiopubic ramus and running forward to form the bulk of the body.
cards.att: Proximally each crus is attached to the ischiopubic ramus and covered by ischiocavernosus; the two bodies meet under the pubic symphysis, are bound by tunica albuginea and an incomplete median septum (pectiniform), and end blunted beneath the glans.
cards.sup: Deep artery of the penis (from the internal pudendal) with helicine branches; drainage via deep dorsal vein to the prostatic venous plexus. Cavernous nerves from the prostatic plexus (parasympathetic S2, S3, S4) mediate erection.
cards.act: Engorgement of its cavernous spaces against the rigid tunica albuginea produces penile rigidity in erection.
cards.rel: Lies dorsal to the corpus spongiosum, deep to the deep fascia of the penis (Buck fascia); the deep dorsal vein, dorsal arteries and dorsal nerves lie in the dorsal groove between the two bodies.
cards.clin: Site of needle aspiration and intracavernosal injection in priapism and erectile dysfunction. Fibrous plaques of the tunica albuginea cause Peyronie disease; tearing of the tunica during intercourse is penile fracture.
cards.exam: Q. Which artery fills the corpus cavernosum during erection? A. The deep artery of the penis, a branch of the internal pudendal artery.

cards.desc: Single ventral (median) erectile column that transmits the spongy urethra, expanded proximally as the bulb of the penis and distally as the glans.
cards.att: The bulb is attached to the inferior surface of the perineal membrane and covered by bulbospongiosus; the body lies in the ventral groove between the corpora cavernosa and expands distally into the glans penis.
cards.sup: Artery of the bulb of the penis and the urethral artery, both from the internal pudendal artery; venous drainage to the deep dorsal vein and prostatic venous plexus.
cards.act: Remains less turgid than the corpora cavernosa during erection, so the spongy urethra stays patent for ejaculation.
cards.rel: Ventral to the corpora cavernosa; the spongy urethra runs through its length. The bulbourethral (Cowper) glands open into the urethra within the bulb.
cards.clin: Straddle injury ruptures the bulb, and urine and blood extravasate into the superficial perineal pouch, spreading into the scrotum and anterior abdominal wall deep to Scarpa fascia but not into the thigh.
cards.exam: Q. Why does the urethra remain patent during erection? A. It runs in the corpus spongiosum, which has a thinner tunica and stays less turgid than the corpora cavernosa.

cards.desc: The only complete cartilaginous ring in the airway, shaped like a signet ring at the lower end of the larynx at the level of the C6 vertebra.
cards.att: A narrow anterior arch and a broad posterior lamina. Articulates above with the inferior horns of the thyroid cartilage and with the bases of the arytenoids at synovial joints. Gives attachment to cricothyroid and posterior and lateral cricoarytenoid muscles, the conus elasticus, the cricopharyngeus, the cricotracheal ligament and the longitudinal muscle of the oesophagus.
cards.sup: Cricothyroid and inferior laryngeal branches of the superior and inferior thyroid arteries.
cards.act: Supports the larynx and holds the airway open; its joints with the thyroid cartilage and arytenoids provide the mechanism for tensing and for abducting and adducting the vocal folds.
cards.rel: Marks the level of C6, where the pharynx becomes oesophagus, the larynx becomes trachea, the middle thyroid vein and inferior thyroid artery are encountered, and the carotid tubercle can be palpated. The isthmus of the thyroid lies just below it.
cards.clin: Backward pressure on the cricoid (Sellick manoeuvre) compresses the oesophagus against the vertebral body during rapid sequence induction. Being a complete ring, the subglottis is the narrowest part of the infant airway, so a tight tube causes subglottic stenosis. Emergency airway access is made through the cricothyroid membrane just above it.
cards.exam: Q. What is anatomically unique about the cricoid cartilage and why does it matter? A. It is the only complete ring in the airway, which allows cricoid pressure to occlude the oesophagus and makes the subglottis the narrowest part of the child's airway.

cards.desc: Cuboidal bone of the lateral side of the distal row of the tarsus, lying between the calcaneus and the lateral two metatarsals.
cards.att: Articulates proximally with the calcaneus at the calcaneocuboid joint, medially with the lateral cuneiform and often with the navicular, and distally with the bases of the fourth and fifth metatarsals. Its plantar surface bears a prominent ridge, the tuberosity of the cuboid, in front of which is a groove for the tendon of fibularis longus; the long plantar ligament converts this groove into a tunnel.
cards.act: Forms part of the lateral longitudinal arch and the transverse arch and acts as a pulley for the tendon of fibularis longus.
cards.rel: Lies lateral to the lateral cuneiform, distal to the calcaneus, and forms the lateral half of the transverse tarsal (Chopart's) joint with the talonavicular joint.
cards.clin: Nutcracker fracture of the cuboid occurs when it is crushed between the calcaneus and the metatarsal bases in forced abduction of the forefoot. Cuboid subluxation, or cuboid syndrome, causes lateral midfoot pain in dancers.
cards.exam: Q. Which tendon grooves the plantar surface of the cuboid? A. The tendon of fibularis longus, held in a tunnel by the long plantar ligament.

cards.desc: Short duct, 3 to 4 cm long, running from the neck of the gallbladder to join the common hepatic duct and form the bile duct.
cards.att: Begins at the neck of the gallbladder, passes backwards, downwards and to the left in the free edge of the lesser omentum, and joins the right side of the common hepatic duct. Its mucosa is thrown into the spiral fold (valve of Heister).
cards.sup: Cystic artery, usually from the right hepatic artery. Lymph drains to the cystic node (of Lund) at the neck of the gallbladder.
cards.act: Conducts bile both into and out of the gallbladder; the spiral fold keeps the lumen patent.
cards.rel: Forms the lower boundary of the cystohepatic triangle of Calot, bounded also by the common hepatic duct medially and the inferior surface of the liver above. The cystic artery lies within this triangle.
cards.clin: Impaction of a stone in the cystic duct causes biliary colic and, if it persists, acute cholecystitis or a mucocele. Correct identification of the cystic duct and cystic artery, and of nothing else, entering the gallbladder is the critical view of safety in laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
cards.exam: Q. Name the boundaries and contents of Calot's triangle. A. Cystic duct below, common hepatic duct medially, inferior surface of the liver above; it contains the cystic artery.

cards.desc: Largest branch of the brachial artery, accompanying the radial nerve behind the shaft of the humerus.
cards.att: Arises from the brachial artery just below the lower border of teres major, passes with the radial nerve through the triangular interval into the spiral (radial) groove between the medial and lateral heads of triceps, and divides into radial collateral and middle collateral branches.
cards.sup: Radial collateral artery, which pierces the lateral intermuscular septum with the radial nerve to meet the radial recurrent artery, the middle collateral artery, which descends behind the lateral epicondyle to meet the interosseous recurrent artery, a nutrient branch to the humerus, and branches to triceps and deltoid.
cards.act: Supplies triceps and the posterior compartment of the arm, the humeral shaft, and contributes to the arterial anastomosis round the elbow.
cards.rel: Lies in the spiral groove directly against the shaft of the humerus with the radial nerve, between the medial and lateral heads of triceps.
cards.clin: Injured with the radial nerve in mid-shaft (spiral groove) fractures of the humerus, which classically produce wrist drop with preserved elbow extension. Its collateral branches keep the forearm perfused if the brachial artery is occluded at the elbow.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve accompanies the profunda brachii artery and where? A. The radial nerve, in the spiral (radial) groove of the humerus.

cards.desc: Arterial arch across the bases of the metacarpals in the deepest plane of the palm.
cards.att: Formed mainly by the terminal part of the radial artery, which enters the palm between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous and then between the heads of adductor pollicis, and is completed on the ulnar side by the deep branch of the ulnar artery; it lies on the interossei and the bases of the metacarpals.
cards.sup: Three palmar metacarpal arteries, three perforating branches that pass back to the dorsal metacarpal arteries, and recurrent branches to the carpal arch; the princeps pollicis and radialis indicis arise from the radial artery as the arch is formed.
cards.act: Supplies the deep structures of the palm and, through the palmar metacarpal arteries, reinforces the digital supply from the superficial arch.
cards.rel: Lies deep to the long flexor tendons, the lumbricals and adductor pollicis, and is accompanied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. It lies about a finger's breadth proximal to the superficial palmar arch.
cards.clin: The Allen test confirms that both radial and ulnar arteries fill the arches before radial artery cannulation or radial forearm flap harvest. A penetrating palmar wound bleeds from both ends of the arch, so ligation of one feeding artery alone does not control it.
cards.exam: Q. Which artery mainly forms the deep palmar arch? A. The radial artery, completed by the deep branch of the ulnar artery.

cards.desc: Thick-walled muscular tube about 45 cm long conveying sperm from the tail of the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct behind the bladder.
cards.att: Begins at the tail of the epididymis, ascends in the spermatic cord, traverses the inguinal canal, hooks around the inferior epigastric artery at the deep ring, crosses the ureter near the ischial spine, dilates as the ampulla behind the bladder and joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct.
cards.sup: Artery to the ductus deferens, usually from the superior vesical artery; sympathetic fibres from the hypogastric plexus (L1, L2) drive its peristalsis.
cards.act: Thick three-layered smooth muscle propels sperm rapidly to the prostatic urethra during emission.
cards.rel: In the spermatic cord it is the firm cord-like structure felt posteriorly. In the pelvis it crosses superior to the ureter, the classic "water under the bridge" relation, and lies medial to the seminal vesicle.
cards.clin: Divided and ligated at vasectomy through a scrotal incision. Congenital bilateral absence of the vas is associated with cystic fibrosis mutations; a beaded, thickened vas suggests genital tuberculosis.
cards.exam: Q. What is the relation of the ductus deferens to the ureter? A. The ductus crosses superior (anterior) to the ureter, water under the bridge.

cards.desc: The whole of the aorta beyond the arch, comprising the thoracic part from T4 to T12 and the abdominal part from T12 to its bifurcation at L4.
cards.att: Begins at the lower border of T4 on the left side of the vertebral column as the continuation of the arch, passes through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at T12 to become the abdominal aorta, and ends at the level of L4 by dividing into the two common iliac arteries.
cards.sup: Thoracic part: posterior intercostal arteries of the 3rd to 11th spaces, subcostal, bronchial, oesophageal, pericardial, mediastinal and superior phrenic arteries. Abdominal part: inferior phrenic, coeliac trunk, superior mesenteric, middle suprarenal, renal, gonadal, inferior mesenteric, lumbar and median sacral arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the posterior thoracic wall, thoracic viscera, the whole of the abdomen and the lower limbs.
cards.rel: Descends on the left of the vertebral bodies in the thorax and comes to lie in the midline in front of them; the azygos vein and thoracic duct lie to its right, the oesophagus in front, and in the abdomen the inferior vena cava is on its right.
cards.clin: Atherosclerotic aneurysm most often affects the infrarenal abdominal part. Aortic dissection distal to the left subclavian is type B and is usually treated medically or by endovascular stenting.
cards.exam: Q. At what vertebral levels does the descending aorta begin and end? A. It begins at the lower border of T4 and ends at L4 by dividing into the common iliac arteries.

cards.desc: Retroperitoneal segment of large intestine running from the left colic (splenic) flexure down the left side of the abdomen to the pelvic brim, where it becomes the sigmoid colon.
cards.att: Begins at the left colic flexure, which is higher, more posterior and more acute than the right and is anchored to the diaphragm by the phrenicocolic ligament. Descends in the left paracolic gutter and ends at the pelvic brim. Peritoneum covers its front and sides only.
cards.sup: Left colic artery and upper sigmoid branches of the inferior mesenteric artery. Veins to the inferior mesenteric vein and thence the splenic vein. Parasympathetic supply from pelvic splanchnic nerves S2, S3, S4; sympathetic from L1, L2 via lumbar splanchnic nerves.
cards.act: Stores and dehydrates faeces; propels contents to the sigmoid colon.
cards.rel: Lies on the lateral border of the left kidney, quadratus lumborum, transversus abdominis and iliacus. The left ureter and the gonadal vessels lie behind it, at risk during mobilisation.
cards.clin: The splenic flexure lies in the watershed between superior and inferior mesenteric territories (Griffiths point) and is the commonest site of ischaemic colitis. Left-sided carcinoma presents with obstruction and altered bowel habit because the stool is solid and the lumen narrow.
cards.exam: Q. Why is the splenic flexure prone to ischaemic colitis? A. It lies in the watershed between the superior and inferior mesenteric arterial territories.

cards.desc: The upper fibres of trapezius, descending from the skull and ligamentum nuchae to the lateral clavicle.
cards.att: Origin: medial third of the superior nuchal line, external occipital protuberance and the ligamentum nuchae down to the C7 spine. Insertion: posterior border of the lateral third of the clavicle.
cards.sup: Accessory nerve (CN XI) for motor supply, with proprioceptive fibres from the ventral rami of C3 and C4.
cards.act: Elevates the scapula and, with the ascending part and serratus anterior, rotates the glenoid cavity upwards; extends the head and neck when the scapula is fixed.
cards.rel: Its anterior border forms the posterior boundary of the posterior triangle of the neck. The accessory nerve crosses the triangle obliquely and passes deep to that border about 5 cm above the clavicle, reaching the deep surface of the muscle.
cards.clin: The accessory nerve is vulnerable during lymph node biopsy in the posterior triangle; injury causes shoulder droop, weak shrugging and inability to abduct the arm fully above the head. Shoulder shrug against resistance is the standard bedside test.
cards.exam: Q. Where is the accessory nerve most at risk of surgical injury? A. In the posterior triangle of the neck, along the anterior border of the descending part of trapezius.

cards.desc: Thoracic segment of the descending aorta, running in the posterior mediastinum from the lower border of T4 to the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at T12.
cards.att: Begins on the left side of the lower border of T4 as the continuation of the aortic arch, descends on the left of the vertebral bodies gradually coming to the midline, and passes behind the median arcuate ligament through the aortic hiatus at T12 with the thoracic duct and azygos vein.
cards.sup: Branches: posterior intercostal arteries to the 3rd to 11th spaces, subcostal arteries, bronchial, oesophageal, pericardial, mediastinal and superior phrenic arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the posterior thoracic wall, bronchi, oesophagus, pericardium and the posterior part of the diaphragm.
cards.rel: Oesophagus lies to its right above and in front of it below; the azygos vein and thoracic duct lie on its right, the hemiazygos vein behind it, and the left lung and pleura on its left. It is crossed by the left greater splanchnic nerve.
cards.clin: Deceleration injury tears the aorta at the isthmus just distal to the left subclavian origin where the ligamentum arteriosum tethers it, giving a widened mediastinum on chest radiograph. The great anterior radicular artery (of Adamkiewicz), usually from a lower left posterior intercostal artery, supplies the lumbar spinal cord, and its sacrifice in aortic surgery causes paraplegia.
cards.exam: Q. Which structures accompany the aorta through the aortic hiatus at T12? A. The thoracic duct and the azygos vein.

cards.desc: Dome-shaped musculotendinous septum separating the thoracic from the abdominal cavity, the principal muscle of respiration.
cards.att: Origin from three parts: sternal, two slips from the back of the xiphoid process; costal, inner surfaces of the lower six costal cartilages and ribs; lumbar, the right crus from bodies of L1 to L3 and the left crus from L1 to L2, with the medial and lateral arcuate ligaments. All fibres insert into the central tendon.
cards.sup: Motor supply is entirely from the phrenic nerve, C3, C4, C5. Sensory supply to the peripheral part is from the lower intercostal (T7 to T11) and subcostal nerves. Arteries: musculophrenic, pericardiacophrenic, superior and inferior phrenic, lower posterior intercostal.
cards.act: Contraction flattens the domes and increases the vertical diameter of the thorax, the chief movement of quiet inspiration; also raises intra-abdominal pressure in straining, coughing and micturition.
cards.rel: Openings: caval opening in the central tendon at T8 for the inferior vena cava and right phrenic nerve; oesophageal opening in the right crus at T10 for the oesophagus, vagal trunks and oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels; aortic opening behind the median arcuate ligament at T12 for the aorta, thoracic duct and azygos vein.
cards.clin: Irritation of the central diaphragmatic pleura or peritoneum refers pain to the shoulder tip through C3, C4, C5. Phrenic nerve injury causes a raised hemidiaphragm with paradoxical movement on sniffing. Congenital posterolateral (Bochdalek) and anterior (Morgagni) hernias, and sliding hiatus hernia, occur at its weak points.
cards.exam: Q. Name the structures passing through the diaphragm at T8, T10 and T12. A. T8 inferior vena cava and right phrenic nerve; T10 oesophagus, vagi and left gastric vessels; T12 aorta, thoracic duct and azygos vein.

cards.desc: A two-bellied suprahyoid muscle slung from the mastoid region to the mandible, defining the digastric (submandibular) triangle of the neck.
cards.att: Posterior belly arises from the mastoid notch on the medial side of the mastoid process; anterior belly arises from the digastric fossa on the inner surface of the lower border of the mandible near the symphysis. The two join in an intermediate tendon which perforates stylohyoid and is held to the body and greater cornu of the hyoid by a fibrous sling.
cards.sup: Anterior belly by the nerve to mylohyoid from the inferior alveolar branch of the mandibular nerve; posterior belly by the digastric branch of the facial nerve. Arteries: facial and occipital.
cards.act: Depresses the mandible and opens the mouth when the hyoid is fixed; elevates the hyoid in swallowing when the mandible is fixed.
cards.rel: Posterior belly crosses superficial to the internal and external carotid arteries, the internal jugular vein, and the hypoglossal, vagus and accessory nerves, and marks the upper limit of the carotid dissection. The submandibular gland lies within the triangle bounded by the two bellies and the lower border of the mandible.
cards.clin: The posterior belly is the key surgical landmark of the upper neck, guiding the surgeon to the carotid vessels, the hypoglossal nerve and the facial nerve trunk. Its two bellies have different nerve supplies because they develop from the first and second pharyngeal arches respectively.
cards.exam: Q. Why do the two bellies of digastric have different nerve supplies? A. The anterior belly is first arch (mandibular nerve) and the posterior belly is second arch (facial nerve) in origin.

cards.desc: Short stout terminal bone of the great toe, much larger than the distal phalanges of the other toes and carrying the nail bed.
cards.att: Consists of a base, a short shaft and a distal tuberosity (tuft) supporting the nail bed. Its base articulates with the head of the proximal phalanx of the hallux at the interphalangeal joint. Flexor hallucis longus inserts on the plantar surface of the base and extensor hallucis longus on the dorsal surface of the base.
cards.act: Provides the final lever for push off through flexor hallucis longus, taking a large share of body weight at toe off.
cards.rel: The interphalangeal joint of the hallux is a hinge joint with collateral ligaments and a plantar plate; two sesamoids lie under the head of the first metatarsal, not under this bone.
cards.clin: Crush injuries produce a subungual haematoma with an underlying tuft fracture. Osteomyelitis of this phalanx is common in the diabetic foot and it is the usual site of ingrowing toenail surgery.
cards.exam: Q. Which tendon inserts into the base of the distal phalanx of the great toe on its plantar surface? A. Flexor hallucis longus.

cards.desc: One of the two terminal branches of the internal pudendal artery, running forward on the dorsum of the penis to the glans.
cards.att: Arises from the internal pudendal artery in the deep perineal pouch, pierces the perineal membrane and the suspensory ligament, then runs forward deep to the deep fascia of the penis (Buck's fascia) on the dorsum to reach the glans, where it anastomoses with the artery of the bulb and the deep artery.
cards.act: Supplies the skin, prepuce, glans penis and the fibrous coverings of the corpora; contributes to tumescence.
cards.rel: On the dorsum, from the midline outwards, lie the single deep dorsal vein, then the dorsal artery, then the dorsal nerve on each side, all deep to Buck's fascia; the superficial dorsal vein lies outside that fascia.
cards.clin: Injury to the internal pudendal or dorsal arteries in pelvic fracture or a straddle injury causes vasculogenic erectile dysfunction. The dorsal nerves, lying lateral to the arteries beneath Buck's fascia, are the target in a penile block for circumcision.
cards.exam: Q. What are the two terminal branches of the internal pudendal artery in the male? A. The deep artery of the penis and the dorsal artery of the penis.

cards.desc: Artery running down the medial border of the scapula deep to the rhomboids.
cards.att: Usually arises from the third part of the subclavian artery, or as the deep branch of the transverse cervical artery from the thyrocervical trunk; passes laterally between the trunks of the brachial plexus, then deep to levator scapulae, and descends along the medial border of the scapula deep to the rhomboids.
cards.sup: Muscular branches to the rhomboids, levator scapulae, trapezius and latissimus dorsi, and branches that anastomose with the suprascapular and circumflex scapular arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the muscles attached to the medial border of the scapula and contributes to the scapular anastomosis.
cards.rel: Accompanies the dorsal scapular nerve (nerve to the rhomboids) along the medial border of the scapula, deep to rhomboid major and minor and levator scapulae.
cards.clin: Encountered and must be controlled in posterior approaches along the medial border of the scapula. Part of the scapular anastomosis that maintains upper limb flow when the subclavian or proximal axillary artery is occluded.
cards.exam: Q. What are the two usual origins of the dorsal scapular artery? A. The third part of the subclavian artery, or the deep branch of the transverse cervical artery.

cards.desc: Superficial venous arch lying in the subcutaneous tissue over the distal dorsum of the foot near the heads of the metatarsals.
cards.att: Formed by the dorsal digital and dorsal metatarsal veins; its medial end continues upwards as the great saphenous vein passing anterior to the medial malleolus, and its lateral end continues as the small saphenous vein passing posterior to the lateral malleolus.
cards.sup: Receives dorsal digital veins and communicates with the plantar venous network and with deep veins by perforating veins.
cards.act: Collects superficial venous blood from the foot and delivers it to the two saphenous veins.
cards.rel: Lies superficial to the extensor tendons in the subcutaneous fat, crossed by branches of the superficial fibular nerve, with the saphenous nerve at its medial end and the sural nerve at its lateral end.
cards.clin: Standard site for intravenous cannulation when arm veins fail. The great saphenous vein at the medial end is the classic site for venous cut-down in shock; the saphenous nerve lies immediately alongside it and can be injured.
cards.exam: Q. Which veins arise from the medial and lateral ends of the dorsal venous arch? A. The great saphenous vein medially, in front of the medial malleolus, and the small saphenous vein laterally, behind the lateral malleolus.

syn: dorsal venous arch of the hand
cards.desc: Network of superficial veins in the subcutaneous tissue over the back of the hand.
cards.att: Receives the three dorsal metacarpal veins and tributaries from the fingers and the palm; drains from its radial end into the cephalic vein over the anatomical snuffbox and from its ulnar end into the basilic vein.
cards.sup: Drains the dorsum of the hand and, through intercapitular and perforating veins, much of the palm and the digits.
cards.rel: Lies in the superficial fascia, superficial to the extensor tendons; the superficial branch of the radial nerve crosses it laterally and the dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve medially.
cards.clin: First-choice site for intravenous cannulation and venepuncture in the hand. Most venous and lymphatic drainage of the hand passes to the dorsum, which is why the dorsum becomes tense and swollen in palmar infection while the pus itself lies in the palm.
cards.exam: Q. Which two named veins arise from the dorsal venous network? A. The cephalic vein from its radial end and the basilic vein from its ulnar end.

cards.desc: Artery of the dorsum of the foot, the direct continuation of the anterior tibial artery.
cards.att: Begins at the ankle joint midway between the malleoli as the continuation of the anterior tibial artery, runs distally over the talus, navicular and intermediate cuneiform, and ends at the proximal end of the first intermetatarsal space by passing into the sole between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous as the deep plantar artery, which completes the plantar arch.
cards.sup: Lateral tarsal, medial tarsal, arcuate (giving the second to fourth dorsal metatarsal arteries), first dorsal metatarsal and deep plantar arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the dorsum of the foot and contributes the deep plantar artery to the plantar arch of the sole.
cards.rel: Lies lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus and medial to the tendon of extensor digitorum longus to the second toe, crossed distally by the tendon of extensor hallucis brevis; the deep fibular nerve lies on its lateral side; it is covered only by skin, fascia and the inferior extensor retinaculum.
cards.clin: Its pulse is felt just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon on the dorsum and is a routine test of distal limb perfusion; it is congenitally absent or aberrant in a small minority of normal people, so absence alone does not prove arterial disease.
cards.exam: Q. Where do you palpate the dorsalis pedis pulse? A. On the dorsum of the foot, immediately lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus, between the first and second metatarsal bases.

cards.desc: C-shaped first part of the small intestine, about 25 cm long, curving around the head of the pancreas from the pylorus to the duodenojejunal flexure.
cards.att: Four parts: superior (first, about 5 cm, at L1, the proximal 2 cm intraperitoneal as the cap), descending (second, 7 to 10 cm, L1 to L3, receives the bile and pancreatic ducts), horizontal (third, 6 to 8 cm, at L3, crossed by the superior mesenteric vessels) and ascending (fourth, about 5 cm, ending at the duodenojejunal flexure at L2 left of the midline). Retroperitoneal except the cap.
cards.sup: Superior pancreaticoduodenal artery from the gastroduodenal (foregut) and inferior pancreaticoduodenal from the superior mesenteric artery (midgut), meeting at the major duodenal papilla. Veins to the portal and superior mesenteric veins. Nerves from the vagus and the greater and lesser splanchnic nerves via the coeliac and superior mesenteric plexuses.
cards.act: Receives chyme, bile and pancreatic juice; neutralises acid and begins the main phase of digestion.
cards.rel: The first part has the quadrate lobe of the liver and the gallbladder in front and above, and behind it the bile duct, gastroduodenal artery, portal vein and inferior vena cava. The second part lies on the hilum of the right kidney and the right renal vessels and is crossed anteriorly by the transverse colon and its mesocolon. The third part is crossed anteriorly by the superior mesenteric vessels and the root of the mesentery, and lies on the inferior vena cava and aorta.
cards.clin: Posterior duodenal ulcers erode the gastroduodenal artery and cause massive haematemesis; anterior ulcers perforate into the peritoneal cavity. The duodenojejunal flexure is suspended by the suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz), the landmark separating upper from lower gastrointestinal bleeding.
cards.exam: Q. Which artery is eroded by a posterior duodenal ulcer? A. The gastroduodenal artery.

cards.desc: Eighth of the twelve ribs, the first of the vertebrochondral or false ribs, whose costal cartilage joins the cartilage of the 7th rib rather than the sternum.
cards.att: Head bears two facets articulating with the inferior demifacet of T7, the superior demifacet of T8 and the disc between; the tubercle articulates with the transverse process of T8; the shaft has an angle and a costal groove. Gives attachment to the last digitation of serratus anterior, to external oblique and latissimus dorsi, and to the diaphragm on its inner aspect.
cards.sup: Eighth posterior intercostal artery with periosteal branches; the 8th intercostal nerve runs in its costal groove.
cards.act: Bucket-handle elevation increases the transverse diameter of the lower thorax in inspiration; contributes to the costal margin through the 7th cartilage.
cards.rel: External, internal and innermost intercostal muscles fill the adjacent spaces; the vein, artery and nerve lie in that order from above down in the costal groove, with endothoracic fascia and parietal pleura inside.
cards.clin: The lower border of the lung crosses the 8th rib in the midaxillary line and the pleural reflection crosses it in the midclavicular line, so a needle placed below the 8th rib anteriorly may enter the abdomen. Fractures of the left 8th to 11th ribs threaten the spleen.
cards.exam: Q. Why is the 8th rib called a false rib? A. Its costal cartilage does not reach the sternum directly; it articulates with the cartilage of the rib above.

cards.desc: Typical mid-thoracic vertebra with a heart-shaped body, a small circular vertebral foramen and a long spine directed downwards.
cards.att: Superior costal demifacet for the head of rib 8 and inferior demifacet for the head of rib 9; the transverse process carries a costal facet for the tubercle of rib 8. Articular facets lie in the coronal plane, the superior facing backwards and the inferior forwards.
cards.sup: Segmental branches of the posterior intercostal arteries; sinuvertebral nerves and medial branches of the thoracic dorsal rami supply the periosteum and facet joints.
cards.act: Transmits axial load, protects the spinal cord, and with its coronal facets and attached ribs permits rotation while limiting flexion.
cards.rel: Descending thoracic aorta anterolaterally on the left, azygos vein and thoracic duct on the right, oesophagus in front; the sympathetic trunk crosses the head of the rib laterally.
cards.clin: The caval opening of the diaphragm lies at the T8 level, transmitting the inferior vena cava and the right phrenic nerve. A thoracic disc prolapse at this level compresses the cord itself, causing spastic paraparesis rather than a simple radiculopathy.
cards.exam: Q. Which structures pass through the diaphragm at the T8 level? A. The inferior vena cava and the right phrenic nerve, through the central tendon.

cards.desc: Short, tapering floating rib whose cartilage-capped anterior end lies free in the muscles of the posterolateral abdominal wall.
cards.att: Head has a single whole facet for the body of T11; there is no tubercle and no articulation with a transverse process, almost no neck, a shallow costal groove and no true angle. Gives attachment to quadratus lumborum, the diaphragm, external and internal oblique, transversus abdominis and latissimus dorsi.
cards.sup: Eleventh posterior intercostal artery; the 11th intercostal nerve runs below it into the abdominal wall.
cards.act: Adds mobility rather than rigidity to the lower thorax and gives attachment to the diaphragm and the flat abdominal muscles.
cards.rel: Crosses the kidney posteriorly; the pleural reflection descends behind to the 12th rib, so the pleural recess may extend over the 11th rib medially.
cards.clin: Fractures of ribs 9 to 11 endanger the spleen on the left and the liver and right kidney on the right. In the posterior approach to the kidney the incision is kept below the 12th rib to avoid opening the pleura.
cards.exam: Q. How does the head of the 11th rib differ from that of a typical rib? A. It has a single facet for its own numbered vertebra only, and the rib has no tubercle or costotransverse joint.

cards.desc: Atypical lower thoracic vertebra with a large body, a single complete costal facet on each side and a short, almost horizontal spine.
cards.att: One whole costal facet on the body and pedicle for the head of rib 11; the transverse process is short and has no costal facet. The body is nearly as large as a lumbar body and the spine is triangular and blunt.
cards.sup: Segmental branches from the lowest posterior intercostal arteries; dorsal rami supply the facet joints and periosteum.
cards.act: Transitional vertebra transmitting load from thorax to lumbar column; facet orientation begins to change from coronal to sagittal, limiting rotation and favouring flexion.
cards.rel: The descending aorta lies anteriorly, approaching the midline before the aortic hiatus at T12; azygos vein and thoracic duct lie to the right of the body; the crura of the diaphragm arise just below.
cards.clin: The thoracolumbar junction, T11 to L1, is the commonest site of vertebral fracture-dislocation because a rigid kyphotic thorax meets a mobile lordotic lumbar spine and the facet planes change. The spinal cord ends around L1, so injury here can damage conus medullaris and cauda equina together.
cards.exam: Q. How is T11 identified from an isolated vertebra? A. A single whole costal facet on each side of the body and a transverse process without a costal facet.

cards.desc: Comma-shaped structure of head, body and tail applied to the posterolateral surface of the testis, holding the single coiled duct of the epididymis.
cards.att: The head receives 12 to 20 efferent ductules from the rete testis; the body and tail lie along the posterior border of the testis, and the tail becomes continuous with the ductus deferens.
cards.sup: Testicular artery with contributions from the artery to the ductus deferens; veins to the pampiniform plexus; lymphatics to the para-aortic (lumbar) nodes.
cards.act: Sperm maturation, acquisition of motility and storage, principally in the tail.
cards.rel: Posterolateral to the testis; the sinus of the epididymis lies between its body and the testis. Covered by the visceral layer of the tunica vaginalis except along its posterior attachment.
cards.clin: Epididymitis is the commonest cause of a painful scrotum in adults (Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae under 35, coliforms above); pain eased by elevating the testis (Prehn sign), unlike torsion. Torsion of the appendix of the epididymis gives the blue dot sign.
cards.exam: Q. Where in the epididymis is sperm mainly stored? A. In the tail, which continues as the ductus deferens.

cards.desc: Muscular tube about 25 cm long conveying food from the pharynx to the stomach, running through the neck, posterior mediastinum and a short abdominal segment.
cards.att: Begins at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage at C6 and ends at the cardiac orifice of the stomach at T11, entering the abdomen through the oesophageal hiatus in the right crus of the diaphragm at T10. Upper third is striated muscle, middle third mixed, lower third smooth muscle.
cards.sup: Arteries: inferior thyroid, oesophageal branches of thoracic aorta and bronchial arteries, left gastric and left inferior phrenic. Veins: inferior thyroid and azygos system above, left gastric (portal) below. Nerves: vagi through the oesophageal plexus, with sympathetic fibres. Lymph: deep cervical, posterior mediastinal and left gastric nodes.
cards.act: Propels the bolus by peristalsis; the lower oesophageal sphincter, a physiological sphincter reinforced by the right crus, prevents reflux.
cards.rel: In the thorax it lies behind the trachea and left main bronchus, behind the left atrium, and in front of the vertebral bodies, thoracic duct and descending aorta; it deviates left in the neck and again at the diaphragm. Three constrictions occur at 15 cm (cricopharyngeal), 22 to 27 cm (aortic arch and left main bronchus) and 40 cm (diaphragmatic) from the incisors.
cards.clin: Foreign bodies lodge and carcinoma and strictures arise at the constrictions. Oesophageal varices at the lower end are a portosystemic anastomosis and bleed in portal hypertension. Achalasia shows a bird beak narrowing on barium swallow.
cards.exam: Q. Give the three constrictions of the oesophagus and their distances from the incisor teeth. A. Cricopharyngeal 15 cm, aortic and bronchial 22 to 27 cm, diaphragmatic 40 cm.

cards.desc: Light, cuboidal midline bone of the cranial base lying between the two orbits and forming the roof and much of the lateral wall of the nasal cavity.
cards.att: Has a horizontal cribriform plate with the crista galli projecting above for the falx cerebri, a vertical perpendicular plate forming the upper part of the nasal septum, and two lateral labyrinths containing the ethmoidal air cells and bearing the superior and middle nasal conchae. Its lateral surface, the lamina papyracea, forms most of the medial wall of the orbit. Articulates with the frontal, sphenoid, nasal, lacrimal, maxillary, palatine and vomer bones and the inferior conchae.
cards.sup: Anterior and posterior ethmoidal branches of the ophthalmic artery and sphenopalatine branches; the cribriform plate transmits the olfactory nerve filaments.
cards.act: Separates the nasal cavity from the anterior cranial fossa and the orbits, supports the conchae that condition inspired air, and transmits the olfactory nerves.
cards.rel: Olfactory bulbs rest on the cribriform plate above; the orbit lies lateral to the lamina papyracea; the sphenoid sinus lies behind and the frontal sinus in front and above.
cards.clin: Fracture of the cribriform plate tears the meninges and causes CSF rhinorrhoea and anosmia, with a risk of meningitis. Ethmoid sinusitis spreads through the paper-thin lamina papyracea to cause orbital cellulitis, the commonest cause of orbital cellulitis in children.
cards.exam: Q. Which part of the ethmoid separates the ethmoidal air cells from the orbit and why is it important? A. The lamina papyracea, so thin that ethmoid sinus infection readily spreads to produce orbital cellulitis.

cards.desc: Superficial extensor of the posterior forearm lying deep to extensor carpi radialis longus, arising from the common extensor origin.
cards.att: Origin: lateral epicondyle of the humerus by the common extensor tendon, and the adjacent intermuscular septa and antebrachial fascia. Insertion: dorsal surface of the base of the third metacarpal.
cards.sup: Deep branch of the radial nerve (C7, C8), given off before or as it becomes the posterior interosseous nerve.
cards.act: Extends the wrist and, with extensor carpi radialis longus and flexor carpi radialis, abducts it (radial deviation); acting together with extensor carpi ulnaris it produces pure wrist extension, essential for making a strong fist by stabilising the wrist in extension.
cards.rel: Lies deep to extensor carpi radialis longus and is crossed distally by abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis; both radial extensor tendons occupy the second extensor compartment under the extensor retinaculum.
cards.clin: Its origin from the common extensor tendon is the site of lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow), and the deep surface of its origin is what is released or debrided surgically.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle origin is chiefly involved in tennis elbow? A. The origin of extensor carpi radialis brevis from the common extensor tendon on the lateral epicondyle.

cards.desc: Long radial wrist extensor arising above the lateral epicondyle, lying between brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis brevis.
cards.att: Origin: lower third of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus and the lateral intermuscular septum. Insertion: dorsal surface of the base of the second metacarpal.
cards.sup: Radial nerve (C6, C7), directly, before the nerve divides into superficial and deep branches.
cards.act: Extends and abducts (radially deviates) the wrist; weakly flexes the elbow.
cards.rel: With brachioradialis it forms the mobile wad of the lateral forearm; its tendon lies in the second extensor compartment with extensor carpi radialis brevis, crossed superficially by abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis.
cards.clin: Because it is supplied by the radial nerve trunk rather than the posterior interosseous nerve, wrist extension is partly preserved with radial deviation in posterior interosseous nerve palsy, so there is no true wrist drop. Its tendon is a standard donor for tendon transfer.
cards.exam: Q. Why is there no complete wrist drop in posterior interosseous nerve palsy? A. Extensor carpi radialis longus is supplied by the radial nerve proper and still extends the wrist, with radial deviation.

cards.desc: Most medial of the superficial extensors, running along the posterior border of the ulna to the fifth metacarpal.
cards.att: Origin: lateral epicondyle by the common extensor tendon and, by an aponeurosis, from the posterior border of the ulna. Insertion: tubercle on the medial side of the base of the fifth metacarpal.
cards.sup: Posterior interosseous nerve (C7, C8).
cards.act: Extends the wrist and, with flexor carpi ulnaris, adducts it (ulnar deviation).
cards.rel: Occupies the sixth extensor compartment, running in a groove between the head and styloid process of the ulna, held by its own subsheath; lies superficial to the distal radioulnar joint and triangular fibrocartilage complex.
cards.clin: Subluxation of its tendon out of the ulnar groove causes painful snapping on forearm rotation. Tenderness here is a common cause of ulnar sided wrist pain and must be distinguished from triangular fibrocartilage complex tears.
cards.exam: Q. Which extensor compartment contains extensor carpi ulnaris? A. The sixth, in the groove between the ulnar head and styloid process.

cards.desc: Slender superficial extensor arising with the common extensor tendon, dedicated to the little finger.
cards.att: Origin: lateral epicondyle by the common extensor tendon and adjacent intermuscular septa. Insertion: dorsal digital expansion of the little finger, joining the extensor digitorum tendon to that digit.
cards.sup: Posterior interosseous nerve (C7, C8).
cards.act: Extends the little finger at the metacarpophalangeal joint, and through the extensor expansion at the interphalangeal joints; assists wrist extension.
cards.rel: Tendon runs in the fifth extensor compartment over the distal radioulnar joint, medial to extensor digitorum; usually splits into two slips on the dorsum of the hand.
cards.clin: Because it is independent of extensor digitorum, extension of the little finger persists after division of the extensor digitorum tendon. Its tendon is a common site of attritional rupture over a prominent distal ulna in rheumatoid arthritis (Vaughan-Jackson lesion begins here).
cards.exam: Q. Which extensor compartment transmits extensor digiti minimi? A. The fifth, lying over the distal radioulnar joint.

cards.desc: Principal superficial extensor of the fingers, arising from the common extensor origin and dividing into four tendons on the dorsum of the hand.
cards.att: Origin: lateral epicondyle of the humerus by the common extensor tendon, and adjacent intermuscular septa and antebrachial fascia. Insertion: by four tendons into the dorsal digital expansions of the index, middle, ring and little fingers, reaching the bases of the middle and distal phalanges.
cards.sup: Posterior interosseous nerve (C7, C8).
cards.act: Extends the medial four fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joints, and with the lumbricals and interossei at the interphalangeal joints; assists wrist extension.
