cards.rel: Occupies the fourth extensor compartment with extensor indicis, the posterior interosseous nerve lying on the floor of that compartment; on the dorsum of the hand its tendons are linked by intertendinous connections (juncturae tendinum).
cards.clin: The intertendinous connections mean a proximal cut tendon may still show weak finger extension, masking the injury. Central slip rupture at the proximal interphalangeal joint produces a boutonniere deformity; terminal slip avulsion produces mallet finger.
cards.exam: Q. What are the juncturae tendinum and why do they matter clinically? A. Oblique bands linking extensor digitorum tendons on the dorsum of the hand; they can mask a proximally divided tendon.

cards.desc: Muscle of the anterior (extensor) compartment of the leg, lateral to tibialis anterior, extending the lateral four toes. Note this is a lower limb muscle.
cards.att: Origin: lateral condyle of the tibia, upper three-quarters of the medial surface of the fibula, interosseous membrane and adjacent intermuscular septa. Insertion: by four tendons into the dorsal digital expansions of the lateral four toes, reaching the bases of the middle and distal phalanges.
cards.sup: Deep fibular (peroneal) nerve (L5, S1).
cards.act: Extends the lateral four toes and dorsiflexes the ankle; assists eversion of the foot.
cards.rel: Lies lateral to tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus, with the anterior tibial vessels and deep fibular nerve medial to it; its tendons pass deep to the superior and inferior extensor retinacula, and fibularis tertius arises from its lower lateral part.
cards.clin: Paralysed in deep fibular nerve injury or common fibular nerve palsy at the fibular neck, contributing to foot drop with a high stepping gait and clawing of the toes when tibialis anterior alone is spared. Its tendons are visible on the dorsum of the foot on active toe extension.
cards.exam: Q. What is the nerve supply of extensor digitorum longus? A. The deep fibular nerve (L5, S1).

cards.desc: Muscle of the anterior compartment of the leg that extends the great toe, its tendon lying between tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus at the ankle.
cards.att: Origin: middle half of the medial surface of the fibula and the adjacent interosseous membrane. Insertion: dorsal surface of the base of the distal phalanx of the great toe.
cards.sup: Deep fibular nerve (L5, S1).
cards.act: Extends the great toe at the interphalangeal and metatarsophalangeal joints; assists dorsiflexion of the ankle and weak inversion of the foot.
cards.rel: Concealed above by tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus. At the ankle the anterior tibial artery and deep fibular nerve lie lateral to its tendon, and the dorsalis pedis pulse is felt immediately lateral to it on the dorsum.
cards.clin: Weakness of great toe extension is the classic single sign of an L5 root lesion from a prolapsed L4 to L5 disc. Its tendon is the landmark for palpating the dorsalis pedis pulse.
cards.exam: Q. Weakness of extensor hallucis longus indicates which root lesion? A. L5.

cards.desc: Deep extensor of the posterior forearm with the most distal origin of the outcropping group, supplying only the index finger.
cards.att: Origin: posterior surface of the ulna distal to extensor pollicis longus and the adjacent interosseous membrane. Insertion: dorsal digital expansion of the index finger, on the ulnar side of the extensor digitorum tendon to that digit.
cards.sup: Posterior interosseous nerve (C7, C8).
cards.act: Extends the index finger independently of the other fingers, and assists wrist extension.
cards.rel: Tendon shares the fourth extensor compartment with extensor digitorum and lies deep and medial to it on the dorsum of the hand; the posterior interosseous nerve and anterior interosseous artery lie deep to the muscle belly.
cards.clin: Its independence allows the pointing index sign. It is the standard donor for tendon transfer to restore thumb extension after rupture of extensor pollicis longus following a distal radius fracture.
cards.exam: Q. Which tendon is transferred for extensor pollicis longus rupture? A. Extensor indicis, transferred to the distal stump of extensor pollicis longus.

cards.desc: Deep outcropping extensor lying medial and distal to abductor pollicis longus, acting on the proximal phalanx of the thumb.
cards.att: Origin: posterior surface of the radius distal to abductor pollicis longus and the adjacent interosseous membrane. Insertion: base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb, dorsal surface.
cards.sup: Posterior interosseous nerve (C7, C8).
cards.act: Extends the thumb at the metacarpophalangeal and carpometacarpal joints; assists abduction of the wrist.
cards.rel: Its tendon lies in the first extensor compartment with abductor pollicis longus and forms the anterior (lateral) boundary of the anatomical snuffbox; extensor pollicis longus forms the posterior boundary.
cards.clin: Inflammation of the first compartment sheath containing it and abductor pollicis longus is de Quervain's tenosynovitis, common in new mothers and confirmed by Finkelstein's test. A separate subsheath for extensor pollicis brevis is a frequent cause of failed conservative treatment.
cards.exam: Q. Which tendons bound the anatomical snuffbox? A. Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis anteriorly, extensor pollicis longus posteriorly.

cards.desc: Deep posterior forearm muscle whose tendon hooks round the dorsal tubercle of the radius to reach the distal phalanx of the thumb.
cards.att: Origin: posterior surface of the middle third of the ulna distal to abductor pollicis longus and the adjacent interosseous membrane. Insertion: base of the distal phalanx of the thumb, dorsal surface.
cards.sup: Posterior interosseous nerve (C7, C8).
cards.act: Extends the distal phalanx of the thumb and, continuing, the metacarpophalangeal and carpometacarpal joints; retroposes the extended thumb.
cards.rel: Runs in the third extensor compartment, turning at almost a right angle round the dorsal (Lister's) tubercle of the radius; forms the posterior (medial) boundary of the anatomical snuffbox, with the radial artery crossing the floor of the box deep to it.
cards.clin: Delayed rupture around Lister's tubercle after an undisplaced Colles fracture is classic, caused by attrition and a watershed blood supply; the patient cannot lift the thumb off a flat table. Repair is by extensor indicis transfer.
cards.exam: Q. Which tendon ruptures late after a distal radius fracture and where? A. Extensor pollicis longus, at the dorsal tubercle of the radius.

cards.desc: The voluntary striated muscle that surrounds the whole length of the anal canal outside the internal sphincter.
cards.att: Described in subcutaneous, superficial and deep parts. The subcutaneous part encircles the anal orifice with no bony attachment; the superficial part is attached in front to the perineal body and behind to the coccyx through the anococcygeal ligament; the deep part is a thick ring blending above with puborectalis.
cards.sup: Inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve (S2, S3), with a contribution from the perineal branch of the fourth sacral nerve.
cards.act: Voluntary closure of the anal canal; it maintains tonic contraction at rest and contracts strongly to defer defaecation, relaxing during defaecation.
cards.rel: Separated from the internal anal sphincter by the intersphincteric plane containing the longitudinal muscle layer; the ischio-anal fossa with its fat and the inferior rectal vessels and nerve lies lateral; the anococcygeal body behind and the perineal body in front.
cards.clin: Obstetric injury tearing the external sphincter is a third degree perineal tear, and extension into the anal mucosa is a fourth degree tear; unrepaired, it causes faecal incontinence. Fistula-in-ano is classified by Parks according to its course relative to this sphincter, and division of the deep part or puborectalis in fistula surgery causes incontinence.
cards.exam: Q. What is the nerve supply of the external anal sphincter? A. The inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve, S2 and S3, with the perineal branch of S4.

cards.desc: The auricle and the external acoustic meatus, ending medially at the tympanic membrane.
cards.att: The auricle has a framework of elastic cartilage covered by adherent skin, except the fibrofatty lobule. The external acoustic meatus is about 24 mm long and S-shaped: the outer one-third is cartilaginous, the inner two-thirds bony in the temporal bone, and the whole is closed medially by the tympanic membrane.
cards.sup: Sensory supply from the great auricular and lesser occipital nerves (cervical plexus), the auriculotemporal nerve (CN V3), the auricular branch of the vagus (CN X), and a contribution from the facial nerve. Arterial supply from the posterior auricular and superficial temporal arteries and the deep auricular branch of the maxillary artery.
cards.act: Collects and channels sound to the tympanic membrane and helps localise sound.
cards.rel: The parotid gland lies anterior and inferior to the meatus, the mastoid process posterior, and the temporomandibular joint immediately in front of its cartilaginous part; the middle cranial fossa lies above the bony meatus.
cards.clin: To straighten the meatus for otoscopy, pull the auricle upwards, backwards and laterally in an adult, and downwards and backwards in an infant. Stimulating the auricular branch of the vagus in the meatus provokes Arnold's cough reflex, and a furuncle in the cartilaginous part is exquisitely painful because the skin is bound down.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve mediates the cough reflex on cleaning the external acoustic meatus? A. The auricular branch of the vagus, Arnold's nerve.

cards.desc: The larger terminal branch of the common iliac artery, running along the pelvic brim to become the femoral artery.
cards.att: Begins in front of the sacroiliac joint, runs downwards and laterally along the medial border of psoas major on the pelvic brim, and passes behind the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point to become the femoral artery. Branches: inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac arteries, both arising just above the inguinal ligament.
cards.act: Principal arterial supply of the lower limb, with branches to the anterior abdominal wall.
cards.rel: Accompanied medially by the external iliac vein; crossed at its origin by the ureter (left) and by the ductus deferens or the round ligament and ovarian vessels; the genitofemoral nerve lies lateral, testicular vessels cross in front; the deep circumflex iliac vein crosses in front of it.
cards.clin: The inferior epigastric artery is the landmark dividing indirect hernias, whose sac lies lateral to it, from direct hernias, which bulge medial to it. The external iliac artery is the usual site of anastomosis of the renal artery in a transplant.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the external iliac artery become the femoral artery? A. Behind the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis.

cards.desc: The continuation of the femoral vein above the inguinal ligament, running along the pelvic brim to join the internal iliac vein.
cards.att: Begins behind the inguinal ligament as the continuation of the femoral vein, ascends along the pelvic brim medial then posteromedial to its artery, and unites with the internal iliac vein in front of the sacroiliac joint to form the common iliac vein. Tributaries: inferior epigastric, deep circumflex iliac and pubic veins.
cards.act: Main venous drainage of the lower limb and lower anterior abdominal wall.
cards.rel: Lies medial to the external iliac artery at first and behind it above; the ureter and, in the female, the ovarian vessels cross it; the obturator nerve and internal iliac vessels lie behind and below.
cards.clin: Iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis here is the usual source of major pulmonary embolism. The vein is used for the venous anastomosis in renal transplantation, and an abnormal obturator (corona mortis) communication with it is a source of troublesome bleeding.
cards.exam: Q. What are the tributaries of the external iliac vein? A. The inferior epigastric, deep circumflex iliac and pubic veins.

cards.desc: Outermost of the three intercostal muscle layers, eleven on each side, filling the posterior and lateral part of each intercostal space.
cards.att: Arises from the lower border of the rib above and inserts into the upper border of the rib below; fibres run downwards, forwards and medially, in the direction of the hands placed in the front trouser pockets. Extends from the tubercle of the rib behind to the costochondral junction in front, where it is replaced by the external intercostal membrane.
cards.sup: Intercostal nerves, the ventral rami of T1 to T11.
cards.act: Elevates the ribs and increases the anteroposterior and transverse diameters of the thorax during inspiration; also supports the intercostal space and resists paradoxical indrawing.
cards.rel: Superficial to the internal intercostal muscle; the neurovascular bundle lies deep to the internal intercostal, not deep to this layer. Covered externally by the serratus anterior, pectoral and back muscles.
cards.clin: An intercostal drain or aspiration needle passes through skin, superficial fascia, external, internal and innermost intercostal muscles and parietal pleura, entering just above the upper border of the lower rib.
cards.exam: Q. What replaces the external intercostal muscle anteriorly? A. The external intercostal membrane, between the costochondral junction and the sternum.

cards.desc: Largest and most superficial of the three flat muscles of the anterolateral abdominal wall, its fibres running downwards and forwards like hands in pockets.
cards.att: Origin from the outer surfaces and lower borders of the lower eight ribs (5 to 12) by fleshy digitations interdigitating with serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi. Inserts into the anterior half of the outer lip of the iliac crest, the pubic tubercle and pubic crest, and through a broad aponeurosis into the linea alba.
cards.sup: Anterior rami of T7 to T12 (thoracoabdominal nerves T7 to T11 and the subcostal nerve T12).
cards.act: Compresses the abdominal contents and raises intra-abdominal pressure; flexes the trunk; acting on one side it turns the trunk to the opposite side.
cards.rel: Superficial to internal oblique; its aponeurosis forms the anterior wall of the rectus sheath throughout. Its lower free border rolls back on itself between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle to form the inguinal ligament, and is deficient above the pubic crest as the superficial inguinal ring.
cards.clin: Its aponeurosis provides the inguinal ligament, lacunar ligament, superficial inguinal ring and the anterior wall of the inguinal canal, and is the layer reinforced in Bassini and Lichtenstein hernia repair. Splitting the muscle along its fibres is the first step of the grid-iron (McBurney) appendicectomy incision.
cards.exam: Q. Which structures are formed by the external oblique aponeurosis? A. The inguinal ligament, lacunar ligament, pectineal ligament, superficial inguinal ring and the anterior wall of the rectus sheath and inguinal canal.

cards.desc: Main artery of the lower limb, running from the inguinal ligament to the adductor hiatus.
cards.att: Continuation of the external iliac artery behind the inguinal ligament at the mid-inguinal point, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis; it passes through the femoral triangle and then the adductor canal, and becomes the popliteal artery at the adductor hiatus in adductor magnus.
cards.sup: Superficial epigastric, superficial circumflex iliac, superficial external pudendal, deep external pudendal, profunda femoris and descending genicular arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the lower limb and the lower anterior abdominal wall and external genitalia through its superficial branches.
cards.rel: In the femoral triangle it lies lateral to the femoral vein and medial to the femoral nerve, within the femoral sheath which does not contain the nerve; in the adductor canal it lies deep to sartorius with the saphenous nerve crossing it from lateral to medial and the nerve to vastus medialis laterally.
cards.clin: The femoral pulse is felt below the mid-inguinal point and is the standard puncture site for coronary and peripheral angiography; puncture above the inguinal ligament risks uncontrollable retroperitoneal haemorrhage. Remember the order from lateral to medial: nerve, artery, vein, empty space, lymphatics (NAVEL).
cards.exam: Q. What are the boundaries of the femoral triangle? A. Inguinal ligament above, medial border of sartorius laterally, medial border of adductor longus medially, with a floor of iliopsoas, pectineus and adductor longus.

cards.desc: Main deep vein of the thigh, continuing the popliteal vein up to the inguinal ligament.
cards.att: Begins as the continuation of the popliteal vein at the adductor hiatus, ascends through the adductor canal and femoral triangle within the femoral sheath, and becomes the external iliac vein at the inguinal ligament.
cards.sup: Receives the deep femoral vein, the great saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction, and the circumflex femoral veins.
cards.act: Carries the whole deep venous return of the lower limb.
cards.rel: Lies posterolateral to the artery at the adductor hiatus, posterior to it in mid-thigh, and medial to it at the inguinal ligament, where it occupies the intermediate compartment of the femoral sheath with the femoral canal medial to it.
cards.clin: Femoral venous puncture for central access is made about a centimetre medial to the femoral arterial pulse below the inguinal ligament. Thrombosis of the femoral vein is a proximal DVT with a high risk of pulmonary embolism, presenting with a swollen, tender, warm limb.
cards.exam: Q. What is the relation of the femoral vein to the femoral artery at the base of the femoral triangle? A. The vein lies medial to the artery.

cards.desc: Longest, heaviest and strongest bone of the body, forming the skeleton of the thigh between the hip and the knee.
cards.att: Upper end: head with the fovea for the ligament of the head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters, intertrochanteric line in front and intertrochanteric crest with the quadrate tubercle behind. Shaft: linea aspera with medial and lateral lips, gluteal tuberosity, pectineal line, popliteal surface. Lower end: medial and lateral condyles, epicondyles, adductor tubercle, intercondylar fossa and patellar surface. Articulates with the acetabulum above and with the tibia and patella below. The neck-shaft angle is about 125 degrees and the angle of anteversion about 15 degrees in the adult.
cards.sup: Retinacular branches of the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries, the medial being dominant, the artery of the ligament of the head, and nutrient arteries from the perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery.
cards.act: Transmits body weight from the hip bone to the tibia and acts as the lever for the muscles of the hip and knee.
cards.rel: The femoral vessels lie in front of the hip and pass through the adductor canal on its medial side; the sciatic nerve runs behind the ischium and the popliteal vessels lie on the popliteal surface. The profunda femoris artery and its perforating branches hug the linea aspera.
cards.clin: Fracture of the femoral neck in the elderly tears the retinacular vessels and leads to avascular necrosis of the head; the limb is short and laterally rotated. A shaft fracture can lose more than a litre of blood, and the ossification centre in the lower end, present at birth, is used medicolegally as a sign of maturity.
cards.exam: Q. Why is avascular necrosis common after an intracapsular fracture of the femoral neck? A. Because the retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery, the main supply to the head, run in the capsule and are torn.

cards.desc: Slender lateral bone of the leg, not weight bearing, giving attachment to muscles and forming the lateral malleolus of the ankle.
cards.att: Parts: head with an apex or styloid process, neck, triangular shaft with three borders and three surfaces, and the lateral malleolus with the malleolar fossa and a groove behind for the fibular tendons. Articulates with the lateral condyle of the tibia at the superior tibiofibular joint, with the tibia through the interosseous membrane and the inferior tibiofibular syndesmosis, and with the lateral surface of the talus at the ankle. Gives origin to the fibularis muscles laterally, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus and fibularis tertius in front, and soleus, flexor hallucis longus and tibialis posterior behind; biceps femoris inserts on the head.
cards.act: Stabilises the ankle mortise, deepens the socket for the talus and provides muscle attachment; it transmits almost no body weight.
cards.rel: The common fibular nerve winds round the neck of the fibula against bone, between it and fibularis longus, before dividing into superficial and deep fibular nerves. The lateral malleolus reaches about 1 cm lower and lies more posterior than the medial malleolus.
cards.clin: Fracture of the neck or tight plaster at this level injures the common fibular nerve and causes foot drop with loss of sensation on the dorsum of the foot. In a Maisonneuve injury a proximal fibular fracture accompanies a medial ankle injury, so the whole fibula must be examined; the middle shaft is the standard donor for a vascularised bone graft.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve is at risk in a fracture of the neck of the fibula, and what is the result? A. The common fibular nerve, producing foot drop with loss of dorsiflexion and eversion.

cards.desc: Shorter and deeper muscle of the lateral compartment of the leg, lying against the fibula.
cards.att: Origin: lower two thirds of the lateral surface of the fibula and the adjacent anterior and posterior intermuscular septa. Insertion: tuberosity on the lateral side of the base of the fifth metatarsal.
cards.sup: Superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1).
cards.act: Everts the foot and assists weak plantarflexion at the ankle.
cards.rel: Its tendon lies anterior to that of fibularis longus behind the lateral malleolus, both sharing a common synovial sheath under the superior fibular retinaculum; below the malleolus it runs above the fibular trochlea of the calcaneus.
cards.clin: Sudden inversion avulses the tuberosity at its insertion, giving the avulsion or pseudo Jones fracture of the base of the fifth metatarsal, to be distinguished from the true Jones fracture of the metaphysial diaphysial junction. Its tendon is used for lateral ligament reconstruction.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle avulses the base of the fifth metatarsal in an inversion injury? A. Fibularis brevis.

cards.desc: Superficial and longer muscle of the lateral compartment, whose tendon crosses the sole to reach the medial side of the foot.
cards.att: Origin: head and upper two thirds of the lateral surface of the fibula and the adjacent intermuscular septa. Insertion: lateral side of the base of the first metatarsal and of the medial cuneiform, after passing behind the lateral malleolus, below the fibular trochlea and through the groove on the cuboid.
cards.sup: Superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1).
cards.act: Everts the foot and plantarflexes the ankle; its sling across the sole supports the transverse and lateral longitudinal arches.
cards.rel: Covers fibularis brevis; the common fibular nerve divides deep to its upper attachment, between the muscle and the neck of the fibula. In the sole its tendon runs in a groove on the cuboid, held by the long plantar ligament, deep to all other structures.
cards.clin: The common fibular nerve is compressed against the fibular neck under this muscle by plaster casts, prolonged squatting or crossed legs, causing foot drop with loss of eversion. A sesamoid, the os peroneum, may lie in the tendon over the cuboid and fracture.
cards.exam: Q. Where is the common fibular nerve most often injured, and what is the deformity? A. Against the neck of the fibula, causing foot drop with loss of dorsiflexion and eversion.

cards.desc: A typical cervical vertebra in the middle of the neck, at the level of the mid thyroid cartilage.
cards.att: Small broad body with raised uncinate processes on the lateral margins of its upper surface, a large triangular vertebral foramen, transverse processes each with a foramen transversarium and anterior and posterior tubercles separated by a groove for the ventral ramus, and a short bifid spine. Articulates with C4 above and C6 below through the intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial joints.
cards.sup: Foramen transversarium transmits the vertebral artery and vein and a sympathetic plexus; segmental branches of the vertebral and ascending cervical arteries supply the bone.
cards.act: Bears the weight of the head and upper neck and, through the obliquely set facet joints, permits flexion, extension, lateral flexion and rotation.
cards.rel: Lies behind the thyroid cartilage and the carotid sheath, with the ventral ramus of C5 in the groove of its transverse process joining the upper trunk of the brachial plexus. Prevertebral fascia and longus colli lie on its anterior surface.
cards.clin: C5 and C6 are the commonest levels for cervical spondylosis, where uncinate osteophytes narrow the intervertebral foramen and compress the nerve root. Compression of the C5 root gives weak shoulder abduction, numbness over the deltoid and a depressed biceps jerk.
cards.exam: Q. Name the features that make C5 a typical cervical vertebra. A. Small broad body with uncinate processes, triangular vertebral foramen, foramen transversarium in the transverse process, and a short bifid spine.

cards.desc: Bar of hyaline cartilage joining the anterior end of the 5th rib to the lateral border of the body of the sternum.
cards.att: Continuous laterally with the 5th rib at the costochondral junction and medially with the sternum at a synovial sternocostal joint reinforced by radiate sternocostal ligaments. Gives attachment to the sternocostal head of pectoralis major, to rectus abdominis below and to transversus thoracis internally.
cards.sup: Avascular hyaline cartilage nourished by diffusion from the perichondrium, which is supplied by the internal thoracic artery.
cards.act: Provides elastic recoil and allows the anterior ends of the ribs to swing upward and forward in inspiration; may calcify with age and stiffen the chest wall.
cards.rel: The internal thoracic vessels descend behind the cartilage about 1 cm from the sternal edge; the pericardium and left ventricle lie deep to the left 5th cartilage and interspace.
cards.clin: The apex beat is felt in the left 5th intercostal space just medial to the midclavicular line, immediately below this cartilage. Costochondritis and Tietze syndrome typically affect the 2nd to 5th costal cartilages and mimic cardiac pain.
cards.exam: Q. What type of joint is the 5th sternocostal joint? A. A synovial plane joint, unlike the 1st, which is a primary cartilaginous synchondrosis.

cards.desc: The largest and lowest lumbar vertebra, sitting on the sacral base and forming the lumbosacral junction.
cards.att: Body is the largest of the vertebrae and wedge-shaped, deeper in front than behind; transverse processes are thick, conical and arise from the whole pedicle and the back of the body. Articulates with L4 above and with the sacrum below through the L5/S1 disc and paired zygapophysial joints.
cards.sup: Segmental supply from lumbar arteries and the iliolumbar artery; venous drainage to the internal and external vertebral venous plexuses.
cards.rel: The iliolumbar ligament runs from the tip of the transverse process to the iliac crest. The L5 nerve root passes below its pedicle; the sympathetic trunk, common iliac vessels and the median sacral vessels lie on the front of the body.
cards.clin: Commonest site of spondylolysis (pars interarticularis defect) and of spondylolisthesis of L5 on S1, producing a palpable step above the sacrum. The wedge shape of the body and disc creates the lumbosacral angle.
cards.exam: Q. At which vertebral level is spondylolisthesis most common? A. L5 on S1, usually through a pars interarticularis defect of L5.

cards.desc: The most medial and second shortest metacarpal, forming the skeleton of the little finger ray.
cards.att: Base articulates with the hamate and with the fourth metacarpal, and bears a tubercle on its medial side for extensor carpi ulnaris. Opponens digiti minimi inserts along its medial border and flexor carpi ulnaris acts on it through the pisometacarpal ligament; the head forms the fifth knuckle and carries the deep transverse metacarpal ligament.
cards.rel: Its base bounds the ulnar side of the carpometacarpal joints; the deep branch of the ulnar nerve and deep palmar arch run across the palmar aspect of its base. The fifth carpometacarpal joint is comparatively mobile, allowing cupping of the palm.
cards.clin: Fracture of the neck with volar angulation of the head is the boxer's fracture, the commonest metacarpal fracture, caused by punching with a clenched fist. Loss of the knuckle prominence and rotational malalignment of the finger are the key clinical signs.
cards.exam: Q. What is a boxer's fracture? A. A fracture of the neck of the fifth metacarpal with volar angulation of the head.

cards.desc: Most lateral metatarsal, recognised by the prominent tuberosity projecting backwards and laterally from its base.
cards.att: Base articulates with the cuboid behind and with the fourth metatarsal medially; the head articulates with the proximal phalanx of the little toe. Fibularis brevis inserts on the tuberosity of the base, fibularis tertius on the dorsal surface of the base. Flexor digiti minimi brevis arises from the plantar surface of the base and the sheath of fibularis longus, the third plantar interosseous from the base and medial side of the shaft, and the fourth dorsal interosseous by one head from the medial side of the shaft, its other head from the fourth metatarsal.
cards.act: Forms the lateral border of the foot and transmits weight to the ground at the base and head; anchors the lateral longitudinal arch.
cards.rel: The tuberosity is palpable at the midpoint of the lateral border of the foot and marks the level of the transverse tarsal joint region on the lateral side.
cards.clin: Forced inversion avulses the tuberosity through fibularis brevis and the lateral band of the plantar aponeurosis, the pseudo-Jones fracture; a true Jones fracture at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction lies in a watershed zone and is prone to non-union. The apophysis in adolescents lies parallel to the shaft and is mistaken for a fracture.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle inserts into the tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal? A. Fibularis brevis.

cards.desc: Typical true rib, articulating in front through its own costal cartilage with the body of the sternum.
cards.att: Head has two facets for the inferior demifacet of T4, the superior demifacet of T5 and the intervening disc; it has a crest, neck, tubercle articulating with the transverse process of T5, angle, shaft with a costal groove, and an anterior end for its cartilage. Gives origin to a digitation of serratus anterior and to external oblique, with intercostal muscles along its borders.
cards.sup: Fifth posterior intercostal artery from the thoracic aorta and anterior intercostal branches of the internal thoracic artery; the 5th intercostal nerve lies in the costal groove.
cards.act: Pump-handle and bucket-handle movement raises the sternum and widens the thorax in inspiration; protects heart and lungs.
cards.rel: Intercostal neurovascular bundle in the costal groove in the order vein, artery, nerve from above down; parietal pleura and endothoracic fascia internally; pectoralis major and serratus anterior superficially.
cards.clin: An intercostal drain is inserted in the safe triangle, usually in the 4th or 5th intercostal space, passing just above the upper border of the rib below to avoid the neurovascular bundle. The apex beat lies in the left 5th intercostal space.
cards.exam: Q. With which vertebrae does the head of the 5th rib articulate? A. The bodies of T4 and T5 and the disc between them; its tubercle articulates with the transverse process of T5.

cards.desc: Typical upper mid-thoracic vertebra with a heart-shaped body, costal demifacets and a long overlapping spine.
cards.att: Superior demifacet for the head of rib 5 and inferior demifacet for the head of rib 6; the transverse process carries a facet for the tubercle of rib 5; the spine points sharply downwards, overlapping the vertebra below.
cards.sup: Segmental posterior intercostal branches; dorsal rami to the facet joints and periosteum.
cards.act: Load transmission and cord protection; the coronal facets permit rotation of the thoracic spine.
cards.rel: The thoracic duct crosses the midline from right to left behind the oesophagus at about this level; the arch of the aorta lies on the left just above, and the oesophagus and thoracic aorta lie anteriorly.
cards.clin: The T4/T5 disc immediately above lies in the plane of the sternal angle, the key landmark of the superior mediastinum. Thoracic bodies are common sites for metastatic deposits and for tuberculous spondylitis with paravertebral cold abscess.
cards.exam: Q. At what vertebral level does the thoracic duct cross to the left side? A. At about the level of T5.

cards.desc: Short, broad, flattened bar of hyaline cartilage uniting the 1st rib to the lateral border of the manubrium sterni.
cards.att: Joins the 1st rib laterally and the manubrium medially by a primary cartilaginous joint, a synchondrosis, unlike the synovial joints of cartilages 2 to 7. Receives the costoclavicular ligament and the attachment of subclavius near its junction with the rib.
cards.sup: Perichondrial supply from the internal thoracic artery.
cards.act: Fixes the 1st rib to the sternum, so manubrium and first ribs move as one unit in the pump-handle movement of inspiration.
cards.rel: The internal thoracic artery enters the thorax behind it; the subclavian vein crosses in front of scalenus anterior above it, and the brachiocephalic vein lies deep to it.
cards.clin: It is the earliest costal cartilage to calcify, often by the third decade, and the calcified shadow is commonly mistaken for a pulmonary nodule on a chest radiograph.
cards.exam: Q. What type of joint is the 1st sternocostal joint? A. A synchondrosis, a primary cartilaginous joint, so it is immobile.

cards.desc: The uppermost lumbar vertebra, at the thoracolumbar junction, with the smallest body and shortest transverse processes of the lumbar series.
cards.att: Kidney-shaped body, short thick pedicles, hatchet-shaped spinous process, triangular vertebral foramen; superior articular facets face posteromedially. Articulates with T12 above and L2 below.
cards.sup: First lumbar arteries from the abdominal aorta; drainage to lumbar veins and the vertebral venous plexuses.
cards.rel: The transpyloric plane crosses the lower border of the body. The right crus of the diaphragm arises from L1 to L3, the left from L1 to L2. The coeliac trunk arises at the upper border and the superior mesenteric artery at the lower border of L1.
cards.clin: The spinal cord ends (conus medullaris) at the L1/L2 disc in the adult, so lumbar puncture is performed below this level. The thoracolumbar junction is the commonest site of burst fracture in a fall from height.
cards.exam: Q. Which structures lie in the transpyloric plane at the lower border of L1? A. Pylorus, neck of pancreas, hila of the kidneys, origin of the superior mesenteric artery, and the ninth costal cartilages.

cards.desc: Most medial of the four small lumbrical muscles of the second layer of the sole, acting on the second toe.
cards.att: Origin: unipennate, from the medial side of the tendon of flexor digitorum longus passing to the second toe. Insertion: medial side of the dorsal digital (extensor) expansion of the second toe, over the proximal phalanx.
cards.sup: Medial plantar nerve (S2, S3).
cards.act: Flexes the metatarsophalangeal joint and extends the interphalangeal joints of the second toe, keeping the toe flat on the ground.
cards.rel: Lies in the second layer of the sole with quadratus plantae and the long flexor tendons, superficial to the interossei and deep to flexor digitorum brevis.
cards.clin: It is the only lumbrical supplied by the medial plantar nerve, the remaining three coming from the deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve, mirroring the arrangement in the hand. Loss of lumbrical action contributes to clawing of the toes in nerve lesions.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve supplies the first lumbrical of the foot? A. The medial plantar nerve (S2, S3); the other three are supplied by the deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve.

cards.desc: The shortest and stoutest metacarpal, rotated about 90 degrees medially relative to the others so the thumb pulp faces the palm.
cards.att: Base carries a saddle-shaped facet for the trapezium, forming the first carpometacarpal joint. Abductor pollicis longus inserts on the lateral side of the base, opponens pollicis along the lateral border of the shaft, and the lateral head of the first dorsal interosseous takes origin from its ulnar side; two sesamoid bones lie at the head.
cards.rel: The radial artery crosses the base in the anatomical snuffbox and passes between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous to enter the palm. The thumb metacarpal moves in a plane at right angles to the other metacarpals.
cards.clin: It is the only metacarpal whose epiphysis lies at the base, matching the phalanges, which is used in bone age assessment. Bennett fracture-dislocation is an oblique intra-articular fracture of the base in which abductor pollicis longus pulls the shaft proximally while the volar ulnar fragment stays attached to the anterior oblique ligament; a comminuted version is the Rolando fracture.
cards.exam: Q. Where is the epiphysis of the first metacarpal, and what fracture affects its base? A. At the base, unlike the other metacarpals; Bennett fracture-dislocation is the intra-articular fracture of that base.

cards.desc: Shortest and stoutest metatarsal, forming the skeleton of the medial border of the forefoot and bearing most of the load at push off.
cards.att: Base articulates with the medial cuneiform and normally has no facet for the second metatarsal; the head articulates with the proximal phalanx of the hallux and is grooved on its plantar surface for two sesamoid bones in the tendon of flexor hallucis brevis. Tibialis anterior inserts on the medial side of the base, fibularis longus on the lateral side of the plantar aspect of the base, and the first dorsal interosseous arises from its lateral shaft.
cards.act: Transmits about twice the load of any other metatarsal head at toe off and forms the anterior pillar of the medial longitudinal arch.
cards.rel: Its head, the ball of the great toe, rests on two sesamoids separated by a crest, with flexor hallucis longus running in the groove between them.
cards.clin: Hallux valgus with metatarsus primus varus produces a bunion over the medial eminence of the head. Sesamoiditis and fracture of the sesamoids cause pain under the first metatarsal head, and the base is the medial anchor of the Lisfranc joint.
cards.exam: Q. Which two tendons insert into the base of the first metatarsal? A. Tibialis anterior on its medial side and fibularis longus on its plantar lateral side.

syn: first posterior intercostal branch of the superior intercostal artery
cards.desc: Artery of the first intercostal space, arising not from the aorta but from the superior (supreme) intercostal artery of the costocervical trunk.
cards.att: Arises from the superior intercostal artery, a branch of the costocervical trunk of the second part of the subclavian artery; descends over the neck of the first rib to run in the first intercostal space and anastomose with the first anterior intercostal branch of the internal thoracic artery.
cards.sup: Gives a dorsal branch to the back muscles and skin and a collateral branch; a lateral cutaneous branch accompanies it.
cards.act: Supplies the first intercostal space, its muscles, parietal pleura and overlying skin.
cards.rel: Crosses the neck of the first rib lateral to the sympathetic trunk and the superior intercostal vein, with the ventral ramus of T1 running below it to join the brachial plexus.
cards.clin: Explains why the thoracic aorta gives only nine pairs of posterior intercostal arteries, for the 3rd to 11th spaces: the first two spaces are supplied from the subclavian through the superior intercostal artery.
cards.exam: Q. What is the source of the first and second posterior intercostal arteries? A. The superior intercostal artery from the costocervical trunk of the subclavian artery.

cards.desc: Shortest, broadest and most sharply curved rib, set almost horizontally with superior and inferior surfaces and outer and inner borders.
cards.att: Head has a single facet for the body of T1; short neck; prominent tubercle articulating with the transverse process of T1; the superior surface bears the scalene tubercle for scalenus anterior, with the groove for the subclavian vein in front of it and the groove for the subclavian artery and lower trunk of the brachial plexus behind it. Scalenus medius attaches behind the arterial groove, subclavius near the costal cartilage, and serratus anterior gives its first digitation to it.
cards.sup: Supreme (superior) intercostal artery from the costocervical trunk; the first thoracic nerve contributes chiefly to the brachial plexus rather than running as a typical intercostal nerve.
cards.act: Its elevation raises the whole rib cage in inspiration; it forms the bony boundary of the thoracic inlet and anchors the suprapleural membrane.
cards.rel: The cervical pleura and apex of the lung rise above its inner border, roofed by the suprapleural membrane of Sibson attached to it; the subclavian vessels and lower trunk of the brachial plexus cross it; the clavicle lies above.
cards.clin: A cervical rib or fibrous band compressing the lower trunk and subclavian artery over the 1st rib produces thoracic outlet syndrome with T1 wasting of the small hand muscles. The 1st rib is deeply protected, so its fracture indicates severe trauma and raises suspicion of great vessel injury.
cards.exam: Q. What separates the grooves for the subclavian artery and vein on the first rib? A. The scalene tubercle, the insertion of scalenus anterior.

cards.desc: Atypical uppermost thoracic vertebra, cervical-like in shape, with a long, thick, nearly horizontal spinous process.
cards.att: Body carries a whole superior costal facet for the head of rib 1 and an inferior demifacet for the upper part of the head of rib 2; the transverse process has a facet for the tubercle of rib 1. The body is broad and its upper surface often shows raised lateral lips as in a cervical vertebra.
cards.sup: Branches of the supreme intercostal and vertebral arteries; dorsal rami supply the facet joints and periosteum.
cards.act: Transmits the load of the head and neck to the thorax and anchors the first rib, making the thoracic inlet a rigid ring.
cards.rel: The apex of each lung and the cervical pleura rise beside it; the oesophagus and trachea lie in front, with the stellate ganglion and the vertebral artery ascending anterolaterally.
cards.clin: The T1 spine is palpable just below the vertebra prominens of C7. Traction injury of the T1 root, as in Klumpke palsy, gives small-muscle wasting of the hand, and interruption of the T1 sympathetic outflow gives Horner syndrome; an apical lung tumour at this level does both.
cards.exam: Q. Which costal facets does T1 carry? A. A complete superior facet for the head of rib 1 and an inferior demifacet for the upper half of the head of rib 2.

cards.desc: Flat quadrilateral muscle of the second layer of the sole that inserts into the tendon of flexor digitorum longus.
cards.att: Origin: by two heads, a medial fleshy head from the medial concave surface of the calcaneus and a lateral head from the lateral border of the plantar surface of the calcaneus, separated by the long plantar ligament. Insertion: posterolateral border and deep surface of the tendon of flexor digitorum longus before it divides.
cards.sup: Lateral plantar nerve (S2, S3).
cards.act: Straightens the oblique line of pull of flexor digitorum longus so that the toes flex directly backwards; assists flexion of the lateral four toes.
cards.rel: Lies deep to flexor digitorum brevis and superficial to the long plantar ligament; the lateral plantar vessels and nerve cross its distal part.
cards.clin: It allows the toes to be flexed with the ankle plantarflexed, when flexor digitorum longus is shortened and inefficient. The nerve to abductor digiti minimi is entrapped between it and abductor hallucis in Baxter neuropathy.
cards.exam: Q. What is the functional importance of quadratus plantae? A. It corrects the oblique pull of the flexor digitorum longus tendons so the toes flex in line.

cards.desc: Superficial flexor of the forearm lying medial to pronator teres, its tendon a key landmark at the wrist.
cards.att: Origin: medial epicondyle of the humerus by the common flexor tendon, and the antebrachial fascia. Insertion: base of the second metacarpal, with a slip to the base of the third metacarpal.
cards.sup: Median nerve (C6, C7).
cards.act: Flexes the wrist and assists abduction (radial deviation); weakly assists elbow flexion and pronation.
cards.rel: Its tendon runs in a separate compartment of the flexor retinaculum in a groove on the trapezium; the radial artery lies immediately lateral to it at the wrist and the median nerve lies medial, between it and palmaris longus.
cards.clin: The tendon is the guide to the radial artery for pulse palpation and arterial line placement, and marks the interval used in the volar (Henry) approach to the distal radius. Its groove on the trapezium is involved in flexor carpi radialis tendinitis with basal thumb arthritis.
cards.exam: Q. Which structure lies immediately lateral to the flexor carpi radialis tendon at the wrist? A. The radial artery.

cards.k: flexor digiti minimi brevis of hand
cards.latin: musculus flexor digiti minimi brevis manus
cards.desc: Middle hypothenar muscle lying lateral to abductor digiti minimi in the ulnar side of the palm.
cards.att: Origin: hook of the hamate and the adjacent flexor retinaculum. Insertion: medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the little finger, with abductor digiti minimi.
cards.sup: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8, T1).
cards.act: Flexes the little finger at the metacarpophalangeal joint.
cards.rel: Lies lateral to abductor digiti minimi and superficial to opponens digiti minimi; the deep branch of the ulnar nerve and the deep palmar arch pass between it and abductor digiti minimi to enter the palm.
cards.clin: Frequently small or absent. Fractures of the hook of the hamate, seen in racquet and club sports, disturb its origin and threaten the adjacent ulnar nerve and artery in the canal of Guyon.
cards.exam: Q. What is the bony origin of flexor digiti minimi brevis of the hand? A. The hook of the hamate.

cards.desc: Central muscle of the first layer of the sole, lying immediately deep to the plantar aponeurosis.
cards.att: Origin: medial process of the tuberosity of the calcaneus, the plantar aponeurosis and the intermuscular septa. Insertion: by four tendons; each divides opposite the proximal phalanx and inserts on the sides of the middle phalanx of the lateral four toes.
cards.sup: Medial plantar nerve (S2, S3).
cards.act: Flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints and then the metatarsophalangeal joints of the lateral four toes; grips the ground and supports the medial longitudinal arch.
cards.rel: Lies between the plantar aponeurosis superficially and quadratus plantae with the long flexor tendons deeply; the plantar vessels and nerves lie on either side of it in the medial and lateral plantar spaces.
cards.clin: Its calcaneal origin, shared with the plantar aponeurosis, is the site of pain and traction in plantar fasciitis and calcaneal spur. Each tendon is perforated by the tendon of flexor digitorum longus, exactly as flexor digitorum superficialis is by profundus in the hand.
cards.exam: Q. Where do the tendons of flexor digitorum brevis insert? A. On the sides of the middle phalanges of the lateral four toes, after being perforated by the flexor digitorum longus tendons.

cards.desc: Most medial muscle of the deep posterior compartment of the leg, flexing the lateral four toes.
cards.att: Origin: posterior surface of the shaft of the tibia below the soleal line, medial to the vertical line. Insertion: by four tendons into the plantar surfaces of the bases of the distal phalanges of the lateral four toes, after crossing superficial to the tendon of flexor hallucis longus in the sole.
cards.sup: Tibial nerve (S2, S3).
cards.act: Flexes the distal interphalangeal joints and then the other joints of the lateral four toes; assists plantarflexion and inversion and supports the longitudinal arches.
cards.rel: Its tendon passes behind the medial malleolus in a groove on the tibia, second in the order tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, posterior tibial artery, tibial nerve, flexor hallucis longus. In the sole it crosses the flexor hallucis longus tendon at the knot of Henry, receives quadratus plantae and gives origin to the lumbricals.
cards.clin: Tested by asking the patient to flex the toes against resistance; its tendon is transferred for tibialis posterior dysfunction and for flexible claw toe correction. Traced behind the medial malleolus, it is a fixed landmark in the tarsal tunnel.
cards.exam: Q. What is the knot of Henry? A. The crossing in the sole where the tendon of flexor digitorum longus passes superficial to that of flexor hallucis longus, which sends it a slip.

cards.desc: Deep flexor of the forearm, the only muscle able to flex the distal interphalangeal joints of the fingers.
cards.att: Origin: upper three-quarters of the anterior and medial surfaces of the ulna, the adjacent interosseous membrane and the deep fascia of the forearm. Insertion: by four tendons into the palmar surfaces of the bases of the distal phalanges of the medial four fingers.
cards.sup: Dual: the medial half (ring and little fingers) by the ulnar nerve (C8, T1), the lateral half (index and middle fingers) by the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve (C8, T1).
cards.act: Flexes the distal interphalangeal joints, then the proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints and the wrist.
cards.rel: Lies deep to flexor digitorum superficialis. The four lumbricals arise from the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus in the palm. Its tendons pass through the carpal tunnel, then through the split in the superficialis tendons within the digital fibrous flexor sheaths.
cards.clin: Tested by holding the middle phalanx and asking the patient to bend the fingertip. Avulsion of the tendon from the distal phalanx, usually of the ring finger, is jersey finger. Its dual nerve supply explains the ulnar claw hand and the paradox that a high ulnar lesion causes less clawing than a low one.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerves supply flexor digitorum profundus? A. Ulnar nerve to the medial half and anterior interosseous nerve to the lateral half, both C8, T1.

cards.desc: Intermediate layer flexor of the forearm, forming a plane between the superficial flexors and flexor digitorum profundus.
cards.att: Origin: humeroulnar head from the medial epicondyle, ulnar collateral ligament and medial border of the coronoid process; radial head from the oblique line and upper anterior border of the radius. Insertion: by four tendons that split to attach to the sides of the middle phalanges of the medial four fingers.
cards.sup: Median nerve (C7, C8, T1).
cards.act: Flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints of the medial four fingers, then the metacarpophalangeal joints and the wrist.
cards.rel: The median nerve and ulnar artery enter the forearm by passing deep to its fibrous arch (the sublimis bridge) between the two heads; the median nerve then runs on its deep surface. Its four tendons pass through the carpal tunnel, the middle and ring finger tendons anterior to those of the index and little fingers.
cards.clin: The fibrous arch between the two heads is a site of median nerve entrapment (pronator or sublimis syndrome). Tested by holding the other fingers extended to eliminate profundus and asking the patient to flex the proximal interphalangeal joint.
cards.exam: Q. What passes between the two heads of flexor digitorum superficialis? A. The median nerve and the ulnar artery.

cards.desc: Most lateral and most powerful muscle of the deep posterior compartment of the leg, flexing the great toe.
cards.att: Origin: lower two thirds of the posterior surface of the fibula and the adjacent interosseous membrane. Insertion: plantar surface of the base of the distal phalanx of the great toe, after grooving the posterior surface of the talus and the undersurface of the sustentaculum tali.
cards.sup: Tibial nerve (S2, S3).
cards.act: Flexes the great toe, gives the final thrust in walking and running, plantarflexes the ankle and supports the medial longitudinal arch.
cards.rel: Its tendon is the most lateral structure behind the medial malleolus and lies between the two tubercles of the posterior process of the talus. In the sole it crosses deep to the tendon of flexor digitorum longus at the knot of Henry, to which it sends a slip.
cards.clin: Inflamed where it passes behind the talus in ballet dancers, giving posteromedial ankle pain aggravated in full plantarflexion, often with an os trigonum. Its tendon crossing the sustentaculum tali is a reliable landmark in medial hindfoot surgery.
cards.exam: Q. Which tendon lies most laterally in the tarsal tunnel behind the medial malleolus? A. Flexor hallucis longus.

cards.desc: Thenar muscle medial to abductor pollicis brevis, with two heads and a divided nerve supply.
cards.att: Origin: superficial head from the flexor retinaculum and tubercle of the trapezium; deep head from the trapezoid and capitate. Insertion: lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb, through a tendon containing the radial sesamoid bone.
cards.sup: Superficial head by the recurrent branch of the median nerve (C8, T1); deep head by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8, T1).
cards.act: Flexes the thumb at the metacarpophalangeal joint and assists in opposition and medial rotation of the thumb.
cards.rel: The tendon of flexor pollicis longus passes between its two heads; abductor pollicis brevis lies lateral and superficial, adductor pollicis medial and deep.
cards.clin: Its dual innervation means thumb flexion may be partly preserved in either median or ulnar palsy, so it is unreliable for testing single nerve function; abductor pollicis brevis is used instead. The radial sesamoid in its tendon is a normal radiographic finding.
cards.exam: Q. Why is flexor pollicis brevis a poor test of median nerve function? A. Its deep head is supplied by the ulnar nerve, so thumb flexion persists in median palsy.

cards.desc: Deep flexor of the forearm lying lateral to flexor digitorum profundus, the only long flexor of the thumb.
cards.att: Origin: anterior surface of the radius below the radial tuberosity, the adjacent interosseous membrane and often a slip from the medial epicondyle or coronoid process. Insertion: palmar surface of the base of the distal phalanx of the thumb.
cards.sup: Anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve (C8, T1).
cards.act: Flexes the interphalangeal joint of the thumb, then the metacarpophalangeal and carpometacarpal joints and assists wrist flexion.
cards.rel: Lies lateral to flexor digitorum profundus, with the anterior interosseous nerve and vessels between them on the interosseous membrane; its tendon enters the carpal tunnel in its own synovial sheath, the radial bursa, and passes between the two heads of flexor pollicis brevis.
cards.clin: Inability to flex the interphalangeal joint of the thumb and the distal interphalangeal joint of the index finger gives the abnormal OK sign of anterior interosseous nerve syndrome. Its radial bursa is a route for spread of thumb pulp infection into the forearm.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve supplies flexor pollicis longus and what sign indicates its palsy? A. The anterior interosseous nerve (C8, T1); an abnormal OK sign with the thumb interphalangeal joint held straight.

cards.desc: A thick fibrous band bridging the concavity of the carpus and converting the carpal arch into the carpal tunnel.
cards.att: Attached medially to the pisiform and the hook of the hamate, and laterally to the tubercle of the scaphoid and the ridge of the trapezium; continuous above with the deep fascia of the forearm and below with the palmar aponeurosis.
cards.act: Holds the long flexor tendons against the carpus, preventing bowstringing during wrist flexion, and gives origin to the thenar and hypothenar muscles.
cards.rel: Deep to it in the carpal tunnel run the median nerve and nine tendons: four of flexor digitorum superficialis, four of flexor digitorum profundus and one of flexor pollicis longus. Superficial to it pass the ulnar nerve and artery in the canal of Guyon, the palmar cutaneous branches of the median and ulnar nerves, and the tendon of palmaris longus, which is partly inserted into it.
cards.clin: Thickening or a reduction in tunnel volume compresses the median nerve, causing carpal tunnel syndrome with paraesthesia of the lateral three and a half digits and thenar wasting; sensation over the thenar eminence is spared because the palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to the retinaculum. Surgical release divides the retinaculum.
cards.exam: Q. Why is thenar skin sensation preserved in carpal tunnel syndrome? A. The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises proximally and crosses superficial to the flexor retinaculum.

cards.desc: Arched bundle of white matter forming the principal efferent pathway of the hippocampal formation, running from the temporal lobe beneath the corpus callosum to the hypothalamus.
cards.att: Begins as the alveus on the ventricular surface of the hippocampus, gathers as the fimbria, becomes the crus, the two crura join beneath the corpus callosum to form the body, which divides in front into the two columns; postcommissural fibres end mainly in the mammillary body and precommissural fibres in the septal region.
cards.act: Carries hippocampal output to the mammillary body, septal nuclei and anterior thalamus; a key limb of the Papez circuit and of memory consolidation.
cards.rel: Body forms the roof of the third ventricle with the tela choroidea; the column forms the anterior boundary of the interventricular foramen, with the anterior tubercle of the thalamus behind. The crura lie beneath the splenium, joined by the commissure of the fornix.
cards.clin: Bilateral damage to the fornix, for example during removal of a third ventricular colloid cyst or from a midline tumour, causes anterograde amnesia. A colloid cyst wedged between the columns at the interventricular foramen causes acute obstructive hydrocephalus with positional headache and drop attacks.
cards.exam: Q. What forms the anterior boundary of the interventricular foramen? A. The column of the fornix.

cards.desc: A typical cervical vertebra at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage.
cards.att: Small broad body with uncinate processes, triangular vertebral foramen, transverse processes with a foramen transversarium and anterior and posterior tubercles, and a short bifid spine. Articulates with C3 above and C5 below at the disc and zygapophysial joints.
cards.sup: Foramen transversarium transmits the vertebral artery and vein and its sympathetic plexus.
cards.act: Transmits axial load and, with the other cervical vertebrae, allows the wide range of neck movement while protecting the spinal cord.
cards.rel: Lies at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, where the common carotid artery bifurcates and the carotid sinus and body lie. The ventral ramus of C4 emerges in the groove of its transverse process and contributes the main root of the phrenic nerve.
cards.clin: The C4 dermatome covers the tip of the shoulder, so shoulder tip pain follows diaphragmatic irritation through the phrenic nerve. Cord injury above C4 abolishes diaphragmatic breathing, hence the rule that C3, C4 and C5 keep the diaphragm alive.
cards.exam: Q. What surface landmark corresponds to the C4 vertebral level? A. The upper border of the thyroid cartilage, the level at which the common carotid artery bifurcates.

cards.desc: Hyaline cartilage bar connecting the 4th rib to the lateral border of the body of the sternum.
cards.att: Joins the 4th rib at the costochondral junction and the sternum at a synovial sternocostal joint with radiate ligaments; gives attachment to the sternocostal head of pectoralis major and, internally, to transversus thoracis.
cards.sup: Perichondrial branches of the internal thoracic artery.
cards.act: Transmits rib movement to the sternum and gives springiness to the anterior chest wall.
cards.rel: The internal thoracic vessels lie behind it a finger's breadth from the sternal border; the right atrium and right border of the heart lie deep to the right 3rd to 6th cartilages, and the horizontal fissure of the right lung runs forward to the level of the 4th costal cartilage.
cards.clin: The male nipple usually overlies the 4th intercostal space just below this cartilage, marking the T4 dermatome. Calcification of the costal cartilages with age is a normal radiographic finding.
cards.exam: Q. Which fissure of the lung reaches the anterior chest wall at the 4th costal cartilage? A. The horizontal (transverse) fissure of the right lung.

cards.desc: The fourth lumbar vertebra, the key surface landmark of the lumbar spine because the highest points of the iliac crests lie at its level.
cards.att: Typical lumbar form: large kidney-shaped body, hatchet-shaped spine, mamillary and accessory processes. Articulates with L3 above and L5 below at the discs and zygapophysial joints.
cards.sup: Fourth lumbar arteries from the abdominal aorta; internal and external vertebral venous plexuses.
cards.rel: The abdominal aorta bifurcates into the common iliac arteries at the lower border of L4, a little to the left of the midline. Psoas major and quadratus lumborum arise alongside the body and transverse process.
cards.clin: The supracristal (intercristal, Tuffier) plane joining the highest points of the iliac crests crosses the L4 spinous process or the L4/L5 interspace, the standard landmark for lumbar puncture and spinal anaesthesia in the adult.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the abdominal aorta bifurcate? A. At the lower border of the fourth lumbar vertebra, on the supracristal plane.

cards.desc: Slender metacarpal of the ring finger ray, lying between the third and fifth metacarpals.
cards.att: Base articulates with the hamate and a small part of the capitate proximally, and with the third and fifth metacarpals on either side. The third palmar interosseous and parts of the third and fourth dorsal interossei arise from its shaft; the head carries the deep transverse metacarpal ligament and the collateral ligaments of the metacarpophalangeal joint.
cards.rel: The deep palmar arch and the deep branch of the ulnar nerve cross its palmar surface near the base. The fourth carpometacarpal joint permits slight flexion, contributing to cupping of the palm.
cards.clin: A short fourth metacarpal, seen as a dimple instead of a knuckle when the fist is clenched, is the classic sign of pseudohypoparathyroidism and of Turner syndrome. Fractures of the shaft and neck are managed with attention to rotational alignment, judged by the direction of the flexed fingers.
cards.exam: Q. What is the significance of a short fourth metacarpal? A. It is a feature of pseudohypoparathyroidism and Turner syndrome, seen as an absent knuckle on clenching the fist.

cards.desc: Typical true rib reaching the sternum by its own costal cartilage, at about the level of the male nipple.
cards.att: Head bears two facets for the inferior demifacet of T3, the superior demifacet of T4 and the disc between; the tubercle articulates with the transverse process of T4; the shaft shows an angle and a costal groove. Serratus anterior gives a digitation to it and the intercostal muscles attach along its borders.
cards.sup: Fourth posterior intercostal artery from the thoracic aorta and anterior intercostal branches of the internal thoracic artery; the 4th intercostal nerve lies in its costal groove.
cards.act: Combined pump-handle and bucket-handle elevation enlarges the thorax in inspiration.
cards.rel: Neurovascular bundle in the costal groove, vein above, then artery, then nerve; parietal pleura internally; pectoralis major and the breast lie superficially.
cards.clin: The safe triangle for chest drain insertion, bounded by the lateral border of pectoralis major, the anterior border of latissimus dorsi and the horizontal level of the nipple, uses the 4th or 5th intercostal space; current practice also decompresses a tension pneumothorax here rather than at the 2nd space.
cards.exam: Q. Why is a needle inserted just above the lower rib of an intercostal space? A. To avoid the main intercostal vein, artery and nerve, which run in the costal groove of the rib above.

cards.desc: Typical upper thoracic vertebra whose lower border, with the T4/T5 disc, lies in the plane of the sternal angle.
cards.att: Superior demifacet for the head of rib 4 and inferior demifacet for the head of rib 5; the transverse process carries a facet for the tubercle of rib 4; the long spine slopes downwards over the vertebra below.
cards.sup: Segmental posterior intercostal branches; dorsal rami to the facets and periosteum.
cards.act: Load transmission, cord protection and rib articulation permitting rotation.
cards.rel: The arch of the aorta arches backwards and to the left across its body; the trachea bifurcates and the azygos vein arches forward over the right main bronchus at this level; the oesophagus and thoracic duct lie in front.
cards.clin: The transverse thoracic plane through the sternal angle and the T4/T5 disc separates superior from inferior mediastinum and marks the tracheal bifurcation, the beginning and end of the aortic arch and the level of the 2nd costal cartilage. The T4 dermatome lies at the nipple line, used to check the height of a spinal block.
cards.exam: Q. Name three structures found at the level of the sternal angle. A. Bifurcation of the trachea, the beginning and end of the arch of the aorta, and the articulation of the 2nd costal cartilage, all at the T4/T5 disc.

cards.desc: Tent-shaped cavity of the hindbrain lying between the pons and upper medulla in front and the cerebellum behind, diamond-shaped in its floor.
cards.att: Continuous above with the cerebral aqueduct and below with the central canal of the medulla; communicates with the subarachnoid space through the median aperture of Magendie and the paired lateral apertures of Luschka.
cards.act: Contains cerebrospinal fluid and, through its apertures, is the only route by which cerebrospinal fluid leaves the ventricular system for the subarachnoid space.
cards.rel: Floor, the rhomboid fossa, is formed by the posterior surface of the pons and open part of the medulla and overlies the cranial nerve nuclei, with the facial colliculus, median sulcus, sulcus limitans, vestibular area and hypoglossal and vagal trigones. Roof is formed above by the superior cerebellar peduncles and superior medullary velum, below by the inferior medullary velum and tela choroidea.
cards.clin: Obstruction of the outlet foramina, as in Dandy-Walker malformation, causes hydrocephalus with a grossly dilated fourth ventricle. A lesion at the facial colliculus damages the abducent nucleus and the looping facial fibres, giving ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy with lower motor neuron facial palsy.
cards.exam: Q. Name the apertures of the fourth ventricle. A. The median aperture of Magendie and the two lateral apertures of Luschka.

cards.desc: Unpaired bone forming the forehead, the roofs of the orbits and the floor of the anterior cranial fossa.
cards.att: Has a squamous part with the glabella, superciliary arches and frontal eminences, two orbital plates and a nasal part. Bears the supraorbital margin with a supraorbital notch or foramen, the frontal crest and foramen caecum internally, the lacrimal fossa laterally in the orbital plate and the trochlear fovea medially, and encloses the frontal sinuses. Articulates with the parietals at the coronal suture, and with the sphenoid, ethmoid, nasal, lacrimal, maxillary and zygomatic bones.
cards.sup: Supraorbital and supratrochlear branches of the ophthalmic artery and the middle meningeal artery internally; sensory supply of the overlying skin and sinus by the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves (V1).
cards.act: Protects the frontal lobes, roofs the orbit, and its air sinuses lighten the skull and add resonance to the voice.
cards.rel: Frontal lobes and the falx attachment lie on its internal surface, the orbital contents and the lacrimal gland below the orbital plate, and the frontal sinus drains into the middle meatus through the frontonasal duct and ethmoidal infundibulum.
cards.clin: Persistence of the metopic suture in the adult can be mistaken for a fracture. The supraorbital nerve is blocked at the supraorbital notch, palpable at the junction of the medial third and lateral two thirds of the supraorbital margin. Frontal sinusitis causes tenderness over the floor of the sinus and can spread to the meninges.
cards.exam: Q. What is the metopic suture? A. The persistent midline frontal suture between the two halves of the frontal bone, normally obliterated by about the sixth year.

cards.desc: The largest branch of the ophthalmic nerve, running forwards on the roof of the orbit just beneath the periorbita.
cards.att: Arises from the ophthalmic nerve in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus, enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure outside the common tendinous ring, runs forward on the upper surface of levator palpebrae superioris, and divides about halfway into the supra-orbital and supratrochlear nerves.
cards.act: Sensory to the forehead and scalp as far back as the vertex, the upper eyelid and conjunctiva, and the mucosa of the frontal sinus.
cards.rel: Lies between levator palpebrae superioris below and the periorbita of the orbital roof above; the trochlear nerve lies medial to it as both enter the fissure, and the lacrimal nerve lies lateral.
cards.clin: Its position immediately under the orbital roof makes it the nerve reached by a subperiosteal approach to the superior orbit, and pain over the forehead in frontal sinusitis is referred along it.
cards.exam: Q. Which three nerves enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure outside the common tendinous ring? A. The lacrimal, frontal and trochlear nerves.

cards.desc: Long gyrus on the inferior surface of the temporal and occipital lobes, lying between the collateral sulcus medially and the occipitotemporal sulcus laterally.
cards.att: Part of the ventral visual stream; connected forwards to the temporal pole and backwards to the striate and extrastriate visual cortex through the inferior longitudinal fasciculus.
cards.sup: Branches of the posterior cerebral artery, with the anterior part also receiving temporal branches of the middle cerebral artery.
cards.act: High-order visual recognition of faces, objects, colour and visual word forms; the mid-fusiform region is the fusiform face area.
cards.rel: Lies between the parahippocampal and lingual gyri medially and the inferior temporal gyrus laterally; the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle lies above its medial part.
cards.clin: Bilateral, and sometimes right-sided, lesions of the fusiform gyrus cause prosopagnosia, an inability to recognise familiar faces with preserved recognition by voice. A left posterior fusiform lesion involves the visual word form area and contributes to alexia.
cards.exam: Q. A patient cannot recognise his wife's face but knows her voice. Where is the lesion? A. The fusiform gyrus, typically bilateral or right-sided, causing prosopagnosia.

cards.desc: Pear-shaped sac of about 50 mL capacity lying in a fossa on the inferior surface of the right lobe of the liver, on the line separating the right and left functional lobes.
cards.att: Has a fundus, body and neck. The fundus projects beyond the inferior border of the liver at the tip of the ninth costal cartilage, where the lateral border of the right rectus abdominis crosses the costal margin. The neck narrows into the cystic duct and often bears a posteromedial dilatation, Hartmann's pouch. Its upper surface is attached to the liver, the rest covered by peritoneum.
cards.sup: Cystic artery from the right hepatic artery in Calot's triangle. Cystic veins drain into the portal vein and directly into the liver bed. Lymph to the cystic node of Lund, then hepatic and coeliac nodes. Parasympathetic supply from the vagus; sympathetic and visceral afferent fibres from T7 to T9 via the coeliac plexus.
cards.act: Stores and concentrates bile, and expels it into the duodenum under cholecystokinin stimulation.
cards.rel: The body lies on the transverse colon and the first and second parts of the duodenum. The fundus contacts the anterior abdominal wall at the tip of the ninth costal cartilage.
cards.clin: Murphy's sign is arrest of inspiration on palpation below the right costal margin in acute cholecystitis. Referred pain to the right shoulder tip (C3, C4) indicates diaphragmatic peritoneal irritation. A gallstone eroding into the duodenum can obstruct the terminal ileum (gallstone ileus).
cards.exam: Q. Where does the fundus of the gallbladder meet the anterior abdominal wall? A. At the tip of the ninth costal cartilage, where the lateral border of rectus abdominis crosses the costal margin.

cards.desc: Paired arteries running along the lesser curvature of the stomach between the layers of the lesser omentum, the left from the coeliac trunk and the right usually from the hepatic artery proper.
cards.att: The left gastric artery arises from the coeliac trunk, ascends to the cardia raising the gastropancreatic fold, then turns along the lesser curvature. The right gastric artery arises from the hepatic artery proper or common hepatic artery and runs to the left along the lesser curvature to anastomose with the left.
cards.sup: Oesophageal branches from the left gastric, gastric branches to both surfaces of the stomach; an accessory or replaced left hepatic artery may arise from the left gastric artery.
cards.act: Supply the lesser curvature and adjacent walls of the stomach and the abdominal oesophagus.
cards.rel: Both lie between the two layers of the lesser omentum along the lesser curvature, accompanied by the corresponding veins and by gastric lymph nodes.
cards.clin: The left gastric artery is the usual bleeding vessel in a chronic lesser curve gastric ulcer and is the target of angiographic embolisation. Its oesophageal branches accompany the veins that become oesophageal varices in portal hypertension.
cards.exam: Q. What is the commonest important arterial variant arising from the left gastric artery? A. An accessory or replaced left hepatic artery.

cards.desc: Paired veins accompanying the gastric arteries along the lesser curvature and draining directly into the hepatic portal vein.
cards.att: The left gastric (coronary) vein runs along the lesser curvature to the cardia, then turns backwards and to the right to enter the portal vein. The right gastric vein runs to the right along the lesser curvature and joins the portal vein above the pylorus.
cards.sup: The left gastric vein receives oesophageal tributaries; the right gastric vein receives the prepyloric vein of Mayo.
cards.act: Drain the lesser curvature of the stomach and the lower oesophagus into the portal system.
cards.rel: Both lie in the lesser omentum beside the corresponding arteries; the left gastric vein crosses behind or in front of the hepatic artery proper to reach the portal vein.
cards.clin: Oesophageal tributaries of the left gastric vein anastomose with oesophageal tributaries of the azygos vein; in portal hypertension this becomes oesophageal varices, the most lethal portosystemic shunt. The prepyloric vein of Mayo identifies the pylorus at operation.
cards.exam: Q. Which portosystemic anastomosis involves the left gastric vein? A. Its oesophageal tributaries with the oesophageal tributaries of the azygos vein, at the lower end of the oesophagus.

cards.desc: Paired arteries running along the greater curvature of the stomach between the layers of the greater omentum, the right from the gastroduodenal artery and the left from the splenic artery.
cards.att: The right gastro-omental artery arises from the gastroduodenal artery behind the first part of the duodenum and runs to the left; the left arises from the splenic artery near the splenic hilum and runs to the right; the two anastomose along the greater curvature.
cards.sup: Gastric branches to both surfaces of the stomach and omental (epiploic) branches descending into the greater omentum.
cards.act: Supply the greater curvature of the stomach and the greater omentum.
cards.rel: Lie about a finger's breadth from the greater curvature between the anterior two layers of the greater omentum, with the gastro-omental lymph nodes alongside.
cards.clin: The right gastro-epiploic artery is the pedicle of the gastric conduit after oesophagectomy and is preserved carefully during gastric mobilisation; it is also used as an arterial graft in coronary bypass surgery.
cards.exam: Q. From which arteries do the right and left gastro-omental arteries arise? A. The right from the gastroduodenal artery and the left from the splenic artery.

cards.desc: The largest extrinsic muscle of the tongue, a fan-shaped sheet forming the bulk of its substance close to the midline septum.
cards.att: Arises from the superior genial tubercle on the inner surface of the mandibular symphysis; fibres fan backwards and upwards, the lowest to the body of the hyoid, the rest into the whole length of the ventral surface of the tongue from root to tip.
cards.sup: Hypoglossal nerve; lingual artery.
cards.act: Protrudes the tongue and depresses its central part; the posterior fibres pull the root forwards, keeping the oropharyngeal airway open.
cards.rel: Separated from its fellow by the lingual septum; geniohyoid lies below it and the sublingual gland and lingual nerve lie laterally. The deep lingual artery and vein lie on its lateral surface.
cards.clin: Called the safety muscle of the tongue: loss of its tone in coma or general anaesthesia lets the tongue fall back and obstruct the airway, which is why the jaw is thrust forward. In a unilateral hypoglossal nerve lesion the protruded tongue deviates towards the paralysed side because the intact genioglossus is unopposed.
