cards.exam: Q. Why does the tongue deviate to the side of the lesion in hypoglossal palsy? A. The normal genioglossus protrudes its own half unopposed, pushing the tip towards the paralysed side.

cards.desc: A short narrow suprahyoid muscle lying alongside the midline on the upper surface of mylohyoid in the floor of the mouth.
cards.att: Arises from the inferior genial tubercle on the back of the mandibular symphysis and passes backwards and slightly downwards to insert on the anterior surface of the body of the hyoid bone.
cards.sup: Fibres of the first cervical nerve (C1) carried by the hypoglossal nerve; blood supply from the lingual and submental arteries.
cards.act: Elevates the hyoid and draws it forwards, widening the pharynx during swallowing; depresses the mandible when the hyoid is fixed.
cards.rel: Lies above mylohyoid and below genioglossus, in contact with its fellow of the opposite side across the midline.
cards.clin: Its forward pull on the hyoid enlarges the retrolingual airway, and geniohyoid advancement is used in surgery for obstructive sleep apnoea. Although a suprahyoid muscle, it is supplied by C1 and not by a branchial nerve, so it is spared in mandibular nerve lesions.
cards.exam: Q. What is the nerve supply of geniohyoid? A. C1 fibres travelling with the hypoglossal nerve.

cards.desc: The masticatory mucosa covering the alveolar process of the mandible and encircling the necks of the lower teeth.
cards.att: Firmly bound to the periosteum of the alveolar bone as attached gingiva and to the tooth by the junctional epithelium; the free gingiva forms the gingival sulcus around each tooth and the interdental papillae between them. Continuous with the alveolar mucosa at the mucogingival junction.
cards.sup: Sensory: buccal (labial) surface by the buccal nerve posteriorly, the mental and incisive branches of the inferior alveolar nerve anteriorly; lingual surface by the lingual nerve. All are branches of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. Arteries from the inferior alveolar, lingual, buccal and facial arteries.
cards.act: Forms a protective epithelial seal around the necks of the teeth and resists the shearing forces of mastication.
cards.rel: Continuous with the mucosa of the floor of the mouth lingually and the labial and buccal vestibule externally; overlies the alveolar bone and the roots of the mandibular teeth.
cards.clin: Because the buccal and lingual gingiva have separate nerve supplies, extraction of a lower tooth needs both an inferior alveolar (or mental) block and a lingual nerve block. Plaque-induced gingivitis is the earliest and reversible stage of periodontal disease.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve supplies the lingual gingiva of the lower jaw? A. The lingual nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.

cards.desc: The masticatory mucosa covering the alveolar process of the maxilla and surrounding the necks of the upper teeth.
cards.att: Attached gingiva bound to the periosteum of the maxillary alveolar bone, with free gingiva and interdental papillae around the teeth; continuous with the hard palate mucosa palatally and with the labial and buccal vestibular mucosa externally.
cards.sup: Sensory: labial and buccal surfaces by the anterior, middle and posterior superior alveolar nerves; palatal surface by the greater palatine nerve posteriorly and the nasopalatine nerve anteriorly. All from the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve. Arteries from the superior alveolar, greater palatine and infraorbital arteries.
cards.act: Seals and protects the necks of the upper teeth and withstands masticatory friction.
cards.rel: Overlies the alveolar bone and the roots of the maxillary teeth, with the maxillary sinus lying above the roots of the premolars and molars.
cards.clin: Drug-induced gingival overgrowth is classically caused by phenytoin, ciclosporin and nifedipine. Anaesthesia for an upper molar extraction requires buccal infiltration plus a greater palatine block for the palatal gingiva.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve supplies the palatal gingiva behind the canines? A. The greater palatine nerve.

cards.desc: Conical expansion of the corpus spongiosum capping the distal ends of the corpora cavernosa and bearing the external urethral orifice.
cards.att: Its base overhangs the ends of the corpora cavernosa as the corona, behind which is the constricted neck; it is covered by the prepuce, tethered ventrally by the frenulum.
cards.sup: Arteries: dorsal artery of the penis and the urethral artery from the internal pudendal. Sensory supply: dorsal nerve of the penis from the pudendal nerve (S2, S3, S4). Lymphatics drain to the deep inguinal nodes, including the node of Cloquet, and to external iliac nodes.
cards.act: Densely innervated sensory end organ of the penis; its urethral orifice is the narrowest part of the male urethra.
cards.rel: Continuous proximally with the corpus spongiosum; the navicular fossa of the urethra lies within it; prepuce and preputial sac lie superficially.
cards.clin: Phimosis prevents retraction of the prepuce; a retracted tight prepuce trapped behind the corona causes paraphimosis with venous congestion, a urological emergency. Carcinoma of the glans spreads to inguinal nodes, unlike testicular tumours which go to para-aortic nodes.
cards.exam: Q. Where does lymph from the glans penis drain? A. Mainly to the deep inguinal nodes, including the node of Cloquet.

cards.desc: Pale, heavily myelinated medial part of the lentiform nucleus, wedge-shaped in horizontal section, lying medial to the putamen and lateral to the internal capsule.
cards.att: Divided by the medial medullary lamina into external and internal segments and separated from the putamen by the lateral medullary lamina. Receives from the striatum and subthalamic nucleus; the internal segment projects to the thalamus through the ansa lenticularis and lenticular fasciculus, which join as the thalamic fasciculus.
cards.sup: Lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery and the anterior choroidal artery.
cards.act: Principal output nucleus of the basal ganglia, regulating the thalamocortical drive to the motor cortex and thereby the scaling and smoothness of voluntary movement.
cards.rel: Lateral to the genu and posterior limb of the internal capsule and to the caudate nucleus and thalamus beyond it; the putamen lies lateral, and the optic tract and substantia innominata lie below.
cards.clin: The internal segment is the classic target for pallidotomy and for deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease and dystonia. Bilateral pallidal necrosis is characteristic of carbon monoxide poisoning.
cards.exam: Q. Which structure separates the globus pallidus from the putamen? A. The lateral medullary lamina.

cards.desc: Largest and most superficial muscle of the gluteal region, giving the buttock its shape.
cards.att: Origin: outer surface of the ilium behind the posterior gluteal line, the posterior surface of the lower sacrum and the side of the coccyx, the sacrotuberous ligament and the aponeurosis of erector spinae. Insertion: upper three quarters into the iliotibial tract of the fascia lata; deeper lower quarter into the gluteal tuberosity of the femur.
cards.sup: Inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1, S2).
cards.act: Powerful extensor and lateral rotator of the hip, used chiefly in climbing stairs, running and rising from a seated position; through the iliotibial tract it steadies the femur on the tibia in extension.
cards.rel: Covers the short lateral rotators and the structures leaving the greater sciatic foramen, including the sciatic nerve; three bursae lie deep to it, over the greater trochanter, the ischial tuberosity and the gluteal tuberosity.
cards.clin: Intramuscular injections are given in the upper outer quadrant of the buttock to avoid the sciatic nerve, which lies midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter. Weakness makes the patient lean the trunk backwards over the affected hip during stance, the gluteus maximus lurch.
cards.exam: Q. Why is the upper outer quadrant of the buttock chosen for intramuscular injection? A. To avoid the sciatic nerve and the gluteal vessels, which lie in the lower and medial quadrants.

cards.desc: Thick fan shaped abductor of the hip lying deep to gluteus maximus on the outer surface of the ilium.
cards.att: Origin: outer surface of the ilium between the posterior and anterior gluteal lines, and the overlying gluteal aponeurosis. Insertion: oblique ridge on the lateral surface of the greater trochanter of the femur.
cards.sup: Superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1).
cards.act: Abducts the thigh; anterior fibres medially rotate it. In walking it prevents the pelvis from dropping on the unsupported side when the opposite foot is off the ground.
cards.rel: Covered posteriorly by gluteus maximus and anteriorly only by fascia; covers gluteus minimus and the superior gluteal vessels and nerve, which run forwards between the two muscles. The trochanteric bursa separates its tendon from the greater trochanter.
cards.clin: Paralysis from a superior gluteal nerve injury, badly placed injection or hip disease gives a positive Trendelenburg sign, the pelvis sagging on the opposite unsupported side when standing on the affected leg. Its tendon degenerates in greater trochanteric pain syndrome.
cards.exam: Q. Standing on the right leg the left side of the pelvis drops. Which muscles and nerve are affected? A. Right gluteus medius and minimus, supplied by the right superior gluteal nerve.

cards.desc: Smallest and deepest of the three glutei, fan shaped and lying directly on the ilium.
cards.att: Origin: outer surface of the ilium between the anterior and inferior gluteal lines. Insertion: anterior surface of the greater trochanter of the femur, with a slip to the capsule of the hip joint.
cards.sup: Superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1).
cards.act: Abducts and medially rotates the thigh; with gluteus medius it steadies the pelvis on the weight bearing limb during gait.
cards.rel: Lies deep to gluteus medius, with the superior gluteal vessels and nerve between the two; its deep surface lies on the capsule of the hip joint and on the reflected head of rectus femoris.
cards.clin: Acts with gluteus medius as the abductor mechanism, so both are lost together in a superior gluteal nerve lesion and both give a Trendelenburg gait. Its tendon is a common site of gluteal tendinopathy causing lateral hip pain.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscles are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve? A. Gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae.

cards.desc: Thin strap muscle along the medial border of the thigh, the most superficial of the adductor group and the only one crossing both hip and knee.
cards.att: Origin: medial margins of the lower half of the body of the pubis and the whole inferior pubic ramus and adjacent ramus of the ischium. Insertion: upper part of the medial surface of the shaft of the tibia, as part of the pes anserinus behind sartorius and above semitendinosus.
cards.sup: Obturator nerve, anterior division (L2, L3).
cards.act: Adducts the thigh at the hip; flexes the leg at the knee and medially rotates the flexed knee.
cards.rel: Forms the medial boundary of the thigh; its tendon lies between those of sartorius and semitendinosus at the pes anserinus, with the pes anserine bursa deep to them and the medial collateral ligament beneath.
cards.clin: Harvested with semitendinosus as a hamstring graft for anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, and transferred as a free functioning muscle flap for facial reanimation or as a graciloplasty for faecal incontinence, because its loss causes little functional deficit.
cards.exam: Q. Which three tendons form the pes anserinus? A. Sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus, from anterior to posterior.

cards.desc: Longest vein in the body, running the whole length of the lower limb in the superficial fascia on its medial side.
cards.att: Begins at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch of the foot, passes anterior to the medial malleolus, ascends the medial side of the leg with the saphenous nerve, passes a hand's breadth behind the medial border of the patella at the knee, ascends the medial thigh, and pierces the cribriform fascia at the saphenous opening about 3.5 cm below and lateral to the pubic tubercle to end in the femoral vein.
cards.sup: Near its termination it receives the superficial epigastric, superficial circumflex iliac and superficial and deep external pudendal veins; along its course it receives the accessory saphenous veins and communicates with the deep veins through perforating veins, notably in the leg.
cards.act: Superficial venous drainage of the medial foot, leg and thigh; contains about 10 to 20 valves that direct flow upwards and inwards.
cards.rel: Accompanied by the saphenous nerve from the knee downwards, and lies with the ilio-inguinal and superficial inguinal lymph nodes near the saphenofemoral junction.
cards.clin: Incompetent valves at the saphenofemoral junction and in perforating veins cause varicose veins, tested by the Trendelenburg test. It is the classic conduit for coronary artery bypass grafting, reversed to allow flow past its valves. Stripping below the knee risks saphenous nerve injury with numbness along the medial leg and foot.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the great saphenous vein pass in relation to the medial malleolus, and which nerve accompanies it there? A. Anterior to the medial malleolus, accompanied by the saphenous nerve.

cards.desc: Wedge-shaped bone at the medial end of the distal carpal row, distinguished by the hook (hamulus) projecting from its palmar surface.
cards.att: Articulates with the lunate proximally, the triquetrum medially, the capitate laterally, and the bases of the fourth and fifth metacarpals distally. The hook gives attachment to the flexor retinaculum, the pisohamate ligament, and the origins of flexor and opponens digiti minimi.
cards.rel: The hook forms the medial pillar of the carpal tunnel and the lateral wall of the ulnar canal (canal of Guyon), so the ulnar nerve and artery lie immediately lateral to the pisiform and medial to the hook. The deep branch of the ulnar nerve then curves round the hook into the palm.
cards.clin: Fracture of the hook of the hamate occurs in golfers, cricketers and racquet players from the butt of the handle, and gives deep ulnar-sided palmar tenderness with possible ulnar nerve palsy or attritional rupture of the little finger flexor tendons. It is missed on standard views and needs a carpal tunnel view or CT.
cards.exam: Q. Which structures are at risk in a fracture of the hook of the hamate? A. The ulnar nerve and artery in Guyon's canal, and the flexor tendons of the little finger, which may rupture by attrition.

cards.desc: Left-sided counterpart of the lower azygos vein, draining the lower left posterior intercostal spaces into the azygos vein.
cards.att: Formed at about L1 or L2 by the union of the left ascending lumbar vein and the left subcostal vein, enters the thorax through the left crus of the diaphragm, ascends on the left of the vertebral bodies to about T9, then crosses to the right behind the aorta, oesophagus and thoracic duct to join the azygos vein.
cards.sup: Tributaries: the lower three or four left posterior intercostal veins (usually 9th to 11th), the left subcostal vein, and oesophageal and mediastinal veins; it often communicates with the left renal vein below.
cards.act: Returns blood from the lower left intercostal spaces and posterior abdominal wall into the azygos system and hence to the superior vena cava.
cards.rel: Lies posterior to the descending thoracic aorta at its crossing, in front of the vertebral bodies, with the thoracic duct and azygos vein to its right.
cards.clin: With the ascending lumbar veins it forms a collateral channel in inferior vena caval obstruction. Its variable anatomy is important in posterior mediastinal dissection and in interpreting a paraspinal line on chest radiograph.
cards.exam: Q. At what level does the hemiazygos vein cross the midline? A. At about T9, passing behind the aorta, oesophagus and thoracic duct to join the azygos vein.

cards.desc: Continuation of the common hepatic artery beyond the origin of the gastroduodenal artery, ascending in the free edge of the lesser omentum to the porta hepatis.
cards.att: Begins where the common hepatic artery gives off the gastroduodenal artery, ascends in the hepatoduodenal ligament, and divides at or just below the porta hepatis into the right and left hepatic arteries.
cards.sup: Right and left hepatic arteries; the right hepatic gives the cystic artery, and the right gastric artery often arises from the proper hepatic.
cards.act: Delivers about a quarter of hepatic blood flow and roughly half the liver's oxygen, and is the arterial supply of the gallbladder and of the intrahepatic and upper extrahepatic bile ducts.
cards.rel: In the free edge of the lesser omentum it lies to the left of the bile duct and anterior to the portal vein; these three form the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen.
cards.clin: The cystic artery is sought in the cystohepatic triangle of Calot, bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the inferior surface of the liver; misidentification of structures here is the cause of bile duct injury at cholecystectomy. Hepatic artery thrombosis after liver transplantation causes ischaemic biliary strictures because the ducts have no other arterial supply.
cards.exam: Q. What are the contents of the free edge of the lesser omentum and their arrangement? A. Hepatic artery proper on the left, bile duct on the right, portal vein behind both.

cards.desc: The right and left hepatic ducts, emerging at the porta hepatis to drain the functional right and left halves of the liver and uniting to form the common hepatic duct.
cards.att: The right duct is formed inside the liver by the right anterior and right posterior sectoral ducts and is short, about 1 cm. The left duct drains segments II, III and IV, runs transversely along the base of the quadrate lobe and is longer, about 2 to 3 cm, with a longer extrahepatic course. They unite anterior to the right portal vein at the porta hepatis.
cards.sup: Arterial supply from the right and left hepatic arteries and the cystic artery. Lymph to hilar nodes.
cards.act: Convey bile from each functional half of the liver to the common hepatic duct.
cards.rel: Lie anterior to the portal vein branches and to the right of the hepatic arteries at the porta hepatis, where the arrangement from front to back is duct, artery, vein.
cards.clin: The longer extrahepatic left duct is used for hepaticojejunostomy (Hepp-Couinaud approach). Malignant stricture at the confluence is a Klatskin tumour, classified by the Bismuth-Corlette system. Aberrant right sectoral ducts joining the common hepatic or cystic duct are a common cause of bile leak after cholecystectomy.
cards.exam: Q. Give the front to back order of structures at the porta hepatis. A. Hepatic ducts anteriorly, hepatic arteries in the middle, portal vein posteriorly.

cards.desc: Short, wide, valveless vein about 8 cm long that carries venous blood from the gut, spleen and pancreas to the liver.
cards.att: Formed behind the neck of the pancreas at the level of L2 by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins; ascends behind the first part of the duodenum and then in the free edge of the lesser omentum, ending at the porta hepatis by dividing into right and left branches.
cards.sup: Tributaries: superior mesenteric, splenic, left and right gastric, cystic and para-umbilical veins; the inferior mesenteric vein drains into it indirectly through the splenic vein.
cards.act: Carries about 75 percent of hepatic blood flow, delivering absorbed nutrients from the gut to the hepatic sinusoids.
cards.rel: Lies posterior to the bile duct and the hepatic artery proper in the hepatoduodenal ligament and forms the anterior wall of the epiploic foramen, with the inferior vena cava behind the foramen.
cards.clin: Portal hypertension opens portosystemic anastomoses at the lower oesophagus, anal canal, umbilicus (caput medusae) and retroperitoneum, and causes splenomegaly and ascites. The portal triad including the portal vein is compressed in the free edge of the lesser omentum during the Pringle manoeuvre to control liver bleeding.
cards.exam: Q. Where and by which veins is the hepatic portal vein formed? A. Behind the neck of the pancreas at L2, by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins.

cards.desc: Large intrahepatic veins with almost no extrahepatic course, opening directly into the inferior vena cava in the groove on the bare area of the liver.
cards.att: The right hepatic vein runs in the right portal (intersegmental) plane and drains segments V to VIII; the left hepatic vein runs in the left portal plane and drains segments II and III with part of IV; both open into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm at about T8.
cards.sup: Receive intersegmental tributaries from the segments on either side; the caudate lobe drains separately by small veins directly into the inferior vena cava.
cards.act: Return all hepatic blood, both portal and arterial, to the systemic circulation.
cards.rel: Intersegmental and interlobar in position, lying between the portal triads, which are intrasegmental. The right hepatic vein separates the anterior from the posterior sector of the right hemiliver.
cards.clin: Hepatic venous outflow obstruction (Budd-Chiari syndrome) causes tender hepatomegaly, ascites and hypertrophy of the caudate lobe, which is spared because of its independent drainage. The hepatic veins define the planes of anatomical liver resection.
cards.exam: Q. Why is the caudate lobe spared and enlarged in Budd-Chiari syndrome? A. It drains by its own small veins directly into the inferior vena cava, not through the main hepatic veins.

cards.desc: Large irregular bone of the pelvic girdle formed by fusion of the ilium, ischium and pubis, meeting the sacrum behind and its fellow in front.
cards.att: The three parts fuse at the triradiate cartilage in the acetabulum in the mid-teens. Articulations: with the sacrum at the sacroiliac joint, with the head of the femur at the hip joint, and with the opposite hip bone at the pubic symphysis. Landmarks: iliac crest, anterior and posterior superior and inferior iliac spines, greater and lesser sciatic notches, ischial spine and tuberosity, obturator foramen, acetabulum with its notch, pubic tubercle, pecten pubis and iliopubic eminence.
cards.act: Transmits body weight from the vertebral column to the lower limb in standing and to the ischial tuberosities in sitting; gives attachment to abdominal wall, gluteal, hamstring, adductor and pelvic floor muscles.
cards.rel: The greater sciatic foramen transmits the piriformis, superior and inferior gluteal vessels and nerves, sciatic nerve, pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels; the lesser sciatic foramen transmits the tendon of obturator internus and the pudendal nerve and vessels re-entering the perineum.
cards.clin: The anterior superior iliac spine and pubic tubercle are the ends of the inguinal ligament and standard surface landmarks. The iliac crest is used for bone marrow aspiration and as a bone graft donor site. The ischial spine, palpable per vaginam, guides pudendal nerve block.
cards.exam: Q. At what site and age do the three parts of the hip bone fuse? A. At the triradiate cartilage in the acetabulum, around 15 to 17 years.

cards.desc: Curved elevation of three-layered archicortex in the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle, formed by the medial temporal lobe rolling into the ventricle along the hippocampal fissure.
cards.att: Its expanded anterior end is the pes hippocampi; the ventricular surface is covered by the white alveus, whose fibres gather medially as the fimbria and continue as the crus of the fornix. Principal input is from the entorhinal cortex of the parahippocampal gyrus by the perforant path; output is through the fornix to the mammillary body and septal nuclei.
cards.sup: Branches of the anterior choroidal artery and hippocampal branches of the posterior cerebral artery.
cards.act: Formation and consolidation of new declarative (episodic) memory and spatial memory.
cards.rel: Lies in the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle with the choroid plexus above it along the choroid fissure; the dentate gyrus lies medial and the parahippocampal gyrus and subiculum below and medial; the tail of the caudate nucleus lies in the ventricular roof.
cards.clin: Mesial temporal sclerosis, with neuronal loss maximal in the CA1 (Sommer) sector, is the commonest pathology in drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy and is treated by anterior temporal lobectomy with amygdalohippocampectomy. Bilateral hippocampal damage causes a dense anterograde amnesia, and the hippocampus is the earliest cortical region to atrophy in Alzheimer's disease.
cards.exam: Q. What deficit follows bilateral hippocampal destruction? A. Anterograde amnesia, an inability to form new declarative memories, with old memories retained.

cards.k: humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris
cards.latin: caput humerale musculi flexoris carpi ulnaris
cards.desc: The smaller, more superficial of the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris, arising with the common flexor origin at the elbow.
cards.att: Arises from the medial epicondyle of the humerus by the common flexor tendon; joins the ulnar head, which comes from the medial margin of the olecranon and the upper two thirds of the posterior border of the ulna, and inserts through a common tendon into the pisiform, and thence to the hook of the hamate and the base of the fifth metacarpal.
cards.sup: Ulnar nerve, C7, C8; ulnar artery and the posterior ulnar recurrent artery.
cards.act: Flexes and adducts the wrist; acting with extensor carpi ulnaris it produces pure adduction.
cards.rel: The two heads are joined by a tendinous arch, Osborne's ligament, deep to which the ulnar nerve passes from the cubital tunnel into the forearm. The ulnar nerve and artery lie deep to the muscle, the nerve lateral to the tendon at the wrist.
cards.clin: The aponeurotic arch between the two heads is a common site of ulnar nerve entrapment, giving cubital tunnel syndrome with numbness of the medial one and a half digits and weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles. The tendon at the wrist is the guide to the ulnar nerve and to the pisiform.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the ulnar nerve enter the forearm? A. Between the humeral and ulnar heads of flexor carpi ulnaris, beneath the aponeurotic arch of the cubital tunnel.

cards.desc: The larger superficial head of pronator teres, which forms the medial boundary of the cubital fossa.
cards.att: Arises from the medial supracondylar ridge just above the medial epicondyle and from the common flexor origin and adjacent intermuscular septum; unites with the ulnar head from the medial side of the coronoid process and inserts into the rough impression on the middle of the lateral surface of the radial shaft.
cards.sup: Median nerve, C6, C7; ulnar and radial recurrent arteries.
cards.act: Pronates the forearm and assists flexion at the elbow.
cards.rel: The median nerve enters the forearm between the humeral and ulnar heads, while the ulnar artery passes deep to both heads. The muscle forms the medial boundary of the cubital fossa and the brachial artery lies on it at the elbow.
cards.clin: The median nerve may be compressed between the two heads, giving pronator syndrome with forearm pain and median sensory loss that includes the thenar skin, unlike carpal tunnel syndrome. The muscle is the standard landmark for exposing the median nerve in the proximal forearm.
cards.exam: Q. Which structure passes between the two heads of pronator teres, and which passes deep to both? A. The median nerve passes between the heads; the ulnar artery passes deep to both.

cards.desc: The long bone of the arm, articulating above with the glenoid cavity of the scapula and below with the radius and ulna at the elbow.
cards.att: Upper end: head, anatomical neck, greater and lesser tubercles separated by the intertubercular sulcus, and the surgical neck. Shaft: deltoid tuberosity laterally and the radial (spiral) groove behind. Lower end: capitulum for the radial head, trochlea for the ulna, medial and lateral epicondyles, and the radial, coronoid and olecranon fossae. Rotator cuff, deltoid, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi and teres major attach above; the flexor and extensor common origins arise from the epicondyles.
cards.sup: Nutrient artery from the brachial artery; the head is supplied mainly by the anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries.
cards.rel: The axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels wind round the surgical neck, the radial nerve and profunda brachii lie in the radial groove, the ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle, and the median nerve and brachial artery lie in front of the lower end.
cards.clin: Fracture of the surgical neck injures the axillary nerve, giving loss of sensation over the regimental badge area and weak abduction. A midshaft fracture injures the radial nerve, giving wrist drop. A supracondylar fracture endangers the brachial artery and median nerve and may lead to Volkmann ischaemic contracture, while a medial epicondyle injury threatens the ulnar nerve.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve is injured in a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus and what is the sign? A. The axillary nerve, causing loss of sensation over the regimental badge area and weakness of abduction.

cards.desc: A thin quadrilateral extrinsic muscle of the tongue that forms the key landmark of the submandibular region.
cards.att: Arises from the whole length of the greater cornu and the adjoining lateral part of the body of the hyoid bone; passes vertically upwards to enter the side of the tongue between styloglossus laterally and the inferior longitudinal muscle medially.
cards.sup: Hypoglossal nerve; lingual artery.
cards.act: Depresses the tongue and retracts its protruded tip, making the dorsum convex.
cards.rel: On its lateral (superficial) surface, from above downwards, lie the lingual nerve, the submandibular duct and the hypoglossal nerve with the accompanying lingual vein, the lingual nerve looping under the duct. Deep to it lie the lingual artery, the glossopharyngeal nerve and the stylohyoid ligament.
cards.clin: The classical viva landmark: the lingual artery is ligated by dividing hyoglossus, and in removing a stone from the submandibular duct the lingual nerve, which crosses first lateral then below and then medial to the duct, must be protected.
cards.exam: Q. Name the structures lateral to hyoglossus from above down. A. Lingual nerve, submandibular duct, then the hypoglossal nerve with the lingual vein.

cards.desc: U-shaped bone in the front of the neck at the level of C3, suspended in muscles and ligaments with no bony articulation.
cards.att: Consists of a body, paired greater cornua and paired lesser cornua. Suspended from the styloid processes by the stylohyoid ligaments. Gives attachment above to mylohyoid, geniohyoid, stylohyoid, the anterior and posterior bellies of digastric, hyoglossus, genioglossus and the middle constrictor, and below to sternohyoid, omohyoid and thyrohyoid; the thyrohyoid membrane and the hyo-epiglottic ligament also attach to it.
cards.sup: Lingual and superior thyroid arteries; ossifies from six centres, the greater cornua fusing with the body in middle life.
cards.act: Provides a mobile anchor for the tongue and the floor of the mouth, and is elevated and moved forwards during swallowing and speech; the infrahyoid muscles fix or depress it so the suprahyoid muscles can open the jaw.
cards.rel: The greater cornu is palpable in the carotid triangle at the level of C3 and lies opposite the bifurcation region of the common carotid; the lingual artery arises just above it and the internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels pierce the thyrohyoid membrane just below it.
cards.clin: Fracture of the greater cornu occurs in manual strangulation and is a classic medicolegal finding at autopsy. The greater cornu is the surgical landmark for ligating the lingual artery in Pirogov's triangle, whose floor is hyoglossus.
cards.exam: Q. Why is the hyoid bone called a floating bone? A. It has no articulation with any other bone and is held in position solely by muscles and by the stylohyoid ligaments.

cards.desc: Small region of the diencephalon forming the floor and the lower part of the lateral wall of the third ventricle, below the hypothalamic sulcus.
cards.att: Extends from the lamina terminalis and optic chiasm in front to the mammillary bodies and posterior perforated substance behind; includes the optic chiasm, tuber cinereum with median eminence, infundibulum and mammillary bodies. Receives the fornix and stria terminalis; the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei send the hypothalamohypophysial tract to the neurohypophysis, and the median eminence gives the hypophysial portal vessels to the adenohypophysis.
cards.sup: Branches of the circle of Willis, chiefly the anterior and posterior communicating and posterior cerebral arteries.
cards.act: Chief integrator of the autonomic nervous system and controller of the endocrine system: regulates temperature, appetite and thirst, water balance, sleep and circadian rhythm, sexual behaviour and emotional expression.
cards.rel: Thalamus lies above across the hypothalamic sulcus; the third ventricle is medial; the internal capsule and subthalamus lie laterally; the pituitary gland hangs below from the infundibulum, with the optic chiasm in front of the stalk.
cards.clin: Damage to the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei or the pituitary stalk causes cranial diabetes insipidus with polyuria and dilute urine. Craniopharyngioma and suprasellar germinoma in this region cause growth failure, visual field loss and endocrine disturbance.
cards.exam: Q. Which hypothalamic nuclei produce the hormones released from the posterior pituitary? A. The supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei, producing vasopressin and oxytocin.

cards.desc: Opening of the terminal ileum into the posteromedial wall of the caecum at the junction of caecum and ascending colon, guarded by the ileocaecal valve.
cards.att: The terminal ileum enters obliquely; the ileal orifice is bounded by upper and lower lips (ileocolic and ileocaecal labia) that meet laterally as the frenula of the valve. Viewed endoscopically in the living it appears as a papilla rather than a valve.
cards.sup: Ileocolic artery from the superior mesenteric artery, through its anterior and posterior caecal branches and ileal branch. Veins to the superior mesenteric vein. Lymph to ileocolic nodes.
cards.act: Regulates passage of ileal contents into the caecum and limits reflux of colonic contents and bacteria into the ileum.
cards.rel: Lies in the right iliac fossa. The base of the appendix is about 2 cm below it on the posteromedial caecal wall, where the three taeniae converge.
cards.clin: A competent valve in large bowel obstruction converts the colon into a closed loop, raising the risk of caecal perforation. It is a common site of Crohn's disease and of ileocolic intussusception in children, and is the landmark confirming complete colonoscopy.
cards.exam: Q. Why is caecal perforation a risk in large bowel obstruction? A. A competent ileocaecal valve creates a closed loop, and by Laplace's law the wide caecum bears the highest wall tension.

cards.desc: Fan-shaped muscle filling the iliac fossa, joining psoas major to form iliopsoas, the chief flexor of the hip.
cards.att: Origin from the upper two-thirds of the iliac fossa, the inner lip of the iliac crest, the anterior sacroiliac and iliolumbar ligaments and the ala of the sacrum. Its fibres converge on the lateral side of the psoas tendon and insert with it into the lesser trochanter of the femur.
cards.sup: Femoral nerve (L2, L3).
cards.act: Flexes the thigh at the hip; with the femur fixed it flexes the trunk on the thigh, as in sitting up from lying.
cards.rel: Covered by iliac fascia, which separates it from the peritoneum. The femoral nerve lies in the groove between iliacus and psoas major and the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh crosses it. It passes deep to the inguinal ligament lateral to the femoral artery.
cards.clin: Pus from a psoas or vertebral tuberculous abscess tracks within the fascial sheath beneath the inguinal ligament and points in the femoral triangle. A haematoma within the iliacus sheath, as in haemophilia or over-anticoagulation, compresses the femoral nerve and causes quadriceps weakness with loss of the knee jerk and sensory loss on the anterior thigh.
cards.exam: Q. What is the nerve supply of iliacus, and how does it differ from psoas major? A. Iliacus is supplied by the femoral nerve (L2, L3); psoas major by anterior rami of L1, L2, L3 directly.

cards.desc: Posterior, thinner and more horizontal part of levator ani, forming the bulk of the pelvic diaphragm behind the puborectal sling.
cards.att: Origin: ischial spine and the posterior part of the tendinous arch of levator ani over obturator internus fascia. Insertion: anococcygeal ligament (levator plate), last two coccygeal segments and the midline raphe with the fellow of the opposite side.
cards.sup: Nerve to levator ani from the anterior ramus of S4, with a contribution from the pudendal nerve (S2, S3, S4).
cards.act: Elevates and supports the pelvic floor and pelvic viscera; raises intra-abdominal pressure with the abdominal wall and diaphragm.
cards.rel: Superiorly the pelvic fascia, rectum and bladder; inferiorly the ischioanal fossa. Obturator internus and its fascia lie laterally.
cards.clin: Thin and often largely aponeurotic, so it is the part that stretches and gapes in pelvic organ prolapse. Widening of the levator hiatus after obstetric injury is assessed on translabial ultrasound.
cards.exam: Q. Which part of levator ani arises from the ischial spine? A. Iliococcygeus, from the ischial spine and posterior part of the tendinous arch.

cards.desc: Most lateral column of the erector spinae in the lumbar region, lying in the vertebral groove lateral to longissimus.
cards.att: Arises from the common tendon of erector spinae attached to the median and lateral sacral crests, the posterior part of the iliac crest, the sacrotuberous and sacroiliac ligaments and the lumbar spinous processes. Inserts by tendons into the inferior borders and angles of the lower six or seven ribs.
cards.sup: Posterior (dorsal) rami of the lumbar spinal nerves.
cards.act: Bilaterally extends the vertebral column; unilaterally laterally flexes the trunk to the same side and controls forward flexion by eccentric contraction.
cards.rel: Lies deep to the thoracolumbar fascia and serratus posterior inferior, lateral to longissimus, and superficial to multifidus and quadratus lumborum.
cards.clin: This muscle mass falls electrically silent in full forward flexion (the flexion-relaxation phenomenon), so the flexed lumbar spine relies on ligaments, which is why lifting with a bent back risks disc and ligamentous injury. It is a common site of lumbar muscular strain and of protective spasm.
cards.exam: Q. What is the nerve supply of the erector spinae group? A. Posterior (dorsal) rami of the spinal nerves at the corresponding levels.

cards.desc: Thoracic part of the iliocostalis, the most lateral of the three columns of erector spinae in the back.
cards.att: Origin: upper borders of the angles of the lower six ribs, medial to the insertion of iliocostalis lumborum. Insertion: upper borders of the angles of the upper six ribs and the back of the transverse process of the seventh cervical vertebra.
cards.sup: Dorsal rami of the thoracic spinal nerves.
cards.act: Acting bilaterally, extends the thoracic vertebral column and helps depress the ribs; acting unilaterally, laterally flexes the trunk to the same side and steadies the vertebral column during forward bending.
cards.rel: Lies lateral to longissimus thoracis, deep to the thoracolumbar fascia, serratus posterior muscles and the rhomboids and trapezius. Iliocostalis lumborum lies below it, iliocostalis cervicis above.
cards.clin: Part of the paraspinal muscle mass injured in whiplash and lifting strains; its bulk is used in myocutaneous and paraspinal flaps and is assessed on axial imaging in chronic low back pain.
cards.exam: Q. Name the three columns of erector spinae from lateral to medial. A. Iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis.

cards.desc: Thickened longitudinal band of the fascia lata along the lateral thigh, running from the iliac tubercle to the lateral condyle of the tibia.
cards.att: Above, attached to the iliac tubercle and outer lip of the iliac crest, and receives tensor fasciae latae and the upper three quarters of gluteus maximus. Below, inserts into Gerdy's tubercle on the lateral tibial condyle, with slips to the lateral patellar retinaculum and head of fibula.
cards.act: Transmits the pull of tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus; steadies the pelvis on the femur and helps hold the extended knee braced in standing.
cards.rel: Lies superficial to vastus lateralis and the lateral femoral epicondyle, anchored to the femur through the lateral intermuscular septum. Attaches to the linea aspera indirectly through that septum.
cards.clin: Iliotibial band friction syndrome causes lateral knee pain in runners and cyclists; Ober's test assesses tightness. Gerdy's tubercle is a surgical landmark, and the tract is harvested as a fascial graft.
cards.exam: Q. Which two muscles insert into the iliotibial tract? A. Tensor fasciae latae and the greater part of gluteus maximus.

syn: inferior division of the oculomotor nerve
cards.desc: The larger of the two divisions of the oculomotor nerve, supplying three extra-ocular muscles and carrying the parasympathetic fibres to the eye.
cards.att: Divides from the oculomotor nerve in the anterior cavernous sinus or superior orbital fissure, enters the orbit within the common tendinous ring below the optic nerve, and gives three branches: to medial rectus, to inferior rectus, and a long branch to inferior oblique which also carries the parasympathetic root to the ciliary ganglion.
cards.act: Motor to medial rectus, inferior rectus and inferior oblique, and the pathway for preganglionic parasympathetic fibres to sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle.
cards.rel: Runs below the optic nerve within the muscle cone; the branch to inferior oblique passes forwards between inferior rectus and lateral rectus, close to the ciliary ganglion.
cards.clin: The parasympathetic fibres lie superficially in the nerve, so a compressive lesion such as a posterior communicating artery aneurysm dilates the pupil early, whereas the ischaemic third nerve palsy of diabetes typically spares it.
cards.exam: Q. Which branch of the inferior division of CN III carries the parasympathetic root of the ciliary ganglion? A. The nerve to inferior oblique.

cards.desc: Lower and smaller of the two pairs of rounded eminences of the midbrain tectum, at the level of the caudal midbrain.
cards.att: Receives the lateral lemniscus as its principal input and projects through the brachium of the inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate body; also connected to the superior colliculus and to the contralateral inferior colliculus.
cards.sup: Branches of the superior cerebellar artery and the posterior cerebral artery.
cards.act: Obligatory relay of the ascending auditory pathway; concerned with sound localisation and with reflex turning of the head and eyes towards sound.
cards.rel: Lies below the superior colliculus on the dorsal surface of the midbrain; the trochlear nerve emerges from the dorsal surface immediately below it, and the superior medullary velum and superior cerebellar peduncles lie below and behind.
cards.clin: The dorsal surface just below the inferior colliculus is where the trochlear nerve, the only cranial nerve to leave the brainstem dorsally, emerges and decussates; this makes it vulnerable in tectal lesions and in head injury.
cards.exam: Q. Which cranial nerve emerges just below the inferior colliculus? A. The trochlear nerve, cranial nerve IV.

cards.desc: Branch of the external iliac artery arising just above the inguinal ligament and ascending on the deep surface of the anterior abdominal wall into the rectus sheath.
cards.att: Arises from the external iliac artery immediately proximal to the inguinal ligament, runs upwards and medially along the medial margin of the deep inguinal ring, pierces the transversalis fascia and enters the rectus sheath below the arcuate line, ascending behind rectus abdominis to anastomose with the superior epigastric artery.
cards.sup: Cremasteric artery (artery of the round ligament in the female), a pubic branch that anastomoses with the obturator artery, and muscular and cutaneous perforators.
cards.act: Supplies the lower rectus abdominis and overlying skin, and forms part of the collateral channel between the external iliac and subclavian arteries.
cards.rel: Raises the lateral umbilical fold of peritoneum; lies medial to the deep inguinal ring and forms the lateral boundary of the inguinal (Hesselbach) triangle.
cards.clin: An indirect inguinal hernia enters lateral to the artery and a direct hernia bulges medial to it. It is the source of rectus sheath haematoma, the vessel injured by lateral laparoscopic ports, and its abnormal pubic anastomosis crossing the femoral ring is the corona mortis.
cards.exam: Q. How are direct and indirect inguinal hernias distinguished at operation? A. A direct hernia lies medial and an indirect hernia lateral to the inferior epigastric artery.

cards.desc: Lowest of the three gyri on the lateral surface of the frontal lobe, lying between the inferior frontal sulcus above and the lateral sulcus below.
cards.att: Divided by the anterior horizontal and anterior ascending rami of the lateral sulcus into pars orbitalis in front, pars triangularis between, and pars opercularis behind. Connected to the posterior superior temporal region by the arcuate fasciculus.
cards.sup: Branches of the superior division of the middle cerebral artery.
cards.act: Pars opercularis and pars triangularis of the dominant hemisphere form Broca's motor speech area (areas 44 and 45), which programmes the motor production of speech.
cards.rel: Lies above the lateral sulcus and the insula, in front of the precentral gyrus; the middle frontal gyrus lies above across the inferior frontal sulcus.
cards.clin: A lesion of Broca's area, usually an infarct in the superior division of the left middle cerebral artery, causes an expressive (non-fluent) aphasia: speech is sparse and effortful with agrammatism, comprehension is relatively preserved, and repetition is impaired, often with a right hemiparesis worse in the face and arm.
cards.exam: Q. Which parts of the inferior frontal gyrus form Broca's area? A. Pars opercularis and pars triangularis of the dominant hemisphere, Brodmann areas 44 and 45.

cards.desc: Third and smallest unpaired ventral branch of the abdominal aorta, arising at L3 about 4 cm above the aortic bifurcation, and the artery of the hindgut.
cards.att: Arises from the front of the aorta at L3, passes downwards and to the left behind the peritoneum, crosses the left common iliac artery and continues into the pelvis as the superior rectal artery.
cards.sup: Left colic artery, two to three sigmoid arteries and the superior rectal artery.
cards.act: Supplies the distal third of the transverse colon, the descending and sigmoid colon and the rectum down to the pectinate line.
cards.rel: Lies on the front of the aorta and then on the left psoas major; the left ureter and gonadal vessels lie lateral to it, and the inferior mesenteric vein ascends separately, to the left of the artery.
cards.clin: The marginal artery of Drummond and the arc of Riolan connect it with the superior mesenteric artery; the splenic flexure (Griffiths point) and the rectosigmoid junction (Sudeck point) are watershed zones prone to ischaemic colitis. A high tie of the artery at its aortic origin is performed in left hemicolectomy and anterior resection.
cards.exam: Q. Which gut region does the inferior mesenteric artery supply and where is its pain referred? A. The hindgut, with pain referred to the hypogastrium.

cards.desc: Vein of the hindgut, the upward continuation of the superior rectal vein, ending behind the body of the pancreas in the splenic vein.
cards.att: Begins as the superior rectal vein in the pelvis, ascends retroperitoneally to the left of the inferior mesenteric artery, passes lateral to the duodenojejunal flexure beneath the inferior mesenteric (paraduodenal) fold, and joins the splenic vein; it may instead join the superior mesenteric vein or their angle of union.
cards.sup: Receives superior rectal, sigmoid and left colic tributaries.
cards.act: Returns blood from the descending colon, sigmoid colon and upper rectum to the portal system.
cards.rel: Ascends on psoas major behind the peritoneum, lateral to the duodenojejunal flexure, then passes behind the body of the pancreas to reach the splenic vein.
cards.clin: The superior rectal vein anastomoses with the middle and inferior rectal veins in the anal canal wall, forming a portosystemic anastomosis; the anorectal varices this produces are distinct from ordinary haemorrhoids. The vein is a landmark for the medial-to-lateral mesocolic plane in left colectomy.
cards.exam: Q. Into which vein does the inferior mesenteric vein usually drain? A. The splenic vein, behind the body of the pancreas.

cards.desc: Separate scroll-shaped paired bone attached to the lateral wall of the nasal cavity below the middle concha.
cards.att: Its upper border bears a lacrimal process meeting the lacrimal bone, an ethmoidal process meeting the uncinate process of the ethmoid, and a maxillary process that curves down over the maxillary hiatus. Articulates with the maxilla, lacrimal, ethmoid and palatine bones and overhangs the inferior meatus.
cards.sup: Sphenopalatine and greater palatine arteries with a rich venous plexus; sensory and vasomotor supply from branches of the maxillary nerve and the pterygopalatine ganglion.
cards.act: Increases the surface area of the nasal mucosa to warm, moisten and filter inspired air, and creates turbulent flow that directs air over the mucosa.
cards.rel: The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus beneath its anterior part. The maxillary sinus lies laterally, the nasal septum medially and the middle concha above.
cards.clin: Its venous erectile plexus swells in rhinitis and vasomotor allergy, causing nasal obstruction that is relieved by decongestants or turbinate reduction. Its lower edge marks the floor of the nose, and instruments passed along the floor beneath it reach the inferior meatus and the nasolacrimal duct opening.
cards.exam: Q. Which duct opens beneath the inferior nasal concha? A. The nasolacrimal duct, into the anterior part of the inferior meatus.

syn: inferior oblique muscle of the eyeball
cards.desc: The only extra-ocular muscle to arise from the front of the orbit, running backwards and laterally beneath the globe.
cards.att: Arises from the orbital surface of the maxilla just lateral to the nasolacrimal groove near the anteromedial angle of the orbital floor; passes backwards and laterally below inferior rectus to insert into the sclera in the posterolateral quadrant behind the equator.
cards.sup: Inferior division of the oculomotor nerve, the only muscle in the orbit it supplies from below and laterally; infra-orbital and ophthalmic arteries.
cards.act: From the primary position it elevates, abducts and extorts the eyeball; elevation is greatest when the eye is adducted.
cards.rel: Lies below inferior rectus and above the orbital floor; the nerve to inferior oblique carries the parasympathetic fibres that reach the ciliary ganglion by its motor root.
cards.clin: Tested by asking the patient to look upwards while the eye is adducted. It overacts when the ipsilateral superior oblique is paralysed, producing the upshoot in adduction seen in trochlear nerve palsy.
cards.exam: Q. How is inferior oblique tested clinically? A. Elevation of the adducted eye, that is looking up and medially.

cards.desc: The lowest, thickest and most external of the three overlapping constrictor muscles of the pharyngeal wall, made of a thyropharyngeal and a cricopharyngeal part.
cards.att: Thyropharyngeus arises from the oblique line of the lamina of the thyroid cartilage and the inferior cornu; cricopharyngeus arises from the side of the arch of the cricoid cartilage. Thyropharyngeal fibres pass obliquely upwards to the median raphe on the pharyngobasilar fascia; cricopharyngeal fibres pass horizontally and are continuous with those of the opposite side without a raphe, forming a sphincter.
cards.sup: Pharyngeal plexus, motor fibres from the cranial part of the accessory nerve carried by the vagus; cricopharyngeus receives additional fibres from the external laryngeal and recurrent laryngeal nerves. Arteries: ascending pharyngeal, superior and inferior thyroid.
cards.act: Propels the bolus from the pharynx into the oesophagus; cricopharyngeus is the upper oesophageal sphincter, tonically closed except during swallowing and belching.
cards.rel: The recurrent laryngeal nerve and the inferior laryngeal artery enter the larynx at its lower border; the external laryngeal nerve pierces or runs on it with the superior thyroid vessels. The piriform fossa lies deep to it.
cards.clin: Killian's dehiscence, the weak gap between the oblique thyropharyngeal and horizontal cricopharyngeal fibres, is the site of a pharyngeal (Zenker's) pouch when cricopharyngeus fails to relax. Rigid oesophagoscopy most commonly perforates the pharynx here.
cards.exam: Q. What is Killian's dehiscence and why does it matter? A. The gap between thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus, the site of pharyngeal pouch formation and of instrumental perforation.

cards.desc: First paired branch of the abdominal aorta, arising at T12 just below the aortic hiatus and running upwards and laterally on the abdominal surface of the diaphragm.
cards.att: Arises from the aorta immediately below the hiatus, or from the coeliac trunk, ascends across the corresponding crus, and divides into anterior and posterior branches on the undersurface of the diaphragm.
cards.sup: Superior suprarenal arteries, and diaphragmatic branches that anastomose with the musculophrenic, pericardiacophrenic and lower posterior intercostal arteries.
cards.act: Chief arterial supply of the diaphragm from below and of the upper part of the suprarenal gland.
cards.rel: The right artery passes behind the inferior vena cava; the left passes behind the oesophagus and in front of the left crus.
cards.clin: The commonest extrahepatic collateral artery feeding a hepatocellular carcinoma, so it is sought during transarterial chemoembolisation when tumour persists. It is also a source of significant bleeding after diaphragmatic injury or crural dissection.
cards.exam: Q. What are the three arteries supplying the suprarenal gland? A. Superior from the inferior phrenic artery, middle from the abdominal aorta, inferior from the renal artery.

cards.desc: One of the two pulmonary veins of each lung, carrying oxygenated blood from the lower lobe to the left atrium.
cards.att: Formed within the lung by the union of the segmental veins of the lower lobe, emerges at the hilum below the other structures, runs forwards and medially in the root of the lung and opens into the posterior wall of the left atrium; there are normally four pulmonary veins and none of them has valves.
cards.act: Returns oxygenated blood from the lower lobe to the left atrium; a small amount of deoxygenated bronchial venous blood joins it, accounting for the normal physiological shunt.
cards.rel: The lowest and most anterior structure in the root of the lung; on the right the superior vein drains the upper and middle lobes, and on the left the superior vein drains the upper lobe including the lingula.
cards.clin: The pulmonary vein ostia are the source of ectopic beats in atrial fibrillation and are the target of catheter ablation (pulmonary vein isolation); over-aggressive ablation causes pulmonary vein stenosis. The vein is individually ligated in lobectomy.
cards.exam: Q. What is the most inferior structure in the root of the lung? A. The inferior pulmonary vein.

cards.desc: The extra-ocular muscle running forwards along the floor of the orbit from the common tendinous ring to the underside of the globe.
cards.att: Arises from the lower part of the common tendinous ring and inserts into the sclera on the inferior aspect of the globe about 6.5 mm behind the corneal margin, in front of the equator.
cards.sup: Inferior division of the oculomotor nerve; muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery.
cards.act: Depresses the eyeball; secondarily adducts and extorts it. Depression is greatest when the eye is abducted.
cards.rel: Lies on the orbital floor with inferior oblique below and in front of it, to which its sheath is connected by the suspensory ligament of Lockwood; the nerve enters its ocular surface.
cards.clin: In a blow-out fracture of the orbital floor the muscle and its fascia herniate into the maxillary sinus and become tethered, giving diplopia and limitation of upward gaze, confirmed by a positive forced duction test. It is tested by asking the patient to look down and out.
cards.exam: Q. How is inferior rectus tested? A. Depression of the abducted eye, that is looking down and laterally.

cards.desc: Lowest gyrus on the lateral surface of the temporal lobe, below the inferior temporal sulcus, extending round the inferolateral border onto the inferior surface.
cards.att: Part of the ventral visual stream, connected with occipital visual cortex through the inferior longitudinal fasciculus and with the temporal pole and limbic cortex in front.
cards.sup: Temporal branches of the middle cerebral artery, with the inferior surface receiving branches from the posterior cerebral artery.
cards.act: Higher-order visual association cortex for the recognition and identification of objects, forms and colour.
cards.rel: Lies below the middle temporal gyrus across the inferior temporal sulcus and lateral to the fusiform gyrus across the occipitotemporal sulcus; the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle and the optic radiation lie deep to it.
cards.clin: Lesions of this ventral stream cortex produce visual object agnosia, in which objects are seen but not recognised visually although they are identified at once by touch or sound. Resection here risks the fibres of Meyer's loop deep in the temporal white matter, producing a contralateral upper quadrantanopia.
cards.exam: Q. What visual field defect follows anterior temporal lobe surgery? A. A contralateral homonymous upper quadrantanopia from damage to Meyer's loop.

cards.desc: Chief branch of the thyrocervical trunk, the main artery to the lower pole of the thyroid gland and to both parathyroid glands.
cards.att: Arises from the thyrocervical trunk of the first part of the subclavian artery, ascends behind the carotid sheath, then arches medially at the level of C6 behind the sheath and in front of the vertebral artery to reach the posterior aspect of the lower pole of the thyroid.
cards.sup: Branches: glandular branches to the thyroid and parathyroid glands, ascending cervical, inferior laryngeal, pharyngeal, oesophageal and tracheal branches.
cards.act: Supplies the lower part of the thyroid gland, the parathyroid glands, and the pharynx, oesophagus, trachea and larynx.
cards.rel: The recurrent laryngeal nerve passes in front of, behind, or between the terminal branches of the artery near the lower pole of the thyroid. Its arch lies behind the carotid sheath and the middle cervical sympathetic ganglion lies on it.
cards.clin: In thyroidectomy the inferior thyroid artery is ligated well lateral to the gland, away from the recurrent laryngeal nerve; ligating close to the capsule risks the nerve. It is also the principal blood supply of both parathyroid glands, so it must be preserved to avoid postoperative hypocalcaemia.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve is at risk when the inferior thyroid artery is ligated near the gland? A. The recurrent laryngeal nerve, causing hoarseness.

cards.desc: Largest vein in the body, formed at L5 by the union of the two common iliac veins and returning blood from the lower half of the body to the right atrium.
cards.att: Formed to the right of the aorta at L5, ascends on the right of the vertebral bodies and in the groove on the bare area of the liver, pierces the central tendon of the diaphragm at T8 and opens into the lower part of the right atrium.
cards.sup: Tributaries: common iliac, median sacral, lumbar, right gonadal, renal, right suprarenal, inferior phrenic and hepatic veins.
cards.act: Systemic venous return from the lower limbs, pelvis, perineum, kidneys, posterior abdominal wall and liver.
cards.rel: Anteriorly: right common iliac artery, root of the mesentery, third part of duodenum, head of pancreas, portal vein, epiploic foramen and liver. Posteriorly: right psoas, right crus, right renal and right suprarenal arteries, and the bodies of L3 to L5.
cards.clin: Compressed by the gravid uterus in the supine position, causing supine hypotensive syndrome, relieved by left lateral tilt. Renal cell carcinoma may extend along the renal vein into its lumen, and filters are placed in the infrarenal segment for recurrent pulmonary embolism despite anticoagulation.
cards.exam: Q. At which vertebral level does the inferior vena cava pierce the diaphragm and what accompanies it? A. T8, in the central tendon, with branches of the right phrenic nerve.

cards.desc: Thick triangular rotator cuff muscle filling the infraspinous fossa of the scapula.
cards.att: Origin: medial two-thirds of the infraspinous fossa and the overlying infraspinous fascia. Insertion: middle facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus, blending with the capsule of the shoulder joint.
cards.sup: Suprascapular nerve (C5, C6).
cards.act: Laterally rotates the arm; as part of the rotator cuff it holds the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity and resists upward displacement.
cards.rel: Covered by deltoid and trapezius; teres minor lies below, supraspinatus above the scapular spine; the suprascapular nerve and vessels reach it through the spinoglenoid notch.
cards.clin: Tested by resisted lateral rotation with the elbow flexed at the side. Wasting of the infraspinous fossa with weak lateral rotation suggests suprascapular nerve entrapment at the spinoglenoid notch, often by a ganglion, or a rotator cuff tear. Volleyball players show painless isolated infraspinatus wasting.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscles laterally rotate the arm at the shoulder? A. Infraspinatus and teres minor, with the posterior fibres of deltoid.

cards.desc: Terminal cutaneous branch of the nasociliary nerve running forwards below the trochlea to the medial angle of the eye.
cards.att: Arises from the nasociliary nerve near the anterior ethmoidal foramen, runs forwards along the upper border of medial rectus, passes below the trochlea, and emerges at the medial canthus.
cards.act: Sensory to the skin of the medial part of the upper eyelid and the side of the root of the nose, the conjunctiva and lacrimal caruncle, the lacrimal sac and the upper part of the nasolacrimal duct.
cards.rel: Runs between superior oblique above and medial rectus below along the medial orbital wall, with the supratrochlear nerve emerging above the trochlea.
cards.clin: Blocked together with the supratrochlear nerve for surgery at the medial canthus, including dacryocystorhinostomy. It carries pain from an inflamed lacrimal sac in dacryocystitis.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve supplies sensation to the lacrimal sac? A. The infratrochlear nerve, from the nasociliary.

cards.desc: Deepest of the three intercostal layers, an incomplete sheet lying internal to the intercostal neurovascular bundle.
cards.att: Arises from the internal surface of the rib above and inserts into the internal surface of the rib below, fibres running in the same direction as the internal intercostal. Best developed in the middle two quarters of the space, especially in the lower lateral thoracic wall, and often deficient anteriorly and posteriorly.
cards.sup: Intercostal nerves, the ventral rami of the corresponding thoracic spinal nerves.
cards.act: Acts with the internal intercostal muscle in respiration and supports the intercostal space.
cards.rel: Separated from the internal intercostal by the intercostal vein, artery and nerve; internal to it lie the endothoracic fascia and parietal pleura. It is continuous behind with the subcostal muscles and in front with transversus thoracis.
cards.clin: The plane between internal and innermost intercostal muscles is the target for an intercostal nerve block, and the same plane is where a misdirected needle strikes the neurovascular bundle.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscles lie superficial and deep to the intercostal neurovascular bundle? A. Internal intercostal superficially and innermost intercostal deeply.

cards.desc: Triangular area of cortex buried in the floor of the lateral sulcus, overlapped and hidden by the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula.
cards.att: Outlined by the circular sulcus and divided by the central sulcus of the insula into a larger anterior part with three short gyri and a posterior part with two long gyri; its apex, the limen insulae, is continuous with the anterior perforated substance. Connected with the frontal and parietal opercula, temporal cortex, amygdala and thalamus.
cards.sup: Insular (M2) branches of the middle cerebral artery, which run over its surface.
cards.act: Visceral sensory and visceral motor cortex; contains the primary gustatory area, and is concerned with pain, interoception, autonomic control and, in the anterior dominant insula, with speech articulation.
cards.rel: Covered by the frontal, frontoparietal and temporal opercula; the extreme capsule, claustrum, external capsule and putamen lie deep to it in that order from the surface inwards.
cards.clin: The insula is exposed by separating the opercula in the transsylvian approach; the middle cerebral artery branches crossing it must be preserved during resection of insular gliomas. Damage to the insula and neighbouring opercular cortex can cause loss of taste and, on the dominant side, apraxia of speech.
cards.exam: Q. Name the layers between the insular cortex and the putamen, from superficial to deep. A. Extreme capsule, claustrum, external capsule, putamen.

cards.k: insular part of middle cerebral artery
cards.desc: Second segment of the middle cerebral artery, running over the surface of the insula within the depth of the lateral sulcus.
cards.att: Begins at the genu of the middle cerebral artery at the limen insulae, where the sphenoid part turns, runs backwards and upwards on the insula, and ends at the circular sulcus where the vessel turns laterally over the opercula as the opercular part.
cards.sup: Insular arteries to the insular cortex, and the stems of the frontal, temporal and parietal cortical branches, which usually arise here as a superior and an inferior trunk.
cards.act: Distributes the middle cerebral supply from the insula to the whole lateral convexity of the hemisphere.
cards.rel: Lies deep in the lateral sulcus on the insula, covered by the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula, with the claustrum and lentiform nucleus deep to it.
cards.clin: The commonest site of a proximal large vessel occlusion accessible to mechanical thrombectomy after the sphenoid segment. The insular ribbon loses its grey and white differentiation early on CT and is a key sign of acute middle cerebral artery infarction.
cards.exam: Q. Which segment of the middle cerebral artery is M2, and where does it lie? A. The insular part, on the surface of the insula within the lateral sulcus.

cards.desc: Smallest and shortest of the three cuneiform bones, wedge shaped with its broad base dorsally and its narrow edge plantarwards.
cards.att: Articulates proximally with the navicular, medially with the medial cuneiform, laterally with the lateral cuneiform and distally with the base of the second metatarsal. Gives attachment to slips of tibialis posterior on its plantar surface and to dorsal and plantar tarsometatarsal ligaments.
cards.act: Forms part of the transverse arch of the foot; because it is the shortest cuneiform, the base of the second metatarsal is recessed between the medial and lateral cuneiforms in a mortise that locks the midfoot.
cards.rel: Lies between the other two cuneiforms in the distal row of the tarsus, with the tendon of tibialis anterior passing medial to it and extensor tendons crossing its dorsal surface.
cards.clin: The recessed second metatarsal base is the keystone of the tarsometatarsal complex; disruption of the Lisfranc ligament from the medial cuneiform to the second metatarsal base allows lateral displacement and is easily missed on plain films.
cards.exam: Q. Why is the base of the second metatarsal the keystone of the Lisfranc joint? A. Because the short intermediate cuneiform recesses it into a mortise between the medial and lateral cuneiforms.

cards.desc: The short rounded tendon between the anterior and posterior bellies of digastric, anchored to the hyoid bone at the level of the greater cornu.
cards.att: Receives the posterior belly from the mastoid notch and gives origin to the anterior belly, which runs to the digastric fossa of the mandible. It perforates the tendon of stylohyoid and is held to the junction of the body and greater cornu of the hyoid by a loop of deep cervical fascia that acts as a pulley.
cards.act: Acts as a movable pulley that converts the pull of the two bellies into elevation of the hyoid or depression of the mandible, depending on which end is fixed.
cards.rel: Lies on hyoglossus and the insertion of middle constrictor; the hypoglossal nerve and the lingual and facial vessels are close to it. Omohyoid has a comparable intermediate tendon lower in the neck, bound down by a fascial sling from the clavicle.
cards.clin: The fibrous sling is the landmark for identifying the hyoid in a suprahyoid dissection and in hyoid suspension surgery. The tendon marks the boundary between first arch and second arch derivatives of the muscle.
cards.exam: Q. What holds the intermediate tendon of digastric to the hyoid? A. A fibrous sling of deep cervical fascia at the junction of the body and greater cornu.

cards.desc: Compact, V-shaped sheet of projection fibres, seen in horizontal section with its concavity outwards, lying between the caudate nucleus and thalamus medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally.
cards.att: Divided into an anterior limb between the caudate head and lentiform nucleus, a genu, a posterior limb between the thalamus and lentiform nucleus, and retrolentiform and sublentiform parts. Carries corticonuclear fibres in the genu, corticospinal fibres in the anterior part of the posterior limb, thalamocortical and corticopontine fibres, the optic radiation in the retrolentiform part and the acoustic radiation in the sublentiform part. Continuous above with the corona radiata and below with the crus cerebri.
cards.sup: Lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery to most of it, the medial striate artery of Heubner to the anterior limb, and the anterior choroidal artery to the lower part of the posterior limb.
cards.act: Conveys almost all afferent and efferent fibres between the cerebral cortex and the brainstem and spinal cord.
cards.rel: Caudate head and thalamus lie medial, lentiform nucleus lateral; the tail of the caudate and the optic radiation lie behind and below.
cards.clin: Because the fibres are packed together, a small lacunar infarct or a hypertensive haemorrhage from a lenticulostriate artery in the posterior limb causes a dense contralateral hemiplegia and hemianaesthesia with no cortical signs such as aphasia or neglect. Extension into the retrolentiform part adds a contralateral homonymous hemianopia.
cards.exam: Q. Where in the internal capsule do corticospinal fibres lie? A. In the anterior part of the posterior limb, with corticonuclear fibres in the genu.

cards.desc: Terminal branch of the common carotid supplying most of the cerebral hemisphere, the eye and the forehead, with no branches in the neck.
cards.att: Arises at the carotid bifurcation at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C4). Cervical part ascends in the carotid sheath to the base of the skull; petrous part traverses the carotid canal; cavernous part runs in the cavernous sinus in an S-shaped siphon; cerebral part pierces the roof of the sinus medial to the anterior clinoid process and divides into the anterior and middle cerebral arteries.
cards.sup: Branches: caroticotympanic, ophthalmic, posterior communicating, anterior choroidal, and terminal anterior and middle cerebral arteries. No branches in the neck.
cards.act: Supplies the frontal, parietal and much of the temporal lobe, the eye and orbit, the forehead and part of the nose.
cards.rel: In the neck it lies deep to the external carotid, with the internal jugular vein lateral and the vagus behind. In the cavernous sinus the abducent nerve lies against it, with the oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic and maxillary nerves in the lateral wall.
cards.clin: Atheroma at the origin causes transient ischaemic attacks and amaurosis fugax through emboli to the retina. A cavernous carotid aneurysm or a caroticocavernous fistula gives pulsatile exophthalmos, chemosis and multiple cranial nerve palsies.
cards.exam: Q. Does the internal carotid artery branch in the neck? A. No, absence of cervical branches distinguishes it from the external carotid at operation.

cards.desc: The medial terminal branch of the common iliac artery, the main artery of the pelvis, perineum and gluteal region.
cards.att: Arises in front of the sacroiliac joint, descends about 4 cm to the upper border of the greater sciatic foramen, and divides into anterior and posterior divisions. Anterior division: superior vesical (from the patent proximal part of the umbilical artery), inferior vesical (in the female the vaginal artery), middle rectal, uterine, obturator, internal pudendal and inferior gluteal. Posterior division: iliolumbar, lateral sacral and superior gluteal.
cards.act: Supplies the pelvic viscera, pelvic walls, perineum, external genitalia and the gluteal region.
cards.rel: The ureter descends in front of it and the internal iliac vein and lumbosacral trunk lie behind; the external iliac vein lies anterolateral above, and the obturator nerve runs below and lateral on the pelvic wall.
cards.clin: Bilateral internal iliac ligation or embolisation is used for uncontrollable postpartum or pelvic fracture haemorrhage; collateral flow keeps the pelvis viable. The obliterated umbilical artery persists as the medial umbilical ligament.
cards.exam: Q. Name the three branches of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery. A. Iliolumbar, lateral sacral and superior gluteal.

cards.desc: The vein draining the pelvis, formed above the greater sciatic foramen and ending by joining the external iliac vein.
cards.att: Formed by tributaries corresponding to the branches of the artery, except that there are no umbilical or iliolumbar veins draining into it directly; ascends behind and medial to the artery to join the external iliac vein in front of the sacroiliac joint and form the common iliac vein. It receives the superior gluteal, inferior gluteal, internal pudendal, obturator, lateral sacral, middle rectal, vesical, prostatic or uterine and vaginal veins.
cards.act: Returns blood from the pelvic viscera, pelvic walls, perineum and buttock.
cards.rel: Lies posteromedial to the internal iliac artery on the lateral pelvic wall; the ureter and the pelvic plexuses lie in front; the lumbosacral trunk and sacroiliac joint behind.
cards.clin: Its valveless tributaries form the pelvic plexuses that communicate with the internal vertebral venous plexus of Batson, explaining spread of prostatic and rectal carcinoma to the vertebrae, pelvis and skull without passing through the lungs.
cards.exam: Q. How does prostatic carcinoma reach the vertebral bodies without lung metastases? A. Through valveless communications between the prostatic and internal iliac veins and the internal vertebral venous plexus of Batson.

cards.desc: Middle of the three intercostal layers, eleven on each side, with fibres running at right angles to those of the external intercostal.
cards.att: Arises from the floor of the costal groove of the rib above and from the costal cartilage, and inserts into the upper border of the rib below; fibres run downwards and backwards. Extends from the sternum in front to the angles of the ribs behind, where it is replaced by the internal intercostal membrane.
cards.sup: Intercostal nerves, the ventral rami of T1 to T11.
cards.act: The interosseous part depresses the ribs in forced expiration; the interchondral part, between the costal cartilages, elevates the ribs in inspiration.
cards.rel: Deep to the external intercostal, superficial to the intercostal neurovascular bundle and the innermost intercostal muscle.
cards.clin: Posteriorly, where only the internal intercostal membrane is present, a paravertebral injection spreads readily to adjacent levels. Intercostal muscle tears cause sharp pleuritic-type pain worse on coughing.
cards.exam: Q. Which part of the internal intercostal muscle assists inspiration? A. The interchondral part, between the costal cartilages.

cards.desc: The main venous channel of the neck, draining the brain, face and neck, running in the carotid sheath from the jugular foramen to the root of the neck.
cards.att: Begins as the superior bulb at the jugular foramen as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus, descends in the carotid sheath, and ends behind the sternal end of the clavicle by joining the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein. The inferior bulb near its termination contains a bicuspid valve.
cards.sup: Tributaries: inferior petrosal sinus, facial, lingual, pharyngeal, superior thyroid and middle thyroid veins, and sometimes the occipital vein.
cards.act: Drains blood from the cranial cavity, face and neck to the brachiocephalic vein.
cards.rel: Lies lateral to the internal and common carotid arteries, with the vagus nerve behind and between them; it is overlapped by sternocleidomastoid. The deep cervical lymph nodes lie along it, and the thoracic duct enters the left venous angle at its termination.
cards.clin: Cannulated for central venous access by entering at the apex of the triangle between the sternal and clavicular heads of sternocleidomastoid, aiming towards the ipsilateral nipple. Its pulsation is used clinically to assess the jugular venous pressure; unlike the carotid it is non-palpable, has a double waveform and varies with posture and respiration.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the internal jugular vein begin and end? A. It begins at the jugular foramen as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus and ends behind the sternoclavicular joint by joining the subclavian vein.
