cards.desc: The venae comitantes of the internal pudendal artery, draining the perineum and external genitalia into the internal iliac vein.
cards.att: Begin as the veins of the perineum and external genitalia, including the veins of the bulb of the penis, scrotal or labial veins and the deep veins of the penis or clitoris; run backwards with the artery in the pudendal (Alcock) canal on the fascia over obturator internus, re-enter the pelvis through the lesser and then the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, and end in the internal iliac vein.
cards.act: Venous drainage of the perineum, anal canal below the pectinate line and the external genitalia.
cards.rel: Lie with the internal pudendal artery and the pudendal nerve in the pudendal canal in the lateral wall of the ischio-anal fossa; the inferior rectal vessels and nerve leave them to cross the fossa.
cards.clin: They form the systemic side of the portosystemic anastomosis at the anal canal through the inferior rectal veins. Perineal or ischio-anal sepsis may spread along the pudendal canal, and these vessels are at risk during pudendal nerve block at the ischial spine.
cards.exam: Q. In which fascial canal do the internal pudendal vessels run? A. The pudendal canal of Alcock, in the obturator internus fascia of the lateral wall of the ischio-anal fossa.

cards.desc: Long branch of the first part of the subclavian artery descending just lateral to the sternum behind the upper six costal cartilages.
cards.att: Arises from the inferior surface of the first part of the subclavian artery opposite the thyrocervical trunk, enters the thorax behind the clavicle and first costal cartilage, descends about 1 to 1.25 cm lateral to the sternal border, and divides at the level of the sixth intercostal space into the superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries.
cards.sup: Branches: pericardiacophrenic, mediastinal, thymic, sternal, anterior intercostal arteries to the upper six spaces, perforating branches with medial mammary branches, and the terminal superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the anterior chest wall, sternum, thymus, pericardium, medial part of the breast and, through the superior epigastric artery, the upper anterior abdominal wall.
cards.rel: Above the second costal cartilage it lies on the pleura, below that it is separated from the pleura by transversus thoracis; the phrenic nerve crosses it in front from lateral to medial at the thoracic inlet. Parasternal (internal thoracic) lymph nodes lie alongside it.
cards.clin: The left internal thoracic artery is the graft of choice to the left anterior descending coronary artery, with the best long-term patency. Medial quadrant breast cancer spreads to the parasternal nodes along it. In coarctation of the aorta its enlarged anterior intercostal branches produce inferior rib notching.
cards.exam: Q. Into which two arteries does the internal thoracic artery divide, and where? A. Superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries, in the sixth intercostal space.

cards.desc: Strong fibrous sheet joining the interosseous borders of the radius and ulna, forming the middle radio-ulnar union, a syndesmosis.
cards.att: Attached to the interosseous borders of the radius and ulna along most of the shafts, its main fibres running downwards and medially from the radius to the ulna. It gives origin to the deep flexors in front and the deep extensors behind and is deficient above, where the oblique cord lies.
cards.act: Transmits force from the hand and radius to the ulna and so to the humerus, and separates the flexor from the extensor compartments of the forearm.
cards.rel: The anterior interosseous vessels and nerve run on its anterior surface and the vessels pass to the back through an opening in its lower part; the posterior interosseous vessels reach the extensor compartment through a gap in its upper part.
cards.clin: Because its fibres run downwards and medially, a force falling on the outstretched hand is transferred from the radius to the ulna. Rupture of the central band with a radial head fracture and distal radio-ulnar joint disruption is the Essex-Lopresti injury, in which excision of the radial head alone leads to proximal migration of the radius and wrist pain.
cards.exam: Q. In which direction do the fibres of the interosseous membrane run, and why does it matter? A. Downwards and medially from radius to ulna, so that force transmitted up the radius is passed on to the ulna.

cards.desc: Strong fibrous sheet uniting the interosseous borders of the tibia and fibula along the length of the leg.
cards.att: Attached to the interosseous border of the tibia medially and of the fibula laterally; most fibres pass downwards and laterally from tibia to fibula. There is an aperture in its upper part for the anterior tibial vessels and a lower opening for the perforating branch of the fibular artery.
cards.act: Binds the tibia and fibula together, resists their separation, transmits a small part of the load from tibia to fibula, and provides an extensive surface for muscle attachment on both faces.
cards.rel: Separates the anterior compartment from the deep posterior compartment. Tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus and extensor hallucis longus arise from its anterior surface; tibialis posterior and flexor hallucis longus from its posterior surface.
cards.clin: With the inferior tibiofibular ligaments it forms the syndesmosis; a Maisonneuve fracture tears it up to a proximal fibular fracture, so the whole leg must be imaged. The anterior tibial artery reaches the anterior compartment through the aperture at its upper end.
cards.exam: Q. Which vessel passes through the upper aperture of the interosseous membrane of the leg? A. The anterior tibial artery, entering the anterior compartment.

cards.desc: Deep midline depression on the ventral surface of the midbrain between the two diverging crura cerebri.
cards.att: Bounded laterally by the crura cerebri, in front by the mammillary bodies and optic tracts, and behind by the upper border of the pons; its floor is the posterior perforated substance, pierced by central branches of the posterior cerebral and posterior communicating arteries.
cards.act: Contains no neural tissue of its own; it transmits the oculomotor nerves and the central perforating arteries and holds the interpeduncular cistern of cerebrospinal fluid.
cards.rel: The oculomotor nerve emerges from its side wall; the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries and the basilar bifurcation lie within the interpeduncular cistern here, with the posterior communicating artery running forwards along its lateral edge.
cards.clin: An uncal herniation pushes the medial temporal lobe into this space and compresses the oculomotor nerve against the free edge of the tentorium, giving a fixed dilated pupil and a down-and-out eye on the side of the lesion, followed by contralateral hemiparesis. A posterior communicating artery aneurysm in the same region causes an isolated painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve emerges in the interpeduncular fossa? A. The oculomotor nerve, cranial nerve III.

cards.desc: Short, curved, slit-like channel on each side connecting the lateral ventricle with the third ventricle.
cards.att: Bounded in front by the column of the fornix and behind by the anterior tubercle of the thalamus; the choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle passes through it to become continuous with that of the third ventricle.
cards.act: Conducts cerebrospinal fluid from the lateral ventricle to the third ventricle.
cards.rel: Lies at the junction of the roof and the anterior wall of the third ventricle; the septal and thalamostriate veins unite near it to form the internal cerebral vein, and it is the anatomical origin of the venous angle seen on angiography.
cards.clin: A colloid cyst of the third ventricle lodged at the foramina causes intermittent obstruction with severe positional headache, drop attacks and sudden death, and produces symmetrical dilatation of both lateral ventricles with a normal third ventricle. It is also the target of endoscopic access to the third ventricle.
cards.exam: Q. What are the boundaries of the interventricular foramen? A. The column of the fornix in front and the anterior tubercle of the thalamus behind.

cards.desc: Fibrocartilaginous secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis) uniting adjacent vertebral bodies, from the C2/C3 to the L5/S1 level, twenty-three in all.
cards.att: Peripheral anulus fibrosus of concentric lamellae of fibrocartilage attached to the ring apophyses and blended with the anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments, enclosing the gelatinous nucleus pulposus, a notochordal remnant; hyaline cartilage end-plates cover the vertebral surfaces.
cards.sup: Outer third of the anulus fibrosus is innervated by sinuvertebral (recurrent meningeal) nerves posteriorly and by grey rami communicantes laterally. The adult disc is avascular and is nourished by diffusion through the end-plates.
cards.act: Permits and limits movement between vertebrae, absorbs and distributes axial load; the discs together form about one quarter of the height of the presacral vertebral column.
cards.rel: Anteriorly the anterior longitudinal ligament, posteriorly the narrow posterior longitudinal ligament and the vertebral canal with the cord or cauda equina; the intervertebral foramina and their nerve roots lie posterolaterally.
cards.clin: The posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow in the lumbar region, so herniation of the nucleus pulposus occurs posterolaterally and compresses the traversing nerve root, one level below the named root of the exiting foramen. Disc height and water content fall with age, reducing stature.
cards.exam: Q. Why do disc herniations occur posterolaterally? A. The posterior longitudinal ligament is strong centrally but narrow laterally, so the anulus is weakest posterolaterally.

cards.k: intervertebral disk of eleventh thoracic vertebra
cards.desc: Fibrocartilaginous disc between the bodies of the eleventh and twelfth thoracic vertebrae, the lowest but one disc of the thoracic column.
cards.att: Nucleus pulposus within lamellae of anulus fibrosus, attached to the cartilaginous end plates of T11 and T12 and bound by the anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments.
cards.sup: Avascular in the adult, nourished by diffusion from the end plates; the outer anulus is innervated by sinuvertebral nerves.
cards.act: Shock absorption and limited intervertebral movement; at this level the facet joints begin to turn towards the sagittal plane, so flexion increases and rotation falls away.
cards.rel: The descending aorta lies close to the midline anteriorly as it approaches the aortic hiatus at T12; the crura of the diaphragm, the azygos vein and the thoracic duct pass immediately in front and to the right.
cards.clin: This disc lies in the thoracolumbar transition zone, T11 to L1, where the commonest vertebral fracture-dislocations occur because a rigid kyphotic thorax meets a mobile lumbar spine. The spinal cord ends near L1, so injury here may involve the conus medullaris.
cards.exam: Q. Why is the thoracolumbar junction a common site of spinal injury? A. A rigid, rib-braced thoracic spine meets a mobile lumbar spine and the facet joint planes change from coronal to sagittal.

cards.k: intervertebral disk of fifth cervical vertebra
cards.desc: Fibrocartilaginous disc between the bodies of the fifth and sixth cervical vertebrae, one of the two most mobile and most degenerated cervical levels.
cards.att: Outer anulus fibrosus and central nucleus pulposus bound to the end plates of C5 and C6, reinforced in front by the anterior longitudinal ligament and behind by the narrower posterior longitudinal ligament; it is thicker in front than behind, contributing to the cervical lordosis.
cards.sup: Avascular in the adult, nourished by diffusion through the vertebral end plates; the outer anulus and posterior longitudinal ligament are innervated by the sinuvertebral nerves.
cards.act: Transmits load and permits movement between C5 and C6, the level at which most cervical flexion and extension occurs.
cards.rel: Posteriorly related to the spinal cord through the posterior longitudinal ligament; the C6 nerve root leaves through the C5 to C6 intervertebral foramen, bounded in front by the uncovertebral joint of Luschka and behind by the zygapophysial joint.
cards.clin: With the C6 to C7 disc this is the commonest site of cervical disc prolapse and spondylosis. Because cervical roots leave above the correspondingly numbered pedicle, a C5 to C6 prolapse compresses the C6 root, giving pain down the lateral arm to the thumb, weak elbow flexion and a depressed biceps and supinator jerk.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve root is compressed by a C5 to C6 disc prolapse and what are the signs? A. The C6 root, with numbness over the thumb, weak elbow flexion and wrist extension, and a reduced biceps and brachioradialis reflex.

cards.k: intervertebral disk of fifth lumbar vertebra
cards.desc: The fibrocartilaginous disc between the body of L5 and the base of the sacrum, the lowest disc of the vertebral column.
cards.att: Anulus fibrosus attached to the ring apophyses of L5 and S1 and blended with the anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments; nucleus pulposus lies eccentrically posterior. Markedly wedge-shaped, much thicker anteriorly than posteriorly.
cards.sup: Outer anulus supplied by sinuvertebral (recurrent meningeal) nerves; the disc is avascular in the adult and is nourished by diffusion through the vertebral end-plates.
cards.act: Permits limited flexion, extension, lateral flexion and rotation, and transmits and distributes load from the lumbar spine to the sacrum.
cards.rel: The lumbosacral trunk and the sympathetic trunk lie on its anterolateral aspect; the common iliac vessels and the superior hypogastric plexus lie in front; the S1 nerve roots lie posterolaterally in the vertebral canal.
cards.clin: With L4/L5 this is the commonest site of disc prolapse. A posterolateral herniation here compresses the traversing S1 root: pain down the back of the thigh and calf to the lateral foot, weak plantarflexion, and a lost ankle jerk.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve root is compressed by a posterolateral L5/S1 disc prolapse? A. The S1 root, giving a diminished ankle jerk.

cards.k: intervertebral disk of first lumbar vertebra
cards.desc: The fibrocartilaginous disc between the bodies of the first and second lumbar vertebrae.
cards.att: Anulus fibrosus attached to the ring apophyses of L1 and L2 and to the anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments, enclosing a central nucleus pulposus.
cards.sup: Sinuvertebral nerves supply the outer third of the anulus; the disc itself is avascular in the adult.
cards.act: Allows small movements between L1 and L2 and acts as a shock absorber transmitting axial load.
cards.rel: The conus medullaris of the spinal cord ends at about this level in the adult. The cisterna chyli, aorta and diaphragmatic crura lie anteriorly.
cards.clin: Because the cord terminates at or just above this disc, needles for lumbar puncture are never introduced at this interspace. Disc prolapse here is uncommon but may compress the conus.
cards.exam: Q. Why is lumbar puncture never performed at the L1/L2 interspace in an adult? A. The conus medullaris ends at that level, so the cord would be at risk.

cards.k: intervertebral disk of fourth lumbar vertebra
cards.desc: The fibrocartilaginous disc between the bodies of the fourth and fifth lumbar vertebrae.
cards.att: Anulus fibrosus attached to the ring apophyses of L4 and L5 and to the longitudinal ligaments; nucleus pulposus placed posterior to the centre.
cards.sup: Sinuvertebral nerves to the outer anulus; avascular centrally in the adult, nourished by diffusion through the end-plates.
cards.act: Permits flexion, extension, lateral flexion and slight rotation between L4 and L5 and transmits axial load.
cards.rel: Lies at the supracristal plane. The abdominal aorta bifurcates just above it; the L5 nerve root traverses the canal behind it before leaving below the L5 pedicle.
cards.clin: With L5/S1 the commonest level of disc prolapse. A posterolateral herniation compresses the traversing L5 root: weak great toe extension and foot dorsiflexion, sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot, and a preserved ankle jerk.
cards.exam: Q. Which root is compressed by a posterolateral L4/L5 disc prolapse, and what is the classic sign? A. The L5 root, with weak extensor hallucis longus and foot drop.

cards.k: intervertebral disk of fourth thoracic vertebra
cards.desc: Fibrocartilaginous disc between the fourth and fifth thoracic vertebral bodies, lying in the plane of the sternal angle.
cards.att: Nucleus pulposus within the anulus fibrosus, attached to the end plates of T4 and T5 and reinforced by the anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments.
cards.sup: Avascular in the adult, nourished by diffusion through the end plates; the outer anulus is innervated by sinuvertebral nerves.
cards.act: Cushions axial load and allows slight movement between T4 and T5.
cards.rel: The transverse thoracic plane passes through this disc and the sternal angle; here the trachea bifurcates, the arch of the aorta begins and ends, the azygos vein arches over the right main bronchus and the pulmonary trunk divides.
cards.clin: This is the single most useful vertebral level in thoracic surface anatomy: it divides superior from inferior mediastinum and marks the level of the 2nd costal cartilage, from which ribs are counted clinically.
cards.exam: Q. Which plane passes through the T4/T5 intervertebral disc? A. The transverse thoracic plane of the sternal angle, dividing the superior and inferior mediastinum.

cards.k: intervertebral disk of sixth cervical vertebra
cards.desc: Fibrocartilaginous disc between the bodies of the sixth and seventh cervical vertebrae, the commonest site of cervical disc prolapse.
cards.att: Anulus fibrosus enclosing the nucleus pulposus, bonded to the end plates of C6 and C7 and reinforced by the anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments; wedge-shaped and thicker in front.
cards.sup: Avascular in the adult, nourished by diffusion through the vertebral end plates; the outer anulus is supplied by the sinuvertebral nerves.
cards.act: Transmits load and permits movement between C6 and C7, a level of high mechanical demand at the lower cervical spine.
cards.rel: Lies behind the cricoid cartilage and the carotid tubercle of C6, with the spinal cord behind. The C7 nerve root leaves through the C6 to C7 foramen, bounded anteriorly by the uncovertebral joint.
cards.clin: The commonest cervical disc to prolapse, compressing the C7 root and causing pain down the back of the arm to the middle finger, weak elbow extension and wrist flexion, and a lost triceps jerk. Osteophytes from the uncovertebral joints at this level are the usual cause of spondylotic radiculopathy.
cards.exam: Q. Which is the commonest cervical disc to prolapse and which root does it compress? A. The C6 to C7 disc, compressing the C7 root, with a lost triceps reflex and numbness of the middle finger.

cards.k: intervertebral disk of third lumbar vertebra
cards.desc: The fibrocartilaginous disc between the bodies of the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae.
cards.att: Anulus fibrosus attached to the ring apophyses of L3 and L4 and to the longitudinal ligaments, surrounding the nucleus pulposus.
cards.sup: Sinuvertebral nerves to the outer anulus; avascular in the adult, nourished by diffusion.
cards.act: Permits movement between L3 and L4 and transmits load down the lumbar column.
cards.rel: The cauda equina lies posteriorly in the dural sac; the third part of the duodenum crosses the aorta at about this level anteriorly.
cards.clin: The L3/L4 interspace is a standard site for lumbar puncture and spinal anaesthesia. Prolapse here typically compresses the traversing L4 root, giving weak knee extension and a reduced knee jerk.
cards.exam: Q. Which reflex is lost with an L4 root lesion? A. The knee jerk.

cards.desc: The thin, pigmented, contractile diaphragm of the vascular coat, placed in front of the lens with a central aperture, the pupil.
cards.att: Attached peripherally at its root to the anterior surface of the ciliary body; its free margin bounds the pupil and rests on the anterior surface of the lens. It divides the space between cornea and lens into the anterior and posterior chambers, and contains two muscles: the circular sphincter pupillae around the pupil, and the radial dilator pupillae.
cards.sup: Sphincter pupillae is supplied by parasympathetic fibres from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus, relayed in the ciliary ganglion and carried by the short ciliary nerves. Dilator pupillae is supplied by sympathetic fibres reaching it through the long ciliary nerves. Blood supply from the major arterial circle of the iris.
cards.act: Alters the size of the pupil, controlling the amount of light entering the eye and increasing depth of focus in the near reflex.
cards.rel: Anterior surface faces the aqueous of the anterior chamber and the cornea; posterior surface, covered by the pigmented iridial part of the retina, faces the posterior chamber, the ciliary processes and the lens.
cards.clin: Sympathetic denervation gives the miosis of Horner syndrome; oculomotor palsy gives a dilated unreactive pupil; the Argyll Robertson pupil of neurosyphilis is small, irregular and shows light-near dissociation. A peripheral iridotomy relieves pupillary block in angle-closure glaucoma.
cards.exam: Q. What is the nerve supply of dilator pupillae? A. Sympathetic fibres, reaching it through the long ciliary nerves.

cards.desc: Paired retroperitoneal excretory organ lying on the posterior abdominal wall against the psoas major, extending from about T12 to L3, the right lying slightly lower than the left because of the liver.
cards.att: Bean-shaped, with anterior and posterior surfaces, superior and inferior poles, a convex lateral and concave medial border bearing the hilum. Enclosed in a fibrous capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia and pararenal fat. Entirely retroperitoneal (primarily retroperitoneal). Hilar order from front to back: renal vein, renal artery, renal pelvis.
cards.sup: Renal artery from the abdominal aorta at L1/L2; renal vein to the inferior vena cava, the left vein crossing in front of the aorta below the superior mesenteric artery. Nerves from the renal plexus (T10 to L1 sympathetic via least splanchnic and lumbar splanchnic nerves). Lymph to the lateral aortic (para-aortic) nodes.
cards.act: Filters plasma to form urine, regulates fluid, electrolyte and acid-base balance, and secretes renin and erythropoietin.
cards.rel: Anteriorly on the right: liver, second part of duodenum, right colic flexure. Anteriorly on the left: stomach, spleen, pancreas, jejunum, left colic flexure. Posteriorly both rest on the diaphragm, psoas major, quadratus lumborum and transversus abdominis, crossed by the subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.
cards.clin: Renal angle tenderness (between the twelfth rib and the lateral border of erector spinae) suggests pyelonephritis or perinephric abscess. The renal artery is an end-artery system, so segmental occlusion infarcts that segment. A transplanted kidney is placed extraperitoneally in the iliac fossa, not orthotopically.
cards.exam: Q. Arrange the structures at the renal hilum from anterior to posterior. A. Renal vein, renal artery, renal pelvis.

cards.desc: Smallest and most fragile bone of the face, forming part of the medial wall of the orbit.
cards.att: Has a posterior lacrimal crest ending below in the lacrimal hamulus, and in front of the crest a lacrimal groove which, with the frontal process of the maxilla, forms the fossa for the lacrimal sac. Articulates with the frontal bone above, the maxilla in front, the ethmoid behind and the inferior nasal concha below, and helps form the upper opening of the nasolacrimal canal.
cards.sup: Branches of the ophthalmic and infraorbital arteries.
cards.act: Houses and protects the lacrimal sac and forms the bony beginning of the nasolacrimal canal; its posterior crest gives attachment to the lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi and the medial check ligament.
cards.rel: Lacrimal sac and fascia lie in its groove, the ethmoidal air cells behind it, and the middle meatus of the nose medially, separated only by thin bone.
cards.clin: Removed to create the bony window in dacryocystorhinostomy, because the middle meatus lies immediately medial to it. It is commonly shattered in naso-orbito-ethmoid fractures, which disrupt tear drainage and cause traumatic telecanthus.
cards.exam: Q. Which two bones form the fossa for the lacrimal sac? A. The lacrimal bone behind and the frontal process of the maxilla in front, separated by the posterior and anterior lacrimal crests.

cards.desc: Fine channel, about 10 mm long, carrying tears from the lid margin to the lacrimal sac; there is one in each eyelid.
cards.att: Begins at the lacrimal punctum on the medial part of the lid margin, runs vertically for about 2 mm, turns sharply at a dilated ampulla, then runs medially for about 8 mm behind the medial palpebral ligament. The superior and inferior canaliculi usually unite as a common canaliculus that opens into the lateral wall of the lacrimal sac.
cards.sup: Sensory innervation from the infratrochlear nerve, a branch of the nasociliary nerve, CN V1.
cards.act: Conducts tears from the lacus lacrimalis into the lacrimal sac, aided by the lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi, which acts as a pump on blinking.
cards.rel: Lies deep to the skin at the medial part of the eyelid, in front of the orbital septum, with the medial palpebral ligament and the lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi related to its medial end and the lacrimal sac.
cards.clin: The canaliculus is easily torn in medial eyelid lacerations, particularly dog bites, and must be repaired over a stent to avoid permanent watering. Punctal stenosis or canalicular block causes epiphora, assessed by syringing and probing.
cards.exam: Q. Where do the lacrimal canaliculi begin and end? A. They begin at the lacrimal puncta on the lid margins and open into the lacrimal sac, usually by a common canaliculus.

cards.desc: Serous gland in the lacrimal fossa of the frontal bone, at the superolateral angle of the orbit.
cards.att: Lies in the lacrimal fossa; the aponeurosis of levator palpebrae superioris divides it into a larger orbital part and a smaller palpebral part, which is seen through the everted upper lid. About 10 to 12 ducts open into the lateral part of the superior conjunctival fornix.
cards.sup: Lacrimal artery from the ophthalmic artery; venous drainage to the superior ophthalmic vein. Sensory by the lacrimal nerve (V1). Secretomotor parasympathetic from the superior salivatory (lacrimatory) nucleus by the facial nerve, greater petrosal nerve, nerve of the pterygoid canal, pterygopalatine ganglion, then zygomatic and zygomaticotemporal nerves to the lacrimal nerve.
cards.act: Secretes the aqueous layer of the tear film, which lubricates the cornea, supplies oxygen and lysozyme, and is swept medially by blinking.
cards.rel: Orbital part lies between the levator aponeurosis below and the orbital roof above; the palpebral part lies deep to the conjunctiva of the upper fornix. Related laterally to the lateral rectus and the lacrimal nerve and artery.
cards.clin: Facial nerve lesions proximal to the geniculate ganglion cause loss of reflex lacrimation, and aberrant regeneration produces crocodile tears (lacrimation on eating). Autoimmune destruction in Sjogren syndrome causes keratoconjunctivitis sicca; acute dacryoadenitis gives an S-shaped upper lid.
cards.exam: Q. Trace the secretomotor pathway to the lacrimal gland. A. Superior salivatory nucleus, facial nerve, greater petrosal nerve, nerve of pterygoid canal, pterygopalatine ganglion, maxillary and zygomatic nerves, communicating branch to the lacrimal nerve.

cards.desc: The smallest branch of the ophthalmic nerve, running along the upper border of lateral rectus to the lacrimal gland.
cards.att: Arises from the ophthalmic nerve, enters the orbit through the lateral part of the superior orbital fissure outside the common tendinous ring, runs forwards on the upper border of lateral rectus with the lacrimal artery, pierces the orbital septum and ends in the lateral part of the upper eyelid.
cards.act: Sensory to the lacrimal gland, the adjacent conjunctiva and the skin of the lateral part of the upper eyelid; it also delivers secretomotor fibres to the gland.
cards.rel: Lies lateral to the frontal nerve in the roof of the orbit, above lateral rectus; it receives a communicating branch from the zygomaticotemporal nerve of CN V2.
cards.clin: The secretomotor fibres to the lacrimal gland are postganglionic parasympathetic fibres from the pterygopalatine ganglion, which reach the gland by the zygomatic and zygomaticotemporal nerves and the communicating branch, not from V1 itself. Lesions along this route give a dry eye.
cards.exam: Q. How do secretomotor fibres reach the lacrimal gland? A. From the pterygopalatine ganglion via the zygomatic and zygomaticotemporal nerves to the lacrimal nerve.

cards.desc: Dilated blind upper end of the nasolacrimal passage, about 12 mm long, lodged in the lacrimal groove of the medial orbital wall.
cards.att: Sits in the fossa formed by the frontal process of the maxilla and the lacrimal bone, between the anterior and posterior lacrimal crests, enclosed by the lacrimal fascia. Receives the common canaliculus on its lateral wall and continues below as the nasolacrimal duct.
cards.sup: Branches of the facial and infraorbital arteries and the ophthalmic artery; sensory supply from the infratrochlear nerve (V1).
cards.act: Fills and empties with each blink; the lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi expands the sac to draw in tears, and elastic recoil expels them into the duct.
cards.rel: Medial palpebral ligament crosses its upper part in front; the lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi (Horner muscle) passes behind it. Medially it is separated from the middle meatus by thin bone.
cards.clin: Stasis causes dacryocystitis, with a tender swelling below the medial palpebral ligament and regurgitation of pus through the puncta on pressure (regurgitation test). Dacryocystorhinostomy joins the sac to the nose through the lacrimal bone.
cards.exam: Q. Why does a lacrimal sac swelling lie below the medial palpebral ligament? A. The ligament crosses the upper part of the sac, so distension presents below it; a swelling above the ligament suggests another diagnosis.

cards.desc: Thin sheet of grey matter and pia forming the anterior wall of the third ventricle, stretching from the upper surface of the optic chiasm below to the rostrum of the corpus callosum above.
cards.att: Represents the rostral end of the embryonic neural tube; the anterior commissure crosses in its upper part, and it contains the vascular organ of the lamina terminalis, a circumventricular organ lacking a blood-brain barrier.
cards.sup: Small branches of the anterior cerebral and anterior communicating arteries.
cards.act: Forms the anterior boundary of the third ventricle; its vascular organ senses plasma osmolality and contributes to the control of thirst and vasopressin release.
cards.rel: Lies behind the anterior cerebral and anterior communicating arteries in the cistern of the lamina terminalis, above the optic chiasm and in front of the third ventricle and the optic recess.
cards.clin: The lamina terminalis is opened (fenestrated) during aneurysm surgery to release cerebrospinal fluid, relax the brain and reduce the risk of shunt-dependent hydrocephalus, and it is a route of approach to lesions of the third ventricle.
cards.exam: Q. What forms the anterior wall of the third ventricle? A. The lamina terminalis, with the anterior commissure in its upper part.

cards.desc: Large lateral branch of the profunda femoris artery supplying the lateral thigh and hip.
cards.att: Arises from the lateral side of the profunda femoris artery, occasionally directly from the femoral artery, passes laterally between the divisions of the femoral nerve and deep to sartorius and rectus femoris, and divides into ascending, transverse and descending branches.
cards.sup: Ascending branch to the greater trochanter and the trochanteric anastomosis, transverse branch encircling the femur to the cruciate anastomosis, descending branch to vastus lateralis and the knee.
cards.act: Supplies the extensor compartment muscles, the hip joint region and the skin of the lateral thigh.
cards.rel: Passes between the anterior and posterior divisions of the femoral nerve, deep to sartorius and rectus femoris and superficial to vastus intermedius.
cards.clin: Source of the perforators for the anterolateral thigh free flap. Its ascending branch contributes to the trochanteric anastomosis, but the retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery are the main supply to the head of the femur, so intracapsular femoral neck fracture risks avascular necrosis.
cards.exam: Q. Which artery is the main supply to the head of the femur in an adult? A. The medial circumflex femoral artery, through its retinacular branches.

cards.desc: A small intrinsic laryngeal muscle running obliquely upwards and backwards on the inner aspect of the lamina of the thyroid cartilage.
cards.att: Arises from the upper border of the lateral part of the arch of the cricoid cartilage and inserts into the front of the muscular process of the arytenoid cartilage.
cards.sup: Recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus; superior and inferior laryngeal arteries.
cards.act: Pulls the muscular process forwards, rotating the vocal process medially, so it adducts the vocal folds and closes the rima glottidis. It is the direct antagonist of the posterior crico-arytenoid.
cards.rel: Lies deep to the lamina of the thyroid cartilage, lateral to the conus elasticus and below the level of the vestibular fold; the recurrent laryngeal nerve reaches it from behind the cricothyroid joint.
cards.clin: Damage to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, as in thyroidectomy, paralyses it along with the other adductors and the abductor, leaving the cord near the midline with a hoarse breathy voice; bilateral injury threatens the airway.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle is the sole abductor of the vocal folds and which the chief adductor? A. Posterior crico-arytenoid abducts; lateral crico-arytenoid adducts.

cards.desc: Small oval swelling on the posteroinferior aspect of the thalamus, below the pulvinar, forming the thalamic relay of the visual pathway.
cards.att: Receives the lateral (larger) root of the optic tract and gives rise to the optic radiation (geniculocalcarine tract), which runs through the retrolentiform part of the internal capsule to the visual cortex on the banks of the calcarine sulcus. It has six laminae: layers 1, 4 and 6 receive crossed (contralateral nasal) fibres and layers 2, 3 and 5 uncrossed (ipsilateral temporal) fibres; layers 1 and 2 are magnocellular and layers 3 to 6 parvocellular.
cards.sup: Anterior choroidal artery and the lateral posterior choroidal branch of the posterior cerebral artery.
cards.act: Relays and processes visual information from the retina to the primary visual cortex, keeping the two eyes' inputs in separate layers.
cards.rel: Lies below the pulvinar, lateral to the medial geniculate body, above and lateral to the crus cerebri; the optic tract winds round the crus to reach it.
cards.clin: A lesion of the lateral geniculate body causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often incongruous. Its dual arterial supply produces characteristic sector field defects when one of the two feeding arteries is occluded.
cards.exam: Q. Which lateral geniculate laminae receive crossed retinal fibres? A. Laminae 1, 4 and 6.

cards.desc: The smaller and shorter of the two heads of gastrocnemius, forming the inferolateral boundary of the popliteal fossa and the lateral bulge of the calf.
cards.att: Arises by a strong tendon from an impression on the lateral surface of the lateral condyle of the femur and the adjacent popliteal surface; joins the medial head, and their common aponeurosis fuses with that of soleus to form the calcaneal tendon inserted into the middle of the posterior surface of the calcaneus.
cards.sup: Tibial nerve, S1, S2; sural arteries from the popliteal artery.
cards.act: Plantarflexes the ankle and flexes the knee; provides the propulsive thrust in walking, running and jumping.
cards.rel: Forms the inferolateral boundary of the popliteal fossa; the common fibular nerve lies along its lateral border on its way to the neck of the fibula, and plantaris arises just above it. A sesamoid bone, the fabella, lies in its tendon in a minority of people.
cards.clin: The fabella can be mistaken for a loose body on a knee radiograph. The tendinous origin and the muscle belly may compress the popliteal artery, causing popliteal artery entrapment syndrome in young athletes; the common fibular nerve at its lateral border is at risk in that plane.
cards.exam: Q. What is the fabella? A. A sesamoid bone in the tendon of the lateral head of gastrocnemius behind the lateral femoral condyle.

cards.desc: The head of triceps arising above and lateral to the radial groove on the back of the humerus, forming the lateral contour of the upper arm.
cards.att: Arises from a linear ridge on the posterior surface of the humerus above and lateral to the radial groove and from the upper part of the lateral intermuscular septum; joins the common tendon inserted into the upper surface of the olecranon of the ulna.
cards.sup: Radial nerve, C6, C7, C8; profunda brachii artery.
cards.act: Extends the elbow joint; it is a pure elbow extensor, taking no part in shoulder movement.
cards.rel: Its origin forms the upper lateral wall of the radial (spiral) groove, in which the radial nerve and profunda brachii vessels run between the lateral and medial heads. With the long head, the humerus and teres major it bounds the triangular interval through which the radial nerve leaves the axilla.
cards.clin: A fracture of the humeral shaft at the spiral groove injures the radial nerve as it lies against bone under this head, producing wrist drop. The muscle is the landmark for the posterior (triceps-splitting) approach to the humerus.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve lies in the radial groove deep to the lateral head of triceps? A. The radial nerve, with the profunda brachii vessels.

syn: anterolateral papillary muscle of left ventricle
cards.desc: Anterolateral papillary muscle of the left ventricle, arising from the anterolateral wall and usually formed of two heads.
cards.att: Arises from the junction of the anterior and lateral walls of the left ventricle in its middle third; its chordae tendineae pass to the adjacent halves of both the anterior and the posterior cusps of the mitral valve.
cards.sup: Dual supply from a diagonal branch of the left anterior descending artery and from the circumflex artery.
cards.act: Contracts with the ventricle to hold the mitral cusps apposed and prevent prolapse into the left atrium during systole.
cards.rel: Projects into the left ventricular cavity from the anterolateral wall, with the posteromedial papillary muscle opposite it and the trabeculae carneae between; both send chordae to both mitral cusps.
cards.clin: Each mitral cusp receives chordae from both papillary muscles, so ischaemia of one muscle causes leakage along the whole line of closure. Rupture here is less common than on the posteromedial side because of the dual blood supply.
cards.exam: Q. To which cusps do the chordae of a left ventricular papillary muscle go? A. To the adjacent halves of both mitral cusps, which is why each muscle steadies the whole line of closure.

cards.desc: The extra-ocular muscle on the lateral wall of the orbit that turns the eye outwards.
cards.att: Arises by two heads from the lateral part of the common tendinous ring, one from the ring proper and one from the spina recti lateralis on the greater wing of the sphenoid, and inserts into the sclera on the lateral aspect of the globe about 7 mm behind the corneal margin.
cards.sup: Abducent nerve, which enters its ocular surface; muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery and the lacrimal artery.
cards.act: Abducts the eyeball; it is the only muscle producing pure horizontal abduction.
cards.rel: Between its two heads lie the structures passing through the common tendinous ring: the oculomotor divisions, the nasociliary nerve and the abducent nerve. The lacrimal nerve and artery run along its upper border.
cards.clin: Abducent nerve palsy paralyses it, giving a convergent squint with diplopia maximal on looking to the affected side. Because the nerve has the longest intracranial course and bends over the petrous temporal bone, raised intracranial pressure produces a sixth nerve palsy as a false localising sign.
cards.exam: Q. Why is abducent palsy a false localising sign in raised intracranial pressure? A. The long intracranial course of the nerve is stretched over the petrous ridge, so the palsy does not indicate the site of the lesion.

cards.desc: Branch of the second part of the axillary artery running down the lateral chest wall along the lower border of pectoralis minor.
cards.att: Arises from the second part of the axillary artery behind pectoralis minor, descends along the lower (lateral) border of that muscle on serratus anterior to the chest wall.
cards.sup: Supplies serratus anterior, both pectoral muscles, subscapularis and the axillary lymph nodes; in the female it gives lateral mammary branches to the breast. It anastomoses with the internal thoracic, subscapular, intercostal and thoracoacromial arteries.
cards.act: Principal arterial supply of the lateral chest wall and a major source for the lateral part of the breast.
cards.rel: Runs with the long thoracic nerve on serratus anterior, deep to pectoralis major; the lateral group of axillary nodes lies along it.
cards.clin: Encountered and ligated during axillary clearance and modified radical mastectomy; injury near the long thoracic nerve risks winging of the scapula. It contributes substantially to the blood supply of the breast.
cards.exam: Q. From which part of the axillary artery does the lateral thoracic artery arise? A. The second part, behind pectoralis minor.

cards.desc: Large C-shaped cavity within each cerebral hemisphere, lined by ependyma and containing cerebrospinal fluid and choroid plexus.
cards.att: Consists of an anterior (frontal) horn in the frontal lobe, a body in the parietal region, an atrium or trigone, a posterior (occipital) horn and an inferior (temporal) horn; it communicates with the third ventricle through the interventricular foramen.
cards.sup: Choroid plexus supplied by the anterior choroidal artery and posterior choroidal branches of the posterior cerebral artery; drained by the internal cerebral vein.
cards.act: Contains and circulates cerebrospinal fluid, most of which is produced by its choroid plexus.
cards.rel: Roof formed by the corpus callosum throughout; anterior horn bounded medially by the septum pellucidum and laterally by the head of the caudate nucleus; the thalamus lies in the floor of the body, the hippocampus in the floor of the inferior horn, and the calcar avis and bulb of the corpus callosum indent the posterior horn.
cards.clin: An external ventricular drain is passed into the frontal horn through Kocher's point, about 11 cm behind the nasion and 3 cm from the midline, aimed towards the ipsilateral medial canthus and the tragus. Ventricular size is assessed by the Evans index, the ratio of maximal frontal horn width to maximal inner skull diameter, with a value above 0.3 indicating ventriculomegaly.
cards.exam: Q. Which structure forms the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle? A. The hippocampus, with the collateral eminence laterally.

cards.desc: Transparent, avascular, biconvex body behind the iris, suspended between the aqueous and vitreous chambers.
cards.att: Held by the zonular fibres of the ciliary zonule passing from the ciliary processes to its capsule at the equator. It has a capsule, an anterior subcapsular epithelium, a cortex and a nucleus, and it grows by adding fibres throughout life.
cards.sup: Avascular and non-innervated; nourished by diffusion from the aqueous humour.
cards.act: Refracts light onto the retina, contributing about 15 to 17 dioptres, and increases its curvature during accommodation when ciliary muscle contraction slackens the zonule.
cards.rel: Iris and pupil in front, vitreous body in the hyaloid fossa behind, ciliary processes at the equator.
cards.clin: Opacification is cataract, the leading cause of reversible blindness. Loss of elasticity with age causes presbyopia. The lens dislocates superotemporally in Marfan syndrome and inferonasally in homocystinuria.
cards.exam: Q. What happens to the lens during accommodation for near vision? A. Ciliary muscle contracts, the zonule slackens, and the elastic lens becomes more convex, increasing its refractive power.

cards.desc: A thin triangular muscle in the roof of the orbit that raises the upper eyelid, the only voluntary retractor of the lid.
cards.att: Arises from the orbital surface of the lesser wing of the sphenoid above and in front of the optic canal; ends in a broad aponeurosis whose fibres pass into the skin of the upper lid and to the anterior surface of the superior tarsal plate, with medial and lateral horns anchored to the orbital walls. Deep to the aponeurosis a sheet of smooth muscle, the superior tarsal muscle of Müller, reaches the upper border of the tarsal plate.
cards.sup: Superior division of the oculomotor nerve for the striated part; sympathetic fibres from the internal carotid plexus for the superior tarsal muscle. Ophthalmic artery.
cards.act: Elevates the upper eyelid and opens the palpebral fissure; the smooth part maintains lid elevation tonically.
cards.rel: Lies immediately above superior rectus and shares its nerve supply and fascial sheath, so the lid rises with upward gaze. The frontal and trochlear nerves lie above it beneath the orbital periosteum.
cards.clin: Complete ptosis with a dilated pupil and a down-and-out eye indicates oculomotor nerve palsy; partial ptosis with miosis and anhidrosis indicates Horner syndrome from loss of sympathetic supply to the superior tarsal muscle. Fatigable ptosis suggests myasthenia gravis.
cards.exam: Q. Distinguish the ptosis of third nerve palsy from that of Horner syndrome. A. Third nerve palsy gives complete ptosis with mydriasis and ophthalmoplegia; Horner syndrome gives partial ptosis with miosis, from paralysis of the superior tarsal muscle.

cards.desc: Strap muscle of the posterior triangle running from the upper cervical transverse processes to the superior angle of the scapula.
cards.att: Origin: transverse processes of the atlas and axis and the posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C3 and C4. Insertion: medial border of the scapula between the superior angle and the root of the spine of the scapula.
cards.sup: Dorsal scapular nerve (C5) and branches from the ventral rami of C3 and C4.
cards.act: Elevates the scapula and, with the rhomboids, rotates the glenoid cavity downwards; laterally flexes the neck when the scapula is fixed.
cards.rel: Forms part of the floor of the posterior triangle of the neck, covered there by prevertebral fascia; lies deep to trapezius and sternocleidomastoid, superficial to scalenus posterior and splenius cervicis.
cards.clin: A common site of myofascial trigger points causing pain at the superior angle of the scapula and a stiff neck. It is a landmark in the floor of the posterior triangle during neck dissection, where the dorsal scapular nerve and accessory nerve lie nearby.
cards.exam: Q. What is the nerve supply of levator scapulae? A. The dorsal scapular nerve (C5) with direct branches from C3 and C4.

cards.desc: A cylindrical muscle descending from the base of the skull into the soft palate, the chief elevator of the palate.
cards.att: Arises from the inferior surface of the petrous part of the temporal bone in front of the lower opening of the carotid canal and from the medial lamina of the cartilage of the pharyngotympanic tube; passes downwards, forwards and medially above the upper border of the superior constrictor to insert into the upper surface of the palatine aponeurosis, interdigitating with its fellow.
cards.sup: Pharyngeal plexus, motor fibres from the cranial part of the accessory nerve carried by the vagus; ascending palatine and greater palatine arteries.
cards.act: Elevates the soft palate and pulls it backwards to close the pharyngeal isthmus and seal off the nasopharynx during swallowing and speech; assists opening of the pharyngotympanic tube.
cards.rel: Enters the palate through the sinus of Morgagni, the gap between the upper border of superior constrictor and the base of the skull, alongside the pharyngotympanic tube and the ascending palatine artery.
cards.clin: Paralysis, as in vagal or bulbar lesions, causes nasal regurgitation of fluids and nasal speech, and the uvula deviates to the healthy side. Its abnormal insertion in cleft palate underlies the middle ear effusions of these children, and its repositioning is the aim of palatoplasty.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle of the soft palate is not supplied by the pharyngeal plexus? A. Tensor veli palatini, supplied by the mandibular nerve; the rest, including levator veli palatini, are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus.

cards.desc: Midline fibrous raphe of the anterior abdominal wall, formed by interlacing aponeurotic fibres of the flat abdominal muscles of both sides.
cards.att: Extends from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis, attaching below to the pubic symphysis and pubic crest, and is pierced at its midpoint by the umbilicus. Broad above the umbilicus, narrow and thick below it.
cards.sup: Essentially avascular, crossed only by small perforating vessels and nerves; the segmental nerves and vessels run laterally.
cards.act: Provides midline attachment and transfers tension between the oblique and transverse abdominal muscles of the two sides.
cards.rel: Lies between the two recti, separating the right and left rectus sheaths; the pyramidalis muscles insert into its lower part.
cards.clin: Its avascularity makes the midline (median) laparotomy incision quick and relatively bloodless, but healing is slower and incisional hernia commoner. Divarication of the recti widens it in pregnancy and obesity, and epigastric hernias push through its wider supraumbilical part.
cards.exam: Q. Why is the midline laparotomy incision made through the linea alba? A. It is a relatively avascular, nerveless midline raphe, giving quick access with minimal bleeding or nerve injury.

cards.desc: The mobile musculofibrous folds, upper and lower, that bound the oral fissure anteriorly and meet laterally at the angles of the mouth.
cards.att: From surface inwards: skin, superficial fascia, orbicularis oris and the muscles converging on the modiolus, submucosa containing labial glands, and mucous membrane. The upper lip shows the philtrum and the vermilion border; each lip is tethered to the gum by a median frenulum.
cards.sup: Arteries: superior and inferior labial branches of the facial artery, anastomosing across the midline. Motor: facial nerve, through buccal and marginal mandibular branches. Sensory: infraorbital nerve (V2) for the upper lip, mental nerve (V3) for the lower. Lymph: upper lip and lateral lower lip to the submandibular nodes, central lower lip to the submental nodes bilaterally.
cards.act: Close the oral fissure, contain food during chewing, and act in speech, sucking, whistling and facial expression.
cards.rel: Lie in front of the alveolar arches and teeth, separated from them by the labial vestibule; the labial arteries lie deep to the muscle just inside the vermilion border.
cards.clin: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lower lip is common in outdoor workers; central lesions drain to submental nodes on both sides, so bilateral neck disease occurs. Cleft lip results from failure of fusion of the maxillary and medial nasal prominences and is lateral to the philtrum, not midline.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the central part of the lower lip drain? A. To the submental lymph nodes on both sides.

cards.desc: One of the two asymmetric lobes of the thymus, the primary lymphoid organ for T lymphocyte maturation, lying in the anterior and superior mediastinum behind the manubrium.
cards.att: The right and left lobes are joined by loose connective tissue in the midline; each extends from the lower neck near the thyroid down over the pericardium, and is divided by septa into lobules with a densely packed cortex and a paler medulla containing Hassall's corpuscles. Each lobe develops from the third pharyngeal pouch of its own side.
cards.sup: Arteries: branches of the internal thoracic and inferior thyroid arteries. Veins: drain to the left brachiocephalic vein. Lymph: parasternal, brachiocephalic and tracheobronchial nodes.
cards.act: Site of T lymphocyte development and selection; largest relative to body size at birth, maximal in weight at puberty, then replaced progressively by fat.
cards.rel: Lies behind the manubrium and upper body of sternum, in front of the left brachiocephalic vein, aortic arch and its branches, and the pericardium.
cards.clin: Thymoma presents as an anterior mediastinal mass and is associated with myasthenia gravis, treated by thymectomy. The normal infant thymus gives the sail sign on chest radiograph. Failure of third and fourth pouch development causes DiGeorge syndrome with thymic aplasia and hypocalcaemia.
cards.exam: Q. From which pharyngeal pouch does the thymus develop? A. The ventral part of the third pharyngeal pouch, bilaterally.

cards.desc: Two or three slender nerves given off by the nasociliary nerve as it crosses the optic nerve, running forwards to pierce the sclera.
cards.att: Arise from the nasociliary nerve above the optic nerve, run forwards medial to the optic nerve, pierce the sclera near its entry, and pass forwards in the perichoroidal space to the ciliary body and iris.
cards.act: Sensory to the cornea, iris and ciliary body, and they also carry sympathetic fibres to the dilator pupillae.
cards.rel: Run alongside the short ciliary nerves and the ciliary arteries in the perichoroidal space between sclera and choroid.
cards.clin: They carry corneal sensation, so testing the corneal reflex tests them. Being sympathetic carriers, injury to them or to the sympathetic pathway contributes to the miosis of Horner syndrome.
cards.exam: Q. From which nerve do the long ciliary nerves arise? A. The nasociliary nerve.

cards.desc: The lateral head of biceps brachii, whose tendon arises inside the shoulder joint and descends in the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus.
cards.att: Arises from the supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula and the adjacent glenoid labrum; the tendon arches over the head of the humerus inside the capsule, leaves through the intertubercular sulcus under the transverse humeral ligament, and joins the short head. The common tendon inserts into the posterior rough part of the radial tuberosity, and the bicipital aponeurosis passes medially into the deep fascia of the forearm.
cards.sup: Musculocutaneous nerve, C5, C6; brachial artery and the anterior circumflex humeral artery to the tendon.
cards.act: Powerful supinator of the flexed forearm and flexor of the elbow; the tendon of the long head also helps to stabilise the head of the humerus during abduction.
cards.rel: The tendon is intracapsular but extrasynovial, invested by a tubular sheath of synovial membrane. In the arm the muscle lies over brachialis, with the musculocutaneous nerve between them and the median nerve and brachial artery along its medial border; the bicipital aponeurosis roofs the cubital fossa and protects the brachial artery.
cards.clin: Attrition of the tendon in the intertubercular sulcus causes bicipital tendinitis, and rupture allows the belly to retract distally as the Popeye sign. Tears at its labral attachment are SLAP lesions. The bicipital aponeurosis separates the brachial artery from the median cubital vein during venepuncture.
cards.exam: Q. Is the tendon of the long head of biceps intracapsular or intrasynovial? A. It is intracapsular but extrasynovial, being ensheathed by a tube of synovial membrane.

syn: long head of biceps femoris muscle
cards.desc: The superficial hamstring head arising from the ischial tuberosity that forms the superolateral boundary of the popliteal fossa.
cards.att: Arises with semitendinosus from the inferomedial impression on the ischial tuberosity and from the sacrotuberous ligament; joins the short head from the linea aspera and inserts mainly into the head of the fibula, its tendon split by the fibular collateral ligament, with a slip to the lateral condyle of the tibia.
cards.sup: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve, L5, S1, S2; perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery.
cards.act: Flexes the knee, laterally rotates the flexed leg, and extends the hip.
cards.rel: Crosses the sciatic nerve obliquely in the back of the thigh and forms the superolateral boundary of the popliteal fossa, with the common fibular nerve lying along the medial side of its tendon before winding round the neck of the fibula.
cards.clin: Its proximal tendon is a common site of hamstring strain and of avulsion of the ischial tuberosity apophysis in adolescent sprinters. The common fibular nerve is at risk in operations on its distal tendon and in an injury to the fibular neck; the two heads differ in nerve supply, which is why the short head alone escapes in a tibial division lesion.
cards.exam: Q. Which hamstring head has a different nerve supply and what is it? A. The short head of biceps femoris, supplied by the common fibular division of the sciatic nerve.

cards.desc: The only head of triceps to cross the shoulder joint, descending between teres minor and teres major to divide the interval below them.
cards.att: Arises from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula and the adjoining capsule of the shoulder joint; joins the common tendon inserted into the upper surface of the olecranon.
cards.sup: Radial nerve, C6, C7, C8; profunda brachii and posterior circumflex humeral arteries.
cards.act: Extends the elbow; also extends and adducts the arm at the shoulder and steadies the head of the humerus.
cards.rel: Passing between teres minor and teres major it divides the space into a quadrangular space laterally, transmitting the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels, and an upper triangular space medially, transmitting the circumflex scapular artery. With the humerus and teres major it bounds the triangular interval, through which the radial nerve and profunda brachii vessels pass into the arm.
cards.clin: The definitive landmark for the quadrangular space: the axillary nerve is injured there in shoulder dislocation and in surgical neck fractures, giving deltoid paralysis and numbness over the regimental badge area. Quadrangular space syndrome compresses the same structures.
cards.exam: Q. Name the boundaries and contents of the quadrangular space. A. Teres minor above, teres major below, long head of triceps medially, surgical neck of humerus laterally; it transmits the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels.

cards.desc: Longest ligament of the sole, a strong band running forwards from the calcaneus to the cuboid and the metatarsal bases.
cards.att: Attached behind to the plantar surface of the calcaneus in front of the tuberosity, and in front to the ridge on the cuboid, with superficial fibres continuing beyond the groove to the bases of the second, third and fourth metatarsals.
cards.act: Chief ligamentous support of the lateral longitudinal arch; it resists depression of the calcaneocuboid joint and converts the groove on the cuboid into a tunnel for the tendon of fibularis longus.
cards.rel: Superficial to the short plantar (plantar calcaneocuboid) ligament and deep to the tendon of fibularis longus and the plantar aponeurosis.
cards.clin: Its integrity is essential to the lateral longitudinal arch; injury contributes to flattening of the lateral border of the foot. It is a source of lateral plantar pain in dancers and is used as a landmark in cuboid tunnel release.
cards.exam: Q. Which ligament converts the groove on the cuboid into a tunnel, and for which tendon? A. The long plantar ligament, for the tendon of fibularis longus.

cards.desc: The largest and intermediate of the three columns of erector spinae, extending from the lumbar region to the upper thorax.
cards.att: Origin: the common erector spinae tendon from the sacrum, iliac crest and lumbar spinous processes, and the transverse and accessory processes of the lumbar vertebrae. Insertion: by medial slips into the tips of the transverse processes of all the thoracic vertebrae and by lateral slips into the lower nine or ten ribs between the tubercle and the angle.
cards.sup: Dorsal rami of the thoracic and lumbar spinal nerves.
cards.act: Bilaterally extends the vertebral column and helps depress the ribs; unilaterally produces lateral flexion to the same side and controls trunk flexion eccentrically.
cards.rel: Lies between iliocostalis laterally and spinalis medially, deep to the thoracolumbar fascia, serratus posterior muscles, rhomboids, trapezius and latissimus dorsi.
cards.clin: Forms most of the palpable paraspinal ridge lateral to the spinous processes; a common source of mechanical back pain and the muscle mass retracted in posterior spinal approaches.
cards.exam: Q. Where does longissimus thoracis insert on the ribs? A. Between the tubercle and the angle of the lower nine or ten ribs.

cards.desc: A prevertebral muscle of the neck that broadens as it ascends from the cervical transverse processes to the base of the skull.
cards.att: Arises by four tendinous slips from the anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of the third to sixth cervical vertebrae and inserts into the inferior surface of the basilar part of the occipital bone in front of the pharyngeal tubercle.
cards.sup: Anterior rami of the first to third cervical spinal nerves; ascending pharyngeal and vertebral arteries.
cards.act: Flexes the head on the neck at the atlanto-occipital joint and assists flexion of the upper cervical spine.
cards.rel: Lies in front of longus colli and behind the pharynx, covered by the prevertebral fascia on which the sympathetic trunk lies. The carotid sheath is anterolateral, and the vertebral artery and internal jugular vein lie laterally.
cards.clin: Bounds the retropharyngeal (prevertebral) space, along which pus from cervical spine tuberculosis or a retropharyngeal abscess tracks and bulges into the pharynx. It is retracted in the anterior approach to the cervical spine.
cards.exam: Q. Which fascia covers longus capitis and what lies on it? A. The prevertebral fascia, on which lies the cervical sympathetic trunk.

cards.desc: The largest tooth of the mandibular arch, the first permanent tooth to erupt, appearing behind the deciduous molars at about six years without replacing any deciduous tooth.
cards.att: Two roots, mesial and distal, in the mandibular alveolus; the crown typically bears five cusps, two buccal, two lingual and a distal cusp, with a broad occlusal table.
cards.sup: Sensory: inferior alveolar nerve (V3); buccal gingiva by the buccal nerve and lingual gingiva by the lingual nerve. Artery: inferior alveolar artery.
cards.act: Grinds and crushes food; establishes the key of occlusion with the upper first molar.
cards.rel: Lies behind the second premolar and in front of the second molar; its roots may lie close to the inferior alveolar canal.
cards.clin: The most commonly carious tooth in the mouth, and often mistaken for a deciduous tooth because it erupts without one being shed. Its relation of the mesiobuccal cusp to the buccal groove of the upper first molar defines Angle's classification of occlusion.
cards.exam: Q. Which is the first permanent tooth to erupt? A. The mandibular first molar, at about six years.

cards.desc: Four pairs of parietal branches arising from the back of the abdominal aorta and passing laterally across the bodies of the upper four lumbar vertebrae.
cards.att: Arise from the posterior surface of the aorta opposite L1 to L4, pass laterally behind the sympathetic trunk and the psoas major, and divide into a dorsal branch with a spinal twig and an abdominal branch running between transversus abdominis and internal oblique. A fifth small pair usually arises from the median sacral artery.
cards.sup: Dorsal branches to the back muscles and skin, spinal branches to the vertebral canal and its contents, abdominal branches anastomosing with the lower intercostal, subcostal, iliolumbar and epigastric arteries.
cards.act: Supply the posterior abdominal wall, the muscles of the back, the lumbar vertebrae and the coverings of the spinal cord.
cards.rel: The right lumbar arteries pass behind the inferior vena cava; the upper two pairs on each side pass behind the crura of the diaphragm, and all pass behind the lumbar sympathetic trunk.
cards.clin: A back-bleeding lumbar artery is a common cause of a type II endoleak after endovascular aortic repair, and lumbar arteries must be oversewn from within the sac in open repair. A lumbar branch may give the great anterior radicular artery of Adamkiewicz, which usually arises between T9 and L2, so its interruption risks spinal cord ischaemia.
cards.exam: Q. How many pairs of lumbar arteries arise from the abdominal aorta and where do they pass? A. Four pairs, passing backwards behind the sympathetic trunk and psoas major.

cards.desc: Four pairs of veins accompanying the lumbar arteries on the posterior abdominal wall, draining mainly into the inferior vena cava.
cards.att: Begin from the abdominal wall and back muscles, receive an intervertebral tributary carrying blood from the internal vertebral venous plexus, and pass forwards around the vertebral bodies deep to psoas major; the second and third pairs usually enter the inferior vena cava while the first and fourth drain into the ascending lumbar vein.
cards.sup: Receive dorsal and abdominal tributaries and communicate freely with the ascending lumbar vein and with the internal and external vertebral venous plexuses.
cards.act: Drain the posterior abdominal wall and the vertebral column into the caval and azygos systems.
cards.rel: Lie deep to psoas major and the lumbar sympathetic trunk; the left veins are longer and pass behind the aorta to reach the inferior vena cava.
cards.clin: Their valveless connection with the internal vertebral venous plexus of Batson allows tumour cells from prostate, breast, thyroid, kidney and lung to reach the vertebrae, pelvis and skull without first passing through the lungs, explaining the pattern of skeletal metastases.
cards.exam: Q. Which venous plexus do the lumbar veins communicate with and why does it matter clinically? A. The internal vertebral venous plexus of Batson, a valveless route for tumour spread to the vertebral column.

cards.desc: Crescent-shaped bone in the middle of the proximal carpal row, deeply concave distally to receive the head of the capitate.
cards.att: Articulates with the radius and the articular disc above, the capitate and part of the hamate below, the scaphoid laterally and the triquetrum medially. It is held by the scapholunate and lunotriquetral interosseous ligaments and by the palmar radiolunate ligaments, which carry its blood supply.
cards.rel: Lies in the floor of the carpal tunnel directly behind the median nerve and the long flexor tendons; the radiocarpal joint lies above it.
cards.clin: The lunate is the carpal bone most often dislocated, displacing anteriorly into the carpal tunnel and causing acute median nerve compression, with a triangular rather than quadrilateral lunate outline on the posteroanterior film and the spilled teacup sign laterally. Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the lunate is Kienbock disease.
cards.exam: Q. Which carpal bone is most commonly dislocated and what is the immediate complication? A. The lunate, dislocating anteriorly and compressing the median nerve in the carpal tunnel.

cards.desc: The left principal bronchus, conducting air from the tracheal bifurcation to the left lung; narrower, longer and more horizontal than its right counterpart.
cards.att: Begins at the carina at the level of the sternal angle (T4 to T5) and runs about 5 cm downwards and laterally at roughly 45 degrees to the midline, entering the hilum of the left lung where it divides into superior and inferior lobar bronchi.
cards.sup: Bronchial arteries from the thoracic aorta, usually two on the left; venous drainage to the accessory hemiazygos and azygos veins; nerves from the pulmonary plexuses, vagal and sympathetic.
cards.act: Conducts air; its cartilaginous rings hold the lumen open and the ciliated respiratory epithelium clears mucus towards the trachea.
cards.rel: Passes below the arch of the aorta and in front of the oesophagus and descending thoracic aorta. At the hilum the left pulmonary artery lies above it and the pulmonary veins in front and below.
cards.clin: Widening of the carinal angle on chest radiograph or bronchoscopy suggests subcarinal nodal disease or gross left atrial enlargement, which can also compress the left main bronchus. A left sided double lumen endobronchial tube is standard for one lung ventilation.
cards.exam: Q. Why do inhaled foreign bodies rarely enter the left main bronchus? A. It is narrower, longer and more oblique than the right main bronchus.

cards.desc: The right principal bronchus, wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, conducting air from the carina to the right lung.
cards.att: Begins at the carina at the level of the sternal angle (T4 to T5), runs about 2.5 cm downwards and laterally, gives off the right superior lobar (eparterial) bronchus before entering the hilum, then continues as the intermediate bronchus dividing into middle and inferior lobar bronchi.
cards.sup: A single right bronchial artery, usually from the third right posterior intercostal artery or a common trunk; venous drainage to the azygos vein; nerves from the pulmonary plexuses.
cards.act: Conducts air to the right lung; its cartilage maintains patency and its ciliated epithelium clears secretions.
cards.rel: The azygos vein arches forwards over it to reach the superior vena cava. The right pulmonary artery lies anterior and inferior to it at the hilum, hence the eparterial upper lobe bronchus above the artery.
cards.clin: Inhaled foreign bodies, aspirated fluid and an over-inserted endotracheal tube pass into the right main bronchus. Aspiration in the supine patient collects in the posterior segment of the right upper lobe or the superior segment of the right lower lobe.
cards.exam: Q. Which bronchus is called eparterial and why? A. The right superior lobar bronchus, because it arises above the right pulmonary artery.

cards.desc: Paired small hemispherical grey masses, about the size of a pea, projecting from the posterior part of the floor of the hypothalamus behind the tuber cinereum.
cards.att: Receives the postcommissural fibres of the fornix from the hippocampal formation and the mammillary peduncle from the brainstem; projects by the mammillothalamic tract to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus and by the mammillotegmental tract to the tegmental nuclei of the midbrain.
cards.sup: Perforating branches of the posterior cerebral and posterior communicating arteries.
cards.act: Relay station of the Papez circuit, concerned with the recall and consolidation of episodic memory.
cards.rel: Lie in front of the posterior perforated substance and the interpeduncular fossa, behind the tuber cinereum and infundibulum, medial to the optic tracts and in front of the crura cerebri.
cards.clin: Bilateral haemorrhagic necrosis and later atrophy of the mammillary bodies from thiamine deficiency underlies Wernicke's encephalopathy, with confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia, progressing to the profound anterograde amnesia and confabulation of Korsakoff's psychosis.
cards.exam: Q. Which tract connects the mammillary body to the anterior thalamic nucleus? A. The mammillothalamic tract, the bundle of Vicq d'Azyr.

cards.desc: The largest and strongest bone of the face, carrying the lower teeth and forming the only mobile joint of the skull.
cards.att: A horseshoe-shaped body and two rami meeting at the angle. The body has the mental protuberance, mental foramen below the second premolar, mylohyoid line, digastric fossa, genial tubercles and the alveolar part. Each ramus bears a coronoid process for temporalis, a condylar process for the temporomandibular joint, and on its medial surface the mandibular foramen guarded by the lingula, leading into the mandibular canal. Gives attachment to masseter and medial pterygoid at the angle, lateral pterygoid to the condylar neck, and mylohyoid, geniohyoid, genioglossus, digastric and buccinator to the body.
cards.sup: Inferior alveolar artery from the maxillary artery within the canal, with periosteal supply; sensory supply of the teeth and chin by the inferior alveolar and mental nerves (V3).
cards.act: Carries the lower dentition and, through the muscles of mastication acting at the temporomandibular joints, produces elevation, depression, protrusion, retraction and side to side grinding.
cards.rel: Inferior alveolar nerve and vessels run in the mandibular canal; the facial artery and vein cross the lower border at the anterior border of masseter; the lingual nerve lies against the medial surface opposite the third molar; the parotid gland overlies the ramus.
cards.clin: It usually fractures in two places because it is a bony ring, most often the condylar neck with the opposite angle or parasymphysis. The inferior alveolar nerve is blocked at the lingula. Anterior dislocation of the condyle occurs on wide yawning and is reduced by pressing downwards and backwards on the molars.
cards.exam: Q. Why are mandibular fractures usually multiple? A. The mandible is a ring of bone articulating at both condyles, so a blow at one point transmits force and produces a second fracture elsewhere, classically the contralateral condylar neck or angle.

cards.desc: Quadrangular upper part of the sternum, lying at the level of T3 and T4, forming the front of the thoracic inlet.
cards.att: The superior border carries the jugular (suprasternal) notch with a clavicular notch on each side for the sternoclavicular joint; laterally there is a facet for the 1st costal cartilage, a synchondrosis, and a demifacet for the upper half of the 2nd. It joins the body at the manubriosternal symphysis, the sternal angle. Gives origin to the sternal head of sternocleidomastoid, to sternohyoid, sternothyroid and part of pectoralis major.
cards.sup: Branches of the internal thoracic artery; contains red marrow.
cards.act: Anchors the clavicles and first ribs, forming the rigid anterior part of the thoracic inlet, and moves upward and forward with the first ribs in pump-handle inspiration.
cards.rel: Behind it lie the thymus or its remnant, the left brachiocephalic vein, the arch of the aorta with the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, and more deeply the trachea and oesophagus.
cards.clin: The sternal angle of Louis, the palpable ridge at the manubriosternal joint, identifies the 2nd costal cartilage and is the starting point for counting ribs and intercostal spaces. The manubrium is a standard site for intraosseous access in resuscitation.
cards.exam: Q. What is the vertebral level of the jugular notch and of the sternal angle? A. The lower border of T2 and the T4/T5 disc respectively.

cards.desc: Paired bone forming the upper jaw, most of the hard palate, the floor and lateral wall of the nose and the floor of the orbit.
cards.att: A body containing the maxillary sinus, with four processes: frontal, zygomatic, palatine and alveolar. The body has orbital, nasal, infratemporal and anterior surfaces, the infraorbital groove, canal and foramen, and the maxillary tuberosity. Articulates with the frontal, nasal, lacrimal, ethmoid, vomer, inferior concha, palatine, zygomatic bones and its fellow at the intermaxillary suture. Gives attachment to levator labii superioris, levator anguli oris, buccinator, nasalis and the medial pterygoid at the tuberosity.
cards.sup: Infraorbital, posterior superior alveolar and greater palatine branches of the maxillary artery; sensory supply of the sinus, teeth, cheek and palate by the maxillary nerve through its infraorbital, superior alveolar and palatine branches.
cards.act: Carries the upper dentition, forms the palate separating the mouth from the nose, supports the orbit and encloses the largest paranasal sinus.
cards.rel: Maxillary sinus lies within the body, with the orbit and infraorbital nerve above, the upper molar and premolar roots below, the nose medially and the infratemporal fossa behind. The sinus opens high on its medial wall into the hiatus semilunaris of the middle meatus.
cards.clin: Le Fort I, II and III fractures separate the maxilla from the skull at predictable weak lines. A blow to the globe blows out the thin orbital floor into the sinus, trapping the inferior rectus and causing diplopia on upward gaze and infraorbital numbness. Because the sinus ostium lies near its roof, drainage is against gravity and sinusitis is common; molar root infection can enter the sinus.
cards.exam: Q. Why is maxillary sinusitis common and how does it present? A. The ostium lies high on the medial wall opening into the middle meatus, so drainage is against gravity; it presents with cheek pain worse on stooping, and referred pain to the upper teeth.

cards.desc: Largest of the three cuneiforms, at the medial side of the distal row of the tarsus, wedge shaped with its base plantarwards and its edge dorsally, the reverse of the other two.
cards.att: Articulates proximally with the navicular, laterally with the intermediate cuneiform and often with the base of the second metatarsal, and distally with the base of the first metatarsal. Tibialis anterior inserts on its medial and plantar surface and fibularis longus on its plantar lateral surface; a slip of tibialis posterior also reaches it.
cards.act: Forms the medial pillar of the transverse arch and part of the medial longitudinal arch, and acts as the point where tibialis anterior and fibularis longus form a sling under the foot.
cards.rel: Lies between the navicular behind and the first metatarsal in front, with abductor hallucis and the medial plantar structures on its plantar aspect.
cards.clin: The Lisfranc ligament passes from its lateral surface to the base of the second metatarsal and is the key stabiliser of the tarsometatarsal joints; widening of the gap between the medial cuneiform and the second metatarsal base on a weight bearing film indicates a Lisfranc injury.
cards.exam: Q. Which two tendons attach to the medial cuneiform and act as a stirrup for the foot? A. Tibialis anterior medially and fibularis longus on its plantar lateral aspect.
