cards.desc: Rounded eminence on the posteroinferior surface of the thalamus, medial to the lateral geniculate body and below the pulvinar, forming the thalamic relay of the auditory pathway.
cards.att: Receives the brachium of the inferior colliculus and projects by the acoustic radiation, which passes through the sublentiform part of the internal capsule, to the anterior transverse temporal gyri of Heschl (areas 41 and 42).
cards.sup: Thalamogeniculate branches of the posterior cerebral artery.
cards.act: Relays auditory information from the midbrain to the primary auditory cortex.
cards.rel: Lies medial to the lateral geniculate body and lateral to the superior colliculus and the crus cerebri; the pulvinar overhangs it above.
cards.clin: A unilateral lesion of the medial geniculate body or the auditory radiation causes no significant deafness, because each ear is represented in the auditory cortex of both sides; a subtle deficit in localising sound may be all that is found.
cards.exam: Q. Why does a unilateral lesion above the cochlear nuclei not cause deafness? A. Because auditory pathways are bilaterally represented from the cochlear nuclei upwards.

cards.desc: The larger of the two heads of gastrocnemius, forming the inferomedial boundary of the popliteal fossa and the prominent medial bulge of the calf.
cards.att: Arises by a strong tendon from the popliteal surface of the femur just above the medial condyle and from the adjacent part of the condyle; descends further distally than the lateral head, unites with it and with soleus to form the calcaneal tendon, inserted into the middle of the posterior surface of the calcaneus.
cards.sup: Tibial nerve, S1, S2; sural branches of the popliteal artery.
cards.act: Plantarflexes the ankle and flexes the knee; being a two-joint muscle it works best for propulsion with the knee extended.
cards.rel: Forms the inferomedial boundary of the popliteal fossa, overlying the popliteal vessels and the tibial nerve; a bursa lies between its origin and the capsule of the knee joint and often communicates with the joint cavity.
cards.clin: A tear at its musculotendinous junction causes tennis leg, with sudden calf pain mimicking deep vein thrombosis. The bursa between it and semimembranosus, when distended, forms a popliteal (Baker's) cyst. Its long reliable pedicle makes it the standard muscle flap for covering the upper tibia and knee.
cards.exam: Q. What is tennis leg? A. A tear at the musculotendinous junction of the medial head of gastrocnemius, presenting as sudden calf pain that mimics deep vein thrombosis.

cards.desc: The deepest of the three heads of triceps brachii, lying beneath the long and lateral heads on the posterior surface of the humerus.
cards.att: Origin: posterior surface of the humerus below the radial (spiral) groove, extending to the medial and lateral intermuscular septa. Insertion: posterior part of the superior surface of the olecranon of the ulna through the common triceps tendon.
cards.sup: Radial nerve (C6, C7, C8); the medial head receives its own branch, and the ulnar collateral branch of the radial nerve accompanies it in the arm.
cards.act: Extends the elbow; the chief head active in unresisted low-force extension.
cards.rel: Covered by the long and lateral heads; the radial nerve and profunda brachii vessels lie between it and the lateral head in the radial groove. Its lower fibres are related to the posterior capsule of the elbow joint.
cards.clin: Because it arises below the radial groove, its nerve branch is given off proximally, so a mid-shaft humeral fracture injuring the radial nerve in the groove often spares much of triceps power while causing wrist drop. A few of its deep fibres insert into the elbow capsule and prevent it being nipped during extension.
cards.exam: Q. Which head of triceps arises entirely below the radial groove? A. The medial (deep) head.

syn: medial occipital branch of posterior cerebral artery
cards.desc: Terminal branch of the posterior cerebral artery running on the medial surface of the occipital lobe, the artery of the visual cortex.
cards.att: Arises as a terminal division of the posterior cerebral artery in the quadrigeminal cistern and passes backwards on the medial surface of the hemisphere.
cards.sup: Branches: dorsal branch to the corpus callosum, parietal branch, parieto-occipital branch, calcarine branch and occipitotemporal branch.
cards.act: Supplies the medial surface of the occipital lobe including the primary visual cortex on the banks of the calcarine sulcus, the cuneus and the precuneus.
cards.rel: Runs in the calcarine and parieto-occipital sulci, medial to the lateral occipital artery, with the great cerebral vein and the tentorium nearby.
cards.clin: Occlusion of the calcarine branch causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia; macular sparing may occur because the occipital pole also receives supply from the middle cerebral artery.
cards.exam: Q. What visual field defect follows occlusion of the calcarine branch? A. Contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing.

cards.desc: The thickest and strongest extraocular muscle, running along the medial wall of the orbit to the medial side of the eyeball.
cards.att: Origin: medial part of the common tendinous ring (anulus of Zinn) around the optic canal. Insertion: sclera medially, about 5.5 mm behind the corneal limbus.
cards.sup: Inferior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III).
cards.act: Adducts the eyeball; with its fellow it converges the eyes.
cards.rel: Lies lateral to the medial orbital wall and ethmoidal air cells; the ophthalmic artery and nasociliary nerve cross above it, and the inferior oblique is related to its insertion.
cards.clin: Failure of adduction with nystagmus of the abducting eye indicates internuclear ophthalmoplegia from a medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion; convergence is preserved. Medial rectus recession is the standard operation for esotropia, and the muscle may be injured in endoscopic ethmoid sinus surgery.
cards.exam: Q. Nerve supply of medial rectus? A. Inferior division of the oculomotor nerve.

cards.desc: Superficial vein ascending in the midline of the front of the forearm.
cards.att: Begins in the superficial palmar venous plexus, ascends in the middle of the front of the forearm, and ends in the basilic vein or in the median cubital vein; it may divide into a median basilic and a median cephalic vein, producing the M-shaped pattern at the elbow.
cards.sup: Drains the palmar surface of the hand and the front of the forearm.
cards.rel: Lies in the superficial fascia in front of the flexor muscles, with the medial and lateral cutaneous nerves of the forearm on either side.
cards.clin: Its variability accounts for the different venous patterns seen in the cubital fossa; it is a usable vein for venepuncture when the median cubital vein is thrombosed or absent, but lies closer to the underlying brachial artery in the midline.
cards.exam: Q. What pattern results when the median vein of the forearm divides at the elbow? A. The M-shaped pattern of median basilic and median cephalic veins.

cards.desc: Thick triangular anterior part of the cricothyroid ligament, bridging the gap between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages in the midline.
cards.att: Extends from the upper border of the arch of the cricoid cartilage to the lower border of the thyroid cartilage; laterally it is continuous with the conus elasticus, whose free upper border forms the vocal ligament.
cards.sup: Cricothyroid branches of the superior thyroid arteries, which cross its upper part and anastomose in the midline.
cards.act: Closes the interval between the two cartilages, and as part of the conus elasticus supports the vocal ligaments and the subglottic airway.
cards.rel: Covered by skin, superficial and pretracheal fascia and the anterior jugular veins, with the cricothyroid muscles on each side; the vocal folds lie about a centimetre above it, and the isthmus of the thyroid gland lies below over the second to fourth tracheal rings.
cards.clin: This is the site of emergency cricothyroidotomy and needle cricothyroidotomy, chosen because it is subcutaneous, avascular apart from the cricothyroid arteries, and lies below the vocal cords and above the thyroid isthmus. Transtracheal injection of local anaesthetic for awake intubation is given through it.
cards.exam: Q. Why is the median cricothyroid ligament preferred over the trachea for emergency airway access? A. It is superficial and easily palpable, has no overlying thyroid isthmus or major vessels, and lies below the vocal cords, so the airway can be entered rapidly and safely.

cards.desc: Short oblique communicating vein crossing the cubital fossa from the cephalic to the basilic vein.
cards.att: Leaves the cephalic vein below the elbow, runs upwards and medially across the front of the cubital fossa in the superficial fascia, and joins the basilic vein; it usually receives the median vein of the forearm.
cards.sup: Drains into the basilic vein and connects the superficial venous systems of the two sides of the limb; it is often linked to the deep veins by a perforating vein.
cards.rel: Lies in front of the bicipital aponeurosis, which separates it from the brachial artery and median nerve; the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm lies close to it and the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm lies lateral.
cards.clin: The standard vein for venepuncture, blood donation and cannulation because it is large, constant and separated from the brachial artery by the bicipital aponeurosis, for which reason that aponeurosis is called the grace a Dieu fascia. Too deep a needle passes through it into the artery or strikes the median nerve.
cards.exam: Q. What protects the brachial artery during venepuncture in the cubital fossa? A. The bicipital aponeurosis, which lies between the artery and the median cubital vein.

cards.desc: Lowest part of the brainstem, about 3 cm long, conical in shape, extending from the upper border of the first cervical segment at the foramen magnum to the pontomedullary sulcus.
cards.att: Continuous below with the spinal cord and above with the pons; connected to the cerebellum by the inferior cerebellar peduncle. Bears the pyramids and the olives on its anterior surface, with the decussation of the pyramids below and the gracile and cuneate tubercles behind. Cranial nerves IX, X, XI and XII are attached to it.
cards.sup: Anterior spinal and vertebral arteries to the medial part, and the posterior inferior cerebellar artery, largely a branch of the vertebral artery, to the lateral part.
cards.act: Contains the vital cardiovascular, respiratory and vasomotor centres, the reflex centres for vomiting, coughing, swallowing and sneezing, and the nuclei gracilis and cuneatus of the dorsal column pathway.
cards.rel: Lies on the basiocciput in front, with the cerebellum behind separated by the lower part of the fourth ventricle; the vertebral arteries ascend on its anterolateral surface.
cards.clin: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome from vertebral or posterior inferior cerebellar artery occlusion gives ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss, Horner's syndrome, ataxia and palatal palsy with contralateral pain and temperature loss on the body. Medial medullary syndrome from the anterior spinal artery gives contralateral hemiplegia sparing the face, contralateral loss of proprioception and ipsilateral tongue deviation.
cards.exam: Q. Why is sensory loss crossed in Wallenberg's syndrome? A. The spinal tract of the trigeminal is affected before decussation, causing ipsilateral facial loss, while the spinothalamic tract has already crossed, causing contralateral body loss.

cards.desc: Fan-shaped double fold of peritoneum suspending the jejunum and ileum from the posterior abdominal wall.
cards.att: Root about 15 cm long, running obliquely from the duodenojejunal flexure on the left of L2 downwards and to the right, across the third part of the duodenum, the aorta, the inferior vena cava, the right ureter and psoas major, to the right sacroiliac joint. Its free border is about 6 metres long and its depth about 20 cm.
cards.sup: Contains the jejunal and ileal branches of the superior mesenteric artery with their arcades and vasa recta, accompanying veins, lymphatics (lacteals), mesenteric lymph nodes, autonomic nerves and fat.
cards.act: Suspends the small intestine, allows mobility, and carries its neurovascular supply.
cards.rel: Divides the infracolic compartment into right and left infracolic spaces. Its root crosses the third part of the duodenum, aorta, inferior vena cava, right ureter and right psoas major.
cards.clin: The narrow root permits volvulus of the whole midgut in malrotation. Jejunal mesentery contains less fat with long vasa recta and few arcades; ileal mesentery is fat-laden with short vasa recta and many arcades, and fat creeping onto the bowel is a sign of Crohn's disease.
cards.exam: Q. Describe the line of attachment of the root of the mesentery. A. From the duodenojejunal flexure at L2 on the left, obliquely down to the right sacroiliac joint, about 15 cm long.

cards.desc: Small triangular fold of peritoneum suspending the appendix from the lower (posterior) layer of the mesentery of the terminal ileum.
cards.att: Passes from the posterior layer of the mesentery behind the terminal ileum to the appendix, usually reaching most of the way along it, its length determining how mobile the tip is.
cards.sup: Contains the appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery, running in the free edge of the fold, with the appendicular vein, lymphatics and nerves.
cards.act: Suspends the appendix and carries its blood supply.
cards.rel: Lies behind the terminal ileum at its origin. The appendicular artery in its free edge is the structure ligated at appendicectomy.
cards.clin: The appendicular artery is a functional end artery running in the free edge, so its thrombosis in appendicitis causes rapid gangrene and perforation of the tip. A short mesoappendix produces a curled, retrocaecal appendix.
cards.exam: Q. What lies in the free edge of the mesoappendix? A. The appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery and a functional end artery.

cards.desc: Shortest part of the brainstem, about 2 cm long, joining the pons below to the diencephalon above and traversed by the cerebral aqueduct.
cards.att: Comprises the two crura cerebri in front, the tegmentum behind them separated by the pigmented substantia nigra, and the tectum with the four colliculi behind the aqueduct. Contains the red nucleus, the oculomotor and trochlear nuclei, the mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal and the decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles. The oculomotor nerve emerges into the interpeduncular fossa and the trochlear nerve from the dorsal surface below the inferior colliculus.
cards.sup: Perforating branches of the basilar bifurcation, posterior cerebral, posterior communicating and superior cerebellar arteries.
cards.act: Conducts ascending and descending tracts; controls eye movement and the pupillary reflexes, contains auditory (inferior colliculus) and visual (superior colliculus) reflex centres, and takes part in motor control through the substantia nigra and red nucleus.
cards.rel: Passes through the tentorial notch, with the uncus and parahippocampal gyrus on either side; the posterior cerebral artery and the free edge of the tentorium lie alongside; the pineal gland lies above the superior colliculi.
cards.clin: Weber's syndrome, from infarction of the crus cerebri, gives an ipsilateral oculomotor palsy with contralateral hemiplegia. Degeneration of the pigmented cells of the substantia nigra causes Parkinson's disease, and uncal herniation through the tentorial notch compresses the midbrain and the third nerve.
cards.exam: Q. Which structure separates the crus cerebri from the tegmentum? A. The substantia nigra.

cards.desc: Cardiac vein of the posterior interventricular groove, running on the diaphragmatic surface of the heart from apex to base.
cards.att: Begins at the apex of the heart, ascends in the posterior interventricular sulcus alongside the posterior interventricular artery, and opens into the right end of the coronary sinus close to its termination in the right atrium.
cards.act: Drains the posterior walls of both ventricles and the posterior part of the interventricular septum, the territory of the posterior interventricular artery.
cards.rel: Accompanies the posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery in the sulcus; the coronary sinus lies at its upper end in the coronary groove.
cards.clin: Marks the posterior interventricular groove during surgery, and is the usual route for retrograde perfusion studies of the inferior wall. It drains the region infarcted in an inferior myocardial infarction.
cards.exam: Q. Which cardiac vein accompanies the posterior interventricular artery? A. The middle cardiac vein, which drains into the right end of the coronary sinus.

cards.desc: Broadest of the three gyri on the lateral surface of the frontal lobe, lying between the superior and inferior frontal sulci and running forwards from the precentral sulcus.
cards.att: Its posterior part, in front of the precentral sulcus, contains the frontal eye field (area 8), which projects to the contralateral paramedian pontine reticular formation and to the superior colliculus; the anterior part is dorsolateral prefrontal association cortex.
cards.sup: Branches of the middle cerebral artery, with its upper part also receiving supply from the anterior cerebral artery.
cards.act: Frontal eye field controls voluntary conjugate gaze to the opposite side; the prefrontal part serves working memory, planning and executive function.
cards.rel: Lies between the superior frontal gyrus above and the inferior frontal gyrus below; the precentral gyrus lies behind it across the precentral sulcus.
cards.clin: A destructive lesion of the frontal eye field causes conjugate deviation of the eyes towards the side of the lesion, so the patient looks away from the hemiplegia; an irritative lesion during a seizure drives the eyes to the opposite side.
cards.exam: Q. In a right frontal lobe infarct, which way do the eyes deviate? A. Towards the right, the side of the lesion, and away from the hemiplegic side.

cards.desc: Small unpaired branch of the popliteal artery that enters the knee joint from behind.
cards.att: Arises from the anterior surface of the popliteal artery opposite the knee joint line, passes forwards and pierces the oblique popliteal ligament and the posterior capsule to enter the joint.
cards.sup: Supplies the cruciate ligaments, the synovial membrane and the central part of the knee joint, including the intercondylar region.
cards.act: Sole arterial supply to the interior of the knee joint, including the cruciate ligaments.
cards.rel: Lies between the popliteal artery behind and the posterior capsule in front, in the intercondylar region; it does not join the peripheral genicular anastomosis directly.
cards.clin: Because the cruciate ligaments depend on this single small vessel and lie intracapsular but extrasynovial, a torn anterior cruciate ligament heals poorly and is usually reconstructed rather than repaired.
cards.exam: Q. Which artery supplies the cruciate ligaments? A. The middle genicular branch of the popliteal artery.

cards.desc: Hepatic vein running within the principal plane of the liver, from the gallbladder fossa to the inferior vena cava, between the right and left hemilivers.
cards.att: Formed by tributaries from segments IV, V and VIII, it runs backwards and upwards in the principal (Cantlie) plane and in most people joins the left hepatic vein to form a short common trunk that opens into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm.
cards.sup: Receives intersegmental tributaries from segments IV, V and VIII.
cards.act: Drains the central part of the liver on both sides of the principal plane.
cards.rel: Lies in the plane joining the gallbladder fossa to the inferior vena cava, which divides the liver into right and left hemilivers; the right hepatic vein lies lateral and the left medial to it.
cards.clin: Defines the plane of section in right or left hemihepatectomy. It is preserved in the right lobe living donor graft, or the donor's segments V and VIII congest; because it usually shares a trunk with the left hepatic vein, the left vein is at risk when it is clamped.
cards.exam: Q. Which vein marks the principal plane of the liver? A. The middle hepatic vein, running from the gallbladder fossa to the inferior vena cava.

cards.desc: Fan-shaped muscle of the pharyngeal wall arising from the hyoid region and sweeping backwards to the midline raphe, overlapped below by the inferior constrictor.
cards.att: Origin: lower part of the stylohyoid ligament and the lesser and greater horns of the hyoid bone. Insertion: median pharyngeal raphe, its upper fibres overlapping the superior constrictor.
cards.sup: Pharyngeal plexus, motor fibres from the vagus nerve carrying the cranial accessory component.
cards.act: Constricts the pharynx and propels the bolus downwards during the pharyngeal phase of swallowing.
cards.rel: The glossopharyngeal nerve, stylopharyngeus and the stylohyoid ligament enter the pharynx above it, between it and the superior constrictor. The internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels pass below it, between it and the inferior constrictor.
cards.clin: The gap above it is the route of spread of infection and of the glossopharyngeal nerve; the gap below it is used to identify the internal laryngeal nerve in surgery of the piriform fossa.
cards.exam: Q. What passes between the superior and middle constrictors? A. The stylopharyngeus muscle and the glossopharyngeal nerve.

cards.desc: Terminal lateral branch of the internal thoracic artery, running downwards and laterally behind the costal margin.
cards.att: Arises with the superior epigastric artery from the internal thoracic artery at the sixth intercostal space, passes obliquely along the costal margin behind the costal cartilages, pierces the diaphragm near the eighth or ninth costal cartilage and ends near the last intercostal space.
cards.sup: Gives the anterior intercostal arteries to the 7th, 8th and 9th intercostal spaces, branches to the diaphragm and to the lower intercostal and abdominal wall muscles; anastomoses with the inferior phrenic, lower posterior intercostal and deep circumflex iliac arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the anterior part of the diaphragm, the lower intercostal spaces and the adjacent abdominal wall.
cards.rel: Runs deep to the costal cartilages along the costal margin, between the diaphragm and transversus abdominis, with its vein alongside.
cards.clin: Contributes to the anastomotic network of the anterior abdominal and thoracic wall, an important collateral pathway after ligation of the internal thoracic artery or in coarctation. It is at risk in surgical incisions along the costal margin and in chest drain insertion low in the anterior axillary line.
cards.exam: Q. Which anterior intercostal arteries come from the musculophrenic artery? A. Those of the 7th, 8th and 9th intercostal spaces.

cards.desc: Flat triangular muscle forming the muscular floor of the mouth between the two halves of the mandible.
cards.att: Origin: mylohyoid line on the inner surface of the mandible. Insertion: posterior fibres into the body of the hyoid bone, remaining fibres into a median fibrous raphe running from the mandibular symphysis to the hyoid.
cards.sup: Mylohyoid nerve, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve from the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.
cards.act: Elevates the floor of the mouth and the hyoid bone in the first stage of swallowing; depresses the mandible when the hyoid is fixed.
cards.rel: Sublingual gland, deep part of the submandibular gland, lingual nerve, hypoglossal nerve and submandibular duct lie above it; the superficial part of the submandibular gland, facial artery and anterior belly of digastric lie below. The gland hooks round its free posterior border.
cards.clin: The apices of the lower third molar roots lie below the mylohyoid line, so a periapical abscess there points into the submandibular space, whereas a premolar abscess points into the sublingual space. Bilateral spread across this floor is Ludwig angina, which threatens the airway.
cards.exam: Q. Nerve supply of mylohyoid? A. Mylohyoid nerve from the inferior alveolar branch of the mandibular nerve.

cards.desc: Small paired oblong bone forming the bridge of the nose.
cards.att: Articulates with its fellow at the internasal suture, with the frontal bone above at the frontonasal suture, with the frontal process of the maxilla laterally, and with the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid and the septal cartilage behind. Its lower border gives attachment to the lateral nasal cartilage; procerus and nasalis attach to its surface.
cards.sup: Branches of the ophthalmic and facial arteries; overlying skin supplied by the external nasal branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve and the infratrochlear nerve.
cards.act: Forms and supports the upper third of the external nose and protects the nasal cavity.
cards.rel: The internasal suture meets the frontonasal suture at the nasion; the anterior ethmoidal nerve emerges between the lower border of the bone and the lateral nasal cartilage.
cards.clin: The most commonly fractured bone of the face, presenting with deformity, epistaxis and, if the septum is involved, a septal haematoma that must be drained to prevent cartilage necrosis and saddle nose. Reduction is best performed within about two weeks before union.
cards.exam: Q. Which is the most commonly fractured facial bone and what complication must be excluded? A. The nasal bone; a septal haematoma must be excluded and drained to prevent septal cartilage necrosis and saddle nose deformity.

cards.desc: The intermediate branch of the ophthalmic nerve and the only one to enter the orbit through the common tendinous ring, crossing the optic nerve from lateral to medial.
cards.att: Arises from the ophthalmic nerve in the cavernous sinus, enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure within the common tendinous ring between the two divisions of CN III, crosses above the optic nerve with the ophthalmic artery, runs along the medial orbital wall between superior oblique and medial rectus, and ends by dividing into the infratrochlear and anterior ethmoidal nerves.
cards.act: Sensory to the eyeball, the mucosa of the ethmoidal and sphenoidal sinuses and the anterior nasal cavity, the lacrimal sac, the medial eyelid skin and the skin of the nasal dorsum and tip.
cards.rel: Crosses the optic nerve within the muscle cone, above and medial to the ciliary ganglion; its branches are the communicating branch to the ciliary ganglion, the long ciliary nerves, the posterior ethmoidal, infratrochlear and anterior ethmoidal nerves.
cards.clin: It is the sensory supply of the cornea, so it is the afferent limb of the corneal reflex. Because it supplies both the cornea and the nasal tip, nasal tip vesicles in herpes zoster ophthalmicus predict corneal involvement.
cards.exam: Q. Which branch of the ophthalmic nerve enters the orbit inside the common tendinous ring? A. The nasociliary nerve.

cards.desc: Membranous duct about 18 mm long carrying tears from the lacrimal sac to the inferior meatus of the nose.
cards.att: Begins at the lower end of the lacrimal sac and runs downwards, backwards and laterally in the bony nasolacrimal canal formed by the maxilla, lacrimal bone and lacrimal process of the inferior nasal concha, opening into the anterior part of the inferior meatus.
cards.sup: Mucosal branches of the sphenopalatine and infraorbital arteries; lymphatics to the submandibular nodes.
cards.act: Conducts tears into the nose; its opening is guarded by the plica lacrimalis (valve of Hasner), which prevents air and nasal contents being forced upwards.
cards.rel: Lies in the lateral wall of the nose behind the frontal process of the maxilla, with the maxillary sinus laterally and the middle and inferior meatus medially.
cards.clin: Failure of the valve of Hasner to canalise causes congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction, the usual cause of a watering, sticky eye in infancy, treated by massage and later probing. Blowing the nose forces air up the duct, which is why the eye waters in rhinitis.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the nasolacrimal duct open and what guards the opening? A. Into the inferior meatus of the nose, guarded by the plica lacrimalis or valve of Hasner.

cards.desc: Boat-shaped tarsal bone on the medial side of the midfoot, between the head of the talus and the three cuneiforms.
cards.att: Concave proximal surface receives the head of the talus; distal surface has three facets for the medial, intermediate and lateral cuneiforms; a lateral facet for the cuboid is often present. The prominent tuberosity on the medial side receives the main insertion of tibialis posterior; the plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament attaches to its plantar and proximal surfaces.
cards.act: Keystone of the medial column of the foot, transmitting weight from the talus forwards to the cuneiforms and metatarsals and supporting the medial longitudinal arch.
cards.rel: Tibialis posterior tendon medially and plantarly, tibialis anterior tendon passing to the medial cuneiform, extensor tendons and dorsalis pedis artery dorsally, spring ligament and head of talus proximally.
cards.clin: Köhler disease is osteochondrosis of the navicular in children, causing a limp with a tender midfoot and a dense flattened bone on X-ray. An accessory navicular (os tibiale externum) at the tuberosity causes medial pain and may accompany flat foot; navicular stress fracture is a classic sport injury with a high non-union rate.
cards.exam: Q. Which tendon inserts into the navicular tuberosity? A. Tibialis posterior, which is the main supporter of the medial longitudinal arch.

cards.desc: Ninth rib, a false or vertebrochondral rib whose costal cartilage joins that of the 8th rib to reach the costal margin.
cards.att: Head has two facets for the inferior demifacet of T8, the superior demifacet of T9 and the disc between; the tubercle articulates with the transverse process of T9; the shaft has an angle and a costal groove. Gives attachment to external and internal oblique, latissimus dorsi, serratus posterior inferior and the costal origin of the diaphragm internally.
cards.sup: Ninth posterior intercostal artery; the 9th intercostal nerve runs in the costal groove and continues into the anterior abdominal wall.
cards.act: Bucket-handle elevation widens the lower thorax; forms part of the costal margin and of the attachment ring of the diaphragm.
cards.rel: Diaphragm and costodiaphragmatic recess internally, with the liver on the right and the spleen and stomach on the left below the diaphragm; intercostal bundle in the costal groove.
cards.clin: The tips of the 9th costal cartilages lie in the transpyloric plane of Addison at the level of L1. The fundus of the gallbladder lies where the lateral border of rectus abdominis meets the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage, the point of maximal tenderness in Murphy's sign.
cards.exam: Q. Which surface plane passes through the tips of the 9th costal cartilages? A. The transpyloric plane of Addison, at the level of L1.

cards.desc: Lower thoracic vertebra with a large heart-shaped body, transitional in its costal facets between the typical thoracic and the lumbar pattern.
cards.att: Superior demifacet for the head of rib 9; the inferior demifacet is often absent, because rib 10 commonly articulates by a single whole facet with T10 alone. The transverse process carries a facet for the tubercle of rib 9, and the spine is shorter and less steeply inclined than in the mid-thoracic region.
cards.sup: Segmental posterior intercostal branches; dorsal rami to facet joints and periosteum.
cards.act: Weight transmission and cord protection; ribs and coronally set facets still permit rotation at this level.
cards.rel: The thoracic aorta lies anteriorly and slightly to the left, the azygos vein and thoracic duct to the right, and the diaphragmatic crura arise just below; the oesophagus passes forward towards the T10 hiatus.
cards.clin: The xiphisternal joint lies at the T9 vertebral level. The great anterior radicular artery of Adamkiewicz usually arises between T9 and T12, most often on the left, and its interruption during aortic surgery causes anterior spinal artery syndrome.
cards.exam: Q. Which surface landmark corresponds to the T9 vertebral level? A. The xiphisternal joint.

cards.desc: Superficial pair of intrinsic laryngeal muscles crossing each other as an X on the posterior surface of the arytenoid cartilages.
cards.att: Origin: muscular process of one arytenoid cartilage. Insertion: apex of the opposite arytenoid cartilage; some fibres continue round the aryepiglottic fold as the aryepiglotticus.
cards.sup: Recurrent laryngeal nerve (vagus).
cards.act: Approximates the arytenoid cartilages and, through the aryepiglottic continuation, closes the laryngeal inlet as a sphincter.
cards.rel: Lies superficial to the transverse arytenoid on the posterior aspect of the larynx, deep to the mucosa of the posterior commissure.
cards.clin: Along with aryepiglotticus it protects the airway during swallowing; loss of recurrent laryngeal nerve function abolishes this sphincteric closure and predisposes to aspiration.
cards.exam: Q. Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle continues as the aryepiglotticus? A. The oblique arytenoid.

cards.desc: The larger, fleshy head of adductor hallucis, running obliquely across the sole in the third layer from the metatarsal bases to the great toe.
cards.att: Origin: bases of the second, third and fourth metatarsal bones and the sheath of the tendon of fibularis longus. Insertion: with the transverse head into the lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe and the lateral sesamoid.
cards.sup: Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve (S2, S3).
cards.act: Adducts and flexes the metatarsophalangeal joint of the great toe; supports the longitudinal and transverse arches of the foot.
cards.rel: Lies deep to the long flexor tendons and lumbricals; the deep plantar arch and the deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve run on its deep surface, and the tendon of fibularis longus passes beneath its origin.
cards.clin: Unopposed pull of adductor hallucis contributes to the lateral deviation of the great toe in hallux valgus, and its tendon is released in bunion surgery.
cards.exam: Q. Nerve supply of adductor hallucis? A. Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve.

cards.desc: The proximal, carpally attached head of adductor pollicis, forming the bulk of the muscle in the deep palm.
cards.att: Origin: capitate bone, bases of the second and third metacarpals and the adjacent carpal ligaments. Insertion: with the transverse head into the ulnar side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb through the ulnar sesamoid.
cards.sup: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8, T1).
cards.act: Adducts the thumb and assists opposition; a key component of the power pinch grip.
cards.rel: The radial artery passes between the oblique and transverse heads to enter the palm and form the deep palmar arch; the deep branch of the ulnar nerve runs deep to the muscle. The flexor pollicis longus tendon lies in front of it.
cards.clin: Ulnar nerve palsy weakens adductor pollicis, so the patient compensates by flexing the thumb interphalangeal joint with flexor pollicis longus when gripping paper: a positive Froment sign.
cards.exam: Q. Which artery passes between the two heads of adductor pollicis? A. The radial artery, entering the palm to form the deep palmar arch.

cards.desc: The posterolateral, more horizontally directed part of cricothyroid, running backwards from the cricoid arch to the inferior horn of the thyroid cartilage.
cards.att: Origin: anterolateral surface of the arch of the cricoid cartilage, lateral to the straight part. Insertion: anterior border of the inferior horn and the adjacent lower lamina of the thyroid cartilage.
cards.sup: External laryngeal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (vagus).
cards.act: Draws the thyroid cartilage forwards on the cricothyroid joint, working with the straight part to lengthen and tense the vocal folds and raise the pitch of the voice.
cards.rel: Lies on the external surface of the larynx, covered by the sternothyroid; the external laryngeal nerve descends on it alongside the superior thyroid artery.
cards.clin: The external laryngeal nerve lies close to the superior thyroid artery and is at risk during thyroidectomy; injury produces a weak, monotonous voice with loss of high notes, which is why it is called the singer's nerve.
cards.exam: Q. Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle is not supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve? A. Cricothyroid, supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.

syn: inferior oblique muscle of the head
cards.desc: Thick suboccipital muscle running from the spine of the axis upwards and laterally to the transverse process of the atlas; despite its name it has no attachment to the skull.
cards.att: Origin: spinous process and lamina of the axis. Insertion: posteroinferior aspect of the transverse process of the atlas.
cards.sup: Suboccipital nerve, the posterior ramus of C1.
cards.act: Rotates the atlas and with it the head to the same side at the atlanto-axial joint.
cards.rel: Forms the inferolateral boundary of the suboccipital triangle; the vertebral artery and the suboccipital venous plexus lie in the floor of that triangle, and the greater occipital nerve (C2) winds round its lower border.
cards.clin: It is the landmark for the greater occipital nerve block, the nerve being found as it curls round the inferior border of this muscle. Its rotatory action is tested and treated in cervicogenic headache.
cards.exam: Q. Which suboccipital muscle has no attachment to the skull? A. Obliquus capitis inferior.

syn: superior oblique muscle of the head
cards.desc: Suboccipital muscle passing upwards and medially from the transverse process of the atlas to the occipital bone.
cards.att: Origin: upper surface of the transverse process of the atlas. Insertion: occipital bone between the superior and inferior nuchal lines, lateral to semispinalis capitis.
cards.sup: Suboccipital nerve, the posterior ramus of C1.
cards.act: Extends the head at the atlanto-occipital joint and bends it to the same side.
cards.rel: Forms the superolateral boundary of the suboccipital triangle, deep to semispinalis capitis; the vertebral artery lies medial and deep to it in the groove on the posterior arch of the atlas.
cards.clin: Lies over the vertebral artery in the suboccipital triangle, the region entered in far lateral approaches to the posterior fossa and craniovertebral junction.
cards.exam: Q. Name the three muscles bounding the suboccipital triangle. A. Rectus capitis posterior major, obliquus capitis superior and obliquus capitis inferior.

cards.desc: Flat triangular muscle on the external surface of the obturator membrane, deep in the upper medial thigh, whose tendon curls behind the neck of the femur.
cards.att: Origin: external surface of the obturator membrane and the adjoining bony margins of the obturator foramen on the pubis and ischium. Insertion: trochanteric fossa on the medial surface of the greater trochanter.
cards.sup: Posterior division of the obturator nerve, L3, L4.
cards.act: Lateral rotation of the thigh at the hip; assists adduction and steadies the femoral head in the acetabulum.
cards.rel: Its tendon runs backwards and laterally below the neck of the femur, deep to quadratus femoris, and is separated from the hip capsule by a bursa. Anteriorly it is covered by pectineus and the adductors.
cards.clin: Grouped functionally with the short lateral rotators but is the only one supplied by the obturator nerve, so it is spared in sacral plexus lesions. Its tendon acts as a sling below the femoral neck and is displaced in femoral neck fractures.
cards.exam: Q. Which lateral rotator of the hip is supplied by the obturator nerve? A. Obturator externus, by the posterior division, L3, L4.

cards.desc: Fan-shaped muscle of the lateral pelvic wall that turns through a right angle over the lesser sciatic notch to reach the greater trochanter.
cards.att: Origin: internal surface of the obturator membrane and the adjacent pelvic surfaces of the ischium, pubis and ilium around the obturator foramen. Leaves the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen and inserts on the medial surface of the greater trochanter, above the trochanteric fossa, with the gemelli.
cards.sup: Nerve to obturator internus, L5, S1, S2.
cards.act: Lateral rotation of the extended thigh; abduction of the flexed thigh; stabilises the hip joint.
cards.rel: Forms the lateral wall of the ischio-anal fossa; its fascia splits to form the pudendal canal carrying the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels. A bursa separates its tendon from the grooved lesser sciatic notch.
cards.clin: The pudendal nerve leaves through the greater sciatic foramen, hooks round the ischial spine and re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen to lie in the pudendal canal on this muscle, the site of pudendal nerve block. The muscle is a landmark for the ischial spine on vaginal examination.
cards.exam: Q. Through which foramen does obturator internus leave the pelvis? A. The lesser sciatic foramen, turning at a right angle over the lesser sciatic notch.

cards.desc: The vein accompanying the obturator artery, draining the adductor region of the thigh into the internal iliac vein.
cards.att: Begins in the upper adductor compartment of the thigh, passes backwards through the obturator canal into the pelvis, runs upwards and backwards below the obturator artery on the lateral pelvic wall, and drains into the internal iliac vein. An accessory obturator vein frequently drains instead into the external iliac or inferior epigastric vein.
cards.act: Venous drainage of the adductor region and hip joint.
cards.rel: Runs with the obturator artery and nerve on the lateral pelvic wall, the nerve above the vessels; the ureter and ductus deferens or ovarian vessels lie medial to it; obturator lymph nodes lie alongside.
cards.clin: An abnormal pubic communication between the obturator and external iliac or inferior epigastric vessels is the corona mortis, crossing the superior pubic ramus behind the lacunar ligament; it is torn in femoral hernia repair or superior pubic ramus fracture and bleeds briskly.
cards.exam: Q. What is the corona mortis and why is it named so? A. A vascular anastomosis between the obturator and external iliac or inferior epigastric vessels over the superior pubic ramus, once fatal when divided in femoral hernia surgery.

cards.desc: Unpaired bone of the back and base of the skull, arranged around the foramen magnum.
cards.att: Has a squamous part behind, two lateral (condylar) parts and a basilar part in front of the foramen magnum. Externally it bears the external occipital protuberance (inion), the external occipital crest and the superior and inferior nuchal lines for trapezius, sternocleidomastoid, the semispinales and the suboccipital muscles; internally it shows the cruciform eminence with grooves for the superior sagittal, transverse and sigmoid sinuses. The occipital condyles articulate with the atlas; the hypoglossal canal lies above each condyle, and with the temporal bone it forms the jugular foramen. Articulates with the parietals at the lambdoid suture and with the sphenoid at the basi-occipital synchondrosis.
cards.sup: Occipital and vertebral arteries; the basilar part is crossed internally by the basilar plexus. Transmits the hypoglossal nerve, and with the temporal bone the glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves through the jugular foramen.
cards.act: Encloses the posterior cranial fossa housing the cerebellum and brainstem, transmits the medulla through the foramen magnum, and carries the weight of the head onto the atlas.
cards.rel: Cerebellum and occipital lobes lie internally, separated by the attachment of the tentorium cerebelli; the vertebral arteries and the spinal roots of the accessory nerve enter through the foramen magnum. The pharyngeal tubercle on the basilar part gives attachment to the pharyngeal raphe.
cards.clin: The spheno-occipital synchondrosis fuses in the early twenties, and its position is used in forensic age estimation. Occipital condyle fracture accompanies high energy head injury and threatens the lower cranial nerves in the hypoglossal canal and jugular foramen. Basilar skull fracture through it produces retroauricular bruising and CSF leak.
cards.exam: Q. Which cranial nerves are related to the occipital bone and where? A. The hypoglossal nerve through the hypoglossal canal, the glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves through the jugular foramen it forms with the temporal bone, and the spinal root of the accessory nerve through the foramen magnum.

cards.desc: Smallest and most posterior lobe of the cerebral hemisphere, lying on the tentorium cerebelli behind the parieto-occipital sulcus.
cards.att: Bounded in front on the medial surface by the parieto-occipital sulcus and on the lateral surface by an imaginary line from the preoccipital notch. Divided on the medial surface by the calcarine sulcus into the cuneus above and the lingual gyrus below; receives the optic radiation and is connected to the opposite lobe by the forceps major of the splenium.
cards.sup: Posterior cerebral artery, chiefly the calcarine branch, with a contribution to the occipital pole from the middle cerebral artery.
cards.act: Contains the primary visual cortex (area 17) on the walls of the calcarine sulcus, marked by the stria of Gennari, and the surrounding visual association cortex (areas 18 and 19) for the interpretation of what is seen.
cards.rel: Lies above the tentorium cerebelli and the cerebellum, behind the parietal and temporal lobes, with the posterior horn of the lateral ventricle projecting into it.
cards.clin: Unilateral occipital infarction in the posterior cerebral artery territory causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, the occipital pole being also supplied by the middle cerebral artery. Bilateral occipital infarction causes cortical blindness with normal pupillary reflexes, and if the patient denies the blindness this is Anton's syndrome.
cards.exam: Q. Why is the macula spared in posterior cerebral artery occlusion? A. The occipital pole, where the macula is represented, has a collateral supply from the middle cerebral artery.

cards.desc: Digastric infrahyoid strap muscle with an inferior and a superior belly joined by an intermediate tendon, crossing the neck obliquely from the scapula to the hyoid.
cards.att: Origin: superior border of the scapula near the suprascapular notch and the superior transverse scapular ligament. Insertion: lower border of the body of the hyoid bone, lateral to sternohyoid; the intermediate tendon is bound to the clavicle and first rib by a fascial sling from the investing layer of deep cervical fascia.
cards.sup: Ansa cervicalis (C1, C2, C3); the superior belly is supplied by the superior root of the ansa (C1).
cards.act: Depresses and retracts the hyoid bone; through its fascial sling it tenses the deep cervical fascia and helps keep the internal jugular vein patent.
cards.rel: The inferior belly crosses the posterior triangle and divides it into occipital and supraclavicular triangles; the superior belly divides the anterior triangle into carotid and muscular triangles. Its intermediate tendon crosses the internal jugular vein and carotid sheath.
cards.clin: A surgical landmark in block dissection of the neck and in exposure of the carotid vessels; the muscle is divided to reach the lower carotid sheath and it identifies level III and IV nodes.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle divides the posterior triangle of the neck into two? A. The inferior belly of omohyoid.

cards.desc: First major intracranial branch of the internal carotid artery, the arterial supply of the orbit and its contents.
cards.att: Arises from the internal carotid artery medial to the anterior clinoid process as the artery emerges from the cavernous sinus, enters the orbit through the optic canal inferolateral to the optic nerve within its dural sheath, then crosses above the optic nerve to run forward on the medial wall of the orbit and end as the supratrochlear and dorsal nasal arteries.
cards.sup: Branches: central artery of the retina, lacrimal artery, short and long posterior ciliary arteries, anterior ciliary, muscular, supraorbital, posterior and anterior ethmoidal, medial palpebral, supratrochlear and dorsal nasal arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the eyeball, extraocular muscles, lacrimal gland, eyelids, the ethmoidal air cells and part of the nose and forehead.
cards.rel: Enters the optic canal inferolateral to the optic nerve, then usually crosses superior to the nerve from lateral to medial, accompanied by the nasociliary nerve.
cards.clin: The central artery of the retina is a functional end-artery; its occlusion causes sudden painless total monocular blindness with a cherry-red spot at the macula. Anastomoses between its terminal branches and the facial artery explain the retrograde embolic blindness reported after nasal and glabellar filler injection.
cards.exam: Q. What is the relation of the ophthalmic artery to the optic nerve in the optic canal? A. It lies inferolateral to the nerve, then crosses above it in the orbit.

syn: first division of the trigeminal nerve
cards.desc: The smallest and most superior division of the trigeminal nerve, purely sensory, supplying the eye, upper face and anterior scalp.
cards.att: Arises from the anteromedial part of the trigeminal ganglion in the middle cranial fossa, runs forwards in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus below the trochlear nerve, gives a tentorial (meningeal) branch, and divides into the lacrimal, frontal and nasociliary nerves which enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
cards.act: General sensation from the eyeball and conjunctiva, lacrimal gland, upper eyelid, forehead and scalp to the vertex, the dorsum of the nose, the frontal, ethmoidal and sphenoidal sinuses, and the tentorium cerebelli.
cards.rel: In the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus it lies below the trochlear nerve and above the maxillary nerve, lateral to the internal carotid artery and abducent nerve.
cards.clin: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus follows this division and threatens sight. It is the afferent limb of the corneal reflex, so an absent corneal reflex with preserved facial movement localises the lesion to V1 rather than to the facial nerve.
cards.exam: Q. What is the afferent limb of the corneal reflex? A. The ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, through the nasociliary and ciliary nerves.

cards.desc: Deepest of the three hypothenar muscles, lying directly on the fifth metacarpal.
cards.att: Origin: hook of the hamate and the adjacent flexor retinaculum. Insertion: whole length of the medial border and palmar surface of the shaft of the fifth metacarpal.
cards.sup: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8, T1).
cards.act: Draws the fifth metacarpal forwards and laterally, rotating it to cup the palm and deepen the hollow of the hand in grip and opposition to the thumb.
cards.rel: Deep to abductor digiti minimi and flexor digiti minimi brevis; the deep branch of the ulnar nerve and the deep palmar arch pass deep to or through the hypothenar muscles to enter the palm on its surface.
cards.clin: Loss of palmar cupping and flattening of the hypothenar eminence follow ulnar nerve injury; the flattened palm reduces the power of cylindrical grip.
cards.exam: Q. Which hypothenar muscle deepens the hollow of the palm? A. Opponens digiti minimi, supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.

cards.desc: Thenar muscle lying deep to abductor pollicis brevis and directly on the first metacarpal.
cards.att: Origin: flexor retinaculum and the tubercle of the trapezium. Insertion: whole length of the lateral border and palmar surface of the shaft of the first metacarpal.
cards.sup: Recurrent (muscular) branch of the median nerve (C8, T1), occasionally with a contribution from the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
cards.act: Opposes the thumb: flexes, abducts and medially rotates the first metacarpal at the saddle carpometacarpal joint so the thumb pulp meets the fingers.
cards.rel: Deep to abductor pollicis brevis, lateral to flexor pollicis brevis; overlies the first carpometacarpal joint and the trapezium.
cards.clin: Loss of opposition is the functional disaster of median nerve injury, producing the flat ape hand; opponensplasty, commonly using flexor digitorum superficialis of the ring finger, restores it. The recurrent branch of the median nerve to it lies in the danger area of the thenar eminence and can be cut in careless palmar incisions.
cards.exam: Q. Which movement is uniquely lost in a low median nerve injury? A. Opposition of the thumb, due to paralysis of opponens pollicis and abductor pollicis brevis.

cards.desc: Flattened X-shaped bundle formed by the junction of the two optic nerves, lying above the diaphragma sellae at the junction of the anterior wall and floor of the third ventricle.
cards.att: Receives the two optic nerves in front and gives off the two optic tracts behind; fibres from the nasal half of each retina decussate within it, while temporal fibres pass through uncrossed.
cards.sup: Small branches of the internal carotid, anterior cerebral and anterior communicating arteries.
cards.act: Partial decussation here brings the fibres representing each contralateral half of the visual field together in the opposite optic tract, the basis of binocular visual field representation.
cards.rel: Pituitary gland and diaphragma sellae lie below, the third ventricle and lamina terminalis above and behind, the internal carotid arteries on each side, and the anterior cerebral and anterior communicating arteries above.
cards.clin: A pituitary adenoma expanding upwards compresses the decussating nasal fibres and causes a bitemporal hemianopia, classically beginning in the upper quadrants; a craniopharyngioma pressing from above tends to affect the lower quadrants first.
cards.exam: Q. Which fibres decussate in the optic chiasm and what field defect follows their compression? A. Nasal retinal fibres; compression gives a bitemporal hemianopia.

cards.desc: The nerve of sight, in reality a tract of the central nervous system, carrying axons of retinal ganglion cells from the eyeball to the optic chiasma.
cards.att: Begins at the optic disc, and has four parts: intra-ocular (about 1 mm), intra-orbital (about 25 mm, slightly sinuous), intracanalicular (about 5 mm, in the optic canal with the ophthalmic artery), and intracranial (about 10 mm, ending at the optic chiasma).
cards.sup: Supplied by the ophthalmic artery; its head is supplied by the short posterior ciliary arteries. The central retinal artery pierces it about 1.25 cm behind the eyeball and runs in its centre.
cards.act: Transmits visual information from the retina to the lateral geniculate body via the chiasma and optic tract.
cards.rel: In the orbit it is surrounded by the four recti and the orbital fat, crossed superiorly from lateral to medial by the ophthalmic artery and nasociliary nerve, with the ciliary ganglion lateral to it. It is invested by all three meninges, so its subarachnoid space is continuous with that of the brain.
cards.clin: Raised intracranial pressure is transmitted along the subarachnoid sheath and produces papilloedema. Compression at the chiasma by a pituitary tumour gives bitemporal hemianopia, and demyelination gives optic neuritis with painful monocular visual loss and a relative afferent pupillary defect.
cards.exam: Q. Why does raised intracranial pressure cause papilloedema? A. The subarachnoid space extends along the optic nerve sheath to the eyeball, so pressure is transmitted to the optic disc.

cards.desc: The photosensitive portion of the retina, extending from the optic disc forwards to the ora serrata.
cards.att: Has an outer pigmented layer adherent to the choroid and an inner neural layer of ten laminae containing rods and cones, bipolar cells and ganglion cells. Firmly attached only at the optic disc and the ora serrata. Contains the macula lutea with the fovea centralis about 3 mm lateral to the disc.
cards.sup: Outer layers by diffusion from the choriocapillaris; inner layers by the central artery of the retina, an end artery. Venous drainage by the central vein of the retina into the cavernous sinus or superior ophthalmic vein. Ganglion cell axons form the optic nerve.
cards.act: Converts light into nerve impulses: rods for scotopic and peripheral vision, cones concentrated at the fovea for photopic and colour vision and highest acuity.
cards.rel: Choroid outside, vitreous body inside; continues at the ora serrata as the non-visual ciliary and iridial parts.
cards.clin: Separation of the neural layer from the pigmented layer along the embryonic intraretinal space is retinal detachment, giving flashes, floaters and a curtain-like field loss. Central retinal artery occlusion causes sudden painless blindness with a pale retina and a cherry-red spot at the fovea.
cards.exam: Q. Why does the fovea appear as a cherry-red spot in central retinal artery occlusion? A. The thin fovea is nourished by the intact choroidal circulation and shows through, while the surrounding oedematous ischaemic retina turns pale.

cards.desc: Flattened band of fibres passing backwards and laterally from the posterolateral angle of the optic chiasm, winding round the crus cerebri to reach the lateral geniculate body.
cards.att: Divides near its end into a large lateral root that ends mainly in the lateral geniculate body, some of its fibres continuing through the brachium of the superior colliculus to the pretectal nuclei and superior colliculus, and a small non-visual medial root, made up of the fibres of Gudden's commissure, that ends in the medial geniculate body. Carries fibres from the temporal half of the ipsilateral retina and the nasal half of the contralateral retina.
cards.sup: Anterior choroidal artery and branches of the internal carotid and posterior communicating arteries.
cards.act: Conveys visual information for perception to the thalamus and for the pupillary light reflex and reflex eye movements to the pretectal area and superior colliculus.
cards.rel: Lies on the under surface of the brain between the anterior perforated substance in front and the crus cerebri behind, lateral to the tuber cinereum and mammillary body, with the uncus above it laterally.
cards.clin: An optic tract lesion causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia that is characteristically incongruous, and because it interrupts pupillary afferents it may be accompanied by a relative afferent pupillary defect in the contralateral eye, features that distinguish it from a lesion of the optic radiation.
cards.exam: Q. Which retinal fibres does the right optic tract carry? A. Fibres from the right temporal and left nasal hemiretinae, representing the left half of the visual field.

cards.desc: Irregular gyri on the orbital (inferior) surface of the frontal lobe, arranged as anterior, posterior, medial and lateral orbital gyri around the H-shaped orbital sulcus.
cards.att: Form the orbitofrontal cortex, connected with the amygdala, hypothalamus, dorsomedial nucleus of the thalamus and temporal pole through the uncinate fasciculus.
cards.sup: Orbital branches of the anterior cerebral artery to the medial part and branches of the middle cerebral artery to the lateral part.
cards.act: Orbitofrontal cortex governs social behaviour, impulse control, emotional regulation and the evaluation of reward, and contributes to olfactory processing.
cards.rel: Rest on the orbital plate of the frontal bone and the cribriform plate, above the orbit; the gyrus rectus lies medially, separated from them by the olfactory sulcus, in which the olfactory bulb and tract lie.
cards.clin: The orbital surface is torn against the rough orbital roof and the lesser wings of the sphenoid in frontal contusions and contrecoup injury, producing disinhibition, poor judgement and personality change. An olfactory groove meningioma here causes ipsilateral anosmia and, with optic atrophy and contralateral papilloedema, the Foster Kennedy syndrome.
cards.exam: Q. What lies in the olfactory sulcus, and which gyrus is medial to it? A. The olfactory bulb and tract, with the gyrus rectus medial to the sulcus.

cards.desc: Small L-shaped bone wedged between the maxilla and the pterygoid process of the sphenoid, forming the posterior part of the hard palate and part of the lateral nasal wall.
cards.att: Horizontal plate forms the posterior third of the hard palate and meets its fellow at the median palatine suture; perpendicular plate forms part of the lateral nasal wall and contains the greater palatine canal. Processes: pyramidal, orbital and sphenoidal, the last two separated by the sphenopalatine notch which the sphenoid converts into the sphenopalatine foramen. Articulates with maxilla, sphenoid, ethmoid, inferior nasal concha, vomer and the opposite palatine bone.
cards.act: Completes the bony palate separating nasal and oral cavities, and transmits the greater and lesser palatine neurovascular bundles and the sphenopalatine vessels and nerves.
cards.rel: Pterygopalatine fossa and its ganglion lie lateral to the perpendicular plate; nasal mucosa medial, oral mucoperiosteum inferior.
cards.clin: Greater palatine nerve block is given at the greater palatine foramen, medial to the third molar, to anaesthetise the hard palate. Failure of fusion of the horizontal plates produces cleft of the secondary palate.
cards.exam: Q. Which foramen lies just medial to the maxillary third molar and what does it transmit? A. The greater palatine foramen, transmitting the greater palatine nerve and vessels.

cards.desc: Longitudinal muscle of the pharynx that raises the palatopharyngeal arch, the posterior pillar of the fauces.
cards.att: Origin: two heads from the posterior border of the hard palate and the palatine aponeurosis, embracing levator veli palatini. Insertion: posterior border of the thyroid cartilage and the fibrous wall of the pharynx, blending with stylopharyngeus.
cards.sup: Pharyngeal plexus, motor fibres of the vagus carrying the cranial accessory component.
cards.act: Elevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing, approximates the palatopharyngeal arches and, with the upper fibres, forms the palatopharyngeal sphincter that helps close the nasopharynx.
cards.rel: Raises the posterior tonsillar pillar; the palatine tonsil lies in the fossa between it and the palatoglossal arch, with the superior constrictor forming the tonsillar bed.
cards.clin: Damage during tonsillectomy or adenoidectomy, or in a cleft palate, impairs velopharyngeal closure and causes nasal regurgitation and hypernasal speech. Passavant ridge, formed partly by its upper fibres, is prominent in cleft palate patients.
cards.exam: Q. Which arch of the fauces is formed by palatopharyngeus? A. The posterior, palatopharyngeal arch.

cards.desc: Slender, frequently absent superficial flexor lying between flexor carpi radialis and flexor carpi ulnaris, with a long tendon crossing the flexor retinaculum.
cards.att: Origin: medial epicondyle of the humerus by the common flexor tendon and the adjacent antebrachial fascia. Insertion: anterior surface of the flexor retinaculum and the apex of the palmar aponeurosis.
cards.sup: Median nerve (C7, C8).
cards.act: Weakly flexes the wrist and tenses the palmar aponeurosis, anchoring the skin of the palm during grip.
cards.rel: Its tendon crosses superficial to the flexor retinaculum, not through the carpal tunnel; the median nerve lies deep and slightly lateral to it, and the ulnar artery and nerve lie medial under cover of flexor carpi ulnaris.
cards.clin: Absent unilaterally or bilaterally in a substantial minority of people, and its expendability makes it the first choice tendon graft for flexor tendon and ligament reconstruction. It is the surface landmark for the median nerve at the wrist, which lies just deep and lateral to it.
cards.exam: Q. Why is palmaris longus a favoured tendon graft? A. It is expendable, frequently absent without deficit, and superficial and easily harvested.

cards.desc: Retroperitoneal mixed exocrine and endocrine gland lying transversely across the posterior abdominal wall at the L1 to L2 level, behind the stomach.
cards.att: Head lies in the C of the duodenum with the uncinate process projecting behind the superior mesenteric vessels; the neck overlies the origin of the portal vein; the body crosses the aorta and left kidney; the tail reaches the splenic hilum within the splenorenal ligament, the only intraperitoneal part.
cards.sup: Head from the superior pancreaticoduodenal (gastroduodenal) and inferior pancreaticoduodenal (superior mesenteric) arteries; neck, body and tail from pancreatic branches of the splenic artery including the arteria pancreatica magna. Veins to the splenic, superior mesenteric and portal veins. Lymph to pancreaticosplenic and coeliac nodes. Parasympathetic supply from the vagus; sympathetic and pain fibres from T5 to T9 via the greater splanchnic nerve and coeliac plexus.
cards.act: Secretes about 1.5 litres of alkaline enzyme-rich juice daily into the duodenum, and insulin, glucagon and somatostatin into the blood.
cards.rel: Anteriorly the lesser sac and stomach; posteriorly the aorta, inferior vena cava, bile duct, left kidney and suprarenal gland, with the splenic vein along the back of the body. The splenic artery runs a tortuous course along its upper border and the transverse mesocolon attaches to its anterior border.
cards.clin: Pancreatic pain is epigastric and bores through to the back (T5 to T9), relieved by leaning forwards. Carcinoma of the head compresses the bile duct causing painless obstructive jaundice with a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier's law). Splenic vein thrombosis from pancreatitis causes left-sided segmental portal hypertension with isolated gastric varices.
cards.exam: Q. Which part of the pancreas is intraperitoneal? A. The tail, lying in the splenorenal ligament.

cards.desc: Main excretory duct of the pancreas, running the whole length of the gland from tail to head and opening into the second part of the duodenum.
cards.att: Begins in the tail, runs to the right through the body and neck receiving tributaries at right angles, turns downwards and backwards in the head, and joins the bile duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater), opening on the major duodenal papilla about 8 to 10 cm from the pylorus on the posteromedial wall of the second part of the duodenum.
cards.sup: Supplied by the pancreaticoduodenal arteries and the splenic pancreatic branches. The ampulla and terminal duct are surrounded by the sphincter of the hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Oddi), with separate sphincters on the bile and pancreatic ducts.
cards.act: Conveys alkaline, enzyme-rich pancreatic juice to the duodenum.
cards.rel: Lies nearer the posterior surface of the gland, above and in front of the splenic vein in the body. In the head the bile duct lies to its right and behind.
cards.clin: A gallstone impacted at the ampulla obstructs both ducts and causes gallstone pancreatitis with jaundice. The duct is dilated with a chain-of-lakes appearance in chronic pancreatitis, and is imaged by MRCP or ERCP.
cards.exam: Q. Where do the bile duct and main pancreatic duct open? A. On the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum, through the hepatopancreatic ampulla guarded by the sphincter of Oddi.

cards.desc: Branch of the callosomarginal artery, from the anterior cerebral artery, supplying the paracentral lobule.
cards.att: Arises from the callosomarginal artery in the cingulate sulcus and runs upwards and backwards to the paracentral lobule on the medial surface of the hemisphere, reaching over the superomedial margin.
cards.sup: Supplies the paracentral lobule, that is the medial extensions of the precentral and postcentral gyri, and the adjacent posterior cingulate cortex.
cards.act: Perfuses the motor and sensory cortex of the contralateral lower limb and perineum and the cortical centre for voluntary control of micturition.
cards.rel: Lies on the medial surface of the hemisphere above the corpus callosum, between the cingulate and marginal sulci, with the pericallosal artery below.
cards.clin: Infarction here causes contralateral weakness and sensory loss confined to the lower limb, with urinary incontinence when the paracentral lobule is damaged bilaterally, as in a parasagittal meningioma or anterior cerebral artery territory stroke.
cards.exam: Q. Which artery supplies the paracentral lobule, and what is the deficit if it is occluded? A. The paracentral branch of the callosomarginal artery from the anterior cerebral artery; contralateral leg weakness and sensory loss with incontinence.

cards.desc: Gyrus on the inferomedial surface of the temporal lobe, lying between the hippocampal fissure above and the collateral sulcus below, whose anterior end is recurved to form the uncus.
cards.att: Its anterior cortex is the entorhinal area (area 28), which sends the perforant path to the hippocampus and is the main cortical gateway to the hippocampal formation; it continues behind through the isthmus into the cingulate gyrus and medially into the subiculum.
cards.sup: Branches of the posterior cerebral artery and the anterior choroidal artery.
cards.act: Relays neocortical information to and from the hippocampus; involved in memory encoding and retrieval and in scene and spatial context recognition.
cards.rel: Lies medial to the fusiform gyrus across the collateral sulcus and below the hippocampus; the uncus overlies the free edge of the tentorium and lies close to the midbrain, oculomotor nerve and posterior cerebral artery.
cards.clin: In raised supratentorial pressure the uncus herniates through the tentorial notch and compresses the oculomotor nerve, midbrain and posterior cerebral artery, giving an ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, contralateral hemiparesis and later occipital infarction. Neurofibrillary pathology in Alzheimer's disease appears earliest in the entorhinal cortex of this gyrus.
cards.exam: Q. Which part of the parahippocampal gyrus herniates through the tentorial notch? A. The uncus, its recurved anterior end.

cards.desc: Quadrilateral flat bone of the cranial vault forming much of the roof and side of the skull.
cards.att: Four borders (sagittal, frontal, squamosal, occipital) and four angles (frontal, sphenoidal, occipital, mastoid). Articulates at the sagittal, coronal, lambdoid and squamosal sutures with the opposite parietal, frontal, occipital, temporal and greater wing of sphenoid. Inner surface shows grooves for the middle meningeal vessels, the sagittal sulcus and granular foveolae; the parietal foramen transmits an emissary vein.
cards.act: Protects the cerebral hemispheres and forms part of the calvaria.
cards.rel: Overlies the parietal lobe and, at the sphenoidal angle, the anterior division of the middle meningeal artery; covered externally by temporalis and the scalp.
cards.clin: The pterion, where the sphenoidal angle meets frontal, sphenoid and temporal bones, is the thinnest part of the vault and overlies the anterior division of the middle meningeal artery: fracture here causes extradural haematoma with a lucid interval. Subperiosteal cephalhaematoma of the newborn is limited by the sutures at the bone margins.
cards.exam: Q. What structure lies deep to the pterion? A. The anterior division of the middle meningeal artery.

cards.desc: Largest sesamoid bone in the body, lying in the tendon of quadriceps femoris in front of the knee joint.
cards.att: Base above receives quadriceps tendon, apex below gives origin to the ligamentum patellae which runs to the tibial tuberosity; the medial and lateral retinacula from vastus medialis and lateralis pass on either side. The posterior surface is articular, divided by a vertical ridge into a smaller medial and a larger lateral facet, which meet the patellar surface of the femur; the lower third of the posterior surface is non-articular and covered by the infrapatellar fat pad.
cards.act: Holds the quadriceps tendon away from the knee axis, increasing its lever arm and extensor power by about a third, and protects the front of the joint.
cards.rel: Subcutaneous in front with the prepatellar bursa; patellar surface of the femur behind; infrapatellar fat pad and deep infrapatellar bursa below; genicular anastomosis around it.
cards.clin: Direct blows fracture it transversely and the fragments separate because quadriceps pulls the upper piece up. Dislocation is almost always lateral and is resisted by the forward projection of the lateral femoral condyle and the horizontal fibres of vastus medialis; a bipartite patella at the superolateral corner is a normal variant mistaken for fracture. The knee jerk tests L3, L4 through the femoral nerve.
cards.exam: Q. Why does the patella dislocate laterally and what resists it? A. Because of the valgus Q angle; the prominent lateral femoral condyle and the lowest horizontal fibres of vastus medialis resist it.

cards.desc: Flat quadrangular muscle in the floor of the femoral triangle, between iliopsoas laterally and adductor longus medially.
cards.att: Origin: pecten pubis (pectineal line) and the surface of the superior pubic ramus between the iliopubic eminence and the pubic tubercle. Insertion: pectineal line of the femur, running from the lesser trochanter to the linea aspera.
cards.sup: Femoral nerve, L2, L3; frequently an additional supply from the accessory obturator nerve, L3.
cards.act: Adduction and flexion of the thigh at the hip, with slight medial rotation.
cards.rel: Forms the intermediate part of the floor of the femoral triangle, with the femoral vein and femoral sheath lying on it. Obturator externus and the anterior division of the obturator nerve lie deep to it.
cards.clin: Its dual innervation, femoral nerve with obturator or accessory obturator supply, makes it the classical composite muscle. The pectineal ligament of Cooper lies along the pecten pubis at its origin and is the strong anchor used in the McVay repair of femoral and direct inguinal hernias. A femoral hernia passes in front of that ligament through the femoral ring, lateral to the lacunar ligament and medial to the femoral vein, then descends over pectineus in the femoral canal.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle of the thigh may be supplied by both the femoral and obturator nerves? A. Pectineus.

cards.desc: Descending branch of the thoraco-acromial artery running between the two pectoral muscles.
cards.att: Arises with the acromial, clavicular and deltoid branches where the thoraco-acromial artery, from the second part of the axillary artery, pierces the clavipectoral fascia; it descends between pectoralis major and pectoralis minor.
cards.sup: Supplies pectoralis major and pectoralis minor, and sends branches to the upper and medial parts of the breast, anastomosing with the lateral thoracic and internal thoracic perforating branches.
cards.act: Chief arterial supply of the pectoral muscles.
cards.rel: Runs on the deep surface of pectoralis major with the lateral pectoral nerve; the medial pectoral nerve pierces pectoralis minor close by, and the cephalic vein lies laterally in the deltopectoral groove.
cards.clin: The dominant pedicle of the pectoralis major myocutaneous flap used in head and neck reconstruction, so it must be identified and preserved when the muscle is raised. It is a source of troublesome bleeding during axillary dissection and pectoral muscle splitting.
cards.exam: Q. From which part of the axillary artery does the thoraco-acromial artery arise? A. The second part, behind pectoralis minor.

cards.desc: Thin triangular muscle of the anterior chest wall deep to pectoralis major, forming the key landmark of the axilla.
cards.att: Origin: outer surfaces of the third, fourth and fifth ribs near their costal cartilages, and the fascia over the intercostal muscles. Insertion: medial border and superior surface of the coracoid process of the scapula.
cards.sup: Medial pectoral nerve (C8, T1), often with a communicating branch from the lateral pectoral nerve.
cards.act: Draws the scapula forwards and downwards (protraction and downward rotation); with the scapula fixed it acts as an accessory muscle of inspiration by raising the ribs.
cards.rel: Crosses the axillary artery and divides it into three parts: first part medial to the muscle, second part behind it, third part lateral to it. It lies within the clavipectoral fascia, which is pierced above it by the cephalic vein, thoracoacromial artery, lateral pectoral nerve and lymphatics.
cards.clin: Used to divide the axillary lymph nodes into surgical levels I, II and III in breast cancer surgery, and it is the landmark for the three parts of the axillary artery. A tight pectoralis minor can compress the neurovascular bundle beneath the coracoid, producing pectoralis minor (subcoracoid) thoracic outlet syndrome.
cards.exam: Q. Why is pectoralis minor surgically important in the axilla? A. It crosses the axillary artery, dividing it into three parts, and defines the three levels of axillary lymph nodes.

cards.desc: The paired ventral column of the midbrain on either side of the interpeduncular fossa, carrying descending fibres from the internal capsule into the pons.
cards.att: Crus cerebri carries corticopontine fibres in its medial one-fifth (frontopontine) and lateral one-fifth (temporo-parieto-occipitopontine), with corticospinal and corticonuclear fibres in the middle three-fifths; substantia nigra lies immediately dorsal, tegmentum behind that.
cards.act: Conduit for the entire corticospinal, corticonuclear and corticopontine outflow of one hemisphere to the brainstem and cord.
cards.rel: Oculomotor nerve emerges from the interpeduncular fossa on its medial side; posterior cerebral artery above and superior cerebellar artery below run in the groove between peduncle and pons; optic tract winds round its lateral surface.
cards.clin: Weber syndrome: an infarct of the medial crus and exiting third nerve gives ipsilateral oculomotor palsy with contralateral hemiplegia. Uncal herniation compresses the peduncle and the third nerve against the tentorial notch.
cards.exam: Q. Which fibres occupy the middle three-fifths of the crus cerebri? A. Corticospinal and corticonuclear fibres, somatotopically arranged.

cards.desc: Median fibrous band on the posterior wall of the pharynx into which the constrictor muscles of both sides insert.
cards.att: Extends from the pharyngeal tubercle on the basilar part of the occipital bone above to the level of the cricoid cartilage, where it fades at the junction with the oesophagus. Gives insertion to the superior, middle and inferior constrictors of both sides.
cards.act: Provides a midline anchor so that the paired constrictors act as a single sphincteric sheet during swallowing.
