cards.rel: Lies in front of the prevertebral fascia and the retropharyngeal space, behind the buccopharyngeal fascia; the pharyngeal plexus of nerves and veins lies on the posterior wall lateral to it.
cards.clin: The posterior midline near the raphe, between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior constrictor, is the weak Killian dehiscence through which a pharyngeal (Zenker) pouch herniates.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the pharyngeal raphe attach superiorly? A. To the pharyngeal tubercle of the basilar part of the occipital bone.

cards.desc: Small conical endocrine gland of the epithalamus, projecting backwards from the posterior wall of the third ventricle between the superior colliculi.
cards.att: Attached by the pineal stalk, whose laminae contain the habenular commissure above and the posterior commissure below; receives sympathetic fibres from the superior cervical ganglion driven by the suprachiasmatic nucleus via the retinohypothalamic tract.
cards.act: Pinealocytes secrete melatonin in darkness, entraining circadian rhythm; it exerts an inhibitory influence on gonadal maturation before puberty.
cards.rel: Lies below the splenium of the corpus callosum and the great cerebral vein, above the tectal plate and the entrance of the cerebral aqueduct, behind the suprapineal and pineal recesses of the third ventricle.
cards.clin: Calcifies after adolescence and is a useful midline marker on skull radiographs and CT; shift indicates a space-occupying lesion. Pineal tumours compress the tectum causing Parinaud syndrome and obstruct the aqueduct causing hydrocephalus.
cards.exam: Q. Why does a pineal tumour cause loss of upward gaze? A. It compresses the dorsal midbrain and pretectal vertical gaze centre, producing Parinaud syndrome.

cards.desc: Pear-shaped muscle passing from the front of the sacrum through the greater sciatic foramen to the greater trochanter, the key landmark of the gluteal region.
cards.att: Origin: anterior surface of the sacrum between the second and fourth anterior sacral foramina, with slips from the gluteal surface of the ilium near the posterior inferior iliac spine and from the sacrotuberous ligament. Insertion: upper border of the greater trochanter of the femur.
cards.sup: Nerve to piriformis, from the ventral rami S1, S2.
cards.act: Lateral rotation of the extended thigh; abduction of the flexed thigh; holds the femoral head in the acetabulum.
cards.rel: Divides the greater sciatic foramen: superior gluteal nerve and vessels emerge above it; inferior gluteal nerve and vessels, sciatic nerve, posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, pudendal nerve, internal pudendal vessels and nerves to obturator internus and quadratus femoris emerge below it.
cards.clin: Piriformis syndrome produces sciatic-type pain from compression of the nerve. In about 10 to 15 per cent of people the common fibular division pierces the muscle. Intramuscular injection is confined to the upper outer quadrant of the buttock to avoid the sciatic nerve below piriformis.
cards.exam: Q. Which structures leave the pelvis above piriformis? A. The superior gluteal nerve and superior gluteal vessels.

cards.desc: Pea-shaped sesamoid bone on the palmar surface of the triquetrum, developed in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris, the smallest carpal bone.
cards.att: Has a single articular facet, for the triquetrum. It receives the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris and gives origin to abductor digiti minimi, and to the pisohamate and pisometacarpal ligaments, which are continuations of that tendon; the flexor retinaculum attaches to it.
cards.rel: Forms the medial boundary of the ulnar canal (canal of Guyon), with the hook of the hamate laterally; the ulnar nerve and artery lie immediately lateral to it as they enter the palm. It is easily palpable at the base of the hypothenar eminence.
cards.clin: It is the last carpal bone to ossify, at about 9 to 12 years, and the only one to ossify from a single centre after childhood, which is used in bone age assessment. It is the surface landmark for locating the ulnar nerve and artery at the wrist and for approaching Guyon's canal. Pisotriquetral arthritis causes localised pain on direct pressure.
cards.exam: Q. Which carpal bone is a sesamoid and in which tendon does it lie? A. The pisiform, in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris.

cards.desc: A pea-sized endocrine gland lying in the hypophysial fossa of the sella turcica of the sphenoid, joined to the hypothalamus by the infundibulum.
cards.att: Two parts: the anterior adenohypophysis, derived from Rathke's pouch, comprising pars distalis, pars intermedia and pars tuberalis; and the posterior neurohypophysis, a downgrowth of the diencephalon, comprising pars nervosa, infundibular stem and median eminence. Roofed by the diaphragma sellae, which the infundibulum pierces.
cards.sup: Superior and inferior hypophysial arteries from the internal carotid artery; the superior hypophysial arteries form the hypophysial portal system carrying releasing hormones from the median eminence to the pars distalis. Venous drainage to the cavernous and intercavernous sinuses.
cards.act: Anterior lobe secretes growth hormone, prolactin, ACTH, TSH, FSH and LH under hypothalamic portal control; posterior lobe stores and releases oxytocin and vasopressin made in the supra-optic and paraventricular nuclei.
cards.rel: Above lies the diaphragma sellae with the optic chiasma anterosuperiorly; laterally on each side the cavernous sinus with the internal carotid artery and the oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic, maxillary and abducent nerves; below and in front the sphenoidal air sinus.
cards.clin: An expanding adenoma compresses the decussating fibres of the optic chiasma and causes bitemporal hemianopia, and may invade the cavernous sinus. Its relation to the sphenoidal sinus allows the trans-sphenoidal surgical approach. Postpartum haemorrhagic infarction of the anterior lobe causes Sheehan syndrome.
cards.exam: Q. Why does a pituitary tumour cause bitemporal hemianopia? A. It compresses the crossing nasal retinal fibres in the optic chiasma lying just above the diaphragma sellae.

cards.desc: Deep arterial arch of the sole lying across the bases of the metatarsal bones, the main arterial supply of the forefoot.
cards.att: Formed by the lateral plantar artery, which curves medially at the base of the fifth metatarsal across the sole, and is completed medially by the deep plantar branch of the dorsalis pedis artery, which passes into the sole between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous muscle.
cards.sup: Gives four plantar metatarsal arteries, which divide into plantar digital arteries for the toes, three perforating branches to the dorsal metatarsal arteries, and branches to the tarsal joints and muscles.
cards.act: Supplies the deep structures of the sole and the toes, and links the dorsal and plantar arterial systems of the foot.
cards.rel: Lies deep to the oblique head of adductor hallucis and the long flexor tendons, on the interossei and the metatarsal bases, accompanied by the deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve.
cards.clin: Its deep position and the dual dorsal and plantar supply mean penetrating wounds of the sole bleed profusely and are hard to control by local pressure. The arch provides the collateral circulation that keeps the foot viable when either the anterior or the posterior tibial artery is occluded.
cards.exam: Q. Which two arteries form the deep plantar arch? A. The lateral plantar artery, completed by the deep plantar branch of the dorsalis pedis artery.

syn: plantar metatarsal branch of plantar arch
cards.desc: Four arteries running forwards in the intermetatarsal spaces of the sole, deep to the flexor tendons.
cards.att: Arise from the convexity of the deep plantar arch (lateral plantar artery); each runs distally in an intermetatarsal space and divides near the web space into two plantar digital arteries proper.
cards.sup: Branches: two plantar digital arteries proper each, plus posterior and anterior perforating branches to the dorsal metatarsal arteries.
cards.act: Main arterial supply to the toes and to the interosseous muscles of the sole.
cards.rel: Lie deep to the oblique head of adductor hallucis and the long flexor tendons, on the interossei; the first space also transmits the deep plantar artery from dorsalis pedis.
cards.clin: Perforating branches make the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial systems interdependent, so the foot may stay viable if one is occluded. Digital ischaemia and gangrene in diabetes and Buerger disease begin in these small vessels.
cards.exam: Q. From what does the plantar metatarsal artery arise, and what does it become? A. From the deep plantar arch of the lateral plantar artery, dividing into two plantar digital arteries proper.

cards.desc: Small vestigial muscle of the superficial posterior compartment of the leg with a short belly and a very long slender tendon.
cards.att: Origin: lower part of the lateral supracondylar line of the femur and the oblique popliteal ligament. Insertion: posterior surface of the calcaneus on the medial side of the calcaneal tendon, often blending with it.
cards.sup: Tibial nerve, S1, S2.
cards.act: Weak plantarflexion of the ankle and weak flexion of the knee; rich in muscle spindles, so largely proprioceptive.
cards.rel: Its belly lies in the floor of the popliteal fossa between the lateral head of gastrocnemius and popliteus; the tendon runs obliquely downwards and medially between gastrocnemius and soleus.
cards.clin: Nicknamed the freshman's nerve because students mistake its thin tendon for a nerve. Rupture is a cause of sudden calf pain resembling tennis leg; the muscle is absent in up to a fifth of limbs and is harvested as a tendon graft.
cards.exam: Q. Why is the plantaris tendon called the freshman's nerve? A. Because its long thin tendon in the calf is commonly mistaken for a nerve by beginners in dissection.

cards.desc: Broad, thin sheet of muscle of facial expression lying in the superficial fascia of the neck.
cards.att: Origin: deep fascia covering the upper parts of pectoralis major and deltoid. Insertion: base of the mandible, skin and subcutaneous tissue of the lower face, the modiolus and the muscles around the angle of the mouth, blending with depressor anguli oris.
cards.sup: Cervical branch of the facial nerve (CN VII).
cards.act: Depresses the mandible and draws down the angle of the mouth in expressions of horror and surprise; tenses the skin of the neck and releases pressure on the underlying veins.
cards.rel: Lies in the superficial fascia, superficial to the external jugular vein, the great auricular and transverse cervical nerves and the anterior jugular veins; the deep fascia and sternocleidomastoid lie deep to it.
cards.clin: Neck wounds must be closed in a separate platysma layer, otherwise the muscle pulls the scar apart. Injury to the cervical branch of the facial nerve during submandibular gland surgery causes an asymmetrical lower lip on grimacing.
cards.exam: Q. Nerve supply of platysma? A. Cervical branch of the facial nerve.

cards.desc: The bulging middle part of the brainstem, between the midbrain above and the medulla oblongata below, lying on the clivus in front of the cerebellum.
cards.att: Basilar part contains pontine nuclei and transverse pontocerebellar fibres that gather laterally as the middle cerebellar peduncle; the tegmentum houses the nuclei of the trigeminal, abducent, facial and vestibulocochlear nerves, the facial colliculus and the medial lemniscus.
cards.sup: Pontine branches of the basilar artery, which lies in the shallow midline basilar sulcus.
cards.act: Relays cortical information to the contralateral cerebellar cortex, transmits all long ascending and descending tracts, and contains the pneumotaxic and apneustic respiratory centres.
cards.rel: Fourth ventricle lies behind it; trigeminal nerve emerges from its lateral surface, and the abducent, facial and vestibulocochlear nerves at the pontomedullary junction; the cerebellopontine angle lies at its lateral border.
cards.clin: Basilar artery thrombosis of the ventral pons produces the locked-in syndrome with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movement. Rapid correction of hyponatraemia causes central pontine myelinolysis; a cerebellopontine angle schwannoma compresses cranial nerves VIII, VII and V.
cards.exam: Q. Which cranial nerve nuclei lie in the pons? A. Trigeminal motor and sensory, abducent, facial and vestibulocochlear.

cards.desc: Continuation of the femoral artery behind the knee, the deepest structure in the popliteal fossa.
cards.att: Begins at the adductor hiatus in adductor magnus, runs downwards and laterally across the floor of the popliteal fossa, and ends at the lower border of popliteus by dividing into anterior tibial and posterior tibial arteries.
cards.sup: Branches: superior medial and superior lateral genicular, middle genicular, inferior medial and inferior lateral genicular, sural, and muscular branches; all take part in the anastomosis around the knee.
cards.act: Sole arterial supply to the leg and foot, and supply to the knee joint.
cards.rel: Deepest structure in the fossa, lying on the popliteal surface of the femur, capsule of the knee and popliteus fascia; the popliteal vein is superficial to it and the tibial nerve most superficial of the three.
cards.clin: Tethered at the adductor hiatus and the soleal arch, so it is torn in posterior knee dislocation and supracondylar femoral fracture. Commonest site of peripheral aneurysm, and the pulse is felt only with the knee flexed and deep pressure in the fossa.
cards.exam: Q. What are the three structures of the neurovascular bundle in the popliteal fossa from superficial to deep? A. Tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery.

cards.desc: Deep vein of the popliteal fossa, lying between the tibial nerve and the popliteal artery.
cards.att: Formed at the lower border of popliteus by union of the anterior and posterior tibial veins; ascends through the fossa and passes through the adductor hiatus to become the femoral vein.
cards.sup: Tributaries: small saphenous vein, genicular veins and muscular veins including the sural veins.
cards.act: Returns all deep venous blood from the leg and foot to the femoral vein.
cards.rel: Superficial (posterior) to the popliteal artery and deep to the tibial nerve; enclosed with the artery in a common fibrous sheath.
cards.clin: Common site of deep vein thrombosis and the standard site for duplex compression ultrasound. Being bound to the artery in one sheath, injury here can produce an arteriovenous fistula.
cards.exam: Q. Which superficial vein ends in the popliteal vein? A. The small saphenous vein, at the saphenopopliteal junction.

cards.desc: Flat triangular muscle forming the lower part of the floor of the popliteal fossa, running from the lateral femoral condyle downwards and medially to the tibia.
cards.att: Origin: a tendon from a pit on the lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle, within the knee capsule, with fibres from the arcuate popliteal ligament and the lateral meniscus. Insertion: triangular area on the posterior surface of the tibia above the soleal line.
cards.sup: Tibial nerve, L4, L5, S1.
cards.act: Unlocks the fully extended knee: laterally rotates the femur on the fixed tibia, or medially rotates the tibia when the foot is free. Retracts the lateral meniscus and helps resist posterior displacement of the tibia.
cards.rel: Its posterior surface forms the floor of the lower popliteal fossa, crossed by the popliteal vessels and tibial nerve. Its tendon is intracapsular but extrasynovial, running through the hiatus in the coronary ligament of the lateral meniscus.
cards.clin: Loss of popliteus prevents unlocking of the knee. Its tendon is torn in posterolateral corner injuries, giving rotatory instability, and the popliteal bursa may communicate with the knee joint.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle unlocks the fully extended knee? A. Popliteus, by laterally rotating the femur on the fixed tibia.

cards.latin: ramus dexter et ramus sinister venae portae hepatis
cards.desc: The two terminal branches into which the hepatic portal vein divides at the porta hepatis, one for each hemiliver.
cards.att: The portal vein divides at the right end of the porta hepatis. The short thick right branch enters the right hemiliver and divides into anterior and posterior sectoral branches; the longer left branch runs transversely, then turns forwards into the umbilical fissure, where the ligamentum teres is attached in front and the ligamentum venosum behind.
cards.sup: Right branch: anterior sectoral branches to segments V and VIII, posterior sectoral branches to segments VI and VII. Left branch: branches to segments II, III and IV. Both give branches to the caudate lobe.
cards.act: Deliver portal blood to the sinusoids of each hemiliver; the boundary between their territories is the principal plane, not the falciform ligament.
cards.rel: Each branch lies posterior to the corresponding hepatic artery branch and bile duct within the portal triad, enclosed with them in the perivascular fibrous capsule of Glisson.
cards.clin: Preoperative portal vein embolisation of one side produces hypertrophy of the future liver remnant before major hepatectomy. Recanalisation of the umbilical vein at the left branch produces the para-umbilical collaterals and caput medusae of portal hypertension.
cards.exam: Q. Which structures accompany a portal vein branch inside the liver? A. A branch of the hepatic artery and a bile duct, together forming the portal triad within Glisson's sheath.

cards.desc: The gyrus of the parietal lobe between the central and postcentral sulci, forming the primary somatosensory cortex, Brodmann areas 3, 1 and 2.
cards.att: Receives thalamocortical fibres from the ventral posterolateral nucleus (body) and ventral posteromedial nucleus (head) through the posterior limb of the internal capsule; projects to the superior parietal lobule and to the motor cortex.
cards.sup: Middle cerebral artery for the lateral surface, anterior cerebral artery for the medial extension into the paracentral lobule.
cards.act: Conscious perception and localisation of touch, pressure, vibration, joint position and pain from the opposite half of the body.
cards.rel: Precentral gyrus lies in front across the central sulcus, supramarginal gyrus and superior parietal lobule behind; the sensory homunculus is inverted, with the leg and perineum on the medial surface and the face and tongue lowest laterally.
cards.clin: A lesion causes contralateral loss of discriminative touch, two-point discrimination, proprioception and stereognosis with relative sparing of crude pain. Anterior cerebral artery occlusion produces sensory loss confined to the opposite lower limb.
cards.exam: Q. Which thalamic nucleus projects to the face area of the postcentral gyrus? A. The ventral posteromedial nucleus.

cards.k: postcommunicating part of posterior cerebral artery
cards.desc: Segment of the posterior cerebral artery distal to its junction with the posterior communicating artery, winding round the midbrain.
cards.att: Begins where the posterior communicating artery joins, passes laterally and backwards round the cerebral peduncle in the ambient cistern, and reaches the tentorial surface of the occipital and temporal lobes.
cards.sup: Thalamogeniculate arteries, medial and lateral posterior choroidal arteries, and the cortical inferior temporal, calcarine and parieto-occipital branches.
cards.act: Supplies the lateral thalamus and geniculate bodies, the choroid plexus, and the visual cortex with the inferomedial temporal and occipital lobes.
cards.rel: Curves round the midbrain with the basal vein of Rosenthal and the optic tract above it, on the free edge of the tentorium cerebelli; the oculomotor nerve emerges proximal to it, between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries.
cards.clin: Occlusion produces a contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, since the occipital pole also receives middle cerebral branches. In uncal herniation the artery is compressed against the tentorial edge, causing occipital infarction; thalamogeniculate occlusion gives the thalamic (Dejerine-Roussy) syndrome.
cards.exam: Q. Why is the macula spared in posterior cerebral artery occlusion? A. Because the occipital pole receives a collateral supply from terminal branches of the middle cerebral artery.

cards.desc: Larger of the two circumflex humeral arteries, passing with the axillary nerve through the quadrangular space.
cards.att: Arises from the third part of the axillary artery, passes backwards with the axillary nerve through the quadrangular space, and winds round the surgical neck of the humerus deep to deltoid to anastomose with the anterior circumflex humeral artery.
cards.sup: Branches to deltoid, teres minor, the long head of triceps, the shoulder joint and the overlying skin; anastomoses with the anterior circumflex humeral, profunda brachii and suprascapular arteries.
cards.act: Supplies deltoid, teres minor and the shoulder joint, and contributes to the supply of the surgical neck of the humerus.
cards.rel: The quadrangular space is bounded above by teres minor, below by teres major, medially by the long head of triceps and laterally by the surgical neck of the humerus; the axillary nerve accompanies the artery through it.
cards.clin: Injured with the axillary nerve in fractures of the surgical neck and in inferior shoulder dislocation, giving deltoid paralysis and loss of sensation over the regimental badge area. Compression in the quadrangular space causes posterior shoulder pain with deltoid and teres minor wasting.
cards.exam: Q. Which artery and nerve traverse the quadrangular space? A. The posterior circumflex humeral artery and the axillary nerve.

cards.desc: A compact transverse fibre bundle crossing the midline in the caudal wall of the third ventricle, just above the opening of the cerebral aqueduct and below the pineal stalk.
cards.att: Interconnects the pretectal nuclei, the nuclei of the posterior commissure and interstitial nucleus of Cajal, and the superior colliculi of the two sides.
cards.act: Carries the crossing limb of the pupillary light reflex, so light in one eye constricts both pupils, and contributes fibres for conjugate vertical gaze.
cards.rel: Forms the inferior lamina of the pineal stalk, with the habenular commissure above it; the cerebral aqueduct begins immediately below.
cards.clin: A dorsal midbrain lesion at the commissure gives light-near dissociation, with pupils that do not react to light but constrict on accommodation, part of Parinaud syndrome.
cards.exam: Q. Which reflex pathway crosses in the posterior commissure? A. The consensual limb of the pupillary light reflex, from pretectal nucleus to the opposite Edinger-Westphal nucleus.

cards.desc: The only abductor of the vocal folds, on the posterior surface of the cricoid lamina.
cards.att: Origin: posterior surface of the lamina of the cricoid cartilage, in the shallow depression on either side of the median ridge. Insertion: back of the muscular process of the arytenoid cartilage.
cards.sup: Recurrent laryngeal nerve (vagus).
cards.act: Rotates the arytenoid laterally, abducting the vocal fold and opening the rima glottidis; it also braces the folds against the pull of the adductors during phonation.
cards.rel: Lies on the posterior cricoid lamina behind the pharyngeal mucosa in the piriform fossa region; the transverse and oblique arytenoids lie above it.
cards.clin: Called the safety muscle of the larynx: bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy paralyses both, the cords lie adducted and the patient develops inspiratory stridor requiring emergency tracheostomy.
cards.exam: Q. Which is the only abductor of the vocal folds? A. Posterior crico-arytenoid.

cards.desc: Largest branch of the vertebral artery, supplying the posterolateral medulla and the under surface of the cerebellum.
cards.att: Arises from the vertebral artery near the lower border of the olive, winds backwards between the rootlets of the vagus and accessory nerves, loops round the cerebellar tonsil and divides into medial and lateral branches on the inferior surface of the cerebellum.
cards.sup: Branches to the posterolateral medulla, the choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle, the inferior vermis, the cerebellar tonsil and the inferior cerebellar hemisphere.
cards.act: Supplies the lateral medullary territory containing the spinal nucleus and tract of the trigeminal, nucleus ambiguus, vestibular nuclei, spinothalamic tract, descending sympathetic fibres and inferior cerebellar peduncle.
cards.rel: Related to the roots of the glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves, the olive and the cerebellar tonsil; the vertebral artery gives it off before the two vertebrals unite to form the basilar.
cards.clin: Occlusion, more often of the vertebral artery itself, causes the lateral medullary or Wallenberg syndrome: ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature on the face, Horner syndrome, ataxia, nystagmus and vertigo, dysphagia and hoarseness, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature over the body.
cards.exam: Q. Name the features of lateral medullary syndrome. A. Ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss, Horner syndrome, ataxia, palatal and vocal cord palsy with vertigo, and contralateral pain and temperature loss on the trunk and limbs.

cards.desc: Series of paired arteries supplying the intercostal spaces from behind, running forward in the costal groove of the rib above.
cards.att: First and second arise from the superior (supreme) intercostal artery of the costocervical trunk; third to eleventh, with the subcostal artery, arise from the posterior surface of the descending thoracic aorta. The right vessels are longer and cross the vertebral bodies.
cards.sup: Each gives a dorsal branch (with a spinal branch to the cord), a collateral branch running along the upper border of the rib below, a lateral cutaneous branch, and muscular and mammary branches.
cards.act: Supply the intercostal muscles, parietal pleura, ribs, breast, skin of the thoracic wall and, via spinal branches, the spinal cord.
cards.rel: Run in the costal groove between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, in the order vein, artery, nerve from above downwards. On the right they pass behind the oesophagus, thoracic duct and azygos vein.
cards.clin: Chest drains and thoracocentesis needles are passed just above the upper border of the lower rib, in the mid-axillary line, to avoid the main bundle; the collateral branch still runs there, so the middle of the space is safest. In coarctation of the aorta enlarged posterior intercostal arteries cause inferior rib notching.
cards.exam: Q. Which posterior intercostal arteries do not arise from the aorta? A. The first and second, which come from the superior intercostal artery of the costocervical trunk.

cards.desc: The quadrangular, posterolateral leaflet of the left atrioventricular (mitral) valve, guarding the left atrioventricular orifice.
cards.att: Attached to roughly two-thirds of the circumference of the mitral annulus, posterolaterally; usually scalloped into three parts, P1 lateral, P2 middle, P3 medial. Chordae tendineae pass from its free and rough zones to both the anterolateral and posteromedial papillary muscles.
cards.act: Coapts with the anterior leaflet in systole to close the mitral orifice; it is shorter in height but broader at its base than the anterior leaflet.
cards.rel: Lies posterior and lateral in the orifice, related to the coronary sinus and circumflex artery in the atrioventricular groove behind it. The anterior leaflet lies between it and the aortic outflow tract.
cards.clin: Prolapse of the P2 scallop from myxomatous degeneration is the commonest cause of degenerative mitral regurgitation and is repaired by resection or neochordae. The circumflex artery and coronary sinus are at risk during annuloplasty.
cards.exam: Q. Which mitral leaflet occupies the greater part of the annulus? A. The posterior leaflet, about two-thirds, though the anterior leaflet is the taller.

cards.desc: The posteroinferior of the three cusps of the tricuspid valve, guarding the right atrioventricular orifice.
cards.att: Attached to the posteroinferior part of the tricuspid annulus, between the anterior and septal cusps; receives chordae tendineae mainly from the posterior (inferior) papillary muscle, which commonly has two or three heads.
cards.act: Coapts with the anterior and septal cusps in ventricular systole, closing the right atrioventricular orifice and preventing regurgitation into the right atrium.
cards.rel: Related externally to the right coronary artery in the right atrioventricular groove. Lies against the diaphragmatic wall of the right ventricle.
cards.clin: In Ebstein anomaly the posterior and septal leaflets are displaced apically and adherent to the ventricular wall, atrialising the inflow. The right coronary artery is at risk in tricuspid annuloplasty.
cards.exam: Q. Which papillary muscle supplies chordae to the posterior tricuspid cusp? A. The posterior (inferior) papillary muscle, together with the adjacent anterior papillary muscle.

cards.k: posterior part of superior temporal gyrus
cards.desc: The hindmost third of the superior temporal gyrus, behind the transverse temporal gyri, including the planum temporale on the upper surface.
cards.att: Receives auditory association input from the primary auditory cortex in front of it and connects with the supramarginal and angular gyri; linked to Broca's area by the arcuate fasciculus.
cards.sup: Inferior division of the middle cerebral artery.
cards.act: In the dominant hemisphere this is Wernicke's area, Brodmann area 22, for comprehension of spoken language; in the non-dominant hemisphere it handles prosody and environmental sound.
cards.rel: Lies below the posterior ramus of the lateral sulcus and the supramarginal gyrus, above the middle temporal gyrus; the planum temporale is usually larger on the left.
cards.clin: Infarction of the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery here causes receptive (fluent) aphasia: speech is fluent but meaningless, comprehension and repetition are lost, and the patient is unaware of the deficit.
cards.exam: Q. Where is Wernicke's area and what is its Brodmann number? A. Posterior part of the dominant superior temporal gyrus, area 22.

cards.desc: Larger terminal branch of the popliteal artery, the main artery of the posterior compartment of the leg and of the sole.
cards.att: Begins at the lower border of popliteus, passes deep to the tendinous arch of soleus, descends in the deep posterior compartment on tibialis posterior then flexor digitorum longus, and ends deep to the flexor retinaculum midway between the medial malleolus and the heel by dividing into medial and lateral plantar arteries.
cards.sup: Branches: circumflex fibular branch, fibular (peroneal) artery, nutrient artery to the tibia which is the largest nutrient artery in the body, medial calcaneal branches, muscular and communicating branches.
cards.act: Supplies the posterior and lateral compartments of the leg and, through the plantar arteries, the whole sole.
cards.rel: Accompanied by paired venae comitantes and by the tibial nerve, which crosses from its medial to its lateral side about 2.5 cm below its origin. Behind the medial malleolus the order under the retinaculum is tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, artery, tibial nerve, flexor hallucis longus.
cards.clin: Pulse is felt midway between the medial malleolus and the heel, an essential check in the diabetic foot and in peripheral arterial disease. Injured in tibial shaft fracture and compressed in deep posterior compartment syndrome.
cards.exam: Q. Where is the posterior tibial pulse palpated? A. Midway between the medial malleolus and the medial tubercle of the calcaneus, behind the medial malleolus.

cards.desc: Paired deep veins accompanying the posterior tibial artery in the deep posterior compartment of the leg.
cards.att: Formed behind the medial malleolus by union of the medial and lateral plantar veins; ascend with the artery and join the anterior tibial veins at the lower border of popliteus to form the popliteal vein.
cards.sup: Tributaries: fibular (peroneal) veins, muscular veins from soleus and gastrocnemius, and perforating veins from the great saphenous system.
cards.act: Drain the sole and the deep posterior compartment of the leg.
cards.rel: Lie on either side of the posterior tibial artery within the same fascial sheath, deep to soleus.
cards.clin: With the soleal sinusoids, one of the commonest sites of origin of deep vein thrombosis and therefore of pulmonary embolism. Incompetent perforators draining into them cause medial ankle varicose ulcers.
cards.exam: Q. What two veins unite to form the popliteal vein? A. The anterior tibial and posterior tibial veins, at the lower border of popliteus.

cards.desc: Ascending branch of the ulnar artery that passes behind the medial epicondyle with the ulnar nerve.
cards.att: Arises from the ulnar artery just below the anterior recurrent branch, passes backwards and upwards between flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus, then ascends behind the medial epicondyle between the olecranon and the epicondyle, and anastomoses with the superior and inferior ulnar collateral arteries.
cards.sup: Muscular branches to the flexor muscles and branches to the elbow joint and the cubital tunnel.
cards.act: Supplies the medial side of the elbow joint and the adjacent flexor muscles.
cards.rel: Lies with the ulnar nerve in the groove behind the medial epicondyle, deep to the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris and the arch between them.
cards.clin: Accompanies the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle, so it is encountered in anterior transposition of the ulnar nerve and may be injured in medial epicondyle fractures, contributing to a cubital tunnel haematoma.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve does the posterior ulnar recurrent artery accompany, and where? A. The ulnar nerve, in the groove behind the medial epicondyle.

cards.desc: The gyrus of the frontal lobe between the precentral and central sulci, forming the primary motor cortex, Brodmann area 4.
cards.att: Its layer V giant pyramidal cells of Betz contribute only about 3 per cent of corticospinal fibres, the gyrus (area 4) as a whole about a third; fibres descend through the corona radiata, corticonuclear fibres passing through the genu and corticospinal fibres through the posterior limb of the internal capsule; receives input from the premotor cortex, supplementary motor area and ventral lateral thalamic nucleus.
cards.sup: Middle cerebral artery for the lateral surface, anterior cerebral artery for the medial part in the paracentral lobule.
cards.act: Initiates and controls skilled voluntary movement of the opposite half of the body.
cards.rel: Postcentral gyrus lies behind across the central sulcus; the motor homunculus is inverted and disproportionate, the lower limb and perineum on the medial surface, the hand and face large and low on the lateral surface.
cards.clin: A cortical lesion causes contralateral upper motor neuron weakness with spasticity, hyperreflexia and an extensor plantar response. Irritation gives a Jacksonian march, seizure activity spreading in homuncular order.
cards.exam: Q. Which vessel supplies the lower limb area of the motor cortex? A. The anterior cerebral artery, supplying the paracentral lobule.

cards.k: precommunicating part of posterior cerebral artery
cards.desc: First segment of the posterior cerebral artery, between the bifurcation of the basilar artery and the entry of the posterior communicating artery.
cards.att: Runs laterally in the interpeduncular cistern above the oculomotor nerve, from the basilar bifurcation to the junction with the posterior communicating artery, where the postcommunicating part begins.
cards.sup: Posteromedial central (thalamoperforating) arteries to the midbrain, subthalamus and medial thalamus, and small branches to the interpeduncular fossa.
cards.act: Supplies the rostral midbrain and medial thalamus and completes the posterior part of the circle of Willis.
cards.rel: The oculomotor nerve passes forward between the posterior cerebral artery above and the superior cerebellar artery below; the interpeduncular fossa, cerebral peduncles and posterior perforated substance lie around it.
cards.clin: An aneurysm at the basilar tip or at this segment presses on the oculomotor nerve and gives a painful third nerve palsy with a fixed dilated pupil. In the fetal variant the precommunicating part is hypoplastic and the posterior cerebral territory is supplied from the internal carotid through a large posterior communicating artery.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve lies between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries? A. The oculomotor nerve.

cards.desc: Flat quadrilateral muscle across the front of the distal quarter of the radius and ulna, the deepest muscle of the anterior forearm.
cards.att: Origin: oblique ridge on the anterior surface of the distal quarter of the ulna. Insertion: anterior surface of the distal quarter of the radius.
cards.sup: Anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve (C8, T1).
cards.act: Prime mover of pronation of the forearm; its deep fibres hold the head of the ulna against the ulnar notch of the radius at the distal radio-ulnar joint.
cards.rel: Lies deep to the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus, flexor pollicis longus and flexor carpi radialis, and forms the floor of the distal forearm. The pronator quadratus fat pad lies on its anterior surface.
cards.clin: Loss of the pronator quadratus fat pad shadow or its bowing on a lateral wrist radiograph signals an occult distal radius fracture. It is paralysed in anterior interosseous nerve syndrome, tested by pronation with the elbow fully flexed to eliminate pronator teres.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle is the prime mover of pronation and how is it tested in isolation? A. Pronator quadratus, tested by resisted pronation with the elbow fully flexed.

cards.desc: Walnut-sized fibromuscular and glandular organ lying below the bladder neck and in front of the rectum, surrounding the prostatic urethra.
cards.att: Base fused with the bladder neck above, apex resting on the perineal membrane below; anterior, posterior and two inferolateral surfaces. Zones: peripheral, central, transition and anterior fibromuscular stroma; the median sulcus divides the posterior surface.
cards.sup: Arteries: inferior vesical, middle rectal and internal pudendal. Veins: prostatic venous plexus draining to the internal iliac veins and communicating with the internal vertebral venous plexus. Nerves: inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus. Lymph: internal iliac and sacral nodes.
cards.act: Secretes thin alkaline fluid rich in citric acid, zinc and prostate specific antigen, contributing about 30 per cent of the ejaculate and liquefying the semen.
cards.rel: Bladder above, rectum behind separated by the rectovesical fascia of Denonvilliers, levator ani inferolaterally, retropubic space of Retzius and pubic symphysis in front. Ejaculatory ducts pierce the posterior surface and open at the seminal colliculus.
cards.clin: Benign hyperplasia begins in the transition zone and obstructs the urethra; carcinoma arises mainly in the peripheral zone, hardening the posterior surface and obliterating the median sulcus on digital rectal examination. Spread to the vertebrae and skull occurs through the valveless prostatic and vertebral venous plexuses (Batson).
cards.exam: Q. Which zone gives rise to benign prostatic hyperplasia and which to carcinoma? A. Transition zone for hyperplasia, peripheral zone for carcinoma.

cards.desc: Stout proximal of the two phalanges of the great toe, articulating with the head of the first metatarsal.
cards.att: Concave base meets the head of the first metatarsal at the metatarsophalangeal joint; head articulates with the distal phalanx. Flexor hallucis brevis inserts on the base by two heads through the medial and lateral sesamoids, abductor hallucis on the medial side of the base, adductor hallucis on the lateral side, and extensor hallucis brevis on the dorsum of the base.
cards.act: Bears the greatest load of any toe at push off and gives insertion to the short muscles that stabilise the great toe.
cards.rel: Flexor hallucis longus tendon and the two sesamoids plantarly, extensor hallucis longus dorsally, plantar digital nerves and arteries on each side.
cards.clin: In hallux valgus this phalanx deviates laterally at the metatarsophalangeal joint and the head of the first metatarsal becomes prominent as a bunion. The first metatarsophalangeal joint is the classic site of acute gout (podagra), and forced hyperextension of that joint is turf toe.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscles insert on the base of the proximal phalanx of the hallux? A. Flexor hallucis brevis through the sesamoids, abductor hallucis medially, adductor hallucis laterally, extensor hallucis brevis dorsally.

cards.desc: Longest of the three phalanges of the index finger, extending from the metacarpophalangeal joint to the proximal interphalangeal joint.
cards.att: Base has a concave oval facet for the head of the second metacarpal; the first dorsal interosseous and first palmar interosseous attach to its base and extensor expansion, and the first lumbrical joins the expansion on its radial side. The head is a trochlea for the middle phalanx.
cards.rel: No long flexor tendon inserts into it; the flexor tendons pass along its palmar surface within the fibrous flexor sheath, held by the A1, A2 and A3 pulleys. The extensor expansion covers its dorsum.
cards.clin: Fractures of the shaft angulate with the apex volar, because the interossei flex the proximal fragment while the extensor expansion extends the distal fragment. Rotational malalignment is judged by the fingers converging on the scaphoid tubercle when the fist is closed.
cards.exam: Q. Why do proximal phalangeal shaft fractures angulate with an apex volar? A. The interossei flex the proximal fragment while the central slip of the extensor expansion extends the distal fragment.

cards.desc: Shortest of the proximal phalanges of the fingers, forming the first segment of the little finger.
cards.att: Base bears an oval concave facet for the head of the fifth metacarpal and receives flexor digiti minimi brevis, abductor digiti minimi, the third palmar interosseous and the fourth lumbrical through the base and extensor expansion. The head articulates with the middle phalanx.
cards.rel: Palmar surface grooved for the flexor tendons in their fibrous sheath; the deep transverse metacarpal ligament binds its base to that of the ring finger through the volar plate.
cards.clin: The metacarpophalangeal joint of the little finger is where clawing is most obvious in ulnar nerve palsy, and Wartenberg sign is the persistent abduction of this finger due to unopposed extensor digiti minimi when the palmar interosseous is paralysed.
cards.exam: Q. What is Wartenberg's sign? A. Persistent abduction of the little finger in ulnar nerve palsy, from unopposed extensor digiti minimi with paralysis of the third palmar interosseous.

cards.desc: Longest phalanx in the hand, the first segment of the middle finger.
cards.att: Base carries a concave oval facet for the head of the third metacarpal and receives the second dorsal interosseous on its radial side and the third dorsal interosseous on its ulnar side; there is no palmar interosseous. The second lumbrical joins the extensor expansion on its radial side, and the head forms a trochlea for the middle phalanx.
cards.rel: The long flexor tendons run in the fibrous flexor sheath on its palmar surface, restrained by the A1, A2 and A3 pulleys; the extensor expansion with its lateral bands covers the dorsum.
cards.clin: The A1 pulley over the metacarpophalangeal joint at its base is the site of stenosis in trigger finger, released by division of that pulley. Volar plate injuries at the proximal interphalangeal joint at the head of this bone are the commonest finger sprain.
cards.exam: Q. Which pulley is divided in trigger finger release? A. The A1 pulley, at the level of the metacarpophalangeal joint.

cards.desc: First segment of the ring finger, slightly shorter than that of the middle finger.
cards.att: Base has an oval concave facet for the head of the fourth metacarpal, receives the fourth dorsal interosseous on its ulnar side and the second palmar interosseous on its radial side, and gives passage to the third lumbrical into the extensor expansion. The head articulates with the middle phalanx.
cards.rel: Bound to the neighbouring proximal phalanges through the volar plates by the deep transverse metacarpal ligaments; the long flexor tendons lie palmar to it in the fibrous sheath and the extensor expansion dorsal to it.
cards.clin: Clawing at the metacarpophalangeal joint of this and the little finger characterises ulnar nerve palsy. A tight ring causing swelling and constriction acts at the level of this phalanx and may need to be cut off before circulation is compromised.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscles attach to the base and expansion of a proximal phalanx and what do they do? A. The interossei and lumbricals, which flex the metacarpophalangeal joint and extend the interphalangeal joints.

cards.desc: Long fusiform muscle of the posterior abdominal wall lying alongside the lumbar vertebrae, joining iliacus to form iliopsoas.
cards.att: Origin from the transverse processes of all five lumbar vertebrae, the bodies and intervertebral discs from T12 to L5, and the tendinous arches bridging the vertebral bodies. Passes behind the inguinal ligament and in front of the hip capsule to insert by a tendon into the lesser trochanter of the femur.
cards.sup: Anterior rami of L1, L2 and L3 directly.
cards.act: Chief flexor of the thigh at the hip; laterally rotates the hip; with the lower limb fixed it flexes the trunk and stabilises the lumbar spine.
cards.rel: The lumbar plexus is formed within its substance. The ureter and gonadal vessels descend on its anterior surface, the genitofemoral nerve pierces that surface, the femoral nerve emerges from its lateral border and the obturator nerve from its medial border. The kidney and sympathetic trunk are also related to it.
cards.clin: A psoas abscess, classically tuberculous from a lumbar vertebral body, tracks in the psoas sheath under the inguinal ligament and points as a fluctuant swelling in the femoral triangle with a flexed hip. The psoas sign, pain on passive extension of the right hip, indicates irritation of the muscle by a retrocaecal appendix. It gives the psoas shadow on a plain abdominal radiograph.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerves emerge from the lateral and medial borders of psoas major? A. Femoral nerve laterally, obturator nerve medially.

cards.desc: Tendinous band in the cheek that gives common attachment to buccinator in front and superior constrictor behind.
cards.att: Extends from the tip of the pterygoid hamulus of the medial pterygoid plate above to the posterior end of the mylohyoid line of the mandible below. Buccinator arises from its anterior edge, the superior constrictor from its posterior edge.
cards.act: Acts as a fibrous intersection transmitting tension between buccinator and superior constrictor, keeping the cheek and pharyngeal wall applied to the teeth and bolus.
cards.rel: Forms the medial wall of the pterygomandibular space, which contains the lingual and inferior alveolar nerves and the inferior alveolar vessels; the medial pterygoid lies lateral to that space.
cards.clin: The key landmark for the inferior alveolar nerve block: the needle is inserted just lateral to the raphe, at the pterygomandibular fold, and advanced to the mandibular lingula. Infections of the pterygomandibular space cause trismus.
cards.exam: Q. Which two muscles attach to the pterygomandibular raphe? A. Buccinator anteriorly and superior constrictor of the pharynx posteriorly.

cards.desc: Thick anterior part of levator ani running backwards from the pubis alongside the urethra, prostate and anal canal to the coccyx.
cards.att: Origin: posterior surface of the body of the pubis and the anterior part of the tendinous arch of levator ani. Insertion: anococcygeal ligament and coccyx, with visceral slips as puboprostaticus (levator prostatae) or pubovaginalis, puboperinealis and puboanalis.
cards.sup: Nerve to levator ani from the anterior ramus of S4, with a contribution from the pudendal nerve (S2, S3, S4).
cards.act: Supports and elevates the pelvic viscera, compresses the urethra and anal canal, and reinforces the external urethral sphincter mechanism.
cards.rel: Its medial borders bound the levator hiatus, through which the urethra and anal canal (and the vagina in the female) pass. Lies above the perineal membrane and deep perineal pouch.
cards.clin: The muscle trained by pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises for stress urinary incontinence. Avulsion of its pubic attachment during difficult vaginal delivery is a major cause of later prolapse.
cards.exam: Q. Which structures pass through the levator hiatus bounded by pubococcygeus? A. The urethra and anal canal, plus the vagina in the female.

cards.desc: U-shaped muscular sling of levator ani that loops behind the anorectal junction, the most medial and inferior part of the muscle.
cards.att: Origin: posterior surface of the body of the pubis on each side, close to the symphysis. Insertion: none bony; the two sides unite behind the anorectal junction as a continuous sling blending with the deep part of the external anal sphincter.
cards.sup: Nerve to levator ani (anterior ramus of S4) and the inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve (S2, S3, S4).
cards.act: Pulls the anorectal junction forwards to maintain the anorectal angle of about 80 to 90 degrees, the principal mechanism of faecal continence; it relaxes to straighten the angle during defaecation.
cards.rel: Lies immediately above the deep part of the external anal sphincter, behind the perineal body and prostate or vagina; the anorectal junction and anal canal pass through the sling.
cards.clin: Palpable as a firm posterior shelf on digital rectal examination. Failure of relaxation (anismus, paradoxical contraction) causes obstructed defaecation; division of the sling in fistula surgery causes faecal incontinence.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle maintains the anorectal angle? A. Puborectalis, the U-shaped sling of levator ani around the anorectal junction.

cards.desc: Terminal branch of the pulmonary trunk carrying deoxygenated blood to the lung of its own side; the only artery in the postnatal body conveying deoxygenated blood.
cards.att: Both arise from the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk at the level of the sternal angle (T4), below and to the left of the aortic arch. The right is longer and passes horizontally behind the ascending aorta and superior vena cava to the right hilum; the shorter left arches over the left main bronchus and is joined to the aortic arch by the ligamentum arteriosum.
cards.sup: Divides at the hilum into lobar and then segmental arteries accompanying the bronchi; the right gives its upper lobe branch before or at the hilum.
cards.rel: At the right hilum the artery lies anterior to the right main bronchus; at the left hilum it lies superior to the left main bronchus (RALS). Pulmonary veins are anterior and inferior to both.
cards.clin: A saddle embolus lodges at the bifurcation and causes acute right heart strain. The left pulmonary artery, ligamentum arteriosum and left recurrent laryngeal nerve are close together, so hoarseness may follow enlargement here.
cards.exam: Q. Give the relation of the pulmonary artery to the bronchus at each hilum. A. Right anterior, left superior (RALS).

cards.desc: Short wide artery, about 5 cm long, carrying deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the two pulmonary arteries; it lies entirely within the pericardium.
cards.att: Arises from the conus arteriosus (infundibulum) of the right ventricle at the level of the left third costal cartilage, guarded by the pulmonary valve; runs upwards, backwards and to the left, and bifurcates below the arch of the aorta at the level of the sternal angle (T4).
cards.sup: Divides into right and left pulmonary arteries; the ligamentum arteriosum connects its bifurcation, or the root of the left pulmonary artery, to the concavity of the aortic arch.
cards.rel: Begins anterior to the ascending aorta and passes to its left side; both vessels share a common sheath of serous pericardium. The left coronary artery and left auricle lie behind and to the left of its origin, the transverse pericardial sinus behind it.
cards.clin: Dilates in pulmonary arterial hypertension. Compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve by a dilated pulmonary trunk or left atrium causes hoarseness (Ortner cardiovocal syndrome). The trunk is banded palliatively in some congenital left to right shunts.
cards.exam: Q. At what vertebral level does the pulmonary trunk bifurcate? A. At the level of the sternal angle, lower border of T4.

cards.desc: The large, dark, lateral part of the lentiform nucleus, lying deep in the cerebral hemisphere lateral to the globus pallidus and internal capsule.
cards.att: Separated from the globus pallidus by the lateral medullary lamina and from the caudate nucleus by the internal capsule, though grey bridges cross it; with the caudate nucleus it constitutes the striatum, receiving corticostriate and nigrostriatal fibres and projecting to the globus pallidus and substantia nigra.
cards.sup: Lateral striate (lenticulostriate) branches of the middle cerebral artery.
cards.act: Component of the basal ganglia motor loop, scaling and selecting voluntary movement and suppressing unwanted movement.
cards.rel: External capsule, claustrum and extreme capsule lie lateral to it, then the insular cortex; the internal capsule and globus pallidus lie medially; the caudate nucleus is superomedial.
cards.clin: The commonest site of hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage, from rupture of Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms on lenticulostriate arteries, giving dense contralateral hemiplegia. It shows characteristic changes in Wilson disease and degenerates with the caudate in Huntington disease.
cards.exam: Q. Which arteries bleed in a typical hypertensive putaminal haemorrhage? A. The lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery.

cards.desc: Short flat quadrilateral muscle of the gluteal region running horizontally from the ischial tuberosity to the intertrochanteric crest.
cards.att: Origin: upper part of the lateral border of the ischial tuberosity. Insertion: quadrate tubercle on the intertrochanteric crest of the femur and the bone just below it.
cards.sup: Nerve to quadratus femoris, L4, L5, S1.
cards.act: Lateral rotation of the thigh at the hip; steadies the femoral head in the acetabulum.
cards.rel: Lies below the inferior gemellus and above the upper border of adductor magnus. Deep to it lie the tendon of obturator externus and the ascending branch of the medial circumflex femoral artery.
cards.clin: Ischiofemoral impingement narrows the space between the ischial tuberosity and lesser trochanter and produces oedema of this muscle on MRI. The medial circumflex femoral artery deep to it is the main supply to the femoral head and is at risk in posterior approaches to the hip.
cards.exam: Q. Which artery lies deep to quadratus femoris? A. The ascending branch of the medial circumflex femoral artery, the chief supply to the head of the femur.

cards.desc: Smaller terminal branch of the brachial artery, running down the lateral side of the forearm to the hand.
cards.att: Begins at the level of the neck of the radius in the cubital fossa, descends on the lateral side of the forearm under cover of brachioradialis, becomes superficial at the wrist lateral to the tendon of flexor carpi radialis, crosses the floor of the anatomical snuffbox, and passes between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous and then between the heads of adductor pollicis to form the deep palmar arch.
cards.sup: Radial recurrent artery, muscular branches, palmar and dorsal carpal branches, superficial palmar branch, princeps pollicis and radialis indicis, ending as the deep palmar arch.
cards.act: Supplies the lateral forearm muscles, the radius, the carpus, the thumb and the radial side of the index finger, and the deep structures of the palm.
cards.rel: In the upper forearm the superficial branch of the radial nerve lies lateral to it beneath brachioradialis. At the wrist it lies on the lower end of the radius between the tendons of brachioradialis and flexor carpi radialis, where the pulse is felt; in the snuffbox it lies on the scaphoid and trapezium.
cards.clin: Site of the radial pulse, of arterial lines and of radial access for coronary angiography; the Allen test confirms an adequate ulnar supply before puncture or before raising a radial forearm free flap. In the snuffbox it lies on the scaphoid, tender there after a fall on the outstretched hand.
cards.exam: Q. Between which two tendons is the radial pulse felt at the wrist? A. Brachioradialis laterally and flexor carpi radialis medially.

cards.desc: First branch of the radial artery, ascending in front of the lateral epicondyle.
cards.att: Arises from the radial artery just below its origin in the cubital fossa, ascends between brachioradialis and brachialis, and anastomoses in front of the lateral epicondyle with the radial collateral branch of the profunda brachii artery.
cards.sup: Muscular branches to brachioradialis, brachialis, supinator and the extensor muscles arising from the lateral epicondyle, and branches to the elbow joint.
cards.act: Supplies the lateral side of the elbow joint and the adjacent muscles.
cards.rel: Lies on supinator and brachialis, deep to brachioradialis; the radial nerve and its division into superficial and deep branches lie immediately lateral to it.
cards.clin: Forms the lateral limb of the anastomosis round the elbow, which preserves forearm blood flow after occlusion of the brachial artery; it may bleed during exposure of the radial nerve in the anterolateral approach to the proximal radius.
cards.exam: Q. With which artery does the radial recurrent artery anastomose? A. The radial collateral branch of the profunda brachii artery.

cards.desc: Lateral bone of the forearm, short above and expanded below, carrying the hand with it in pronation and supination.
cards.att: Upper end: disc-shaped head with a circumferential articular margin for the radial notch of the ulna and the annular ligament, a neck, and the radial tuberosity for biceps brachii. Shaft: anterior and posterior oblique lines, sharp interosseous border, and the insertion of pronator teres at its lateral midpoint. Lower end: styloid process, dorsal (Lister) tubercle, ulnar notch, and a distal articular surface for the scaphoid and lunate; brachioradialis inserts at the base of the styloid.
cards.sup: Nutrient artery from the anterior interosseous artery; the head is supplied by the radial recurrent and periarticular vessels.
cards.act: Rotates about the ulna in pronation and supination and transmits the load of the hand to the humerus, mainly through the radiocarpal joint.
cards.rel: Supinator wraps its upper third and is pierced by the deep branch of the radial nerve. Extensor pollicis longus turns round Lister's tubercle. The radial artery lies on the lower anterior surface, lateral to flexor carpi radialis, where the pulse is felt.
cards.clin: Colles fracture is a fracture of the distal radius within 2.5 cm of the wrist with dorsal displacement and the dinner fork deformity, Smith fracture is the volar equivalent. Galeazzi fracture is a distal radial shaft fracture with dislocation of the distal radio-ulnar joint. In a child, sudden traction on the extended pronated forearm slips the radial head from the annular ligament, a pulled elbow.
cards.exam: Q. What deformity does a Colles fracture produce and where is the radial styloid normally? A. The dinner fork deformity, with the radial styloid normally about 1 cm distal to the ulnar styloid, a relationship lost in the fracture.

cards.desc: The terminal 12 cm of the large intestine, continuing the sigmoid colon in front of the third sacral vertebra and ending at the anorectal junction.
cards.att: Follows the curve of the sacrum and coccyx (sacral flexure), then turns sharply backwards at the anorectal junction 2 to 3 cm in front of and below the tip of the coccyx as it pierces the pelvic diaphragm. It has no mesentery, taeniae coli, sacculations or appendices epiploicae; three transverse rectal folds (valves of Houston) indent the lumen. Peritoneum covers the front and sides of the upper third, the front only of the middle third, and none of the lower third.
cards.sup: Arteries: superior rectal from the inferior mesenteric, middle rectal from the internal iliac and inferior rectal from the internal pudendal. Veins: superior rectal to the portal system, middle and inferior rectal to the systemic system. Lymphatics: from the upper part along the superior rectal vessels to inferior mesenteric nodes, from the lower part to internal iliac nodes. Nerves: sympathetic from the inferior hypogastric plexus, parasympathetic from the pelvic splanchnic nerves S2, S3 and S4.
cards.act: Stores faeces; distension initiates the defaecation reflex with reflex relaxation of the internal anal sphincter.
cards.rel: Behind lie the sacrum, coccyx, piriformis, the sacral plexus and the median sacral vessels; in front in the male the rectovesical pouch, base of the bladder, seminal vesicles, ductus deferens and prostate; in the female the rectouterine pouch of Douglas, vagina and cervix. The ampulla rests on the levator ani.
cards.clin: The prostate, cervix and pouch of Douglas are palpable on digital rectal examination, so pelvic abscess and peritoneal deposits can be felt. Rectal carcinoma is staged by the peritoneal reflection and the mesorectal fascia; total mesorectal excision follows this plane while preserving the hypogastric nerves to avoid impotence.
cards.exam: Q. At what level does the rectum begin and end? A. It begins in front of the third sacral vertebra and ends at the anorectal junction, 2 to 3 cm in front of and below the tip of the coccyx.

cards.desc: Triangular suboccipital muscle forming the medial boundary of the suboccipital triangle.
cards.att: Origin: spinous process of the axis. Insertion: lateral part of the inferior nuchal line of the occipital bone and the bone below it.
cards.sup: Suboccipital nerve, the posterior ramus of C1.
cards.act: Extends the head and rotates the face to the same side.
cards.rel: Medial boundary of the suboccipital triangle, whose floor holds the posterior arch of the atlas, the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane, the third part of the vertebral artery and the suboccipital venous plexus. Semispinalis capitis covers it.
cards.clin: Together with the other suboccipital muscles it is a source of tenderness in cervicogenic headache; the triangle it bounds is the site of vertebral artery exposure and of the C1 nerve.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve supplies all four suboccipital muscles? A. The suboccipital nerve, the posterior ramus of C1.

cards.desc: Smallest suboccipital muscle, lying medial to rectus capitis posterior major and outside the suboccipital triangle.
cards.att: Origin: posterior tubercle of the posterior arch of the atlas. Insertion: medial part of the inferior nuchal line of the occipital bone and the area between it and the foramen magnum.
cards.sup: Suboccipital nerve, the posterior ramus of C1.
cards.act: Extends the head at the atlanto-occipital joint; rich in muscle spindles, it acts largely in proprioceptive control of head position.
cards.rel: Lies deep to semispinalis capitis, medial to rectus capitis posterior major; its deep surface is connected to the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane and the spinal dura by the myodural bridge.
cards.clin: The myodural bridge links this muscle to the cervical dura and is implicated in cervicogenic headache and in dural tension after whiplash injury.
cards.exam: Q. Which suboccipital muscle arises from the posterior tubercle of the atlas? A. Rectus capitis posterior minor.

cards.desc: Fusiform superficial head of quadriceps femoris running straight down the front of the thigh, the only part crossing both hip and knee.
cards.att: Origin: straight head from the anterior inferior iliac spine, reflected head from a groove above the acetabulum on the ilium. Insertion: base of the patella through the quadriceps tendon, and through the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity.
cards.sup: Femoral nerve, L2, L3, L4.
cards.act: Extends the leg at the knee and flexes the thigh at the hip; the two actions are most effective together in kicking.
cards.rel: Lies between tensor fasciae latae and sartorius, superficial to vastus intermedius. The descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery and the nerve to vastus intermedius lie deep to it.
cards.clin: Avulsion of the anterior inferior iliac spine occurs in adolescent sprinters and footballers. Proximal rectus femoris strain is a common kicking injury, and the muscle is tested by Ely's test for tightness.
cards.exam: Q. Which part of quadriceps femoris crosses two joints, and from where does it arise? A. Rectus femoris, from the anterior inferior iliac spine and a groove above the acetabulum.

cards.desc: Large paired lateral visceral branches of the abdominal aorta, arising at the L1 to L2 level just below the superior mesenteric artery and passing laterally to the renal hilum.
cards.att: Arise from the sides of the aorta below the superior mesenteric artery; each divides near the hilum into an anterior and a posterior division which give five segmental arteries. The right artery is longer and passes behind the inferior vena cava; the left is shorter and slightly higher.
cards.sup: Five segmental arteries (apical, upper, middle and lower from the anterior division, posterior from the posterior division), the inferior suprarenal artery and ureteric branches.
cards.act: Supplies the kidney, the lower part of the suprarenal gland and the upper ureter; the kidneys receive about one fifth of the cardiac output.
cards.rel: At the hilum, from front to back, lie the renal vein, the renal artery and the renal pelvis. The right artery passes behind the inferior vena cava, and the left renal vein crosses in front of the aorta above the left artery.
cards.clin: The segmental arteries are end arteries, so occlusion of one infarcts a whole segment; the relatively avascular plane between the anterior and posterior territories, Brodel's bloodless line, is used for nephrolithotomy. Accessory renal arteries are common, and atherosclerotic stenosis of the main artery causes renovascular hypertension with an epigastric bruit.
cards.exam: Q. Arrange the structures at the renal hilum from anterior to posterior. A. Renal vein, renal artery, renal pelvis.

cards.desc: Paired veins draining the kidneys into the inferior vena cava at the L1 to L2 level, lying anterior to the renal arteries.
cards.att: Formed from segmental veins at the hilum, each passes medially in front of the renal artery. The left renal vein is about three times longer and crosses in front of the aorta in the angle between it and the superior mesenteric artery; the short right vein enters the inferior vena cava directly.
cards.sup: The left receives the left suprarenal, left gonadal and left inferior phrenic veins and communicates with the ascending lumbar vein; the right usually has no named tributaries.
cards.act: Venous drainage of the kidney; unlike the segmental arteries, the intrarenal veins anastomose freely, so no venous segments exist.
cards.rel: Both lie anterior to the renal arteries; the right lies behind the second part of the duodenum and head of pancreas, the left behind the body of the pancreas and splenic vein and within the aortomesenteric angle.
cards.clin: Nutcracker syndrome: compression of the left renal vein between the aorta and superior mesenteric artery causes haematuria, left flank pain and, in men, a left varicocele. A left varicocele of recent onset also raises suspicion of a renal tumour obstructing or invading the vein.
cards.exam: Q. Why is a varicocele commoner on the left side? A. The left testicular vein drains at a right angle into the left renal vein, which may be compressed in the aortomesenteric angle.

cards.desc: Flat rhomboidal muscle of the back that slings the medial border of the scapula to the upper thoracic spines.
cards.att: Origin: spinous processes of T2 to T5 and the intervening supraspinous ligaments. Insertion: medial border of the scapula between the root of the spine and the inferior angle.
cards.sup: Dorsal scapular nerve (C4, C5).
cards.act: Retracts the scapula and rotates it so the glenoid cavity faces downwards; steadies the scapula against the thoracic wall.
cards.rel: Deep to trapezius, superficial to erector spinae and the serratus posterior superior. Rhomboid minor lies immediately above it, levator scapulae above that.
cards.clin: Injury to the dorsal scapular nerve, or its entrapment as it pierces scalenus medius, lets the scapula drift laterally and produces a mild winging that increases when the arm is pushed forwards against resistance. The muscle is a landmark for the triangle of auscultation at its lower lateral border.
cards.exam: Q. Nerve supply of the rhomboids? A. Dorsal scapular nerve (C4, C5), arising from the anterior ramus (root) of C5 of the brachial plexus, before the trunks are formed.

cards.desc: Narrow band above rhomboid major running from the lower ligamentum nuchae to the root of the spine of the scapula.
cards.att: Origin: lower part of the ligamentum nuchae and the spinous processes of C7 and T1. Insertion: medial border of the scapula opposite the root of the spine.
cards.sup: Dorsal scapular nerve (C4, C5).
cards.act: Retracts and stabilises the scapula and assists downward rotation of the glenoid.
cards.rel: Deep to trapezius, above rhomboid major and below the insertion of levator scapulae. The dorsal scapular nerve and the deep branch of the transverse cervical artery run along its deep surface at the medial border of the scapula.
cards.clin: The neurovascular bundle on its deep surface is at risk in medial parascapular approaches, so incisions are kept close to the medial border of the scapula.
cards.exam: Q. Which two rhomboid attachments distinguish minor from major? A. Minor arises from ligamentum nuchae and C7 to T1 and inserts at the root of the spine; major arises from T2 to T5 and inserts below the root of the spine.

cards.desc: Large triangular bone formed by fusion of the five sacral vertebrae, wedged between the two hip bones to complete the posterior wall of the pelvis.
cards.att: Base above bears the promontory, the superior articular processes for L5 and the alae; the apex below articulates with the coccyx. Articulations: L5 above, coccyx below, and the ilium on each side at the auricular surface. Features: four pairs of anterior and posterior sacral foramina, median, intermediate and lateral sacral crests, sacral canal, sacral hiatus and cornua.
cards.act: Transmits body weight from the vertebral column to the pelvic girdle and forms the posterior wall of the pelvic cavity; anchors the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments.
cards.rel: Anteriorly the sigmoid colon, rectum, superior rectal vessels and the sympathetic trunks with the median sacral vessels; the sacral plexus lies on piriformis in front of the anterior foramina. The dural sac ends at the level of S2.
cards.clin: Caudal epidural anaesthesia is given through the sacral hiatus between the sacral cornua. The sacral promontory is the landmark for measuring the obstetric conjugate and for pelvic inlet assessment. Sacralisation of L5 and lumbarisation of S1 are common variants.
cards.exam: Q. At what vertebral level does the dural sac end in the adult? A. The lower border of S2, marked on the sacrum.

cards.desc: Slender longitudinal pharyngeal muscle descending from the auditory tube, raising the salpingopharyngeal fold of mucosa.
cards.att: Origin: inferior part of the cartilage of the pharyngotympanic (auditory) tube near its pharyngeal opening. Insertion: blends with palatopharyngeus in the lateral wall of the pharynx.
cards.sup: Pharyngeal plexus, motor fibres of the vagus carrying the cranial accessory component.
cards.act: Elevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing and helps open the auditory tube to equalise middle ear pressure.
cards.rel: Its mucosal fold runs down from the torus tubarius on the lateral nasopharyngeal wall, in front of the pharyngeal recess (fossa of Rosenmuller); levator and tensor veli palatini are related to the tube above.
cards.clin: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma typically arises in the fossa of Rosenmuller behind this fold and presents with unilateral serous otitis media from tubal obstruction and a neck node.
cards.exam: Q. Which fold does salpingopharyngeus raise, and what lies behind it? A. The salpingopharyngeal fold, with the pharyngeal recess (fossa of Rosenmuller) behind it.

cards.desc: Long narrow strap muscle, the longest in the body, crossing the front of the thigh obliquely from lateral above to medial below.
cards.att: Origin: anterior superior iliac spine and the upper half of the notch below it. Insertion: upper part of the medial surface of the tibia, in front of gracilis and semitendinosus, forming the pes anserinus.
cards.sup: Femoral nerve, L2, L3.
cards.act: Flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the thigh at the hip and flexes the leg at the knee, the combination used to sit cross-legged.
cards.rel: Forms the lateral boundary of the femoral triangle and then the roof of the adductor canal, under which lie the femoral vessels, saphenous nerve and nerve to vastus medialis.
cards.clin: A key surgical landmark: the adductor canal is opened deep to it, and the saphenous nerve becomes subcutaneous at its posterior border. It is used as a muscle flap to cover groin vessels.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle forms the roof of the adductor canal? A. Sartorius, with the subsartorial fascia beneath it.

cards.desc: Key landmark muscle of the root of the neck, descending from the cervical transverse processes to the first rib.
cards.att: Origin: anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of the third to sixth cervical vertebrae. Insertion: scalene tubercle on the inner border of the upper surface of the first rib.
cards.sup: Anterior rami of C4, C5 and C6.
cards.act: Elevates the first rib in forced inspiration; with the first rib fixed it bends the neck laterally to the same side, and the two muscles acting together flex the neck forwards.
cards.rel: The phrenic nerve descends on its anterior surface from lateral to medial, and the subclavian vein, transverse cervical and suprascapular arteries pass in front of it. The subclavian artery and the trunks of the brachial plexus pass behind it in the interscalene interval; the cervical pleura and the thoracic duct on the left lie at its lower medial edge.
cards.clin: The muscle separates the subclavian vein in front from the artery behind, which is why a supraclavicular subclavian vein puncture spares the artery. Compression in the interscalene interval produces thoracic outlet syndrome, and the interscalene block is placed in this groove.
cards.exam: Q. What structure lies on the anterior surface of scalenus anterior? A. The phrenic nerve.

cards.desc: The largest scalene muscle, forming the posterior wall of the interscalene interval.
cards.att: Origin: posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of the lower six cervical vertebrae, often extending to the atlas and axis. Insertion: upper surface of the first rib behind the subclavian groove, between the tubercle and the groove.
cards.sup: Anterior rami of the cervical spinal nerves, C3 to C8.
cards.act: Elevates the first rib; bends the neck laterally to the same side.
cards.rel: The subclavian artery and the roots and trunks of the brachial plexus emerge between it and scalenus anterior. The dorsal scapular and long thoracic nerves pierce it, and the upper part of its lateral surface lies in the floor of the posterior triangle.
cards.clin: A cervical rib or a fibrous band from it narrows the interscalene interval and compresses the lower trunk of the brachial plexus, giving wasting of the small muscles of the hand and pain along the medial forearm.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerves pierce scalenus medius? A. The dorsal scapular nerve and the long thoracic nerve.

cards.desc: Largest bone of the proximal carpal row, boat-shaped and set obliquely, bridging both carpal rows on the radial side of the wrist.
cards.att: Articulates with five bones: the radius proximally, the lunate medially, the capitate distomedially, and the trapezium and trapezoid distally. Its tubercle projects palmarly and gives attachment to the flexor retinaculum and a slip of abductor pollicis brevis; the scapholunate and radioscaphocapitate ligaments stabilise it.
cards.sup: Blood supply enters mainly through the dorsal ridge from the dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery and runs in a retrograde direction to supply the proximal pole.
cards.rel: Forms the floor of the anatomical snuffbox, where the radial artery crosses it; its tubercle forms the lateral boundary of the carpal tunnel. It is palpable in the snuffbox and just distal to the radial styloid.
cards.clin: Fracture of the waist after a fall on the outstretched hand is the commonest carpal fracture, giving tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. Because the blood supply is retrograde, the proximal fragment risks avascular necrosis and non-union. Initial radiographs are often normal, so a clinically suspected scaphoid fracture is immobilised and reimaged, or assessed by MRI.
cards.exam: Q. Why does a fracture of the waist of the scaphoid cause avascular necrosis of the proximal fragment? A. The blood supply enters distally at the dorsal ridge and runs retrograde, so a waist fracture cuts off the proximal pole.

cards.desc: Flat triangular bone on the posterolateral thoracic wall overlying ribs 2 to 7, connected to the trunk skeleton only through the clavicle.
cards.att: Costal surface (subscapular fossa) and dorsal surface divided by the spine into supraspinous and infraspinous fossae; acromion, coracoid process, glenoid cavity with supraglenoid and infraglenoid tubercles; superior, medial and lateral borders; superior, inferior and lateral angles; suprascapular notch. Articulates with the head of the humerus at the glenohumeral joint and with the clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint.
cards.act: Provides a mobile base for the upper limb and attachment for seventeen muscles; upward rotation of the scapula contributes about 60 of the 180 degrees of arm elevation (scapulohumeral rhythm 2:1).
cards.rel: Subscapularis lines the costal surface, supraspinatus and infraspinatus fill the dorsal fossae, and serratus anterior inserts along the costal aspect of the medial border. The suprascapular nerve passes through the suprascapular notch deep to the superior transverse scapular ligament while the suprascapular artery passes above the ligament.
