cards.clin: Winging of the scapula follows long thoracic nerve injury paralysing serratus anterior. The inferior angle lies at the level of the T7 spine and is a standard surface landmark in chest examination.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve passes through the suprascapular notch beneath the superior transverse scapular ligament? A. The suprascapular nerve; the suprascapular artery passes above the ligament.

cards.desc: Opaque, dense fibrous coat forming the posterior five-sixths of the outer tunic of the eyeball.
cards.att: Continuous in front with the cornea at the corneoscleral junction (limbus) and behind with the dural sheath of the optic nerve, where it is perforated as the lamina cribrosa. Gives insertion to the four recti and two oblique muscles; pierced by the ciliary vessels and nerves and by the vorticose veins.
cards.sup: Anterior and posterior ciliary arteries; sensory supply from the long and short ciliary nerves (V1).
cards.act: Maintains the shape of the globe, resists intraocular pressure, and provides a firm base for the pull of the extraocular muscles.
cards.rel: Covered in front by bulbar conjunctiva and episclera within the fascial sheath of the eyeball; the choroid lies internal to it with the suprachoroid lamina between.
cards.clin: Thin sclera showing the underlying choroid gives blue sclerae in osteogenesis imperfecta. Bilirubin binds the elastic tissue of the sclera, so scleral icterus is an early sign of jaundice. Scleritis is deep and painful, unlike episcleritis.
cards.exam: Q. Which structures pierce the sclera? A. The optic nerve at the lamina cribrosa, the ciliary arteries and nerves, and the four vorticose veins.

cards.desc: Hyaline cartilage bar joining the 2nd rib to the sternum exactly at the manubriosternal joint, the sternal angle.
cards.att: Articulates laterally with the 2nd rib at the costochondral junction and medially by a synovial joint that straddles the sternal angle, taking a demifacet from the manubrium and one from the body; an intra-articular ligament divides the joint cavity in two.
cards.sup: Perichondrial branches of the internal thoracic artery.
cards.act: Transmits the movement of the 2nd rib to the sternum in inspiration.
cards.rel: The internal thoracic vessels lie behind it about 1 cm from the sternal border; the arch of the aorta lies deep to the manubrium at this level.
cards.clin: The palpable sternal angle identifies this cartilage and therefore the 2nd rib, so all ribs and intercostal spaces are counted from here. Classical teaching places needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax in the 2nd intercostal space in the midclavicular line, just below this cartilage.
cards.exam: Q. Which costal cartilage articulates at the sternal angle? A. The 2nd, taking a demifacet from both the manubrium and the body of the sternum.

cards.desc: The second lumbar vertebra, at the level where the spinal cord ends in the adult.
cards.att: Typical lumbar form: kidney-shaped body, triangular vertebral foramen, hatchet-shaped spine, mamillary and accessory processes. Articulates with L1 above and L3 below.
cards.sup: Second lumbar arteries from the abdominal aorta; internal and external vertebral venous plexuses.
cards.rel: The cisterna chyli lies behind and to the right of the aorta at the L1/L2 level. Psoas major arises from the body and transverse process; the sympathetic trunk descends on the anterolateral surface.
cards.clin: The conus medullaris ends at the L1/L2 disc, so all lumbar punctures are placed below the body of L2. The lowest preganglionic sympathetic outflow leaves at L2.
cards.exam: Q. What is the lowest safe upper limit for lumbar puncture in an adult? A. Below the body of L2, as the cord ends at L1/L2.

cards.desc: Longest of the metacarpals, forming the skeleton of the palm proximal to the index finger.
cards.att: Base, shaft and head; the deeply notched base articulates chiefly with the trapezoid and also with the trapezium, capitate and the third metacarpal, while the head articulates with the proximal phalanx of the index finger. Extensor carpi radialis longus inserts on the dorsal surface of the base and flexor carpi radialis on its palmar surface; the first and second dorsal interossei and the first palmar interosseous arise from the shaft.
cards.act: With the third metacarpal it forms the fixed longitudinal axis of the hand, about which the mobile first, fourth and fifth rays move during grip.
cards.rel: Extensor tendons of the index finger lie dorsally; the long flexor tendons and the first lumbrical lie palmar to it. The radial artery reaches the palm by passing between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous in the space between the first and second metacarpals.
cards.clin: Because the second ray is part of the fixed unit of the hand, fractures here tolerate far less angulation than fifth metacarpal (boxer's) fractures and displaced fractures usually require fixation. The dorsal base is the site of avulsion of extensor carpi radialis longus.
cards.exam: Q. Where does extensor carpi radialis longus insert? A. On the dorsal aspect of the base of the second metacarpal.

cards.desc: Longest metatarsal, its base recessed between the cuneiforms so that it forms the rigid central strut of the forefoot.
cards.att: Base is wedged in a mortise formed by the medial, intermediate and lateral cuneiforms, articulating chiefly with the intermediate cuneiform and also with the first and third metatarsals; head articulates with the proximal phalanx of the second toe. The oblique head of adductor hallucis arises from the bases of the second to fourth metatarsals; a slip of tibialis posterior reaches its base, and the Lisfranc ligament runs from the medial cuneiform to its base.
cards.act: Transmits load through the central forefoot and, being fixed in its mortise, acts as the rigid keystone of the transverse tarsal arch.
cards.rel: Dorsalis pedis artery passes between the bases of the first and second metatarsals to become the plantar arch; deep peroneal nerve accompanies it dorsally; interossei fill the spaces on either side.
cards.clin: Classic site of the march or stress fracture of the shaft, from repeated loading in soldiers and runners, with normal early X-rays and later callus. Disruption of the Lisfranc ligament with widening between the first and second metatarsal bases is the key sign of a tarsometatarsal fracture dislocation.
cards.exam: Q. Which metatarsal is the commonest site of a march fracture and why? A. The second, because its base is locked between the cuneiforms and it cannot yield to repetitive load.

cards.desc: Second rib, about twice as long as the first but similar in curvature, joining the sternum at the level of the sternal angle.
cards.att: Head has two facets for the body of T1 and the body of T2 with the intervening disc; the tubercle articulates with the transverse process of T2. The outer surface bears a rough tuberosity for the first two digitations of serratus anterior; scalenus posterior attaches near the tubercle and the costal groove is shallow.
cards.sup: Second posterior intercostal artery, usually from the supreme intercostal artery of the costocervical trunk; the 2nd intercostal nerve gives off the intercostobrachial nerve.
cards.act: Elevation in inspiration; provides the palpable reference for counting the chest wall.
cards.rel: Lies deep to pectoralis major and the clavipectoral region; parietal pleura and the upper lobe of the lung lie internally.
cards.clin: The 2nd rib is found by sliding laterally from the sternal angle, and the space below it is the 2nd intercostal space. The intercostobrachial nerve from the 2nd intercostal nerve supplies the floor of the axilla and medial arm, and is often divided in axillary clearance, leaving numbness there.
cards.exam: Q. How do you identify the 2nd rib clinically? A. Palpate the sternal angle and move laterally; the rib articulating there is the 2nd.

cards.desc: Deep medial hamstring, flattened and membranous in its upper half, lying deep to semitendinosus on the back of the thigh.
cards.att: Origin: upper lateral impression on the ischial tuberosity, by a long flat membranous tendon. Insertion: groove on the posterior aspect of the medial condyle of the tibia, with expansions forming the oblique popliteal ligament and the fascia over popliteus.
cards.sup: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve, L5, S1, S2.
cards.act: Extends the thigh at the hip, flexes the leg at the knee and medially rotates the flexed leg.
cards.rel: Forms the superomedial boundary of the popliteal fossa with semitendinosus. Bursae separate it from the medial head of gastrocnemius and from the medial tibial condyle.
cards.clin: The semimembranosus and medial gastrocnemius bursa is the usual site of a popliteal (Baker's) cyst, which may communicate with the knee joint. Proximal hamstring avulsion from the ischial tuberosity occurs in sprinters and hurdlers.
cards.exam: Q. Which hamstring tendon gives rise to the oblique popliteal ligament? A. Semimembranosus, by an expansion passing upwards and laterally across the back of the knee.

cards.desc: Coiled sacculated gland about 5 cm long lying obliquely on the base of the bladder, lateral to the ampulla of the ductus deferens and in front of the rectum.
cards.att: Upper end is covered by peritoneum of the rectovesical pouch; its duct joins the ampulla of the ductus deferens to form the ejaculatory duct, which pierces the prostate and opens on the seminal colliculus.
cards.sup: Arteries: inferior vesical and middle rectal. Veins to the vesical and prostatic plexuses. Nerves from the inferior hypogastric plexus. Lymph to the internal iliac nodes.
cards.act: Secretes viscous alkaline fructose-rich fluid, about 70 per cent of the ejaculate volume; it does not store spermatozoa despite the name.
cards.rel: Base of bladder and terminal ureter above and medially, ampulla of the vas medially, rectum behind separated by rectovesical fascia, prostate below.
cards.clin: Not normally palpable, but felt on digital rectal examination when inflamed or infiltrated by prostate cancer. Absence of the vas and seminal vesicles with low-volume fructose-negative semen suggests cystic fibrosis related congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens.
cards.exam: Q. Does the seminal vesicle store sperm? A. No, it secretes fructose-rich alkaline fluid; sperm are stored in the tail of the epididymis.

cards.desc: Thick, powerful muscle of the back of the neck lying deep to splenius and trapezius, running to the occipital bone.
cards.att: Origin: transverse processes of the upper six thoracic vertebrae and the articular processes of the lower four cervical vertebrae. Insertion: occipital bone between the superior and inferior nuchal lines, close to the midline.
cards.sup: Posterior rami of the cervical spinal nerves, chiefly the greater occipital nerve (C2) and C3.
cards.act: Extends the head, the chief extensor of the head and neck; acting on one side it bends the head to that side with slight rotation.
cards.rel: Covers the suboccipital triangle and its contents; deep to trapezius, splenius capitis and longissimus capitis. Its medial part, the biventer cervicis, has a tendinous intersection.
cards.clin: The greater occipital nerve pierces it before piercing trapezius, so entrapment here causes occipital neuralgia, with pain and paraesthesia over the back of the scalp.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve pierces semispinalis capitis? A. The greater occipital nerve, the posterior ramus of C2.

cards.desc: Thin fascicular muscle of the transversospinalis group in the upper back, spanning about five or six vertebral segments.
cards.att: Origin: transverse processes of the sixth to tenth thoracic vertebrae. Insertion: spinous processes of the upper four thoracic and lower two cervical vertebrae, roughly C6 to T4.
cards.sup: Dorsal rami of the thoracic spinal nerves.
cards.act: Bilaterally extends the thoracic and cervical vertebral column; unilaterally rotates the trunk to the opposite side.
cards.rel: Deep to erector spinae and serratus posterior superior, superficial to multifidus and rotatores; continuous above with semispinalis cervicis and capitis.
cards.clin: Part of the deep extensor sleeve whose atrophy and fatty infiltration on MRI correlates with chronic neck and upper back pain and with postural kyphosis.
cards.exam: Q. Name the three muscles of the transversospinalis group from superficial to deep. A. Semispinalis, multifidus, rotatores.

cards.desc: Superficial medial hamstring with a fusiform belly and a long cord-like tendon occupying the lower half of the muscle.
cards.att: Origin: inferomedial impression on the ischial tuberosity, by a tendon common with the long head of biceps femoris. Insertion: upper part of the medial surface of the tibia behind sartorius and below gracilis, forming the pes anserinus.
cards.sup: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve, L5, S1, S2.
cards.act: Extends the thigh at the hip, flexes the leg at the knee and medially rotates the flexed leg.
cards.rel: Lies superficial to semimembranosus and forms the superomedial boundary of the popliteal fossa; a tendinous intersection crosses its belly.
cards.clin: Its tendon, with gracilis, is the standard hamstring autograft for anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. Pes anserine bursitis causes medial knee pain about 5 cm below the joint line.
cards.exam: Q. Which three tendons form the pes anserinus? A. Sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus, in that order from front to back.

cards.desc: The medial cusp of the tricuspid valve, attached along the interventricular septum, guarding the right atrioventricular orifice.
cards.att: Attached to the membranous and muscular interventricular septum and to the medial part of the annulus; receives chordae directly from the septum and from the small septal (medial) papillary muscle, the muscle of Lancisi. Its annular attachment lies more apically than that of the anterior mitral leaflet, creating the atrioventricular septum.
cards.act: Coapts with the anterior and posterior cusps in systole to close the right atrioventricular orifice.
cards.rel: Its annular attachment forms the anterior boundary of the triangle of Koch, with the tendon of Todaro and the orifice of the coronary sinus; the atrioventricular node lies within this triangle. The membranous septum lies immediately deep to it.
cards.clin: Offset of the septal leaflet relative to the anterior mitral leaflet is the echocardiographic marker of Ebstein anomaly. Catheter ablation or valve surgery near the septal leaflet risks complete heart block from injury to the atrioventricular node.
cards.exam: Q. Which structures bound the triangle of Koch? A. The septal leaflet attachment of the tricuspid valve, the tendon of Todaro and the ostium of the coronary sinus.

cards.desc: Quadrangular plate of hyaline cartilage forming the anterior part of the nasal septum.
cards.att: Attached posterosuperiorly to the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid, posteroinferiorly to the vomer and the nasal crests of the maxillae and palatine bones, and anteriorly to the internal aspect of the nasal bones and the medial crura of the major alar cartilages.
cards.act: Supports the nasal dorsum and tip and divides the anterior nasal cavity into two passages.
cards.rel: Covered on both sides by mucoperichondrium; its anteroinferior part underlies Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus) of the vestibule.
cards.clin: Deviated nasal septum obstructs airflow and is corrected by septoplasty. A septal haematoma after trauma must be drained urgently: pressure necrosis of the cartilage causes a saddle nose deformity. Most epistaxis arises from Little's area on the anterior septum.
cards.exam: Q. Name the arteries anastomosing in Little's area. A. Anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine and septal branch of the superior labial artery.

cards.desc: The midline telencephalic partition between the two lateral ventricles, comprising the thin two-layered septum pellucidum above and the septal nuclei below and in front.
cards.att: Bounded above by the corpus callosum and below by the fornix; the septal nuclei connect with the hippocampus through the fornix, with the amygdala through the stria terminalis and diagonal band, and with the habenula through the stria medullaris thalami.
cards.act: Part of the limbic system, involved in emotional and autonomic responses, reward and the hippocampal theta rhythm.
cards.rel: Forms the medial wall of the frontal horn and body of each lateral ventricle; the interventricular foramina lie at its posteroinferior angle behind the columns of the fornix.
cards.clin: A persistent cavum septi pellucidi between the two laminae is a normal variant and is frequent in boxers with chronic traumatic encephalopathy. The septum pellucidum is absent in septo-optic dysplasia, with optic nerve hypoplasia and hypopituitarism.
cards.exam: Q. What forms the roof and floor of the septum pellucidum? A. The corpus callosum above and the body and columns of the fornix below.

cards.desc: Large fan-shaped muscle covering the lateral thoracic wall, forming the medial wall of the axilla.
cards.att: Origin: fleshy digitations from the outer surfaces of the upper eight ribs. Insertion: costal surface of the medial border of the scapula, the bulk of it concentrated at the inferior angle.
cards.sup: Long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7).
cards.act: Protracts the scapula and holds it against the chest wall; the lower fibres rotate the scapula upwards, which is essential for raising the arm above the head.
cards.rel: Forms the medial wall of the axilla; the long thoracic nerve descends on its outer surface, the lateral thoracic artery along its anterior border. Deep to it lie the ribs and external intercostals.
cards.clin: Damage to the long thoracic nerve during axillary node clearance, mastectomy or by a blow to the side of the chest causes winging of the scapula and inability to raise the arm above 90 degrees. Test by pushing against a wall.
cards.exam: Q. What deformity follows long thoracic nerve palsy and why? A. Winging of the scapula, because paralysed serratus anterior can no longer hold the medial border against the chest wall or rotate the scapula upwards.

cards.desc: Thin quadrilateral muscle of the intermediate layer of back muscles, sloping upwards and laterally from the thoracolumbar junction to the lower ribs.
cards.att: Origin: spinous processes of the eleventh and twelfth thoracic and first and second lumbar vertebrae and their supraspinous ligaments, through the thoracolumbar fascia. Insertion: by four slips into the inferior borders of the lower four ribs, lateral to their angles.
cards.sup: Ventral rami of the ninth to twelfth thoracic spinal nerves, that is the lower intercostal and subcostal nerves.
cards.act: Draws the lower ribs downwards and backwards, traditionally described as fixing them against the pull of the diaphragm; its true respiratory role is minor and it is largely proprioceptive.
cards.rel: Deep to latissimus dorsi, superficial to the erector spinae and the thoracolumbar fascia.
cards.clin: Its supply by ventral rami confirms it as a muscle of the thoracic wall migrated backwards, not a true muscle of the back; the same is true of serratus posterior superior.
cards.exam: Q. What is the nerve supply of serratus posterior inferior? A. Ventral rami of T9 to T12.

cards.desc: Thin quadrilateral muscle of the intermediate layer of back muscles, passing downwards and laterally from the cervicothoracic spines to the upper ribs.
cards.att: Origin: lower part of the ligamentum nuchae and the spinous processes of the seventh cervical to third thoracic vertebrae with their supraspinous ligaments. Insertion: by four slips into the upper borders of the second to fifth ribs, lateral to their angles.
cards.sup: Ventral rami of the second to fifth thoracic spinal nerves, that is the upper intercostal nerves.
cards.act: Elevates the second to fifth ribs, assisting inspiration.
cards.rel: Deep to the rhomboids and trapezius, superficial to the erector spinae and the splenius muscles.
cards.clin: Divided in posterolateral thoracotomy approaches; a recognised though uncommon source of deep interscapular myofascial pain referred to the shoulder and arm.
cards.exam: Q. Which ribs does serratus posterior superior insert into? A. The second to fifth ribs, lateral to their angles.

cards.desc: Two constant sesamoid bones, medial and lateral, embedded in the tendons of flexor hallucis brevis beneath the head of the first metatarsal.
cards.att: Each lies in one head of flexor hallucis brevis and is bound to the base of the proximal phalanx of the hallux by the plantar plate and to its fellow by the intersesamoid ligament; the crista on the under surface of the first metatarsal head separates their grooved articular facets. Inconstant sesamoids also occur under the heads of the other metatarsals and in the tendons of peroneus longus and tibialis posterior.
cards.act: Protect the tendon of flexor hallucis longus, which passes in the groove between them, absorb weight under the first metatarsal head and increase the lever arm of flexor hallucis brevis.
cards.rel: Flexor hallucis longus tendon lies between them; the medial sesamoid is related to abductor hallucis and the lateral to adductor hallucis; both articulate with the plantar surface of the first metatarsal head.
cards.clin: Sesamoiditis, stress fracture and osteonecrosis cause pain under the first metatarsal head. A bipartite medial sesamoid is a common variant misread as a fracture; in hallux valgus the sesamoids stay tethered to the adductor and appear to displace laterally on X-ray.
cards.exam: Q. Which tendon runs between the two hallucal sesamoids? A. Flexor hallucis longus.

cards.k: set of dorsal interossei of hand
cards.desc: Four bipennate muscles filling the intervals between the metacarpals on the dorsum of the hand.
cards.att: Origin: each by two heads from the adjacent sides of the two metacarpals bounding its space. Insertion: base of the proximal phalanx and the dorsal extensor expansion of the index (radial side), middle (both sides) and ring (ulnar side) fingers.
cards.sup: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8, T1).
cards.act: Abduct the fingers away from the axis of the middle finger; with the lumbricals they flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints. Mnemonic DAB, dorsals abduct.
cards.rel: Deeper than the palmar interossei when viewed from the front; the deep branch of the ulnar nerve and deep palmar arch cross the interossei of the palm. The first dorsal interosseous forms the bulk of the thumb web space.
cards.clin: Wasting of the first dorsal interosseous gives the guttered web space that is the earliest visible sign of ulnar nerve palsy. Card test: the patient cannot hold a card between adducted fingers when the interossei are paralysed.
cards.exam: Q. Nerve supply and action of the dorsal interossei? A. Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8, T1); they abduct the fingers from the midline of the middle finger.

cards.desc: Group of three or four small arteries running distally in the intermetacarpal spaces on the back of the hand.
cards.att: Arise from the dorsal carpal arch, formed by the dorsal carpal branches of the radial and ulnar arteries, and run distally on the dorsal interossei; the first usually comes directly from the radial artery before it dives between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous. Each divides at the web space into two dorsal digital arteries.
cards.sup: Dorsal digital arteries to the adjacent sides of the fingers, and communicating branches that receive the perforating branches of the deep palmar arch and the palmar metacarpal arteries.
cards.act: Supply the dorsum of the hand and the dorsal aspect of the proximal segments of the fingers; the distal segments and nail beds are supplied by the palmar digital arteries.
cards.rel: Lie on the dorsal interossei deep to the extensor tendons, and are connected to the deep palmar arch by perforating branches passing between the heads of the interossei.
cards.clin: The first dorsal metacarpal artery carries the kite flap raised from the dorsum of the index finger to resurface the thumb, and reverse-flow dorsal metacarpal artery flaps depend on the distal perforating connections with the palmar arches.
cards.exam: Q. From what do the dorsal metacarpal arteries arise? A. The dorsal carpal arch, formed by the dorsal carpal branches of the radial and ulnar arteries.

cards.desc: Four small worm-like muscles in the palm arising from the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus, unique in taking origin from a tendon and inserting into a tendon.
cards.att: Origin: first and second are unipennate from the radial sides of the profundus tendons to the index and middle fingers; third and fourth are bipennate from adjacent sides of the profundus tendons to the middle, ring and little fingers. Insertion: radial side of the dorsal extensor expansion of the corresponding digit.
cards.sup: First and second by the median nerve (C8, T1); third and fourth by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8, T1).
cards.act: Flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints, the writing position of the fingers.
cards.rel: Lie on the radial side of their digits, superficial to the deep transverse metacarpal ligaments, with the digital vessels and nerves alongside. The lumbrical canal continues proximally from the web space.
cards.clin: Loss of the ulnar two lumbricals and the interossei produces clawing of the ring and little fingers. Because the median nerve supplies the radial two, a high ulnar lesion claws less than a low one, the ulnar paradox. Infection can track along the lumbrical canal into the palm.
cards.exam: Q. Why does the ring and little finger claw in ulnar nerve palsy? A. The medial two lumbricals and the interossei are paralysed, so the metacarpophalangeal joints hyperextend and the interphalangeal joints flex.

cards.k: set of oesophageal branches of thoracic aorta
cards.desc: Four or five small unpaired branches arising from the anterior surface of the descending thoracic aorta to supply the thoracic oesophagus.
cards.att: Arise between roughly T5 and T9 and pass forwards and medially to the oesophagus, forming a longitudinal anastomotic chain on its wall.
cards.sup: Supply the middle third of the oesophagus; anastomose above with oesophageal branches of the inferior thyroid artery and bronchial arteries, and below with ascending branches of the left gastric and left inferior phrenic arteries.
cards.rel: Cross the posterior mediastinum from the aorta to the oesophagus, near the thoracic duct and the oesophageal plexus of the vagi.
cards.clin: The segmental, longitudinally anastomosing supply is why extensive mobilisation of the oesophagus during oesophagectomy risks ischaemia and anastomotic leak.
cards.exam: Q. Name the arteries supplying the thoracic oesophagus. A. Oesophageal branches of the thoracic aorta and bronchial arteries, with inferior thyroid above and left gastric and left inferior phrenic below.

cards.k: set of palmar interossei of hand
cards.desc: Three small unipennate muscles on the palmar aspect of the metacarpals, one for each of the index, ring and little fingers; some texts describe a fourth for the thumb.
cards.att: Origin: palmar surface of the metacarpal of the digit on which the muscle acts, the first from the ulnar side of the second metacarpal, the second from the radial side of the fourth, the third from the radial side of the fifth. Insertion: base of the proximal phalanx and the extensor expansion of the same digit.
cards.sup: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8, T1).
cards.act: Adduct the index, ring and little fingers towards the axis of the middle finger; assist flexion at the metacarpophalangeal joints and extension at the interphalangeal joints. Mnemonic PAD, palmars adduct.
cards.rel: Lie anterior to the dorsal interossei, deep to the long flexor tendons, the lumbricals and the deep palmar arch with the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
cards.clin: Weak finger adduction is demonstrated by the card test in ulnar neuropathy. The middle finger has no palmar interosseous because it is the reference axis for abduction and adduction.
cards.exam: Q. Which digit has no palmar interosseous and why? A. The middle finger, because it is the axis about which abduction and adduction of the fingers are defined.

cards.desc: Usually four arteries in the thigh that pierce adductor magnus close to the linea aspera to reach the posterior compartment.
cards.att: Three arise from the deep artery of the thigh (profunda femoris) and the fourth is its terminal part; each pierces the tendinous insertion of adductor magnus near the linea aspera and winds round the back of the femur.
cards.sup: Supply the adductors, hamstrings and vastus lateralis; the second perforating artery usually gives the nutrient artery of the femur; each divides into ascending and descending branches which anastomose with each other in a chain.
cards.act: Chief arterial supply to the posterior compartment of the thigh and the shaft of the femur.
cards.rel: Lie against the back of the femur under cover of the hamstrings; the first passes above and the others below the insertion of adductor brevis.
cards.clin: The first perforating artery completes the cruciate anastomosis, and the linked chain from the inferior gluteal artery to the popliteal artery provides collateral circulation if the femoral artery is occluded. They bleed briskly in femoral shaft fracture and can be torn during adductor magnus surgery.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle do the perforating arteries pierce? A. Adductor magnus, close to the linea aspera.

cards.desc: Veins that pierce the deep fascia to connect the superficial saphenous system with the deep veins of the limb.
cards.att: Run from the great or small saphenous system and their tributaries through the deep fascia into the posterior tibial, fibular, popliteal or femoral veins; the important groups are the medial ankle and calf perforators, the mid-calf perforators and the thigh perforators of the adductor canal region.
cards.sup: Contain valves directed so that blood flows only from superficial to deep. In the thigh, perforating veins also accompany the perforating arteries into the profunda femoris vein.
cards.act: Channel blood from the superficial to the deep system, where the calf muscle pump drives it upwards.
cards.rel: Pierce the deep fascia at fairly constant points, most clinically on the medial side of the lower leg above and behind the medial malleolus.
cards.clin: Incompetent valves in these perforators reverse the flow, cause varicose veins and produce the gaiter area of lipodermatosclerosis and venous ulceration just above the medial malleolus. Duplex mapping of perforators guides varicose vein surgery and ablation.
cards.exam: Q. In which direction do valves of the perforating veins allow flow, and what happens when they fail? A. Superficial to deep; failure causes reversed flow, varicose veins and medial gaiter ulceration.

cards.desc: The lowest cervical vertebra, identified by its long, non-bifid spinous process that is palpable at the root of the neck.
cards.att: Small body with uncinate processes; triangular vertebral foramen; transverse process has a large posterior tubercle and a small or absent anterior tubercle; foramen transversarium is small and transmits accessory vertebral veins, not the vertebral artery. Articulates above with C6, below with T1 by the intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial joints.
cards.act: Transitional vertebra between the mobile cervical and rigid thoracic regions; gives attachment to ligamentum nuchae, trapezius and rhomboid minor at its spine.
cards.rel: The C8 spinal nerve emerges above the T1 pedicle, that is below the C7 vertebra; the vertebral artery usually passes anterior to the C7 transverse process before entering the foramen transversarium of C6.
cards.clin: The spine of C7 is the standard surface landmark for counting vertebrae. An enlarged C7 costal element forms a cervical rib, which may compress the lower trunk of the brachial plexus and the subclavian artery causing thoracic outlet syndrome.
cards.exam: Q. Why is the vertebral artery not found in the foramen transversarium of C7? A. It enters the foramen transversarium of C6 and passes anterior to the C7 transverse process.

cards.desc: Longest costal cartilage, joining the 7th rib to the sternum at the xiphisternal junction; the last cartilage to reach the sternum directly.
cards.att: Articulates with the 7th rib laterally and with the lower end of the body of the sternum and the xiphoid medially by a synovial joint. Gives attachment to rectus abdominis and the aponeurosis of external oblique in front, and to transversus abdominis and the costal origin of the diaphragm behind.
cards.sup: Perichondrial supply from the internal thoracic and musculophrenic arteries.
cards.act: Forms the summit of the infrasternal (subcostal) angle and transmits movement of the 7th rib to the sternum.
cards.rel: The internal thoracic artery divides into superior epigastric and musculophrenic branches near the 6th space just above; the diaphragm and the liver lie deep to it.
cards.clin: The costal margin is formed by the cartilages of ribs 7 to 10, and the 7th cartilage marks the xiphisternal joint at the T9 level. Costochondritis of the lower cartilages and slipping rib syndrome of the vertebrochondral cartilages both present as chest wall pain.
cards.exam: Q. Which is the lowest costal cartilage to articulate directly with the sternum? A. The 7th.

cards.desc: Longest rib and the lowest true rib, reaching the sternum by its own cartilage at the xiphisternal junction.
cards.att: Head has two facets for the inferior demifacet of T6, the superior demifacet of T7 and the disc between; the tubercle articulates with the transverse process of T7; the shaft has an angle and a costal groove. Gives attachment to serratus anterior, external oblique and latissimus dorsi and, on its inner surface, to the costal part of the diaphragm.
cards.sup: Seventh posterior intercostal artery and anterior intercostal branches of the internal thoracic artery; the 7th intercostal nerve runs in the costal groove and continues into the abdominal wall.
cards.act: Bucket-handle elevation widens the thorax; anchors the costal origin of the diaphragm.
cards.rel: Pleura and lung above the diaphragm, liver on the right and stomach and spleen on the left below it; the neurovascular bundle lies in the costal groove.
cards.clin: The costal origin of the diaphragm arises from the inner surfaces of the lower six costal cartilages, so a penetrating wound below the 7th rib may cross the diaphragm and injure abdominal viscera even though it looks like a chest wound.
cards.exam: Q. Which is the longest rib? A. The 7th.

cards.desc: Typical mid-thoracic vertebra with a heart-shaped body, a small circular vertebral foramen and a long, steeply sloping spine.
cards.att: Superior demifacet for the head of rib 7 and inferior demifacet for the head of rib 8; the transverse process carries a facet for the tubercle of rib 7; the tip of its spine lies opposite the body of T8.
cards.sup: Segmental posterior intercostal branches; dorsal rami supply the facets and periosteum.
cards.act: Load transmission and cord protection; coronally oriented facets allow rotation.
cards.rel: The oesophagus and thoracic aorta lie anteriorly, the azygos vein on the right, and the hemiazygos crosses the midline behind the aorta at about this level.
cards.clin: The T7 spinous process lies at the level of the inferior angle of the scapula with the arms by the sides, the standard landmark for counting thoracic spines and for siting a thoracic epidural. The mid-thoracic cord is a watershed zone for blood supply.
cards.exam: Q. Which spinous process lies at the inferior angle of the scapula? A. T7.

cards.desc: Eight to ten fine nerves leaving the front of the ciliary ganglion and running forwards around the optic nerve to enter the eyeball.
cards.att: Arise from the anterior aspect of the ciliary ganglion in two groups, run forwards with the posterior ciliary arteries, pierce the sclera around the optic nerve, and pass forwards in the perichoroidal space to the ciliary body and iris.
cards.act: Carry postganglionic parasympathetic fibres to sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle, sensory fibres from the cornea, iris and ciliary body, and sympathetic fibres to the ocular vessels and dilator pupillae.
cards.rel: Lie around the optic nerve behind the eyeball, alongside the long ciliary nerves and the short posterior ciliary arteries.
cards.clin: They are the efferent limb of the light reflex and of accommodation. Aberrant regeneration of these fibres after ciliary ganglion damage produces the tonic pupil of Adie syndrome, with light-near dissociation.
cards.exam: Q. What is the efferent pathway of the pupillary light reflex after the ciliary ganglion? A. The short ciliary nerves to sphincter pupillae.

cards.desc: The medial head of biceps brachii, arising outside the shoulder joint from the coracoid process as part of the conjoint tendon.
cards.att: Origin: apex of the coracoid process of the scapula by a tendon shared with coracobrachialis, the conjoint tendon. Insertion: with the long head into the posterior part of the radial tuberosity, and through the bicipital aponeurosis into the deep fascia of the medial forearm.
cards.sup: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6).
cards.act: Flexes the elbow and supinates the flexed forearm; assists flexion and adduction at the shoulder.
cards.rel: Lies medial to the long head in the arm; the musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis and runs between biceps and brachialis. The bicipital aponeurosis separates the brachial artery and median nerve from the median cubital vein in the cubital fossa.
cards.clin: Because its origin is extracapsular, it is unaffected in long head tendon rupture, where the muscle belly balls up in the lower arm as the Popeye sign. The conjoint tendon is transferred with the coracoid in the Latarjet procedure for recurrent shoulder dislocation.
cards.exam: Q. From where does the short head of biceps brachii arise? A. The apex of the coracoid process, by the conjoint tendon with coracobrachialis.

cards.desc: The femoral head of biceps femoris, the only part of the hamstring group that does not cross the hip joint.
cards.att: Origin: lateral lip of the linea aspera and the upper part of the lateral supracondylar line of the femur. Insertion: joins the tendon of the long head and inserts into the head of the fibula, split by the fibular collateral ligament.
cards.sup: Common fibular (peroneal) division of the sciatic nerve (L5, S1, S2), unlike every other hamstring, which is supplied by the tibial division.
cards.act: Flexes the knee and rotates the flexed leg laterally; it has no action at the hip.
cards.rel: Forms the upper lateral boundary of the popliteal fossa; the common fibular nerve runs along its medial border to reach the neck of the fibula.
cards.clin: Its distinct innervation makes it the anatomical marker of the hamstring group; the common fibular nerve lies on its tendon and is at risk in avulsion of the fibular head and in lateral knee injuries, causing foot drop.
cards.exam: Q. Which hamstring component is supplied by the common fibular division of the sciatic nerve? A. The short head of biceps femoris.

cards.desc: Typical cervical vertebra whose transverse process carries a prominent anterior tubercle, the carotid tubercle.
cards.att: Small broad body with uncinate processes, large triangular vertebral foramen, bifid spinous process, and transverse process with anterior and posterior tubercles and a foramen transversarium. Articulates with C5 above and C7 below.
cards.act: Supports the neck and, through the foramen transversarium, transmits the vertebral artery, which enters the cervical transverse foramina at this level.
cards.rel: The anterior tubercle of C6 is the carotid tubercle of Chassaignac: the common carotid artery lies directly in front of it and can be compressed against it. The vertebral artery lies behind the anterior tubercle as it enters the foramen transversarium of C6. At the same level lie the middle cervical sympathetic ganglion and the inferior thyroid artery.
cards.clin: The carotid tubercle (Chassaignac's tubercle) is used to compress the common carotid artery and as the target for a stellate ganglion block. The C6 vertebral level marks the cricoid cartilage, the junction of larynx with trachea and of pharynx with oesophagus, and the entry of the vertebral artery into the transverse foramen.
cards.exam: Q. What structures lie at the level of the sixth cervical vertebra? A. Cricoid cartilage, larynx becoming trachea, pharynx becoming oesophagus, carotid tubercle, and entry of the vertebral artery into the foramen transversarium.

cards.desc: Hyaline cartilage joining the 6th rib to the lower part of the body of the sternum.
cards.att: Articulates with the 6th rib at the costochondral junction and with the sternum at a synovial sternocostal joint; gives attachment to rectus abdominis in front and to transversus thoracis and the diaphragm behind.
cards.sup: Perichondrial branches of the internal thoracic artery.
cards.act: Transmits rib movement to the sternum and contributes to the elastic recoil of the chest wall.
cards.rel: The internal thoracic artery ends behind the 6th costal cartilage or in the 6th intercostal space by dividing into superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries; the inferior border of the heart and the diaphragm lie deep to it.
cards.clin: Rectus abdominis inserts into the 5th, 6th and 7th costal cartilages, so the upper limit of the rectus sheath lies here. The oblique fissure of the lung reaches the chest wall at the 6th costal cartilage anteriorly.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the internal thoracic artery terminate? A. At the level of the 6th costal cartilage or 6th intercostal space, dividing into superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries.

cards.desc: Typical true rib articulating with the sternum through its own costal cartilage.
cards.att: Head bears two facets for the inferior demifacet of T5, the superior demifacet of T6 and the intervening disc; the tubercle articulates with the transverse process of T6; the shaft shows an angle and a costal groove. Gives attachment to a digitation of serratus anterior, to external oblique and to the intercostal muscles.
cards.sup: Sixth posterior intercostal artery and anterior intercostal branches of the internal thoracic artery; the 6th intercostal nerve lies in the costal groove.
cards.act: Pump-handle and bucket-handle elevation in inspiration; protects the heart, lung bases and upper abdominal viscera.
cards.rel: Intercostal bundle in the costal groove; parietal pleura internally; the diaphragm and liver lie deep to the rib anteriorly in expiration.
cards.clin: The lower border of the lung crosses the 6th rib in the midclavicular line, the 8th in the midaxillary line and the 10th at the paravertebral line, while the pleural reflections are two ribs lower at 8, 10 and 12. Knowing this pair of rules prevents entering the abdomen when draining a chest.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the lower border of the lung lie in the midclavicular line? A. At the 6th rib, with the pleural reflection two ribs lower at the 8th.

cards.desc: The outer covering of the body, the largest organ, made of a superficial ectodermal epidermis and a deeper mesodermal dermis resting on subcutaneous tissue.
cards.att: Epidermis is keratinised stratified squamous epithelium with five layers, basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum in thick skin and corneum; the dermis contains collagen and elastic fibres, vessels, nerve endings, hair follicles, sebaceous and sweat glands, and lies on the superficial fascia. Over the pelvis and perineum the skin is thin, mobile and hair bearing, with abundant sebaceous and apocrine glands, and the scrotal skin contains the smooth muscle dartos.
cards.sup: Segmental cutaneous nerves define dermatomes; perineal skin is supplied by the pudendal, ilioinguinal, genitofemoral and posterior femoral cutaneous nerves. Lymph from the perineum, scrotum and skin of the penis and from the anal canal below the pectinate line drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.
cards.act: Barrier against water loss, trauma and infection, thermoregulation through sweat and cutaneous blood flow, sensory reception, and vitamin D synthesis.
cards.rel: Attached to the deep fascia by the superficial fascia, which in the perineum has a membranous layer (Colles' fascia) continuous with Scarpa's fascia of the abdominal wall and attached to the ischiopubic rami and the posterior border of the perineal membrane.
cards.clin: Rupture of the spongy urethra extravasates urine into the superficial perineal pouch, so it spreads into the scrotum, penis and anterior abdominal wall but never into the thigh, because Colles' fascia is fixed to the fascia lata. Carcinoma of the scrotum, penile skin and anal margin metastasises to superficial inguinal nodes.
cards.exam: Q. Why does extravasated urine from a ruptured spongy urethra not enter the thigh? A. The membranous layer of superficial fascia (Colles' fascia) is attached to the fascia lata just below the inguinal ligament.

cards.desc: Superficial vein of the back of the leg, running from behind the lateral malleolus to the popliteal fossa.
cards.att: Begins behind the lateral malleolus as the continuation of the lateral end of the dorsal venous arch, ascends lateral to the calcaneal tendon, then in the midline of the calf, pierces the deep fascia in the lower part of the popliteal fossa and ends in the popliteal vein between the two heads of gastrocnemius.
cards.sup: Tributaries: superficial veins of the back of the leg, communicating branches to the great saphenous vein and perforating veins to the deep veins of the calf.
cards.act: Drains the lateral part of the foot and the posterior aspect of the leg.
cards.rel: Accompanied by the sural nerve below and the medial sural cutaneous nerve above; lies in a fascial canal between the superficial and deep layers of fascia in the calf.
cards.clin: The level of the saphenopopliteal junction is variable, so it is marked by ultrasound before surgery. The sural nerve lies against the vein and is the nerve most often injured in stripping or in harvesting it, giving numbness over the lateral border of the foot.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve accompanies the small saphenous vein behind the lateral malleolus? A. The sural nerve.

cards.desc: Broad flat multipennate muscle of the superficial posterior compartment of the leg, lying deep to gastrocnemius and shaped like a sole fish.
cards.att: Origin: soleal line and the middle third of the medial border of the tibia, the posterior surface of the head and upper quarter of the shaft of the fibula, and the tendinous soleal arch bridging between them. Insertion: with gastrocnemius through the calcaneal tendon into the middle of the posterior surface of the calcaneus.
cards.sup: Tibial nerve, S1, S2.
cards.act: Powerful plantarflexion of the ankle, especially with the knee flexed; a postural antigravity muscle that steadies the leg on the foot in standing.
cards.rel: Deep to gastrocnemius and superficial to the deep flexor group. The popliteal artery and tibial nerve pass deep to its tendinous arch to enter the posterior compartment.
cards.clin: Called the peripheral heart: contraction pumps blood from the soleal venous sinuses, and immobility there predisposes to deep vein thrombosis. The tendinous soleal arch is a site of tibial nerve or popliteal artery entrapment.
cards.exam: Q. Which structures pass deep to the tendinous arch of soleus? A. The popliteal artery, dividing into its terminal branches, and the tibial nerve.

cards.desc: Unpaired bone in the middle of the skull base that articulates with all the other cranial bones and forms much of the middle cranial fossa.
cards.att: Parts: body containing the sphenoidal sinuses and bearing the sella turcica with the hypophysial fossa; lesser wings with the anterior clinoid processes; greater wings; and pterygoid processes with medial and lateral plates. Foramina: optic canal, superior orbital fissure, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale, foramen spinosum, and the carotid groove on the body. Articulates with the frontal, ethmoid, occipital, parietal, temporal, vomer, palatine and zygomatic bones.
cards.act: Keystone of the cranial base; transmits the optic nerve, the ophthalmic and maxillary and mandibular divisions of the trigeminal nerve, the middle meningeal artery, and gives attachment to the pterygoid muscles.
cards.rel: Pituitary gland in the hypophysial fossa with the cavernous sinuses and internal carotid arteries lateral to it; optic chiasma above; sphenoidal sinus and nasopharynx below.
cards.clin: The pituitary is approached surgically through the nose and sphenoidal sinus (trans-sphenoidal hypophysectomy). Fracture of the sphenoid may tear the dura and cause CSF rhinorrhoea, and may injure the cavernous sinus contents or the internal carotid artery.
cards.exam: Q. Which structures pass through the superior orbital fissure? A. Oculomotor, trochlear and abducent nerves, the three branches of the ophthalmic nerve, and the superior ophthalmic vein.

cards.k: sphenoid part of middle cerebral artery
cards.desc: First and horizontal segment of the middle cerebral artery, running laterally below the anterior perforated substance to the limen insulae.
cards.att: Begins at the bifurcation of the internal carotid artery lateral to the optic chiasm, runs laterally in the stem of the lateral sulcus behind the lesser wing of the sphenoid, and ends at the genu at the limen insulae, where the insular part begins.
cards.sup: Anterolateral central (lenticulostriate) arteries, which pass up through the anterior perforated substance, and often the lateral frontobasal and anterior temporal branches.
cards.act: Supplies the lentiform nucleus, the internal capsule and the caudate nucleus through its lenticulostriate branches, and carries the whole middle cerebral supply to the lateral hemisphere.
cards.rel: Lies in the stem of the lateral sulcus with the anterior perforated substance above and the temporal pole below; the internal carotid bifurcation is medial to it.
cards.clin: Rupture of a lenticulostriate branch, the artery of cerebral haemorrhage of Charcot, causes the common capsular haemorrhage with a dense contralateral hemiplegia. Occlusion of this segment infarcts the whole middle cerebral territory and is the classical target for thrombectomy.
cards.exam: Q. Which arteries are called the arteries of cerebral haemorrhage? A. The lenticulostriate branches of the sphenoid (M1) part of the middle cerebral artery.

cards.desc: The posterior, multipennate-free portion of deltoid arising from the spine of the scapula and covering the back of the shoulder.
cards.att: Origin: lower lip of the crest of the spine of the scapula as far medially as the flat triangular area at its root. Insertion: deltoid tuberosity on the lateral surface of the shaft of the humerus, with the other parts.
cards.sup: Axillary nerve, posterior branch (C5, C6).
cards.act: Extends and laterally rotates the arm at the shoulder; with the anterior fibres it steadies the joint, and once abduction is begun it assists it.
cards.rel: Overlies infraspinatus, teres minor and teres major, and its lower border roofs the quadrangular space through which the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels reach its deep surface.
cards.clin: The posterior branch of the axillary nerve supplies this part and continues as the upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm, so sensation over the regimental badge area is lost with it. Deltoid is a common intramuscular injection site: inject into the upper third to stay clear of the axillary nerve, which runs about 5 to 6 cm below the acromion.
cards.exam: Q. Which part of deltoid extends the shoulder and what nerve supplies it? A. The spinal (posterior) part, supplied by the axillary nerve (C5, C6).

cards.desc: The most medial of the three columns of erector spinae, lying against the sides of the spinous processes.
cards.att: Comprises spinalis thoracis, spinalis cervicis and the inconstant spinalis capitis; each part passes from spinous processes below to spinous processes above, blending laterally with longissimus.
cards.sup: Dorsal rami of the spinal nerves.
cards.act: Bilaterally extends the vertebral column and helps maintain erect posture; unilaterally assists lateral flexion to the same side.
cards.rel: Medial to longissimus and iliocostalis, immediately lateral to the spinous processes; deep to the thoracolumbar fascia and the superficial back muscles.
cards.clin: The three erector spinae columns are the target of the erector spinae plane block, in which local anaesthetic is deposited deep to the muscle mass on the transverse process.
cards.exam: Q. Which erector spinae column lies closest to the midline? A. Spinalis.

cards.desc: Largest lymphoid organ, intraperitoneal, lying in the left hypochondrium along the axis of the tenth rib under cover of ribs 9 to 11.
cards.att: Held by the gastrosplenic ligament (containing short gastric and left gastro-omental vessels) and the splenorenal ligament (containing the splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas). Has diaphragmatic and visceral surfaces, a hilum, and a notched superior (anterior) border. Classic 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 rule: 1 by 3 by 5 inches, about 7 ounces, behind ribs 9 to 11.
cards.sup: Splenic artery, the largest branch of the coeliac trunk, running tortuously along the upper border of the pancreas; the splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein. Lymph to pancreaticosplenic and coeliac nodes. Nerves from the coeliac plexus.
cards.act: Filters and removes aged red cells and encapsulated organisms, mounts immune responses, and is haemopoietic in the fetus.
cards.rel: The diaphragm, left pleural recess and ninth to eleventh ribs lie posterolaterally; the stomach, left colic flexure, left kidney and tail of the pancreas contact the visceral surface.
cards.clin: Fracture of the left lower ribs is the classic cause of splenic rupture, with left shoulder tip pain from diaphragmatic irritation (Kehr's sign). The spleen must enlarge two to three times before it is palpable, and it enlarges towards the right iliac fossa with a palpable notch, moves with respiration and one cannot get above it, distinguishing it from a kidney. After splenectomy patients need vaccination against encapsulated organisms.
cards.exam: Q. How is an enlarged spleen distinguished from an enlarged left kidney? A. The spleen has a notch, enlarges towards the right iliac fossa, moves with respiration, is dull to percussion and you cannot get above it.

cards.desc: Largest branch of the coeliac trunk, characteristically tortuous, running to the left along the upper border of the pancreas to the hilum of the spleen.
cards.att: Arises from the coeliac trunk, passes to the left behind the omental bursa along the superior border of the body and tail of the pancreas, enters the splenorenal ligament and divides into about five terminal branches that enter the splenic hilum.
cards.sup: Pancreatic branches including the dorsal pancreatic and the arteria pancreatica magna, short gastric arteries, left gastro-omental artery and terminal splenic branches.
cards.act: Supplies the spleen, the neck, body and tail of the pancreas, and the fundus and greater curvature of the stomach.
cards.rel: Lies above the splenic vein along the back of the pancreas, behind the omental bursa and stomach, with the left kidney and left suprarenal gland behind; it reaches the spleen in the splenorenal ligament with the tail of the pancreas.
cards.clin: Commonest site of visceral artery aneurysm, with a high risk of rupture in pregnancy and in portal hypertension. Its tortuous course and pancreatic branches govern the dissection in distal pancreatectomy, and proximal embolisation is used to salvage the spleen after trauma.
cards.exam: Q. Which ligament conveys the splenic vessels to the hilum of the spleen? A. The splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament, which also contains the tail of the pancreas.

cards.desc: Large vein formed at the splenic hilum that runs to the right behind the body of the pancreas and unites with the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein.
cards.att: Formed by five or six tributaries at the hilum of the spleen, passes right in the splenorenal ligament and then in a groove on the posterior surface of the pancreas below the artery, crossing in front of the left kidney and the aorta, and joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the neck of the pancreas.
cards.sup: Receives short gastric, left gastro-omental, pancreatic and usually the inferior mesenteric veins.
cards.act: Drains the spleen, much of the pancreas and the greater curvature of the stomach into the portal vein.
cards.rel: Runs below and behind the splenic artery on the back of the pancreas, anterior to the left renal vein, the left suprarenal gland and the aorta, and below the coeliac trunk.
cards.clin: Thrombosis, usually from chronic pancreatitis or carcinoma of the pancreatic body, causes left-sided (sinistral) portal hypertension with isolated gastric fundal varices, curable by splenectomy. The vein is used for the distal splenorenal (Warren) shunt.
cards.exam: Q. What causes isolated gastric varices with a normal liver? A. Splenic vein thrombosis, usually secondary to pancreatic disease.

cards.desc: Strap-like muscle bandaging the deeper neck muscles, running upwards and laterally from the midline to the skull.
cards.att: Origin: lower half of the ligamentum nuchae and the spinous processes of the seventh cervical and upper three or four thoracic vertebrae. Insertion: mastoid process of the temporal bone and the lateral third of the superior nuchal line, deep to sternocleidomastoid.
cards.sup: Posterior rami of the middle cervical spinal nerves (C3, C4).
cards.act: Acting alone it rotates the head and turns the face to the same side and bends the head laterally; acting with its fellow it extends the head and neck.
cards.rel: Deep to trapezius and sternocleidomastoid, superficial to semispinalis capitis and longissimus capitis; its upper lateral part appears in the floor of the posterior triangle between sternocleidomastoid and levator scapulae.
cards.clin: It rotates the head to the same side, the opposite of sternocleidomastoid, and the two act together on one side to produce pure lateral rotation; involvement contributes to acquired torticollis and cervicogenic headache.
cards.exam: Q. Compare the rotatory action of splenius capitis and sternocleidomastoid. A. Splenius capitis turns the face to the same side, sternocleidomastoid to the opposite side.

cards.desc: The great oblique landmark muscle of the neck, dividing it into anterior and posterior triangles.
cards.att: Origin: by a rounded tendinous sternal head from the front of the manubrium sterni and a flat muscular clavicular head from the medial third of the upper surface of the clavicle. Insertion: lateral surface of the mastoid process and the lateral half of the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone.
cards.sup: Motor supply from the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI); proprioceptive fibres from the anterior rami of C2 and C3.
cards.act: Acting alone it tilts the head to the same side and turns the face to the opposite side and upwards; acting together the muscles flex the neck and extend the head, and act as accessory muscles of inspiration.
cards.rel: Covered by platysma, the external jugular vein and the great auricular nerve; deep to it lie the carotid sheath, the ansa cervicalis, the cervical plexus, the scalene muscles and the phrenic nerve. Its posterior border forms the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle.
cards.clin: Congenital muscular torticollis follows fibrosis of the muscle, tilting the head to the affected side with the face turned away. The accessory nerve is at risk in lymph node biopsy behind its posterior border, and the triangle between the two heads is the surface landmark for internal jugular vein cannulation.
cards.exam: Q. What is the nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid? A. Motor from the spinal accessory nerve, proprioceptive from C2 and C3.

cards.desc: The large lower head of pectoralis major arising from the sternum and costal cartilages, separated from the clavicular head by a slight cleft.
cards.att: Origin: anterior surface of the sternum and the upper six costal cartilages, with a small slip from the aponeurosis of external oblique. Insertion: lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus, forming the deeper (posterior) lamina of the bilaminar tendon, its lowest fibres twisting to lie highest at the insertion.
cards.sup: Medial pectoral nerve (C8, T1), with a contribution from the lateral pectoral nerve.
cards.act: Adducts and medially rotates the arm, and from the flexed position it extends the arm powerfully, as in climbing or throwing a ball downwards.
cards.rel: Forms most of the anterior wall of the axilla and its lower border makes the anterior axillary fold. Deep to it lie pectoralis minor, the clavipectoral fascia and the axillary vessels and brachial plexus.
cards.clin: The sternocostal part is the portion torn in bench-press injuries, giving a bruised, hollowed anterior axillary fold and a medially retracted muscle belly. The twisted bilaminar tendon explains why the fold retains its sharp edge and why partial tears preserve some function.
cards.exam: Q. Which part of pectoralis major is chiefly responsible for extending the flexed arm? A. The sternocostal part, supplied mainly by the medial pectoral nerve (C8, T1).

cards.desc: Thin superficial infrahyoid strap muscle running from the manubrium to the hyoid bone.
cards.att: Origin: posterior surface of the manubrium sterni, the posterior sternoclavicular ligament and the adjoining medial end of the clavicle. Insertion: medial part of the lower border of the body of the hyoid bone.
cards.sup: Ansa cervicalis (C1, C2, C3).
cards.act: Depresses the hyoid bone after it has been elevated in swallowing and speech.
cards.rel: Superficial to sternothyroid and thyrohyoid and to the thyroid gland; the two muscles of opposite sides are separated below by a triangular interval containing the jugular venous arch in the suprasternal space.
cards.clin: The strap muscles are separated in the midline, an avascular plane, and retracted in thyroidectomy; they are divided only for a very large goitre.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles apart from thyrohyoid? A. The ansa cervicalis (C1, C2, C3).

cards.desc: Deeper and shorter infrahyoid strap muscle lying on the thyroid gland and larynx.
cards.att: Origin: posterior surface of the manubrium sterni below the origin of sternohyoid and the adjacent first costal cartilage. Insertion: oblique line on the lamina of the thyroid cartilage.
cards.sup: Ansa cervicalis (C1, C2, C3).
cards.act: Depresses the larynx after it has been elevated in swallowing and in the production of low notes.
cards.rel: Lies deep to sternohyoid and directly on the thyroid gland, the trachea and the common carotid artery; it is continued upwards by the thyrohyoid from the same oblique line.
cards.clin: Its attachment to the oblique line limits the upward extension of an enlarging thyroid gland, so a large goitre tends to grow downwards behind the sternum as a retrosternal goitre.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle limits upward enlargement of the thyroid gland? A. Sternothyroid, through its attachment to the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage.

cards.desc: Most dilated part of the alimentary canal, lying in the left hypochondrium and epigastrium between the oesophagus and the duodenum.
cards.att: Parts: cardia, fundus (above the cardiac orifice under the left dome of the diaphragm), body, pyloric antrum and pylorus. The lesser curvature gives attachment to the lesser omentum and bears the incisura angularis; the greater curvature gives attachment to the gastrosplenic ligament and greater omentum. Also held by the gastrophrenic and gastrocolic ligaments.
cards.sup: Left gastric from the coeliac trunk and right gastric from the hepatic artery along the lesser curvature; right gastro-omental from the gastroduodenal and left gastro-omental from the splenic artery along the greater curvature; short gastric arteries to the fundus. Veins drain to the portal system. Lymph ultimately to coeliac nodes. Parasympathetic supply from the anterior and posterior vagal trunks; sympathetic from T6 to T9 via the greater splanchnic nerve.
cards.act: Stores food, mixes it with acid and pepsin to form chyme, releases it into the duodenum, and secretes intrinsic factor.
cards.rel: Anteriorly the diaphragm, left lobe of the liver and anterior abdominal wall. Posteriorly, across the lesser sac, lies the stomach bed: diaphragm, left suprarenal gland, upper left kidney, pancreas, splenic artery, transverse mesocolon and spleen.
cards.clin: Gastric pain is referred to the epigastrium (T6 to T9). Carcinoma spreads to the left supraclavicular node (Virchow's node, Troisier's sign) and can seed the ovaries (Krukenberg tumour). Fluid collecting in the lesser sac forms a pseudocyst behind the stomach.
cards.exam: Q. Name the structures forming the stomach bed. A. Diaphragm, left suprarenal gland, upper part of the left kidney, pancreas, splenic artery, transverse mesocolon and spleen.

cards.desc: The anterior, more vertically directed part of cricothyroid, the external tensor of the vocal folds.
cards.att: Origin: anterolateral surface of the arch of the cricoid cartilage near the midline. Insertion: lower border of the lamina of the thyroid cartilage.
cards.sup: External laryngeal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (vagus).
cards.act: Tilts the thyroid cartilage forwards and downwards on the cricothyroid joint, lengthening and tensing the vocal folds and raising the pitch of the voice.
cards.rel: Lies on the outer surface of the larynx in the cricothyroid space, covered by sternothyroid; the cricothyroid membrane lies medial to it in the midline.
cards.clin: The midline cricothyroid membrane between the two muscles is the site of emergency cricothyroidotomy. Injury to the external laryngeal nerve during ligation of the superior thyroid artery weakens the muscle and flattens the voice.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle tenses the vocal folds and what is its nerve supply? A. Cricothyroid, supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.

cards.desc: Slender suprahyoid muscle running from the styloid process to the hyoid bone, perforated near its insertion by the digastric tendon.
cards.att: Origin: posterior surface of the styloid process of the temporal bone near its base. Insertion: body of the hyoid bone at its junction with the greater horn, just above the omohyoid; the tendon splits to allow the intermediate tendon of digastric to pass through.
cards.sup: Facial nerve (CN VII), by its stylohyoid branch in the parotid region.
cards.act: Elevates and retracts the hyoid bone, lengthening the floor of the mouth during swallowing.
cards.rel: Lies along the upper border of the posterior belly of digastric, which it accompanies; both cross the external and internal carotid arteries and mark the upper limit of the carotid triangle. The facial artery and the retromandibular vein are related deep to it.
cards.clin: Derived from the second pharyngeal arch with the posterior belly of digastric, which is why both are supplied by the facial nerve. Ossification of the associated stylohyoid ligament produces the elongated styloid process of Eagle syndrome, with throat pain on turning the head.
cards.exam: Q. Nerve supply of stylohyoid, and why? A. The facial nerve, because it is a second pharyngeal arch muscle.

cards.desc: Fibrous cord running from the tip of the styloid process of the temporal bone to the lesser horn of the hyoid bone.
cards.att: Origin from the tip of the styloid process; insertion into the lesser horn of the hyoid. It is a remnant of the cartilage of the second pharyngeal arch (Reichert's cartilage).
cards.act: Suspends the hyoid bone from the skull base and gives partial origin to the middle constrictor of the pharynx.
cards.rel: Lies deep to the stylohyoid muscle and the posterior belly of digastric; the glossopharyngeal nerve and the external carotid artery are related to it; it separates the parotid from the submandibular region.
cards.clin: Ossification or elongation of the styloid process and ligament produces Eagle syndrome: pain in the throat and neck on swallowing or turning the head, sometimes with referred otalgia.
cards.exam: Q. From which pharyngeal arch cartilage does the stylohyoid ligament develop? A. The second arch cartilage, Reichert's cartilage.

cards.desc: Longitudinal muscle of the pharynx descending from the styloid process, the only muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.
cards.att: Origin: medial side of the base of the styloid process of the temporal bone. Insertion: posterior border of the lamina of the thyroid cartilage and the wall of the pharynx, blending with palatopharyngeus.
cards.sup: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), its only motor muscle.
cards.act: Elevates and widens the pharynx and elevates the larynx during swallowing.
cards.rel: Enters the pharyngeal wall through the gap between the superior and middle constrictors, with the glossopharyngeal nerve winding round its lateral surface. It separates the internal from the external carotid artery at the base of the skull.
cards.clin: The glossopharyngeal nerve is identified surgically by following it along the lateral surface of this muscle; the muscle is a third pharyngeal arch derivative, matching its nerve supply.
cards.exam: Q. Which is the only muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve? A. Stylopharyngeus.

cards.desc: Main artery of the upper limb in the root of the neck, also supplying the brain, neck and anterior chest wall before it becomes the axillary artery.
cards.att: The right arises from the brachiocephalic trunk behind the right sternoclavicular joint; the left arises from the arch of the aorta and has an additional intrathoracic course. Each arches over the cervical pleura and ends at the outer border of the first rib as the axillary artery. Scalenus anterior divides it into three parts.
cards.sup: First part: vertebral artery, internal thoracic artery, thyrocervical trunk. Second part: costocervical trunk. Third part: usually nothing, but often the dorsal scapular artery.
cards.act: Conveys blood to the upper limb, and through its branches to the brain and spinal cord, thyroid, neck and anterior thoracic wall.
cards.rel: Second part lies behind scalenus anterior with the cervical pleura and apex of the lung below and the brachial plexus trunks above and behind. The subclavian vein lies anterior to scalenus anterior, the phrenic nerve on its front. The thoracic duct arches over the left first part.
cards.clin: The third part can be compressed against the first rib in the supraclavicular fossa to arrest bleeding in the limb. Proximal stenosis before the vertebral origin causes subclavian steal syndrome: exercising the arm reverses vertebral flow and produces vertebrobasilar symptoms. A cervical rib may compress the artery and the lower trunk of the brachial plexus.
cards.exam: Q. Name the branches of the first part of the subclavian artery. A. Vertebral artery, internal thoracic artery and thyrocervical trunk.

cards.desc: Continuation of the axillary vein in the root of the neck, joining the internal jugular vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.
cards.att: Begins at the outer border of the first rib as the continuation of the axillary vein, arches over the first rib in front of scalenus anterior, and ends behind the medial end of the clavicle by uniting with the internal jugular vein at the venous angle to form the brachiocephalic vein.
cards.sup: Tributaries: the external jugular vein and sometimes the dorsal scapular vein. The thoracic duct enters the left venous angle and the right lymphatic duct the right venous angle.
cards.act: Drains the upper limb and, through the external jugular vein, part of the scalp and face.
cards.rel: Lies anterior to scalenus anterior, with the subclavian artery and the phrenic nerve behind that muscle; the clavicle and subclavius lie in front and the cervical pleura below and behind.
cards.clin: Cannulated by the infraclavicular route at the junction of the medial two thirds and lateral third of the clavicle; the pleural dome lies immediately behind, so pneumothorax is the classic complication. Fascial attachments hold the vein open, so a laceration can draw in air and cause air embolism.
cards.exam: Q. What forms the brachiocephalic vein? A. Union of the subclavian and internal jugular veins behind the sternoclavicular joint.

cards.desc: Small cylindrical muscle lying under cover of the clavicle between the first rib and the clavicle.
cards.att: Origin: junction of the first rib with its costal cartilage. Insertion: subclavian groove on the inferior surface of the middle third of the clavicle.
cards.sup: Nerve to subclavius (C5, C6), from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus.
cards.act: Depresses the clavicle and pulls the shoulder forward and downward; steadies the clavicle during movements of the shoulder girdle.
cards.rel: Enclosed in the clavipectoral fascia; the subclavian vein, subclavian artery and the trunks of the brachial plexus lie immediately behind and below it, separated only by the fascia.
cards.clin: The muscle and the clavipectoral fascia cushion the underlying subclavian vessels and brachial plexus, which is why these structures usually escape injury in the common midshaft clavicular fracture. The nerve to subclavius often gives an accessory phrenic root that must be sought in phrenic nerve surgery.
cards.exam: Q. Which structures lie immediately deep to subclavius? A. The subclavian vein, subclavian artery and the trunks of the brachial plexus.

cards.desc: The smallest of the three paired major salivary glands, an almond-shaped predominantly mucous gland lying under the mucosa of the floor of the mouth.
cards.att: Lies in the sublingual fossa on the inner surface of the mandible, above mylohyoid, raising the sublingual fold of mucosa; bounded medially by genioglossus, laterally by the mandible, below by mylohyoid and behind by the deep part of the submandibular gland. It drains by 8 to 20 small ducts (of Rivinus) opening along the sublingual fold, one of which may join the submandibular duct as the major sublingual duct.
cards.sup: Arteries: sublingual branch of the lingual artery and submental branch of the facial artery. Secretomotor: parasympathetic fibres of the chorda tympani, carried by the lingual nerve, relaying in the submandibular ganglion. Lymph to the submandibular nodes.
cards.act: Secretes predominantly mucous saliva, lubricating the floor of the mouth and the food bolus.
cards.rel: The submandibular duct and the lingual nerve run medial to it, the lingual nerve looping under the duct; the sublingual gland lies immediately deep to the mucosa lateral to the frenulum of the tongue.
cards.clin: Obstruction or trauma of the gland or its ducts produces a ranula, a bluish translucent mucous extravasation cyst in the floor of the mouth; a plunging ranula extends through mylohyoid into the neck.
cards.exam: Q. What is a ranula? A. A mucous extravasation cyst arising from the sublingual gland in the floor of the mouth.

cards.desc: J-shaped mixed seromucous salivary gland with a large superficial part in the submandibular triangle and a small deep part that hooks around the posterior border of mylohyoid.
cards.att: Superficial part lies in the digastric (submandibular) triangle on mylohyoid, hyoglossus and the mandible; the deep part lies between mylohyoid below and hyoglossus above. Its duct (of Wharton), about 5 cm long, runs forward between mylohyoid and hyoglossus to open at the sublingual papilla beside the frenulum of the tongue.
cards.sup: Arteries: facial and lingual arteries; veins to the common facial and lingual veins. Secretomotor: parasympathetic fibres of the chorda tympani via the lingual nerve, relaying in the submandibular ganglion; sympathetic from the superior cervical ganglion. Lymph to the submandibular and then deep cervical nodes.
cards.act: Produces mixed saliva, predominantly serous, and contributes most of the resting salivary volume.
cards.rel: The facial artery grooves its deep surface and the facial vein lies superficial. The lingual nerve crosses the duct laterally, passes below it and turns up medially; the hypoglossal nerve lies below the duct on hyoglossus. The marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve lies superficial to the capsule.
cards.clin: About 80 per cent of salivary calculi occur here, because the duct runs uphill and the secretion is viscid, causing pain and swelling on eating. In gland excision the skin incision is placed two finger-breadths below the mandible to spare the marginal mandibular nerve, and the lingual and hypoglossal nerves must be identified.
cards.exam: Q. Why are calculi commonest in the submandibular gland? A. Its long duct ascends against gravity and its saliva is viscid and rich in mucin and calcium.

cards.desc: Large triangular rotator cuff muscle filling the subscapular fossa on the costal surface of the scapula.
cards.att: Origin: medial two-thirds of the subscapular fossa. Insertion: lesser tubercle of the humerus and the front of the capsule of the shoulder joint.
cards.sup: Upper and lower subscapular nerves (C5, C6), from the posterior cord.
cards.act: Medially rotates the arm; as part of the rotator cuff it holds the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity.
cards.rel: Forms the posterior wall of the axilla with teres major and latissimus dorsi, and the anterior wall of the quadrangular space. The subscapular bursa lies between its tendon and the neck of the scapula and communicates with the joint cavity through the opening in the capsule.
cards.clin: It is the only rotator cuff muscle in front of the joint and is the main check to anterior dislocation, so it is divided and repaired in the deltopectoral approach to the shoulder. Tested by the lift-off test, in which the patient cannot lift the dorsum of the hand off the lower back.
cards.exam: Q. Which rotator cuff muscle inserts into the lesser tubercle and how is it tested? A. Subscapularis, tested by the lift-off (Gerber) test.

cards.k: superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis
cards.latin: caput superficiale musculi flexoris pollicis brevis
cards.desc: The larger, lateral head of flexor pollicis brevis, forming part of the thenar eminence beneath abductor pollicis brevis.
cards.att: Origin: distal border of the flexor retinaculum and the tubercle of the trapezium. Insertion: radial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb, through a tendon containing the radial sesamoid bone.
cards.sup: Recurrent (motor) branch of the median nerve (C8, T1); the deep head is supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
cards.act: Flexes the metacarpophalangeal joint of the thumb and assists opposition.
cards.rel: Lies deep to abductor pollicis brevis and lateral to the tendon of flexor pollicis longus, which passes between the two heads; the deep head lies deeper and more medial with the oblique head of adductor pollicis.
