cards.clin: Wasting of the thenar eminence with loss of thumb abduction and opposition follows median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel; the recurrent branch lies superficially just distal to the retinaculum and is at risk in incisions in the thenar area.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve supplies the superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis? A. The recurrent branch of the median nerve.

cards.desc: Arterial arch across the palm just deep to the palmar aponeurosis, the chief supply of the fingers.
cards.att: Direct continuation of the ulnar artery after it enters the palm lateral to the pisiform, completed on the radial side by the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery; its convexity lies level with the distal border of the fully extended and abducted thumb.
cards.sup: A proper palmar digital artery to the ulnar side of the little finger and three common palmar digital arteries, each dividing near the web space into two proper palmar digital arteries for adjacent sides of the fingers.
cards.act: Supplies the medial three and a half digits and the superficial structures of the palm; the thumb and radial side of the index finger are supplied from the radial artery.
cards.rel: Lies deep to the palmar aponeurosis and superficial to the long flexor tendons and the lumbricals; in the palm the digital branches of the median and ulnar nerves lie superficial to the corresponding arteries.
cards.clin: A transverse palmar laceration bleeds from both ends of the arch, so ligation of the ulnar artery alone does not control it and exploration is needed. The Allen test assesses whether both arteries fill the arches before radial artery puncture.
cards.exam: Q. Which artery mainly forms the superficial palmar arch? A. The ulnar artery, completed by the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery.

syn: superior division of the oculomotor nerve
cards.desc: The smaller of the two divisions of the oculomotor nerve, supplying the two muscles of the orbital roof.
cards.att: Separates from the oculomotor nerve in the anterior cavernous sinus or superior orbital fissure, enters the orbit within the common tendinous ring, ascends lateral to the optic nerve, pierces or passes medial to superior rectus and ends in levator palpebrae superioris.
cards.act: Motor to superior rectus and levator palpebrae superioris.
cards.rel: Runs within the muscle cone lateral to the optic nerve and the ophthalmic artery, below superior rectus; the nasociliary nerve enters the ring between it and the inferior branch.
cards.clin: An isolated superior division palsy gives ptosis with impaired elevation of the eye but a normal pupil. Because the same branch supplies the lid elevator and the eye elevator, the two fail together.
cards.exam: Q. Which two muscles does the superior division of the oculomotor nerve supply? A. Superior rectus and levator palpebrae superioris.

cards.desc: The rostral pair of rounded elevations on the dorsal surface of the midbrain, at the level of the red nucleus, forming the upper half of the corpora quadrigemina.
cards.att: Receives fibres from the retina, the visual cortex and the spinotectal tract; its brachium connects it with the lateral geniculate body and the pretectal area; it gives origin to the tectospinal and tectobulbar tracts, which cross in the dorsal tegmental decussation.
cards.sup: Branches of the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries.
cards.act: Reflex centre for orientation of the head and eyes towards visual stimuli, and control of saccadic eye movement.
cards.rel: Pineal body lies between and above the two superior colliculi; the trochlear nerve emerges just below the inferior colliculus and winds round the midbrain; the cerebral aqueduct lies deep to the tectum.
cards.clin: Compression by a pineal tumour causes Parinaud syndrome: paralysis of upward gaze, light-near dissociation and convergence-retraction nystagmus.
cards.exam: Q. What tract arises from the superior colliculus and what does it do? A. The tectospinal tract, mediating reflex turning of the head towards visual stimuli.

cards.desc: One of the two terminal branches of the internal thoracic artery, entering the rectus sheath from above to supply the upper anterior abdominal wall.
cards.att: Arises from the internal thoracic artery at the level of the sixth costal cartilage, enters the rectus sheath by passing between the sternal and costal slips of the diaphragm, and descends behind rectus abdominis to anastomose with the inferior epigastric artery.
cards.sup: Muscular branches to rectus abdominis, cutaneous perforators, and small branches to the diaphragm and the falciform ligament.
cards.act: Supplies the upper part of rectus abdominis and the overlying skin, and forms a collateral link between the subclavian and external iliac arteries.
cards.rel: Runs between rectus abdominis and the posterior wall of its sheath, accompanied by its venae comitantes; it passes through the sternocostal triangle of the diaphragm.
cards.clin: The superior to inferior epigastric anastomosis enlarges to form a visible collateral in coarctation of the aorta and in inferior vena caval obstruction. The artery is the pedicle of the pedicled TRAM flap, and its diaphragmatic gap is the site of a Morgagni hernia.
cards.exam: Q. Which two arteries anastomose within the rectus sheath? A. The superior epigastric from the internal thoracic and the inferior epigastric from the external iliac artery.

cards.desc: The uppermost gyrus of the frontal lobe, running anteroposteriorly above the superior frontal sulcus and continuing over the superomedial margin onto the medial surface.
cards.att: Its posterior part on the medial surface is the supplementary motor area, Brodmann area 6, which projects to the primary motor cortex and the corticospinal tract; the anterior part belongs to the prefrontal cortex, connected with the thalamic dorsomedial nucleus.
cards.sup: Anterior cerebral artery for the medial surface and superior margin, middle cerebral artery for the adjacent lateral surface.
cards.act: Supplementary motor area plans and sequences complex and bimanual movement and prepares postural adjustment; the prefrontal part serves working memory, judgement and social behaviour.
cards.rel: Lies above the middle frontal gyrus, from which it is separated by the superior frontal sulcus; on the medial surface it lies above the cingulate sulcus and ends behind at the paracentral lobule.
cards.clin: Anterior cerebral artery occlusion damages the medial part, giving contralateral lower limb weakness with a grasp reflex and, if the supplementary motor area is involved, transient akinesia and mutism.
cards.exam: Q. Which functional area occupies the posteromedial part of the superior frontal gyrus? A. The supplementary motor area, part of Brodmann area 6.

cards.desc: The venae comitantes of the superior gluteal artery, the largest tributaries of the internal iliac vein.
cards.att: Begin in the gluteal region draining gluteus medius, minimus and tensor fasciae latae, accompany the superior gluteal artery through the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis, and unite to drain into the internal iliac vein.
cards.act: Return blood from the deep gluteal muscles and the posterior pelvic wall.
cards.rel: Emerge above piriformis with the superior gluteal artery and nerve, between the lumbosacral trunk and the first sacral ventral ramus, close to the greater sciatic notch and the posterior surface of the ilium.
cards.clin: Torn superior gluteal vessels at the sciatic notch in posterior pelvic ring fracture or during a posterior approach to the acetabulum cause severe, poorly accessible haemorrhage; they retract into the pelvis and often require embolisation.
cards.exam: Q. Which structures leave the pelvis above piriformis? A. The superior gluteal artery, vein and nerve.

cards.desc: Descending branch of the costocervical trunk that supplies the upper two intercostal spaces, the only spaces not supplied from the thoracic aorta.
cards.att: Arises from the costocervical trunk of the second part of the subclavian artery behind scalenus anterior, arches backwards over the cervical pleura and descends in front of the necks of the first and second ribs.
cards.sup: Gives the first and second posterior intercostal arteries, each with dorsal, spinal and collateral branches.
cards.rel: Descends anterior to the necks of the first two ribs, lateral to the sympathetic trunk and the ventral ramus of T1, and medial to the ventral ramus of T1 in some descriptions; the superior intercostal vein lies on its medial side.
cards.clin: At risk during first rib resection and in supraclavicular approaches to the brachial plexus; injury also threatens the underlying cervical pleura.
cards.exam: Q. From which vessel does the superior intercostal artery arise? A. The costocervical trunk of the second part of the subclavian artery.

cards.desc: Vein draining the upper posterior intercostal spaces below the first, differing in its termination on the two sides.
cards.att: The right superior intercostal vein drains the second, third and fourth right posterior intercostal veins and ends in the arch of the azygos vein. The left superior intercostal vein drains the second, third and sometimes fourth left posterior intercostal veins, crosses the left side of the aortic arch and ends in the left brachiocephalic vein.
cards.sup: Receives the upper posterior intercostal veins and communicates inferiorly with the accessory hemiazygos vein; the first posterior intercostal vein drains separately into the brachiocephalic vein.
cards.rel: On the left it crosses the aortic arch lateral to the left vagus nerve and medial to the left phrenic nerve.
cards.clin: Seen end-on against the aortic arch on a frontal chest radiograph as the aortic nipple; it enlarges in superior vena caval obstruction and in azygos continuation of the inferior vena cava.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the left superior intercostal vein end? A. In the left brachiocephalic vein, after crossing the arch of the aorta.

cards.desc: Second unpaired ventral branch of the abdominal aorta, arising at L1 about 1 cm below the coeliac trunk, and the artery of the midgut.
cards.att: Arises behind the body of the pancreas, passes forwards over the uncinate process and the third part of the duodenum, then downwards and to the right in the root of the mesentery, ending in the right iliac fossa by anastomosing with a branch of its own ileocolic artery.
cards.sup: Inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery, jejunal and ileal branches, middle colic, right colic and ileocolic arteries.
cards.act: Supplies the duodenum distal to the major duodenal papilla, jejunum, ileum, caecum, appendix, ascending colon and proximal two thirds of the transverse colon.
cards.rel: The splenic vein and neck of the pancreas cross in front of its origin, the left renal vein, uncinate process and third part of the duodenum lie behind it, and the superior mesenteric vein lies on its right.
cards.clin: Embolic occlusion causes acute mesenteric ischaemia, with pain out of proportion to abdominal signs and a rising serum lactate. Narrowing of the aortomesenteric angle after rapid weight loss compresses the third part of the duodenum, producing superior mesenteric artery (Wilkie) syndrome; the same angle compresses the left renal vein in nutcracker syndrome.
cards.exam: Q. Which two structures may be compressed in the aortomesenteric angle? A. The third part of the duodenum in SMA syndrome and the left renal vein in nutcracker syndrome.

cards.desc: Large tributary of the portal vein draining the whole midgut, ascending in the root of the mesentery to the right of the superior mesenteric artery.
cards.att: Begins in the right iliac fossa from the ileocolic and appendicular veins, ascends in the mesenteric root anterior to the third part of the duodenum and uncinate process, and ends behind the neck of the pancreas by joining the splenic vein to form the portal vein.
cards.sup: Receives jejunal and ileal veins, ileocolic, right colic and middle colic veins, the right gastro-omental vein and the anterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal vein.
cards.act: Carries nutrient-rich venous blood from the small intestine and proximal colon to the liver.
cards.rel: Lies to the right of the superior mesenteric artery in the mesenteric root; the third part of the duodenum and uncinate process lie behind it. The neck of the pancreas is anterior at its termination.
cards.clin: Absence or inversion of the normal SMA/SMV relationship on CT (the SMV lying to the left of the artery) is the classic sign of intestinal malrotation. Tumour contact with the SMV determines resectability in pancreatic head carcinoma.
cards.exam: Q. Where is the portal vein formed? A. Behind the neck of the pancreas, by union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins.

cards.desc: Extra-ocular muscle of the superomedial orbit whose tendon turns through a fibrocartilaginous pulley, the trochlea, on the frontal bone before reaching the eyeball.
cards.att: Origin: body of the sphenoid, superomedial to the optic canal. The tendon passes through the trochlea, turns posterolaterally and inserts into the sclera in the posterolateral quadrant, deep to superior rectus.
cards.sup: Trochlear nerve, CN IV.
cards.act: From the primary position: depression, abduction and intorsion (medial rotation) of the eyeball. Tested clinically as depression with the eye adducted.
cards.rel: Lies along the superomedial orbital wall above medial rectus; the nasociliary nerve and ophthalmic artery run between it and medial rectus. Its tendon passes deep to the tendon of superior rectus.
cards.clin: CN IV palsy gives vertical diplopia that is worst on looking down and in, so patients trip on stairs, and they tilt the head to the opposite shoulder (positive Bielschowsky head-tilt test). Brown syndrome is restricted elevation in adduction from a tight superior oblique tendon sheath.
cards.exam: Q. In which position of gaze is the superior oblique tested as a pure depressor? A. With the eye adducted.

cards.desc: The part of the parietal lobe above the intraparietal sulcus and behind the postcentral sulcus, corresponding to Brodmann areas 5 and 7.
cards.att: Receives fibres from the postcentral gyrus and from the pulvinar and lateral posterior thalamic nuclei; connects with the premotor cortex and, through the medial surface precuneus, with the cingulate gyrus.
cards.sup: Middle cerebral artery on the lateral surface, anterior cerebral artery for the precuneus medially.
cards.act: Somatosensory association area: integrates tactile and proprioceptive information into body image and guides visually directed reaching, as part of the dorsal stream.
cards.rel: Bounded below by the intraparietal sulcus separating it from the inferior parietal lobule, in front by the postcentral sulcus, behind by the parieto-occipital sulcus; it becomes the precuneus on the medial surface.
cards.clin: A lesion causes contralateral astereognosis and loss of two-point discrimination with intact primary sensation; a right-sided lesion produces contralateral sensory neglect and dressing apraxia, and bilateral damage gives optic ataxia in Balint syndrome.
cards.exam: Q. Which sulcus separates the superior from the inferior parietal lobule? A. The intraparietal sulcus.

cards.desc: Uppermost of the three overlapping constrictors forming the pharyngeal wall, quadrilateral and the thinnest of the three.
cards.att: Origin, from above down: lower part of the posterior border of the medial pterygoid plate and the pterygoid hamulus, the pterygomandibular raphe, the posterior end of the mylohyoid line of the mandible, and the side of the tongue. Insertion: pharyngeal tubercle of the occipital bone and the median pharyngeal raphe.
cards.sup: Pharyngeal plexus, motor fibres from the vagus, CN X.
cards.act: Constricts the upper pharynx to propel the bolus; its upper fibres form Passavant's ridge, which helps close the nasopharyngeal isthmus.
cards.rel: Buccinator is continuous with it through the pterygomandibular raphe. Through the gap above its upper border (sinus of Morgagni) pass levator veli palatini, the auditory tube and the ascending palatine artery; through the gap below it pass the stylopharyngeus and the glossopharyngeal nerve.
cards.clin: Palatal or pharyngeal weakness produces nasal regurgitation and hypernasal speech, seen after cleft palate and in vagal lesions. The sinus of Morgagni is a route by which nasopharyngeal infection and tumour spread to the parapharyngeal space.
cards.exam: Q. What passes through the gap above the upper border of the superior constrictor? A. Levator veli palatini, the auditory tube and the ascending palatine artery.

cards.desc: Upper of the two pulmonary veins of each lung, carrying oxygenated blood from the lung to the left atrium.
cards.att: On the right it is formed by veins from the upper and middle lobes; on the left it drains the upper lobe including the lingula. Each passes medially through the hilum, anterior and inferior to the other hilar structures, and opens into the upper part of the posterior wall of the left atrium.
cards.sup: Receives segmental and intersegmental tributaries which run in the intersegmental planes, unlike the arteries and bronchi which are intrasegmental.
cards.rel: At the hilum it is the most anterior and inferior structure. The right superior pulmonary vein passes behind the superior vena cava; the left passes anterior to the descending thoracic aorta and below the left main bronchus.
cards.clin: Muscular sleeves extending from the left atrium into the pulmonary vein ostia are the commonest source of ectopic beats triggering atrial fibrillation, hence pulmonary vein isolation. Pulmonary vein stenosis is a recognised complication of ablation.
cards.exam: Q. Which lobes drain into the right superior pulmonary vein? A. The right upper and middle lobes.

cards.desc: Extra-ocular muscle running forwards and laterally in the roof of the muscle cone to the upper sclera.
cards.att: Origin: upper part of the common tendinous ring (anulus tendineus communis) at the orbital apex. Insertion: sclera on the superior aspect of the eyeball, just behind the corneal limbus.
cards.sup: Superior branch of the oculomotor nerve, CN III, which enters its ocular surface.
cards.act: Elevation, with adduction and intorsion. Tested as pure elevation with the eye abducted.
cards.rel: Levator palpebrae superioris lies immediately above it, with the frontal nerve on the levator; the tendon of superior oblique passes deep to its insertion. The ophthalmic artery and nasociliary nerve cross the optic nerve beneath it.
cards.clin: Oculomotor palsy causes ptosis with the eye down and out. Because superior rectus and levator share a nerve and a common developmental origin, they are affected together, and overaction of one lifts the lid with the other in aberrant regeneration.
cards.exam: Q. In which position of gaze is superior rectus tested as a pure elevator? A. With the eye abducted.

cards.desc: Slender branch of the brachial artery arising near the middle of the arm, just below profunda brachii, and running with the ulnar nerve to the back of the medial epicondyle.
cards.att: Arises from the medial side of the brachial artery about the middle of the arm; pierces the medial intermuscular septum with the ulnar nerve and descends in front of the medial head of triceps; ends behind the medial epicondyle.
cards.sup: Gives muscular twigs to triceps and the medial intermuscular septum region, and an articular branch to the elbow.
cards.act: Supplies the ulnar nerve in the arm and contributes to the arterial anastomosis around the elbow.
cards.rel: Runs with the ulnar nerve throughout its course; lies deep to the medial head of triceps behind the medial epicondyle, superficial to the elbow capsule.
cards.clin: Anastomoses behind the medial epicondyle with the posterior ulnar recurrent artery, so the elbow stays perfused after brachial artery ligation above the anastomosis. Its close relation to the ulnar nerve means it is at risk during ulnar nerve transposition.
cards.exam: Q. Which artery accompanies the ulnar nerve through the medial intermuscular septum? A. The superior ulnar collateral artery, a branch of the brachial artery.

cards.desc: Great vein returning blood from the head, neck, upper limbs and thoracic wall to the right atrium, lying in the right side of the superior and middle mediastinum.
cards.att: Formed behind the lower border of the right first costal cartilage by the union of the right and left brachiocephalic veins; about 7 cm long, it descends and opens into the upper part of the right atrium at the level of the third right costal cartilage. Its lower half lies within the fibrous pericardium.
cards.sup: Receives the azygos vein, which arches forward over the root of the right lung at T4, and small pericardial and mediastinal veins. It has no valves.
cards.rel: Ascending aorta and brachiocephalic artery lie medially; the right phrenic nerve and mediastinal pleura lie laterally; the trachea and right main bronchus lie posteromedially; the right lung and pleura are lateral.
cards.clin: Superior vena cava obstruction, most often by bronchogenic carcinoma or lymphoma, causes facial and upper limb oedema, distended non-pulsatile neck veins and dilated chest wall collaterals. Central venous catheter tips are sited at the cavoatrial junction.
cards.exam: Q. Which vein is the last tributary of the superior vena cava? A. The azygos vein, entering just above the pericardial reflection at the level of T4.

cards.desc: Broad muscle wrapping around the upper third of the radius, forming the floor of the cubital fossa laterally.
cards.att: Origin: lateral epicondyle of the humerus, radial collateral and annular ligaments, and the supinator crest and fossa of the ulna. Insertion: lateral and anterior surfaces of the upper third of the radius, above and below the anterior oblique line.
cards.sup: Deep branch of the radial nerve (posterior interosseous nerve), C6.
cards.act: Supinates the forearm; it acts alone in slow unresisted supination with the elbow extended, biceps being recruited for power.
cards.rel: Its two heads are pierced by the deep branch of the radial nerve, which enters between them at the arcade of Frohse and leaves posteriorly as the posterior interosseous nerve. It covers the upper radius and the tuberosity, deep to the mobile wad and brachioradialis.
cards.clin: Compression of the deep branch of the radial nerve at the arcade of Frohse gives posterior interosseous nerve syndrome, with finger drop and preserved wrist extension in radial deviation, and no sensory loss. Supinator is released in surgery for this entrapment.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve pierces supinator and what does its compression cause? A. The deep branch of the radial nerve; compression at the arcade of Frohse causes posterior interosseous nerve syndrome with finger drop and no sensory loss.

cards.desc: The larger terminal branch of the frontal nerve, leaving the orbit at the supra-orbital notch or foramen to supply the forehead and scalp.
cards.att: Arises from the frontal nerve about the middle of the orbit, passes forwards on levator palpebrae superioris, leaves through the supra-orbital notch or foramen with the supra-orbital vessels, and divides into medial and lateral branches that ascend over the forehead.
cards.act: Sensory to the conjunctiva and skin of the upper eyelid, the skin of the forehead and scalp as far back as the vertex and the lambdoid suture, and the mucous membrane of the frontal sinus.
cards.rel: Lies deep to frontalis and the galea aponeurotica on the forehead, with the supra-orbital artery; the supratrochlear nerve lies medial to it.
cards.clin: The supra-orbital notch lies at the junction of the medial third and lateral two-thirds of the supra-orbital margin, in line with the pupil, and is the point for a supra-orbital nerve block in forehead laceration repair. Frontal sinusitis refers pain to its territory.
cards.exam: Q. How far back on the scalp does the supra-orbital nerve supply sensation? A. To the vertex, up to the lambdoid suture.

cards.desc: The gyrus of the inferior parietal lobule that arches round the upturned posterior end of the posterior ramus of the lateral sulcus, Brodmann area 40.
cards.att: Connected to the inferior frontal gyrus by the arcuate fasciculus and to the superior temporal and angular gyri; part of the wider Wernicke's territory in the dominant hemisphere.
cards.sup: Inferior division of the middle cerebral artery.
cards.act: Phonological processing and verbal working memory in the dominant hemisphere, and spatial attention and body awareness in the non-dominant hemisphere.
cards.rel: Lies above and behind the posterior end of the lateral sulcus, in front of the angular gyrus, which caps the superior temporal sulcus; the superior temporal gyrus lies below.
cards.clin: Dominant lesions cause conduction aphasia with disproportionate loss of repetition, and ideomotor apraxia. Non-dominant lesions cause contralateral hemispatial neglect and anosognosia.
cards.exam: Q. Damage to which tract beneath the supramarginal gyrus causes conduction aphasia? A. The arcuate fasciculus.

cards.desc: Branch of the thyrocervical trunk that crosses the root of the neck to reach the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae.
cards.att: Arises from the thyrocervical trunk of the first part of the subclavian artery; runs laterally across scalenus anterior, the phrenic nerve and the third part of the subclavian artery, then behind the clavicle; passes above the superior transverse scapular ligament into the supraspinous fossa and round the spinoglenoid notch into the infraspinous fossa.
cards.sup: Suprasternal, acromial and articular branches, and a branch to the subscapular fossa.
cards.act: Supplies supraspinatus, infraspinatus, the acromioclavicular and shoulder joints, and forms a key link in the scapular anastomosis.
cards.rel: Passes above the superior transverse scapular ligament while the suprascapular nerve passes below it; lies deep to the clavicle and subclavius.
cards.clin: With the dorsal scapular and subscapular arteries it forms the scapular anastomosis, which maintains upper limb flow when the subclavian or axillary artery is occluded between the thyrocervical trunk and the subscapular artery. Spared in thoracic outlet ligations.
cards.exam: Q. What is the relation of the suprascapular artery and nerve to the superior transverse scapular ligament? A. Artery above the ligament, nerve below it.

cards.desc: Rotator cuff muscle occupying the supraspinous fossa above the spine of the scapula.
cards.att: Origin: medial two-thirds of the supraspinous fossa and the overlying supraspinous fascia. Insertion: superior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus and the capsule of the shoulder joint.
cards.sup: Suprascapular nerve (C5, C6).
cards.act: Initiates abduction of the arm for roughly the first 15 degrees and holds the head of the humerus against the glenoid cavity while deltoid continues the movement.
cards.rel: Its tendon runs beneath the coracoacromial arch, separated from the acromion and the deltoid by the subacromial bursa. The suprascapular nerve reaches it through the suprascapular notch under the superior transverse scapular ligament, while the vessels pass above the ligament.
cards.clin: The most commonly torn tendon of the rotator cuff, especially in its relatively avascular critical zone near the insertion; tears give a painful arc between 60 and 120 degrees of abduction and a positive empty can test. Calcific tendinitis and subacromial impingement occur at the same site.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle initiates abduction of the arm and what nerve supplies it? A. Supraspinatus, supplied by the suprascapular nerve (C5, C6).

cards.desc: The smaller, medial terminal branch of the frontal nerve, leaving the orbit above the trochlea of superior oblique.
cards.att: Arises from the frontal nerve in the orbit, passes forwards and medially above the trochlea, gives a branch to the infratrochlear nerve, and ascends on the forehead deep to corrugator supercilii and frontalis.
cards.act: Sensory to the skin and conjunctiva of the medial part of the upper eyelid and the skin of the lower medial forehead.
cards.rel: Runs above the trochlea, medial to the supra-orbital nerve, accompanied by the supratrochlear artery, a branch of the ophthalmic artery.
cards.clin: Blocked with the supra-orbital nerve for forehead procedures. The paramedian forehead flap used to reconstruct the nose is raised on the supratrochlear artery, which runs with this nerve about 1.7 to 2 cm from the midline.
cards.exam: Q. Which two nerves are the terminal branches of the frontal nerve? A. The supra-orbital and supratrochlear nerves.

cards.desc: System of fine radial fibres that slings the lens from the ciliary body, holding it in the optical axis behind the iris.
cards.att: Fibres arise from the ciliary processes and the pars plana of the ciliary body and insert into the lens capsule at and around its equator.
cards.act: Transmits the pull of the ciliary body to the lens: ciliary muscle contraction relaxes the zonule so the elastic lens becomes more convex for near vision, and relaxation of the muscle tightens the zonule and flattens the lens for distance.
cards.rel: Bounded in front by the posterior chamber and iris, behind by the vitreous body and the hyaloid fossa; the spaces between the fibres form the zonular spaces.
cards.clin: Zonular weakness causes ectopia lentis: superotemporal subluxation of the lens in Marfan syndrome and inferonasal subluxation in homocystinuria. Zonular dehiscence complicates cataract surgery. Accommodation is driven by parasympathetic fibres of the oculomotor nerve relaying in the ciliary ganglion.
cards.exam: Q. What happens to the zonular fibres and the lens when the ciliary muscle contracts? A. The zonule slackens and the lens becomes more convex, increasing its refractive power for near vision.

cards.desc: One of the three longitudinal bands of thickened outer smooth muscle of the large intestine, the one free from any peritoneal or omental attachment.
cards.att: Runs the length of the caecum and colon as far as the rectosigmoid junction, where the taeniae spread out into a continuous longitudinal layer. It lies on the anterior surface of the ascending and descending colon and on the inferior (anteroinferior) surface of the transverse colon. All three taeniae converge at the base of the appendix.
cards.sup: Smooth muscle supplied by the enteric nervous system with sympathetic and parasympathetic modulation, through the mesenteric arterial territory of the segment concerned.
cards.act: Its tonic shortening gathers the colonic wall into sacculations (haustra); with the circular muscle it produces segmental and mass movements.
cards.rel: Free of attachment, unlike the mesocolic taenia (mesenteric attachment) and the omental taenia (attachment of the appendices epiploicae and greater omentum). Appendices epiploicae are related along its length except on the caecum and rectum.
cards.clin: Following the taeniae to their convergence is the reliable way to find the base of the appendix at operation. Being free of attachment, this band is the safest line for a longitudinal colotomy, and the taeniae are the feature that identifies large from small bowel at laparotomy.
cards.exam: Q. Where does the free taenia lie on the transverse colon? A. On its inferior (anteroinferior) surface, having been anterior on the ascending colon.

cards.desc: Longitudinal muscular band of the large intestine that lies along the line of mesenteric or mesocolic attachment.
cards.att: Runs from the base of the appendix, where all three taeniae converge, to the rectosigmoid junction. It lies posteromedial on the ascending and descending colon and posterosuperior on the transverse colon along the attachment of the transverse mesocolon; on the sigmoid colon it follows the sigmoid mesocolic attachment.
cards.sup: Smooth muscle under enteric, sympathetic and parasympathetic control, supplied by the vessels of the corresponding colonic segment.
cards.act: Shortens the colon and, with the other two taeniae, forms the haustra.
cards.rel: Marks the line of the mesocolon; the omental taenia lies posterolateral on the ascending and descending colon and anterosuperior on the transverse colon, and the free taenia lies anteriorly or inferiorly.
cards.clin: It identifies the mesenteric border of the colon and so the plane for safe division of the mesocolon with preservation of the marginal artery in colonic resection. Because the omental and mesocolic taeniae mark attachment sites, the free taenia rather than this one is chosen for a longitudinal colotomy.
cards.exam: Q. Name the three taeniae coli and their positions on the transverse colon. A. Mesocolic (posterosuperior), omental (anterosuperior) and free (inferior).

cards.desc: One of the three longitudinal bands of thickened outer muscle coat of the colon, the band along which the greater omentum is attached to the transverse colon.
cards.att: Runs the length of the caecum and colon; on the transverse colon it lies along the anterosuperior surface at the line of omental attachment, and on the ascending and descending colon it lies posterolaterally. All three taeniae converge at the base of the appendix and fan out on the rectum.
cards.sup: Smooth muscle: enteric plexuses, with sympathetic fibres from the superior and inferior mesenteric plexuses and parasympathetic supply from the vagus proximal to the left colic flexure and pelvic splanchnic nerves distal to it.
cards.act: Being shorter than the colon, the taeniae gather the wall into sacculations (haustra) and shorten the bowel during mass peristalsis.
cards.rel: The greater omentum hangs from it on the transverse colon; the taenia libera lies free anteriorly on the ascending and descending colon and the taenia mesocolica at the mesenteric attachment.
cards.clin: Tracing any taenia distally on the caecum leads to the base of the appendix, the standard surgical manoeuvre for finding a retrocaecal appendix. Loss of taeniae distally marks the rectosigmoid junction.
cards.exam: Q. Which taenia coli carries the attachment of the greater omentum? A. The taenia omentalis, on the anterosuperior aspect of the transverse colon.

cards.desc: Tarsal bone that transmits the whole body weight from the tibia to the foot and has no muscle attached to it.
cards.att: Has a head, neck and body. The trochlea of the body, wider in front than behind, articulates with the lower end of the tibia, with the medial malleolus medially and the lateral malleolus laterally; the head articulates with the navicular and rests on the spring ligament. The inferior surface has posterior, middle and anterior facets for the calcaneus separated by the sulcus tali, which with the calcaneal sulcus forms the sinus tarsi. The posterior process has medial and lateral tubercles with the groove for flexor hallucis longus between them.
cards.act: Transmits body weight from the leg to the foot, dividing it backwards to the calcaneus and forwards to the navicular; its trochlea is the moving part of the ankle joint.
cards.rel: Tibia and both malleoli above and at the sides, calcaneus below, navicular in front. Flexor hallucis longus runs in the groove on its posterior process; the deltoid ligament and lateral collateral ligaments attach to it.
cards.clin: Blood supply enters mainly through the neck, from the artery of the tarsal canal off the posterior tibial, deltoid branches and the artery of the sinus tarsi, so a fracture of the neck can render the body avascular. An os trigonum is a separated lateral tubercle and causes posterior ankle impingement in dancers and footballers. The wedge shaped trochlea makes the ankle most stable in dorsiflexion, and sprains occur in plantar flexion.
cards.exam: Q. Why does avascular necrosis follow a fracture of the neck of the talus? A. Because the blood supply to the body enters through the neck and runs backwards, and there are no muscular attachments to bring a second supply.

cards.desc: Dense fibrous plate about 10 mm high forming the skeleton of the upper eyelid.
cards.att: Attached medially and laterally by the palpebral ligaments; the aponeurosis of levator palpebrae superioris inserts into its anterior surface and the overlying skin, and the superior tarsal muscle of Muller passes from the levator to its upper border. Contains about 25 to 30 tarsal (Meibomian) glands.
cards.sup: Superior palpebral arcade from the ophthalmic artery; sensory supply from the supraorbital, supratrochlear and lacrimal nerves (V1). Levator is supplied by the oculomotor nerve, the superior tarsal muscle by sympathetic fibres.
cards.act: Gives the lid its form and, through the levator inserting on it, raises the upper lid; the superior tarsal muscle maintains lid elevation tonically.
cards.rel: Skin, orbicularis oculi and levator aponeurosis in front; palpebral conjunctiva behind, closely adherent, which is why the lid can be everted over a glass rod.
cards.clin: Loss of sympathetic supply to the superior tarsal muscle gives the partial ptosis of Horner syndrome, unlike the complete ptosis of an oculomotor palsy. Foreign bodies lodge in the subtarsal sulcus and are found by everting the lid.
cards.exam: Q. Compare the ptosis of Horner syndrome with that of a third nerve palsy. A. Horner gives slight ptosis from paralysis of the smooth superior tarsal muscle, with miosis; third nerve palsy gives complete ptosis from levator paralysis, with a dilated pupil and a down and out eye.

cards.desc: Paired bone of the side and base of the skull that houses the middle and internal ear.
cards.att: Parts: squamous (with the zygomatic process and mandibular fossa), petrous (containing the ear and the internal acoustic meatus), mastoid (with the mastoid process and air cells), tympanic (forming the external acoustic meatus), and the styloid process. Openings include the external and internal acoustic meatus, carotid canal, jugular fossa, stylomastoid foramen, facial canal and the petrotympanic fissure. Articulates with the parietal, occipital, sphenoid, zygomatic and mandible.
cards.act: Encloses the auditory and vestibular apparatus, forms the temporomandibular joint, and gives attachment to sternocleidomastoid, the digastric posterior belly, and the styloid muscles.
cards.rel: Temporal lobe above the petrous part, sigmoid sinus in the mastoid, internal carotid artery in the carotid canal, internal jugular vein in the jugular fossa, facial nerve in the facial canal.
cards.clin: Fracture of the petrous temporal bone may cause CSF otorrhoea, haemotympanum, facial nerve palsy and deafness, with bruising over the mastoid (Battle's sign). Middle ear infection can spread to the mastoid air cells causing mastoiditis, and thence intracranially.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve emerges from the stylomastoid foramen? A. The facial nerve.

syn: white line of pelvic fascia (levator ani origin)
cards.desc: Linear thickening of the obturator internus fascia stretching from the posterior aspect of the body of the pubis to the ischial spine, giving origin to levator ani.
cards.att: Extends from the pubis anteriorly to the ischial spine posteriorly across the fascia of obturator internus; gives origin to the posterior fibres of pubococcygeus and to iliococcygeus.
cards.act: Provides a fixed fascial line of origin that allows the pelvic diaphragm to span the side wall of the pelvis without a bony attachment along its length.
cards.rel: Overlies obturator internus and its fascia; the obturator nerve and vessels lie above it, the ischioanal fossa below and lateral to the levator ani arising from it.
cards.clin: Must be distinguished from the arcus tendineus fasciae pelvis, the more medial line that suspends the bladder and vagina and is reattached in paravaginal repair. It is a key landmark in pelvic floor reconstructive surgery and in defining a cystocele.
cards.exam: Q. What are the bony ends of the tendinous arch of levator ani? A. The body of the pubis in front and the ischial spine behind.

cards.desc: The flat terminal tendon of levator palpebrae superioris, which fans out over the upper eyelid as the levator aponeurosis.
cards.att: Continues from the muscle belly at the level of the superior orbital margin, passes through the orbital septum, and inserts into the skin of the upper eyelid and the anterior surface of the superior tarsal plate; its medial and lateral horns attach to the orbital walls at the canthi.
cards.sup: The muscle it belongs to is supplied by the superior branch of the oculomotor nerve, CN III; the deep smooth muscle sheet on its undersurface, the superior tarsal muscle of Muller, is sympathetic.
cards.act: Transmits the pull of levator palpebrae superioris to elevate and retract the upper eyelid.
cards.rel: Lies deep to the orbital septum and superficial to the superior tarsal muscle and conjunctiva; the whitnall (superior transverse) ligament crosses above it, and superior rectus lies immediately beneath the muscle belly.
cards.clin: Dehiscence or disinsertion of this aponeurosis from the tarsal plate is the commonest cause of acquired ptosis in the elderly, giving a high lid crease with normal levator function. Loss of the sympathetic superior tarsal muscle gives the partial ptosis of Horner syndrome.
cards.exam: Q. Why is the ptosis of Horner syndrome only partial? A. Only the smooth superior tarsal muscle is denervated; the striated levator, supplied by CN III, still works.

cards.desc: Short muscle enclosed between the two layers of the fascia lata on the upper anterolateral thigh, ending in the iliotibial tract.
cards.att: Origin: outer lip of the iliac crest between the anterior superior iliac spine and the iliac tubercle, and the notch below the anterior superior iliac spine. Insertion: iliotibial tract, about one third of the way down the thigh.
cards.sup: Superior gluteal nerve, L4, L5, S1.
cards.act: Tenses the fascia lata and iliotibial tract, assists abduction, medial rotation and flexion of the thigh, and helps steady the pelvis and the extended knee in standing and walking.
cards.rel: Lies in front of gluteus medius and lateral to sartorius and rectus femoris; the ascending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery supplies it and lies on its deep surface.
cards.clin: Injury to the superior gluteal nerve, which also supplies gluteus medius and minimus, gives a positive Trendelenburg sign. A tight iliotibial tract from this muscle is detected by Ober's test and contributes to lateral knee pain.
cards.exam: Q. What is the nerve supply of tensor fasciae latae? A. The superior gluteal nerve, L4, L5, S1.

cards.desc: Thin triangular muscle of the soft palate lateral to the auditory tube, whose tendon hooks around the pterygoid hamulus to become the palatine aponeurosis.
cards.att: Origin: scaphoid fossa of the sphenoid, the spine of the sphenoid, and the lateral wall of the cartilaginous part of the auditory tube. Its tendon turns medially round the pterygoid hamulus and expands as the palatine aponeurosis, attached to the posterior border of the hard palate.
cards.sup: Nerve to medial pterygoid, from the mandibular nerve, CN V3.
cards.act: Tenses the soft palate and opens the auditory tube during swallowing and yawning.
cards.rel: Lies lateral to levator veli palatini and the auditory tube, medial to the medial pterygoid; the mandibular nerve, otic ganglion and chorda tympani lie on its lateral surface at the skull base, the ganglion between the nerve trunk and the muscle.
cards.clin: The only palatal muscle not supplied by the pharyngeal plexus, so it is spared in vagal lesions. In cleft palate its abnormal insertion impairs tubal opening, causing persistent otitis media with effusion and conductive deafness.
cards.exam: Q. Which is the only muscle of the soft palate not supplied by the pharyngeal plexus, and what supplies it? A. Tensor veli palatini, by the nerve to medial pterygoid from CN V3.

cards.desc: Tenth rib, the lowest vertebrochondral rib, whose cartilage joins that of the 9th to complete the costal margin.
cards.att: Head usually has a single whole facet articulating with the body of T10 alone; the tubercle articulates with the transverse process of T10, unlike ribs 11 and 12 which have no such articulation. Gives attachment to the oblique abdominal muscles, latissimus dorsi, serratus posterior inferior and the costal part of the diaphragm.
cards.sup: Tenth posterior intercostal artery; the 10th intercostal nerve runs in its groove and continues into the abdominal wall towards the umbilical dermatome.
cards.act: Bucket-handle elevation of the lower thorax; completes the costal margin, the palpable lower limit of the chest wall.
cards.rel: Diaphragm and costodiaphragmatic recess internally; liver on the right and spleen and stomach on the left beneath the diaphragm; kidney posteriorly.
cards.clin: The pleural reflection crosses the 10th rib in the midaxillary line, so a needle placed below it there enters the abdomen. Fracture of the left lower ribs 9 to 11 is the classic mechanism for splenic rupture.
cards.exam: Q. Which is the lowest rib to articulate with a transverse process? A. The 10th; ribs 11 and 12 have no tubercle and no costotransverse joint.

cards.desc: Lower thoracic vertebra with a large body bearing a single complete costal facet on each side for the head of the 10th rib.
cards.att: One whole superior costal facet on each side, encroaching on the pedicle, for the head of rib 10; the transverse process still carries a facet for the tubercle of rib 10, the last vertebra to do so. The spine is shorter and less inclined than in the mid-thoracic region.
cards.sup: Segmental branches of the lower posterior intercostal arteries; dorsal rami to the facet joints.
cards.act: Load transmission at the transition towards the lumbar column; facet orientation begins to change from coronal to sagittal.
cards.rel: The oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm lies at this level in the muscular right crus; the aorta lies posterior and slightly to the left, the azygos vein to the right.
cards.clin: The oesophageal hiatus at T10 transmits the oesophagus, the anterior and posterior vagal trunks and the oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels, and is the site of sliding hiatus hernia. The T10 dermatome lies at the umbilicus.
cards.exam: Q. Which structures pass through the diaphragm at T10? A. The oesophagus, both vagal trunks, and the oesophageal branches of the left gastric artery and vein.

cards.desc: A crescentic, tent-shaped fold of dura mater roofing the posterior cranial fossa, separating the cerebellum below from the occipital lobes above.
cards.att: Its convex attached margin is fixed behind and laterally to the lips of the transverse sulci of the occipital bone and the posteroinferior parietal angle, and in front to the superior border of the petrous temporal bone and the posterior clinoid process; the free concave margin runs forward to the anterior clinoid process, bounding the tentorial notch.
cards.sup: Enclosed sinuses: transverse sinuses in the attached posterior margin, superior petrosal sinuses in the petrous attachment, straight sinus along the line where the falx cerebri joins it.
cards.act: Supports the occipital lobes, restricts displacement of the brain, and divides the cranial cavity into supratentorial and infratentorial compartments.
cards.rel: The midbrain passes through the tentorial notch, with the oculomotor nerve and posterior cerebral artery running close to the free edge; the falx cerebri is attached to its upper surface in the midline and the falx cerebelli below.
cards.clin: Raised supratentorial pressure forces the uncus through the tentorial notch: the third nerve is compressed, giving an ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, and the opposite crus is pressed on the free edge, producing a false localising ipsilateral hemiparesis (Kernohan notch).
cards.exam: Q. What structures pass through the tentorial notch? A. The midbrain, with the oculomotor and trochlear nerves and the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries nearby.

cards.desc: Thick rounded muscle running from the inferior angle of the scapula to the humerus, forming the lower border of the posterior axillary wall.
cards.att: Origin: oval area on the dorsal surface of the inferior angle and lower part of the lateral border of the scapula. Insertion: medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus.
cards.sup: Lower subscapular nerve (C5, C6).
cards.act: Adducts, medially rotates and extends the arm at the shoulder joint.
cards.rel: With the long head of triceps it forms the boundaries of the triangular and quadrangular spaces, and it makes the lower border of both spaces. Latissimus dorsi wraps round its lower border to reach the floor of the intertubercular sulcus. It is not part of the rotator cuff.
cards.clin: The lower border of teres major marks the point where the axillary artery becomes the brachial artery, an important surgical and radiological landmark. The muscle is used as a pedicled transfer to restore external rotation in brachial plexus injury.
cards.exam: Q. At what level does the axillary artery become the brachial artery? A. At the lower border of teres major.

cards.desc: Narrow rotator cuff muscle on the upper part of the lateral border of the scapula, blending with the back of the shoulder capsule.
cards.att: Origin: upper two-thirds of the dorsal surface of the lateral border of the scapula. Insertion: inferior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus and the capsule of the shoulder joint.
cards.sup: Axillary nerve (C5, C6), usually through the branch bearing the pseudoganglion.
cards.act: Laterally rotates the arm and holds the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity.
cards.rel: Forms the upper boundary of the quadrangular space, with teres major below, the long head of triceps medially and the surgical neck of the humerus laterally. Infraspinatus lies above and often blends with it.
cards.clin: Isolated fatty atrophy of teres minor on MRI suggests quadrilateral space syndrome, compression of the axillary nerve between teres minor, teres major, the long head of triceps and the humerus. It is the only cuff muscle supplied by the axillary nerve.
cards.exam: Q. Which rotator cuff muscle is supplied by the axillary nerve? A. Teres minor (C5, C6).

cards.desc: Long, slender branch of the abdominal aorta that descends retroperitoneally to supply the testis and epididymis.
cards.att: Arises from the anterolateral aorta just below the renal artery at about the L2 vertebral level, descends on psoas major crossing the ureter and the external iliac artery, enters the deep inguinal ring and runs in the spermatic cord to the posterior border of the testis.
cards.sup: Gives ureteric branches and an epididymal branch; anastomoses with the artery to the ductus deferens and the cremasteric artery.
cards.act: Supplies the testis and epididymis.
cards.rel: Crosses anterior to the ureter and the genitofemoral nerve on psoas major. The right artery passes anterior to the inferior vena cava. In the cord it lies among the veins of the pampiniform plexus.
cards.clin: Its high origin explains why testicular pain is referred to the loin and periumbilical region (T10). The pampiniform plexus acts as a countercurrent heat exchanger around it, and the artery is at risk during varicocele ligation and inguinal hernia repair.
cards.exam: Q. At what vertebral level does the testicular artery arise? A. L2, from the abdominal aorta just below the renal artery.

cards.desc: Vein formed from the pampiniform plexus of the spermatic cord, ascending retroperitoneally to drain into the inferior vena cava on the right and the left renal vein on the left.
cards.att: Begins as the pampiniform plexus around the testicular artery, condenses to a single vein near the deep inguinal ring, ascends on psoas major, and ends in the inferior vena cava at an acute angle on the right and in the left renal vein at a right angle on the left.
cards.sup: Drains the testis, epididymis and coverings; communicates with the cremasteric and deferential veins.
cards.act: Venous drainage of the testis; the pampiniform plexus cools arterial blood entering the testis.
cards.rel: Runs with the testicular artery anterior to the ureter and psoas major. The left vein passes behind the descending colon and its termination lies close to the left suprarenal vein.
cards.clin: Varicocele is far commoner on the left because of the right-angled drainage into the left renal vein, the longer column of blood and possible compression of the left renal vein between the aorta and superior mesenteric artery. A sudden left varicocele in an older man suggests a left renal carcinoma invading the renal vein.
cards.exam: Q. Why are varicoceles commoner on the left? A. The left testicular vein drains at a right angle into the left renal vein, giving a longer, higher-resistance column of blood.

cards.desc: Paired oval male gonad suspended in the scrotum by the spermatic cord, producing spermatozoa and testosterone.
cards.att: Enclosed in the tough tunica albuginea, which sends septa from the mediastinum testis dividing it into about 250 lobules of seminiferous tubules; tubules drain through the rete testis and efferent ductules into the head of the epididymis. The tunica vaginalis covers all but the posterior bare area.
cards.sup: Testicular artery from the abdominal aorta at L2; veins form the pampiniform plexus, the right testicular vein draining into the inferior vena cava and the left into the left renal vein. Nerves from the T10 sympathetic segment via the renal and aortic plexuses. Lymph drains to the para-aortic (lumbar) nodes at L2.
cards.act: Spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules; testosterone secretion by interstitial (Leydig) cells.
cards.rel: Epididymis posterolateral, spermatic cord above, tunica vaginalis in front and at the sides; the scrotal skin and dartos are superficial.
cards.clin: Testicular pain is referred to the periumbilical region because of the T10 supply. Torsion occurs with a bell-clapper deformity and demands surgery within six hours. Varicocele is far commoner on the left, where the testicular vein joins the left renal vein at a right angle. Testicular tumours spread to para-aortic nodes, while scrotal skin drains to superficial inguinal nodes.
cards.exam: Q. To which lymph nodes does the testis drain? A. Para-aortic (lumbar) nodes at L2, following its embryological origin, not the inguinal nodes.

cards.desc: A large ovoid mass of grey matter forming the greater part of the diencephalon on each side of the third ventricle, the great sensory relay station to the cortex.
cards.att: Nuclei are divided by the internal medullary lamina; ventral posterolateral and ventral posteromedial nuclei relay the medial lemniscus, spinothalamic and trigeminal pathways to the postcentral gyrus, the lateral and medial geniculate bodies relay vision and hearing, ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei relay cerebellar and basal ganglia input to the motor cortex, the dorsomedial nucleus connects with the prefrontal cortex and the anterior nucleus with the cingulate gyrus through the mammillothalamic tract.
cards.sup: Thalamoperforating and thalamogeniculate branches of the posterior cerebral artery and branches of the posterior communicating artery.
cards.act: Relays all sensory modalities except olfaction to the cerebral cortex, and participates in motor control, memory, arousal and the affective response to pain.
cards.rel: Third ventricle medially, with the interthalamic adhesion crossing it; posterior limb of the internal capsule laterally; caudate nucleus and body of the lateral ventricle above, separated by the stria terminalis and thalamostriate vein; hypothalamic sulcus below; the pulvinar overhangs the geniculate bodies and superior colliculus behind.
cards.clin: Thalamogeniculate infarction gives contralateral hemianaesthesia followed by Dejerine-Roussy syndrome, spontaneous burning thalamic pain with hyperpathia. Thalamic haemorrhage classically produces downward and inward deviation of the eyes.
cards.exam: Q. Which thalamic nucleus relays the medial lemniscus and spinothalamic tract from the body? A. The ventral posterolateral nucleus.

cards.desc: Bar of hyaline cartilage joining the anterior end of the third rib to the lateral border of the body of the sternum.
cards.att: Runs medially and slightly downwards from the costochondral junction of the third rib to the third sternocostal joint, a synovial joint on the side of the sternal body just below the sternal angle.
cards.act: Gives elasticity to the thoracic cage, allowing the rib to spring during inspiration and to recoil in expiration.
cards.rel: Pectoralis major arises from its anterior surface and pectoralis minor from the third rib close by; transversus thoracis and the internal thoracic vessels lie behind it. The third intercostal space lies immediately below.
cards.clin: Costochondritis and Tietze syndrome typically affect the second to fourth costal cartilages, causing anterior chest pain that mimics cardiac pain but is reproduced by local pressure. Costal cartilage is harvested as graft material for rhinoplasty and ear reconstruction.
cards.exam: Q. Which sternocostal joints are synovial? A. The second to the seventh; the first is a primary cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis).

cards.desc: The middle lumbar vertebra, bearing the longest transverse processes of the lumbar series.
cards.att: Large kidney-shaped body, short stout pedicles, long transverse processes, hatchet-shaped spinous process. Articulates with L2 above and L4 below.
cards.sup: Third lumbar arteries from the abdominal aorta; vertebral venous plexuses.
cards.rel: The subcostal plane crosses this vertebra. The inferior mesenteric artery arises at its level; the third part of the duodenum crosses the aorta here; the umbilicus overlies the L3/L4 region in the adult.
cards.clin: Its long transverse processes are the commonest lumbar transverse process to be avulsed or fractured in direct trauma. The L3/L4 interspace is a routine site for spinal anaesthesia.
cards.exam: Q. Which lumbar vertebra has the longest transverse processes? A. The third.

cards.desc: Metacarpal of the middle finger, distinguished from the others by a styloid process projecting from the radial side of its dorsal base.
cards.att: Base articulates with the capitate and with the second and fourth metacarpals; the head articulates with the proximal phalanx of the middle finger. Extensor carpi radialis brevis inserts on the dorsal surface of the base, the transverse head of adductor pollicis arises from the palmar ridge of the shaft, and the second and third dorsal interossei arise from its sides.
cards.act: Forms the central axis of the hand: abduction and adduction of the fingers by the interossei are defined as movement away from and towards a line drawn through the third digit.
cards.rel: Capitate proximally; the deep palmar arch and the deep branch of the ulnar nerve cross the bases of the metacarpals palmar to it, under cover of the long flexor tendons and adductor pollicis.
cards.clin: A hard fixed dorsal lump over the second and third carpometacarpal joints, the carpal boss, is a common cause of dorsal wrist pain and can be mistaken for a ganglion. The styloid process may be misread as a carpal fracture fragment on radiographs.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle inserts into the base of the third metacarpal? A. Extensor carpi radialis brevis, on the dorsal surface of the base.

cards.desc: A typical rib of the upper thorax, the first rib with the full typical form of head, neck, tubercle, angle and shaft.
cards.att: The head bears two facets that articulate with the bodies of T2 and T3 and the disc between them; the tubercle articulates with the transverse process of T3; the anterior end joins the third costal cartilage. A costal groove runs along the inner aspect of the lower border.
cards.act: Forms part of the thoracic wall and moves at its vertebral joints in the pump-handle and bucket-handle manner during respiration.
cards.rel: The third intercostal nerve and vessels lie in the costal groove on its inferior aspect. Pectoralis minor arises from ribs 3, 4 and 5 in front, and a digitation of serratus anterior arises from its outer surface.
cards.clin: The upper three ribs are shielded by the clavicle and scapula, so a fracture here indicates high-energy trauma and should prompt a search for brachial plexus, subclavian vessel and lung injury.
cards.exam: Q. With which vertebrae does the head of the third rib articulate? A. The bodies of T2 and T3 and the intervertebral disc between them.

cards.desc: Typical upper thoracic vertebra, lying at the level of the medial end (root) of the spine of the scapula.
cards.att: Heart-shaped body carrying superior and inferior costal demifacets for the heads of the third and fourth ribs; the transverse process bears a facet for the tubercle of the third rib; the spinous process is long and directed sharply downwards, overlapping the vertebra below.
cards.act: Transmits axial load, articulates with two pairs of ribs, and permits rotation while its facet orientation limits flexion and extension.
cards.rel: The trachea, oesophagus and the arch of the aorta lie in front of the upper thoracic bodies; the spinal cord occupies a relatively narrow canal at this level. The medial end of the scapular spine is at the T3 spine.
cards.clin: The T3 spinous process is the standard surface landmark for the root of the spine of the scapula, used when counting vertebral levels. The upper thoracic spine is a common site of metastatic deposits and tuberculous spondylitis, where the narrow canal makes cord compression likely.
cards.exam: Q. Which spinous process lies level with the root of the spine of the scapula? A. T3.

cards.desc: A narrow midline cleft of the diencephalon between the two thalami and hypothalami, part of the ventricular system.
cards.att: Communicates in front with each lateral ventricle through the interventricular foramen of Monro, and behind with the fourth ventricle through the cerebral aqueduct; it has supraoptic, infundibular, pineal and suprapineal recesses.
cards.sup: Choroid plexus in the roof supplied by the medial posterior choroidal arteries; the plexus secretes cerebrospinal fluid.
cards.act: Contains and conducts cerebrospinal fluid from the lateral ventricles to the fourth ventricle.
cards.rel: Roof formed by ependyma and the tela choroidea with the internal cerebral veins; floor from front to back by the optic chiasma, tuber cinereum and infundibulum, mammillary bodies, posterior perforated substance and tegmentum of the midbrain; anterior wall by the lamina terminalis and anterior commissure; posterior wall by the pineal stalk with the habenular and posterior commissures.
cards.clin: A colloid cyst at the interventricular foramen causes intermittent obstructive hydrocephalus with positional headache and drop attacks. Endoscopic third ventriculostomy makes an opening in the floor between the infundibulum and mammillary bodies to bypass aqueduct stenosis.
cards.exam: Q. Name the boundaries of the floor of the third ventricle from front to back. A. Optic chiasma, tuber cinereum and infundibulum, mammillary bodies, posterior perforated substance, midbrain tegmentum.

cards.desc: Terminal continuation of the subscapular artery, the chief artery of latissimus dorsi, running on the posterior wall of the axilla.
cards.att: Arises as the larger terminal branch of the subscapular artery from the third part of the axillary artery, the other being the circumflex scapular artery; it descends along the lateral border of the scapula with the thoracodorsal nerve and enters the deep surface of latissimus dorsi, where it divides into transverse and descending branches.
cards.sup: Supplies latissimus dorsi, serratus anterior, subscapularis and the adjacent chest wall skin.
cards.rel: Runs with the thoracodorsal nerve (C6, C7, C8) on the deep surface of latissimus dorsi, behind the axillary vein and lateral to the long thoracic nerve on the medial axillary wall.
cards.clin: The vascular pedicle of the latissimus dorsi myocutaneous flap in breast and chest wall reconstruction. It and its nerve are at risk during axillary lymph node clearance.
cards.exam: Q. What is the parent vessel of the thoracodorsal artery? A. The subscapular artery, from the third part of the axillary artery.

cards.desc: Broad intrinsic laryngeal muscle forming the muscular bulk of the vocal fold, lateral to the vocal ligament.
cards.att: Origin: inner surface of the thyroid lamina near the angle and the adjacent cricothyroid ligament. Insertion: anterolateral surface and vocal process of the arytenoid cartilage; upper fibres continue into the aryepiglottic fold as the thyro-epiglottic muscle.
cards.sup: Recurrent laryngeal nerve, a branch of the vagus, CN X.
cards.act: Relaxes and shortens the vocal ligament, lowering pitch, and adducts the vocal fold. Its medial fibres form the vocalis.
cards.rel: Lies lateral to the vocal ligament and conus elasticus, medial to the thyroid lamina and the paraglottic space, and anterolateral to lateral cricoarytenoid.
cards.clin: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury during thyroidectomy paralyses it with the other intrinsic muscles except cricothyroid, giving hoarseness. The paraglottic space lateral to it is a route of deep spread for glottic carcinoma.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve supplies all the intrinsic muscles of the larynx except cricothyroid? A. The recurrent laryngeal nerve.

cards.desc: Short quadrilateral infrahyoid (strap) muscle, effectively the upward continuation of sternothyroid, bridging thyroid cartilage to hyoid bone.
cards.att: Origin: oblique line on the lamina of the thyroid cartilage. Insertion: lower border of the body and greater horn of the hyoid bone.
cards.sup: Fibres of the anterior ramus of C1 that travel with the hypoglossal nerve.
cards.act: Depresses the hyoid bone; with the hyoid fixed it elevates the larynx, as in swallowing and high-pitched phonation.
cards.rel: Deep to sternohyoid and omohyoid, superficial to the thyrohyoid membrane, which is pierced by the internal laryngeal nerve and the superior laryngeal vessels.
cards.clin: The thyrohyoid membrane beneath it is the target for an internal laryngeal nerve block before awake intubation or endoscopy. C1 fibres to it and to geniohyoid leave the hypoglossal nerve, so both are spared in a true hypoglossal lesion.
cards.exam: Q. What is the nerve supply of thyrohyoid? A. Fibres of C1 carried by the hypoglossal nerve.

cards.desc: Broad fibro-elastic sheet joining the upper border of the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone.
cards.att: Attached below to the upper border of the thyroid lamina and the superior horn, and above to the upper border of the posterior surface of the body and greater horn of the hyoid, so that a bursa lies between it and the back of the hyoid. Thickened in the midline as the median thyrohyoid ligament and posteriorly as the lateral thyrohyoid ligaments, which contain the triticeal cartilages.
cards.act: Suspends the larynx from the hyoid bone and closes the interval between them; it is pierced on each side by the internal laryngeal nerve and the superior laryngeal vessels.
cards.rel: Covered by thyrohyoid and the infrahyoid muscles; the piriform fossa of the laryngopharynx lies deep to its posterior part.
cards.clin: Local anaesthetic injected just above the superior horn of the thyroid cartilage blocks the internal laryngeal nerve as it pierces the membrane, anaesthetising the supraglottis for awake fibreoptic intubation. A sharp foreign body in the piriform fossa can injure the same nerve.
cards.exam: Q. What pierces the thyrohyoid membrane? A. The internal laryngeal nerve and the superior laryngeal artery and vein.

cards.desc: Largest laryngeal cartilage, made of two hyaline laminae that meet in front to form the laryngeal prominence.
cards.att: Laminae fuse anteriorly at the laryngeal prominence with the superior thyroid notch above; each lamina bears an oblique line and superior and inferior horns. The inferior horn articulates with the cricoid cartilage at the synovial cricothyroid joint; the superior horn gives attachment to the lateral thyrohyoid ligament. Internally the vocal ligaments, thyro-epiglottic ligament and thyroarytenoid muscles are attached to the angle.
cards.act: Shields the larynx anteriorly and, by tilting on the cricoid at the cricothyroid joints, allows cricothyroid muscle action to lengthen and tense the vocal ligaments and raise pitch.
cards.rel: Oblique line gives attachment to sternothyroid, thyrohyoid and the inferior constrictor; lobes of the thyroid gland and the carotid sheath lie lateral; the laryngeal inlet and piriform fossae lie behind.
cards.clin: The laryngeal prominence, at vertebral level C4 to C5, is the key surface landmark of the neck and is more marked in men. The cricothyroid membrane immediately below it is the site for emergency cricothyroidotomy. Fracture from strangulation or blunt trauma causes airway obstruction and surgical emphysema.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle tenses the vocal ligament and what is its nerve supply? A. Cricothyroid, supplied by the external laryngeal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

cards.desc: Medial and larger of the two leg bones, the only one that transmits body weight from the femur to the talus.
cards.att: Upper end has medial and lateral condyles with the intercondylar eminence between, the tibial tuberosity in front for the ligamentum patellae, and Gerdy tubercle laterally for the iliotibial tract. The shaft is triangular with a subcutaneous anterior border and medial surface, a soleal line for soleus, and a nutrient foramen in the upper posterior surface directed downwards. The lower end forms the medial malleolus, the fibular notch and the inferior articular surface for the talus. It articulates at the knee with the femur through the menisci, with the fibula at the superior and inferior tibiofibular joints, and with the talus at the ankle.
cards.act: Carries the whole body weight through the knee and ankle and gives attachment to the extensor mechanism of the knee at the tibial tuberosity.
cards.rel: Anteromedial surface subcutaneous throughout; anterior compartment muscles and anterior tibial vessels with the deep peroneal nerve lateral to the anterior border; popliteus, tibialis posterior and the posterior tibial vessels behind; pes anserinus (sartorius, gracilis, semitendinosus) on the upper medial surface.
cards.clin: Commonest long bone to be fractured and the commonest site of compound fracture because the anteromedial surface is subcutaneous. Union is slow at the junction of the middle and lower thirds where the blood supply is poorest. The tibial tuberosity is the site of Osgood-Schlatter apophysitis in adolescents, and the proximal anteromedial surface is the standard site for intraosseous access in a child.
cards.exam: Q. Why is delayed union common at the junction of the middle and lower thirds of the tibia? A. Because it is the watershed between the nutrient artery territory and the periosteal supply, with little surrounding muscle.

cards.desc: Most medial and most superficial muscle of the anterior compartment of the leg, running down beside the anterior border of the tibia to the medial side of the foot.
cards.att: Origin: lateral condyle and upper half or two thirds of the lateral surface of the tibia, the adjoining interosseous membrane and the deep fascia. Insertion: medial and inferior surfaces of the medial cuneiform and the adjacent base of the first metatarsal.
cards.sup: Deep fibular (peroneal) nerve, L4, L5.
cards.act: Dorsiflexion of the ankle and inversion of the foot; controls lowering of the foot after heel strike and clears the toes during the swing phase.
cards.rel: Its tendon is the most medial structure passing deep to the superior and inferior extensor retinacula. The anterior tibial vessels and deep fibular nerve lie on its lateral side against the interosseous membrane.
cards.clin: Paralysis in common or deep fibular nerve injury gives foot drop with a high-stepping gait. The muscle is the main content of the anterior compartment in anterior compartment syndrome and in shin splints; its tendon is transferred for drop foot.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve is injured in foot drop with loss of dorsiflexion and inversion? A. The deep fibular nerve, or the common fibular nerve at the neck of the fibula, supplying tibialis anterior, L4, L5.

cards.desc: Deepest and most central muscle of the posterior compartment of the leg, the chief invertor of the foot and the main dynamic support of the medial longitudinal arch.
cards.att: Origin: posterior surface of the interosseous membrane and the adjoining posterior surfaces of the tibia and fibula. Insertion: tuberosity of the navicular, with slips to the sustentaculum tali, all three cuneiforms, the cuboid and the bases of the second, third and fourth metatarsals.
cards.sup: Tibial nerve, L4, L5.
cards.act: Inversion of the foot and plantarflexion of the ankle; supports the medial longitudinal arch and locks the transverse tarsal joint for push off.
cards.rel: Lies between flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus, deep to the tibial vessels and nerve. Behind the medial malleolus its tendon is the most anterior structure in the tarsal tunnel: tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, posterior tibial artery, tibial nerve, flexor hallucis longus.
cards.clin: Tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction is the commonest cause of acquired flat foot in adults, with a positive too-many-toes sign and inability to perform a single heel raise. The tendon may be ruptured or entrapped in tarsal tunnel syndrome.
cards.exam: Q. Name the structures behind the medial malleolus from front to back. A. Tibialis posterior tendon, flexor digitorum longus tendon, posterior tibial artery, tibial nerve, flexor hallucis longus tendon.

cards.desc: Mobile muscular organ occupying the floor of the mouth and the anterior wall of the oropharynx, concerned with taste, mastication, deglutition and speech.
cards.att: Has a root attached to the mandible and hyoid bone, a tip, a dorsum and an inferior surface. The V-shaped sulcus terminalis, with the foramen caecum at its apex, divides the oral (anterior two thirds) from the pharyngeal (posterior third) part. Intrinsic muscles (superior and inferior longitudinal, transverse, vertical) lie wholly within it; extrinsic muscles are genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus and palatoglossus.
cards.sup: Motor: hypoglossal nerve to all muscles except palatoglossus, which is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus, cranial accessory). Sensation: anterior two thirds, general by the lingual nerve (V3) and taste by the chorda tympani (VII); posterior third, general and taste by the glossopharyngeal nerve; vallecular region by the internal laryngeal branch of the vagus. Artery: lingual artery. Lymph: tip to submental nodes, anterior two thirds to submandibular then deep cervical nodes, posterior third to deep cervical nodes bilaterally.
cards.act: Alters shape by the intrinsic muscles and position by the extrinsic muscles: protrusion by genioglossus, retraction by styloglossus, depression by hyoglossus, elevation of the root by palatoglossus. Essential for chewing, bolus formation, swallowing, taste and articulation.
cards.rel: Rests on mylohyoid and geniohyoid; lies within the arch of the mandible, related to the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches behind and to the sublingual glands and lingual nerves below.
cards.clin: A unilateral hypoglossal lesion causes the protruded tongue to deviate towards the paralysed side, because the normal genioglossus is unopposed. Genioglossus holds the tongue forward, so it falls back and obstructs the airway in an unconscious supine patient, hence the jaw thrust. Carcinoma of the posterior third metastasises early to both sides of the neck because its lymphatics cross the midline.
cards.exam: Q. Which way does the tongue deviate in a hypoglossal nerve lesion? A. Towards the side of the lesion.

cards.desc: Fibrocartilaginous air tube, about 10 to 11 cm long, running in the midline from the lower border of the cricoid cartilage at C6 to its bifurcation at the level of the sternal angle (T4/T5).
cards.att: Continuous above with the cricoid cartilage; ends at the carina by dividing into right and left principal bronchi. Wall carries 16 to 20 C-shaped hyaline cartilages, incomplete posteriorly where the trachealis muscle bridges the gap.
cards.sup: Upper part from inferior thyroid arteries, lower part from bronchial arteries; veins to the inferior thyroid venous plexus. Nerves from recurrent laryngeal and vagus, and from the sympathetic trunk. Lymph to pretracheal and paratracheal nodes.
cards.act: Conducts, warms and humidifies air; the mucociliary escalator clears secretions; trachealis contraction narrows the lumen and raises expiratory air velocity in coughing.
cards.rel: Cervical part: thyroid isthmus crosses rings 2 to 4, inferior thyroid veins and jugular venous arch in front, carotid sheaths lateral, oesophagus behind with the recurrent laryngeal nerves in the tracheo-oesophageal grooves. Thoracic part: brachiocephalic artery, left brachiocephalic vein, thymic remnant and arch of the aorta anteriorly.
cards.clin: Tracheostomy is performed through rings 2 to 4; the thyroid isthmus may need division. The right principal bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so inhaled foreign bodies lodge on the right; tracheal deviation away from the side of a tension pneumothorax is a bedside sign.
cards.exam: Q. At what level does the trachea bifurcate? A. At the plane of the sternal angle, the lower border of T4 or the T4/T5 disc, marked internally by the carina.

cards.desc: The single unpaired intrinsic muscle of the larynx, bridging the posterior surfaces of the two arytenoid cartilages.
cards.att: Attached to the posterior surface and lateral border of each arytenoid cartilage, passing transversely from one to the other.
cards.sup: Recurrent laryngeal nerve, CN X; it receives fibres from both sides.
cards.act: Approximates the arytenoid cartilages, closing the posterior intercartilaginous part of the rima glottidis.
cards.rel: Lies on the posterior surfaces of the arytenoids, deep to the mucosa of the interarytenoid fold and superficial to nothing; the oblique arytenoid muscles cross superficial to it.
cards.clin: Because it is unpaired and receives fibres from both recurrent laryngeal nerves, closure of the posterior rima is relatively preserved in a unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy. Interarytenoid mucosal changes are a classic endoscopic sign of laryngopharyngeal reflux.
cards.exam: Q. Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle is unpaired? A. The transverse arytenoid (interarytenoid) muscle.

cards.desc: Mobile, intraperitoneal part of the large intestine, about 45 to 50 cm long, slung between the right and left colic flexures by the transverse mesocolon.
cards.att: Runs from the right colic flexure, below the right lobe of the liver, across the abdomen with a downward loop, to the higher and more acute left colic flexure held up by the phrenicocolic ligament. Suspended by the transverse mesocolon, with the greater omentum attached to its anterosuperior surface.
