cards.sup: Proximal two-thirds by the middle colic artery from the superior mesenteric artery; distal third by the left colic artery from the inferior mesenteric artery, through the marginal artery. Veins to the superior and inferior mesenteric veins. Parasympathetic supply is vagal proximally and from pelvic splanchnic nerves distally, the change occurring at the junction of the proximal two-thirds and distal third.
cards.act: Absorbs water and electrolytes and stores faeces; site of mass movements.
cards.rel: Lies against the second part of the duodenum, the head of the pancreas and the gallbladder above and behind; the greater omentum hangs from it anteriorly and coils of small bowel lie below.
cards.clin: The midgut to hindgut junction lies at the distal third, the watershed most vulnerable to ischaemia. Its mobility allows it to be brought out as a colostomy, and the middle colic artery in the transverse mesocolon is at risk during gastric and pancreatic surgery.
cards.exam: Q. Where is the midgut-hindgut junction in the colon? A. At the junction of the proximal two-thirds and distal third of the transverse colon.

cards.desc: The smaller, transversely running head of adductor hallucis, lying across the heads of the lateral metatarsals in the third layer of the sole.
cards.att: Origin: plantar metatarsophalangeal ligaments of the third, fourth and fifth toes and the deep transverse metatarsal ligament. Insertion: joins the oblique head to reach the lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe and the lateral sesamoid.
cards.sup: Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve, S2 and S3.
cards.act: Adducts the great toe and, running transversely, helps maintain the transverse arch of the foot.
cards.rel: Lies deep to the long flexor tendons and lumbricals, superficial to the interossei and the deep plantar arch; the oblique head lies proximal and medial to it.
cards.clin: A contracted adductor hallucis holds the great toe in valgus, and release of this tendon from the lateral sesamoid and proximal phalanx is a standard step in hallux valgus (bunion) surgery.
cards.exam: Q. What is the nerve supply of both heads of adductor hallucis? A. The deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve, S2 and S3.

cards.desc: The larger, fan-shaped head of adductor pollicis arising from the third metacarpal in the deepest layer of the palm.
cards.att: Origin: the palmar surface of the shaft of the third metacarpal. Insertion: with the oblique head, into the ulnar side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb and the ulnar sesamoid, with a slip to the extensor expansion.
cards.sup: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve, T1 (C8, T1).
cards.act: Adducts the thumb towards the palm and assists opposition and pinch grip.
cards.rel: Lies deep to the long flexor tendons and the deep palmar arch, superficial to the interossei. The radial artery enters the palm by passing between the oblique and transverse heads to complete the deep palmar arch.
cards.clin: Adductor pollicis weakness in ulnar nerve palsy gives a positive Froment's sign: the thumb interphalangeal joint flexes, using flexor pollicis longus, when the patient grips paper between thumb and index finger.
cards.exam: Q. Which structure passes between the two heads of adductor pollicis? A. The radial artery, entering the palm to form the deep palmar arch.

cards.desc: Broad double fold of peritoneum suspending the transverse colon from the posterior abdominal wall.
cards.att: Root runs transversely across the anterior border of the head and body of the pancreas, the second part of the duodenum and the lower pole of the left kidney, from the right to the left colic flexure. Its two layers separate to enclose the transverse colon, and the posterior layers of the greater omentum fuse with its upper surface.
cards.sup: Contains the middle colic artery and vein with their branches, lymphatics, middle colic nodes and autonomic nerves.
cards.act: Suspends and mobilises the transverse colon and carries its neurovascular supply.
cards.rel: Divides the peritoneal cavity into the supracolic compartment (liver, stomach, spleen) and the infracolic compartment (small intestine, ascending and descending colon). Its upper surface forms part of the floor of the lesser sac.
cards.clin: The plane is used surgically to enter the lesser sac and to perform a retrocolic gastrojejunostomy. Collections in the supracolic compartment are separated from infracolic collections by this fold, which shapes the spread of peritoneal sepsis.
cards.exam: Q. What does the root of the transverse mesocolon cross? A. The second part of the duodenum, the head and anterior border of the body of the pancreas, and the lower pole of the left kidney.

cards.desc: The horizontal middle sheet of trapezius running from the lower cervical and upper thoracic spines laterally to the shoulder.
cards.att: Origin: spinous processes and supraspinous ligaments of about C7 to T3, largely through a tendinous aponeurosis. Insertion: medial margin of the acromion and the superior lip of the crest of the spine of the scapula.
cards.sup: Spinal accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) for motor supply, with C3 and C4 carrying proprioception.
cards.act: Retracts the scapula, drawing it towards the midline, and steadies it during use of the arm.
cards.rel: The aponeurotic part of both sides makes the tendinous ellipse over the C7 to T3 spines. The spinal accessory nerve descends on the deep surface of trapezius after crossing the posterior triangle. Rhomboids and levator scapulae lie deep to it.
cards.clin: The spinal accessory nerve lies superficially in the posterior triangle and is commonly injured during lymph node biopsy: the result is a drooping shoulder, loss of scapular retraction and difficulty abducting the arm above the head. The trapezius is examined by asking the patient to shrug and to brace the shoulders back against resistance.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve supplies trapezius and where is it most often injured? A. The spinal accessory nerve, most often injured in the posterior triangle during lymph node biopsy.

cards.desc: Thin fan-shaped muscle on the inner surface of the anterior thoracic wall, radiating from the sternum to the costal cartilages.
cards.att: Origin: posterior surface of the lower third of the body of the sternum, the xiphoid process and the adjacent costal cartilages. Insertion: by four or five slips into the lower borders and inner surfaces of the second to sixth costal cartilages.
cards.sup: Intercostal nerves of the corresponding spaces, the ventral rami of T2 to T6.
cards.act: Draws the costal cartilages downwards, a weak muscle of expiration; also has a proprioceptive role in respiratory control.
cards.rel: Lies deep to the internal thoracic vessels, which descend across its anterior surface about 1 cm lateral to the sternal margin; the endothoracic fascia and parietal pleura lie behind it. It is continuous inferiorly with transversus abdominis.
cards.clin: Identified when harvesting the internal thoracic artery for coronary bypass, since the artery lies superficial to it. The plane between transversus thoracis and the internal intercostal muscle is used for the transversus thoracis plane block after sternotomy.
cards.exam: Q. What is the relation of the internal thoracic artery to transversus thoracis? A. The artery lies on its anterior (superficial) surface.

cards.desc: Most lateral bone of the distal carpal row, lying between the scaphoid and the base of the first metacarpal at the root of the thumb.
cards.att: Saddle-shaped distal facet for the first metacarpal; articulates proximally with the scaphoid, medially with the trapezoid and distomedially with the base of the second metacarpal. Its palmar surface carries a groove for the tendon of flexor carpi radialis, with the tubercle of the trapezium lateral to the groove giving attachment to the flexor retinaculum and to abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis.
cards.act: Its saddle (sellar) joint with the first metacarpal allows flexion, extension, abduction, adduction and opposition of the thumb, the movements that make the human hand prehensile.
cards.rel: With the tubercle of the scaphoid it forms the lateral attachment of the flexor retinaculum and so the lateral wall of the carpal tunnel; flexor carpi radialis runs in its own compartment in the groove. The radial artery crosses its dorsal aspect in the floor of the anatomical snuffbox.
cards.clin: Osteoarthritis of the trapeziometacarpal joint is common, especially in older women, and is treated by trapeziectomy. Bennett fracture-dislocation is an intra-articular fracture of the base of the first metacarpal at this joint.
cards.exam: Q. Which tendon grooves the palmar surface of the trapezium? A. Flexor carpi radialis.

cards.desc: Pyramidal bone at the medial end of the proximal carpal row, carrying the pisiform on its palmar surface.
cards.att: Articulates with the lunate laterally, the hamate distally by a spiral (helicoid) facet, and the pisiform by an oval facet on its palmar surface. It does not articulate with the ulna directly, contacting the articular disc of the distal radioulnar joint only when the wrist is adducted.
cards.act: Transmits load from the medial side of the hand to the forearm through the articular disc, and its helicoid joint with the hamate guides the wrist through ulnar deviation.
cards.rel: The pisiform lies on its palmar surface; the ulnar nerve and artery pass lateral to the pisiform in the canal of Guyon. The triangular fibrocartilage (articular disc) separates it from the head of the ulna.
cards.clin: Second most commonly fractured carpal bone after the scaphoid, usually a dorsal chip (avulsion) fracture causing tenderness just distal to the ulnar head. Perilunate dislocations commonly disrupt the lunotriquetral ligament.
cards.exam: Q. Does the triquetral articulate with the ulna? A. No, the articular disc of the distal radioulnar joint separates the two.

cards.desc: Fibrocartilaginous loop attached to the trochlear fovea of the frontal bone in the superomedial angle of the orbit, through which the tendon of superior oblique passes.
cards.att: Anchored to the trochlear fovea or spine of the frontal bone just behind the superomedial orbital margin; the tendon of superior oblique runs through it and turns posterolaterally to insert into the sclera in the superolateral posterior quadrant of the eyeball, deep to the tendon of superior rectus.
cards.act: Acts as the functional origin of superior oblique, redirecting its pull so the muscle depresses, abducts and intorts the eye, its depressing action being greatest with the eye adducted.
cards.rel: Lies between the orbital plate of the frontal bone above and the tendon below; the supratrochlear and infratrochlear nerves pass close by at the orbital margin.
cards.clin: Inflammation of the trochlea (trochleitis) causes localised superomedial orbital pain. Brown syndrome is restriction of the superior oblique tendon at the trochlea, limiting elevation of the adducted eye. Trochlear damage in orbital surgery or trauma causes torsional diplopia.
cards.exam: Q. Why is superior oblique tested by asking the patient to look down and in? A. Its depressing action on the eye is maximal when the eye is adducted, because of the direction of pull from the trochlea.

cards.desc: The slenderest cranial nerve, and the only one to emerge from the dorsal surface of the brainstem, supplying a single muscle, the superior oblique.
cards.att: Fibres from the trochlear nucleus in the midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus decussate in the superior medullary velum and emerge dorsally below the inferior colliculus. The nerve winds round the cerebral peduncle, runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus below the oculomotor nerve, and enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure outside the common tendinous ring to reach superior oblique.
cards.act: Motor to superior oblique, producing depression, abduction and intorsion of the eyeball.
cards.rel: Passes between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries, then lies in the free margin of the tentorium cerebelli and in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus between the oculomotor nerve above and the ophthalmic nerve below. In the orbit it crosses above levator palpebrae superioris medially.
cards.clin: It is the only entirely crossed cranial nerve, so a nuclear lesion causes a contralateral superior oblique palsy while a lesion of the nerve causes an ipsilateral one. Its long slender intracranial course makes it the nerve most often injured in closed head injury; the patient has vertical diplopia worst on looking down and tilts the head away from the affected side.
cards.exam: Q. Which cranial nerve emerges from the dorsal aspect of the brainstem? A. The trochlear nerve.

cards.desc: The initial undivided stem of a coronary artery, arising from an aortic sinus above the aortic valve and supplying the heart.
cards.att: The left coronary trunk arises from the left aortic sinus, passes behind the pulmonary trunk and in front of the left auricle for about 1 to 2 cm, then divides into the anterior interventricular (left anterior descending) and circumflex arteries. The right coronary trunk arises from the right aortic sinus and descends in the right atrioventricular groove between the right auricle and the pulmonary trunk.
cards.sup: Left trunk gives the anterior interventricular and circumflex arteries, sometimes an intermediate (ramus) branch; right trunk gives the sinu-atrial nodal, right marginal, atrioventricular nodal and posterior interventricular branches in a right dominant heart.
cards.rel: Both trunks lie in the atrioventricular groove beneath the epicardium, embedded in fat. The left trunk lies deep between the pulmonary trunk and left auricle, the right trunk anterior to the right atrioventricular groove.
cards.clin: Left main stem stenosis threatens most of the left ventricle and is an indication for coronary artery bypass grafting. Dominance is defined by which trunk gives the posterior interventricular artery, right in about 70 per cent of hearts.
cards.exam: Q. Which branch defines coronary dominance? A. The posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery.

cards.desc: Main arterial stem to the liver, running in the free edge of the lesser omentum before dividing into right and left hepatic arteries at the porta hepatis.
cards.att: Continues from the common hepatic artery (branch of the coeliac trunk) after the gastroduodenal artery is given off, ascends in the hepatoduodenal ligament, and divides into right and left hepatic trunks which enter the liver at the porta hepatis.
cards.sup: Gives the right gastric artery, the cystic artery (usually from the right hepatic trunk), and the right and left hepatic arteries; supplies about 25 percent of hepatic blood flow but most of the oxygen to the bile ducts.
cards.act: Arterial supply to the liver parenchyma and, critically, to the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts.
cards.rel: In the free edge of the lesser omentum it lies to the left of the bile duct and anterior to the portal vein. The epiploic foramen (of Winslow) lies behind these three structures.
cards.clin: The bile ducts depend almost entirely on hepatic arterial blood, so hepatic artery thrombosis after liver transplantation causes ischaemic biliary strictures. A replaced or accessory right hepatic artery from the superior mesenteric artery is a common variant that must be identified before pancreatic or gallbladder surgery.
cards.exam: Q. Name the three structures in the free edge of the lesser omentum and their arrangement. A. Bile duct to the right, hepatic artery to the left, portal vein posterior.

cards.desc: Main venous trunk carrying blood from the whole gastrointestinal tract, spleen and pancreas to the liver, about 8 cm long.
cards.att: Formed behind the neck of the pancreas at about the L2 level by union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins, ascends in the free edge of the lesser omentum behind the bile duct and hepatic artery, and divides at the porta hepatis into right and left portal trunks.
cards.sup: Receives the left and right gastric veins, the cystic vein, the para-umbilical veins and the superior pancreaticoduodenal vein; the inferior mesenteric vein usually drains into the splenic vein.
cards.act: Delivers about 75 percent of hepatic blood flow, carrying absorbed nutrients to the liver for first-pass metabolism.
cards.rel: Posterior to the bile duct and hepatic artery in the hepatoduodenal ligament, and forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen. The inferior vena cava lies behind the foramen.
cards.clin: Portal hypertension opens portosystemic anastomoses at the lower oesophagus (varices), the anal canal, the umbilicus (caput medusae) and retroperitoneal sites. Pringle's manoeuvre compresses the portal triad in the free edge of the lesser omentum to control liver bleeding.
cards.exam: Q. Which veins unite to form the portal vein and where? A. Superior mesenteric and splenic veins, behind the neck of the pancreas.

cards.desc: Large lateral branch of the abdominal aorta running to the hilum of the kidney at about the L1 to L2 level.
cards.att: Arises from the aorta just below the superior mesenteric artery, passes laterally behind the renal vein, and divides near the hilum into an anterior division (four segmental arteries) and a posterior division (one segmental artery).
cards.sup: Gives the inferior suprarenal artery and ureteric branches; segmental arteries are end arteries dividing into interlobar, arcuate and interlobular vessels.
cards.act: Supplies the kidney; carries about 20 percent of cardiac output to the two kidneys.
cards.rel: At the hilum the order from front to back is renal vein, renal artery, renal pelvis. The right renal artery is longer and passes behind the inferior vena cava.
cards.clin: Segmental arteries are end arteries, so occlusion of one causes infarction of that segment. The relatively avascular plane between the anterior and posterior divisions (Brodel's bloodless line) along the posterolateral border is used for nephrolithotomy. Renal artery stenosis causes renovascular hypertension.
cards.exam: Q. Give the anteroposterior order of structures at the renal hilum. A. Renal vein, renal artery, renal pelvis.

cards.desc: Midline ventral branch of the abdominal aorta at the L1 level, the artery of the midgut.
cards.att: Arises from the aorta about 1 cm below the coeliac trunk, passes behind the neck of the pancreas and splenic vein, crosses anterior to the uncinate process and the third part of the duodenum, and runs in the root of the mesentery to the right iliac fossa.
cards.sup: Branches: inferior pancreaticoduodenal, jejunal and ileal branches, middle colic, right colic and ileocolic arteries. Supplies gut from the major duodenal papilla to the distal third of the transverse colon.
cards.act: Arterial supply of the midgut derivatives.
cards.rel: Lies to the left of the superior mesenteric vein. The left renal vein passes between the SMA and the aorta; the third part of the duodenum and the uncinate process pass between the same two vessels.
cards.clin: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome is compression of the third part of the duodenum in the aortomesenteric angle after marked weight loss. Embolic occlusion causes acute mesenteric ischaemia with pain out of proportion to signs. Referred midgut pain is periumbilical (T10).
cards.exam: Q. Which two structures pass between the SMA and the aorta? A. The left renal vein and the third part of the duodenum (with the uncinate process).

cards.desc: A convex mass of grey matter in the floor of the third ventricle, between the optic chiasma in front and the mammillary bodies behind, from which the infundibulum descends.
cards.att: Contains the tuberal and arcuate nuclei of the hypothalamus, which project to the median eminence; the median eminence on its lower surface holds the primary capillary plexus of the hypophysial portal system that carries releasing hormones to the anterior pituitary.
cards.sup: Branches of the circle of Willis, chiefly the posterior communicating and posterior cerebral arteries; drained into the hypophysial portal veins.
cards.act: Hypothalamic control of anterior pituitary secretion by releasing and inhibiting hormones, including dopamine as prolactin inhibitory factor.
cards.rel: Lies within the interpeduncular cistern, bounded in front by the optic chiasma and tracts, behind by the mammillary bodies, laterally by the optic tracts; the infundibulum passes downwards and forwards to the pituitary gland in the sella turcica.
cards.clin: A hypothalamic hamartoma of the tuber cinereum causes gelastic (laughing) seizures with central precocious puberty. Damage to the median eminence or stalk removes dopaminergic inhibition and produces hyperprolactinaemia.
cards.exam: Q. What arises from the tuber cinereum? A. The infundibulum, continuous with the pituitary stalk, and its median eminence contains the hypophysial portal capillary plexus.

cards.desc: Short atypical floating rib whose anterior tipped end lies free in the muscle of the posterior abdominal wall.
cards.att: Head bears a single facet articulating only with the body of T12; it has no neck, no tubercle, no angle and no costal groove. Gives attachment to the lateral arcuate ligament of the diaphragm, quadratus lumborum, serratus posterior inferior, latissimus dorsi and the thoracolumbar fascia.
cards.act: Anchors the lateral arcuate ligament and quadratus lumborum, and is fixed by quadratus lumborum so that the diaphragm can act from a stable base.
cards.rel: The subcostal vessels and nerve run along its lower border. The pleural reflection crosses its medial part, and the upper pole of the kidney with the suprarenal gland lies deep to it in front.
cards.clin: Landmark for the posterior loin approach to the kidney: an incision made above or too medial to the twelfth rib opens the costodiaphragmatic recess of the pleura. Renal angle tenderness, between the twelfth rib and the lateral border of erector spinae, is elicited in pyelonephritis and renal stone disease.
cards.exam: Q. What lies immediately deep to the medial part of the twelfth rib and is at risk in loin incisions? A. The pleural reflection of the costodiaphragmatic recess.

cards.desc: Transitional vertebra at the thoracolumbar junction, thoracic above and lumbar below.
cards.att: Large body with a single whole costal facet on each side for the head of the twelfth rib; the superior articular facets face backwards in the thoracic pattern while the inferior facets face laterally in the lumbar pattern. The transverse process is small and represented by superior, inferior and lateral tubercles.
cards.act: Marks the change from a rotating thoracic segment to a flexing lumbar segment, so torsional and shearing forces concentrate here.
cards.rel: The aortic hiatus of the diaphragm lies at the T12 level and the coeliac trunk arises just below it; the crura of the diaphragm descend on to the upper lumbar bodies. The conus medullaris of the adult spinal cord ends at the L1/L2 disc, just below.
cards.clin: The thoracolumbar junction is the commonest site of vertebral fracture because facet orientation and mobility change abruptly here. A burst fracture at T12/L1 can produce a conus medullaris syndrome with saddle anaesthesia and early bladder and bowel involvement.
cards.exam: Q. Why is T12 called transitional? A. Its superior articular facets are thoracic in orientation and its inferior facets lumbar, so rotation is allowed above and prevented below.

cards.desc: Medial bone of the forearm, longer than the radius and the principal bone at the elbow joint.
cards.att: Olecranon and coronoid process enclose the trochlear notch proximally; radial notch laterally, ulnar tuberosity below the coronoid, supinator crest, a triangular shaft with a sharp interosseous border, and distally a rounded head with the styloid process. Articulates with the trochlea of the humerus, with the head of the radius at the proximal radioulnar joint and with the ulnar notch of the radius at the distal radioulnar joint. Triceps brachii inserts on the olecranon and brachialis on the ulnar tuberosity.
cards.act: Forms the hinge of the elbow with the humerus and provides the fixed axis about which the radius rotates in pronation and supination; it takes no part in the wrist joint, being separated from the carpus by the articular disc.
cards.rel: The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle and enters the forearm between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris, then runs distally on flexor digitorum profundus medial to the ulnar artery. Flexor digitorum profundus, pronator quadratus, supinator and extensor carpi ulnaris take origin from its shaft.
cards.clin: Monteggia fracture-dislocation is a fracture of the proximal ulna with dislocation of the head of the radius. An isolated mid-shaft fracture from a direct blow is the nightstick fracture, and olecranon fractures are pulled apart proximally by triceps, so they need tension band fixation.
cards.exam: Q. What is a Monteggia fracture-dislocation? A. Fracture of the proximal ulna combined with dislocation of the head of the radius at the proximal radioulnar joint.

cards.desc: The larger terminal branch of the brachial artery, running down the medial side of the forearm to form the superficial palmar arch in the hand.
cards.att: Arises from the brachial artery in the cubital fossa at the level of the neck of the radius; passes deep to pronator teres, the ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis and the other superficial flexors, then lies on flexor digitorum profundus; enters the hand superficial to the flexor retinaculum lateral to the pisiform and ends as the superficial palmar arch.
cards.sup: Anterior and posterior ulnar recurrent arteries, common interosseous artery (dividing into anterior and posterior interosseous), muscular branches, palmar and dorsal carpal branches, and the deep palmar branch.
cards.act: Main supply to the medial forearm and, through the superficial palmar arch, to the fingers.
cards.rel: The ulnar nerve lies on its medial side in the distal two-thirds of the forearm; at the wrist both lie lateral to the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris and pass through the canal of Guyon, with the artery lateral to the nerve.
cards.clin: Allen's test checks ulnar patency before radial artery cannulation or harvest. In the canal of Guyon, an ulnar artery aneurysm from repeated palmar trauma (hypothenar hammer syndrome) can compress the ulnar nerve.
cards.exam: Q. What is the relation of the ulnar artery to the ulnar nerve at the wrist? A. The artery lies lateral to the nerve, both superficial to the flexor retinaculum.

cards.k: ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris
cards.latin: caput ulnare musculi flexoris carpi ulnaris
cards.desc: The longer of the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris, arising from the ulna and joined to the humeral head by a tendinous arch.
cards.att: Origin: medial margin of the olecranon and the upper two-thirds of the posterior border of the ulna by an aponeurosis shared with extensor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum profundus. Insertion: with the humeral head into the pisiform, and thence into the hook of the hamate and the base of the fifth metacarpal by the pisohamate and pisometacarpal ligaments.
cards.sup: Ulnar nerve, C7, C8 and T1.
cards.act: Flexes and adducts (ulnar deviates) the wrist.
cards.rel: The ulnar nerve enters the forearm by passing between this head and the humeral head, beneath the tendinous arch (arcade of Osborne). The ulnar nerve and artery run deep to the muscle in the forearm, the nerve lying medial to the artery.
cards.clin: The arch between the two heads is the roof of the cubital tunnel, the commonest site of ulnar nerve entrapment; symptoms worsen on elbow flexion. The tendon and pisiform are the surface guide to the ulnar nerve and artery at the wrist.
cards.exam: Q. Between which two structures does the ulnar nerve enter the forearm? A. Between the humeral and ulnar heads of flexor carpi ulnaris.

cards.desc: The small deep head of pronator teres, arising from the ulna and separated from the humeral head by the median nerve.
cards.att: Origin: medial side of the coronoid process of the ulna. Insertion: joins the humeral head and inserts, by a common tendon, into the rough impression on the middle of the lateral surface of the radius.
cards.sup: Median nerve, C6 and C7.
cards.act: Pronates the forearm and weakly flexes the elbow.
cards.rel: The median nerve passes between the humeral and ulnar heads, and the ulnar artery passes deep to both heads. The muscle forms the medial boundary of the cubital fossa.
cards.clin: Compression of the median nerve between the two heads is pronator syndrome, giving forearm pain and median sensory loss including the palmar cutaneous territory, which distinguishes it from carpal tunnel syndrome.
cards.exam: Q. What passes between the two heads of pronator teres, and what passes deep to both? A. The median nerve passes between them; the ulnar artery passes deep to both.

cards.desc: The most medial permanent tooth of the maxillary arch, and the widest of the incisors, erupting at about 7 to 8 years.
cards.att: Single stout conical root in the maxillary alveolus; the crown is trapezoid from the labial aspect with a broad, straight incisal edge, a convex labial surface and a lingual cingulum with marginal ridges.
cards.sup: Sensory: anterior superior alveolar branch of the infraorbital nerve (V2); labial gingiva by the same nerve and palatal gingiva by the nasopalatine nerve. Artery: anterior superior alveolar branch of the infraorbital artery.
cards.act: Cuts food against the lower incisors and is a major determinant of appearance and of the articulation of dental sounds.
cards.rel: Its mesial surface contacts its fellow at the midline, its distal surface the upper lateral incisor; the root is related to the floor of the nose and the incisive canal.
cards.clin: The tooth most frequently fractured or avulsed in childhood facial trauma; an avulsed permanent incisor should be replanted as soon as possible or transported in milk or saline. A midline diastema is often caused by a low labial frenulum between the two central incisors.
cards.exam: Q. Which nerve is blocked to anaesthetise the upper central incisor? A. The anterior superior alveolar nerve, a branch of the infraorbital nerve (V2), with a nasopalatine block for the palatal tissue.

cards.desc: The largest tooth of the maxillary arch, third from the midline behind the two premolars, and the first permanent tooth to erupt, at about 6 years.
cards.att: Crown carries four cusps: mesiobuccal, distobuccal, mesiopalatal and distopalatal, with a fifth accessory cusp of Carabelli on the mesiopalatal cusp. Three roots: mesiobuccal, distobuccal and a large palatal root; the oblique ridge joins the mesiopalatal and distobuccal cusps.
cards.sup: Posterior superior alveolar nerve, except the mesiobuccal root which is usually supplied by the middle superior alveolar nerve. Posterior superior alveolar artery and vein.
cards.act: Grinding and crushing of food; the first molars establish the occlusal key of the dentition.
cards.rel: Root apices lie close to, and may project into, the floor of the maxillary sinus, separated only by a thin plate of bone. Buccal to it lies the buccinator and the buccal pad of fat.
cards.clin: The most frequently carious and most frequently lost permanent tooth; often mistaken for a deciduous tooth because it erupts without a predecessor being shed. Periapical infection may cause maxillary sinusitis, and extraction risks an oro-antral communication.
cards.exam: Q. Which is the first permanent tooth to erupt and at what age? A. The first molar, at about 6 years, behind the deciduous second molar.

cards.desc: The fourth tooth from the midline in the upper arch, lying between the canine and the second premolar, erupting at about 10 to 11 years.
cards.att: Crown has two cusps, buccal and palatal, the buccal being longer and sharper. The root is usually bifid, giving buccal and palatal roots with two canals, and the mesial surface of the root shows a deep developmental depression.
cards.sup: Middle superior alveolar nerve, with the superior alveolar branches of the maxillary artery.
cards.act: Tears and crushes food, transitional in form between canine and molar.
cards.rel: Lies against the canine mesially and the second premolar distally; the root apex may approach the floor of the maxillary sinus.
cards.clin: The tooth most often extracted for orthodontic space creation in crowding. The bifid root and mesial root concavity make extraction and root canal treatment more difficult than in the second premolar.
cards.exam: Q. Which permanent tooth is most commonly extracted for orthodontic reasons? A. The maxillary first premolar.

cards.desc: The second tooth from the midline in the upper arch, smaller and narrower than the central incisor, erupting at about 8 to 9 years.
cards.att: Single conical root, usually with a distal curve at the apex; crown has a chisel-shaped incisal edge, prominent marginal ridges and a well-marked cingulum on the palatal surface often containing a lingual pit.
cards.sup: Anterior superior alveolar nerve, a branch of the infra-orbital nerve; anterior superior alveolar branch of the infra-orbital artery.
cards.act: Cutting and shearing of food.
cards.rel: Lies between the central incisor and the canine; its root is related to the incisive fossa and its apex points distally.
cards.clin: After the third molar, the most commonly congenitally absent tooth, and the tooth most often malformed as a peg-shaped lateral. The palatal pit is a common site of caries and of dens invaginatus.
cards.exam: Q. Which tooth is most commonly congenitally missing after the third molar? A. The maxillary lateral incisor.

cards.desc: The seventh tooth from the midline in the upper arch, distal to the first molar, erupting at about 12 years.
cards.att: Crown smaller than the first molar, with a reduced or absent distopalatal cusp giving a rhomboidal outline, and no cusp of Carabelli. Three roots, mesiobuccal, distobuccal and palatal, which are less divergent and frequently fused.
cards.sup: Posterior superior alveolar nerve; posterior superior alveolar artery and vein.
cards.act: Grinding of food.
cards.rel: Root apices are closely related to the floor of the maxillary sinus, often more intimately than those of the first molar. The tuberosity of the maxilla lies distal to it.
cards.clin: Its apices are a common source of odontogenic maxillary sinusitis, and a displaced root during extraction may be pushed into the antrum. Distal position makes it difficult to clean, so distal caries is common.
cards.exam: Q. Which teeth most commonly cause odontogenic maxillary sinusitis? A. The maxillary first and second molars, whose apices lie beneath the antral floor.

cards.desc: The fifth tooth from the midline in the upper arch, lying between the first premolar and the first molar, erupting at about 10 to 12 years.
cards.att: Crown with two cusps of nearly equal height, buccal and palatal, and a less prominent central groove than the first premolar. Usually a single root with a single canal.
cards.sup: Middle superior alveolar nerve where present, otherwise the posterior superior alveolar nerve; superior alveolar branches of the maxillary artery.
cards.act: Crushes and grinds food.
cards.rel: Root apex is close to the floor of the maxillary sinus; mesially the first premolar, distally the first molar.
cards.clin: Simpler single root and single canal make it an easier tooth for extraction and endodontics than the first premolar. It is a frequent site of developmental absence after the lateral incisor.
cards.exam: Q. How does the maxillary second premolar differ from the first? A. Cusps of nearly equal height and a single root with one canal, versus a dominant buccal cusp and a bifid root.

cards.desc: The third tooth from the midline in the upper arch, the longest tooth in the dentition, erupting at about 11 to 12 years.
cards.att: Single pointed cusp with mesial and distal slopes, a strong palatal cingulum, and the longest and stoutest single root of any tooth, which raises the canine eminence on the anterior surface of the maxilla.
cards.sup: Anterior superior alveolar nerve from the infra-orbital nerve; anterior superior alveolar artery.
cards.act: Tears and grasps food; provides canine guidance that disoccludes the posterior teeth in lateral excursion.
cards.rel: Root lies between the incisive fossa and the canine fossa; the apex is directed towards the infra-orbital foramen. Stands at the corner of the arch between incisors and premolars.
cards.clin: The cornerstone of the arch, usually the last tooth to be lost. After the third molar it is the most commonly impacted tooth, typically palatally. Periapical infection may spread into the canine fossa and thence via the angular vein to the cavernous sinus.
cards.exam: Q. Which is the longest tooth in the human dentition? A. The maxillary canine, because of its long single root.

cards.desc: Muscular tube about 25 to 30 cm long conveying urine from the renal pelvis to the urinary bladder, retroperitoneal throughout its abdominal course.
cards.att: Begins at the pelviureteric junction opposite L2, descends on psoas major crossing the tips of the lumbar transverse processes, crosses the bifurcation of the common iliac artery at the pelvic brim, runs on the lateral pelvic wall and turns forward to pierce the bladder wall obliquely at the upper lateral angle of the trigone.
cards.sup: Arteries from the renal, gonadal, abdominal aortic, common and internal iliac, and vesical arteries, forming a longitudinal anastomosis in its adventitia. Nerves from the renal, aortic, superior and inferior hypogastric plexuses (T11 to L2).
cards.act: Propels urine to the bladder by peristalsis of its smooth muscle; the oblique intramural course acts as a valve preventing reflux.
cards.rel: Crossed anteriorly by the gonadal vessels in the abdomen and, near the bladder, by the uterine artery in the female and the ductus deferens in the male. The right ureter lies behind the second part of the duodenum and the root of the mesentery, the left behind the sigmoid mesocolon.
cards.clin: Three normal constrictions, at the pelviureteric junction, at the pelvic brim, and at the ureterovesical junction, are where calculi lodge. Ureteric colic radiates from loin to groin (T11 to L2 referral). At hysterectomy the ureter is at risk where the uterine artery crosses above it, "water under the bridge", near the lateral fornix of the vagina.
cards.exam: Q. Name the three sites of normal ureteric narrowing. A. Pelviureteric junction, crossing of the pelvic brim (common iliac vessels), and the ureterovesical junction.

cards.desc: Muscular tube about 18 to 20 cm long carrying urine and semen from the internal urethral orifice of the bladder to the external urethral orifice on the glans penis.
cards.att: Four parts: preprostatic (intramural), prostatic, membranous and spongy. The prostatic part is the widest and bears the urethral crest, seminal colliculus with the prostatic utricle and ejaculatory duct openings, and the prostatic sinuses. The membranous part traverses the deep perineal pouch and perineal membrane, encircled by the external urethral sphincter. The spongy part runs in the corpus spongiosum, dilated in the bulb and as the navicular fossa in the glans.
cards.sup: Arteries: inferior vesical, middle rectal and internal pudendal branches (urethral and bulbar arteries). Nerves: prostatic plexus and the dorsal nerve of the penis (pudendal, S2, S3, S4).
cards.act: Conducts urine during micturition and semen during ejaculation; the internal sphincter at the bladder neck closes during ejaculation to prevent retrograde flow.
cards.rel: Prostatic part is surrounded by the prostate; membranous part lies between the prostatic apex and the bulb, with the bulbourethral glands lateral to it; spongy part lies within the corpus spongiosum with the bulbourethral ducts opening into it.
cards.clin: The external urethral orifice is the narrowest part and the membranous urethra the least dilatable, so a catheter that will pass the meatus will usually pass throughout. Straddle injury ruptures the bulbous urethra with extravasation into the superficial perineal pouch; pelvic fracture ruptures the membranous urethra with extravasation above the perineal membrane and a high-riding prostate.
cards.exam: Q. Which part of the male urethra is narrowest and which is least dilatable? A. The external urethral orifice is narrowest; the membranous part is least dilatable.

cards.desc: Distensible muscular reservoir for urine lying in the anterior part of the lesser pelvis behind the pubic symphysis when empty.
cards.att: Has an apex connected to the umbilicus by the median umbilical ligament (urachal remnant), a fundus (base) posteriorly, a body, and a neck resting on the prostate in the male and the pelvic fascia in the female. The trigone on the internal surface of the base is smooth and lies between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice.
cards.sup: Arteries: superior and inferior vesical branches of the internal iliac artery (vaginal artery replacing the inferior vesical in the female). Veins: vesical venous plexus to the internal iliac veins. Nerves: parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2, S3, S4) motor to the detrusor, sympathetic from L1, L2 via the hypogastric plexuses, pain from the superior surface travelling with sympathetics and from the base with parasympathetics. Lymph: external and internal iliac nodes.
cards.act: Stores urine and expels it by detrusor contraction with relaxation of the sphincters during micturition.
cards.rel: Peritoneum covers the superior surface only; anteriorly the retropubic space of Retzius; posteriorly the rectovesical pouch, seminal vesicles and ductus deferens in the male, and the uterus and vagina in the female; below, the prostate or the pelvic floor.
cards.clin: A full bladder rises above the pubic symphysis and strips the peritoneum upward, allowing suprapubic puncture or catheterisation without entering the peritoneal cavity. Rupture of the distended dome is intraperitoneal, while rupture of the base with pelvic fracture is extraperitoneal. The trigone is derived from the mesonephric ducts and is the commonest site of cystoscopic pathology.
cards.exam: Q. What is the nerve supply of the detrusor muscle? A. Parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves from S2, S3, S4.

cards.desc: Small paired muscle running backwards within the soft palate to form the bulk of the uvula.
cards.att: Origin: posterior nasal spine of the hard palate and the palatine aponeurosis. Insertion: mucosa and connective tissue of the uvula.
cards.sup: Pharyngeal plexus, motor fibres from the vagus, CN X.
cards.act: Shortens, thickens and elevates the uvula, helping the soft palate seal the nasopharyngeal isthmus during swallowing and speech.
cards.rel: Lies above the palatine aponeurosis in the median plane, between the two levator veli palatini muscles, deep to the nasopharyngeal mucosa.
cards.clin: In a unilateral vagal or pharyngeal plexus lesion the uvula deviates to the normal side on saying "aah". A bifid uvula signals submucous cleft palate, in which adenoidectomy risks velopharyngeal insufficiency.
cards.exam: Q. In a right vagus nerve lesion, to which side does the uvula deviate? A. To the left, the normal side.

cards.desc: Deepest part of quadriceps femoris, lying directly on the front of the femoral shaft beneath rectus femoris.
cards.att: Origin: anterior and lateral surfaces of the upper two thirds of the shaft of the femur and the lower part of the lateral intermuscular septum. Insertion: deep part of the quadriceps tendon to the base of the patella, and through the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity.
cards.sup: Femoral nerve, L2, L3, L4.
cards.act: Extends the leg at the knee joint.
cards.rel: Deep to rectus femoris, blending laterally with vastus lateralis and medially with vastus medialis. Its deepest fibres form articularis genus, which attaches to the suprapatellar bursa.
cards.clin: Articularis genus retracts the suprapatellar bursa during extension and prevents it being nipped. Fibrosis of vastus intermedius after femoral shaft fracture or repeated intramuscular injection causes quadriceps contracture with loss of knee flexion.
cards.exam: Q. What is the function of articularis genus? A. It pulls the suprapatellar bursa upwards during extension of the knee, preventing it from being trapped.

cards.desc: Largest component of quadriceps femoris, forming the bulk of the lateral aspect of the thigh.
cards.att: Origin: upper part of the intertrochanteric line, anterior and inferior borders of the greater trochanter, lateral lip of the gluteal tuberosity, upper half of the lateral lip of the linea aspera, and the lateral intermuscular septum. Insertion: lateral border of the patella through the quadriceps tendon and the lateral patellar retinaculum, and through the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity.
cards.sup: Femoral nerve, L2, L3, L4.
cards.act: Extends the leg at the knee; its retinacular fibres pull the patella laterally.
cards.rel: Covered laterally by the iliotibial tract, with the lateral intermuscular septum separating it from the short head of biceps femoris.
cards.clin: The middle third of the anterolateral thigh over this muscle is the recommended site for intramuscular injection in infants because there are no large vessels or nerves. A tight lateral retinaculum contributes to patellar maltracking and is divided in lateral release.
cards.exam: Q. Which muscle is used for intramuscular injection in infants and why? A. Vastus lateralis in the anterolateral thigh, because it is bulky and free of major nerves and vessels.

syn: VMO for its oblique lowest fibres
cards.desc: Medial component of quadriceps femoris, its lowest oblique fibres reaching almost to the level of the patella on the medial side.
cards.att: Origin: lower part of the intertrochanteric line, spiral line, medial lip of the linea aspera, upper part of the medial supracondylar line, and the tendons of adductor longus and adductor magnus. Insertion: medial border of the patella through the quadriceps tendon and the medial patellar retinaculum, and through the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity.
cards.sup: Femoral nerve, L2, L3, L4.
cards.act: Extends the leg at the knee; the lowest oblique fibres hold the patella medially and stabilise it in the last part of extension.
cards.rel: Forms the anterolateral wall of the adductor canal, in which the saphenous nerve crosses in front of the femoral artery from lateral to medial while the nerve to vastus medialis lies lateral to the artery.
cards.clin: Wasting of vastus medialis is the earliest and most obvious sign of knee joint disease or disuse and is measured by thigh circumference. Its weakness allows lateral dislocation of the patella, which is commoner in women because of the wider Q angle.
cards.exam: Q. Which part of the quadriceps prevents lateral dislocation of the patella? A. The lowest oblique fibres of vastus medialis.

cards.desc: First and largest branch of the first part of the subclavian artery, the principal arterial supply of the hindbrain and cervical spinal cord.
cards.att: Arises from the first part of the subclavian artery, ascends in the prevertebral region to enter the foramen transversarium of C6, ascends through the transverse foramina of C6 to C1, winds backwards on the posterior arch of the atlas through the suboccipital triangle, pierces the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane and dura, enters the foramen magnum and unites with its fellow at the lower border of the pons to form the basilar artery.
cards.sup: Branches: spinal and muscular branches in the neck; meningeal, anterior and posterior spinal arteries and the posterior inferior cerebellar artery intracranially.
cards.act: Supplies the medulla, cervical spinal cord, cerebellum and, through the basilar artery, the pons and midbrain.
cards.rel: Its first part lies in the triangle between longus colli and scalenus anterior with the vertebral vein in front and the inferior thyroid artery crossing it; the stellate ganglion lies behind. In the suboccipital triangle it lies in a groove on the upper surface of the posterior arch of the atlas, with the suboccipital nerve (dorsal ramus of C1) lying between the artery and the arch.
cards.clin: Vulnerable to dissection by sudden neck rotation or manipulation, causing posterior circulation stroke. Occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery gives the lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome: ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss, Horner syndrome, dysphagia and ataxia with contralateral body pain and temperature loss.
cards.exam: Q. Through which transverse foramina does the vertebral artery ascend? A. Those of C6 up to C1; it usually does not pass through the C7 foramen.

cards.desc: Transparent avascular gel of about 4 mL filling the posterior four-fifths of the eyeball behind the lens.
cards.att: Occupies the vitreous chamber, bounded by the retina, the ciliary body and the lens, which rests in its anterior hyaloid fossa. Enclosed by the vitreous membrane and traversed by the hyaloid canal of Cloquet from the optic disc to the back of the lens; it is 99 per cent water with hyaluronan and type II collagen.
cards.sup: Avascular and non-innervated after regression of the hyaloid artery.
cards.act: Transmits light, supports the retina against the choroid, and helps maintain intraocular pressure and the shape of the globe.
cards.rel: Lens and zonule in front, retina behind and laterally, firmly adherent at the vitreous base astride the ora serrata and more loosely at the optic disc and macula.
cards.clin: With age the gel liquefies and separates from the retina as posterior vitreous detachment, giving floaters and flashes; traction at the vitreous base can tear the retina and cause detachment. Vitreous haemorrhage obscures the fundal red reflex.
cards.exam: Q. Why is a sudden shower of floaters with flashes an ophthalmic emergency? A. It suggests posterior vitreous detachment with traction that may have torn the retina, risking retinal detachment.

cards.desc: Thickened free upper border of the conus elasticus, forming the core of the vocal fold.
cards.att: Extends from the vocal process of the arytenoid cartilage posteriorly to the back of the angle of the thyroid cartilage anteriorly, midway between its upper and lower borders; the two ligaments meet anteriorly at the anterior commissure.
cards.act: Forms the sharp medial edge of the vocal fold and vibrates in phonation; the interval between the two folds and the arytenoids is the rima glottidis.
cards.rel: Covered medially by tightly adherent stratified squamous mucosa with no submucosa; thyroarytenoid and vocalis muscles lie lateral to it; the vestibular fold lies above, separated by the sinus of the larynx.
cards.clin: The rima glottidis is the narrowest part of the adult airway and determines tracheal tube size. Vocal nodules and most benign lesions occur at the junction of the anterior third and posterior two thirds of the fold. Because the fold has no submucosa, oedema tracks above it and Reinke's space swelling causes hoarseness.
cards.exam: Q. What is the sensory nerve supply above and below the vocal folds? A. Internal laryngeal nerve above, recurrent laryngeal nerve below.

cards.desc: The medial, deeper fibres of thyroarytenoid that lie alongside and attach to the vocal ligament in the vocal fold.
cards.att: Origin: inner surface of the angle of the thyroid cartilage, below the attachment of the vocal ligament. Insertion: the vocal process and lateral surface of the arytenoid cartilage, with fibres running into the vocal ligament along its length.
cards.sup: Recurrent laryngeal nerve, CN X.
cards.act: Alters the tension of individual segments of the vocal ligament, making the fine adjustments of pitch and vocal fold stiffness needed for phonation and singing.
cards.rel: Lies immediately lateral to the vocal ligament and medial to the rest of thyroarytenoid; the conus elasticus lies below it and the laryngeal ventricle above.
cards.clin: Its selective action lets the anterior part of the fold vibrate while the posterior is tensed, the basis of pitch control. It lies within the layer resected in cordectomy for early glottic carcinoma, so voice quality is affected.
cards.exam: Q. Vocalis is the medial part of which muscle? A. The thyroarytenoid.

cards.desc: Thin unpaired plate of bone forming the posteroinferior part of the bony nasal septum.
cards.att: Its upper border splits into two alae that grasp the rostrum of the sphenoid body; anterosuperiorly it meets the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid, anteroinferiorly the septal cartilage, and inferiorly the nasal crest formed by the maxillae and palatine bones. Its free posterior border separates the two choanae.
cards.act: Forms the bony partition of the posterior nasal cavity and supports the septal cartilage.
cards.rel: Covered on both sides by nasal mucoperiosteum; a groove on each side carries the nasopalatine nerve and the sphenopalatine vessels forwards to the incisive canal.
cards.clin: The vomer is a landmark in trans-sphenoidal pituitary surgery, its keel pointing to the sphenoid sinus in the midline. It is disrupted in Le Fort I fractures and its deviation contributes to nasal obstruction.
cards.exam: Q. Which three structures form the nasal septum? A. Perpendicular plate of the ethmoid, vomer, and the septal nasal cartilage.

cards.desc: Three layered wall of a cardiac ventricle: endocardium within, thick myocardium, and epicardium (visceral serous pericardium) outside.
cards.att: Extends from the atrioventricular and arterial fibrous rings to the apex, with the interventricular septum shared between the two ventricles. Its inner surface bears trabeculae carneae, the papillary muscles and, in the right ventricle, the septomarginal trabecula. The left ventricular wall is about 8 to 12 mm thick, roughly three times the thickness of the right.
cards.sup: Supplied by the coronary arteries, drained by the coronary sinus and anterior cardiac veins, innervated by sympathetic fibres from T1 to T5 and vagal parasympathetic fibres.
cards.act: Contracts in systole to eject blood; its spiral muscle bundles shorten the ventricle and twist it to empty the cavity efficiently.
cards.rel: Right ventricular wall lies behind the body of the sternum and left costal cartilages, the left ventricular wall forms the apex and left border and lies on the diaphragm posteroinferiorly.
cards.clin: Transmural infarction of the free wall may rupture 3 to 7 days later into the pericardium, causing tamponade, or heal as a ventricular aneurysm with persistent ST elevation. Left ventricular wall thickness above 11 mm in men and 10 mm in women on echocardiography defines hypertrophy; 15 mm or more, in the absence of abnormal loading conditions, suggests hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
cards.exam: Q. Why is the left ventricular wall three times thicker than the right? A. Because it pumps against the high resistance of the systemic circulation while the right pumps into the low pressure pulmonary circulation.

cards.desc: The myelinated core of each cerebral hemisphere beneath the cortex, appearing on a horizontal section above the corpus callosum as the centrum semiovale.
cards.att: Contains three fibre types: projection fibres of the corona radiata converging on the internal capsule; commissural fibres in the corpus callosum and anterior commissure crossing to the other hemisphere; association fibres, short arcuate fibres between adjacent gyri and long bundles such as the superior longitudinal (arcuate), inferior longitudinal, uncinate fasciculus and cingulum.
cards.sup: Deep penetrating medullary branches of the anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arteries, with poor collateral supply in the periventricular zone.
cards.act: Conducts impulses between cortical areas, between the two hemispheres and between cortex and subcortical structures.
cards.rel: Lies between the cerebral cortex superficially and the basal ganglia and lateral ventricles deeply; the corpus callosum roofs the lateral ventricles and its fibres radiate as the forceps minor and forceps major.
cards.clin: The periventricular white matter is an arterial border zone, the site of leukoaraiosis in chronic small vessel disease and of periventricular leukomalacia in the preterm infant. Multiple sclerosis plaques are typically periventricular and perpendicular to the ventricle (Dawson's fingers).
cards.exam: Q. Name the three classes of fibre in the cerebral white matter. A. Projection, commissural and association fibres.

cards.desc: Smallest and lowest of the three parts of the sternum, lying in the floor of the infrasternal angle.
cards.att: Joined above to the body of the sternum at the xiphisternal joint, a symphysis that ossifies in later life; it remains cartilaginous until about the fortieth year. Gives attachment to the linea alba, the medial fibres of rectus abdominis and the anterior abdominal aponeuroses in front, and to the diaphragm behind.
cards.act: Anchor point for the linea alba and the anterior fibres of the diaphragm.
cards.rel: The xiphisternal joint lies at the level of the T9 vertebra and marks the anterior inferior limit of the thoracic cavity, with the central tendon of the diaphragm, the upper surface of the liver and the inferior surface of the heart behind it.
cards.clin: The xiphisternal joint is the landmark for hand position in chest compressions; hands placed too low fracture the xiphoid and can lacerate the liver. It is also the entry point for subxiphoid pericardiocentesis, the needle passed upwards and aimed at the left shoulder.
cards.exam: Q. At what vertebral level is the xiphisternal joint? A. T9.

cards.desc: Quadrangular bone forming the prominence of the cheek and part of the lateral wall and floor of the orbit.
cards.att: Frontal process articulates with the zygomatic process of the frontal bone, temporal process with the zygomatic process of the temporal bone to form the zygomatic arch, and the maxillary surface with the maxilla; it also meets the greater wing of the sphenoid in the lateral orbital wall. Pierced by the zygomaticofacial and zygomaticotemporal foramina; the marginal tubercle on the frontal process and the whitnall tubercle inside the orbital margin give attachment to the lateral palpebral ligament and check ligament.
cards.act: Supports the cheek and protects the globe; the arch gives origin to masseter and transmits the temporalis tendon beneath it.
cards.rel: Masseter arises from its lower border and the arch; temporalis tendon passes deep to the arch; the orbital contents lie medial; the infraorbital nerve emerges from the maxilla just below the inferolateral orbital margin.
cards.clin: Zygomaticomaxillary complex (tripod) fracture flattens the cheek, causes numbness in the infraorbital nerve territory, subconjunctival haemorrhage and diplopia, and a depressed arch may impinge on the coronoid process and temporalis causing trismus.
cards.exam: Q. Why does trismus occur with a depressed zygomatic arch fracture? A. The displaced arch impinges on the coronoid process and the temporalis tendon, blocking mandibular movement.

posterior part of superior temporal gyrus

anterior interventricular branch of coronary artery
anterior interventricular branch of coronary artery

groups.name: Rotator cuff
groups.why: The four scapulohumeral muscles whose tendons blend with the shoulder capsule and hold the humeral head in the glenoid.

groups.name: Hamstrings
groups.why: Posterior thigh group from the ischial tuberosity, extending the hip and flexing the knee, supplied by the sciatic nerve.

groups.name: Quadriceps femoris
groups.why: The four heads converging on the patella and tibial tuberosity, the sole extensor of the knee.

groups.name: Triceps surae
groups.why: The three heads that form the calcaneal tendon and plantarflex the ankle.

groups.name: Gluteal muscles
groups.why: Superficial gluteal group: extensor and abductors of the hip, tested by the Trendelenburg sign.

groups.name: Short lateral rotators of the hip
groups.why: Deep gluteal group taught together as the landmark relations of the sciatic nerve in the buttock.

groups.name: Adductor compartment of the thigh
groups.why: Medial thigh compartment supplied by the obturator nerve, examined as one unit in groin pain.

groups.name: Pes anserinus
groups.why: Three tendons from three different nerves inserting together on the medial tibia.

groups.name: Anterior compartment of the leg
groups.why: Dorsiflexor compartment supplied by the deep fibular nerve; its failure gives foot drop.

groups.name: Lateral compartment of the leg
groups.why: Evertors of the foot supplied by the superficial fibular nerve.

groups.name: Deep posterior compartment of the leg
groups.why: Deep calf group behind the soleal line, supplied by the tibial nerve and passing behind the medial malleolus.

groups.name: First layer of the sole
groups.why: The plantar muscles are dissected in four named layers; this is the layer under the plantar aponeurosis.

groups.name: Tarsal bones
groups.why: The seven bones of the ankle and hindfoot, asked as a set in osteology vivas.

groups.name: Carpal bones
groups.why: The eight wrist bones in two rows, a standard mnemonic set in first-year osteology.

groups.name: Thenar muscles
groups.why: Thumb ball muscles supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve, wasted in carpal tunnel syndrome.
members: superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis

groups.name: Hypothenar muscles
groups.why: Little finger group supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
members: flexor digiti minimi brevis of hand

groups.name: Contents of the carpal tunnel
groups.why: Structures deep to the flexor retinaculum, the anatomy behind carpal tunnel syndrome.

groups.name: Superficial flexors of the forearm
groups.why: Common flexor origin group from the medial epicondyle, dissected as one layer.
members: humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris
ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris

groups.name: Deep flexors of the forearm
groups.why: Deep flexor layer supplied largely by the anterior interosseous nerve.

groups.name: Superficial extensors of the forearm
groups.why: Common extensor origin group from the lateral epicondyle, the site of tennis elbow.

groups.name: Deep extensors of the forearm
groups.why: Deep extensor layer crossing to the thumb and index finger, supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.

groups.name: Anatomical snuffbox
groups.why: Boundaries, floor and contents of the snuffbox: tenderness here means a scaphoid fracture until proved otherwise.

groups.name: Superficial veins of the upper limb
groups.why: The venepuncture and cannulation map of the arm.

groups.name: Intrinsic muscles of the hand
groups.why: Interossei and lumbricals, the ulnar and median nerve muscles tested for claw hand.
members: set of dorsal interossei of hand
set of palmar interossei of hand

groups.name: Cubital fossa
groups.why: Boundaries, floor and contents of the triangular hollow in front of the elbow.

groups.name: Suprahyoid muscles
groups.why: Floor of mouth group elevating the hyoid in swallowing, with four different nerve supplies.

groups.name: Infrahyoid strap muscles
groups.why: Strap muscles depressing the hyoid and larynx, supplied by the ansa cervicalis.

groups.name: Scalene muscles
groups.why: Lateral vertebral muscles bounding the interscalene triangle where the brachial plexus and subclavian artery emerge.

groups.name: Suboccipital muscles
groups.why: Four muscles bounding the suboccipital triangle, the landmark for the vertebral artery.

groups.name: Intrinsic muscles of the larynx
groups.why: Muscles moving the vocal folds; only posterior crico-arytenoid abducts, and only cricothyroid is superior laryngeal.

groups.name: Laryngeal cartilages
groups.why: Skeleton of the larynx; the cricoid is the only complete ring in the airway.

groups.name: Pharyngeal constrictors
groups.why: Three overlapping constrictors of the pharyngeal wall, all supplied by the pharyngeal plexus.

groups.name: Muscles of the soft palate
groups.why: Palatal group closing the nasopharynx in swallowing; tensor veli palatini alone is mandibular nerve.

groups.name: Extra-ocular muscles
groups.why: The four recti, two obliques and the lid elevator, examined together in cranial nerve III, IV and VI palsies.

groups.name: Lacrimal apparatus
groups.why: The route of tears from gland to inferior meatus, taught as one drainage pathway.

groups.name: Coats of the eyeball
groups.why: Fibrous, vascular and nervous tunics of the eye in order from outside in.

groups.name: Branches of the ophthalmic nerve
groups.why: The three divisions of cranial nerve V1 entering the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.

groups.name: Bones of the orbit
groups.why: Seven bones forming the orbital walls; the thin ethmoid and maxilla give way in blow-out fractures.

groups.name: Bones of the cranial vault
groups.why: The neurocranium, the bones enclosing the brain and forming the cranial fossae.

groups.name: Nasal septum
groups.why: Bony and cartilaginous parts of the septum, the site of septal deviation and anterior epistaxis.

groups.name: Permanent upper teeth
groups.why: One maxillary quadrant of the permanent dentition, the unit of dental notation.

groups.name: Cervical vertebrae
groups.why: The seven cervical vertebrae, including the two atypical ones and the vertebra prominens.

groups.name: Lumbar vertebrae
groups.why: Five large weight-bearing vertebrae; the cord ends at L1 and lumbar puncture is done below it.

groups.name: Erector spinae
groups.why: The three vertical columns of the intermediate back layer, extensors of the vertebral column.

groups.name: Sternum
groups.why: Three parts of the breastbone; the sternal angle marks the second costal cartilage and the T4/T5 disc.

groups.name: Muscles of respiration
groups.why: Principal and accessory muscles moving the thoracic cage in quiet and forced breathing.

groups.name: Heart valves
groups.why: Cusps and leaflets of the cardiac valves, each with its own surface area of auscultation.

groups.name: Great vessels
groups.why: Vessels entering and leaving the heart, the fixed landmarks of the mediastinum on a chest film.

groups.name: Azygos system
groups.why: Posterior thoracic veins linking the superior and inferior caval systems, the collateral route in caval obstruction.

groups.name: Branches of the coeliac trunk
groups.why: Three branches supplying the foregut derivatives at the T12 level.

groups.name: Tributaries of the portal vein
groups.why: Veins draining the gut to the liver, the anatomy behind portal hypertension and varices.

groups.name: Branches of the abdominal aorta
groups.why: Ventral, lateral and dorsal branches with their vertebral levels, a standard viva sequence.

groups.name: Biliary tree
groups.why: Path of bile from the liver to the duodenum, the anatomy of obstructive jaundice.

groups.name: Taeniae coli
groups.why: Three longitudinal muscle bands of the colon; they converge at the base of the appendix.

groups.name: Urinary tract
groups.why: The continuous path of urine, followed as one unit in obstruction and stone disease.

groups.name: Levator ani and pelvic floor
groups.why: The pelvic diaphragm supporting the pelvic viscera and maintaining continence.

groups.name: Male reproductive tract
groups.why: Path of sperm from testis to urethra, traced as one continuous duct system.

groups.name: Circle of Willis
groups.why: Anastomotic ring at the base of the brain linking carotid and vertebrobasilar supply.
members: precommunicating part of posterior cerebral artery
postcommunicating part of posterior cerebral artery

groups.name: Basal ganglia
groups.why: Deep grey masses of the corpus striatum, damaged in Parkinson's disease and Huntington's disease.

groups.name: Limbic system
groups.why: Circuit for memory and emotion, taught as the Papez loop.

groups.name: Brainstem
groups.why: Three parts carrying the long tracts and giving off cranial nerves III to XII.

groups.name: Ventricular system
groups.why: Cerebrospinal fluid pathway in order; blockage at any point causes hydrocephalus.

groups.name: Diencephalon
groups.why: Structures around the third ventricle, including the sensory relay and endocrine nuclei.

groups.name: Gyri of the frontal lobe
groups.why: Surface anatomy of the frontal lobe: motor cortex, frontal eye field and Broca's area.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vessel and state the vertebral level at which it divides.
spotters.answer: Common iliac artery. It arises from the aortic bifurcation at L4 and divides in front of the sacroiliac joint at the level of L5 (lumbosacral disc) into external and internal iliac arteries. The ureter crosses the bifurcation anteriorly, the key landmark for finding the ureter at pelvic surgery.
spotters.followup: Which structure crosses the bifurcation of this vessel, and why does that matter in hysterectomy?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery and name its two divisions.
spotters.answer: Internal iliac artery (hypogastric artery). About 4 cm long, it begins at the L5 level anterior to the sacroiliac joint and divides at the upper border of the greater sciatic foramen into an anterior division (mainly visceral: superior and inferior vesical, middle rectal, uterine, internal pudendal, inferior gluteal, obturator, umbilical) and a posterior division (parietal: iliolumbar, lateral sacral, superior gluteal). It is the main supply to the pelvic viscera, perineum and gluteal region.
spotters.followup: Why does ligation of this artery for postpartum haemorrhage often fail to stop bleeding completely?

spotters.prompt: The pinned vessel is being traced towards the greater sciatic foramen. Identify it and name the branch that most commonly passes above piriformis.
spotters.answer: Internal iliac artery. Its posterior division gives the superior gluteal artery, which leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis; the inferior gluteal artery from the anterior division leaves below piriformis. This above and below piriformis rule is the standard identification test in the gluteal region.
spotters.followup: Name three visceral branches of the anterior division of this artery.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery and state what it becomes distally.
spotters.answer: External iliac artery. It runs along the medial border of psoas major on the pelvic brim and becomes the femoral artery as it passes deep to the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point. Its two branches within the pelvis are the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac arteries.
spotters.followup: Which branch of this artery forms the lateral boundary of the inguinal (Hesselbach) triangle?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vessel and name the structure lying immediately medial to it behind the inguinal ligament.
spotters.answer: External iliac artery. Behind the inguinal ligament the external iliac vein lies medial to it, and the femoral canal with its lymph node lies medial to the vein. This lateral to medial order (artery, vein, canal) is the basis of the NAVEL mnemonic in the femoral triangle.
spotters.followup: Where would you palpate this vessel's continuation for a femoral pulse?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and state where the two of them unite.
spotters.answer: Common iliac vein. Formed by union of the external and internal iliac veins in front of the sacroiliac joint, the right and left common iliac veins unite at the level of L5, to the right of the midline, to form the inferior vena cava. The left vein is longer and more horizontal and is crossed anteriorly by the right common iliac artery.
spotters.followup: Why is left leg deep vein thrombosis commoner than right (May-Thurner)?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and name the vein it is continuous with distally.
spotters.answer: External iliac vein. It is the upward continuation of the femoral vein from behind the inguinal ligament and runs medial, then posteromedial, to the external iliac artery to join the internal iliac vein. It receives the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac veins and, when present, an accessory obturator vein.
spotters.followup: What is the corona mortis and why does it matter in hernia repair?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and name three tributaries.
spotters.answer: Internal iliac vein. It is formed above the greater sciatic foramen by tributaries that correspond to branches of the internal iliac artery: superior and inferior gluteal, internal pudendal, obturator, lateral sacral, middle rectal and vesical or uterine veins. It ascends behind and lateral to the internal iliac artery to join the external iliac vein and form the common iliac vein.
spotters.followup: Which artery-corresponding tributary does this vein NOT receive, and where does that vessel drain instead?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein running on the pelvic side wall towards the obturator canal.
spotters.answer: Obturator vein. It accompanies the obturator artery and nerve on the pelvic side wall, drains the adductor compartment through the obturator canal and normally ends in the internal iliac vein. In roughly a fifth to a quarter of people an accessory obturator vein drains instead into the external iliac or inferior epigastric vein, crossing the superior pubic ramus as the corona mortis, which can bleed severely in pubic ramus fracture or during hernia and pelvic node surgery.
spotters.followup: Through which canal does this vein leave the pelvis, and what forms the roof of that canal?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein lying on the fascia over obturator internus in the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa.
spotters.answer: Internal pudendal vein. It runs with the internal pudendal artery and pudendal nerve in the pudendal canal (Alcock canal), a fascial tunnel on obturator internus about 4 cm above the ischial tuberosity. It receives the inferior rectal and perineal veins and the deep dorsal vein territory of the penis, leaves the perineum through the lesser sciatic foramen and drains into the internal iliac vein.
spotters.followup: Name the two other contents of the pudendal canal and state the landmark for a pudendal nerve block.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein leaving the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis.
spotters.answer: Superior gluteal vein. It accompanies the superior gluteal artery, drains gluteus medius, minimus and tensor fasciae latae, passes above piriformis through the greater sciatic foramen and ends in the internal iliac vein. It is the largest tributary of the internal iliac vein.
spotters.followup: Which nerve accompanies this vessel, and what gait abnormality follows its injury?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein leaving the pelvis below piriformis, and name the artery it accompanies.
spotters.answer: Inferior gluteal vein. It accompanies the inferior gluteal artery, a branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery, drains gluteus maximus and the upper thigh, exits below piriformis through the greater sciatic foramen and drains into the internal iliac vein. It communicates with veins around the sciatic nerve.
spotters.followup: Which other two named structures leave the pelvis below piriformis alongside this vein?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein running vertically on the anterior surface of the sacrum lateral to the midline.
spotters.answer: Lateral sacral vein. It accompanies the lateral sacral artery from the posterior division of the internal iliac artery, communicates through the anterior sacral foramina with the internal vertebral venous plexus, and drains into the internal iliac vein. It is part of the presacral venous plexus, a source of torrential and hard to control bleeding in rectal surgery.
spotters.followup: How does this vein provide a route for pelvic tumour to reach the vertebral column and skull?

spotters.prompt: Identify the single midline vein pinned on the front of the sacrum and state where it usually drains.
spotters.answer: Median sacral vein. Unpaired, it accompanies the median sacral artery (a branch of the back of the aorta just above the bifurcation) on the anterior surface of the sacrum and usually drains into the left common iliac vein, less often into the junction forming the inferior vena cava.
spotters.followup: From which artery does the accompanying midline artery arise?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned bone and state how many vertebrae fuse to form it.
spotters.answer: Sacrum. Five fused sacral vertebrae forming the wedge-shaped posterior wall of the pelvis. Its base carries the sacral promontory, its auricular surface articulates with the ilium at the sacroiliac joint, and four pairs of anterior and posterior sacral foramina transmit the sacral anterior and posterior rami.
spotters.followup: At what vertebral level does the dural sac normally end in the adult, and why does that matter for caudal anaesthesia?

spotters.prompt: The pin is on the lower posterior aspect of this bone at the deficient laminae. Identify the bone and name the aperture there.
spotters.answer: Sacrum. The gap is the sacral hiatus, formed by failure of fusion of the laminae of the fifth (and often fourth) sacral vertebra, bounded by the sacral cornua. It is the entry point for caudal epidural anaesthesia, widely used in paediatric and obstetric practice, since the dural sac ends higher at about S2.
spotters.followup: Which bony landmarks do you palpate to locate this aperture?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned bone and name its three constituent parts.
spotters.answer: Hip bone (os coxae). Ilium, ischium and pubis, fused at the acetabulum through the triradiate cartilage, which typically ossifies between about 15 and 25 years. The two hip bones with the sacrum and coccyx form the bony pelvis; the obturator foramen is closed by the obturator membrane except at the obturator canal.
spotters.followup: Which part of this bone bears weight in the sitting position?

spotters.prompt: The pin is on the sharp projection at the posterior margin of this bone separating the greater and lesser sciatic notches. Identify the bone and name that projection.
spotters.answer: Hip bone. The projection is the ischial spine, which separates the greater from the lesser sciatic notch and gives attachment to the sacrospinous ligament and to coccygeus. It is palpable per vaginam and is the landmark for a transvaginal pudendal nerve block, since the pudendal nerve hooks round it. It also defines station zero in obstetric assessment of fetal descent.
spotters.followup: Which ligament converts the lesser sciatic notch into a foramen?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned triangular muscle behind levator ani and state its attachments.
spotters.answer: Coccygeus (ischiococcygeus). It runs from the ischial spine to the lateral margin of the coccyx and lowest sacral segment, lying on the pelvic surface of the sacrospinous ligament, with which it is coextensive. With levator ani it completes the pelvic diaphragm and supports the pelvic viscera. Supplied by branches of the anterior rami of S4 and S5.
