spotters.followup: Which ligament lies on the posterior surface of this muscle, and what foramen does that ligament help form?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned posterolateral part of levator ani and state its origin.
spotters.answer: Iliococcygeus. The most posterior and lateral part of levator ani, arising from the tendinous arch of levator ani (the thickened obturator internus fascia) and the ischial spine, inserting into the coccyx and the anococcygeal raphe. It is often thin and largely aponeurotic. Supplied by branches from the anterior rami of S3 and S4 (nerve to levator ani).
spotters.followup: Name the three parts of levator ani and state which is the most important for continence.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned part of levator ani arising from the back of the pubis.
spotters.answer: Pubococcygeus. It arises from the posterior surface of the body of the pubis and the anterior part of the tendinous arch of levator ani and passes backwards to the anococcygeal body and coccyx, with slips to the prostate or vagina, the urethra and the anal canal. It is the part torn or stretched in prolonged second stage labour, contributing to prolapse and stress incontinence, and is the muscle trained by pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises.
spotters.followup: Which structure in the female does the medial slip of this muscle support, and how does its injury cause prolapse?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned U-shaped sling at the anorectal junction and state its functional importance.
spotters.answer: Puborectalis. The medial, thickest part of levator ani, arising from the back of the pubic bodies and forming a sling behind the anorectal junction with no posterior bony attachment. It pulls the junction forwards, maintaining the anorectal angle of roughly 80 to 90 degrees, which is essential for faecal continence. With the deep external anal sphincter it forms the palpable anorectal ring; division of that ring in fistula surgery causes incontinence.
spotters.followup: Which fistula-in-ano operations risk dividing the anorectal ring, and what is the consequence?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle surrounding the anal canal and state its nerve supply.
spotters.answer: External anal sphincter. Voluntary striated muscle in subcutaneous, superficial and deep parts, surrounding the whole length of the anal canal, supplied by the inferior rectal (inferior anal) branch of the pudendal nerve, S2 to S4. It is responsible for voluntary continence; the internal anal sphincter, in contrast, is smooth muscle under autonomic control and maintains resting tone.
spotters.followup: How would you distinguish this muscle from the internal anal sphincter on structure and control?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and name the fibromuscular mass into which its superficial fibres decussate anteriorly.
spotters.answer: External anal sphincter. Its superficial part is anchored anteriorly to the perineal body and posteriorly to the coccyx by the anococcygeal ligament. The perineal body is the central tendon of the perineum, the meeting point of the external anal sphincter, bulbospongiosus, both transverse perinei and levator ani fibres. Third and fourth degree obstetric tears through the perineal body into this sphincter cause faecal incontinence if not repaired.
spotters.followup: Which degrees of perineal tear involve this muscle, and how are they classified?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned linear thickening on the fascia of the lateral pelvic wall and state what arises from it.
spotters.answer: Tendinous arch of levator ani. A thickened band of obturator internus fascia running from the body of the pubis to the ischial spine, giving origin to iliococcygeus and the posterior fibres of pubococcygeus. It should be distinguished from the arcus tendineus fasciae pelvis, the more medial white line to which the vaginal wall and endopelvic fascia attach.
spotters.followup: Which muscle's fascia forms this arch, and which nerve lies on that muscle's fascia in the pudendal canal?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned viscus and state where it begins and ends.
spotters.answer: Rectum. About 12 to 15 cm long, it begins at the level of the S3 vertebra as the continuation of the sigmoid colon and ends at the anorectal junction, where it pierces the pelvic diaphragm to become the anal canal. Unlike the colon it has no taeniae coli, no sacculations and no appendices epiploicae, and it shows three transverse folds (valves of Houston).
spotters.followup: Name three features that distinguish this structure from sigmoid colon on inspection.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned viscus and name its three arteries of supply.
spotters.answer: Rectum. Supplied by the superior rectal artery (continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery, the main supply), the middle rectal artery from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery, and the inferior rectal artery from the internal pudendal artery. Venous drainage is correspondingly portal above and systemic below, making the anorectal junction a site of portosystemic anastomosis, and it explains why rectal carcinoma metastasises to liver and lung.
spotters.followup: Explain why carcinoma of the lower part of this organ can metastasise to lung without passing through liver.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned viscus and state the muscle that forms its wall and the nerve that makes it contract.
spotters.answer: Urinary bladder. Its wall is the detrusor muscle, smooth muscle supplied by parasympathetic fibres from the pelvic splanchnic nerves S2, S3 and S4, which contract the detrusor and relax the internal sphincter for micturition. In the adult the empty bladder lies entirely within the pelvis behind the pubic symphysis.
spotters.followup: Why can a full bladder be tapped suprapubically without entering the peritoneal cavity?

spotters.prompt: The pin is on the smooth triangular area on the internal aspect of the posterior wall of this organ. Identify the organ and name that area and its three corners.
spotters.answer: Urinary bladder. The area is the trigone, bounded by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice, with the interureteric ridge running between the ureteric orifices. Its mucosa is smooth and firmly adherent (unlike the rugose remainder), it is mesodermal in origin from the absorbed mesonephric ducts, and it is highly sensitive, a common site for cystitis, tuberculous ulceration and tumour.
spotters.followup: Which part of this organ is covered by peritoneum, and where does urine collect when it ruptures there?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned gland and state its relations to bladder and urethra.
spotters.answer: Prostate. A fibromuscular glandular organ about the size of a chestnut (roughly 3 by 4 by 2 cm, 8 to 20 g), with its base fused to the neck of the bladder above and its apex resting on the external urethral sphincter below. The prostatic urethra runs through it, and the two ejaculatory ducts enter its posterosuperior aspect to open on the seminal colliculus.
spotters.followup: Which surface of this gland is palpated on digital rectal examination, and what feature is felt in the midline?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned gland and explain its route of metastasis to the vertebral column.
spotters.answer: Prostate. The prostatic venous plexus lies in the fascial sheath around the gland, receives the deep dorsal vein of the penis, drains to the internal iliac veins and communicates with the internal vertebral venous plexus (Batson plexus) through valveless connections. A rise in intra-abdominal pressure can therefore carry tumour emboli directly to the lumbar vertebrae, pelvis and skull, producing characteristically osteosclerotic (osteoblastic) secondaries.
spotters.followup: Which zone of this gland gives rise to most carcinomas, and which enlarges in benign hypertrophy?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned structure lying on the posterior surface of the bladder and state its function.
spotters.answer: Seminal vesicle. A coiled sacculated tube about 5 cm long, lying obliquely on the base of the bladder lateral to the ampulla of the deferent duct and above the prostate, separated from the rectum by the rectovesical (Denonvilliers) fascia. It does not store sperm: it secretes the alkaline fructose-rich, prostaglandin-containing fluid that forms the bulk of seminal volume. Its duct joins the ampulla of the deferent duct to form the ejaculatory duct.
spotters.followup: With which duct does this structure unite, and where does the resulting duct open?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned duct and state where it begins and ends.
spotters.answer: Deferent duct (ductus deferens, vas deferens). It begins at the tail of the epididymis, ascends in the spermatic cord through the inguinal canal, enters the pelvis at the deep inguinal ring, and ends by joining the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct. Its very thick smooth muscle wall gives it a characteristic whipcord feel on palpation in the scrotum, where it is divided at vasectomy.
spotters.followup: At vasectomy, where is this duct most conveniently approached and why?

spotters.prompt: The pin is on this duct in the pelvis, near the ischial spine. Identify it and state its relation to the ureter.
spotters.answer: Deferent duct. In the pelvis it crosses the ureter from lateral to medial, lying anterior and superior to it near the ischial spine, before reaching the base of the bladder and dilating as the ampulla. This is the male counterpart of the uterine artery and ureter relation, 'water under the bridge', and orientates the surgeon to the ureter in pelvic dissection.
spotters.followup: What is the female equivalent of this crossing relation, and why is it surgically important?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned structure on the testis and name its three parts.
spotters.answer: Epididymis. A comma-shaped coiled duct on the posterolateral surface of the testis with a head (receiving the efferent ductules), a body and a tail, from which the deferent duct continues. It is the site of sperm storage and functional maturation. Tuberculous involvement classically starts in the tail (globus minor), giving a craggy, sometimes beaded, swelling.
spotters.followup: How does epididymo-orchitis differ from testicular torsion on clinical examination?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned organ and state its arterial supply.
spotters.answer: Testis. Supplied by the testicular artery, which arises directly from the abdominal aorta just below the renal artery at about L2, reflecting the organ's development on the posterior abdominal wall and its later descent. It is covered by the tunica albuginea and, anteriorly and laterally, the tunica vaginalis, a closed serous sac in which fluid collects as a hydrocele.
spotters.followup: Where do the veins draining this organ end on each side, and why is varicocele commoner on the left?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned organ and state its lymphatic drainage.
spotters.answer: Testis. Lymph drains along the testicular vessels to the para-aortic (lumbar) nodes at the L2 level, not to the inguinal nodes, because the organ develops on the posterior abdominal wall. Scrotal skin, by contrast, drains to the superficial inguinal nodes. Hence a testicular tumour is staged by abdominal imaging, while a scrotal skin lesion is assessed at the groin.
spotters.followup: A patient has an enlarged inguinal node and a testicular mass. What does that combination suggest anatomically?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned paired erectile body and state where its proximal end is attached.
spotters.answer: Corpus cavernosum of penis. The paired dorsal erectile bodies; each begins as a crus attached to the ischiopubic ramus and covered by ischiocavernosus, then the two run forward side by side enclosed in the tough tunica albuginea. The deep artery of the penis, a branch of the internal pudendal artery, runs within each and gives the helicine arteries responsible for erection.
spotters.followup: Which nerves mediate erection and which mediate emission, and where do they arise?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned single ventral erectile body and state what it transmits.
spotters.answer: Corpus spongiosum of penis. The single midline ventral erectile body, expanded proximally as the bulb of the penis (covered by bulbospongiosus) and distally as the glans. It transmits the spongy (penile) urethra throughout its length. Its tunica is thin and it stays at lower pressure during erection, so the urethra is not occluded and ejaculation can occur.
spotters.followup: Which muscle covers the proximal expansion of this body, and what is its action?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned structure and state its sensory nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Glans penis. The expanded distal end of the corpus spongiosum, capped over the ends of the corpora cavernosa, bearing the external urethral meatus and bounded proximally by the corona and neck. Sensory supply is the dorsal nerve of the penis, a branch of the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4). It is the most densely innervated part of the penis and mediates the afferent limb of the reflex.
spotters.followup: Which nodes receive lymph from this structure, and how does that differ from the skin of the penis?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery on the dorsum of the penis and name its parent vessel.
spotters.answer: Dorsal artery of penis. A terminal branch of the internal pudendal artery, it runs forward deep to the deep fascia of the penis (Buck fascia), lying between the deep dorsal vein medially and the dorsal nerve of the penis laterally, and supplies the skin, prepuce and glans. The deep artery of the penis, its companion terminal branch, lies inside the corpus cavernosum instead.
spotters.followup: List the structures on the dorsum of the penis from midline outwards, deep to Buck fascia.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein lying superficial to the deep fascia of the penis and state where it drains.
spotters.answer: Superficial dorsal vein of penis. It lies in the superficial (dartos) fascia, superficial to Buck fascia, drains the skin and prepuce and ends in the superficial external pudendal vein and so into the great saphenous and femoral vein. This is the systemic route, in contrast to the deep dorsal vein, which passes deep to Buck fascia and beneath the pubic symphysis to the prostatic venous plexus.
spotters.followup: Contrast the drainage of this vein with that of the deep dorsal vein, and give the clinical significance.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned tube and name its parts in the male.
spotters.answer: Urethra. In the male it is about 18 to 20 cm long with preprostatic, prostatic, membranous and spongy (penile) parts; the spongy part is often subdivided into bulbar and penile portions. In the female it is short, about 4 cm, running from the bladder neck to open in the vestibule anterior to the vaginal orifice, which explains the far higher incidence of ascending urinary infection in women.
spotters.followup: Which is the widest and most dilatable part, and which is the narrowest point in the male?

spotters.prompt: The pin is on the short segment of this tube passing through the perineal membrane. Identify the structure and state the injury pattern associated with this segment.
spotters.answer: Urethra, membranous part. About 1 to 2 cm long, it is the shortest and least dilatable part, surrounded by the external urethral sphincter (sphincter urethrae), supplied by the pudendal nerve, and fixed as it pierces the perineal membrane. Because it is fixed, it is the part torn in fractures of the pelvis, and extravasated urine collects in the deep perineal pouch or, with bladder neck disruption, above the perineal membrane. A straddle injury instead ruptures the bulbar spongy part, and urine then tracks into the superficial perineal pouch, scrotum, penis and anterior abdominal wall, but never into the thigh.
spotters.followup: Trace the path of extravasated urine after a straddle injury and state why it does not enter the thigh.

spotters.prompt: The pin is on the segment of this tube traversing the prostate. Identify the structure and name the elevation on which the ejaculatory ducts open.
spotters.answer: Urethra, prostatic part. The widest and most dilatable part, about 3 cm long, showing on its posterior wall the urethral crest with the seminal colliculus (verumontanum) in the middle. The prostatic utricle opens on the summit of the colliculus with an ejaculatory duct on either side, and the prostatic sinuses on each side of the crest receive the 20 to 30 prostatic ducts.
spotters.followup: What is the developmental origin of the prostatic utricle?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned gland and explain why its enlargement obstructs micturition.
spotters.answer: Prostate. Benign hyperplasia arises in the transition zone around the preprostatic and prostatic urethra, so the enlarging tissue compresses the urethral lumen and elevates the bladder neck, producing hesitancy, poor stream, terminal dribbling and eventually retention with detrusor hypertrophy and trabeculation. Carcinoma, in contrast, arises mostly in the peripheral zone, which is why it is felt as a hard nodule on rectal examination but often obstructs late.
spotters.followup: Why does the median lobe of this gland cause obstruction out of proportion to its size?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and explain how pelvic sepsis can reach the lung through it.
spotters.answer: Internal iliac vein. The pelvic venous plexuses (prostatic or uterovaginal, vesical, rectal) drain into it, and it has valveless communications with the vertebral venous plexus. Septic thrombophlebitis of these plexuses, for instance after pelvic sepsis or puerperal infection, propagates into this vein and then via the common iliac vein and inferior vena cava to the right heart and pulmonary arteries, producing septic pulmonary emboli.
spotters.followup: Name the pelvic venous plexuses that drain into this vein in the male.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and state the two foramina its associated ligament helps to form.
spotters.answer: Coccygeus. It lies on the pelvic surface of the sacrospinous ligament, running from the ischial spine to the coccyx and lowest sacrum. The sacrospinous ligament converts the greater sciatic notch into the greater sciatic foramen and, with the sacrotuberous ligament, converts the lesser sciatic notch into the lesser sciatic foramen. The pudendal nerve crosses the ischial spine between the two ligaments, the site of the ischial spine pudendal block.
spotters.followup: Which nerve and vessels are at risk during a sacrospinous fixation for vault prolapse?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and name the midline raphe into which it inserts posteriorly.
spotters.answer: Iliococcygeus. Its fibres from each side meet in the midline behind the anal canal in the anococcygeal raphe (levator plate), also inserting on the coccyx. Loss of tone in this plate lets the levator hiatus widen and the pelvic organs descend, an anatomical basis of pelvic organ prolapse.
spotters.followup: What passes through the levator hiatus in the male and in the female?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vessel in the femoral triangle and state where you would palpate it in a shocked patient.
spotters.answer: Femoral artery. Continuation of the external iliac artery distal to the inguinal ligament, palpated at the mid-inguinal point, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis. In the triangle it lies lateral to the femoral vein and medial to the femoral nerve, NAVEL from lateral to medial being nerve, artery, vein, empty space, lymphatics.
spotters.followup: Trace it distally: name the canal it enters and the opening through which it leaves the thigh.

spotters.prompt: Identify this vessel and state its relation to the artery beside it at the base of the femoral triangle.
spotters.answer: Femoral vein. Lies medial to the femoral artery at the inguinal ligament and posterior to it lower in the triangle. It is the continuation of the popliteal vein from the adductor hiatus and becomes the external iliac vein behind the inguinal ligament. Standard site for femoral central venous access, one finger medial to the palpable arterial pulse.
spotters.followup: Which two named tributaries join it within the femoral triangle?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned superficial vein and state the bony landmark used to find it at the ankle.
spotters.answer: Great saphenous vein. Constant position one centimetre anterior to the medial malleolus, the classic venous cut-down site. It ascends on the medial leg and thigh and drains into the femoral vein at the saphenous opening, roughly four centimetres inferolateral to the pubic tubercle. Accompanied by the saphenous nerve below the knee, so a cut-down risks saphenous neuralgia.
spotters.followup: Why is this the vein of choice for coronary artery bypass grafting, and which way must the graft be oriented?
spotters.sub: Superficial veins, medial leg and thigh

spotters.prompt: Identify this superficial vein and name the vein it drains into.
spotters.answer: Small saphenous vein. Begins at the lateral end of the dorsal venous arch of foot, passes behind the lateral malleolus, ascends in the midline of the calf, pierces the deep popliteal fascia and drains into the popliteal vein in the popliteal fossa. The sural nerve accompanies it, and is at risk during stripping or harvest.
spotters.followup: Which nerve travels with it, and what sensory deficit follows if that nerve is divided?

spotters.prompt: Identify this strap muscle and give its nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Sartorius. Femoral nerve, root value L2 and L3. Longest muscle in the body, running from the anterior superior iliac spine to the upper medial tibia as part of the pes anserinus. It forms the lateral boundary of the femoral triangle and the roof of the adductor canal, and produces the cross-legged tailor position: flexion, abduction and lateral rotation at the hip with flexion at the knee.
spotters.followup: Name the other two tendons that form the pes anserinus with it, and give their nerve supplies.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned quadriceps component and state what makes it different from the other three heads.
spotters.answer: Rectus femoris. Femoral nerve, L2 to L4. The only part of quadriceps femoris that crosses the hip joint, so it flexes the hip as well as extending the knee, and is weakest as a knee extensor when the hip is already flexed. Two heads: a straight head from the anterior inferior iliac spine and a reflected head from the ilium just above the acetabulum.
spotters.followup: Where do all four heads converge, and what is the patella functionally within that structure?

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle and state its clinical importance at the patellofemoral joint.
spotters.answer: Vastus medialis. Femoral nerve, L2 to L4. Arises from the intertrochanteric line, spiral line, linea aspera and medial supracondylar line. Its low horizontal fibres, the oblique part, insert on the medial patellar border and are the main dynamic check against lateral patellar dislocation. It wastes visibly and early in knee joint pathology, and is the last part to recover after immobilisation.
spotters.followup: Name the two bony and one muscular factor that resist lateral dislocation of the patella.

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle and state one procedural use of it.
spotters.answer: Vastus lateralis. Femoral nerve, L2 to L4. Arises from the greater trochanter, intertrochanteric line and lateral lip of the linea aspera. It is the largest quadriceps component and the preferred site for intramuscular injection in infants and small children, the middle third of the anterolateral thigh, because the gluteal muscles are poorly developed at that age.
spotters.followup: Which fibrous band lies superficial to it laterally, and what inserts into that band?

spotters.prompt: Identify this adductor and state which border of the femoral triangle its medial edge forms.
spotters.answer: Adductor longus. Anterior division of the obturator nerve, L2 to L4. Arises by a narrow tendon from the body of the pubis below the pubic crest and fans out into the middle third of the linea aspera. Its medial border forms the medial boundary of the femoral triangle, and it is the most anterior adductor, easily made prominent by resisted adduction. Common site of adductor strain, or rider's sprain.
spotters.followup: Which structure lies immediately deep to it, and what nerve divisions straddle that structure?

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle and state which joints it acts on.
spotters.answer: Gracilis. Anterior division of the obturator nerve, L2 and L3. The most superficial and medial muscle of the compartment, and the only adductor that crosses the knee, so it adducts and flexes the hip and flexes and medially rotates the flexed knee. Runs from the body and inferior ramus of the pubis to the upper medial tibia in the pes anserinus. Its length and dispensable action make it a standard muscle transfer for facial reanimation and for anal sphincter reconstruction.
spotters.followup: Give the two other tendons of the pes anserinus and the order in which they lie.

spotters.prompt: Identify this quadrangular muscle and state its nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Pectineus. Usually the femoral nerve, L2 and L3, with a frequent additional supply from the obturator or accessory obturator nerve. This dual innervation reflects its position at the boundary between the anterior and medial compartments. Runs from the pecten pubis to the pectineal line of the femur, and forms part of the floor of the femoral triangle along with iliopsoas laterally and adductor longus medially.
spotters.followup: Name the three muscles forming the floor of the femoral triangle from lateral to medial.
spotters.sub: Medial thigh, floor of femoral triangle

spotters.prompt: Identify this large composite muscle and account for its double nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Adductor magnus. Composite muscle with two parts. The adductor part, from the ischiopubic ramus to the linea aspera, is supplied by the posterior division of the obturator nerve. The hamstring part, from the ischial tuberosity to the adductor tubercle, is supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve. The gap between the aponeurotic insertion and the adductor tubercle is the adductor hiatus, transmitting the femoral vessels into the popliteal fossa.
spotters.followup: Name the openings in this muscle and state what passes through each.

spotters.prompt: Identify this deep muscle and state its nerve supply and action.
spotters.answer: Obturator externus. Posterior division of the obturator nerve, L3 and L4. Arises from the outer surface of the obturator membrane and adjacent bone, and its tendon runs backwards and laterally below the neck of the femur to the trochanteric fossa. It is a lateral rotator of the hip and stabilises the head in the acetabulum. Despite acting with the short lateral rotators it is developmentally an adductor compartment muscle, which is why the obturator nerve supplies it.
spotters.followup: Its tendon crosses the neck of the femur. Which fracture pattern therefore threatens the retinacular vessels running alongside?

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle and give its nerve supply and principal action.
spotters.answer: Gluteus maximus. Inferior gluteal nerve, L5, S1 and S2. Coarse-fibred, quadrilateral muscle from the posterior gluteal line of the ilium, sacrum, coccyx and sacrotuberous ligament, inserting mostly into the iliotibial tract with a deeper quarter into the gluteal tuberosity. Chief extensor and lateral rotator of the hip, recruited for rising from sitting, climbing stairs and running, not for ordinary level walking.
spotters.followup: Which quadrant of the buttock is safe for intramuscular injection and which nerve is at risk if you inject elsewhere?

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle and state the clinical sign produced by its paralysis.
spotters.answer: Gluteus medius. Superior gluteal nerve, L4, L5 and S1. Runs from the outer ilium between the posterior and anterior gluteal lines to the lateral surface of the greater trochanter. With gluteus minimus it abducts the hip and, critically, holds the pelvis level on the stance side during walking. Paralysis gives a positive Trendelenburg sign: the pelvis drops on the unsupported swing side when the patient stands on the affected leg.
spotters.followup: Name three causes of a positive Trendelenburg sign other than nerve injury.

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle and state why it is the key landmark of the gluteal region.
spotters.answer: Piriformis. Nerve to piriformis, S1 and S2. Arises from the front of the sacrum between the anterior sacral foramina, passes out through the greater sciatic foramen and inserts on the upper border of the greater trochanter. It fills the greater sciatic foramen, so every structure entering or leaving the gluteal region is identified as passing above or below it. Lateral rotator of the extended hip, abductor of the flexed hip.
spotters.followup: Name the structures leaving the pelvis above this muscle and those leaving below it.

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle and describe the unusual course of its tendon.
spotters.answer: Obturator internus. Nerve to obturator internus, L5 and S1. Arises from the inner surface of the obturator membrane and surrounding pelvic wall, leaves the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen and turns almost ninety degrees around the lesser sciatic notch, which is covered with cartilage and cushioned by a bursa, before inserting into the medial surface of the greater trochanter. Flanked above and below by the gemelli, forming the tricipital tendon. Lateral rotator of the hip.
spotters.followup: Its nerve leaves the pelvis, crosses the ischial spine and re-enters. Name the two foramina involved.

spotters.prompt: Identify this flat quadrangular muscle and state its nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Quadratus femoris. Nerve to quadratus femoris, L4, L5 and S1, arising from the sacral plexus and running deep to the muscle. Runs horizontally from the lateral border of the ischial tuberosity to the quadrate tubercle on the intertrochanteric crest. Lowest of the short lateral rotators, lying between gemellus inferior above and the upper fibres of adductor magnus below. The trochanteric anastomosis lies deep to it.
spotters.followup: Which artery runs deep to this muscle and why does its integrity matter after a femoral neck fracture?

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle and state what it inserts into.
spotters.answer: Tensor fasciae latae. Superior gluteal nerve, L4, L5 and S1, the same nerve as gluteus medius and minimus. Arises from the anterior part of the outer lip of the iliac crest and the anterior superior iliac spine, and inserts not into bone but into the iliotibial tract about a third of the way down the thigh. It tenses the fascia lata, assists hip abduction and flexion, and helps stabilise the extended knee.
spotters.followup: Name the other muscle that inserts into the same fibrous band and give its nerve supply.

spotters.prompt: Identify this fibrous band and state its distal bony attachment.
spotters.answer: Iliotibial tract. Longitudinally thickened lateral part of the fascia lata, running from the iliac tubercle to Gerdy's tubercle on the anterolateral aspect of the lateral tibial condyle. It receives the insertions of tensor fasciae latae and about three quarters of gluteus maximus. Acts as a lateral tension band for the femur and stabilises the knee in extension. Friction over the lateral femoral epicondyle causes iliotibial band syndrome, a common runner's complaint.
spotters.followup: Name the two muscles inserting into it and the nerve supplying each.

spotters.prompt: Identify this hamstring and state its nerve supply and distal attachment.
spotters.answer: Semitendinosus. Tibial division of the sciatic nerve, L5, S1 and S2. Arises with the long head of biceps from the ischial tuberosity, and its long cord-like tendon begins at mid-thigh and inserts on the upper medial surface of the tibia as the most posterior and lowest of the three pes anserinus tendons. Extends the hip, flexes and medially rotates the knee. Commonly harvested for anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
spotters.followup: Which hamstring is supplied by the common fibular division of the sciatic nerve, and why does that matter in a proximal hamstring injury?

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle and state which boundary of the popliteal fossa it forms.
spotters.answer: Semimembranosus. Tibial division of the sciatic nerve, L5, S1 and S2. Broad membranous proximal tendon from the ischial tuberosity, inserting mainly into the groove on the posterior aspect of the medial tibial condyle. It forms the superomedial boundary of the popliteal fossa, lying deep to semitendinosus. An expansion from its tendon passes upwards and laterally as the oblique popliteal ligament, which reinforces the posterior capsule of the knee.
spotters.followup: Name the four boundaries of the popliteal fossa and the structure crossing its floor most deeply.

spotters.prompt: Identify this vessel and state why it is the hardest pulse in the limb to feel.
spotters.answer: Popliteal artery. Continuation of the femoral artery from the adductor hiatus, ending at the lower border of popliteus by dividing into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries. It is the deepest structure in the popliteal fossa, lying directly on the popliteal surface of the femur and the posterior capsule of the knee, so it must be palpated with the knee passively flexed and the fingers pressed forward against the bone. Tethered at both ends, it is torn or intimally injured in supracondylar fracture of the femur and in posterior knee dislocation.
spotters.followup: Name its genicular branches and the anastomosis they form.

spotters.prompt: Identify this vessel and give its relation to the artery and the nerve in the fossa.
spotters.answer: Popliteal vein. Formed by union of the anterior tibial vein and posterior tibial vein at the lower border of popliteus, and becomes the femoral vein at the adductor hiatus. In the fossa the three main structures lie superficial to deep as tibial nerve, then vein, then artery, so from the surface the order is nerve, vein, artery. It is firmly bound to the artery in a common sheath, which is why a penetrating injury here readily produces an arteriovenous fistula.
spotters.followup: Which superficial vein pierces the deep fascia to end in it?

spotters.prompt: Identify this triangular muscle on the floor of the popliteal fossa and state its unlocking action.
spotters.answer: Popliteus. Tibial nerve, L4, L5 and S1. Runs from a groove on the lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle, inside the knee capsule, downwards and medially to the tibia above the soleal line. It unlocks the fully extended knee by laterally rotating the femur on the fixed tibia, or medially rotating the tibia on the fixed femur, so flexion can begin. Its tendon is intracapsular but extrasynovial, and it attaches to the lateral meniscus, pulling it back during flexion.
spotters.followup: What locks the knee in full extension, and which ligament tightens during that mechanism?

spotters.prompt: Identify this small muscle with a long tendon and state its nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Plantaris. Tibial nerve, S1 and S2. Small fusiform belly arising from the lateral supracondylar line of the femur just above the lateral head of gastrocnemius, with a very long slender tendon running inferomedially between gastrocnemius and soleus to insert on the calcaneus medial to the calcaneal tendon. Functionally negligible, absent in around ten percent of limbs, and harvested as a tendon graft. Its long thin tendon is the classic structure mistaken for a nerve by beginners.
spotters.followup: Which injury is popularly attributed to rupture of this muscle, and what is the more usual pathology?

spotters.prompt: Identify this broad multipennate muscle and state its role in venous return.
spotters.answer: Soleus. Tibial nerve, S1 and S2. Arises from the soleal line and medial border of the tibia, the head and upper posterior fibula, and the fibrous arch between them. Joins gastrocnemius to form the calcaneal tendon. Predominantly slow twitch and postural, it is the chief plantar flexor in standing. Its large venous sinuses are emptied by contraction during walking, the calf muscle pump or peripheral heart, and stasis in these sinuses during immobility is where deep vein thrombosis typically begins.
spotters.followup: Which vessels and nerve pass deep to its fibrous arch, and what does the arch cause if it is tight?

spotters.prompt: Identify this tendon, name the muscles contributing to it, and give one clinical test for its rupture.
spotters.answer: Calcaneal tendon, the tendo Achillis. Formed by gastrocnemius and soleus, inserting into the middle of the posterior surface of the calcaneal tuberosity with a retrocalcaneal bursa between it and the upper part of the bone. Thickest and strongest tendon in the body. Rupture, typically two to six centimetres above the insertion in a relatively avascular zone, gives a palpable gap, weak plantar flexion and a positive Simmonds or Thompson test, in which squeezing the calf fails to plantar flex the foot.
spotters.followup: Which nerve root value is tested by the ankle jerk transmitted through this tendon?

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle, give its nerve supply and state the deformity produced by its paralysis.
spotters.answer: Tibialis anterior. Deep fibular nerve, L4 and L5. Arises from the lateral tibial condyle, upper half of the lateral tibial surface and interosseous membrane, and inserts into the medial cuneiform bone and base of the first metatarsal bone. Strongest dorsiflexor and an invertor of the foot. Paralysis, typically from common fibular nerve injury at the neck of the fibula, gives foot drop with a high stepping gait and slapping of the foot on heel strike.
spotters.followup: Name the other contents of the anterior compartment and the artery running with the nerve.

spotters.prompt: Identify this tendon and state which vessel is found alongside it at the ankle.
spotters.answer: Extensor hallucis longus. Deep fibular nerve, L5 and S1. Arises from the middle half of the medial surface of the fibula and the interosseous membrane, emerges between tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus, and inserts into the base of the distal phalanx of the big toe. The dorsalis pedis artery is palpated immediately lateral to its tendon on the dorsum of the foot. Weakness of great toe extension is a sensitive early sign of an L5 root lesion.
spotters.followup: Which root value is tested by resisted extension of the great toe, and what other muscle group would you test to confirm it?

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle, give its nerve supply, and state where its tendon ends.
spotters.answer: Fibularis longus. Superficial fibular nerve, L5, S1 and S2. Arises from the head and upper two thirds of the lateral surface of the fibula, its tendon passes behind the lateral malleolus, then grooves the cuboid bone and crosses the sole obliquely to insert into the lateral side of the medial cuneiform bone and the base of the first metatarsal bone. Everts and plantar flexes the foot, and its sling across the sole is the main dynamic support of the transverse arch.
spotters.followup: Which muscle has an almost identical insertion approached from the opposite side, and what arch do the two together support?

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle and name its bony insertion and the fracture associated with it.
spotters.answer: Fibularis brevis. Superficial fibular nerve, L5, S1 and S2. Arises from the lower two thirds of the lateral surface of the fibula, lies deep and anterior to fibularis longus at the malleolus, and inserts into the tuberosity on the base of the fifth metatarsal bone. Chief evertor of the foot. Forced inversion of the plantar flexed foot avulses that tuberosity, the pseudo-Jones or dancer's fracture, which is often mistaken clinically for a simple lateral ligament sprain.
spotters.followup: Distinguish the avulsion fracture at that site from a true Jones fracture, and say why the distinction matters.

spotters.prompt: Identify this small muscle and state its nerve supply, noting the compartment it belongs to.
spotters.answer: Fibularis tertius. Deep fibular nerve, L5 and S1. It is a separated lateral part of extensor digitorum longus, so despite its name it lies in the anterior compartment and is not supplied by the superficial fibular nerve. Arises from the lower anterior surface of the fibula and inserts on the dorsal surface of the base of the fifth metatarsal bone. Dorsiflexes and everts the foot, and is absent in a substantial minority of limbs.
spotters.followup: Two tendons attach at the base of the fifth metatarsal. Name both and state which surface each takes.

spotters.prompt: Identify this artery and state how it reaches the compartment it lies in.
spotters.answer: Anterior tibial artery. Smaller terminal branch of the popliteal artery, arising at the lower border of popliteus and entering the anterior compartment through the oval gap in the upper part of the interosseous membrane of leg. It descends on the anterior surface of that membrane with the deep fibular nerve, lying between tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus in the lower leg, and becomes the dorsalis pedis artery at the front of the ankle midway between the malleoli.
spotters.followup: Name its recurrent branch at the knee and the anastomosis it enters.

spotters.prompt: Identify this artery and state exactly where you palpate it.
spotters.answer: Dorsalis pedis artery. Continuation of the anterior tibial artery distal to the ankle. Palpated on the dorsum of the foot lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus, in the proximal part of the first intermetatarsal space, against the intermediate cuneiform bone. It passes between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous muscle as the deep plantar artery to complete the plantar arch. Congenitally absent or aberrant in roughly one in twenty limbs, so absence alone is not proof of disease.
spotters.followup: Which artery does its deep plantar branch join in the sole, and what does that anastomosis form?

spotters.prompt: Identify this artery and give the surface marking for its pulse.
spotters.answer: Posterior tibial artery. Larger terminal branch of the popliteal artery. It descends deep to soleus on tibialis posterior, then passes behind the medial malleolus under the flexor retinaculum in the tarsal tunnel, where its pulse is felt midway between the posterior border of the medial malleolus and the medial border of the calcaneal tendon. It terminates by dividing into the medial and lateral plantar arteries and is the dominant blood supply to the sole.
spotters.followup: List the contents of the tarsal tunnel from anterior to posterior and name the syndrome caused by their compression.
spotters.sub: Posterior compartment of leg and ankle

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle and state its role in the arches of the foot.
spotters.answer: Tibialis posterior. Tibial nerve, L4 and L5. Deepest muscle of the posterior compartment, arising from the interosseous membrane of leg and the adjacent posterior surfaces of tibia and fibula. Its tendon is the most anterior structure behind the medial malleolus and inserts mainly into the tuberosity of the navicular bone of foot with slips to the cuneiforms and middle metatarsals. Chief invertor of the foot and the principal dynamic support of the medial longitudinal arch. Tendon dysfunction produces acquired adult flatfoot.
spotters.followup: Give the mnemonic order of the structures behind the medial malleolus, and name the retinaculum that holds them.

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle and trace its tendon into the foot.
spotters.answer: Flexor hallucis longus. Tibial nerve, S1 and S2. Arises from the lower two thirds of the posterior surface of the fibula and adjacent interosseous membrane. Its tendon grooves the posterior process of the talus and the undersurface of the sustentaculum tali of the calcaneus, crosses beneath flexor digitorum longus in the sole at the knot of Henry, then runs between the two sesamoid bones to the base of the distal phalanx of the big toe. It gives the final push off in walking and supports the medial longitudinal arch.
spotters.followup: Which two structures does its tendon pass between at the head of the first metatarsal, and what condition affects them?

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle and state its nerve supply and the muscles that attach to its tendons.
spotters.answer: Flexor digitorum longus. Tibial nerve, L5, S1 and S2. Arises from the medial part of the posterior surface of the tibia below the soleal line, passes behind the medial malleolus between tibialis posterior and the posterior tibial vessels, then divides into four tendons for the distal phalanges of the lateral four toes. Flexor accessorius inserts into its tendon in the sole and the four lumbricals arise from its tendons. Flexes the lateral four toes and grips the ground in propulsion.
spotters.followup: Name the muscle that corrects its oblique line of pull, and give that muscle's nerve supply.

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle of the first layer and give its nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Abductor hallucis. Medial plantar nerve, S1 and S2. Most medial muscle of the first layer, arising from the medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity and the flexor retinaculum, and inserting with flexor hallucis brevis into the medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the big toe. Abducts and flexes the great toe and braces the medial longitudinal arch. Its deep fascia can entrap the medial plantar nerve or the first branch of the lateral plantar nerve, a cause of medial heel pain.
spotters.followup: Name all three muscles of the first layer of the sole and the nerve supplying each.

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle and describe what happens to its tendons at the toes.
spotters.answer: Flexor digitorum brevis. Medial plantar nerve, S1 and S2. Central muscle of the first layer, arising from the medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity and the plantar aponeurosis, giving four tendons to the lateral four toes. Each tendon splits to allow the corresponding flexor digitorum longus tendon to pass through, then reunites and inserts on the sides of the middle phalanx, exactly as flexor digitorum superficialis does in the hand. Its calcaneal origin is involved in plantar fasciitis and heel spur pain.
spotters.followup: Which muscle in the upper limb is its exact structural counterpart, and on which phalanx do both insert?

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle of the second layer and explain its functional purpose.
spotters.answer: Flexor accessorius, also called quadratus plantae. Lateral plantar nerve, S1, S2 and S3. Arises by two heads from the medial surface and the lateral border of the plantar surface of the calcaneus and inserts into the lateral border of the tendon of flexor digitorum longus. Because that tendon enters the sole obliquely from the medial side, this muscle pulls it into line so the toes flex straight rather than being drawn medially. It is a muscle without any counterpart in the hand.
spotters.followup: Name the other components of the second layer of the sole and state the nerve supply of each lumbrical.

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle and give its nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Abductor digiti minimi of foot. Lateral plantar nerve, S2 and S3. Most lateral muscle of the first layer, arising from both processes of the calcaneal tuberosity and the plantar aponeurosis and inserting with flexor digiti minimi brevis of foot into the lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the little toe. Abducts and flexes the fifth toe and supports the lateral longitudinal arch. The nerve to it, the first branch of the lateral plantar nerve or Baxter's nerve, is a recognised cause of chronic heel pain.
distractors: flexor digiti minimi brevis of foot
spotters.followup: Which branch of which nerve supplies it, and what heel symptom follows if that branch is entrapped?

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle and state which toe it moves and in which direction.
spotters.answer: First plantar interosseous of foot. Lateral plantar nerve, S2 and S3. Unipennate muscle arising from the medial side of the base and shaft of the third metatarsal bone and inserting into the medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the third toe. The three plantar interossei adduct toes three, four and five towards the axis of the second toe, PAD, and also flex the metatarsophalangeal joints while extending the interphalangeal joints. There is no plantar interosseous for the second toe because that toe is the reference axis.
spotters.followup: State the reference axis for abduction and adduction in the foot and how it differs from the hand.

spotters.prompt: Identify this arterial arch and name the two vessels that form it.
spotters.answer: Plantar arch, the deep plantar arch. Formed by the lateral plantar artery, the larger terminal branch of the posterior tibial artery, curving medially across the bases of the metatarsals in the fourth layer, completed medially by the deep plantar branch of the dorsalis pedis artery passing between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous. It lies deep to the oblique head of adductor hallucis and gives the plantar metatarsal arteries, which divide into the plantar digital arteries proper.
spotters.followup: Name the branches arising from its convexity and explain how they supply the toes.

spotters.prompt: Identify this structure and state what passes through it and where.
spotters.answer: Interosseous membrane of leg. Fibrous sheet between the interosseous borders of the tibia and fibula, with fibres running downwards and laterally from tibia to fibula, so it transmits load from the tibia to the fibula. It gives origin to muscles of both the anterior and deep posterior compartments and separates them. The anterior tibial artery passes forward through an oval gap in its upper part, and the perforating branch of the fibular artery passes through it near its lower end.
spotters.followup: Name the two compartments it separates and one muscle arising from each of its surfaces.

spotters.prompt: Identify this bone and state the vascular consequence of a fracture of its neck.
spotters.answer: Femur. Longest and strongest bone in the body. The head is supplied mainly by retinacular branches of the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries running along the neck under the retinacular fibres, with a small contribution from the artery of the ligamentum teres. An intracapsular fracture of the neck tears these retinacular vessels and commonly causes avascular necrosis of the head, which is why such fractures in the elderly are usually treated with replacement rather than fixation.
spotters.followup: Distinguish intracapsular from extracapsular neck fractures and explain why the prognosis differs.

spotters.prompt: Identify this bone and state what kind of bone it is.
spotters.answer: Patella. Largest sesamoid bone in the body, developed in the tendon of quadriceps femoris. Its posterior surface is articular with a larger lateral and smaller medial facet, articulating with the femoral condyles. It increases the leverage of quadriceps by holding the tendon away from the joint axis and protects the front of the knee. Dislocation is almost always lateral, resisted by the prominent lateral femoral condyle and the oblique fibres of vastus medialis.
spotters.followup: Name the fibrous structure connecting it to the tibia and give the bony landmark of its attachment.

spotters.prompt: Identify this bone and state why fractures of its shaft are often compound.
spotters.answer: Tibia. The weight-bearing bone of the leg. Its anterior border and anteromedial surface are subcutaneous throughout, covered only by skin and periosteum, so shaft fractures readily become open or compound. The junction of the middle and lower thirds is the narrowest part and the commonest fracture site, and it is also the least vascular, so delayed union and non-union are frequent. Its nutrient artery arises from the posterior tibial artery and runs downwards.
spotters.followup: Name the four compartments of the leg and say which is most often affected by compartment syndrome after a tibial fracture.

spotters.prompt: Identify this bone and state the nerve injured at its upper end.
spotters.answer: Fibula. Non weight-bearing bone of the leg, providing muscle attachment and forming the lateral malleolus of the ankle mortise. The common fibular nerve winds around its neck, where it lies against bone with almost no soft tissue cover. Fracture of the neck, a tight plaster, or prolonged crossed-leg posture injures the nerve and produces foot drop with loss of dorsiflexion and eversion and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and lateral leg.
spotters.followup: Which muscles are paralysed in that lesion, and which single movement is preserved that distinguishes it from an L5 root lesion?

spotters.prompt: Identify this bone and name the shelf on its medial surface.
spotters.answer: Calcaneus. Largest and strongest tarsal bone, forming the heel and transmitting body weight to the ground. The sustentaculum tali projects medially from its upper part, supporting the talus above and grooved below by the tendon of flexor hallucis longus. Its posterior tuberosity gives insertion to the calcaneal tendon and origin to the first layer of the sole. A fall from a height drives the talus into it and causes a comminuted fracture, classically with an associated burst fracture of the lumbar spine.
spotters.followup: Which tendon grooves the undersurface of the sustentaculum tali, and which ligament attaches to its upper border?

spotters.prompt: Identify this bone and state the two features that make its fractures troublesome.
spotters.answer: Talus. It has no muscular or tendinous attachment at all, and about two thirds of its surface is covered with articular cartilage, leaving little area for vessels to enter. Its blood supply enters mainly through the neck and runs backwards into the body, so a fracture of the neck interrupts the supply and causes avascular necrosis of the body, Hawkins classification. It transmits body weight from the tibia to the calcaneus and the forefoot, and is the only bone linking the leg to the foot.
spotters.followup: Name the joints it takes part in and state which movement occurs at each.

spotters.prompt: Identify this bone and name the tendon inserting on its tuberosity.
spotters.answer: Navicular bone of foot. Boat-shaped tarsal bone lying between the head of the talus behind and the three cuneiforms in front, on the medial side of the foot. Its prominent medial tuberosity receives the main insertion of tibialis posterior and is palpable about two and a half centimetres in front of and below the medial malleolus, the standard surface landmark for the medial longitudinal arch. An accessory ossicle at this site is a common incidental finding, and childhood osteochondritis of the bone is Kohler's disease.
spotters.followup: Which ligament runs from the sustentaculum tali to this bone, and what does it support?

spotters.prompt: Identify this ossicle, name the tendon it lies within, and state what passes between the pair.
spotters.answer: Sesamoid bone of foot. The medial and lateral sesamoids lie in the two tendons of flexor hallucis brevis beneath the head of the first metatarsal bone, embedded in the plantar plate. They protect the tendon of flexor hallucis longus, which runs in the groove between them, take weight during push off and increase the leverage of the short flexor. They are a site of sesamoiditis, avascular necrosis and stress fracture in dancers and runners, and a bipartite medial sesamoid is a common normal variant.
spotters.followup: Name the largest sesamoid bone in the body and the tendon it develops in.

spotters.prompt: Identify this ligament, give its attachments, and state the tunnel it helps form.
spotters.answer: Long plantar ligament. Longest ligament of the sole, running from the plantar surface of the calcaneus in front of the tuberosity to the ridge on the cuboid bone, with superficial fibres continuing forward to the bases of the middle three metatarsals. By bridging the groove on the cuboid it converts it into a tunnel for the tendon of fibularis longus. It is the principal passive support of the lateral longitudinal arch, working with the short plantar ligament deep to it and the plantar aponeurosis superficially.
spotters.followup: Name the three passive supports of the lateral longitudinal arch in order from superficial to deep.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned bone and state the commonest site of fracture in it.
spotters.answer: Clavicle. It is the only bony strut connecting the upper limb to the axial skeleton, articulating medially at the sternoclavicular joint and laterally at the acromioclavicular joint. The commonest fracture site is the junction of the middle and lateral thirds. The lateral fragment is pulled down by the weight of the limb and the medial fragment pulled up by sternocleidomastoid. It is the first bone in the body to ossify and the last to complete ossification.
spotters.followup: Which vessels and nerve trunk lie immediately deep to the middle third and are at risk in a displaced fracture, and which muscle protects them?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned bone. Name the muscle whose paralysis makes its medial border stand away from the chest wall.
spotters.answer: Scapula. Winging of the scapula follows paralysis of serratus anterior due to long thoracic nerve injury (C5, C6, C7). Key surface landmarks: spine at T3 vertebral level, inferior angle at T7, coracoid process palpable in the deltopectoral triangle.
spotters.followup: Name the three bony processes of this bone and one muscle attaching to each.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned bone and state which nerve is injured in a fracture of its surgical neck.
spotters.answer: Humerus. A surgical neck fracture endangers the axillary nerve and the posterior circumflex humeral artery, which wind around the neck through the quadrangular space. Loss gives deltoid paralysis, failure of abduction beyond the initial range, and a patch of anaesthesia over the regimental badge area.
spotters.followup: Which nerve runs in the spiral groove of this bone, and which nerve is at risk in a fracture of the medial epicondyle?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned bone. Name the classical fracture of its lower end and the resulting deformity.
spotters.answer: Radius. Colles fracture: a fracture of the distal radius within 2.5 cm of the wrist with dorsal displacement and dorsal angulation of the distal fragment, often with radial shift and an associated ulnar styloid fracture. It produces the dinner fork deformity. It follows a fall on the outstretched hand, typically in an osteoporotic elderly woman.
spotters.followup: Which extensor tendon may rupture weeks after this fracture, and why?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned bone and name one muscle inserting on it at the elbow.
spotters.answer: Ulna. Brachialis inserts on the ulnar tuberosity and the coronoid process, making it the chief flexor of the elbow. The olecranon forms the point of the elbow and receives triceps. The bone is subcutaneous along its whole posterior border, so its shaft is easily palpated from olecranon to styloid process.
spotters.followup: Define a Monteggia fracture dislocation and say which nerve is at risk in it.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned carpal bone and explain why its fracture is prone to avascular necrosis.
spotters.answer: Scaphoid. It is the commonest carpal bone to fracture, usually at the waist after a fall on the outstretched hand, and gives tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. Its blood supply enters mainly through the dorsal surface distally and runs retrograde, so a waist or proximal fracture devascularises the proximal pole and causes avascular necrosis and non-union.
spotters.followup: Name the two tendons forming the anterior border and the one forming the posterior border of the anatomical snuffbox.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned carpal bone and state what is special about it.
spotters.answer: Pisiform. It is a sesamoid bone developing in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris, sitting on the palmar surface of the triquetral. It gives attachment to the pisohamate and pisometacarpal ligaments and to abductor digiti minimi of hand. It forms the medial boundary of the ulnar canal of Guyon, through which the ulnar nerve and ulnar artery enter the palm superficial to the flexor retinaculum.
spotters.followup: Which structure forms the lateral wall of Guyon canal, and which nerve is compressed there in cyclists?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned carpal bone and name the boundary it forms.
spotters.answer: Hamate. Its hook forms the medial pillar for the distal attachment of the flexor retinaculum, so it is part of the medial wall of the carpal tunnel, and it forms the lateral wall of Guyon canal. Fracture of the hook occurs in racquet and club sports and can injure the deep branch of the ulnar nerve, weakening the interossei.
spotters.followup: Name the four bony points to which the flexor retinaculum attaches.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned fibrous structure and state the direction of its fibres and its functional importance.
spotters.answer: Interosseous membrane of forearm. Its principal fibres run downwards and medially from the interosseous border of the radius to the interosseous border of the ulna. It binds the two bones, transmits force from the radius to the ulna and thence to the humerus when weight is taken on the hand, and gives origin to deep flexor and extensor muscles on its two surfaces.
spotters.followup: Which two vessels arise from the common interosseous artery in relation to this membrane, and where does each run?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle part and give its nerve supply and chief action.
spotters.answer: Acromial part of deltoid, the middle multipennate part arising from the acromion. Nerve supply is the axillary nerve (C5, C6). It is the main abductor of the arm from about 15 to 90 degrees, taking over from supraspinatus. Its multipennate architecture gives it power for this action.
spotters.followup: How would you test the axillary nerve clinically in a patient with a painful shoulder who cannot abduct?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle. State its nerve supply and its role in abduction.
spotters.answer: Supraspinatus. Arising from the supraspinous fossa and inserting on the superior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus, supplied by the suprascapular nerve (C5, C6). It initiates abduction through the first 15 degrees and stabilises the humeral head against the glenoid. It is the most commonly torn rotator cuff tendon and produces the painful arc between 60 and 120 degrees.
spotters.followup: Name the four rotator cuff muscles and say which one is not attached to the greater tubercle.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and give its nerve supply and action.
spotters.answer: Infraspinatus muscle. It arises from the infraspinous fossa and inserts into the middle facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus. Nerve supply is the suprascapular nerve (C5, C6), which reaches it by winding around the lateral border of the spine of the scapula through the spinoglenoid notch. It is a lateral rotator of the humerus and part of the rotator cuff.
spotters.followup: Where can this nerve be entrapped, and how do the clinical findings differ between entrapment at the suprascapular notch and at the spinoglenoid notch?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and name the space it helps to bound.
spotters.answer: Teres minor. It arises from the upper part of the lateral border of the scapula and inserts on the inferior facet of the greater tubercle. Nerve supply is the axillary nerve (C5, C6), the only rotator cuff muscle supplied by that nerve. It forms the upper boundary of the quadrangular space, through which pass the axillary nerve and the posterior circumflex humeral artery.
spotters.followup: Name all four boundaries of the quadrangular space and its contents.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle. State its nerve supply and one surgical landmark it provides.
spotters.answer: Teres major. It arises from the dorsal surface of the inferior angle and lower lateral border of the scapula and inserts on the medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus. Nerve supply is the lower subscapular nerve (C5, C6). It adducts and medially rotates the arm. Its lower border marks the point at which the axillary artery becomes the brachial artery, and it forms the lower boundary of both the quadrangular and the triangular spaces.
spotters.followup: Which structure passes through the triangular space, and which structure passes through the triangular interval?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and give its nerve supply and action.
spotters.answer: Subscapularis. It fills the subscapular fossa on the costal surface of the scapula and inserts into the lesser tubercle of the humerus, the only rotator cuff muscle to do so. Nerve supply is the upper and lower subscapular nerves (C5, C6, C7). It is the chief medial rotator of the arm and reinforces the anterior capsule of the shoulder, resisting anterior dislocation.
spotters.followup: How is this muscle tested clinically, and in which direction do most shoulder dislocations occur?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and state the consequence of paralysing its nerve.
spotters.answer: Serratus anterior. It arises by digitations from the upper eight ribs and inserts along the costal surface of the medial border of the scapula. Nerve supply is the long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7). It protracts the scapula and, with trapezius, rotates it upwards to allow elevation of the arm above the head. Injury during axillary dissection or from a blow to the chest wall produces winging of the scapula and inability to raise the arm above shoulder level.
spotters.followup: How do you elicit winging at the bedside, and how does winging from accessory nerve palsy differ?
spotters.sub: Upper limb, thoracic wall and axilla

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and state its importance to the axillary artery.
spotters.answer: Pectoralis minor. It arises from ribs 3, 4 and 5 and inserts into the coracoid process of the scapula. Nerve supply is the medial pectoral nerve (C8, T1). It divides the axillary artery into three parts: the first part proximal to the muscle, the second deep to it, and the third distal to it. The first part gives one branch, the second gives two, and the third gives three.
spotters.followup: Name the branches of each of the three parts of the axillary artery.
spotters.sub: Upper limb, thoracic wall and axilla

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle part and give its nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Descending part of trapezius, the upper fibres running from the external occipital protuberance, ligamentum nuchae and upper cervical spines to the lateral third of the clavicle. Motor supply is the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), with C3 and C4 carrying proprioception. It elevates the scapula and, with serratus anterior, rotates the glenoid cavity upwards.
spotters.followup: Where does this nerve lie superficially in the posterior triangle of the neck, and what deformity follows its division at that point?
spotters.sub: Upper limb, back and scapular region

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and state what is anatomically distinctive about its nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Coracobrachialis. It arises from the tip of the coracoid process and inserts on the middle of the medial surface of the humeral shaft. Nerve supply is the musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6, C7), which characteristically pierces the substance of the muscle before running between biceps and brachialis. It flexes and adducts the arm and is the medial marker of the floor of the axilla.
spotters.followup: Into what cutaneous nerve does the musculocutaneous nerve continue, and where does it emerge?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle. Give its nerve supply and its insertion.
spotters.answer: Brachialis. It arises from the lower half of the anterior surface of the humerus and inserts into the coronoid process and tuberosity of the ulna. Nerve supply is the musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6), with the lateral part receiving a twig from the radial nerve. Because it inserts on the ulna it is the workhorse flexor of the elbow in every position of the forearm, unlike biceps whose power is greatest in supination.
spotters.followup: Which muscle forms the floor of the cubital fossa, and name the contents of that fossa from lateral to medial.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle. State its nerve supply and explain why its supply is exceptional for its action.
spotters.answer: Brachioradialis. It arises from the upper two thirds of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus and inserts on the base of the styloid process of the radius. It is supplied by the radial nerve (C5, C6) yet it is a flexor of the elbow, which is exceptional because the radial nerve otherwise supplies extensors. It is most efficient with the forearm midprone and forms the lateral boundary of the cubital fossa.
spotters.followup: Which reflex tests the C5 and C6 segments through this muscle, and where do you strike to elicit it?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and state the clinical landmark its tendon provides at the wrist.
spotters.answer: Flexor carpi radialis. It arises from the common flexor origin on the medial epicondyle and inserts on the bases of the second and third metacarpal bones. Nerve supply is the median nerve (C6, C7). It flexes and abducts the wrist. At the wrist the radial artery is palpated immediately lateral to its tendon, and the median nerve lies between it and palmaris longus.
spotters.followup: Does this tendon pass through the carpal tunnel? Explain your answer.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and state two clinically relevant facts about it.
spotters.answer: Palmaris longus. It arises from the common flexor origin and inserts into the flexor retinaculum and the apex of the palmar aponeurosis. Nerve supply is the median nerve (C7, C8). It is congenitally absent in roughly one in seven people, often unilaterally, and is a favoured donor for tendon grafting. Its tendon crosses superficial to the flexor retinaculum, not through the carpal tunnel, and the median nerve lies immediately deep and slightly lateral to it.
spotters.followup: How do you demonstrate this tendon in the living subject, and why does its absence matter to the surgeon planning carpal tunnel decompression?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle. State its insertion and the joint it flexes.
spotters.answer: Flexor digitorum superficialis. Arising by humero-ulnar and radial heads, its four tendons split around those of flexor digitorum profundus at the chiasma tendinum and insert into the sides of the middle phalanges of the medial four fingers. Nerve supply is the median nerve (C7, C8, T1). It flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints principally, and can act on each finger independently.
spotters.followup: How do you test this muscle in isolation in one finger at the bedside?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and give its dual nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Flexor digitorum profundus. It arises from the upper three quarters of the anterior and medial surfaces of the ulna and the adjacent interosseous membrane, and inserts into the bases of the distal phalanges of the medial four fingers. Its lateral half, to the index and middle fingers, is supplied by the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve, and its medial half, to the ring and little fingers, by the ulnar nerve (C8, T1). It is the only muscle able to flex the distal interphalangeal joints.
spotters.followup: Explain the ulnar paradox: why is the claw hand more marked in a low ulnar nerve lesion at the wrist than in a high lesion at the elbow?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and give its nerve supply and insertion.
spotters.answer: Flexor pollicis longus. It arises from the anterior surface of the radius and the adjacent interosseous membrane and inserts into the base of the distal phalanx of the thumb. Nerve supply is the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve (C7, C8). It flexes the interphalangeal joint of the thumb, and its tendon runs through the carpal tunnel in its own radial bursa.
spotters.followup: Which clinical sign tests the anterior interosseous nerve, and which two muscles besides this one does that nerve supply?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle. Give its attachments, nerve supply and action.
spotters.answer: Pronator quadratus. It is the deepest muscle of the anterior compartment, running transversely from the lower quarter of the anterior surface of the ulna to the lower quarter of the anterior surface of the radius. Nerve supply is the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve (C7, C8). It is the prime mover of pronation, with pronator teres recruited for power and speed, and its deep fibres hold the radius and ulna together at the inferior radio-ulnar joint.
spotters.followup: Name the muscles of pronation and supination and say which is the more powerful movement, with a practical example.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and name the nerve that pierces it.
spotters.answer: Supinator. It arises by superficial and deep heads from the lateral epicondyle, the radial collateral and anular ligaments and the supinator crest of the ulna, and wraps around the upper third of the radius to insert on its lateral surface. Nerve supply is the deep branch of the radial nerve (C6, C7). That nerve passes between the two heads at the arcade of Frohse and emerges posteriorly as the posterior interosseous nerve, so a fracture of the radial neck or a tumour here causes finger drop with the wrist deviating radially.
spotters.followup: Why is there no true wrist drop in a posterior interosseous nerve lesion, and which two muscles account for that?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and give its insertion and nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Extensor carpi ulnaris. It arises from the common extensor origin on the lateral epicondyle and from the posterior border of the ulna, and inserts into the medial side of the base of the fifth metacarpal bone. Nerve supply is the posterior interosseous nerve (C7, C8). It extends and adducts the wrist. Acting with flexor carpi ulnaris it produces pure ulnar deviation, and its tendon runs in the sixth extensor compartment in the groove between the head and styloid process of the ulna.
spotters.followup: Name the six extensor compartments under the extensor retinaculum and their contents in order from radial to ulnar.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and describe how its tendons end in the fingers.
spotters.answer: Extensor digitorum. It arises from the common extensor origin on the lateral epicondyle and gives four tendons to the medial four fingers. Nerve supply is the posterior interosseous nerve (C7, C8). Over the proximal phalanx each tendon expands into the extensor hood or dorsal digital expansion, which receives the lumbrical and interosseous tendons and divides into a central slip to the base of the middle phalanx and two collateral slips to the base of the distal phalanx.
spotters.followup: Why is independent extension of the ring finger limited, and what is a mallet finger?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle. State the relation of its tendon to the extensor digitorum tendon of the same finger.
spotters.answer: Extensor indicis. It arises from the posterior surface of the lower ulna and the adjacent interosseous membrane, deep to the superficial extensors, and its tendon runs in the fourth extensor compartment to join the ulnar side of the extensor digitorum tendon of the index finger. Nerve supply is the posterior interosseous nerve (C7, C8). It permits independent extension of the index finger and is commonly harvested for tendon transfer after rupture of extensor pollicis longus.
spotters.followup: Which two fingers can be extended independently and why?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and name the bony landmark around which its tendon turns.
spotters.answer: Extensor pollicis longus. It arises from the middle third of the posterior surface of the ulna and the interosseous membrane and inserts into the base of the distal phalanx of the thumb. Nerve supply is the posterior interosseous nerve (C7, C8). Its tendon hooks around the dorsal tubercle of the radius, Lister tubercle, which acts as a pulley and turns it laterally. It forms the posterior or medial border of the anatomical snuffbox.
spotters.followup: Why may this tendon rupture some weeks after an undisplaced Colles fracture, and how is function restored?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and name the condition affecting the compartment its tendon occupies.
spotters.answer: Abductor pollicis longus. It arises from the posterior surfaces of the ulna, radius and interosseous membrane and inserts on the base of the first metacarpal bone. Nerve supply is the posterior interosseous nerve (C7, C8). With extensor pollicis brevis it forms the anterior or lateral border of the anatomical snuffbox and shares the first extensor compartment, where stenosing tenovaginitis produces de Quervain disease, positive on the Finkelstein test.
spotters.followup: Name the boundaries, floor and contents of the anatomical snuffbox.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and state its nerve supply and clinical importance.
spotters.answer: Abductor pollicis brevis. It arises from the flexor retinaculum and the tubercles of the scaphoid and trapezium and inserts into the lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb. Nerve supply is the recurrent branch of the median nerve (C8, T1). It abducts the thumb at right angles to the palm and is the muscle tested to confirm median nerve function, since wasting of the thenar eminence and loss of true thumb abduction are the cardinal motor signs of carpal tunnel syndrome.
spotters.followup: Why is sensation over the thenar eminence preserved in carpal tunnel syndrome but lost in a median nerve laceration higher in the forearm?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and give its origin and nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Abductor digiti minimi of hand. It arises from the pisiform and the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris and inserts on the medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the little finger. Nerve supply is the deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8, T1). It abducts the little finger and is the most superficial and medial of the hypothenar muscles.
distractors: flexor digiti minimi brevis of hand
spotters.followup: Name the three hypothenar muscles and the fourth small muscle of the medial palm that is not classed with them.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscles. State their unusual origin and their dual nerve supply.
