spotters.answer: Set of lumbricals of hand. There are four, and uniquely among skeletal muscles they arise from tendon rather than bone, from the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus in the palm. Each passes on the radial side of its finger to join the dorsal digital expansion. The lateral two are supplied by digital branches of the median nerve and the medial two by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. They flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints.
distractors: set of palmar interossei of hand
set of dorsal interossei of hand
spotters.followup: Explain the position of the hand in an ulnar claw and why only the ring and little fingers are clawed.

spotters.target: set of dorsal interossei of hand
spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscles. State their number, action and nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Set of dorsal interossei of hand. There are four, each bipennate and arising from the adjacent sides of two metacarpal bones. They abduct the fingers away from the midline of the middle finger, remembered as DAB, and through the extensor expansions they also flex the metacarpophalangeal and extend the interphalangeal joints. Nerve supply is the deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8, T1). The first is the largest and forms the visible mass in the first web space.
distractors: set of palmar interossei of hand
spotters.followup: Which artery passes between the two heads of the first of these muscles, and what does it form in the palm?

spotters.target: set of palmar interossei of hand
spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscles and contrast their action with that of their dorsal counterparts.
spotters.answer: Set of palmar interossei of hand. They are unipennate and arise from the shaft of a single metacarpal bone. They adduct the fingers towards the midline of the middle finger, remembered as PAD, the opposite of the dorsal group which abduct. Nerve supply is the deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8, T1). Both groups insert into the extensor expansion and so flex the metacarpophalangeal and extend the interphalangeal joints.
distractors: set of dorsal interossei of hand
flexor digiti minimi brevis of hand
spotters.followup: Describe the card test and Froment sign, and state which nerve lesion they detect.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery and state where it begins and ends.
spotters.answer: Axillary artery. It is the continuation of the subclavian artery, beginning at the outer border of the first rib and ending at the lower border of teres major, where it becomes the brachial artery. It is divided into three parts by pectoralis minor and is enclosed with the cords of the brachial plexus in the axillary sheath, a prolongation of the prevertebral fascia.
spotters.followup: How are the cords of the brachial plexus arranged around the second part of this artery, and what is the scapular anastomosis?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery. State where it terminates and its relation to the biceps tendon.
spotters.answer: Brachial artery. It begins at the lower border of teres major as the continuation of the axillary artery and ends at the level of the neck of the radius, roughly 2.5 cm below the elbow crease, by dividing into the radial and ulnar arteries. In the cubital fossa it lies medial to the biceps tendon and lateral to the median nerve, and it is separated from the median cubital vein by the bicipital aponeurosis, which protects it during venepuncture.
spotters.followup: Where do you place the stethoscope to record blood pressure, and what is Volkmann ischaemic contracture?
spotters.sub: Upper limb, arm and cubital fossa

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery and name the nerve accompanying it.
spotters.answer: Deep brachial artery, the profunda brachii. It is the largest branch of the brachial artery, arising just below the lower border of teres major, and it accompanies the radial nerve through the triangular interval into the spiral groove of the humerus. It divides into radial collateral and middle collateral branches which take part in the anastomosis around the elbow, so both the artery and the radial nerve are at risk in a mid shaft fracture of the humerus.
spotters.followup: Name the arteries taking part in the anastomosis around the elbow joint and pair each collateral with its recurrent partner.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery. Name the space it traverses and its companion nerve.
spotters.answer: Posterior circumflex humeral artery. It arises from the third part of the axillary artery and passes backwards through the quadrangular space with the axillary nerve, winding around the surgical neck of the humerus deep to deltoid. It anastomoses with the anterior circumflex humeral artery and with ascending branches from the profunda brachii. It is torn along with the axillary nerve in a surgical neck fracture or an anterior shoulder dislocation.
spotters.followup: Which vessel supplies most of the humeral head, and by which route does it reach it?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery. State its origin and its relation to the superior transverse scapular ligament.
spotters.answer: Suprascapular artery. It arises from the thyrocervical trunk of the first part of the subclavian artery, crosses the posterior triangle of the neck, and passes over, that is superficial to, the superior transverse scapular ligament to reach the supraspinous fossa, while the suprascapular nerve passes under the ligament. It supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus and is a key contributor to the scapular anastomosis.
spotters.followup: Why does the scapular anastomosis allow ligation of the axillary artery between the origins of the subscapular and the thyrocervical contributions to remain safe, and where must ligation be avoided?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery, name the nerve it accompanies and the vessel with which it anastomoses.
spotters.answer: Superior ulnar collateral artery. It arises from the brachial artery near the middle of the arm, pierces the medial intermuscular septum and accompanies the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus. It anastomoses with the posterior ulnar recurrent artery. Its inferior counterpart, the inferior ulnar collateral artery, arises just above the elbow and anastomoses in front of the medial epicondyle with the anterior ulnar recurrent artery.
spotters.followup: Why does the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle give the sensation known as hitting the funny bone, and what sensory loss follows a lesion at that point?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery. Give its origin, course and the nerve running with it.
spotters.answer: Anterior interosseous artery. It is a branch of the common interosseous artery, itself a branch of the ulnar artery just below the elbow. It descends on the anterior surface of the interosseous membrane between flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus, accompanied by the anterior interosseous nerve. It pierces the membrane at the upper border of pronator quadratus to enter the posterior compartment and join the dorsal carpal arch.
spotters.followup: Which three muscles are supplied by the nerve accompanying this artery, and what is the clinical sign of its palsy?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery. State where its pulse is felt and how it enters the palm.
spotters.answer: Radial artery. It is the smaller terminal branch of the brachial artery. Its pulse is felt at the wrist between the tendon of flexor carpi radialis and the anterior border of the radius, where it lies on the lower end of the radius. It then winds backwards through the floor of the anatomical snuffbox, crosses the scaphoid and trapezium, and enters the palm by passing between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous and then between the heads of adductor pollicis to form the deep palmar arch.
spotters.followup: Describe the Allen test and say why it is performed before radial artery cannulation or harvesting.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery and describe how it enters the hand.
spotters.answer: Ulnar artery. It is the larger terminal branch of the brachial artery. It passes deep to the superficial flexors, then descends on flexor digitorum profundus with the ulnar nerve on its medial side. At the wrist it enters the palm superficial to the flexor retinaculum through Guyon canal, lateral to the pisiform, and continues as the main contributor to the superficial palmar arterial arch.
spotters.followup: Name the branches of this artery in the forearm and say which one gives the interosseous supply.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned arch. State its main contributor and its surface marking.
spotters.answer: Superficial palmar arterial arch. It is formed mainly by the ulnar artery, completed laterally by the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery. It lies deep to the palmar aponeurosis and superficial to the long flexor tendons and digital branches of the median nerve. Its convexity reaches the level of a line drawn across the palm from the distal border of the fully extended thumb. It gives three common palmar digital arteries and one proper digital artery to the medial side of the little finger.
spotters.followup: Which arch lies more proximal, and how would you control bleeding from a deep laceration of the palm?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned arch and state its main contributor and its level relative to the superficial arch.
spotters.answer: Deep palmar arch. It is formed mainly by the terminal part of the radial artery, completed medially by the deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery. It lies across the bases of the metacarpal bones on the interossei, deep to the long flexor tendons, roughly one finger breadth, about 1 cm, proximal to the superficial arch. It gives palmar metacarpal arteries, perforating branches to the dorsal metacarpal arteries, and recurrent branches to the carpus.
spotters.followup: Which nerve accompanies this arch, and what motor loss follows injury to it in the palm?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery. Name its parent vessel and its territory.
spotters.answer: Arteria princeps pollicis. It arises from the radial artery as that vessel turns medially between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous, and it runs along the palmar surface of the first metacarpal bone deep to the oblique head of adductor pollicis before dividing into two proper palmar digital arteries for the two sides of the thumb. The radialis indicis to the radial side of the index finger arises close to it, often from the same trunk.
spotters.followup: Why is the arterial supply of the thumb and index finger largely radial in origin, and what is the practical consequence in a replantation?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and trace its termination.
spotters.answer: Cephalic vein. It begins from the lateral end of the dorsal venous network of the hand, crosses the anatomical snuffbox, ascends along the lateral border of the forearm and arm, runs in the deltopectoral groove between deltoid and pectoralis major, then pierces the clavipectoral fascia in the deltopectoral triangle to drain into the axillary artery's companion vessel, the axillary vein, just below the clavicle.
spotters.followup: Which three structures besides this vein pierce the clavipectoral fascia?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein. State where it becomes deep and what it becomes.
spotters.answer: Basilic vein. It begins from the medial end of the dorsal venous network of the hand, ascends on the medial side of the forearm and the medial side of the arm, and pierces the deep fascia at about the middle of the arm. It then runs alongside the brachial artery and, at the lower border of teres major, joins the venae comitantes of the brachial artery to become the axillary vein.
spotters.followup: Which cutaneous nerve accompanies this vein in the forearm, and why is that relevant to cannulation?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and state why it is the preferred site for venepuncture.
spotters.answer: Median cubital vein. It runs obliquely across the front of the cubital fossa from the cephalic vein below and laterally to the basilic vein above and medially. It is large, superficial, relatively fixed by the underlying bicipital aponeurosis and the deep fascia, and that aponeurosis separates it from the brachial artery and median nerve beneath, which is why it is chosen for venepuncture and blood donation.
spotters.followup: Which structures could be damaged by a needle passed too deeply at this site, and what symptom would each produce?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein. State its beginning, end and its relation to the axillary artery.
spotters.answer: Axillary vein. It begins at the lower border of teres major as the continuation of the basilic vein joined by the venae comitantes of the brachial artery, and it ends at the outer border of the first rib by becoming the subclavian vein. It lies anteromedial to the axillary artery throughout, so it is the vessel first encountered in an anterior approach and the one at risk of air embolism if opened when the patient is upright.
spotters.followup: Into which group of axillary lymph nodes does most of the lymph from the breast drain, and why does axillary clearance risk lymphoedema of the arm?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and state its motor nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Sternocleidomastoid. Motor supply from the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), with sensory and proprioceptive fibres from the anterior rami of C2 and C3. It has a sternal (tendinous) and a clavicular (fleshy) head, and it divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles. Unilateral shortening produces torticollis, with the chin turned to the opposite side.
spotters.followup: Which large vein lies deep to its sternal head in the lower neck, and why does that matter clinically?

spotters.prompt: Identify this thin sheet in the superficial fascia and state its nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Platysma. Supplied by the cervical branch of the facial nerve (CN VII), because it is a muscle of facial expression carried into the neck. It lies in the superficial fascia, so neck lacerations must be closed in layers, and its pull on skin edges is why neck incisions are placed in skin creases.
spotters.followup: Why is platysma supplied by the facial nerve and not by a cervical nerve?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and give the nerve supply of BOTH its bellies.
spotters.answer: Digastric. The anterior belly is supplied by the nerve to mylohyoid, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (mandibular division, CN V3). The posterior belly is supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII). Its two bellies have different pharyngeal arch origins, first and second respectively. The posterior belly is the key landmark of the carotid triangle and overlies the carotid vessels.
spotters.followup: Name the two triangles of the neck bounded by this muscle.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and state one structure that passes around its posterior free border.
spotters.answer: Mylohyoid, forming the muscular floor of the mouth (oral diaphragm). Supplied by the nerve to mylohyoid from the inferior alveolar nerve (CN V3). The deep part of the submandibular gland and its duct, along with the lingual and hypoglossal nerves, hook around its free posterior border into the floor of the mouth. Infection of a lower molar can spread above or below this muscle, which determines whether pus points into the mouth or into the neck (Ludwig angina).
spotters.followup: Which tooth root position decides whether an abscess drains above or below mylohyoid?
spotters.sub: Head and neck, floor of mouth

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and state its nerve supply and main action.
spotters.answer: Genioglossus. Supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). It arises from the superior genial tubercle of the mandible and fans into the tongue. It is the chief protrusor and the safety muscle of the tongue: it pulls the tongue forward and keeps the airway open. With a hypoglossal lesion the protruded tongue deviates towards the paralysed side.
spotters.followup: Which way does the tongue deviate in a right hypoglossal nerve lesion, and why?

spotters.prompt: Identify this quadrilateral muscle and name the structures superficial and deep to it.
spotters.answer: Hyoglossus, from the greater cornu and body of the hyoid to the side of the tongue. Supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). It is the surgical landmark of the submandibular region: the lingual nerve, submandibular duct and hypoglossal nerve run on its superficial (lateral) surface, while the lingual artery and glossopharyngeal nerve lie deep (medial) to it. The lingual artery is therefore ligated deep to hyoglossus.
spotters.followup: Where exactly would you ligate the lingual artery in relation to this muscle?
spotters.sub: Head and neck, tongue and submandibular region

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned strap muscle and state its nerve supply and its distinguishing feature.
spotters.answer: Omohyoid. Supplied by the ansa cervicalis (C1, C2, C3). It is the only strap muscle with two bellies joined by an intermediate tendon, which is tethered to the clavicle by a fascial sling from the investing layer of deep cervical fascia. Its inferior belly subdivides the posterior triangle into occipital and supraclavicular triangles, and its superior belly subdivides the anterior triangle into carotid and muscular triangles.
spotters.followup: Name the four triangles that this muscle helps to bound.

spotters.prompt: Identify this most superficial strap muscle and state its nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Sternohyoid. Supplied by the ansa cervicalis (C1, C2, C3). It runs from the posterior surface of the manubrium and medial clavicle to the lower border of the body of the hyoid, and it depresses the hyoid after swallowing. The strap muscles are separated in the midline at thyroidectomy, and they can be divided transversely in their upper half without denervation because the ansa enters low.
spotters.followup: Why are the strap muscles divided high rather than low when extra access is needed?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and name the nerve on its anterior surface.
spotters.answer: Scalenus anterior. The phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5) descends vertically on its anterior surface, from lateral to medial, under the prevertebral fascia. The muscle runs from the anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C3 to C6 to the scalene tubercle of the first rib, and is supplied by the anterior rami of C4 to C6. It is the key landmark at the root of the neck: the subclavian vein passes anterior to it, and the subclavian artery and the trunks of the brachial plexus pass posterior to it.
spotters.followup: Which structures pass through the interscalene interval between this muscle and scalenus medius?
spotters.sub: Head and neck, root of neck

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and state its nerve supply and action.
spotters.answer: Splenius capitis. Supplied by the posterior rami of the middle cervical spinal nerves. It runs from the lower half of the ligamentum nuchae and the spines of C7 to T3 upwards and laterally to the mastoid process and lateral third of the superior nuchal line. Acting alone it rotates the head to the same side, acting with its fellow it extends the head. It forms the floor of the posterior triangle in its upper part.
spotters.followup: Which muscle lies immediately deep to it in the upper posterior neck, and which nerve pierces that deeper muscle?

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle of the suboccipital triangle and state its attachments and nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Obliquus capitis inferior. It runs from the spine of the axis to the transverse process of the atlas, and is supplied by the posterior ramus of C1 (suboccipital nerve). Despite its name it is the only capitis muscle with no attachment to the skull. It forms the lower or inferolateral boundary of the suboccipital triangle and rotates the atlas, and therefore the head, to the same side. The greater occipital nerve (posterior ramus of C2) winds around its lower border.
spotters.followup: Name the contents of the suboccipital triangle.

spotters.prompt: Identify this prevertebral muscle and state its attachments and nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Longus capitis. It arises from the anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C3 to C6 and ascends to the inferior surface of the basilar part of the occipital bone. Supplied by the anterior rami of C1 to C3. It flexes the head on the neck. It lies under the prevertebral fascia, behind the retropharyngeal space, so a retropharyngeal abscess presents as a swelling in front of it.
distractors: superior oblique part of longus colli
spotters.followup: Which fascial space lies immediately anterior to this muscle and where can pus in it track?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery and state the vertebral level at which it divides.
spotters.answer: Common carotid artery. It divides into the internal and external carotid arteries at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, at the level of the C3 to C4 disc. It gives no branches in the neck. It lies in the carotid sheath with the internal jugular vein laterally and the vagus nerve posteriorly between them. The right arises from the brachiocephalic trunk, the left directly from the arch of the aorta.
spotters.followup: What is the carotid sinus, where is it, and which nerve supplies it?

spotters.prompt: Identify this artery and state how you distinguish it from its neighbour at the bifurcation.
spotters.answer: Internal carotid artery. It is identified by the fact that it gives no branches in the neck, unlike the external carotid, and it starts posterolateral to the external carotid before passing deep to it. It ascends in the carotid sheath, enters the carotid canal of the temporal bone, traverses the cavernous sinus and gives its first branch, the ophthalmic artery, intracranially. Atheroma at its origin is the classic source of embolic stroke and amaurosis fugax.
spotters.followup: Name the first intracranial branch of this artery and the canal it enters the orbit through.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and state where it begins and ends.
spotters.answer: Internal jugular vein. It begins at the jugular foramen as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus, descends in the carotid sheath lateral to the carotid artery, and ends behind the sternal end of the clavicle by joining the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein. Its surface marking runs from the lobule of the ear to the medial end of the clavicle, and it is the standard site for central venous cannulation, entered at the apex of the triangle between the two heads of sternocleidomastoid.
spotters.followup: What is the venous angle, and which duct drains into it on the left?

spotters.prompt: Identify this artery and state how it is divided into parts.
spotters.answer: Subclavian artery. It is divided into three parts by scalenus anterior: the first part medial to the muscle, the second part behind it, the third part lateral to it as far as the outer border of the first rib, where it becomes the axillary artery. The first part gives the vertebral artery, the internal thoracic artery and the thyrocervical trunk. The right arises from the brachiocephalic trunk, the left directly from the arch of the aorta.
spotters.followup: Name the three branches of the first part of this artery.
spotters.sub: Head and neck, root of neck

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery and trace its course to the cranial cavity.
spotters.answer: Vertebral artery. It is the first branch of the first part of the subclavian artery. It ascends through the foramina transversaria of C6 up to C1, does not pass through the foramen transversarium of C7, then grooves the posterior arch of the atlas in the floor of the suboccipital triangle, pierces the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane and dura, and enters the skull through the foramen magnum. The two vertebral arteries unite at the lower border of the pons to form the basilar artery.
spotters.followup: Which cervical transverse foramen does it NOT pass through, and what vessel do the two vertebral arteries form?
spotters.sub: Head and neck, root of neck and suboccipital region

spotters.prompt: Identify this artery and state its origin and the nerve related to it.
spotters.answer: Inferior thyroid artery, a branch of the thyrocervical trunk from the first part of the subclavian artery. It arches medially behind the carotid sheath to reach the lower pole and posterior surface of the thyroid lobe. The recurrent laryngeal nerve is intimately related to its terminal branches, passing in front of, behind, or between them. It is therefore ligated well away from the gland, on its main trunk, in contrast to the superior thyroid artery, which is ligated close to the gland to spare the external laryngeal nerve.
spotters.followup: Why is this artery ligated away from the gland while the superior thyroid artery is ligated close to it?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery in the orbit and state its origin and route of entry.
spotters.answer: Ophthalmic artery. It is the first intracranial branch of the internal carotid artery, arising as that vessel emerges from the cavernous sinus. It enters the orbit through the optic canal, inferolateral to the optic nerve within the dural sheath, then crosses above the nerve from lateral to medial. Its central artery of the retina is an end artery: occlusion causes sudden painless total blindness in that eye.
spotters.followup: Which branch of this artery is a true end artery, and what happens when it occludes?

spotters.prompt: Identify this cartilage and state the vertebral level of its upper border.
spotters.answer: Thyroid cartilage. It is a hyaline cartilage formed by two laminae meeting anteriorly at the laryngeal prominence, and its upper border lies at the C4 vertebral level, where the common carotid artery bifurcates. The vocal ligaments attach to the middle of its inner angle. Its superior horn is connected to the hyoid by the lateral thyrohyoid ligament, its inferior horn articulates with the cricoid at a synovial joint.
spotters.followup: Which joint does its inferior horn form, and what movement occurs there?

spotters.prompt: Identify this cartilage and state the single feature that makes it unique in the airway.
spotters.answer: Cricoid cartilage. It is the only complete cartilaginous ring in the entire airway, signet-ring shaped with a narrow anterior arch and a broad posterior lamina. It lies at the C6 vertebral level, marking where the pharynx becomes oesophagus and the larynx becomes trachea. Because it is a complete ring, backward pressure on it occludes the oesophagus against the vertebral column (cricoid pressure) during rapid sequence induction.
spotters.followup: Name two other structures that lie at the same vertebral level as this cartilage.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned bone and state what makes it anatomically unusual.
spotters.answer: Hyoid bone. It is the only bone in the body that articulates with no other bone: it is slung by muscles and ligaments, suspended from the styloid processes by the stylohyoid ligaments. It lies at the C3 vertebral level. Its greater cornu is a fracture site in manual strangulation, and it is derived from the second and third pharyngeal arches, the lesser cornu and upper body from the second, the greater cornu and lower body from the third.
spotters.followup: Which pharyngeal arches form its parts, and which ligament suspends it from the skull?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned intrinsic laryngeal muscle and state its action and nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Posterior crico-arytenoid. It arises from the posterior surface of the cricoid lamina and inserts on the muscular process of the arytenoid. Supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. It is the ONLY abductor of the vocal folds, so it is the sole opener of the rima glottidis. Bilateral paralysis leaves the cords adducted and causes stridor and airway obstruction requiring tracheostomy.
spotters.followup: What happens to the airway in bilateral paralysis of this muscle?
spotters.sub: Head and neck, intrinsic laryngeal muscles

spotters.prompt: Identify this part of the muscle on the outer surface of the larynx and state its nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Straight part of cricothyroid, the vertical belly of cricothyroid, running from the arch of the cricoid up to the lower border of the thyroid lamina. Cricothyroid is the ONLY intrinsic laryngeal muscle NOT supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve: it is supplied by the external laryngeal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. It tilts the thyroid cartilage forward, lengthening and tensing the vocal folds. Injury during superior thyroid artery ligation gives a monotonous voice and loss of high notes.
spotters.followup: Which nerve is injured in thyroidectomy to cause loss of the high register of the voice, and where is it at risk?
spotters.sub: Head and neck, intrinsic laryngeal muscles

spotters.prompt: Identify this midline ligament and state its surgical importance.
spotters.answer: Median cricothyroid ligament, the thickened anterior midline part of the cricothyroid membrane (conus elasticus), spanning between the arch of the cricoid and the lower border of the thyroid cartilage. It is the site of emergency cricothyroidotomy: it is subcutaneous, avascular in the midline apart from a small anastomosis of the cricothyroid arteries, and lies below the level of the vocal folds.
spotters.followup: Why is an emergency airway made here rather than through the thyrohyoid membrane?

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle, name its two parts, and state its nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Inferior pharyngeal constrictor. It has two parts: the thyropharyngeus, arising from the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage, and the cricopharyngeus, arising from the cricoid, which acts as the upper oesophageal sphincter. Supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (cranial accessory fibres carried by the vagus). Killian dehiscence, the weak area between the two parts, is where a pharyngeal pouch (Zenker diverticulum) herniates.
spotters.followup: Name the dehiscence between its two parts and the lesion that arises there.

spotters.prompt: Identify this longitudinal pharyngeal muscle and state its nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Stylopharyngeus. It is the ONLY muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), which winds round its posterior border to reach the tongue. It arises from the medial side of the base of the styloid process and enters the pharyngeal wall through the gap between the superior and middle constrictors, inserting into the posterior border of the thyroid cartilage. It elevates the larynx and pharynx and widens the pharynx during swallowing.
spotters.followup: Between which two constrictors does it enter the pharynx, and what else passes through that gap?

spotters.prompt: Identify this palatal muscle and state the feature that separates it from every other palatal muscle.
spotters.answer: Tensor veli palatini. It is the ONLY muscle of the soft palate not supplied by the pharyngeal plexus: it is supplied by the nerve to medial pterygoid from the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3). Its tendon hooks around the pterygoid hamulus to turn medially into the palatine aponeurosis. It tenses the soft palate and opens the auditory tube during swallowing and yawning, which is why the ears pop.
spotters.followup: Around which bony process does its tendon turn, and what does that muscle do to the auditory tube?

spotters.prompt: Identify this palatal muscle and state its action and nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Levator veli palatini. It arises from the petrous temporal bone and the cartilage of the auditory tube, descends medial to the tube, and inserts into the upper surface of the palatine aponeurosis. Supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (cranial accessory through vagus). It elevates the soft palate to seal the nasopharynx from the oropharynx during swallowing and speech. Failure gives nasal regurgitation and nasal (hypernasal) speech.
spotters.followup: What clinical sign appears when this muscle fails to close the nasopharynx?

spotters.prompt: Identify this vertebra and state its two defining features.
spotters.answer: Atlas, the first cervical vertebra. It has no body and no spinous process: it is a ring of two lateral masses joined by anterior and posterior arches. The absent body is represented by the dens of the axis, held against the anterior arch by the transverse ligament of the atlas. Its superior articular facets take the occipital condyles at the atlanto-occipital joint, which is the joint of nodding (yes movement). The vertebral artery grooves the upper surface of its posterior arch.
spotters.followup: Which movement occurs at the atlanto-occipital joint and which at the atlanto-axial joint?

spotters.prompt: Identify this vertebra and state the feature that identifies it.
spotters.answer: Axis, the second cervical vertebra, identified by the dens (odontoid process) projecting upwards from its body. The dens is the developmental body of the atlas. It is held by the transverse ligament of the atlas posteriorly, and by the alar and apical ligaments to the occipital condyles and foramen magnum. The median atlanto-axial joint is the pivot for rotation of the head (no movement). Fracture of the dens or rupture of the transverse ligament, as in rheumatoid arthritis, risks cord compression.
spotters.followup: Which ligament holds the dens in place, and what is the consequence of its rupture?

spotters.prompt: Identify this bone and name the canal within it and its contents.
spotters.answer: Mandible, the only mobile bone of the skull, articulating at the temporomandibular joint. The mandibular foramen on the medial surface of the ramus leads into the mandibular canal, carrying the inferior alveolar nerve, artery and vein to the lower teeth, emerging at the mental foramen as the mental nerve. The lingula guards the foramen, and the inferior alveolar nerve block is given just above and behind it, lateral to the pterygomandibular raphe.
spotters.followup: Which nerve is anaesthetised at the mandibular foramen, and what area goes numb?

spotters.prompt: Identify this bone and state which cavities it helps to form.
spotters.answer: Maxilla. It forms the upper jaw and alveolar arch, the anterior three quarters of the hard palate (palatine process), the floor and medial wall of the orbit, the lateral wall and floor of the nasal cavity, and it contains the maxillary sinus, the largest paranasal sinus. The infra-orbital nerve (from CN V2) leaves through its infra-orbital foramen. The maxillary sinus ostium lies high on its medial wall, which is why it drains poorly in the upright position.
spotters.followup: Which teeth roots project into the maxillary sinus, and what symptom can that produce?

spotters.prompt: Identify this bone and name three foramina in its greater wing.
spotters.answer: Sphenoid bone, the keystone of the skull base, articulating with all the other cranial bones. Its greater wing carries the foramen rotundum (maxillary nerve), foramen ovale (mandibular nerve, accessory meningeal artery, lesser petrous nerve) and foramen spinosum (middle meningeal artery). Its body contains the sphenoid sinus and the hypophyseal fossa of the sella turcica, which houses the pituitary gland, and the superior orbital fissure lies between its greater and lesser wings.
spotters.followup: Which fissure lies between its greater and lesser wings, and what passes through it?

spotters.prompt: Identify this bone and state the clinical consequence of fracturing its horizontal plate.
spotters.answer: Ethmoid. Its cribriform plate transmits the olfactory nerve filaments from the nasal roof to the olfactory bulb. Fracture of the cribriform plate tears the dura and arachnoid, causing anosmia and CSF rhinorrhoea, with a risk of ascending meningitis. The bone also contributes the perpendicular plate to the bony nasal septum, the ethmoidal air cells and the superior and middle conchae, and the crista galli for the falx cerebri.
spotters.followup: Which two bones and which cartilage form the nasal septum?
spotters.sub: Head and neck, skull base and nasal cavity

spotters.prompt: Identify this bone and name its parts and the canal transmitting the internal carotid artery.
spotters.answer: Temporal bone, made of squamous, petrous, mastoid, tympanic and styloid parts. The carotid canal in the petrous part transmits the internal carotid artery into the cranial cavity. It houses the middle and inner ear, and the facial nerve runs in the facial canal within it to emerge at the stylomastoid foramen. Its mandibular fossa takes the head of the mandible, and a fracture of the petrous part causes bleeding from the ear, Battle sign and facial nerve palsy.
spotters.followup: Through which foramen of this bone does the facial nerve leave the skull?

spotters.prompt: Identify this small bone and state what its groove lodges.
spotters.answer: Lacrimal bone, the smallest bone of the face, in the anterior part of the medial wall of the orbit. Its lacrimal groove, completed by the frontal process of the maxilla, forms the fossa for the lacrimal sac, which continues down as the bony nasolacrimal canal into the inferior meatus. Its posterior lacrimal crest gives attachment to the lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi.
spotters.followup: Into which meatus of the nose does the nasolacrimal duct open?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned nerve and state why it is not a true peripheral nerve.
spotters.answer: Optic nerve (CN II). It is a tract of the brain, not a peripheral nerve: it is myelinated by oligodendrocytes and is invested by all three meninges, with an extension of the subarachnoid space around it. Raised intracranial pressure is therefore transmitted along the sheath and produces papilloedema. It leaves the orbit through the optic canal in the lesser wing of the sphenoid, accompanied by the ophthalmic artery.
spotters.followup: Explain the visual field defect produced by a lesion at the optic chiasma.

spotters.prompt: Identify this cranial nerve and state the muscle it supplies and its unique features.
spotters.answer: Trochlear nerve (CN IV). It supplies only superior oblique. It is the only cranial nerve to emerge from the dorsal surface of the brainstem and the only one to decussate completely before emerging, and it has the longest intracranial course. It enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure OUTSIDE the common tendinous ring. Palsy causes vertical diplopia worst on looking down and in, with a compensatory head tilt away from the affected side.
spotters.followup: What compensatory head posture does the patient adopt in a palsy of this nerve, and why?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned extra-ocular muscle and state its nerve supply and action.
spotters.answer: Lateral rectus. Supplied by the abducent nerve (CN VI). It abducts the eye. It arises from the common tendinous ring, and the abducent nerve enters its ocular (medial) surface within the cone. The abducent nerve has a long intracranial course over the petrous temporal ridge, so it is the first nerve affected by raised intracranial pressure, giving a false localising sign with convergent squint and horizontal diplopia.
spotters.followup: Why is a palsy of the nerve to this muscle called a false localising sign?

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle and state its nerve supply and the direction in which you test it.
spotters.answer: Superior oblique. Supplied by the trochlear nerve (CN IV). It arises from the body of the sphenoid above and medial to the optic canal, outside the common tendinous ring, and its tendon passes through the fibrocartilaginous trochlea on the frontal bone, then turns posterolaterally to insert into the sclera behind the equator. It depresses, abducts and medially rotates (intorts) the eye. It is tested clinically by asking the patient to look downwards and medially (down and in) with the eye adducted.
spotters.followup: What is the trochlea, where is it attached, and what does it do to the pull of this muscle?

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle and state its origin, which is unlike any other extra-ocular muscle.
spotters.answer: Inferior oblique. It is the only extra-ocular muscle to arise from the FRONT of the orbit, from the orbital surface of the maxilla lateral to the nasolacrimal groove, and it passes backwards and laterally below inferior rectus to the sclera behind the equator. Supplied by the inferior branch of the oculomotor nerve (CN III), the branch that also carries the parasympathetic root to the ciliary ganglion. It elevates, abducts and laterally rotates (extorts) the eye, and is tested by looking up and in.
spotters.followup: Which branch of the oculomotor nerve supplies it, and what parasympathetic fibres travel with that branch?

spotters.prompt: Identify this muscle and state its DUAL nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Levator palpebrae superioris. Its main striated part is supplied by the superior branch of the oculomotor nerve (CN III). Its deep smooth muscle slip, the superior tarsal muscle of Muller, inserting into the upper tarsal plate, is supplied by sympathetic fibres from the superior cervical ganglion. This dual supply explains the two grades of ptosis: complete ptosis in a third nerve palsy, partial ptosis in Horner syndrome with miosis and anhidrosis.
spotters.followup: Contrast the ptosis of a third nerve palsy with the ptosis of Horner syndrome.
spotters.sub: Head and neck, orbit and eyelid

spotters.prompt: Identify this structure at the orbital apex and name what passes through it.
spotters.answer: Common tendinous ring (annulus of Zinn), a fibrous ring at the apex of the orbit bridging the superior orbital fissure and enclosing the optic canal. All four recti arise from it. Passing through it are the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery (through the optic canal), the superior and inferior branches of the oculomotor nerve, the nasociliary nerve and the abducent nerve. The lacrimal, frontal and trochlear nerves, plus the superior ophthalmic vein, pass through the superior orbital fissure OUTSIDE the ring.
spotters.followup: Which three nerves entering the orbit pass outside this ring?

spotters.prompt: Identify this ganglion and state its three roots and what its postganglionic fibres supply.
spotters.answer: Ciliary ganglion, lying between the optic nerve and lateral rectus about 1 cm in front of the orbital apex. It is a parasympathetic ganglion. Its parasympathetic (motor) root comes from the nerve to inferior oblique from the inferior branch of the oculomotor nerve and RELAYS here; the sympathetic root from the internal carotid plexus and the sensory root from the nasociliary nerve pass through WITHOUT relay. Its postganglionic fibres run in the short ciliary nerves to sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle, giving the constrictor and accommodation responses.
spotters.followup: Which of its roots relays in the ganglion and which pass through it unrelayed?

spotters.prompt: Identify this nerve and state its parent trunk and terminal branches.
spotters.answer: Frontal nerve, the largest branch of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1). It enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure ABOVE and outside the common tendinous ring and runs forward on the upper surface of levator palpebrae superioris, immediately under the periorbita, dividing into the supra-orbital and supratrochlear nerves. It is purely sensory to the forehead, scalp to the vertex, upper eyelid and frontal sinus.
spotters.followup: Name its two terminal branches and the skin territory each supplies.

spotters.prompt: Identify this nerve and name three of its branches.
spotters.answer: Nasociliary nerve, a branch of the ophthalmic nerve (CN V1). It enters through the superior orbital fissure WITHIN the common tendinous ring and crosses above the optic nerve from lateral to medial. Its branches are the communicating branch to the ciliary ganglion (sensory root), the long ciliary nerves to the cornea and iris, the posterior ethmoidal nerve, the infratrochlear nerve, and the anterior ethmoidal nerve, which ends as the external nasal nerve to the nasal tip. Vesicles on the nasal tip in herpes zoster ophthalmicus (Hutchinson sign) warn of corneal involvement.
spotters.followup: Explain Hutchinson sign in herpes zoster ophthalmicus using the branches of this nerve.

spotters.prompt: Identify this gland and state its secretomotor pathway.
spotters.answer: Lacrimal gland, in the fossa on the anterolateral roof of the orbit, divided into orbital and palpebral parts by the tendon of levator palpebrae superioris. Its parasympathetic secretomotor fibres arise in the superior salivatory nucleus, travel in the facial nerve, then the greater petrosal nerve and nerve of the pterygoid canal, relay in the pterygopalatine ganglion, and reach the gland via the zygomatic and then the lacrimal nerve. Sensory supply is by the lacrimal nerve from CN V1.
spotters.followup: In which ganglion do the secretomotor fibres to this gland relay?

spotters.prompt: Identify this duct and state where it opens.
spotters.answer: Nasolacrimal duct. It runs downwards, backwards and laterally from the lower end of the lacrimal sac in the bony nasolacrimal canal and opens into the INFERIOR meatus of the nose, under cover of the inferior nasal concha, guarded by the valve of Hasner. Tears therefore run into the nose, which is why the nose runs when crying. Blockage in the newborn causes epiphora and dacryocystitis.
spotters.followup: Trace the whole path of a tear from the gland to the nose.
spotters.sub: Head and neck, orbit and nasal cavity

spotters.prompt: Identify this structure and state its blood and nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Cornea. It is avascular, nourished by the aqueous humour and by diffusion from the limbal capillaries and tear film, which is why it can be grafted with little rejection. Its sensory supply is dense, via the long ciliary nerves from the nasociliary branch of the ophthalmic nerve (CN V1). It is the afferent limb of the corneal (blink) reflex, whose efferent limb is the facial nerve to orbicularis oculi.
spotters.followup: Name the afferent and efferent limbs of the corneal reflex.

spotters.prompt: Identify this gland and state its duct and secretomotor supply.
spotters.answer: Submandibular gland, with a large superficial part below mylohyoid and a small deep part that hooks around its posterior free border. Its duct (Wharton duct) runs forward on hyoglossus and opens at the sublingual papilla beside the frenulum of the tongue. The lingual nerve crosses the duct twice, passing lateral then below and medial to it. Secretomotor fibres come from the facial nerve via the chorda tympani and lingual nerve, relaying in the submandibular ganglion. It is the commonest site of salivary calculi because its duct runs uphill and its secretion is mucus-rich.
spotters.followup: Why is this gland the commonest site of salivary calculi?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned organ and state its complete sensory and motor innervation.
spotters.answer: Tongue. Anterior two thirds: general sensation by the lingual nerve (CN V3), taste by the chorda tympani (CN VII). Posterior one third: general sensation and taste both by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). Vallecular region and epiglottis: internal laryngeal branch of the vagus (CN X). Motor supply is by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) to all muscles except palatoglossus, which is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus). The sulcus terminalis and foramen caecum mark the junction of the two developmental parts.
spotters.followup: Which single tongue muscle is NOT supplied by the hypoglossal nerve, and what supplies it?

spotters.prompt: Identify this gland and state where it lies and its important surgical relations.
spotters.answer: Pituitary gland (hypophysis cerebri), in the hypophyseal fossa of the sella turcica of the sphenoid body, covered by the diaphragma sellae which the infundibulum pierces. The sphenoid sinus lies directly below and in front, which is the route for trans-sphenoidal hypophysectomy. The optic chiasma lies above and in front, so an enlarging adenoma compresses the decussating nasal fibres and causes bitemporal hemianopia. The cavernous sinus lies on each side, with CN III, IV, V1, V2 and VI and the internal carotid artery.
spotters.followup: Which visual field defect does an enlarging tumour here cause, and why that pattern?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned tooth and state its eruption age and nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Lower first secondary (permanent) molar tooth. It erupts at about six years and is the FIRST permanent tooth to erupt, appearing behind the deciduous molars without replacing any deciduous tooth, hence the name six-year molar. Its sensory supply is the inferior alveolar nerve from the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3), with buccal gingiva supplied by the buccal nerve and lingual gingiva by the lingual nerve. Its early eruption and deep fissures make it the most commonly carious tooth.
spotters.followup: Which nerves must be anaesthetised to extract this tooth painlessly?
spotters.sub: Head and neck, oral cavity, mandibular dentition

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vessel and name its three branches in order from right to left.
spotters.answer: Arch of aorta. It lies entirely in the superior mediastinum, beginning and ending at the level of the sternal angle (T4/T5 plane). Branches from right to left: brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery, left subclavian artery. Applied point: the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the arch lateral to the ligamentum arteriosum, so an arch aneurysm or bulky subaortic nodal disease causes left vocal cord palsy and a bovine cough.
spotters.followup: At what vertebral level does the arch begin and end, and what plane is that?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vessel and state the only branches that arise from it.
spotters.answer: Ascending aorta. It runs from the aortic orifice at the level of the third left costal cartilage upward to the sternal angle. Its only branches are the right and left coronary arteries, arising from the right and left aortic sinuses. Applied point: it is entirely intrapericardial, so rupture or dissection here bleeds into the pericardial sac and causes tamponade.
spotters.followup: Why does the ascending aorta and the pulmonary trunk share a single serous pericardial sleeve, and what is the embryological reason?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vessel. State where it begins, where it divides, and one clinical relation.
spotters.answer: Pulmonary trunk. It arises from the infundibulum of the right ventricle at the level of the left third costal cartilage, runs upward and backward, and divides at about T4/T5 below the arch of aorta into right and left pulmonary arteries. Applied point: the ligamentum arteriosum connects its bifurcation to the arch, and the left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops beneath it at that point.
spotters.followup: The pulmonary trunk lies anterior to the ascending aorta at its origin. Which embryological process explains that spiral relationship?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vessel. State how it is formed and where it ends.
spotters.answer: Superior vena cava. Formed behind the lower border of the right first costal cartilage by union of the right and left brachiocephalic veins, it ends in the upper right atrium at the level of the third right costal cartilage. Its lower half is intrapericardial and it has no valves. Applied point: the azygos vein arches forward over the root of the right lung to enter its posterior surface, and SVC obstruction by right upper lobe carcinoma produces facial and upper limb oedema with distended non pulsatile neck veins.
spotters.followup: Name the collateral routes that open up in superior vena caval obstruction.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein. State its origin and its termination.
spotters.answer: Azygos vein. It usually begins at the level of L1 or L2 from the right ascending lumbar vein joined by the right subcostal vein, enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus or the right crus, ascends on the right side of the vertebral bodies, and arches forward over the root of the right lung at about T4 to drain into the superior vena cava. Applied point: it is the key porto systemic and caval collateral channel, so it enlarges in inferior vena caval obstruction and shows on chest radiograph as a widened azygos knob.
spotters.followup: Which posterior intercostal veins drain directly into the azygos vein on the right side?

spotters.prompt: Identify this vein on the left of the vertebral column and state which segmental veins it receives.
spotters.answer: Hemiazygos vein. It begins from the left ascending lumbar vein and left subcostal vein, ascends on the left of the thoracic vertebral bodies, and at about T8 or T9 crosses behind the aorta, oesophagus and thoracic duct to join the azygos vein. It receives the lower left posterior intercostal veins, roughly the ninth to eleventh, plus some oesophageal and mediastinal tributaries.
spotters.followup: Which structures does the hemiazygos vein cross anterior to as it passes to the right side?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and state which intercostal spaces drain into it.
spotters.answer: Accessory hemiazygos vein. It descends on the left of the vertebral bodies from about T4 or T5 to T8, receiving the fourth to eighth left posterior intercostal veins, and then crosses to the right at about T7 or T8 to join the azygos vein, sometimes joining the hemiazygos vein first. Applied point: it is highly variable, and its termination is one of the commoner venous variants encountered at posterior mediastinal dissection.
spotters.followup: Which vein drains the left second, third and fourth intercostal spaces when they do not reach the accessory hemiazygos vein?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and state how its drainage differs on the two sides.
spotters.answer: Superior intercostal vein. On the left it drains the second, third and sometimes fourth intercostal spaces, crosses the left side of the arch of aorta lateral to the vagus and phrenic nerves, and ends in the left brachiocephalic vein. On the right it drains the second to fourth spaces and ends in the azygos vein. Applied point: a dilated left superior intercostal vein is the aortic nipple seen on a frontal chest radiograph.
spotters.followup: Which nerves does the left superior intercostal vein cross as it passes over the arch of aorta?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned structure in the posterior atrioventricular groove and state where it opens.
spotters.answer: Coronary sinus. It lies in the posterior atrioventricular groove and opens into the right atrium between the opening of the inferior vena cava and the right atrioventricular orifice, guarded by the valve of the coronary sinus, the Thebesian valve. It is the remnant of the left horn of the sinus venosus and drains most of the venous blood of the heart. Applied point: its ostium is the route used for retrograde cardioplegia and for left ventricular pacing leads in cardiac resynchronisation therapy.
spotters.followup: Name the tributaries of the coronary sinus.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and state the groove it occupies and the artery accompanying it.
spotters.answer: Middle cardiac vein, also called the posterior interventricular vein. It runs in the posterior interventricular groove alongside the posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery and drains into the right end of the coronary sinus near its ostium. It drains the diaphragmatic aspect of both ventricles and the posterior third of the interventricular septum.
spotters.followup: In a right dominant circulation, which artery gives the posterior interventricular branch that runs with this vein?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein, name the groove it lies in and the vessel it accompanies.
spotters.answer: Anterior interventricular vein. It ascends in the anterior interventricular groove with the anterior interventricular (left anterior descending) branch of the left coronary artery, then turns left into the coronary sulcus and continues as the great cardiac vein to the coronary sinus. It drains the anterior surface of both ventricles and the anterior two thirds of the interventricular septum.
spotters.followup: Into which vessel does the great cardiac vein continue, and where does the valve of Vieussens lie?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned cardiac vein and state which border of the heart it follows and where it ends.
spotters.answer: Marginal vein. The right marginal vein runs along the acute (inferior) margin of the heart draining the right ventricle and usually ends directly in the right atrium or in the coronary sinus; the left marginal vein runs along the obtuse margin and joins the great cardiac vein. Applied point: marginal veins that open directly into the atrium bypass the coronary sinus, which matters in retrograde cardioplegia.
spotters.followup: Which artery accompanies the right marginal vein along the acute margin?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein on the diaphragmatic surface of the left ventricle and state its termination.
spotters.answer: Posterior vein of ventricle, that is the posterior vein of the left ventricle. It runs on the diaphragmatic surface of the left ventricle to the left of the middle cardiac vein and drains into the coronary sinus, occasionally into the great cardiac vein. Applied point: it is one of the target tributaries cannulated through the coronary sinus for left ventricular lead placement in biventricular pacing.
spotters.followup: Why is a posterolateral tributary preferred over an anterior one for a left ventricular pacing lead?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned arterial trunk arising from the aortic sinus and state its terminal divisions. Note that the model labels the undivided stem generically.
spotters.answer: Trunk of coronary artery. In the standard station this is the short left main stem, arising from the left aortic sinus, passing behind the pulmonary trunk and between it and the left auricle, then dividing into the anterior interventricular (left anterior descending) branch and the circumflex branch. Applied point: left main stem disease threatens the whole anterior wall and septum and is an indication for bypass grafting rather than stenting in many patients. Be honest with the examiner that the tag reads as a generic coronary trunk, and state which sinus it arises from.
spotters.followup: Which sinuses of the aortic valve give rise to coronary arteries, and which one does not?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned leaflet and state one reason its position is functionally critical.
spotters.answer: Anterior leaflet of mitral valve, also called the aortic leaflet. It is the larger, deeper, quadrangular leaflet, occupying about one third of the annular circumference, and it is in fibrous continuity with the non coronary and left coronary cusps of the aortic valve, the aortomitral curtain. Applied point: because it forms the posterior wall of the left ventricular outflow tract, systolic anterior motion of this leaflet produces outflow obstruction and mitral regurgitation in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.
spotters.followup: Where is the mitral valve best auscultated on the chest wall, and why is that not over the anatomical valve position?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned leaflet and state its usual scallop arrangement.
spotters.answer: Posterior leaflet of mitral valve, also called the mural leaflet. It is shallower but occupies about two thirds of the annulus and is conventionally divided into three scallops, P1 lateral, P2 middle and P3 medial. Applied point: P2 prolapse from chordal rupture in myxomatous degeneration is the commonest cause of severe degenerative mitral regurgitation and is the classic target of surgical repair.
spotters.followup: Which papillary muscles supply chordae to both mitral leaflets, and which coronary artery supplies the anterolateral one?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned leaflet and state its relation to the conducting system.
spotters.answer: Septal leaflet of tricuspid valve. It attaches to the membranous and muscular interventricular septum and its annular attachment lies more apically than that of the anterior leaflet of mitral valve, producing the normal offsetting of the two atrioventricular valves. Applied point: the atrioventricular node and the penetrating bundle of His lie in the triangle of Koch immediately behind and above this leaflet's septal attachment, so it is the structure at risk in tricuspid annuloplasty and in septal ablation.
spotters.followup: Name the three boundaries of the triangle of Koch.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned leaflet and state which papillary muscle and which specialised muscular band relate to it.
spotters.answer: Anterior leaflet of tricuspid valve. It is the largest of the three leaflets, hanging between the atrioventricular orifice and the infundibulum, and receives chordae from the anterior papillary muscle. The moderator band, the septomarginal trabecula carrying the right bundle branch, runs from the interventricular septum to the base of that anterior papillary muscle. Applied point: apical displacement of the septal and posterior leaflets with a large sail like anterior leaflet is the picture of Ebstein anomaly.
spotters.followup: Where on the chest wall is the tricuspid valve auscultated?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned semilunar cusp and state the valve, its location in the ventricle and its surface marking. Comment on the cusp nomenclature.
spotters.answer: Anterior cusp of pulmonary valve. The pulmonary valve sits at the top of the infundibulum of the right ventricle behind the medial end of the left third costal cartilage; the three semilunar cusps are avascular, have a nodule and lunules at the free edge, and close in diastole to fill the pulmonary sinuses. Be explicit that Terminologia Anatomica names the pulmonary cusps anterior, right and left, so a paired anterior and posterior labelling in this model follows the older developmental orientation rather than TA. Applied point: pulmonary stenosis at cusp level produces an ejection systolic murmur in the left second intercostal space that increases on inspiration.
spotters.followup: Why do the semilunar cusps not need chordae tendineae or papillary muscles?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned chamber wall and state the two developmentally distinct parts of the right atrial wall and the ridge between them.
spotters.answer: Wall of atrium. The right atrial wall has a rough anterior part with pectinate muscles derived from the primitive atrium and including the auricle, and a smooth posterior part, the sinus venarum, derived from the right horn of the sinus venosus, which receives the superior vena cava, inferior vena cava and coronary sinus. The crista terminalis, marked externally by the sulcus terminalis, separates them. Applied point: the sinoatrial node lies in the upper crista terminalis at the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium, supplied by the sinuatrial nodal artery, which arises from the right coronary artery in about 60 percent of hearts.
spotters.followup: Where in the atrial septum does the fossa ovalis lie, and what is its floor derived from?

spotters.prompt: Station repeat with a different pin: the vessel arching over the right lung root. Identify it and name the structure it drains into.
spotters.answer: Superior vena cava. Recognise this as the drainage of the arching azygos vein, which passes over the root of the right lung to reach the posterior aspect of the superior vena cava at about T4. Applied point: the azygos vein arching into the superior vena cava is the surgical landmark for the upper limit of a right posterolateral thoracotomy approach to the oesophagus.
spotters.followup: Name the structures in the root of the right lung from anterior to posterior.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery, state its origin and its two terminal branches.
spotters.answer: Internal thoracic artery. It arises from the first part of the subclavian artery, descends about 1 to 1.25 cm lateral to the sternal margin behind the upper six costal cartilages, and at the sixth intercostal space divides into the superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries. It gives the anterior intercostal arteries to the upper six spaces, perforating branches including the lateral mammary branches, and the pericardiacophrenic artery. Applied point: it is the graft of choice, as the left internal mammary artery, for the anterior interventricular artery in coronary bypass surgery.
spotters.followup: Which muscle separates the internal thoracic artery from the pleura in the lower part of its course?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein running with the artery behind the costal cartilages and state where it terminates.
spotters.answer: Internal thoracic vein. The paired venae comitantes of the lower internal thoracic artery unite into a single vein at about the third costal cartilage, which ascends medial to the artery and drains into the brachiocephalic vein of its own side. It receives the anterior intercostal veins, the musculophrenic vein and the superior epigastric vein. Applied point: it forms a caval to caval collateral through the superior epigastric to inferior epigastric route in superior vena caval obstruction.
spotters.followup: Through which route does the internal thoracic vein connect the superior and inferior caval systems?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery, state its parent vessel and the territory it supplies.
spotters.answer: Musculophrenic artery. It is one of the two terminal branches of the internal thoracic artery at the sixth intercostal space, and it runs downward and laterally behind the costal cartilages along the line of diaphragmatic attachment. It supplies the anterior intercostal arteries of the seventh, eighth and ninth spaces, the lower intercostal muscles, the peripheral diaphragm and the upper abdominal wall.
spotters.followup: Which artery is the other terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery, and what does it anastomose with?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned group of veins and state where they drain.
spotters.answer: Set of anterior intercostal veins. They accompany the anterior intercostal arteries in the intercostal spaces near the sternum, and drain medially into the internal thoracic vein for the upper spaces and into the musculophrenic vein for the lower spaces. Applied point: they anastomose freely with the posterior intercostal veins, so the intercostal spaces provide a continuous circumferential venous channel between the caval systems.
spotters.followup: Which veins do the posterior intercostal veins of the right side drain into?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned arterial group and state the source of these vessels and the order of the neurovascular bundle.
spotters.answer: Posterior intercostal arteries. The third to eleventh, with the subcostal artery, arise directly from the descending thoracic aorta; the first and second come from the superior intercostal artery of the costocervical trunk. Each runs in the costal groove between the internal intercostal muscle and the innermost intercostal muscle, with the order from above downward being vein, artery, nerve, VAN. Applied point: a chest drain or needle is inserted just above the upper border of the rib below to avoid the main bundle, though the collateral branch running along the upper border of the lower rib means no interspace is truly safe.
spotters.followup: Why are the right posterior intercostal arteries longer than the left, and what do they cross?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery and state its parent trunk and its branches.
spotters.answer: Superior intercostal artery, the descending branch of the costocervical trunk of the second part of the subclavian artery. It descends in front of the neck of the first and second ribs and gives the first and second posterior intercostal arteries, then anastomoses with the third posterior intercostal artery from the aorta. Applied point: it is why the upper two intercostal spaces are not supplied by the aorta and why aortic coarctation collaterals reach the descending aorta through the upper intercostal route.
spotters.followup: Which structures cross the superior intercostal artery on the left side of the neck of the first rib?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery in the first intercostal space and state its source.
spotters.answer: First posterior intercostal artery. It is a branch of the superior intercostal artery from the costocervical trunk, not of the aorta, and supplies the first intercostal space, anastomosing anteriorly with the first anterior intercostal branch of the internal thoracic artery. Applied point: knowing that the first two spaces come from the subclavian and not the aorta explains why rib notching in coarctation of the aorta spares the first and second ribs.
spotters.followup: Which ribs show notching in coarctation of the aorta, and why are the first two spared?

spotters.target: set of oesophageal branches of thoracic aorta
spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned branches and state the full arterial supply of the oesophagus by part.
spotters.answer: Set of oesophageal branches of thoracic aorta. Usually four or five unpaired branches arise from the anterior surface of the descending thoracic aorta between about T4 and T8 to supply the middle third of the oesophagus. The cervical part is supplied by the inferior thyroid artery, the thoracic part by these aortic branches and bronchial arteries, and the abdominal part by the left gastric and left inferior phrenic arteries. Applied point: the submucosal venous plexus of the lower oesophagus is the site of the porto systemic anastomosis that becomes varices in portal hypertension.
spotters.followup: Name the veins forming the porto systemic anastomosis at the lower end of the oesophagus.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned viscus and state its normal anatomical constrictions.
spotters.answer: Esophagus. About 25 cm long from the cricoid at C6 to the cardia at T11, it passes through the diaphragm at the T10 oesophageal hiatus in the right crus with the vagal trunks. Constrictions, measured from the incisor teeth, are at the cricopharyngeal sphincter about 15 cm, the crossing of the arch of aorta and the left main bronchus about 22 to 27 cm, and the diaphragmatic hiatus about 40 cm. Applied point: swallowed foreign bodies and corrosive strictures lodge at these constrictions, and this is where instrumentation most often perforates.
spotters.followup: Which vagal trunk lies anterior to the oesophagus at the hiatus, and why?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned airway. State where it begins and where it bifurcates.
spotters.answer: Trachea. It begins at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage at C6 and bifurcates at the sternal angle, the T4/T5 plane, at the carina. It is about 10 to 12 cm long, held open by 16 to 20 incomplete C shaped cartilages with the trachealis muscle closing the posterior gap. Blood supply is mainly from the inferior thyroid artery, with bronchial arteries below. Applied point: a widened subcarinal angle on chest radiograph indicates subcarinal nodal enlargement or left atrial dilatation.
spotters.followup: At the level of tracheal bifurcation, which nerve lies in the tracheo oesophageal groove?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned airway and state the differences between the right and left of this structure.
spotters.answer: Main bronchus. The right main bronchus is shorter, about 2.5 cm, wider and more vertical, and gives its upper lobe branch before entering the hilum; the left is longer, about 5 cm, narrower and more horizontal, passing under the arch of aorta and in front of the oesophagus. Applied point: aspirated foreign bodies and misplaced endotracheal tubes go preferentially into the right main bronchus, and aspiration pneumonia therefore favours the right lower lobe.
spotters.followup: Into which bronchopulmonary segment does aspirated material most often pass in a supine patient?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned airway segment. Note the labelling convention that distinguishes it from the main bronchus as a whole.
spotters.answer: Main bronchus proper. Flag honestly that this is an ontology label rather than a Terminologia Anatomica term: it denotes the segment of the main bronchus proximal to the origin of the first lobar bronchus, that is the undivided stem, whereas main bronchus in the same scheme covers the whole tree segment named for that side. Clinically the equivalent is the extrapulmonary main stem, which on the right is short because the right upper lobe bronchus arises about 2.5 cm from the carina. Applied point: this short right stem is the reason a right main bronchus intubation occludes the right upper lobe.
spotters.followup: Which is the eparterial bronchus and why is it named so?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned soft structure behind the manubrium and state its blood supply and one clinical association.
spotters.answer: Lobe of thymus. The bilobed thymus lies in the superior and anterior mediastinum behind the manubrium and in front of the pericardium and great vessels, largest at puberty and then replaced by fat. It develops from the third pharyngeal pouch, is supplied by branches of the internal thoracic and inferior thyroid arteries, and drains to the left brachiocephalic vein. Applied point: thymic hyperplasia and thymoma are associated with myasthenia gravis, and thymectomy is performed through a median sternotomy or a transcervical approach.
spotters.followup: Failure of which pharyngeal pouches produces thymic and parathyroid aplasia, and what is that syndrome called?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vessel. State its extent and one of its visceral branches.
spotters.answer: Descending thoracic aorta. It begins at the lower border of T4 as the continuation of the arch and ends at T12 by passing through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm to become the abdominal aorta. Branches: posterior intercostal arteries three to eleven and the subcostal artery, bronchial, oesophageal, mediastinal and superior phrenic arteries. Applied point: the aorta passes behind the diaphragm rather than through it, so aortic flow is unaffected by diaphragmatic contraction; note also that the pericardial sac and the thoracic duct lie anterior and to the right respectively.
spotters.followup: Name the three structures passing through the aortic hiatus at T12.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vessel. Distinguish this label from the descending thoracic aorta.
spotters.answer: Descending aorta. In the labelling used here the descending aorta is the whole continuation of the arch below T4, comprising the thoracic part above the diaphragm and the abdominal part below it, while descending thoracic aorta names only the segment between T4 and the aortic hiatus at T12. State the distinction to the examiner explicitly, because both labels exist in this model and only the level of the pin separates them.
spotters.followup: At which vertebral level does the aorta bifurcate into the common iliac arteries?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vessel at the lung root and state its relation to the bronchus on each side.
spotters.answer: Pulmonary artery. It carries deoxygenated blood to the lung. At the right hilum the artery lies anterior to the bronchus; at the left hilum it lies above the bronchus, hence the mnemonic RALS. The right pulmonary artery is longer and passes to the right behind the ascending aorta and superior vena cava and in front of the oesophagus. Applied point: a saddle embolus lodging at the bifurcation obstructs both pulmonary arteries and causes acute right heart failure.
spotters.followup: What is the functional difference between the pulmonary arteries and the bronchial arteries?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and state what it drains on each side and where it ends.
spotters.answer: Superior pulmonary vein. It lies most anterior and inferior in the lung root and drains into the left atrium. On the right it drains the upper and middle lobes; on the left it drains the upper lobe including the lingula. Applied point: the pulmonary vein ostia in the left atrium contain sleeves of myocardium that are the commonest trigger site for atrial fibrillation, which is why pulmonary vein isolation is the standard ablation target.
spotters.followup: How many pulmonary veins normally open into the left atrium, and where do they open?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and state its position in the lung root and its relation to the pulmonary ligament.
spotters.answer: Inferior pulmonary vein. It is the most inferior and posterior structure of the lung root, draining the lower lobe into the left atrium. The pulmonary ligament, the double fold of pleura hanging below the lung root, extends downward from just below it. Applied point: the pulmonary ligament is divided at lobectomy to mobilise the lower lobe, and the inferior pulmonary vein is the structure immediately at risk during that division.
spotters.followup: What is the function of the pulmonary ligament?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle. State its nerve supply and the levels of its three major openings.
spotters.answer: Diaphragm. Motor supply is entirely from the phrenic nerve, C3, C4 and C5, with the periphery receiving sensory fibres from the lower intercostal nerves. Openings: caval opening at T8 in the central tendon transmitting the inferior vena cava and the right phrenic nerve, oesophageal hiatus at T10 in the right crus with the oesophagus and vagal trunks, aortic hiatus at T12 behind the median arcuate ligament with the aorta, thoracic duct and azygos vein. Applied point: diaphragmatic irritation refers pain to the shoulder tip over the C4 dermatome.
spotters.followup: Why does a subphrenic abscess cause shoulder tip pain?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle. State its fibre direction, its extent, and its action.
spotters.answer: External intercostal muscle. Fibres run downward, forward and medially, from the lower border of the rib above to the upper border of the rib below. It extends from the tubercle of the rib behind to the costochondral junction in front, where it is replaced by the external intercostal membrane. It elevates the ribs in inspiration and is supplied segmentally by the intercostal nerves.
spotters.followup: Where does the external intercostal muscle end anteriorly, and what replaces it?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle. State its fibre direction and how far it extends posteriorly.
spotters.answer: Internal intercostal muscle. Fibres run downward and backward, at right angles to the external layer, from the floor of the costal groove of the rib above to the upper border of the rib below. It extends from the sternum in front to the angle of the rib behind, where it becomes the internal intercostal membrane. It depresses the ribs, acting in forced expiration, and is supplied by the intercostal nerves.
spotters.followup: Between which two muscle layers does the intercostal neurovascular bundle run?
