spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle layer and state what lies immediately superficial and immediately deep to it.
spotters.answer: Innermost intercostal muscle, the intercostalis intimus. It occupies the middle two quarters of the intercostal space, its fibres running in the same direction as the internal intercostal. The intercostal neurovascular bundle lies superficial to it, between it and the internal intercostal muscle; deep to it lie the endothoracic fascia and the parietal pleura. Applied point: this plane is the target of the serratus anterior and erector spinae plane blocks and explains why local anaesthetic spreads segmentally.
spotters.followup: Name the three subdivisions of the deepest intercostal muscle layer.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle on the inner surface of the anterior chest wall and state which vessel lies on it.
spotters.answer: Transversus thoracis, also called sternocostalis. It arises from the posterior surface of the lower sternum and xiphoid process and fans upward and laterally to the inner surfaces of the second to sixth costal cartilages. The internal thoracic artery and vein descend on its anterior surface, so it separates them from the parietal pleura. It is supplied by the intercostal nerves and weakly depresses the costal cartilages.
spotters.followup: Which vessels lie superficial to transversus thoracis, and what does this mean for internal thoracic artery harvest?
spotters.sub: Thorax, internal surface of anterior chest wall

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle, state its attachments and its nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Serratus posterior superior. It arises from the lower part of the ligamentum nuchae and the spines of C7 to T3 and inserts into the upper borders of the second to fifth ribs lateral to their angles. It is supplied by the second to fifth intercostal nerves, that is ventral rami, which is the key point distinguishing it from the true back muscles supplied by dorsal rami. It elevates the ribs.
spotters.followup: Why is serratus posterior superior classed as an intermediate rather than a deep back muscle?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle, state its attachments and its action.
spotters.answer: Serratus posterior inferior. It arises from the spines of T11 to L2 through the thoracolumbar fascia and passes upward and laterally to the lower borders of the ninth to twelfth ribs lateral to their angles. Supplied by the ninth to eleventh intercostal nerves and the subcostal nerve, all ventral rami. It depresses and fixes the lower ribs against the pull of the diaphragm.
spotters.followup: Which muscle group lies immediately deep to serratus posterior inferior?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle column, state which column of erector spinae it belongs to and its nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Iliocostalis thoracis. It is the lateral column of erector spinae, arising from the angles of the lower six ribs and inserting into the angles of the upper six ribs and the transverse process of C7. It is supplied by the dorsal rami of the thoracic spinal nerves and acts to extend and laterally flex the vertebral column and to keep the trunk erect.
spotters.followup: Name the three columns of erector spinae from lateral to medial.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and state its position within erector spinae and its attachments.
spotters.answer: Longissimus thoracis. It is the intermediate and largest column of erector spinae, arising from the erector spinae aponeurosis and the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae, and inserting by medial slips into the transverse processes of the thoracic vertebrae and by lateral slips into the lower nine or ten ribs between tubercle and angle. Supplied by dorsal rami of the spinal nerves. Applied point: erector spinae plane blocks deposit anaesthetic deep to this muscle at the transverse process for multi level thoracic analgesia.
spotters.followup: What is the common tendinous origin of erector spinae, and where does it attach inferiorly?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle. State which erector spinae column it forms and its attachments.
spotters.answer: Spinalis thoracis. It is the most medial and smallest column of erector spinae, arising from the spinous processes of T11 to L2 and inserting into the spinous processes of the upper four to eight thoracic vertebrae. Supplied by dorsal rami of the thoracic spinal nerves; it extends the vertebral column. Its medial position hard against the spines is what separates it from longissimus thoracis at the spotter table.
spotters.followup: Which muscle lies immediately deep to spinalis thoracis in the transversospinalis group?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle. State how many segments its fibres span and its group.
spotters.answer: Semispinalis thoracis. It belongs to the transversospinalis group, deep to erector spinae. Its fibres run from the transverse processes of the lower thoracic vertebrae upward and medially across about four to six segments to the spinous processes of the upper thoracic and lower cervical vertebrae. Supplied by dorsal rami; it extends and contralaterally rotates the vertebral column. The long oblique span is what distinguishes it from multifidus, which spans two to four, and the rotators, which span one to two.
spotters.followup: Name the three muscles of the transversospinalis group in order of decreasing fibre length.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle. State how far its fibres span and its main functional role.
spotters.answer: Thoracic rotator, the rotatores thoracis. These are the deepest and shortest of the transversospinalis group, best developed in the thoracic region, running from the transverse process of one vertebra to the lamina and root of the spine of the vertebra one or two above. Supplied by dorsal rami. Because of their short lever arm and very high density of muscle spindles they act mainly as proprioceptive organs and postural stabilisers rather than powerful rotators.
spotters.followup: Why is a high muscle spindle density taken as evidence of a proprioceptive rather than a prime mover role?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and state its attachments and nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Interspinalis thoracis. Short paired slips passing between the adjacent spinous processes of the thoracic vertebrae, one on each side of the interspinous ligament, poorly developed in the thoracic region compared with the cervical and lumbar. Supplied by dorsal rami of the spinal nerves; they assist extension and act as segmental stabilisers.
spotters.followup: In which regions of the vertebral column are the interspinales best developed, and why?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle group and state how the long slips differ from the short ones.
spotters.answer: Set of levatores costarum longi. These arise from the transverse processes of T7 to T11 and pass downward and laterally to insert on the rib two levels below, skipping one rib; the breves insert on the rib immediately below. Both are supplied by dorsal rami of the thoracic spinal nerves, which is unusual for rib elevators, and they elevate the ribs and assist lateral flexion and rotation.
spotters.followup: Why is dorsal ramus supply to levatores costarum notable when almost every other rib muscle is supplied by ventral rami?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned bone and state what articulates with it and the level of its lower joint.
spotters.answer: Manubrium. It articulates with the clavicles at the sternoclavicular joints, with the first costal cartilage by a primary cartilaginous joint, with the upper half of the second costal cartilage, and inferiorly with the body of sternum at the manubriosternal joint, a secondary cartilaginous joint forming the sternal angle of Louis. Applied point: the sternal angle marks the second costal cartilage, the T4/T5 disc, the start and end of the arch of aorta, the tracheal bifurcation and the plane dividing the superior from the inferior mediastinum. The suprasternal notch lies at T2.
spotters.followup: List the structures that lie at the level of the sternal angle.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned bone and state which costal cartilages articulate with it.
spotters.answer: Body of sternum. It articulates with the lower half of the second costal cartilage at its upper end, with the third to sixth costal cartilages along its lateral margins, and with the upper half of the seventh at the xiphisternal junction. It is formed by fusion of four sternebrae. Applied point: it is the site for sternal marrow aspiration and it is split in the midline for a median sternotomy.
spotters.followup: Which vertebral level does the xiphisternal joint correspond to?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned structure and state its vertebral level and one clinical use.
spotters.answer: Xiphoid process. It is cartilaginous in youth and ossifies and fuses with the body of sternum after about the fortieth year. The xiphisternal joint lies at the T9 level and marks the superior limit of the liver and the central tendon of the diaphragm. It gives attachment to the linea alba, the medial fibres of the diaphragm and the rectus sheath. Applied point: it is the landmark used to position the hands above it for chest compressions and for the subxiphoid approach to pericardiocentesis.
spotters.followup: Why are chest compressions delivered over the lower body of sternum and not over the xiphoid process?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned rib and state the structures related to the grooves on its upper surface.
spotters.answer: First rib. It is the shortest, broadest and most curved rib, flat in the horizontal plane with superior and inferior surfaces. The scalene tubercle on its inner border gives insertion to the anterior scalene muscle; in front of it is the groove for the subclavian vein and behind it the groove for the subclavian artery and the lower trunk of the brachial plexus. It has a single facet on its head articulating only with T1. Applied point: a cervical rib or fibrous band compresses the lower trunk and the subclavian artery in this interscalene interval, producing thoracic outlet syndrome.
spotters.followup: Which structures pass anterior to the anterior scalene and therefore in front of the first rib?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned rib and state the features that distinguish it from a typical rib.
spotters.answer: Twelfth rib. It is atypical: short, with a single facet on its head articulating only with T12, and it has no neck, no tubercle, no angle and no costal groove. It is a floating rib with no anterior attachment. Applied point: it is the surgical landmark for the posterior extraperitoneal approach to the kidney, and the pleural reflection crosses it, so an incision above the twelfth rib risks entering the pleural cavity.
spotters.followup: Where does the pleura cross the twelfth rib posteriorly, and what does that mean for a loin incision?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned rib and state what distinguishes it from the twelfth and from a typical rib.
spotters.answer: Eleventh rib. Like the twelfth it is a floating rib with a single articular facet on its head and no tubercle and no articulation with a transverse process, but unlike the twelfth it retains a slight angle and a shallow costal groove and is longer. Ribs eleven and twelve end in free cartilaginous tips in the abdominal wall musculature.
spotters.followup: Which ribs are true, which are false and which are floating, and on what criterion?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned cartilage and state its clinical significance for surface anatomy.
spotters.answer: Second costal cartilage. It articulates with the sternum at the manubriosternal joint, the sternal angle, so it is the first rib that can be reliably palpated on the anterior chest wall and the reference point for counting ribs and intercostal spaces. Applied point: the second intercostal space in the midclavicular line, immediately below this cartilage, is the classic site for needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax, and the pulmonary valve is auscultated in the left second space.
spotters.followup: Why can the first rib not be palpated anteriorly for counting?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned cartilage and state its significance for the costal margin.
spotters.answer: Seventh costal cartilage. It is the last cartilage to reach the sternum directly, articulating at the xiphisternal junction, so ribs one to seven are the true or vertebrosternal ribs. The eighth, ninth and tenth cartilages articulate with the cartilage above, and together with the seventh they form the costal margin. Applied point: the costal margin is the surface landmark for the liver edge, the gallbladder at the tip of the ninth cartilage in the right midclavicular line, and the site of Tietze syndrome costochondritis.
spotters.followup: Which cartilages form the costal margin, and which rib tip marks the fundus of the gallbladder?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned rib and describe the features of a typical rib and its two vertebral joints.
spotters.answer: Fifth rib. A typical rib has a head with two demifacets separated by a crest, a neck, a tubercle with an articular part for the transverse process and a non articular part for the costotransverse ligament, an angle, and a shaft with a costal groove on the inner aspect of the lower border. The head articulates with its own vertebra and the one above, so the fifth rib meets T4 and T5, and the tubercle articulates with the transverse process of T5. Applied point: the intercostal bundle in the costal groove is the reason intercostal drains are placed just above the lower rib of the space.
spotters.followup: Name the boundaries of the triangle of safety for intercostal drain insertion.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vertebra and state what makes its costal facets atypical.
spotters.answer: First thoracic vertebra. It is atypical because it carries a complete circular costal facet on each side for the whole head of the first rib plus an inferior demifacet for the upper half of the head of the second rib. Its body is more cervical in shape with uncinate processes, and its spinous process is long, thick and nearly horizontal, the vertebra prominens after C7. Applied point: T1 is the level of the suprapleural membrane and the cervical dome of the pleura, which rises about 2.5 cm above the medial third of the clavicle.
spotters.followup: Which thoracic vertebrae carry whole facets rather than demifacets, and for which ribs?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vertebra and state why it is transitional.
spotters.answer: Twelfth thoracic vertebra. It is transitional: it has a single complete costal facet on each side for the twelfth rib, its transverse processes bear no costal facets and are replaced by superior, inferior and lateral tubercles, and its inferior articular facets face laterally in the lumbar pattern while the superior facets remain thoracic. Applied point: this change of facet orientation makes the thoracolumbar junction a common site of fracture dislocation in flexion distraction injury, and the aortic hiatus lies at this level.
spotters.followup: Why is the thoracolumbar junction the commonest site of vertebral fracture in a fall from height?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vertebra and state the significance of the plane at its lower border.
spotters.answer: Fourth thoracic vertebra. The plane of the intervertebral disc between T4 and T5 is the transverse thoracic plane of Ludwig, passing through the sternal angle. At this level: the arch of aorta begins and ends, the trachea bifurcates at the carina, the pulmonary trunk divides, the azygos vein arches into the superior vena cava, the thoracic duct crosses from right to left, and the superior mediastinum is separated from the inferior mediastinum. It is a typical vertebra with superior and inferior costal demifacets and a long downward sloping spine.
spotters.followup: Which rib head articulates with the superior demifacet of the fourth thoracic vertebra?

spotters.target: intervertebral disk of fourth thoracic vertebra
spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned disc and state its structure and why thoracic discs prolapse less often than lumbar discs.
spotters.answer: Intervertebral disk of fourth thoracic vertebra, the fibrocartilaginous disc between T4 and T5 forming the sternal angle plane. Each disc has a peripheral anulus fibrosus of concentric lamellae and a central nucleus pulposus, the notochordal remnant. Thoracic discs are the thinnest in the column relative to vertebral body height, and the thoracic cage and the rib to vertebra articulations splint the segment, so mobility and disc prolapse are both much less common than in the lumbar region. Applied point: a thoracic disc prolapse, when it does occur, tends to present with myelopathy rather than radiculopathy because the canal is narrow and the cord, not a cauda equina, lies behind it.
distractors: intervertebral disk of fifth thoracic vertebra
intervertebral disk of third thoracic vertebra
spotters.followup: Why does thoracic cord compression cause upper motor neurone signs in the legs while a lumbar disc causes lower motor neurone signs?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery, state its origin and the structures it supplies.
spotters.answer: Lateral thoracic artery. It arises from the second part of the axillary artery, behind or at the lower border of pectoralis minor, and descends along the lateral border of that muscle on serratus anterior. It supplies serratus anterior, pectoral muscles and the axillary nodes, and in the female gives lateral mammary branches to the breast. Applied point: the long thoracic nerve runs with it on serratus anterior and is the nerve at risk in axillary clearance, producing winging of the scapula.
spotters.followup: Which nerve accompanies the lateral thoracic artery on serratus anterior, and what deficit follows its injury?
spotters.sub: Thorax, lateral chest wall and axilla

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery, state its origin and its surgical importance.
spotters.answer: Thoracodorsal artery. It is the continuation of the subscapular artery, itself the largest branch of the third part of the axillary artery, and it runs down the posterior axillary wall with the thoracodorsal nerve to supply latissimus dorsi. Applied point: this pedicle is the basis of the pedicled latissimus dorsi myocutaneous flap used in breast reconstruction, and it is preserved deliberately during axillary node clearance for that reason.
spotters.followup: Which three structures form the contents of the posterior axillary wall alongside this artery?
spotters.sub: Thorax, posterolateral chest wall and axilla

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned cartilage and state the type of joint it makes with the sternum.
spotters.answer: First costal cartilage. It joins the manubrium by a primary cartilaginous joint, a synchondrosis, which is immobile, unlike the second to seventh which are synovial. It is the shortest and broadest costal cartilage and lies deep to the medial end of the clavicle, which is why the first rib cannot be palpated anteriorly. Applied point: the superior vena cava is formed behind the lower border of the right first costal cartilage.
spotters.followup: Which type of joint do the second to seventh costal cartilages form with the sternum?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and state which vein it drains into and what it receives.
spotters.answer: Musculophrenic vein. It accompanies the musculophrenic artery along the line of diaphragmatic attachment behind the lower costal cartilages, receives the anterior intercostal veins of the seventh to ninth spaces and veins from the diaphragm and abdominal wall, and drains into the internal thoracic vein. Applied point: with the superior epigastric vein it is part of the anterior thoracoabdominal venous route linking the caval systems.
spotters.followup: Which anterior intercostal veins drain into the internal thoracic vein rather than the musculophrenic vein?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein on the thoracic surface of the diaphragm and state its drainage.
spotters.answer: Superior phrenic vein. It drains the upper, thoracic surface of the diaphragm, accompanying the superior phrenic arteries which arise from the lower descending thoracic aorta, and drains into the azygos and hemiazygos systems and into the internal thoracic and pericardiacophrenic veins. Distinguish it from the inferior phrenic veins, which drain the abdominal surface into the inferior vena cava on the right and into the left suprarenal vein or inferior vena cava on the left.
spotters.followup: Which vein and which artery accompany the phrenic nerve on the pericardium?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vessel. State the vertebral level at which it begins and the level at which it ends.
spotters.answer: Abdominal aorta. Enters through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at T12, descends slightly left of the midline on the bodies of L1 to L4, and bifurcates into the common iliac arteries at the lower border of L4, the supracristal plane. Three unpaired ventral branches: celiac trunk T12, superior mesenteric L1, inferior mesenteric L3.
spotters.followup: Name the paired branches in craniocaudal order and give the level of each.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vessel and state where it is formed and where it pierces the diaphragm.
spotters.answer: Inferior vena cava. Formed at L5 by the union of the two common iliac veins, ascends to the right of the aorta on the bodies of the lumbar vertebrae, grooves the bare area of the liver, and pierces the central tendon of the diaphragm at T8. Tributaries: lumbar, right gonadal, both renal, right suprarenal, inferior phrenic and hepatic veins.
spotters.followup: Why does the left gonadal vein not drain directly into this vessel?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery and name its branches.
spotters.answer: Celiac trunk. Arises from the front of the abdominal aorta at T12 just below the aortic hiatus, about 1.5 cm long, and divides into left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries. It is the artery of the foregut, supplying abdominal esophagus to the second part of the duodenum, plus liver, gallbladder, pancreas and spleen.
spotters.followup: Foregut pain is referred to which region, and through which splanchnic nerves?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery and state the gut segment it supplies.
spotters.answer: Superior mesenteric artery. Arises from the aorta at L1, about 1 cm below the celiac trunk, passes behind the neck of the pancreas and in front of the uncinate process, the third part of the duodenum and the left renal vein. Artery of the midgut: distal duodenum to the distal third of the transverse colon. Branches: inferior pancreaticoduodenal, jejunal and ileal, ileocolic, right colic, middle colic.
spotters.followup: Which two structures are compressed between this artery and the aorta, and what are those syndromes called?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery, state its level of origin and its territory.
spotters.answer: Inferior mesenteric artery. Arises from the front of the aorta at L3, about 3 to 4 cm above the bifurcation. Artery of the hindgut: distal third of transverse colon to the upper rectum. Branches: left colic, sigmoid, superior rectal. Its territory meets the superior mesenteric territory at the splenic flexure, the watershed of Griffiths, via the marginal artery of Drummond.
spotters.followup: Why is the splenic flexure the commonest site of ischemic colitis?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery and describe its course.
spotters.answer: Splenic artery. Largest branch of the celiac trunk, runs a characteristically tortuous course to the left along the superior border of the body and tail of the pancreas, then in the splenorenal ligament to the hilum. Branches: pancreatic branches, short gastric arteries, left gastro-epiploic artery, terminal splenic branches. Commonest site of visceral artery aneurysm.
spotters.followup: Why is the tail of the pancreas at risk during splenectomy?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery and name its two terminal branches.
spotters.answer: Common hepatic artery. Branch of the celiac trunk, passes to the right along the upper border of the head of the pancreas, then turns up into the free edge of the lesser omentum. It divides into the hepatic artery proper and the gastroduodenal artery, the latter giving the right gastro-epiploic and superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries.
spotters.followup: Which artery bleeds when a posterior duodenal ulcer perforates the wall of the first part of the duodenum?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery and state its relations in the free edge of the lesser omentum.
spotters.answer: Hepatic artery proper. Ascends in the free edge of the lesser omentum, lying to the left of the bile duct and anterior to the hepatic portal vein. It divides into right and left hepatic arteries at the porta hepatis. The right hepatic artery usually gives the cystic artery within the cystohepatic triangle of Calot.
spotters.followup: Give the three boundaries of the cystohepatic triangle of Calot.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein, state how it is formed and where.
spotters.answer: Hepatic portal vein. Formed behind the neck of the pancreas at the level of L2 by union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins, about 8 cm long. Ascends in the free edge of the lesser omentum behind the bile duct and hepatic artery proper, forming the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen, then divides into right and left branches at the porta hepatis. It has no valves.
spotters.followup: Name four sites of portosystemic anastomosis and the clinical sign at each.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and name its major tributary.
spotters.answer: Splenic vein. Formed at the splenic hilum, runs to the right behind the body of the pancreas, below the splenic artery, receiving short gastric, left gastro-epiploic and pancreatic veins, and the inferior mesenteric vein. It joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the neck of the pancreas to form the hepatic portal vein.
spotters.followup: How does carcinoma of the body of the pancreas produce isolated gastric varices?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and give its relation to the artery of the same name.
spotters.answer: Superior mesenteric vein. Lies to the right of the superior mesenteric artery in the root of the mesentery, drains the midgut plus the right gastro-epiploic and pancreaticoduodenal veins, crosses the third part of the duodenum and the uncinate process, and unites with the splenic vein behind the neck of the pancreas.
spotters.followup: Which vein lies to the left of the artery in the mesenteric root, and what is the significance of a reversed relation on CT?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and state where it terminates.
spotters.answer: Inferior mesenteric vein. Continuation of the superior rectal vein, ascends to the left of the midline, does not accompany its artery, passes lateral to the duodenojejunal flexure and behind the body of the pancreas to end in the splenic vein. Variants end at the superior mesenteric vein or at the splenoportal confluence. It is a route for portosystemic anastomosis at the anorectum.
spotters.followup: Which fold of peritoneum marks this vein at the duodenojejunal flexure?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery, state its level and one asymmetry between the two sides.
spotters.answer: Renal artery. Arises from the lateral wall of the aorta at L1 to L2, just below the superior mesenteric artery. The right is longer and passes behind the inferior vena cava. Each divides into five segmental arteries which are functional end arteries, the posterior segmental branch passing behind the pelvis. Accessory renal arteries are common and must be preserved in transplant work.
spotters.followup: Give the order of structures at the renal hilum from anterior to posterior.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and list the tributaries received on the left side.
spotters.answer: Renal vein. Lies anterior to the renal artery at the hilum. The left renal vein is about three times longer, crosses the midline anterior to the aorta and posterior to the superior mesenteric artery, and receives the left suprarenal, left gonadal and left inferior phrenic veins before entering the inferior vena cava. The right renal vein is short and has no named tributaries.
spotters.followup: What is nutcracker syndrome and which vein is compressed?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vessel and state its origin.
spotters.answer: Testicular artery. Arises from the front of the abdominal aorta at L2, just below the renal artery, reflecting the embryonic lumbar position of the gonad. It runs retroperitoneally on psoas major, crosses in front of the ureter and the external iliac artery, enters the deep inguinal ring and runs in the spermatic cord to the testis.
spotters.followup: Which structure does this vessel cross anteriorly, and what surgical error does that relation guard against?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and give the drainage on each side.
spotters.answer: Testicular vein. Begins as the pampiniform plexus in the spermatic cord, condenses to a single vein in the retroperitoneum. The right drains obliquely into the inferior vena cava, the left drains at a right angle into the left renal vein. That right angled drainage plus the higher column of blood explains the left sided predominance of varicocele.
spotters.followup: A new left varicocele that does not decompress on lying down suggests what diagnosis?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and state where it drains.
spotters.answer: Hepatic vein. Three main veins, right, middle and left, are intersegmental in position and drain into the inferior vena cava immediately below the diaphragm, in the groove on the bare area of the liver. They have almost no extrahepatic length, which is why the liver cannot be mobilised off the cava without control here. Occlusion produces Budd-Chiari syndrome.
spotters.followup: Which lobe of the liver is spared and hypertrophies in Budd-Chiari syndrome, and why?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and state the plane in which it lies.
spotters.answer: Middle hepatic vein. Runs in the principal plane, Cantlie line, from the gallbladder fossa to the inferior vena cava, dividing the liver into functional right and left hemilivers. It drains segments IV, V and VIII and usually joins the left hepatic vein in a common trunk before entering the cava. Its position dictates the transection plane in right or left hepatectomy and in living donor grafts.
spotters.followup: Which Couinaud segment drains directly into the cava and not through this vein?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery and name the important branch it gives.
spotters.answer: Inferior phrenic artery. The first paired branch of the abdominal aorta, arising just below the aortic hiatus, often from the celiac trunk. It supplies the undersurface of the diaphragm and gives the superior suprarenal arteries. It is a common source of collateral supply to hepatocellular carcinoma at the bare area.
spotters.followup: Name all three arterial sources of the suprarenal gland.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery, state how many pairs there are and their course.
spotters.answer: Lumbar artery. Four pairs arise from the posterior surface of the abdominal aorta opposite L1 to L4, the fifth pair usually coming from the median sacral artery. They pass backwards around the vertebral bodies, deep to the sympathetic trunk and the tendinous arches of psoas major, and divide into dorsal and abdominal branches. They anastomose with the epigastric and intercostal systems.
spotters.followup: Why are these vessels a source of persistent bleeding after aortic aneurysm repair?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery and state its surgical importance at the groin.
spotters.answer: Inferior epigastric artery. Arises from the external iliac artery just above the inguinal ligament, raises the lateral umbilical fold, runs upward and medially to enter the rectus sheath at the arcuate line and anastomose with the superior epigastric artery. Its origin is the landmark for hernias: indirect sacs lie lateral to it, direct sacs medial to it in Hesselbach triangle.
spotters.followup: Which vessel is at risk at a lateral laparoscopic port and how do you site the port to avoid it?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery and state the curvature it supplies.
spotters.answer: Gastric artery. The left gastric artery is the smallest branch of the celiac trunk, ascends to the cardia, gives esophageal branches, then turns along the lesser curvature between the layers of the lesser omentum to anastomose with the right gastric artery from the hepatic artery proper. Its esophageal branches form the portosystemic anastomosis responsible for esophageal varices.
spotters.followup: Name the four named arteries of the stomach and their parent vessels.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned artery and state where it runs.
spotters.answer: Gastro-epiploic artery. Runs along the greater curvature of the stomach between the two layers of the gastrocolic ligament, about a finger breadth from the wall. The right arises from the gastroduodenal artery, the left from the splenic artery, and the two anastomose. It gives gastric and omental branches.
spotters.followup: Which of the two contributing vessels is preserved when the stomach is used as a conduit after esophagectomy?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vein and state its clinical significance.
spotters.answer: Gastric vein. The left gastric or coronary vein runs along the lesser curvature and drains directly into the hepatic portal vein. Its esophageal tributaries communicate with the azygos system in the lower esophagus, the classical portosystemic anastomosis, so portal hypertension diverts flow here and produces esophageal varices. The right gastric vein also enters the portal vein.
spotters.followup: Why do variceal bleeds arise at the gastro-esophageal junction rather than in the mid esophagus?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned arterial branch and state which Couinaud segment it supplies.
spotters.answer: Anterior superior segmental hepatic artery. A division of the right hepatic artery supplying the right anterior sector superiorly, Couinaud segment VIII. Its partner, the anterior inferior segmental branch, supplies segment V. Segmental arteries in the liver are functional end arteries, which is the basis of anatomical segmentectomy and of arterial embolisation of tumours.
spotters.followup: Which segments make up the right posterior sector and which artery supplies them?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned organ and name the structures forming its bed.
spotters.answer: Stomach. Foregut derivative in the left hypochondrium and epigastrium, with cardia, fundus, body, pyloric antrum and pylorus. The stomach bed behind the lesser sac comprises the diaphragm, left crus, spleen, left suprarenal gland, upper left kidney, splenic artery, pancreas and transverse mesocolon. Pain is referred to the epigastrium through T6 to T9.
spotters.followup: Name the arteries of the lesser and greater curvatures with their origins.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned segment of gut and state its parts and length.
spotters.answer: Duodenum. About 25 cm, C shaped around the head of the pancreas, in four parts. The first part is intraperitoneal for its proximal 2 cm and is the site of peptic ulcer. The second part is retroperitoneal and receives the hepatopancreatic ampulla at the major duodenal papilla, about 10 cm from the pylorus, the foregut to midgut junction. The third part is crossed by the superior mesenteric vessels. The fourth ends at the duodenojejunal flexure, held by the suspensory muscle of Treitz.
spotters.followup: Which artery supplies the duodenum above and below the ampulla, and why does that matter embryologically?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned organ and state which part is not retroperitoneal.
spotters.answer: Pancreas. Retroperitoneal except the tail, which lies in the splenorenal ligament. Head sits in the duodenal C with the uncinate process behind the superior mesenteric vessels, the neck overlies the portal confluence, the body crosses L1 and L2, the tail reaches the splenic hilum. Blood supply from pancreaticoduodenal arcades and splenic branches. Pain is epigastric and bores through to the back.
spotters.followup: Why does carcinoma of the head produce painless obstructive jaundice with a palpable gallbladder?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned duct and state where it opens.
spotters.answer: Pancreatic duct, duct of Wirsung. Runs the whole length of the gland, receives tributaries at right angles, turns caudally at the head and joins the bile duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla of Vater, opening on the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum, guarded by the sphincter of Oddi. The accessory duct of Santorini opens 2 cm proximally on the minor papilla.
spotters.followup: Explain how a gallstone impacted at the ampulla causes pancreatitis.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned organ and give the surface marking of its fundus.
spotters.answer: Gallbladder. Pear shaped, 30 to 50 mL, lying in a fossa on the visceral surface of the right lobe of the liver. The fundus projects at the tip of the ninth costal cartilage, where the lateral border of the right rectus abdominis crosses the costal margin, near the transpyloric plane. Fundus, body, infundibulum with Hartmann pouch, and neck. Supplied by the cystic artery, usually from the right hepatic artery.
spotters.followup: Explain Murphy sign and why cholecystitis may refer pain to the right shoulder.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned duct and name the fold within it.
spotters.answer: Cystic duct. About 3 to 4 cm, runs from the neck of the gallbladder to join the common hepatic duct and form the bile duct. Its mucosa is thrown into the spiral valve of Heister, which keeps the lumen patent. It forms the lower boundary of the cystohepatic triangle of Calot and is the structure clipped and divided first in cholecystectomy after the critical view of safety.
spotters.followup: Which duct is at risk of being mistaken for this one and clipped, and how is that avoided?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned duct and state how it is formed and what it becomes.
spotters.answer: Common hepatic duct. Formed at the porta hepatis by union of the right and left hepatic ducts, about 3 cm long, descends in the free edge of the lesser omentum to the right of the hepatic artery proper and anterior to the hepatic portal vein. It joins the cystic duct to form the bile duct. External compression by a stone in Hartmann pouch causes Mirizzi syndrome.
spotters.followup: Give the arrangement of the three structures in the free edge of the lesser omentum.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned part of the liver and state its boundaries.
spotters.answer: Caudate lobe of liver, Couinaud segment I. Lies on the posterior surface, bounded by the inferior vena cava on the right, the fissure for the ligamentum venosum on the left, and the porta hepatis below. It is functionally independent: it receives blood from both right and left portal and arterial branches, and drains by several small veins directly into the inferior vena cava rather than through the main hepatic veins.
spotters.followup: Why does this lobe hypertrophy in Budd-Chiari syndrome?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned organ and state its rib relations.
spotters.answer: Spleen. Intraperitoneal organ of the left hypochondrium, lying against ribs 9 to 11 with its long axis along the tenth rib, separated from them by the diaphragm and the costodiaphragmatic recess. Classical 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 rule: 1 by 3 by 5 inches, about 7 ounces, ribs 9 to 11. Attached by gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments, the latter carrying the splenic vessels and tail of pancreas.
spotters.followup: In which direction does this organ enlarge, and which palpable feature confirms it clinically?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned organ and state its vertebral levels.
spotters.answer: Kidney. Retroperitoneal, extending from T12 to L3, the right lying about 2 cm lower because of the liver. The hilum is at the transpyloric plane, L1, facing anteromedially. Coverings from within out: fibrous capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia of Gerota, pararenal fat. The upper pole is related to the suprarenal gland and the twelfth rib crosses the posterior surface.
spotters.followup: Name the structures at the hilum from anterior to posterior and the posterior muscular relations.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned organ and describe its venous drainage.
spotters.answer: Adrenal gland. Retroperitoneal, capping the upper pole of the kidney within the renal fascia but separated from it by a septum. Supplied by three arteries: superior from the inferior phrenic, middle from the aorta, inferior from the renal artery. Drainage is by a single vein: on the right, short and directly into the inferior vena cava, on the left into the left renal vein. Cortex is mesodermal, medulla is neural crest.
spotters.followup: Why is the right sided gland technically harder to remove than the left?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned structure and name its three sites of normal constriction.
spotters.answer: Ureter. Muscular tube about 25 cm, retroperitoneal, running on psoas major and crossing the tips of the lumbar transverse processes, then crossing the bifurcation of the common iliac artery at the pelvic brim over the sacroiliac joint. Constrictions at the pelviureteric junction, at the pelvic brim where it crosses the iliac vessels, and at the vesicoureteric junction, the commonest sites of stone impaction. Crossed anteriorly by the gonadal vessels.
spotters.followup: Which artery crosses it in the female pelvis, and what is the operative aphorism for that relation?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned structure and give the surface marking of its base.
spotters.answer: Appendix. Arises from the posteromedial wall of the cecum where the three taeniae coli converge, about 2 cm below the ileocecal junction. Base marked at McBurney point, the junction of the lateral one third and medial two thirds of the line from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. Retrocecal is the commonest position. Supplied by the appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery, which runs in the mesoappendix and is an end artery.
spotters.followup: Explain the shift of pain from the periumbilical region to the right iliac fossa.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned peritoneal fold and state its contents.
spotters.answer: Mesoappendix. Triangular fold of peritoneum passing from the posterior layer of the mesentery behind the terminal ileum to the appendix. It carries the appendicular artery and vein and the appendicular lymphatics. It is ligated and divided first at appendicectomy, and inflammation thrombosing the artery in it produces gangrene and perforation.
spotters.followup: Why does thrombosis of the vessel in this fold cause gangrene so rapidly?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned segment of bowel and state its peritoneal status and blood supply.
spotters.answer: Ascending colon. About 15 cm from the ileocecal junction to the right colic or hepatic flexure, secondarily retroperitoneal with peritoneum on its front and sides, creating the right paracolic gutter laterally. Supplied by the ileocolic and right colic branches of the superior mesenteric artery. The hepatic flexure is related to the right kidney, the descending duodenum and the gallbladder.
spotters.followup: Which plane is developed to mobilise this segment, and which structures lie behind it at risk?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned segment of bowel and state how it is suspended.
spotters.answer: Transverse colon. Intraperitoneal, about 45 cm, suspended by the transverse mesocolon and carrying the greater omentum on its anterior surface. Proximal two thirds are midgut supplied by the middle colic artery from the superior mesenteric, the distal third is hindgut supplied by the left colic artery from the inferior mesenteric. The splenic flexure is the higher, more acute and more fixed of the two flexures.
spotters.followup: Name the ligament that fixes the splenic flexure and state its surgical importance.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned segment of bowel and state its blood supply and peritoneal status.
spotters.answer: Descending colon. About 25 cm from the splenic flexure to the pelvic brim, secondarily retroperitoneal, narrower and more deeply placed than the ascending colon, with a left paracolic gutter lateral to it. Supplied by the left colic branch of the inferior mesenteric artery. Related posteriorly to the left kidney, quadratus lumborum and the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.
spotters.followup: Which venous system drains this segment, and where does that vein terminate?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned peritoneal fold and state what it divides.
spotters.answer: Transverse mesocolon. Two layered fold suspending the transverse colon, its root crossing the second part of the duodenum and the anterior border of the pancreas. It divides the abdominal cavity into the supracolic and infracolic compartments and its layers contain the middle colic vessels. Its upper layer is continuous with the posterior layers of the greater omentum.
spotters.followup: Through which structure does pus track between the supracolic and infracolic compartments?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned structure and describe the line of its root.
spotters.answer: Mesentery of small intestine. Fan shaped double fold about 15 cm at the root and 20 cm deep, the root running obliquely from the duodenojejunal flexure to the left of L2 down to the right sacroiliac joint, crossing the third part of the duodenum, the aorta, the inferior vena cava, the right ureter and the right psoas major. It contains the superior mesenteric vessels, jejunal and ileal arcades, lymphatics, nodes and autonomic nerves.
spotters.followup: Why does a narrow root predispose to midgut volvulus in malrotation?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned band and state what it represents.
spotters.answer: Taenia libera. One of the three longitudinal bands into which the outer smooth muscle coat of the large intestine is condensed, the free band, visible on the anterior surface of the ascending and descending colon. The three bands are shorter than the gut, producing sacculation into haustra, and they converge at the base of the appendix, the reliable landmark for finding it. They are absent on the appendix, rectum and cecal tip.
spotters.followup: Name the other two bands and state what is attached along each.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle, state its fibre direction and nerve supply.
spotters.answer: External oblique. Outermost of the three flat muscles, arising from the outer surfaces of the lower eight ribs, fibres running downwards and forwards, hands in pockets direction. It inserts into the xiphoid, linea alba, pubic crest and anterior half of the iliac crest. Its aponeurosis forms the anterior wall of the inguinal canal, the inguinal ligament and the superficial inguinal ring. Supplied by the ventral rami of T7 to T12.
spotters.followup: Which parts of the aponeurosis form the lacunar ligament and the conjoint tendon?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned structure and state what forms it.
spotters.answer: Linea alba. Midline fibrous raphe from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis formed by decussation of the aponeuroses of the external oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominis of both sides. It is broad above the umbilicus and narrow below, and is relatively avascular and free of nerves, which is why the midline incision is used, at the cost of slower healing and incisional hernia.
spotters.followup: What is divarication of the recti and how does it differ from an epigastric hernia?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and give its attachments and nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Psoas major. Arises from the bodies, intervertebral discs and transverse processes of T12 to L5, descends along the pelvic brim, joins iliacus and inserts by a common tendon into the lesser trochanter of the femur. Supplied directly by ventral rami of L1 to L3. It is a flexor of the hip and its fascia is the plane along which a tuberculous abscess of the lumbar spine tracks to the femoral triangle.
spotters.followup: Which nerves emerge from the lateral, medial and anterior surfaces of this muscle?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and state its nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Iliacus. Fan shaped muscle from the upper two thirds of the iliac fossa, the inner lip of the iliac crest and the ala of the sacrum, converging on the lateral side of the psoas tendon to insert into the lesser trochanter. Supplied by the femoral nerve, L2 to L4, unlike psoas major which takes direct branches from the lumbar plexus. It is the chief flexor of the hip with psoas.
spotters.followup: A haematoma in this muscle in a haemophiliac compresses which nerve, and what deficit results?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle, state which column it belongs to and its nerve supply.
spotters.answer: Iliocostalis lumborum. The most lateral of the three columns of erector spinae, arising from the common tendon on the sacrum, iliac crest and thoracolumbar fascia and inserting into the angles of the lower six or seven ribs. Supplied segmentally by the dorsal rami of the lumbar spinal nerves. Acts bilaterally to extend the trunk and unilaterally to side bend it, and controls flexion eccentrically.
spotters.followup: Name the other two columns of erector spinae and their order from lateral to medial.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned muscle and state its innervation compared with its lateral counterpart.
spotters.answer: Medial lumbar intertransversarius. Small paired muscle running between the accessory and mamillary processes of adjacent lumbar vertebrae, deep in the back. It is supplied by the dorsal rami of the lumbar spinal nerves, whereas the lateral lumbar intertransversarius, lying between the transverse processes proper, is supplied by ventral rami. It acts mainly as a proprioceptive stabiliser and side bender.
spotters.followup: State the general rule that decides whether a deep back muscle takes dorsal or ventral rami.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vertebra and name the plane at its level with three structures found there.
spotters.answer: First lumbar vertebra. Its level corresponds to the transpyloric plane of Addison, midway between the jugular notch and the pubic symphysis. Structures at this plane: pylorus, fundus of the gallbladder, neck of the pancreas, hila of both kidneys, origin of the superior mesenteric artery, formation of the hepatic portal vein, end of the spinal cord at the L1 to L2 disc, and the ninth costal cartilage.
spotters.followup: Why must a lumbar puncture be performed below this level in an adult?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned vertebra and name the surface plane at its level.
spotters.answer: Fourth lumbar vertebra. Lies at the supracristal plane, the line joining the highest points of the iliac crests, the standard landmark for lumbar puncture at the L3 to L4 or L4 to L5 interspace. The abdominal aorta bifurcates at its lower border, and the inferior vena cava is formed one level lower at L5. Its transverse process is the highest point of the crest reference in the standing patient.
spotters.followup: Why is lumbar puncture safe at this level in an adult but not in a neonate?

spotters.target: intervertebral disk of fourth lumbar vertebra
spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned structure and state the commonest direction of its herniation and the root affected.
spotters.answer: Intervertebral disk of the fourth lumbar vertebra, the L4 to L5 disc. Made of an outer annulus fibrosus and inner nucleus pulposus, a remnant of the notochord. Herniation is posterolateral because the posterior longitudinal ligament is strong centrally and weak laterally. A posterolateral prolapse here spares the exiting L4 root and compresses the traversing L5 root: weak extensor hallucis longus, foot drop, sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and the great toe, with no ankle jerk change.
distractors: intervertebral disk of third lumbar vertebra
intervertebral disk of fifth lumbar vertebra
spotters.followup: Which root would a large central prolapse at this level threaten, and what emergency does that produce?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned gyrus and state its functional cortex and arterial supply.
spotters.answer: Precentral gyrus, primary motor cortex, Brodmann area 4, containing the giant pyramidal cells of Betz in layer V and giving origin to most corticospinal fibres. Lateral two thirds are supplied by the middle cerebral artery, the medial extension into the paracentral lobule by the anterior cerebral artery. A lesion produces contralateral upper motor neuron weakness.
spotters.followup: A patient has weakness of the contralateral foot and thigh with a spared face and hand. Which artery is occluded and why does the deficit stop at that level?

spotters.prompt: Name the pinned gyrus and state which thalamic nuclei project to it.
spotters.answer: Postcentral gyrus, primary somatosensory cortex, Brodmann areas 3, 1 and 2. It receives the ventral posterolateral nucleus for body and the ventral posteromedial nucleus for face, fibres reaching it through the posterior limb of the internal capsule. Lesion causes contralateral loss of discriminative touch, position sense and two point discrimination.
spotters.followup: Draw the sensory homunculus on this gyrus. Which part is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned gyrus and name the functional area in its posterior part.
spotters.answer: Middle frontal gyrus, lying between the superior and inferior frontal sulci. Its posterior part carries the frontal eye field, Brodmann area 8, for contralateral conjugate saccades. A destructive lesion drives the eyes towards the side of the lesion, an irritative focus drives them away.
spotters.followup: Which artery supplies the frontal eye field, and what eye sign accompanies a large right middle cerebral artery infarct?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned gyrus and state the clinical consequence of a dominant hemisphere lesion here.
spotters.answer: Inferior frontal gyrus. Its pars opercularis and pars triangularis, Brodmann areas 44 and 45, form the motor speech area of Broca in the dominant hemisphere. Supplied by the superior division of the middle cerebral artery, a lesion gives non fluent expressive aphasia with preserved comprehension and impaired repetition.
spotters.followup: Name the three parts of this gyrus and state which structure separates the pars orbitalis from the pars triangularis.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned gyrus on the medial surface and state one connection.
spotters.answer: Cingulate gyrus, arching above the corpus callosum inside the cingulate sulcus, a limbic lobe component in the circuit of Papez. The cingulum bundle links it to the parahippocampal gyrus. Blood supply is the anterior cerebral artery, and bilateral infarction produces akinetic mutism.
spotters.followup: Trace the circuit of Papez starting from the hippocampus and ending back at this gyrus.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned gyrus and state the aphasia produced by a dominant side lesion.
spotters.answer: Supramarginal gyrus, Brodmann area 40, capping the upturned end of the posterior ramus of the lateral sulcus. In the dominant hemisphere it forms part of the inferior parietal lobule, and a lesion involving the arcuate fasciculus here produces conduction aphasia with fluent speech, good comprehension and grossly impaired repetition. Supplied by the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery.
distractors: posterior part of superior temporal gyrus
spotters.followup: Which sulcus does this gyrus curve around, and which gyrus lies immediately posterior to it?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned gyrus and name the syndrome caused by a dominant hemisphere lesion.
spotters.answer: Angular gyrus, Brodmann area 39, curving around the upturned end of the superior temporal sulcus. A dominant side lesion produces Gerstmann syndrome: finger agnosia, right and left disorientation, agraphia and acalculia, often with alexia. Supplied by the angular branch of the middle cerebral artery.
distractors: posterior part of superior temporal gyrus
spotters.followup: Which sulcus does this gyrus surround, and how does that distinguish it from the gyrus immediately anterior?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned region and state its sensory function.
spotters.answer: Superior parietal lobule, Brodmann areas 5 and 7, lying above the intraparietal sulcus behind the postcentral gyrus. It is somatosensory association cortex for stereognosis and spatial awareness of the contralateral half of the body. A non dominant lesion causes contralateral neglect and dressing apraxia, a dominant lesion causes astereognosis.
spotters.followup: Which sulcus separates this lobule from the inferior parietal lobule, and which two gyri make up that inferior lobule?

spotters.target: posterior part of superior temporal gyrus
spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned region and state the deficit produced by a dominant hemisphere lesion.
spotters.answer: Posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus, the sensory speech area of Wernicke, Brodmann area 22, behind the transverse temporal gyri. A dominant side lesion produces fluent receptive aphasia with paraphasic errors, impaired comprehension and impaired repetition, with no insight into the deficit. Supplied by the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery.
distractors: anterior part of superior temporal gyrus
spotters.followup: Which fibre bundle connects this area to the motor speech area, and what aphasia follows if only that bundle is cut?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned gyrus on the inferior surface and state one functional role.
spotters.answer: Fusiform gyrus, the occipitotemporal gyrus, lying between the collateral sulcus medially and the occipitotemporal sulcus laterally. It carries the fusiform face area, and bilateral lesions cause prosopagnosia. Its posterior part is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery.
spotters.followup: Name the two sulci bounding this gyrus and the gyrus lying medial to the collateral sulcus.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned gyrus and state its significance in herniation.
spotters.answer: Parahippocampal gyrus, whose anterior end hooks backwards as the uncus and whose cortex includes the entorhinal area, Brodmann area 28, the source of the perforant path to the hippocampus. In raised intracranial pressure the uncus herniates through the tentorial notch, compressing the oculomotor nerve and the midbrain. Earliest site of neurofibrillary change in Alzheimer disease.
spotters.followup: List the signs of uncal herniation in order of appearance and explain the false localising pupillary sign.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned cortex buried in the lateral sulcus and name its coverings.
spotters.answer: Insula, the island of Reil, covered by the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula and separated from them by the circular sulcus. It handles visceral sensation, taste, autonomic control and visceral pain, and the M2 branches of the middle cerebral artery run over its surface. The extreme capsule, claustrum and external capsule lie deep to it.
distractors: insular part of middle cerebral artery
spotters.followup: Name in order the structures a probe crosses passing from this cortex medially to the thalamus.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned lobe and state its arterial supply and the field defect after unilateral infarction.
spotters.answer: Occipital lobe, containing the primary visual cortex, Brodmann area 17, on the banks of the calcarine sulcus. It is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery. Unilateral infarction gives a contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, attributed to collateral supply from the middle cerebral artery at the occipital pole.
spotters.followup: Which bank of the calcarine sulcus represents the upper visual field, and where does a lesion produce a superior quadrantanopia?
spotters.sub: Cerebral hemisphere, medial and lateral surface

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned structure and name its parts from front to back.
spotters.answer: Corpus callosum, the largest commissure of the brain: rostrum, genu, body, splenium. Fibres of the genu sweep forward as the forceps minor, those of the splenium backwards as the forceps major. It forms the roof of the lateral ventricle, and its splenium is supplied by the splenial artery from the posterior cerebral artery.
spotters.followup: A left occipital infarct extending into the splenium causes alexia without agraphia. Explain the disconnection.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned white matter bundle and state its origin and destination.
spotters.answer: Fornix, the main efferent bundle of the hippocampus, running as fimbria, crus, body and column to end mainly in the mammillary body, with precommissural fibres to the septal area. The column forms the anterior boundary of the interventricular foramen. Bilateral section causes dense anterograde amnesia.
spotters.followup: Where do the two crura exchange fibres, and what is that decussation called?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned commissure and state what it connects.
spotters.answer: Anterior commissure, crossing in the upper part of the lamina terminalis. Its smaller anterior limb connects the olfactory regions, the larger posterior limb connects the middle and inferior temporal gyri and the amygdalae of the two sides. With the posterior commissure it defines the AC PC line used in stereotactic surgery and imaging.
spotters.followup: State the relation of this commissure to the column of the fornix and to the interventricular foramen.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned commissure and state its role in a reflex.
spotters.answer: Posterior commissure, lying at the junction of the third ventricle and cerebral aqueduct, in the inferior lamina of the pineal stalk. Its fibres carry the crossing limb of the pupillary light reflex from the pretectal area to the contralateral Edinger Westphal nucleus. Compression by a pineal tumour gives light near dissociation as part of Parinaud syndrome.
spotters.followup: List the components of Parinaud syndrome and name the commonest tumour producing it in a young male.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned white matter and name the fibres in its posterior limb.
spotters.answer: Internal capsule, V shaped in horizontal section with anterior limb, genu, posterior limb, retrolenticular and sublenticular parts. The posterior limb carries corticospinal fibres in face, arm, leg order from the genu backwards, plus thalamocortical sensory fibres, while the retrolenticular part carries the optic radiation. Supplied mainly by lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery.
spotters.followup: Which structures form the medial and lateral boundaries of the genu, and what deficit follows a lacunar infarct there?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned nucleus and state its relation to the ventricular system.
spotters.answer: Caudate nucleus, a C shaped mass with head, body and tail following the curve of the lateral ventricle. The head bulges into the lateral wall of the frontal horn, the tail runs in the roof of the temporal horn to end at the amygdala. With the putamen it forms the striatum, and its atrophy in Huntington disease gives boxcar dilatation of the frontal horns.
spotters.followup: Which structure separates the head of this nucleus from the putamen, and which vessels supply the head?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned nucleus and state its clinical importance in stroke.
spotters.answer: Putamen, the lateral and largest part of the lentiform nucleus, separated from the claustrum by the external capsule and from the globus pallidus by the medial medullary lamina. It is supplied by lenticulostriate branches of the sphenoid part of the middle cerebral artery, and is the commonest site of hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage.
spotters.followup: Name the nucleus with which this one forms the striatum, and state the neurotransmitter of its main afferent from the substantia nigra.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned nucleus and state its output pathways.
spotters.answer: Globus pallidus, the medial, paler part of the lentiform nucleus, divided by the medial medullary lamina into external and internal segments. The internal segment is the major output nucleus, projecting to the thalamus through the ansa lenticularis and lenticular fasciculus. It is the classical target for deep brain stimulation in dystonia and is damaged in carbon monoxide poisoning and kernicterus.
spotters.followup: Which segment is inhibited in the indirect pathway, and what movement disorder follows a lesion of the subthalamic nucleus?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned nuclear mass and state its main efferent bundle.
spotters.answer: Amygdala, lying in the roof of the tip of the temporal horn just anterior and superior to the head of the hippocampus, deep to the uncus. Its principal efferent is the stria terminalis, running in the groove between the caudate nucleus and thalamus to the septal area and hypothalamus, with a second route through the ventral amygdalofugal pathway. Bilateral destruction produces Kluver Bucy syndrome.
spotters.followup: List the features of Kluver Bucy syndrome and name a viral encephalitis that targets this region.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned structure and state its position relative to the ventricle.
spotters.answer: Hippocampus, forming the floor and medial wall of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle, with head, body and tail. Its efferents leave through the fimbria and fornix to the mammillary body. The CA1 or Sommer sector is the most vulnerable field to hypoxia, and its sclerosis is the classic substrate of mesial temporal lobe epilepsy.
spotters.followup: Name the arteries supplying this structure and state the memory deficit after bilateral resection.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned mass of grey matter and state its relation to the third ventricle.
spotters.answer: Thalamus, forming the upper part of the lateral wall of the third ventricle, joined across the midline by the interthalamic adhesion. All sensory modalities except olfaction relay here before reaching cortex, the ventral posterolateral and ventral posteromedial nuclei being the somatosensory relays. Supplied largely by branches of the posterior cerebral artery and the posterior communicating artery.
spotters.followup: Which sulcus separates this structure from the hypothalamus, and what is Dejerine Roussy syndrome?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned region and state two of its functions.
spotters.answer: Hypothalamus, forming the floor and lower lateral wall of the third ventricle below the hypothalamic sulcus, extending from the optic chiasm to the mammillary body. It controls temperature, water balance, appetite, circadian rhythm and autonomic outflow, and its supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei send axons to the posterior pituitary carrying vasopressin and oxytocin. Damage causes diabetes insipidus or the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone.
spotters.followup: Name the structures forming the floor of the third ventricle from front to back.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned pair of swellings and state their main afferent and efferent.
spotters.answer: Mammillary bodies, on the posterior part of the floor of the third ventricle in front of the posterior perforated substance. They receive the fornix from the hippocampus and project through the mammillothalamic tract to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus, completing the circuit of Papez. They show haemorrhagic necrosis in thiamine deficiency, the anatomical basis of Wernicke Korsakoff syndrome.
spotters.followup: Name the triad of Wernicke encephalopathy and the second tract leaving these bodies.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned area of the hypothalamic floor and state its endocrine significance.
spotters.answer: Tuber cinereum, the grey eminence between the optic chiasm in front and the mammillary bodies behind, from which the infundibulum descends to the pituitary. Its median eminence is the site where hypophysiotropic hormones enter the hypophyseal portal system, and it lies outside the blood brain barrier. A hamartoma here causes gelastic seizures and central precocious puberty.
spotters.followup: Trace the hypophyseal portal circulation from this region to the anterior pituitary.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned structure and state which fibres decussate in it.
spotters.answer: Optic chiasm, lying on the diaphragma sellae above the pituitary and forming part of the anterior floor of the third ventricle. Fibres from the nasal half of each retina, carrying the temporal visual fields, cross here, while temporal retinal fibres remain uncrossed. Compression from below by a pituitary adenoma gives a bitemporal hemianopia beginning in the upper quadrants.
spotters.followup: Why does a craniopharyngioma above this structure typically affect the lower fields first?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned band and state where its fibres terminate.
spotters.answer: Optic tract, running from the chiasm around the peduncle of the midbrain, carrying uncrossed temporal fibres of the same side and crossed nasal fibres of the opposite eye. The great majority end in the lateral geniculate body, with a smaller contingent passing through the brachium of the superior colliculus to the pretectal area and superior colliculus for the light reflex and visual reflexes. A lesion gives a contralateral, characteristically incongruous, homonymous hemianopia.
spotters.followup: Why is a relative afferent pupillary defect sometimes present with a lesion here but never with an occipital lesion?
spotters.sub: Base of brain, around the midbrain

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned swelling and state its input and output.
spotters.answer: Lateral geniculate body, a six layered thalamic nucleus receiving the optic tract, with crossed fibres in layers 1, 4 and 6 and uncrossed fibres in layers 2, 3 and 5. Layers 1 and 2 are magnocellular, layers 3 to 6 parvocellular. Its output forms the optic radiation to the primary visual cortex, the anterior loop of which sweeps into the temporal lobe as Meyer loop.
spotters.followup: Which arteries supply this body, and what field defect follows damage to Meyer loop?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned swelling and state the pathway it belongs to.
spotters.answer: Medial geniculate body, the thalamic auditory relay, lying medial to the lateral geniculate body below the pulvinar. It receives the brachium of the inferior colliculus and projects through the sublenticular part of the internal capsule as the auditory radiation to the transverse temporal gyri of Heschl. Unilateral lesions do not cause deafness because of bilateral representation.
spotters.followup: Trace the auditory pathway from the cochlear nuclei to the cortex, naming the decussation.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned elevation and state its function.
spotters.answer: Superior colliculus, the upper pair of the corpora quadrigemina at the level of the oculomotor nucleus. It is a centre for visual reflexes and reflex orientation of head and eyes, giving origin to the tectospinal tract. It receives retinal and cortical fibres through the brachium of the superior colliculus.
spotters.followup: Name the structures forming the roof of the midbrain and state the syndrome caused by compression of this region.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned elevation and state its place in a sensory pathway.
spotters.answer: Inferior colliculus, the lower pair of the corpora quadrigemina at the level of the trochlear nucleus. It is the obligatory relay for the ascending auditory pathway, receiving the lateral lemniscus and projecting through the brachium of the inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate body. The trochlear nerve emerges from the dorsal surface just below it and decussates in the superior medullary velum.
spotters.followup: Which is the only cranial nerve to leave the dorsal surface of the brainstem, and what is the clinical effect of its palsy?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned ridge and state what it carries.
spotters.answer: Brachium of the inferior colliculus, a ridge running upwards and forwards from the inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate body, carrying ascending auditory fibres from the inferior colliculus and the lateral lemniscus. It lies below and behind its counterpart running from the superior colliculus to the lateral geniculate body and pretectal area.
spotters.followup: Name the ridge lying immediately superior to this one and state which two structures it connects.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned structure and state its secretion and radiological use.
spotters.answer: Pineal body, an endocrine gland projecting backwards from the epithalamus above the superior colliculi, attached by a stalk containing the habenular and posterior commissures. Its pinealocytes secrete melatonin under sympathetic control from the superior cervical ganglion, entraining circadian rhythm. It calcifies after puberty as corpora arenacea and serves as a midline marker on plain films and computed tomography.
spotters.followup: Which tumour of this region causes precocious puberty and upgaze palsy, and by what mechanism does hydrocephalus develop?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned structure and state its connections.
spotters.answer: Habenula, the small triangular epithalamic region at the posterior end of the stria medullaris of the thalamus, containing the medial and lateral habenular nuclei. It receives the stria medullaris from the septal and hypothalamic regions and projects through the fasciculus retroflexus, the habenulointerpeduncular tract, to the interpeduncular nucleus. It is a relay in the olfacto visceral and limbic to midbrain pathway.
spotters.followup: Name the two commissures related to the stalk of the pineal body and state which of them relates to this structure.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned band and state its origin and termination.
spotters.answer: Stria medullaris of the thalamus, a fibre band along the superomedial border of the thalamus running backwards to the habenula. It carries fibres from the septal nuclei, lateral preoptic and hypothalamic areas, and anterior perforated substance. The tela choroidea of the third ventricle is attached along it, so it marks the line of ventricular roof attachment.
spotters.followup: Distinguish this band from the fibre bundle running in the groove between the caudate nucleus and thalamus, and state where each ends.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned membrane and state its boundaries and clinical use.
spotters.answer: Lamina terminalis, the thin sheet forming the anterior wall of the third ventricle, stretching from the optic chiasm below to the rostrum of the corpus callosum above, with the anterior commissure in its upper part. It represents the rostral end of the embryonic neural tube. It carries the vascular organ of the lamina terminalis, a circumventricular organ for osmoreception, and is the site of fenestration in endoscopic third ventriculostomy approaches.
spotters.followup: Name the circumventricular organs and state why they lack a blood brain barrier.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned midline structure and state what it separates.
spotters.answer: Septum of the telencephalon, comprising the septum pellucidum above and the septal nuclei below. The septum pellucidum is a double sheet stretched between the corpus callosum above and the fornix below, separating the frontal horns of the two lateral ventricles. Persistence of the cavum septi pellucidi is a normal variant, and the septum is absent in septo optic dysplasia.
spotters.followup: Name the cholinergic projection from the septal nuclei to the hippocampus and the bundle it travels in.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned cavity and name its parts.
spotters.answer: Lateral ventricle, with anterior or frontal horn, body, atrium or trigone, posterior or occipital horn, and inferior or temporal horn. Its roof is the corpus callosum and its floor in the body is formed by the thalamus, caudate nucleus and fornix. Choroid plexus is present in the body, atrium and temporal horn but absent from the frontal and occipital horns.
spotters.followup: Which structure forms the medial wall of the frontal horn, and where in this ventricle does the choroid plexus form the glomus?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned cavity and state its lateral wall and communications.
spotters.answer: Third ventricle, a midline slit between the two halves of the diencephalon. Its lateral wall is the thalamus above and the hypothalamus below the hypothalamic sulcus, the anterior wall is the lamina terminalis, and the floor runs from optic chiasm to tegmentum. It communicates with each lateral ventricle through the interventricular foramen and with the fourth ventricle through the cerebral aqueduct.
spotters.followup: Name the recesses of this ventricle and state which tumour classically obstructs it at the foramen.

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned aperture and state its boundaries.
spotters.answer: Interventricular foramen of Monro, connecting the lateral ventricle to the third ventricle. It is bounded anteriorly by the column of the fornix and posteriorly by the anterior tubercle of the thalamus. A colloid cyst lodged here causes intermittent positional headache and acute obstructive hydrocephalus with sudden collapse.
spotters.followup: Which structures pass through this foramen, and which ventricles enlarge if it is blocked on one side only?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned channel and state what it connects and the effect of its obstruction.
spotters.answer: Cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius, running through the tegmentum of the midbrain and connecting the third to the fourth ventricle, surrounded by periaqueductal grey. It is the narrowest part of the ventricular system and contains no choroid plexus. Congenital stenosis or extrinsic compression produces non communicating hydrocephalus with dilatation of the third and both lateral ventricles and a normal fourth ventricle.
spotters.followup: Which cranial nerve nuclei lie in the grey matter surrounding this channel at each collicular level?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned cavity and state its boundaries and apertures.
spotters.answer: Fourth ventricle, a tent shaped space between the pons and upper medulla oblongata in front and the cerebellum behind. Its floor is the rhomboid fossa, showing the medial eminence, facial colliculus, vestibular area and hypoglossal and vagal trigones. Cerebrospinal fluid escapes through the median aperture of Magendie and the two lateral apertures of Luschka into the subarachnoid space.
spotters.followup: Which structures raise the facial colliculus, and what deficit does a lesion there produce?

spotters.prompt: Identify the pinned structure and state its function.
